p.seg: Preface to the Confucian School's Economic Strategies: The Long and Short of Governing by Zhào Ruí of Táng, the Grassland Subject of Ānchāng Cliff on Chángpíng Mountain in Qī County of Zǐ Prefecture
Master Zhào says:
The carriage maker
worries that people will not value it;
the arrow maker
fears that people will not be harmed.
Do they have likes and dislikes?
It is truly driven by their skills and professions.
Thus it is known that scholars of the current era, those rushing about,
when reading about vertical and horizontal alliances,
think of the changes among the feudal lords;
when skilled in the unusual and orthodox,
they ponder the opportunities in turbulent times.
This is also the theory of the past,
an inevitable principle.
Therefore, our late teacher Confucius deeply explored its roots and worried about its branches,
thus composing the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
emphasizing the Kingly Way;
establishing the "Classic of Filial Piety",
praising virtuous conduct.
Preventing sprouts and blocking gradual decline,
he preemptively restrained.
This is the original intent of the sage's creation.
However, establishing methods based on principle,
their flaws inevitably lead to chaos.
If it reaches chaos,
how can it be saved?
Hence, in governing the world and managing people,
rarely is there blind adherence to tradition.
The three dynasties had different rites,
the five hegemons different laws.
Not that they opposed each other,
but to rescue from flaws.
Therefore,
though state decorum is consistent,
the ways of loyalty and culture must differ;
though sages share the same ethos,
the names of emperors and kings may vary.
Is it not that setting teachings according to the times follows this,
and accomplishing tasks based on circumstances is influenced by that?
Following this,
purity or thinness depends on what is encountered;
influenced by that,
the kingly or hegemonic way exists in the situation faced.
Thus, the ancient rulers
had three types of governance:
the kingly governance transforms,
the hegemonic governance intimidates,
the strong state's governance coerces.
Each has its application,
not to be interchanged.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"The sage can assist the times,
but cannot defy them.
The wise are good at planning,
but not as good as acting timely."
Zōuzǐ said:
"Administrative teachings, cultural refinement,
are means to rectify and save.
Use them when timely,
discard them when past."
From this perspective,
to practice kingly transformation in a hegemonic court
would be perverse.
To exercise hegemonic intimidation in a strong state's era
would be contrary.
If the times are full of deceit,
and the right path is in decline,
wishing to emulate the ancient kings,
and broadly promote virtuous transformation,
is like asking a Yuè guest to save a drowning person,
or explaining to an elder to put out a fire.
Good as it may be,
is it what is called understanding the changes of the times?
Now, the hegemonic way
is a mixed path.
It blends black and white,
not purely using virtue.
Aiming for success,
it does not question the means;
considering the overall situation,
it does not cling to minor details.
Though citing benevolence and righteousness,
it falls short of the Three Sovereigns,
yet in supporting the falling and stabilizing the toppling,
the outcome is the same.
Fearing that Confucians might drown in their knowledge,
unaware of the different strategies of kingly and hegemonic ways,
I thus compile the art of strengths and weaknesses,
for those who manage affairs with adaptability,
creating topics,
totaling sixty-three chapters,
combined into ten volumes,
named "The Long and Short of Governing".
The main purpose lies in stabilizing roots, reforming current flaws, and addressing rise and fall, order and chaos.
Detailed in each chapter,
as a long-term plan for continuity,
and the ultimate way of statecraft,
not to correct the world or boast customs,
nor seek fame or reputation.
I merely reveal my knowledge,
awaiting the wise of the future.
All those in position,
I hope you will examine it in detail.
The Great Framework First
I have heard Lǎozǐ say:
"Govern the state with orthodoxy,
use the military with unorthodoxy,
gain the world through non-interference."
Xúnzǐ said:
"The ruler's ability
lies in appointing officials;
the commoner's ability
lies in self-reliance."
Fùzǐ said:
"When scholar-officials divide duties and heed,
feudal lords divide lands and guard,
and the three excellencies oversee regions and deliberate,
then the Son of Heaven can fold his hands and be correct."
How to clarify this?
In Yáo's time,
Shùn was Minister of Education,
Xiè was Minister of War,
Yǔ was Minister of Works,
Hòujì oversaw agriculture,
Kuí was Director of Music,
Chuí was Chief Artisan,
Bóyí was Minister of Rites,
Gāoyáo was Chief Judge,
Yì managed hunting.
Yáo could not perform any single one,
yet he was the sovereign,
and the nine were ministers.
What is the reason?
Yáo understood the nine responsibilities,
assigning each to the nine,
all excelling in their tasks to achieve the nine accomplishments.
Yáo then rode on these successes to rule the world.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn said:
"Planning strategies within the tent,
deciding victory a thousand miles away,
I am not as good as Zǐfáng;
pacifying the state,
comforting the people,
supplying provisions,
keeping the supply routes open,
I am not as good as Xiāo Hé;
leading a million troops,
winning every battle,
capturing every fortress,
I am not as good as Hán Xìn.
These three men
are all outstanding.
I could use them,
this is how I gained the world."
"The Records of Human Nature" says:
"The duty of one official
is like one flavor harmonizing five;
the governance of a state
is like no flavor harmonizing five.
Thus, ministers consider self-reliance as ability,
the ruler considers employing others as ability;
ministers consider speaking as ability,
the ruler considers listening as ability;
ministers consider action as ability,
the ruler considers reward and punishment as ability.
Because they differ,
thus the ruler can oversee the many abilities."
Therefore it is said:
Understanding people
is the way of the king;
understanding affairs
is the way of the minister.
The formless
is the master of things;
the endless
is the root of affairs.
The drum does not partake in the five notes,
but is the master of the five notes;
one who has the Way does not perform the duties of the five offices,
but is the master of managing affairs.
The ruler maintains his Way,
officials know their duties,
this has long been so.
The ancient kings knew this well,
thus using what is not theirs as if it were their own,
this is understanding the ruler's Way.
Discussion:
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
"The skilled craftsman building a palace,
for circles must use compasses,
for squares must use rulers,
for straightness must use plumb lines."
When the achievement is already accomplished,
without knowing the tools of measurement,
the skillful craftsman is rewarded.
When the palace is already built,
without recognizing the skillful craftsman,
all say it is the palace of such-and-such lord or king.
Xúnzǐ said:
"If a ruler desires to have one who shoots well and hits the mark,
then none is better than employing Yì;
if he desires to have one who drives well and covers long distances,
then none is better than employing Wáng Liáng;
if he desires to harmonize and unify the world,
then none is better than employing the wise gentleman.
His use of wisdom is very simple,
his handling of affairs is not laborious,
yet his achievements and fame are very great."
This is being able to use what is not originally his as if it were his own.
A ruler who does not understand the way of rulership is not like this.
Doing things himself, he cannot appoint the worthy;
being unable to appoint the worthy, the worthy detest him.
This is why achievements and fame are damaged,
and why the state is endangered.
Discussion says:
"Shēnzǐ stated:
'The ruler knows the way,
the ministers know the affairs.
Speaking ten times and being appropriate ten times,
speaking a hundred times and being appropriate a hundred times,
this is the affair of ministers,
not the way of the ruler.'
Shīzǐ stated:
'For ministers, recommending the worthy is their achievement;
for the ruler, employing the worthy is his achievement.'
Jiǎ Yì stated:
'I have heard that the sage ruler consults his ministers,
and does not personally initiate affairs,
thus enabling his ministers to fully express their sincere loyalty,
I beg Your Majesty to consider this favorably.'
From this perspective,
if the ruler cannot manage authority through delegation
but instead envies the worthy and detests the capable,
this is the path to failure."
King Tāng and King Wǔ in one day possessed all the wealth of the Xià and Shāng,
using their lands to enfeoff,
and no one in the world dared not to submit joyfully;
using their wealth to reward,
and everyone in the world competed to be encouraged,
this exemplifies using what is not originally theirs.
Discussion says:
Xúnzǐ stated:
"He who cultivates rites becomes king,
he who governs effectively becomes strong,
he who wins over people becomes secure,
he who amasses wealth perishes.
Thus the king enriches the people,
the hegemon enriches the scholars,
the barely surviving state enriches the high officials,
the doomed state enriches the coffers and fills the treasuries.
This is called overflow above and leakage below."
He also said:
"The Son of Heaven does not speak of how much or how little,
the feudal lords do not speak of benefit and harm,
the high officials do not speak of gain and loss."
Formerly, King Lì of Zhōu was fond of profit and drew close to Róng Gōng.
Ruì Liángfū admonished him:
"Is the royal house about to decline?
Róng Gōng loves monopolizing profit and does not know great calamity.
Profit
is produced by all things,
and borne by heaven and earth;
yet to monopolize it,
its harm is great indeed.
Heaven, earth, and all things will all take from it,
how can it be monopolized!
The benefits are many
but he does not prepare for great calamity,
using this to teach the king,
can it last long?"
Later King Lì indeed failed.
When the granary of Wèi Wén Hóu caught fire,
he wore plain clothes and avoided the main hall,
and all his ministers had already arrived.
Gōngzǐ Chéngfǔ hurried in to congratulate him:
"I have heard that the Son of Heaven stores his wealth throughout the four seas,
the feudal lords store theirs within their borders.
If it is not where it should be stored,
if there is no fire disaster,
there must be human calamity.
Fortunately, there is no human calamity,
isn't that good!"
Confucius said:
"When the common people have enough,
how can the ruler not have enough?"
A Zhōu proverb says: "What leaks from the bag is stored in the bin."
From this perspective,
when the sage king uses his lands to enfeoff,
uses his wealth to reward,
and does not compete with others for profit,
then he can comprehend the way of kingship,
this is using what is not originally his.
Thus it is said: Establishing offices and dividing duties,
is the substance of rulership;
delegating authority and demanding completion,
is the substance of rulership;
loving strategy without weariness,
is the substance of rulership;
being generous to win the multitude,
is the substance of rulership;
containing disgrace and concealing flaws,
is the substance of rulership.
When the ruler possesses the substance of ruling people,
his ministers fear and love him,
this is how emperors and kings accomplish their enterprises.
Employing Strengths - Second
I have heard that assessing talents and examining abilities
is essential for governing the world.
Unless one is a sage,
who can combine all these hundred conducts
and master all principles?
Thus Shǔn assembled all officials,
assigning positions according to their talents;
the Hàn recorded meritorious ministers,
with three heroes receiving different titles.
How much more for those not of this caliber,
can they be fully demanded?
"The Records of Human Characters" states:
Those who are bold and strategic
cannot handle subtleties,
thus when discussing major principles,
they are broad in strategy and lofty in vision;
when dealing with fine details,
they are erratic and negligent.
Those who are stern and severe cannot yield,
when discussing laws and standards,
they are constrained yet fair;
when speaking of adaptation, they are obstinate and unyielding.
Those who are tolerant and forgiving
cannot act quickly,
when discussing benevolence and righteousness,
they are comprehensive and elegant;
when addressing current affairs, they are slow and跟不上.
Those who love novelty
act rebelliously seeking difference,
when creating power and stratagem, they are unconventional and magnificent;
when following pure principles, they are abnormal and impractical.
It also says:
Policies of kingly transformation
are suitable for governing broadly,
using them for small matters is impractical;
Policies of strategy and technique
are suitable for managing difficulties,
using them for peace lacks wonder;
Policies of correction and restraint
are suitable for governing extravagance,
using them for addressing shortcomings becomes cruel;
Policies of strictness and harshness
are suitable for rectifying evil,
using them for border administration loses the people;
Policies of authority and fierceness
are suitable for suppressing rebellion,
using them for good governance becomes violent;
Policies of skill and cunning
are suitable for managing wealth,
using them for poverty leads to toil and hardship below.
All the above are partial talents.
Formerly, when Yīyǐn initiated construction work,
he had the strong-backed carry soil,
the one-eyed push carts,
the hunchbacked apply plaster,
each being suitable for their role,
thus human nature was equalized.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In ceremonial etiquette,
and polished manners,
I am not as good as Xí Péng,
I request he be appointed as Grand Master of Ceremonies;
in opening lands and gathering grain,
exhausting the benefits of the land,
I am not as good as Nìng Qì,
I request he be appointed as Minister of Agriculture;
on vast plains and open fields,
with chariots not turning back,
soldiers not retreating,
when drums beat and the three army troops look upon death as returning home,
I am not as good as Wángzǐ Chéngfǔ,
I request he be appointed as Grand Marshal;
in deciding cases and judging fairly,
not killing the innocent,
not falsely accusing the guiltless,
I am not as good as Bīn Xūwú,
I request he be appointed as Chief Justice;
in confronting the ruler's countenance,
presenting remonstrance with utmost loyalty,
not avoiding death,
not yielding to the wealthy and noble,
I am not as good as Dōngguō Yá,
If a ruler wishes to govern the state and strengthen the military,
then the five worthies are available;
if he seeks hegemony,
then I, Yíwú, am here."
Huáng Shígōng said:
"Employ the wise, employ the brave,
employ the greedy, employ the foolish.
The wise delight in establishing achievements,
the brave prefer to act on their aspirations,
the greedy decisively pursue profit,
the foolish do not cherish their lives.
Utilize them according to their inherent tendencies—
this is the subtle art of military command."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Under heaven, nothing is more poisonous
than the venom of ravines
and aconite,
yet skilled physicians store it in bags,
for it has its uses.
When a elk climbs mountains,
even Dàzhāng cannot keep pace;
but when it descends,
a shepherd boy can chase it.
Talents have their strengths and weaknesses.
The Hú people are adept with horses,
the Yuè people skilled with boats.
Different forms and distinct kinds
become confused when forced to exchange tasks."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi decreed:
"Ambitious individuals
may lack virtuous conduct.
Those with virtuous conduct
may lack ambition.
Was Chén Píng known for steadfast virtue,
or Sū Qín for keeping promises?
Yet Chén Píng secured the Hàn dynasty
and Sū Qín aided weak Yān—
each was employed according to his strengths."
From this perspective,
had Hán Xìn been confined to scholarly pursuits,
Dǒng Zhòngshū sent to battle,
Yú Gōng dispatched as envoy,
or Lù Jiǎ assigned to judge lawsuits,
they would never have achieved their historic merits
nor earned their present fame.
Therefore, the principle of employing strengths
must not be overlooked.
Discussion:
Wèi Huán Fàn remarked:
"When emperors employ people,
they assess the era to assign talents.
In times of contention,
strategic plans take precedence.
After stability is established,
loyalty and righteousness come first.
Thus Duke Wén of Jìn followed Jiùfàn's schemes
but rewarded Yōng Jì's counsel,
while Emperor Gāozǔ used Chén Píng's wisdom
but entrusted his successor to Zhōu Bó."
An ancient saying goes:
"In eras upholding civil order,
the virtuous receive high rank;
in times of crisis,
the accomplished gain rich rewards."
Zhūgě Liàng said:
"Lǎozi excelled at self-cultivation,
but couldn't handle emergencies;
Shāng Yāng mastered law enforcement,
but couldn't promote education;
Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí were skilled debaters,
but couldn't secure alliances;
Bái Qǐ excelled in conquest,
but couldn't pacify the masses;
Wǔ Zǐxū surpassed in strategizing against enemies,
but couldn't protect himself;
Wěi Shēng upheld faithfulness,
but couldn't adapt to change;
Wáng Jiā thrived under wise rulers,
but couldn't serve incompetent ones;
Xǔ Zǐjiàng discerned character well,
but couldn't nurture talent."
This illustrates the method of employing strengths.
Third: Classification of Individuals
For the sacred vessels of empire
and the great lineage of kings,
none fails to labor in discerning talents
to gain ease through proper appointments.
Thus Confucius said:
"Humans have five categories:
the mediocre person,
the scholar,
the noble person,
the sage,
and the worthy.
Understanding these five
completes the art of governance."
The so-called mediocre person
lacks consideration for consequences,
utters no instructive words
or principles;
chooses no worthy models for self-improvement,
exerts no effort for self-establishment;
sees trifles but misses essentials, not knowing priorities,
drifts with currents without firm principles.
Such is the mediocre person.
The so-called scholar
has settled convictions,
and steadfast plans.
Though not mastering all fundamental principles,
has guiding standards
(standards meaning guidelines);
though not perfect in all virtues,
has firm foundations.
Thus wisdom seeks not abundance,
but thorough understanding;
speech seeks not volume,
but precision of expression
(precision meaning essential points);
action seeks not quantity,
but examination of motives.
When wisdom comprehends,
speech captures essence
(grasping the crucial),
and action follows principles,
these become as unchangeable as life and body.
Wealth and honor cannot enhance them,
poverty and lowliness cannot diminish them.
Such is the scholar.
The so-called noble person
speaks with loyalty and sincerity, harboring no resentment
(resentment meaning
malice or harm),
embodies benevolence and righteousness without boasting,
has clear thoughts but unassuming speech,
acts earnestly in pursuit of truth,
striving tirelessly,
appearing surpassable yet ultimately unreachable.
Such is the noble person.
Appearing surpassable
means unassuming demeanor.
Surpassable
means exceeded.
Xúnzǐ said:
"The noble person can make himself worthy of honor,
but cannot force others to honor him;
can make himself trustworthy,
but cannot force others to trust him;
can make himself useful,
but cannot force others to employ him.
Thus the noble person feels shame at lack of cultivation,
not at being slandered;
shame at untrustworthiness,
not at being distrusted;
shame at incompetence,
not at being unused.
Not enticed by praise,
not resentful of slander,
following the Way,
correcting oneself uprightly—
this defines the noble person."
The so-called worthy person
has virtue not exceeding bounds
(bounds meaning
standards),
conduct conforming to rules,
speech worthy of universal emulation without self-harm
(words filling the world without verbal missteps),
Way sufficient to transform people without self-injury
(self-injury meaning harming oneself),
when rich causes no hoarded wealth worldwide
(hoarded meaning
accumulated),
when generous causes no poverty in society.
Such is the worthy person.
The so-called sage
has virtue matching heaven and earth,
adapting infinitely,
exhausting all things' beginnings and ends,
harmonizing with nature's myriad beings,
spreading the great Way
to fulfill inherent dispositions,
bright as sun and moon,
transformative as divine power,
common people unaware of his virtue,
observers unable to discern his boundaries.
Such is the sage.
Boundaries meaning limits.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Forcing intentions and exalting actions,
withdrawing from society with peculiar customs,
high-sounding criticisms and complaints,
merely constitute eccentricity:
these are the preferences of mountain recluses,
world-detractors,
and those embracing austerity or drowning themselves."
Speaking of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
courtesy, frugality, deference, and yielding,
is for self-cultivation alone:
These are the scholars of peaceful times,
the people who teach and enlighten,
favored by those who travel, reside, and pursue broad learning.
Speaking of great achievements,
establishing great fame,
ritualizing the roles of ruler and minister,
rectifying the distinctions between high and low,
is for governance alone:
These are the court scholars,
those who honor the ruler and strengthen the state,
favored by those who seek achievements and territorial expansion.
Withdrawing to marshes and lakes,
dwelling in leisure and open spaces,
fishing and resting idly,
is for non-action alone:
These are the scholars of rivers and seas,
the people who avoid the world,
favored by those who cherish leisure and idleness.
Breathing in and out,
expelling the old and taking in the new,
imitating the bear's hang and the bird's stretch,
is for longevity alone:
These are the masters of guiding and pulling,
the people who nurture their forms,
favored by those like Péng Zǔ who seek long life.
As for those who are lofty without deliberate effort,
cultivated without benevolence and righteousness,
governing without achievements and fame,
leisurely without rivers and seas,
long-lived without guiding and pulling,
they forget everything,
yet possess everything.
Serene and boundless,
all beauties follow them.
This is the Way of Heaven and Earth,
the virtue of the sage. 」
The "Qián Jīng" says:
「Virtue sufficient to embrace the distant,
trust sufficient to unify differences,
insight sufficient to mirror antiquity,
talent sufficient to lead the age,
these are the essence of humanity;
laws sufficient to complete education,
conduct sufficient to cultivate righteousness,
benevolence sufficient to win the masses,
clarity sufficient to illuminate those below,
these are the excellence of humanity;
person sufficient to serve as a model,
wisdom sufficient to resolve doubts,
integrity sufficient to deter greed and baseness,
trust sufficient to embrace different customs,
these are the heroism of humanity;
maintaining integrity without yielding,
dwelling in righteousness without anger,
facing suspicion without hastily avoiding,
encountering profit without hastily taking,
these are the outstandingness of humanity. 」
The "Rénwù Zhì" says:
「With virtuous conduct sublime,
appearance and demeanor worthy of emulation,
this is called pure integrity,
exemplified by Yánlíng and Yàn Yīng.
Thought penetrating the transformative Way,
strategies and schemes wondrously clever,
this is called the strategist school,
exemplified by Fàn Lǐ and Zhāng Liáng.
Their virtue sufficient to influence customs,
their laws sufficient to rectify the world,
their methods sufficient to plan temple victories,
this is called the state's backbone,
exemplified by Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng.
Their virtue sufficient to lead a state,
their laws sufficient to rectify villages and towns,
their methods sufficient to handle affairs appropriately,
this is called practical ability,
exemplified by Zǐchǎn and Xīmén Bào.
Those of the pure integrity stream,
unable to be broadly forgiving,
fond of criticizing and censuring,
distinguishing right from wrong,
this is called judgmental,
exemplified by the followers of Zǐxià.
Those of the Legalist stream,
unable to create ideas for long-term plans,
but capable of undertaking an official post,
focusing intent and applying skill,
this is called technical craft,
exemplified by Zhāng Chǎng and Zhào Guǎnghàn.
Those of the strategist stream,
unable to establish systems and set examples,
but capable of adapting to change using expediency;
expedient wisdom abundant,
impartial justice insufficient,
this is called clever insight,
exemplified by Chén Píng and Hán Ānguó.
Able to write and compose works,
this is called literary talent,
exemplified by Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
Able to transmit the sagely legacy,
but incapable of handling affairs and administering governance,
this is called Confucian scholarship,
exemplified by Máo Gōng and Guàn Gōng.
Debate not entering the Way,
but responsive and resourceful in replies,
this is called eloquent debate,
exemplified by Yuè Yì and Cáo Qiūshēng.
Courage and strength surpassing all,
talent and strategy exceeding others,
this is called fierce heroism,
exemplified by Bái Qǐ and Hán Xìn. 」
The "Jiāyǔ" says:
「In the past, enlightened kings necessarily knew all the names of the fine scholars in the world,
knowing not only their names,
but also their realities,
then using the world's ranks to honor them,
thus the world was well-governed. 」
This refers to that.
Assessing Talent, Part Four
Now, human talents vary, differing in magnitude,
just as a shēng cannot hold a hú,
overflowing leads to waste.
If one employs the wrong person,
how can it not be perilous?
Fù Zǐ says:
「Generally, talent assessment has nine categories:
First is virtuous conduct,
to establish the foundation of the Way;
second is administrative talent,
to investigate the mechanics of affairs;
third is political talent,
to manage the governance structure;
fourth is scholarly talent,
to synthesize canonical texts;
fifth is military talent,
to command armies;
sixth is agricultural talent,
to teach farming;
to create tools and implements;
eighth is commercial talent,
to enhance state profits;
ninth is rhetorical talent,
to excel in persuasion and discussion. 」
This is assessing talent.
Thus Yī Yǐn said:
「Wisdom penetrating the great Way,
adapting to change without exhaustion,
discerning the nature of all things,
his words sufficient to harmonize yin and yang,
rectify the four seasons,
and regulate wind and rain.
Such a person is recommended to be one of the Three Dukes. 」
Thus the affairs of the Three Dukes constantly lie in the Way.
Emperor Wén of Hàn asked Chén Píng:
「What matters do you, sir, oversee? 」
He replied:
「Your Majesty, unaware of my incompetence,
has made me bear the blame as chancellor.
The chancellor's role
is above to assist the Son of Heaven,
harmonizing yin and yang,
below to fulfill the appropriateness of all things,
externally to pacify the four barbarians,
internally to draw the people close,
ensuring that the dukes, ministers, and officials
each fulfill their duties. 」
The Emperor said:
「Good! 」
Hàn Wèi Xiàng wrote:
「I have heard the 'Yì' says: 'Heaven and Earth act through accord,
thus the sun and moon do not err,
the four seasons do not deviate;
the sage acts through accord,
then punishments are clear and the people submit.'
The changes of Heaven and Earth
necessarily arise from yin and yang.
The division of yin and yang
is marked by the sun and moon.
Each has its constant duties,
and must not interfere.
The enlightened king is reverent in honoring Heaven,
cautious in nurturing people.
Thus establishing the offices of Xī and Hé,
to ride the four seasons,
respectfully imparting human affairs.
If the ruler's actions and stillness follow the Way,
honoring and complying with yin and yang,
then the sun and moon shine brightly,
wind and rain come in season,
cold and heat are harmonized.
When these three are properly ordered,
calamities and disasters will not arise,
people will not suffer premature death or illness,
and clothing and food will be abundant.
This is the essence of harmonizing yīn and yáng."
The details are recorded in the "Hóng Fàn" chapter.
Not missing the four seasons,
understanding the benefits of the land,
able to make passable what is impassable,
able to make beneficial what is unbeneficial—
such persons are recommended as the Nine Ministers.
Thus the affairs of the Nine Ministers always lie in virtue.
Understanding human affairs,
their actions are like following a plumb line,
adept at managing passes and bridges,
filling treasuries and storehouses—
such persons are recommended as Grand Masters.
Thus the affairs of Grand Masters always lie in benevolence.
Yáng Yóng, the Registrar of Shǔ Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng, said:
"Those who sit and discuss the Way
are called the Three Dukes;
those who act and implement it
are called the Ministers and Grand Masters."
Loyal and upright, strongly remonstrating
without any deceit or fraud,
abandoning selfishness for public good
and speaking with legal standards—
such persons are recommended as Exemplary Officers.
Thus the affairs of Exemplary Officers always lie in righteousness.
Therefore, when the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are established, the world is well-governed.
(The "Rénwù Zhì" says:
"The virtue of pure integrity
is the responsibility of the Instructors;
the talent of legalists
is the responsibility of the Minister of Justice;
the talent of strategists
is the responsibility of the Three Solitaries;
the talent of assessment
assists the Instructors;
the talent of skillfulness
is the responsibility of the Minister of Works;
the talent of Confucian scholarship
is the responsibility of the Guardians;
the talent for literary composition
is the responsibility of the State Historian;
the talent of bravery and heroism
is the responsibility of generals and commanders.")
Tàigōng said:
"Those who talk and chatter much,
with foul and malicious tongues,
speaking ill all day long,
never ceasing even in bed,
hated by the masses,
resented by people—
these can be used to patrol alleys and lanes,
detecting treachery and watching for trouble.
Calculating and meddlesome,
sleeping late and rising early,
unregretful even under strain—
these are leaders of wives and children.
Speaking first to observe affairs,
encouraging and sharing food,
honest, elder-like, and sparing in words,
distributing wealth evenly—
these are leaders of ten men.
Anxious and sharp,
attentive and solemn,
not heeding advice,
frequently executing punishments,
ensuring blood is seen in penalties,
not sparing relatives—
these are leaders of a hundred men.
Argumentative and competitive,
envious and oppressive,
punishing others with penalties,
seeking to unify the masses—
these are leaders of a thousand men.
Outwardly hesitant,
speaking occasionally,
knowing people's hunger and fullness,
familiar with their hardships and ease—
these are leaders of ten thousand men.
Trembling with caution,
growing more careful each day,
drawing near to the worthy and adopting counsel,
making people understand discipline,
speech not disrespectful,
loyalty sincere and complete—
these are leaders of a hundred thousand men."
The "Jīng" says:
"Although a general should value thoroughness and gravity,
he must not have irresolvable doubts;
although he should be skilled in broad consultation,
he should not suffer from multiple confusions."
This is the subtlety of discussing generalship.
Gentle, kind, honest, and elder-like,
single-minded in intent;
seeing the worthy, promoting them,
enforcing laws without injustice—
these are leaders of a million men.
Energetic and bustling,
known throughout neighboring states,
moving among the mighty,
beloved by the common people,
sincere, trustworthy, broad-minded,
clear in leading the age,
capable of accomplishing tasks,
and also able to rescue from failure,
knowledgeable in astronomy above,
understanding geography below,
treating all within the four seas
as his own wife and children—
this is the paragon of heroes,
the lord of the world."
The "Rénwù Zhì" says:
"Those with outstanding intelligence and brilliance are called yīng (elite);
those with surpassing courage and strength are called xióng (hero).
These are the general distinctions in terminology.
Intelligence and brilliance
belong to the category of yīng,
but without the courage of xióng, their plans cannot be implemented;
courage and strength
belong to the category of xióng,
but without the wisdom of yīng, their endeavors cannot be established.
If one is wise enough to plan the beginning,
but not clear-sighted enough to perceive opportunities,
they can sit and discuss but cannot handle affairs;
if one is wise enough to plan the beginning,
clear-sighted enough to perceive opportunities,
but lacks the courage to act,
they can follow routine but cannot contemplate change;
if one's strength surpasses others,
but courage to act is lacking,
they can be a strong person,
but not a vanguard;
if one's strength surpasses others,
and courage to act is present,
but wisdom is insufficient to assess affairs,
they can be a vanguard,
but not adequate as a general.
One must be wise enough to plan the beginning,
clear-sighted enough to perceive opportunities,
and courageous enough to make decisions—
only then can they be called yīng,
as was Zhāng Liáng.
With qi and strength surpassing others,
courage to act,
and wisdom sufficient to assess affairs—
only then can they be called xióng,
as was Hán Xìn.
If one person's character
combines both yīng and xióng,
then they can rule the age,
as were Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ."
The "Jīng" says:
"Those whose wisdom is like a spring,
and whose conduct can serve as a model,
are teachers of people;
those whose wisdom can sharpen others,
and whose conduct can serve as a warning,
are friends of people;
those who adhere to laws, uphold duties, and dare not do wrong
are clerks of people;
those who please immediately,
responding with multiple affirmations to a single call,
are servants of people.
Thus, the superior ruler employs teachers as aides,
the middling ruler employs friends as aides,
the inferior ruler employs clerks as aides,
the ruler facing peril and ruin employs servants as aides."
To observe their downfall,
one must look at their subordinates.
Thus, those with the same clarity see each other,
those with the same hearing hear each other,
those with the same purpose follow each other—
unless one is worthy, they cannot employ the worthy.
Therefore, the aides and assistants one wishes to appoint
are the pivot of survival or perish,
the crux of gain or loss.
Sūn Wǔ said:
"Which ruler has the Way?"
Formerly, when the Hàn king was besieged at Xíngyáng,
he said to Chén Píng:
"The world is in turmoil;
when will it be settled?"
Píng replied:
"As for King Xiàng's character,
he is respectful and loves people;
scholars of integrity and propriety mostly join him.
But when it comes to awarding merits and titles,
those who value land and honors
do not attach themselves for this reason.
Now, Your Majesty is rude and lacking in courtesy;
yet stubborn, greedy, shameless scholars
also mostly join Hàn.
Truly, each should discard their two shortcomings
and combine their two strengths—
then pointing and commanding would suffice to settle the world."
Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi said to Guō Jiā:
"Yuán Běnchū possesses vast territory and strong armies.
I wish to attack him,
but my strength is insufficient to match his.
What should I do?"
Jiā replied:
"The historical instance where Liú Bāng could not match Xiàng Yǔ
is something you, my lord, are aware of.
The Hàn founder triumphed solely through wisdom;
though Xiàng Yǔ was strong,
he was ultimately captured.
In my humble opinion,
Yuán Shào has ten points of failure,
while you, my lord, have ten points of superiority.
Though his troops are strong,
he can accomplish nothing.
Shào adheres to complex rituals and numerous formalities,
while you, my lord, embody natural simplicity,
this is superiority in the Way,
the first point.
Shào moves against the natural order,
while you, my lord, act in accordance with it,
leading all under heaven,
this is superiority in righteousness,
the second point.
At the end of Hàn, governance failed due to excessive leniency,
and Shào continues with leniency,
thus failing to inspire awe;
you, my lord, correct this with strictness,
so both high and low understand discipline,
this is superiority in governance,
the third point.
Shào appears tolerant outwardly but is suspicious inwardly,
employing men yet quickly doubting them,
appointing only his relatives and sons;
you, my lord, are straightforward outwardly yet astute inwardly,
employing men without suspicion,
considering only their suitability in talent and ability,
regardless of their closeness or distance,
this is superiority in judgment,
the fourth point.
Shào has many plans but few decisions,
failing in timely action;
you, my lord, implement strategies as soon as they are formed,
adapting to changes infinitely,
this is superiority in planning,
the fifth point.
Shào relies on the resources accumulated over generations,
engages in lofty discussions and ceremonial courtesies,
to gain reputation,
so scholars who enjoy empty talk and superficial appearances mostly flock to him;
you, my lord, treat others with utmost sincerity,
acting with genuine trust,
not engaging in false praises,
leading your subordinates with frugality,
never stinting in rewarding the meritorious,
so scholars who are loyal, upright, far-sighted, and substantial
are all willing to serve you,
this is superiority in virtue,
the sixth point.
Shào, upon seeing people in hunger and cold,
shows compassion and concern,
visible in his expression,
but for what he does not see,
his consideration may not reach,
what is called the kindness of a woman;
you, my lord, may occasionally overlook minor matters at hand,
from time to time,
but when it comes to major affairs,
connected to the whole realm,
the grace you bestow
always exceeds expectations,
even for what is not seen,
your considerations are comprehensive,
and nothing fails to be accomplished,
this is superiority in benevolence,
the seventh point.
Shào's ministers contend for power,
with slander causing confusion;
you, my lord, guide your subordinates with the Way,
so insinuations do not work,
this is superiority in clarity,
the eighth point.
With Shào, right and wrong are indistinguishable;
for what you, my lord, affirm, you promote with propriety;
for what you do not affirm, you correct with law,
this is superiority in culture,
the ninth point.
Shào is fond of empty displays of power,
not understanding the essentials of military affairs;
you, my lord, overcome many with few,
employing troops like a deity,
your soldiers rely on you,
your enemies fear you,
this is superiority in military prowess,
the tenth point."
Cáo Gōng said:
"I understand;
Yuán Shào as a person
has great ambitions but little wisdom,
fierce in appearance but timid at heart,
jealous and lacking authority,
with many troops but unclear organization,
his generals arrogant and his orders inconsistent,
though his land is vast,
and his provisions abundant,
they are merely provisions for me."
Yáng Fù said:
"Lord Yuán is lenient but indecisive,
fond of planning but slow to decide.
Indecisiveness leads to lack of authority,
slowness in decision results in delayed action.
Though he is strong now,
he will ultimately be captured.
Lord Cáo has great talent and far-reaching strategy,
decisive without hesitation,
his laws unified and truly refined,
he will surely accomplish great deeds."
Which general has the ability?
When Yuán Shào led a massive force to attack Xǔ,
Kǒng Róng said to Xún Yù:
"Yuán Shào has vast territory and strong armies,
with Tián Fēng and Xǔ Yōu,
men of wisdom and strategy, planning for him;
Shěn Pèi and Péng Jì,
loyal ministers, managing his affairs;
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu,
bravest in the three armies, commanding his troops.
Is it not difficult to overcome him?"
Yù said:
"Though Shào's troops are numerous,
his laws and orders are not well-ordered.
Tián Fēng is stubborn and offends his superiors,
Xǔ Yōu is greedy and unprincipled,
Shěn Pèi is autocratic and lacking in strategy,
Péng Jì is decisive but self-willed.
If these two remain, we know the aftermath.
Xǔ Yōu, being greedy, will break the law,
and certainly will not be indulged;
if not indulged, he will surely rebel.
As for Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu,
they are merely brave on an individual level,
and can be captured in a single battle."
Later, Xǔ Yōu, being greedy, did not abide by the law,
and Shěn Pèi seized his wife and children,
causing Yōu to rage and defect to Lord Cáo.
Also, Yán Liáng was beheaded in battle,
and Tián Fēng died for his remonstrance.
All turned out as Yù had predicted.
From this, I understand what is meant by foreseeing victory."
Fifth: Knowing People
I have heard that the method for a ruler and general
is to thoroughly understand the hearts of heroes.
Yet people are not easy to know,
and knowing people is not easy.
Hàn Guāngwǔ, an emperor of keen perception,
erred regarding Páng Méng;
Cáo Mèngdé, a sage in knowing people,
was misled by Zhāng Miào.
Why is this?
The categories of things
are what confuse the world.
Hence it is said:
The cunning appear wise but are not truly wise,
(Note: "cunning" pronounced zì shū fǎn, meaning deceitful.)
the foolish appear like gentlemen but are not gentlemen,
the simple-minded appear brave but are not truly brave.
A ruler of a doomed state may seem intelligent,
a minister of a doomed state may seem loyal,
young darnel weeds resemble grain,
a yellow ox may resemble a tiger,
white bones may be mistaken for ivory,
and inferior stones may resemble jade.
These are all cases of seeming so but not being so.
The "Character Records" says:
"Those who lightly make promises seem earnest but are seldom trustworthy,
those who take many things lightly seem capable but achieve little,
those who advance sharply seem precise but withdraw quickly,
the inquisitive seem observant but complicate matters,
false generosity seems kind but does not last,
surface compliance seems loyal but contradicts in private.
These are cases of seeming so but not being so.
There are also cases of seeming not so but being so:
great authority may seem treacherous but brings achievement,
great wisdom may seem foolish but is inwardly clear,
broad love may seem empty but is truly profound,
straightforward speech may seem critical but is sincerely loyal.
If not the most refined in the world,
who can discern their true nature?"
Confucius said:
"Human hearts are more treacherous than mountains and rivers,
harder to fathom than the heavens.
The heavens at least have the cycles of spring, autumn, winter, summer, dawn and dusk,
but humans conceal profound feelings behind thick appearances.
Thus, there are those who appear sincere yet are arrogant,
those who seem virtuous but are unworthy
(zhǎng, pronounced with two tones),
those who appear compliant yet are resolute,
those who seem firm yet are pliable,
and those who appear gentle yet are fierce
(hàn, pronounced as hàn)."
Tàigōng said:
"Among scholars, there are those strict in appearance but unworthy in character,
those gentle and kind yet become thieves,
those with outwardly respectful demeanor
but deceitful and arrogant at heart,
those seemingly diligent yet lack true feeling,
those imposing in presence but achieve nothing,
those who appear decisive yet hesitate when action is needed,
those seemingly vague and indistinct but prove loyal and honest,
those who appear hesitant and indirect yet accomplish their goals,
those with a brave and fierce exterior but timid inside,
and those who seem muddled yet easily influence others.
There is no trait that does not exist,
no outcome that does not occur.
What the world despises,
the sages value;
what ordinary people fail to perceive,
only the greatly discerning can see clearly."
These are cases where a scholar's outward appearance does not match their inner feelings.
Huán Fàn said:
"The difference between the worthy and the foolish
is like that between the sunflower and the amaranth—
how can one not know it?
But if it's like the darnel resembling grain,
seemingly alike yet not truly so,
appearing worthy but not actually worthy."
Yángzǐ's "Model Sayings" states:
Someone asked about what is hard to discern.
The reply was:
'Tàishān compared to an anthill,
the Jiāng and Hé rivers to a puddle—
these are not difficult.
But the great sage versus the great hypocrite—
that is hard!
Alas!
Only those who can distinguish semblances
find nothing difficult!'"
To know such scholars, there are methods:
Subtly observe and question them
to see their responses;
press them with words
to observe their adaptability;
consult them on confidential plans
to gauge their sincerity;
ask clearly and directly
to assess their virtue;
send them on distant missions with wealth
to examine their integrity
It is also said:
Entrust them with wealth
to observe their benevolence;
confront them with profit
to test their integrity;
tempt them with beauty
to check their chastity
It is also said:
Delight them with beauty
to see if they remain unswayed;
inform them of difficulties
to evaluate their courage
It is also said:
Tell them of dangers to observe their bravery.
Also said:
Frighten them to test their steadfastness;
make them drunk with wine
to watch their behavior
It is also said:
Make them drunk to see if they keep their composure.
Also said:
Make them drunk with wine
to observe if they remain proper.
"Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"Send them afar to observe their loyalty
It is also said:
Send them far to see if they remain steadfast;
keep them close to watch their respectfulness
It is also said:
Bring them near with familiarity
to see if they become disrespectful;
burden them with tasks to assess their capability
It is also said:
Trouble them with affairs
to observe their management;
suddenly
question them to test their
wisdom
It is also said: Present them with
strategies to observe
his wisdom.
Tài Gōng said: "He who handles affairs
without reaching an impasse,
possesses strategy." ;
Press him with urgent deadlines,
to observe his trustworthiness
Tài Gōng said:
"He who is employed without concealment,
is called trustworthy." ;
Mix him in diverse situations,
to observe his demeanor
Also said:
"Give him free rein to observe,
and see if he remains unchanged." . 」
《Lǚshì Chūnqiū》 says:
"When he is successful,
observe whom he respects
'Tōng' means
successful. ;
When noble,
observe whom he promotes
Also said:
"When in high position,
look at whom he recommends." ;
When wealthy,
observe how he nurtures
Also said:
"When rich,
observe whom he associates with.
Also said:
"When meeting wealthy and noble people,
observe if they are courteous and charitable.
Tài Gōng said:
"He who becomes wealthy without becoming arrogant or indulgent,
is called benevolent." ;
When listening,
observe his actions
Actions then reflect benevolence;
When close,
observe his preferences
Also said:
"In residence,
observe whom he is intimate with.
Also said:
"Examine his dwelling place,
to observe his integrity and goodness;
examine his social interactions,
to observe his aspirations and alliances." ;
In habits,
observe his words
Preferences reflect righteousness, words then
speak of the Way. ;
When in hardship,
observe what he does not covet
Also said:
"In poverty,
observe what he refrains from doing wrong.
Also said:
"When poor,
observe what he does not take." ;
When lowly,

Also said:
"With poor and lowly people,
observe if they possess virtue and integrity." .
Make him happy,
to test his restraint
'Shǒu' means
careful restraint.
Also said:

Entertain him,

'Jié' means
nature.
Also said:

Grieve him,

A benevolent person,
grieves when seeing something sorrowful. ;
Harden him,
to test his will
Also said:
"Test him,
to observe his ability to remain calm." . 」
《The Classic》 says:
"For those entrusted with favor,
observe if they are not arrogant or extravagant
Tài Gōng said:
"Those who become noble
without being arrogant or extravagant,
are righteous." ;
For those neglected and dismissed,
observe if they do not betray or overstep;
for those honored and prominent,
observe if they are not boastful;
for those in obscurity and poverty,
observe if they are not fearful;
for the young,
observe if they are respectful, studious, and capable of fraternal duty
《Rénwù Zhì》 says:
"The signs of intelligent individuals,
appear in childhood,
all have initial indications.
Thus literary talent emerges from verbose speech,
debate begins with a ready tongue,
benevolence arises from compassion,
generosity manifests in excessive giving,
caution stems from fear,
integrity starts with not taking what is not one's own." ;
For the mature,
observe their integrity, dedication to action, and overcoming personal desires;
for the elderly,
observe their thoughtful caution,
strengthening their shortcomings without overstepping.
Between father and son,
observe their kindness and filial piety;
among brothers,
observe their harmony and friendship;
within the village community,
observe their trustworthiness and righteousness;
between ruler and minister,
observe their loyalty and benevolence
Tài Gōng said:
"He who is entrusted without shifting allegiance,
is loyal." . 」
This is called observing sincerity.
Fù Zǐ said:
"The difficulty in knowing people,
lies most in distinguishing truth from falsehood.
If one's cultivation stems from Daoism,
then they speak of naturalness and value profound mystery;
if one's cultivation stems from Confucianism,
then they speak of social divisions and value fairness and justice;
if one's cultivation stems from the School of Diplomacy,
then they speak of expediency and value changing norms.
The nine schools have different pursuits,
each with their own strengths,
this is not what is called difficult.
With the silent, observe their actions;
with the talkative, observe their rhetoric;
with those in office, observe their governance;
with those in retirement, observe their learning.
These four virtues may differ,
the observations have subtleties,
yet this is still not what is called difficult.
What is called difficult,
is when classical sayings are deceptively matched,
responses shift endlessly,
the lowly speak of loftiness,
the greedy speak of integrity,
the cruel speak of benevolence,
the cowardly speak of courage,
the deceitful speak of trustworthiness,
the licentious speak of chastity.
They can create semblances to confuse truth,
use multiple approaches to baffle the dim-witted.
This is what commonly confuses ordinary people,
and what wise rulers deeply detest.
The noble person cleanses his mind internally,
to receive others with emptiness,
stands firm without changing direction,
this is the way of steadfast observation.
The nine schools have their masters,
this is the way of steadfast unity.
Internally steadfast in observation and externally steadfast in unity,
then those who hold falsehood have no place to escape.
Empty words are easy to fabricate,
but if we demand the actual effects of their deeds,
then the verification of right and wrong becomes immediately visible."
Therefore Hán Zǐ said:
"If everyone is asleep,
The blind do not know;
all people are silent,
the mute do not recognize.
Awaken them and make them see,
question them and make them respond,
then the mute and blind are at a loss.
Examining the teeth and lips,
observing the coat color,
even Liáng and Yuè could not determine a horse's quality;
hitching it to a carriage and driving it,
testing it on the road,
then even a stable hand can judge its worth.
Observing the color,
inspecting the forging and tempering,
even Ōu Yě could not ascertain a sword's quality;
cutting dogs and horses on land,
slicing flood dragons in water,
even a fool can recognize its sharpness or dullness.
Thus we know that clear testing demands substance,
which is the achievement of sages. "
The Rénwùzhì says:
All living beings,
without exception, receive yīn and yáng to establish their nature,
embody the five phases to manifest form.
In the body,
wood represents bones, metal represents sinews, fire represents breath, earth represents flesh, water represents blood -
these are the images of the five elements.
The substance of these five elements,
each contributes something. :
"Those with upright yet pliable bones
are called magnanimous and resolute.
Magnanimity and resolution,
are the substance of benevolence
Wood provides shade,
forming the substance of benevolence.
Without magnanimous substance,
benevolence cannot be achieved. .
Those with clear and bright breath
are called cultured and patterned.
Culture and patterning,
are the foundation of ritual
Fire illuminates,
forming the foundation of ritual.
Without cultural foundation,
ritual cannot be achieved. .
Those with proper and substantial bodies
are called steadfast and firm.
Steadfastness and firmness,
are the basis of trustworthiness
Earth produces growth,
forming the basis of trustworthiness.
Without steadfast basis,
trustworthiness cannot be achieved. .
Those with strong and refined sinews
are called courageous and bold.
Courage and boldness,
are the decision of righteousness
Metal can cut,
forming the decision of righteousness.
Without courageous decision,
righteousness cannot be achieved. .
Those with even and smooth complexion
are called penetrating and subtle.
Penetration and subtlety,
are the source of wisdom
Water flows freely,
forming the source of wisdom.
Without penetrating source,
wisdom cannot be achieved. .
These five substances form constant nature,
therefore called the five constants.
Thus it is said:
Straight but not firm is like wood
Wood strong yet deceptive,
loses its proper quality. ,
Strong but not refined is mere force
Carrying cauldrons breaking knees,
loses its proper strength. ,
Firm but not proper is foolishness
Self-opinionated and self-righteous,
falls into foolish stubbornness. ,
Breath but not clear is scattered
Speech unclear and不顺,
scatters without achievement. ,
Smooth but not even is unrestrained
Wisdom without bounds,
becomes wildly lost. .
Thus even and uneven substance lies in spirit
Spirit is
the master of substance.
So when spirit is even, substance is even;
when spirit is uneven, substance is uneven. ,
Bright and dark reality lies in essence
Essence is
the foundation of reality.
So when essence is sharp, reality is bright;
when essence is turbid, reality is dark. ,
Courage and timidity potential lies in sinews
Sinews are
the application of potential.
So when sinews are strong, potential is courageous;
when sinews are weak, potential is timid. ,
Strength and weakness foundation lies in bones
Bones are
the mechanism of foundation.
So when bones are thick, foundation is strong;
when bones are thin, foundation is weak. ,
Restlessness and calm decision lies in breath
Breath is
the ground of decision.
When breath is abundant,
decision tends to restlessness;
when breath is balanced,
decision tends to calm. ,
Grief and joy emotion lies in complexion
Complexion is
the indicator of emotion.
So haggard complexion comes from grievous emotion;
joyful complexion comes from happy emotion. ,
Decline and propriety form lies in demeanor
Demeanor is
the expression of form.
So declined demeanor comes from perilous form;
proper demeanor comes from dignified form. ,
Attitude movement lies in countenance
Countenance is
the sign of movement.
So when movements are improper, countenance shows sorrow;
when attitude is proper, countenance shows measure. ,
Slowness and urgency manifestation lies in speech
Speech is
the manifestation of heart.
So when heart is tolerant, speech is slow;
when heart is biased, speech is urgent. .
If substance is plain and tranquil,
wise within and bright without,
sinews strong and foundation firm,
voice clear and complexion joyful,
demeanor noble and countenance upright,
then this is pure virtue. "
People possess breath.
Breath means
that sincerity within
must manifest outwardly.
Thus those with rough and contentious heart-breath
have deep and scattered voices;
those with careful and cautious heart-breath
have harmonious and measured voices;
those with mean and violent heart-breath
have coarse and rough voices;
those with broad and gentle heart-breath
have warm and smooth voices.
Sincere breath is balanced and easy,
righteous breath is timely and relaxed,
harmonious breath is simple and brief,
courageous breath is strong and established.
This is called listening to breath.
Through their voice,
assess their substance.
Breath generates things,
things generated have sound.
Sounds have firmness and softness, clarity and turbidity,
all emerging from the voice.
Listen to their voice,
observe their breath,
examine their actions,
all can be known.
There is also observing complexion.
Observing complexion
means heart-breath stored within
can all be discerned through complexion.
Genuine wisdom
must have an inexhaustible appearance
Also said:
Genuine wisdom,
must have a clear and penetrating appearance. ;
Genuine benevolence,
must have a respectable appearance
Also said:
One who is truly benevolent
must have a gentle and soft countenance.;
One who is truly courageous
must have a countenance that is difficult to intimidate.
It is also said:
One who is truly courageous
must have a resolute and vigorous countenance;
one who is truly loyal
must have a respectable appearance;
one who is truly pure
must have a countenance that is hard to defile;
one who is truly steadfast
must have a trustworthy expression.
A genuine countenance is vast and firm, thus serene;
a false countenance is unrestrained, chaotic, and agitated.
This is what is called observing the countenance.
The "Rénwù Zhì" says:
"If one's inner nature is upright and honest,
their demeanor is firm and solid;
if one's inner nature is balanced and rational,
their demeanor is calm and leisurely.
The essence of benevolence in the eyes
is sincere and proper;
the essence of courage in the spirit
is bright and strong.
The countenance of distress
is weary and desolate;
the countenance of illness
is disordered and grimy;
an expression of joy
is cheerful and delighted;
an expression of anger
is stern and heightened;
an expression of jealousy and confusion
is reckless and inconsistent.
Therefore, if one's words are very pleasant but their inner expression does not follow,
it means there is inner contradiction;
if one's words are contradictory but their inner expression is trustworthy,
it is due to inarticulateness;
if an angry expression appears before words are spoken,
it indicates overflowing indignation;
if anger accompanies spoken words,
it is forcing what is not so."
All cases like these,
even if one tries to contradict them,
the inner expression does not comply,
making the truth clear through astonishment,
and even changes can be known.
There is also the examination of intentions.
Examining intentions means
to speak with someone
and observe their aims.
If their demeanor is broad and gentle,
their expression restrained and not flattering,
their courtesy precedes others,
their words come after others,
and they often show awareness of their own shortcomings,
they are a beneficial person.
If they enjoy imposing on others with their expression, looking down on others with their demeanor, or overpowering others with their words,
concealing their shortcomings,
and abandoning what they cannot do,
they are a harmful person.
Tàigōng said:
"Those who are widely learned and eloquent in debate,
who uphold high conduct and engage in discussions,
yet oppose the customs of the time,
are treacherous people.
A ruler must be cautious not to favor them."
If their appearance is upright without insult,
their words are just without selfishness,
they do not embellish their virtues, conceal their faults, or cover up their errors,
they are a person of substance.
It is also said:
Giving to them does not bring joy,
taking from them does not cause anger,
they are calm and speak little,
sincere with few outward displays,
they are a person of substance and tranquility.
Discussion says:
Tàigōng said:
"Those who dress plainly,
wear shabby clothes,
speak of non-action to seek fame,
talk of having no desires to gain something,
are hypocrites.
A ruler must be cautious not to approach them.
Among people of substance, there are such hypocrites."
If their appearance is fawning and ingratiating,
their words sycophantic and clever,
they adorn their visible traits,
focus on minor proofs,
and use these to promote themselves,
they are a person without substance.
Discussion says:
Yànzǐ said:
"Slanderers and flatterers by the ruler's side,
their talents are all extraordinary.
Those who harbor great insincerity within
must be careful with small sincerities outwardly,
to achieve their great insincerity."
This is difficult to detect and know.
Xún Yuè said:
"To examine human nature and methods,
observe their words and actions;
if they do not necessarily conform to the Way,
but please oneself,
they must be flatterers;
if their words and actions
do not necessarily please oneself but conform to the Way,
they must be upright people."
This is one aspect of examining human nature.
If they do not change expression over material joys and angers,
do not become confused in purpose amid chaotic affairs,
do not shift in heart despite deep temptations of profit,
and do not become submissive in spirit when threatened with authority,
they are a person with an even mind and firm integrity.
It is also said:
If they are not entertained by material honors,
not frightened by sudden offenses,
do not waver when righteousness is established,
and do not turn back when faced with wealth,
they are truly upright people.
Discussion says:
Confucius stated:
"In selecting people,
do not choose the aggressive.
Aggressiveness
is greed.
The弊端 of aggressiveness are as such."
If their heart changes with material joys and angers,
their purpose becomes unsettled in chaotic affairs,
their heart moves at the sight of profit,
and their spirit becomes fearful when threatened with authority,
they are a person with a base heart and false courage.
It is also said:
If their will cannot be firm when challenged with words,
and they cannot make decisions after promises,
they are a person of weak character.
If they decide quickly when presented with situations,
respond frequently when startled suddenly,
and are wise without eloquence,
they are a person with intelligence and thought.
Discussion says:
Tàigōng said:
"Those who have a name but no substance,
whose words differ inside and outside,
who promote the good and conceal the bad,
and make progress and retreat for merit,
a ruler must be cautious not to consult with them.
People with intelligence and thought
have this弊端."
If they are hard to test with situations,
hard to persuade with words,
stick to one thing without knowing change,
and are stubborn without knowing reform,
they are foolish and obstinate people.
Discussion says:
A person of principle holds to their integrity,
while the foolish and obstinate are hard to change.
Though not changing is the same,
the difference between foolish and wise
lies in their grasp of the Way.
How to explain this?
The "Xīnyǔ" says:
"Those skilled in change
cannot be exhausted by deceit;
those who understand the Way
cannot be startled by the strange;
those discerning in speech
cannot be confused by words;
those who comprehend righteousness
cannot be moved by profit.
Thus, a gentleman seeks broad knowledge but chooses carefully,
desires extensive learning but acts with earnestness.
Their eyes are not captivated by dazzling colors,
their ears are not disturbed by flattering words.
Even tempted by the wealth of Qí and Lǔ, their will does not shift;
even offered the longevity of Sōng and Qiáo, their conduct does not change.
Only then can they embody the Way and establish their integrity,
achieve their tasks and accomplish their merits,
observing their path and work."
This is why they differ from the foolish and obstinate.
If they ignore words without regard,
are selfish without self-protection,
and force what is wrong,
they are deceptive and envious people.
Discussion says:
Liú Bèi had a guest see Zhūgě Liàng, who found him worthy,
but Liàng said:
"I observe the guest's expression changing and spirit fearful,
gaze lowered and counting on fingers.
A treacherous form leaks outward,
an evil heart hides within.
He must be an assassin sent by Cáo."
It turned out so later.
The demeanor of treacherous people
is mostly like this.
Hé Yàn, Xiàhóu Xuán, Dèng Yáng, and others,
He sought friendship with Fù Jiǎ but was not accepted.
Someone found it strange and asked him about it,
Fù Jiǎ said:
"Tàichū has grand ambitions,
but his capacity can only accommodate empty reputation without real talent;
Hé Píngshū speaks of distant matters but his concerns are near,
fond of argument but lacking sincerity,
what is called a person whose sharp tongue overturns states;
Dèng Yuánmào has initiative but no follow-through,
externally seeks fame and profit,
internally lacks restraint,
values conformity and dislikes difference,
talks much and envies those ahead.
Much talk leads to many failures and conflicts,
envying those ahead brings no achievement.
In my view of these three men,
all have flawed character.
Keeping them at a distance still fears disaster may reach me,
how much more becoming intimate with them?"
Later events all proved Fù Jiǎ right.
The conduct of the envious,
has examples like these.
This is called examining aspirations.
The Rénwù Zhì says:
"Essence should be profound and subtle,
substance should be virtuous and substantial,
aspirations should be vast and great,
mind should be humble and small.
Profundity and subtlety are what enter divine wonder,
virtue and substance are what honor the abode of character,
great aspirations are what overcome the obstacles of things,
a small mind is what cautions against fault and regret.
Thus the Odes praise King Wén:
'With cautious care,'
not raising his voice or changing countenance,
is the small mind;
'The king blazed with wrath,'
in response to the world,
is the great aspiration.
Arguing from this,
those with small mind and great aspiration,
are the class of sages and worthies;
those with great mind and great aspiration,
are the outstanding among heroes;
those with great mind and small aspiration,
are the type of arrogant and dissipated;
those with small mind and small aspiration,
are constrained and timid people."
There is also testing concealment.
Testing concealment means,
if one gives small favors but likes to gain,
yields in small matters but contends in great,
presents words of honesty as his substance,
feigns affection as loyalty,
exalts his conduct to gather reputation.
This is concealment in benevolence and worthiness.
Xún Qīng said:
"Among the disciples of Zhòngní,
even a five-foot boy would be ashamed to speak of the way of hegemony,
why is that?
It is not based on governance and teaching,
does not win people's hearts,
uses yielding to adorn contention,
relies on benevolence while treading the path of profit.
They are but outstanding among petty men,
how can they be worthy of the gate of the great gentleman?"
If questioned then does not respond,
appears detailed but not exhaustive,
outwardly shows surplus,
borrows the way to follow himself,
pressed by things,
when cornered then feigns profundity.
This is concealment in arts and literature.
Also said:
When thoughts are truly inadequate but pretends not to speak,
inner sincerity is insufficient but expression shows surplus,
this is concealment in wisdom and strategy.
The Rénwù Zhì says:
"Some take position behind and maintain duration,
follow what the multitude finds comfortable,
seeming capable of hearing and deciding;
some avoid difficulty without response,
seeming as if having surplus but actually not understanding;
some take advantage of winning momentum to cover errors, cornered yet claiming subtlety,
seeming as if principle cannot be bent.
These several semblances,
are what confuse the multitude."
If using lofty words to appear upright,
affecting sternness to appear brave,
inwardly fearful but outwardly boastful,
urgently making claims,
approaching others with fraudulent air.
This is concealment in integrity and courage.
Discussion says:
Tàigōng said:
"Without wisdom or grand strategy,
and because of heavy rewards and high rank,
forcibly brave and reckless in battle,
hoping for luck externally.
The king must carefully not make such a one a general."
This is the flaw of feigned courage.
If serving ruler or parents personally but likes to tell others,
adorning visible actions without inner sincerity,
launching reputation through ruler and parents,
using reputation for personal gain.
This is concealment in loyalty and filial piety.
This is called testing concealment.
The Rénwù Zhì says:
"The exceptionally subtle person,
contains essence within genuine,
externally without adorned manner;
the exceptionally hollow person,
grand speech and splendid appearance,
inwardly actually contradictory.
Yet people's search for the extraordinary,
not using subtlety to measure their profound mechanism,
some consider meager appearance as insufficiency,
some consider splendid manner as greatness,
some consider genuine revelation as empty flourish,
some consider clever adornment as true reality."
How can they attain it?
Thus testing concealment is needed.
When a person's words and deeds do not match,
end and beginning contradict each other,
outer and inner do not accord,
yet establishing false integrity to move sight and hearing,
this is called destroying aspiration.
The Rénwù Zhì says:
"Purely accusatory nature is contrary,
cannot be fair and upright,
relying on accusation seems straightforward,
using schemes to accuse the good;
purely unrestrained seems fluid,
cannot penetrate the way,
relying on unrestraint seems penetrating,
conduct arrogant exceeding measure.
Therefore it is said:
The straightforward also accuse,
the accusatory also accuse,
their accusation is the same,
but their reason for accusing differs;
the penetrating also are unrestrained,
the unrestrained also are unrestrained,
their unrestraint is the same,
but their reason for being unrestrained differs.
Observing their reliance on semblance,
then destroyed aspiration can be known."
If using food and drink to become intimate,
goods and bribes to make friends,
loss and gain to unite,
obtaining power and reputation while concealed by things,
this is called greedy and base.
Tàigōng said:
"Decisive and bold, lightly regarding death,
merely to greedily obtain,
high rank and heavy salary,
not planning great affairs,
waiting for profit to act,
the king must carefully not use such."
If having small knowledge but no great understanding,
small ability but no great achievement,
planning small matters without knowing great principles,
this is called flowery and boastful.
Wénzǐ said:
"In human nature none lack some shortcoming:
if their main outline is correct,
even having minor faults,
is not enough to burden them;
if their main outline is incorrect,
village conduct,
is not worth praising."
There is also assessing virtue.
Assessing virtue means,
if one has words loyal and conduct even,
upholding aims without selfishness,
giving without seeking return, sentiment loyal and
discerning,
appearance clumsy yet calm,
this is called benevolent heart.
If one can manage effects when affairs change,
can reach through when cornered,
positioning oneself to achieve merit and able to succeed,
this is called having wisdom.
If one is wealthy and honored yet respectful and frugal, able to be威严,
having courtesy without arrogance,
this is called having virtue.
Discussion says:
Yú Huàn said:
"The poor do not learn frugality,
the lowly do not learn respect,
it is not human nature's portion,
but circumstance that makes it so."
Thus knowing to distinguish respect and frugality,
must be among the wealthy and honored.
If one lives in obscurity without fear,
in comfort without extravagance,
with merit and labor unchanged,
joy and anger having measure,
this is called having integrity.
If one serves the ruler with reverence and respect,
To serve one's parents with affection and love,
even when feelings are at odds, not to rebel,
and to exert all effort without defiance,
this defines loyalty and filial piety.
This is what is called assessing virtue.
Huán Fàn said:
"The sovereigns of emperors and kings,
through successive dynasties,
all admire the hegemon's employment of the worthy,
and detest the fallen state's loss of talents.
Yet they still entrust power to the vicious and foolish,
leading to successive collapses and ruins,
what is the reason for this?
It is because in selecting people, they do not seek alignment with the Way,
but rather alignment with themselves."
Hence, the *Rénwùzhì* states:
"Those of pure integrity,
take genuineness and uprightness as their standard,
thus when evaluating various talents,
they can recognize the constancy of nature and conduct but may doubt the deceit of methods and tactics;
those of strategic planning,
take deep contemplation as their standard,
thus they can recognize the marvel of strategies but may miss the goodness of adhering to laws;
those of skill and craft,
take seeking merit as their standard,
thus they can recognize the achievements of advancement but do not comprehend the transformation of morality;
those of speech and debate,
take analysis and discrimination as their standard,
thus they can recognize the wisdom of quick-wittedness but are unaware of the beauty of含蓄 elegance,
hence they refute each other,
unwilling to affirm one another.
All such types
are referred to as belonging to one stream.
Thus, a person of one stream can recognize the goodness of that stream,
and a person of two streams can recognize the beauty of two streams.
If one encompasses all streams,
then they can also comprehensively understand all talents."
It also says:
"Those who strive for fame cannot surpass those who excel beyond themselves,
therefore,
if natures are similar but abilities differ,
they support and rely on each other;
if natures are similar and strengths are equal,
they compete and harm each other.
This is the variation among those of the same type,
which must not be overlooked."
What the sages and worthies praise,
nothing is more praised than intelligence;
what intelligence values,
nothing is more valued than knowing people.
Knowing people and recognizing wisdom,
then all talents find their proper order,
and the achievements of various tasks will flourish.
It also says:
One cannot interact with all the people under heaven.
How can one know them?
To observe one aspect of them,
a single morning is enough to recognize it;
to investigate them in detail,
three days are necessary to suffice.
Why say three days are necessary?
Because a person of state caliber,
combines three talents,
thus without discussing for three days,
it is insufficient to fully understand them.
First, discuss morality,
second, discuss laws and institutions,
third, discuss strategies and tactics.
Only then can one exhaust their strengths,
and recommend them without doubt.
So how can one know if they are comprehensive or biased and speak with them accordingly?
If a person strives to follow the flow of categories,
elucidate others' strengths,
and define their attributes,
such a person is comprehensive;
if one likes to display their own goodness,
desires others to praise them,
and does not wish to know what others possess,
such a person is called biased.

The Zuo Zhuan says:
"Zhōu Nèishǐ Shūfú went to Lǔ,
Gōngsūn Ào heard he was skilled at reading faces,
presented his two sons to him.
Shūfú said:
'Gǔ will feed you,
Nán will bury you.
Gǔ has a full lower face,
he will surely have descendants in the State of Lǔ.'"
Dù Yù comments:
"Full lower face
means having a square jaw."
When the Earl of Zhèng entertained Zhào Mèng at Chuílǒng,
seven ministers accompanied him.
Zhào Mèng said:
"The seven ministers follow their lord
to honor me.
I ask that you all recite poetry
to complete your lord's kindness."
Zǐzhǎn recited "Grass Insects".
Zhào Mèng said:
"Excellent!
You are a master of men.
But I am not worthy to match it."
Yìn Duàn recited "Cricket".
Zhào Mèng said:
"Excellent!
A master of preserving his house.
I have hope now."
Zǐzhǎn would be the last to perish,
for being high yet remembering humility.
Yìn's clan would be next,
joyful but not dissolute.
Using joy to comfort people,
not leading them with excess -
perishing last,
is this not fitting?"
The Hàn Shū says:
"Gāozǔ appointed Bì as King of Wú.
After the appointment,
the emperor read his face and said:
'Your facial features show rebellion,
fifty years from now,
there will be rebellion in the southeast -
could it not be you?
All under heaven is one family,
take care not to rebel.'"
The Classic says:
"When the brow bone is high and prominent,
it is called the nine-fold rebellion bone.
Such a person often harbors treacherous ambitions."
It also says:
"When yellow color encircles the celestial midpoint,
extending from the hairline to both temples,
and yellow appears below each eyebrow,
with more yellow descending straight down the nose -
this is the mark of a Three Lord.
If a lowly person has this coloring,
they can kill their ruler or father."
The Spring and Autumn Annals: Zuo Tradition says:
When the King of Chǔ wanted to make Shāng Chén crown prince,
he consulted Lingyǐn Zǐshàng.
Zǐshàng said:
"This man
has wasp eyes and jackal's voice -
a cruel man.
He should not be established."
The king did not listen.
Later he rebelled,
using palace guards to surround King Chéng,
and strangled him.
It also says:
When Chǔ's Simǎ Zǐliáng gave birth to Zǐ Yuèjiāo,
Zǐwén said:
"You must kill him.
This man
has the appearance of bear and tiger with the voice of wolf.
If not killed,
he will surely destroy the Ruò'áo clan.
As the proverb says:
'The wolf cub has wild ambitions.'
This is a wolf -
can it be kept?"
Zǐliáng refused,
and later he indeed rebelled,
attacking the king.
The King of Chǔ advanced with drums,
and destroyed the Ruò'áo clan.
It also says:
When Jìn's Hán Xuānzǐ went to Qí,
he met Zǐyǎ.
Zǐyǎ called his son Zǐqí
to meet Xuānzǐ.
Xuānzǐ said:
"Not one to preserve his house.
Disloyal."
Dù Yù comments:
"Meaning Zǐqí's ambitions and bearing were arrogant."
Ten years later,
he fled to another state.
When Zhōu King Líng's brother Dān Jì died,
his son Kuò was about to see the king but sighed.
Prince Qiānqí of Shàn heard his sigh,
entered and told the king:
"Not grieving yet ambitious,
restless gaze and lofty step -
his mind is elsewhere.
If not killed, he will surely cause harm."
The king said:
"What does a youth know?"
When King Líng died,
Dān Kuò wanted to establish Prince Nìngfū.
Zhōu ministers killed Nìngfū.
When Qí's Cuī Zhù led troops against us,
the duke was worried.
Mèng Gōngchuò said:
"Cuī Zǐ has greater ambitions -
his concern is not harming us.
He will surely return quickly -
why worry?
His coming shows no hostility,
his men lack discipline,
unlike other times."
The Qí army returned empty-handed,
and he indeed assassinated Duke Zhuāng.
When Jìn and Chǔ met with other states to swear covenant,
Chǔ's Prince Wéi displayed regal attire and separate guards.
Lǔ minister Shūsūn Mùzǐ said:
"Prince Wéi of Chǔ is magnificent -
like a ruler!"
Dù Yù comments:
"Displayed
royal garments."
That year, Zǐ Wéi usurped the throne.
When Wèi's Sūn Wénzǐ came on mission,
he ascended steps equally with the ruler.
Shūsūn Mùzǐ hurried forward and said:
"In meetings of lords,
our humble lord has never lagged behind Wèi's ruler.
Now you do not yield to our humble lord -
we know not our fault.
Please restrain yourself."
Sūnzǐ offered no apology,
