nor showed remorse.
Mù Shū said:
"Sūnzǐ will surely perish.
As minister acting like ruler,
erring without remorse -
this is the root of ruin."
Fourteen years later,
Lín Fǔ expelled his ruler.
Earlier,
when the Earl of Zhèng entertained Zhào Mèng,
seven ministers recited poetry,
Bó Yǒu recited "The Flaunting Pheasant".
After the feast,
Zhào Mèng told Shū Xiàng:
"Bó Yǒu will face execution.
Poetry expresses intent -
his intent slanders his superior,
yet publicly resents him,
taking it as guest's glory -
can this last long?"
In Wèi times, Guǎn Lù read the faces of Hé Yàn and Dèng Yáng as doomed.
After their deaths,
Lù's uncle asked him,
and he said:
"Dèng Yáng's walk -
joints not controlling bones,
pulses not restraining flesh,
rising and leaning,
as if limbless -
this is called ghost agitation.
Hé's appearance -
soul not guarding its abode,
face without bloom,
spirit floating like smoke,
visage like dead wood -
this is called ghost gloom.
Those with ghost agitation
are taken by wind;
those with ghost gloom
are burned by fire.
This is nature's sign,
not to be concealed."
Sòng's Kǒng Xīguāng told Yáo Shēng:
"In reading faces,
heaven should be round,
earth should be square,
eyes should shine bright,
nose must be pillar-strong.
Four rivers should be clear, five
Yuè desired to be strong.
Among these traits,
you possess not a single one.
Moreover, your pupils,
darting restlessly as if gazing afar,
your gait meandering like a sheep losing its footing,
and your voice hoarse and scattered, failing to project—
not only will you lose your blessings and prosperity,
but you shall also meet with calamity."
Later, they all plotted rebellion,
and were executed.
From this, we observe that
using physiognomy to examine individuals
has a long history indeed.
Thus it is said:
Wealth and honor lie in the bone structure;
sorrow and joy reside in the facial complexion.
The Classic states:
"Blue indicates sorrow,
white signifies mourning,
black portends illness,
red foretells fright and fear,
yellow heralds celebration and joy.
All these five colors
are judged according to the four seasons.
In the three months of spring,
blue is dominant,
red is supporting,
white is imprisoned,
yellow and black both perish.
In the three months of summer,
red is dominant,
white and yellow are both supporting,
blue perishes,
black is imprisoned.
In the three months of autumn,
white is dominant,
black is supporting,
red perishes,
blue and yellow are both imprisoned.
In the three months of winter,
black is dominant,
blue is supporting,
white perishes,
yellow and red are imprisoned.
If the season matches,
colors that are dominant or supporting
bring good fortune;
if the season does not match,
colors that are dominant or supporting, or if imprisoned or perishing,
bring misfortune."
When Wèi Guǎn Lù visited his cousin's home,
he saw two guests.
After they left,
Lù said to his cousin:
"These two men,
between their foreheads, mouths, and ears,
share an ominous aura;
unusual changes will arise together,
their dual souls have no abode,
their wandering spirits will drift to the sea,
and their bones will return home."
Later, they indeed drowned.
This briefly illustrates the effect of color changes.
Success or failure lies in decisive judgment.
Using this as reference,
there will be not one error in ten thousand.
The Classic states:
"To speak of nobility or baseness,
it resides in the bone structure;
to speak of longevity or brevity,
it resides in the void and solidity."
The Classic states:
"A person's breathing
is where life resides.
Breathing smoothly and evenly,
long and gentle in pattern,
indicates a long-lived person;
breathing hurried and rapid,
uneven in inhalation and exhalation,
indicates a short-lived person."
It also says:
"Bones and flesh hard and firm,
long-lived but not joyful;
body flesh soft,
joyful but not long-lived."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
When Lǔ sent Xiāng Zhòng to Qí,
he reported back:
"I heard the people of Qí are about to consume Lǔ's wheat.
From what I observed,
they will not succeed.
The ruler of Qí's speech is frivolous.
Zāng Wénzhòng once said:
'If a ruler is frivolous,
he is bound to die.'" Later, it indeed happened.
When the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn to acknowledge the peace,
he received the jade east of the eastern pillar.
The Jìn minister Zhēn Bó said:
"Will the Earl of Zhèng die?
He has abandoned himself!
His gaze wanders and his steps are hasty,
unsettled in his position,
he likely will not last long."
Dù Yù commented:
"This means the Earl of Zhèng lacked solemn dignity."
In June, he died.
The Heavenly King sent Duke Kāng of Liú and Duke Sù of Chéng to meet with the Marquis of Jìn to attack Qín.
Chéng Zǐ received the sacrificial meat at the altar,
but was disrespectful.
Duke of Liú said:
"I have heard that
humans are born receiving the balance of heaven and earth,
which is called destiny;
thus there are rules for actions, rituals, righteousness, dignity, and decorum
to stabilize that destiny.
The capable nurture it to attain blessings,
the incapable ruin it and bring upon disaster.
Therefore,
the nobleman is diligent in rituals,
the commoner exhausts his strength.
Diligence in rituals is best shown by reverence,
exhausting strength is best shown by sincerity and diligence.
Reverence lies in nurturing the spirit,
diligence in preserving one's duties.
The great affairs of state
are sacrifice and war.
In sacrifice, there is the holding of offerings,
in war, there is the receiving of sacrificial meat—
these are major ceremonies for the spirits.
Now Chéng Zǐ has lapsed,
abandoning his destiny.
Will he not perish?"
In May,
he died at Xiá.
The Marquis of Jìn favored Chéng Zhèng,
making him assistant commander of the lower army.
When the Zhèng envoy Gōngsūn Yǔ went to Jìn on a diplomatic mission,
Chéng Zhèng asked him,
saying:
"May I ask how one can lower one's rank?"
Zǐyǔ could not answer.
Returning, he told Rán Míng,
who said:
"He is about to die!
If not, he will flee.
Being noble yet knowing fear,
fearing and thus thinking of lowering rank,
he would find his place,
merely humbling himself—
why even ask?
Moreover, one who seeks to lower rank after having risen
is a wise man,
which Chéng Zhèng is not.
Is there a sign of his flight?
If not,
does he have a delusional illness,
worrying as he faces death?"
The next year,
Chéng Zhèng died.
The Heavenly King sent Duke of Shàn to meet with Hán Xuānzǐ at Qī,
where he looked down and spoke slowly.
Shū Xiàng said:
"Will Duke of Shàn die soon?
At court, there are fixed positions,
meetings have markers,
robes have collars and sashes have knots.
Words spoken in meetings or court
must be heard from the marked positions,
to clarify the order of affairs.
The gaze should not go beyond the knot and collar,
to guide one's demeanor.
Speech is used to command,
demeanor to express it clearly—
to fail in this is a defect.
Now Duke of Shàn, as the king's chief officer commanding affairs at the meeting,
looks not above the sash,
speaks not beyond a step,
his demeanor lacks guidance,
and his words are not clear.
Without guidance, there is no respect;
without clarity, there is no followership—
he has lost his vital energy."
That winter,
Duke of Shàn died.
When Duke Píng of Sòng hosted Zhāo Zǐ,
they feasted joyfully,
but their conversation ended in tears.
Lè Qí assisted
and afterward told others:
"This year, the lord and Shūsūn will likely die?
I have heard:
To mourn at joy and rejoice at sorrow
both mean losing one's mind.
The essence of the mind
is called the húnpò.
If the hún is about to depart,
how can one last long?"
That year,
both Shūsūn and the Duke of Sòng died.
The Duke Yǐn of Zhū came for an audience,
holding the jade high,
his countenance lifted upward;
the Duke of Lǔ received the jade low,
his countenance bowed down.
Zǐgòng said:
"Judging by the rites,
both rulers have an air of death about them.
Holding high and looking up,
is arrogance;
bowing low and looking down,
is decline.
Arrogance approaches chaos,
decline approaches illness.
Our lord is the host,
will he be the first to perish?"
That year,
the duke passed away.
In the seventh year of Duke Āi,
they took Yì, the Viscount of Zhū, back with them,
and the Marquis of Wèi met with the King of Wú at Yún.
The men of Wú fenced in the lodging of the Marquis of Wèi.
Zǐgòng persuaded Grand Steward Pǐ and thus secured his release.
When the Marquis of Wèi returned,
he imitated the barbarian speech.
Zǐzhī, still young, said:
"Our lord will surely not escape misfortune.
Will he die among the barbarians?
Having been detained and then pleased with their speech,
his submission to them is certain."
Later, he eventually died in Chǔ.
The Duke of Lǔ built a Chǔ-style palace,
and Mù Shū said:
"The 'Great Oath' says:
'What men desire,
heaven is sure to grant.'
Our lord desires Chǔ,
hence he builds its palace.
If he does not go to Chǔ again,
he will surely die in this palace."
On the xīnsì day of the sixth month,
the duke died in the Chǔ palace.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Chōu to escort Sūn Línfǔ to Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi hosted a feast for him,
and Kǔchéng Shū (Xì Chōu) was arrogant.
The Wèi great officer Nìngzǐ said:
"Will the house of Kǔchéng perish?
In ancient feasts,
one observed dignity and demeanor to discern fortune and misfortune.
Thus the 'Book of Songs' says:
'The rhinoceros cups are curved,
the good wine is soft.
Neither frivolous nor arrogant,
all blessings come seeking.'
Now this gentleman is arrogant,
which is the way to invite disaster."
In the seventeenth year,
the Xì clan perished.
The Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi met at Shāngrén,
and were disrespectful.
Shūxiàng said:
"These two rulers will surely not escape misfortune.
Meetings and audiences
are the constant rules of ritual.
Ritual
is the vehicle of governance.
Governance
is the guardian of one's person.
Neglecting ritual and losing governance,
one cannot stand firm,
hence chaos arises."
In the twenty-fifth year,
Qí assassinated Guāng.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Wèi assassinated Piāo.
Those who speak of innate spirit focus on demeanor and bearing.
This is the general principle.
In reading faces, first look at the countenance.
The face has five peaks and four rivers;
the five peaks are:
the forehead as Héng Shān,
the chin as Héng Shān,
the nose as Sōng Shān,
the left cheekbone as Tài Shān,
the right cheekbone as Huà Shān.
The four rivers are:
the nostrils as the Jǐ River,
the mouth as the Hé River,
the eyes as the Huái River,
the ears as the Jiāng River.
The five peaks should be lofty, steep, round, and full;
the four rivers should be deep and broad,
with well-formed banks.
If the five peaks are well-formed,
one is a wealthy person;
if not full, then poor;
if the four rivers are well-formed,
one is a noble person;
if not well-formed, then lowly.
The five offices and six treasuries;
the five offices are:
first the mouth,
second the nose,
third the ears,
fourth the eyes,
fifth the philtrum.
The six treasuries are:
the two lines above as the second treasury,
the two auxiliary angles as the fourth treasury,
above the two cheekbones as the sixth treasury.
If one office is good,
it brings ten years of nobility;
if one treasury is good,
it brings ten years of wealth.
If all five offices and six treasuries are good,
wealth and nobility are endless.
The left side represents civil,
the right side represents military.
The nine provinces and eight extremities;
the nine provinces are:
the forehead from left to right,
without vertical lines,
not broken or cut off,
shaped like an inverted liver is good.
The eight extremities are:
looking from the bridge of the nose,
the eight directions taking shape,
not leaning to one side is excellent.
The seven gates and two aspects;
the seven gates are:
two villain gates,
two watchtower gates,
two life gates,
one central court.
The two aspects are:
the head round, modeling heaven,
the feet square, symbolizing earth.
Heaven should be high,
earth should be thick.
If the head is small and feet thin,
one is a poor and lowly person;
if all seven gates are good,
one is a wealthy and noble person.
To summarize,
the forehead represents heaven,
the chin represents earth,
the nose represents man,
the left eye represents the sun,
the right eye represents the moon.
Heaven should be expansive,
earth should be square,
man should be deep and broad,
the sun and moon should be bright.
Good heaven brings nobility,
good earth brings wealth,
good man brings longevity,
good sun and moon bring prosperity.
The upper section is heaven,
governing the status of parents;
the middle section is man,
governing brothers, wife, children, benevolence, righteousness, age, and longevity;
the lower section is earth,
governing fields, residences, slaves, livestock, and food and drink.
If the cheekbones are just prominent,
and the skin color is moist and glossy,
one is a marquis of the ninth rank.
It is also said:
waist and abdomen proportionate,
buttocks and thighs just thick, and walking with a high gaze and broad steps,
these all indicate a marquis of the ninth rank.
The complexion must be heavy and substantial,
the waist must be broad and long.
Therefore, the 'Classic' says:
face like a yellow melon,
brings wealth, honor, and glory.
White like cut lard,
black like lacquer,
purple like mulberry,
waist broad and long,
belly like a hanging pouch,
walking like a goose or turtle,
these are all signs of wealthy and noble people.
Generally, when referring to dukes, marquises, generals, and ministers below,
their specific ranks are not discussed.
If the auxiliary bones are slightly visible,
and the nose bridge is slightly straight,
one is a marquis of the eighth rank.
It is also said:
chest and back slightly full,
hands and feet pleasant and glossy,
and body upright with even steps,
these all indicate a marquis of the eighth rank.
The nose must be large, straight, and long,
the chest and back must be full and thick like a turtle's shape,
the color of hands and feet must be reddish-white,
these are all signs of wealthy and noble people.
Therefore, the 'Classic' says:
hands and feet like silk,
bring lifelong wealth and nobility.
Hands and feet thick and well-formed,
The envoy stands by the side.
Auxiliary angles forming edges,
and both storage areas being level
are signs of a seventh-rank official.
It is also said:
A thick chest and thick neck,
arms and shins well-proportioned,
along with a steady gaze and speech,
these are all indications of a seventh-rank official.
The neck must be thick and short,
the arms and hands slender and long,
and the speech should resemble the sound of bamboo flutes or phoenixes,
all of which are noble signs.
Thus the Classic says:
High and prominent forehead corners
bring superior and heavy positions.
A round, thick tiger-like neck
yields abundant wealth and honor.
An ox-like gaze and tiger-like stare
bring unparalleled wealth and honor.
Full heavenly storage
grants heavenly emoluments;
full earthly storage
enriches with wine and meat.
A full and prominent Tiānzhōng,
and an upright Yìntáng,
are signs of a sixth-rank official.
It is also said:
A full head and square body,
thick hands and round waist,
along with a clear and bright voice,
these are all indications of a sixth-rank official.
On a person's forehead, connecting to the heavens,
from the middle down to Sīkōng,
if there is flesh or bone like a ring,
it is called the Heavenly Wall.
If it is complete without gaps, it signifies great nobility;
if it has a gap like a door, it indicates one of the Three Dukes.
The voice must be deep and solid,
loud but not muddled,
small yet clear,
far-reaching but not scattered,
close yet not lost,
with lingering tones that are sharp and pure,
as if from a bamboo flute,
winding with flowing melody,
capable of being round and long,
this is a good voice.
The gōng sound is heavy, broad, and deep;
the shāng sound firm, strong, and extensive;
the jué sound round, long, and penetrating;
the zhǐ sound rising and falling smoothly;
the yǔ sound gentle, low, and trailing—
these are called the correct sounds.
A prominent and steep Fúxī,
with full and lush auxiliary angles,
are signs of a fifth-rank official.
It is also said:
A short neck and raised back,
broad breasts and drooping belly,
and a goose-like walk with tiger-like steps
are all indications of a fifth-rank official.
If a person's cranial sutures have raised bones,
long and large front and back,
they will be a general of two thousand shí,
a military commander.
Emerging from the hairline,
is the Fúxī,
which must be towering, steep, and sharp—
the sign of a duke or marquis.
It should not be wide and flat;
having depressions
brings adversity;
having peaks
is very good.
If it is wide and flat,
it still brings official emoluments.
The belly must be端正 and beautiful.
Thus it is said:
A massive horse's belly
signifies abundant silks and grains.
High and deep Biāndì,
and broad and thick Fútáng,
are signs of a fourth-rank official.
It is also said:
A high and full head,
long upper and short lower body,
and a half-turn dragon walk
are all indications of a fourth-rank official.
Biāndì
is near the hairline at the forehead corners;
Fútáng
is near the upper part of the eyebrow tails.
The head must be high and large.
Thus the Classic says:
An ox head, square and four-sided,
brings wealth, honor, and prosperity.
A tiger head, high and towering,
brings unparalleled wealth and honor.
An elephant head, high and broad,
brings long and thick fortune and emoluments.
A rhinoceros head, steep and lofty,
brings lush wealth and honor.
A camel head, vast and grand,
is where fortune and emoluments gather.
A tiger walk makes a general;
a wild goose walk brings great wealth.
Rhinoceros-like and at Sīkōng,
with dragon horns slender and straight,
are signs of a third-rank official.
It is also said:
Extremely thick chest and back,
a deep and pointed head,
and a heroic will with a soft body
are all indications of a third-rank official.
Sīkōng runs straight down from the hairline,
next to Tiāntíng.
Dragon horns are above the eyebrows.
A high and deep crown of the head,
with accomplished dragon and rhinoceros features,
are signs of a second-rank official.
It is also said:
Strange rises in the head and angles,
limbs and joints well-proportioned,
and a fierce appearance with a calm nature
are all indications of a second-rank official.
A countenance that is generous and bold,
movements that are poised and graceful,
a spirit that is sharp and clear,
a demeanor that is calm and stable,
speech that is careful and precise,
neither hasty nor slow,
actions and rest that are constant,
neither light nor agitated,
joy and anger not rashly expressed,
advances and retreats fitting the situation,
emotions unchanged by sounds and sights,
integrity unaltered by glory or decay—
this is called having abundant spirit,
and presages a noble position.
All four storage areas full,
bones and angles all clear,
are signs of a first-rank official.
A good head and neck,
limbs and joints all well-formed,
along with beautiful appearance and quality,
and a clear and steady gaze,
these are all indications of a first-rank official.
Those resembling a dragon are civil officials;
resembling a dragon is very noble.
A dragon walker becomes one of the Three Dukes.
Those resembling a tiger are generals;
a tiger walker becomes a general.
High Yìmǎ bones
make a general.
Those resembling an ox are prime ministers;
those resembling a horse are military officials;
resembling a horse is also very noble.
Those resembling a dog hold clear offices and become regional governors;
those resembling pigs or monkeys
attain great wealth and honor.
Those resembling rats
only have wealth.
In general, to be called a resemblance,
means both movement and stillness resemble it.
If only partially resembling in one aspect,
it indicates poverty and lowliness.
Tiānzhōng governs nobility;
if the energy is level and full, it suits official emoluments.
Tiānzhōng is the highest,
near the hairline;
if yellow energy appears,
ascending to the proper angles,
reaching high and broad,
it leads to promotion as a regional inspector or governor.
Yellow like the sun and moon,
to the left and right of Tiānzhōng,
signifies serving the Son of Heaven.
Yellow emerging from Tiānzhōng,
round, large, and brightly heavy,
indicates a sudden audience with the Son of Heaven.
Extending over years and to Jǐngzào,
it brings merit and enfeeffment.
Constant yellow energy,
like a hanging bell or drum,
is the sign of one of the Three Dukes.
Also, yellow energy in the shape of a dragon
also brings enfeeffment.
Seasonal official energy emerging from the heavenly region,
like mirror light,
is a sign of sudden nobility.
Tiāntíng governs the highest duke,
the energy of the grand chancellor.
Tiāntíng goes straight down,
next to Tiānzhōng;
if there is a mole,
The master dies. .
The Minister of Works governs the celestial palace,
also the aura of the Three Excellencies.
Directly below the Minister of Works,
next to the center of heaven,
if the color is bad,
it indicates submitting memorials,
great misfortune. .
The central rectifier governs the aura of all officials,
the office that evaluates people and things.
Directly below the central rectifier,
next to the Minister of Works,
if the color is good,
it means promotion or change of position.
If the Minister of Works and central rectifier show a distinct reddish hue,
at the central rectifier, it signifies a county official;
at the celestial court, it indicates commandery, prefectural, or county officials, as well as those in the Orchid Terrace or the Imperial Secretariat,
each according to their jurisdiction. .
The seal hall governs all official seals and ribbons,
the office in charge of tally seals.
The seal hall is between the two eyebrows,
slightly below the inner ends of the eyebrows,
next to the central rectifier.
If a reddish color appears,
like connected knives,
extending up to the celestial court,
down to the tip of the nose,
it signifies a county magistrate;
if it reaches the palace gate court,
and the color appears,
it indicates a senior official.
If it resembles a wheel and corresponds with the auxiliary angles,
it signifies great nobility.
The seal hall is also called the palace gate court. .
If the root of the mountain is level and fine,
and there are extraordinary bones hidden or rising,
it indicates marriage into the imperial family,
being a princess's consort.
Directly below the root of the mountain,
next to the seal hall,
it also governs having or lacking influence. .
The high and broad area governs the seat of a regional lord.
Running horizontally from the center of heaven to the hairline,
there are seven names in total,
with the high and broad area in the third position.
If the high and broad area suddenly shows a yellow color,
like two people holding a drum,
it is the sign of a general. .
The yang foot governs the office of a provincial assistant.
Horizontally next to the high and broad area,
it is in the fourth position.
The yang foot also governs early departure;
if the regional lord has aura,
it worries about long journeys. .
The armory governs officials in charge of weapons and storehouses.
Horizontally next to the yang foot,
it is in the fifth position. .
The auxiliary angles govern the office of a distant provincial inspector.
Horizontally next to the armory,
it is in the sixth position.
If the bones are prominent and the color is good,
it indicates officials like eunuchs or attendants. .
The border land governs appointments in frontier provinces.
Horizontally next to the auxiliary angles,
it is in the seventh position.
If there is a black mole,
it signifies falling into hardship and becoming a slave. .
The sun angle governs the seat of dukes and marquises.
Running horizontally from the celestial court to the hairline,
there are eight names in total,
with the sun angle in the first position.
If it is level, full, and straight,
it suits official positions. .
The chamber and heart govern appointments in the capital.
Horizontally next to the sun angle,
it is in the second position.
The left side of the chamber and heart is for civil,
the right for military.
If the bones are prominent, it is suitable to be a teacher.
If a yellow color appears in the chamber and heart,
extending up to the celestial court,
it signifies a chief clerk or magistrate.
If it appears directly in the chamber and heart and is glossy,
one will be summoned as a royal tutor. .
The post horse governs officials in charge of urgent matters.
Horizontally next,
it is in the seventh position.
If the post horse has a good color corresponding to the seal hall above,
one will obtain office in autumn or winter. .
The forehead angle governs the positions of ministers and court officials.
Running horizontally from the Minister of Works to the hairline,
there are eight names in total,
with the forehead angle horizontally next,
in the first position.
If the color is red or yellow,
it signifies great luck and prosperity. .
The high minister governs the position of an imperial minister.
Horizontally next to the forehead angle,
if the high minister is vibrant,
one will be enfeoffed as a minister with great joy. .
The tiger eyebrow governs the great general.
Running horizontally from the central rectifier to the hairline,
there are nine names in total,
with the tiger eyebrow horizontally next,
in the second position.
If it shows a bluish-white color,
it indicates travel. .
The ox horn governs the king's commander or junior general.
Horizontally next to the tiger eyebrow,
it is in the third position,
also governing enfeoffment as a noble and receiving emoluments.
If it forms a horn,
it is even better than flesh. .
The primordial horn governs the appearance of a general.
Horizontally next,
it is in the fifth position.
If there is no horn,
one cannot seek office.
To know how long one will hold an office,
first look at the length of the aura on the year point;
an aura length of one part indicates one year,
two parts two years,
and by such calculations,
it can be known.
If there is an evil color interspersed,
it indicates something happening that year.
White color means encountering mourning,
red color means impeachment or dismissal,
black color means illness,
blue color means prison or calamity.
If there is a horizontal aura in the center of heaven,
it means no office.
However, if the official color has been long present,
and suddenly a fatal calamity color appears interspersed,
it means dying in place of another.
If the year point has a good color,
like clouds and rain emerging from connected mountains,
reaching everywhere,
then there is no place not reached.
If there is a yellow aura at the hairline,
it means already having obtained office;
if a black aura,
not yet.
If there is a yellow aura like a sash,
appearing on the forehead,
it means promotion and increased emoluments. .
There are six types of lowliness in a person:
small head and large body,
is the first lowliness.
Also said:
sunken and defective forehead angles,
the center of heaven drooping downward,
is also the first lowliness.
The Classic says:
a cramped and narrow forehead,
leads to poverty and hardship until old age.
A thin, curved snake-like neck,
means not even enough for husks.
A flat, thin snake-like head,
means scarce wealth and goods.
A sharp, pointed badger-like head,
means no plan for poverty and hardship. .
Eyes without luster,
is the second lowliness.
Also said:
thin chest and back,
is also the second lowliness.
The Classic says:
sunken chest, thin buttocks, and monkey-like eyes,
are all signs of poverty. .
Awkward movements,
is the third lowliness.
Also said:
a faint, scattered feminine voice,
is also the third lowliness.
The Classic says:
chattering speech,
dry and withered facial skin,
bristling facial hair,
dust without wind,
These are all signs of poverty and lowliness.
As for the qualities of an unpleasant voice,
it is dusty, turbid, scattered, and flying,
thin, hoarse, intermittent, and chaotic,
rising as if exhausted,
going without return,
shallow, disordered, harsh, and fine,
deep, turbid, weak, and impaired,
with a short tongue and stiff spirit,
stammering without resonance—
these are unfavorable signs.
When a person does not laugh but seems to laugh,
does not scowl but seems to scowl,
does not rejoice but seems to rejoice,
does not fear but seems to fear,
is not drunk but seems drunk,
always as if hungover from a night's drinking,
not sorrowful but seeming so,
constantly as if grieving and distressed,
with a deficient and lacking countenance,
as if afflicted by epilepsy,
a mournful and distressed spirit and complexion,
always as if having suffered a loss,
restless and flustered in demeanor,
ever as if rushing urgently,
speech that is halting and hesitant,
as if concealing something,
a body and appearance low and downtrodden,
as if having endured humiliation—
these all indicate insufficiency of spirit.
Those with insufficient spirit
often face imprisonment and calamity.
Some lose their official positions through concealment,
others are demoted and dismissed from their posts..
A nose that is undeveloped,
with the bridge bending forward and low,
constitutes the fourth sign of lowliness.
It is also said:
Squinting and looking askance with one eye,
also counts as the fourth sign of lowliness.
The "Classic" says:
A flat and full philtrum,
ears without defined rims,
are all signs of poverty and lowliness..
Long feet and a short waist,
constitute the fifth sign of lowliness.
It is also said:
Lips tilted and nose crooked,
also count as the fifth sign of lowliness.
The "Classic" says:
Walking like a snake, scurrying like a sparrow,
indicates no stored wealth or goods.
A thin nose bridge,
signifies making promises while standing.
A drooping nose tip,
means cooking alone until old age.
Swaying the waist and walking hastily,
ensures one will have nothing to employ.
Those with a short waist will have their positions taken by others..
Lack of literary strategy,
lips thin and horizontally long,
constitute the sixth sign of lowliness.
It is also said:
Talkative but seldom truthful,
also counts as the sixth sign of lowliness.
The "Classic" says:
A mouth like a rush mat,
means no one will support you;
crooked and slanted,
you will be slandered by others.
A mouth like a burning fire,
means sitting alone until old age.
A tongue pale in color,
belongs to a lowly person;
a short tongue,
indicates a poor and humble person.
To recognize a lowly person,
noble traits are few, base traits many,
many meaning broad,
few meaning narrow.
If all six signs of lowliness are present,
one is destined to be a servant or slave..
This is how nobility and baseness reside in the bones.
It is discussed:
Yáo had eyebrows of eight colors,
Shùn pupils doubled in his eyes,
Yǔ ears with three perforations,
King Wén four nipples,
yet ordinary people sometimes also have four nipples,
which is like a mediocre horse having one hair resembling a steed's.
As for the marvel of a sun-angle and moon-arch, the beauty of a dragon's perch and tiger's crouch,
the earth's stillness anchored in city walls,
the sky's movement turning in the palm and strategy,
golden hammers and jade pillows,
ruggedly facing each other,
a hidden rhinoceros horn rising like a canopy,
interwoven and shimmering.
With both well and dwelling combined,
granaries and coffers already full,
these are clear signs of ministers and chancellors.
If one has deep-set eyes and a long neck,
a crumbling face and pinched nose,
snake-like walk and vulture-like stance,
with a boar's snout and bird's beak,
sinews not binding the body,
face without radiant color,
hands without the softness of spring buds,
hair with the withering of cold thistles,
these are proofs of destitution and hardship.
Formerly, Gūbù Zǐqīng said to Zǐgòng:
"East of Zhèng's gate, there is a man,
tall at nine chi six cun,
with river-eyes and a prominent forehead,
his head resembling Yáo's,
his neck like Gāo Yáo's,
his shoulders akin to Zǐchǎn's,
yet from the waist down, three cun short of Yǔ,
weary as a homeless dog."
River-eyes mean upper and lower rims long.
Forehead,
is the brow.
Hàn高祖 had a prominent nose bridge and dragon-like countenance.
Nose bridge,
is the nose.
Countenance,
refers to the forehead.
Two angles are dragon horns,
one angle is a rhinoceros horn.
It is said that高祖 resembled a dragon in his two eyebrows,
with high forehead bones and a raised nose bridge.
Wèi's Chénliú King had a full lower part and sharp upper,
bearing the appearance of Yáo's chart.
Chén Xuāndì had a sturdy neck,
yet his appearance seemed unwise.
Initially lowly,
Yáng Zhōng saw him and marveled, saying:
"This man has a tiger's neck,
surely he will achieve great nobility."
Later, it all came true.
This is the effect of nobility and baseness.
Wood governs spring,
the phase of growth
Spring governs the liver,
the liver governs the eyes,
the eyes govern benevolence.
Growth and flourishing
imply the intention to forgive and bestow kindness;
Fire governs summer,
the time of abundance
Summer governs the heart,
the heart governs the tongue,
the tongue governs propriety.
Abundance and prosperity
signify the meaning of richness and broad understanding;
Metal governs autumn,
the season of harvesting
Autumn governs the lungs,
the lungs govern the nose,
the nose governs righteousness.
Gathering and storing
reflect the sentiment of stinginess and miserliness;
Water governs winter,
the time when all things hide
Winter governs the kidneys,
the kidneys govern the ears,
the ears govern wisdom.
Hiding and concealing
harbor the feelings of deceit and flattery;
Earth governs late summer,
the month when all things bear fruit
Late summer governs the spleen,
the spleen governs the lips,
the lips govern trustworthiness.
Firm and solid fruiting
embodies the virtue of faithfulness and caution.
Hence it is said:
Those with beautiful eyebrows and eyes, fine fingers and nails
are likely to be generous people.
The liver manifests in the eyes,
also governs the sinews,
ends at the nails,
flourishes in the eyebrows,
and stores the soul.
The "Classic" says:
Those with straight eyebrows and raised head
have a strong and heroic spirit.
If damaged or thin,
they are untrustworthy people.
Arched like a bow,
they are good people.
Eyes with bright light and charming beauty
belong to those who understand principles and are wise.
If the eye's light overflows beyond the lids,
neither scattered nor still,
neither hasty nor slow,
and the essence is not exposed—
A person with wisdom and intelligence.
Eyelids that are sunken and contracted,
with no luster in the essence,
indicate a foolish and dull person.
Eyes that do not extend beyond the eyelids
signify a person who conceals their emotions,
and if combined with dry, furtive glances,
they are certain to engage in theft.
If the eyes are constantly darting and shifting,
it indicates an envious and jealous person.
A person with a hasty gaze
is either jealous or deceitful and delusional.
Eyes that glare fiercely with a bloodshot appearance
indicate a person with a malicious nature.
Eyes that are unfocused and wandering
signify a simple-minded person.
Eyes that are dull and lifeless,
with a turbid gaze,
indicate a licentious and disorderly person.
A person who frequently squints and peers sideways
is cunning and deceitful.
Eyes that are rigid and fixed
indicate a stubborn and unyielding person.
Eyes like those of a goat, with vertical pupils,
signify a poisonous and harmful person.
Eyes that are wide and flickering
indicate a devious and wicked person.
When the essence and color are mixed and the luster is shallow and floating,
it signifies an unsettled mind,
and an untrustworthy person.
When the essence is clear and the luster overflows,
it indicates an intelligent person.
When the essence is deep and the luster is steady,
it signifies a bold person.
When the upper and lower canthi are deep and thick,
and the energy and color are rich and dense,
it indicates a person with authority and great courage.
When the energy and color are faint and elusive,
it signifies a shallow person.
When the facial complexion is impure,
it indicates a person without authority, timid and cowardly.
When the essence is purplish-black and the luster is stable and firm,
it signifies a resolute and fierce person.
When the essence is pure white and steady,
it indicates a person who prefers seclusion and retreat.
When the essence is abundant with luster but not scattered,
clear and pure, with a steady and discerning gaze,
it signifies a straightforward person.
When the essence is yellow and the luster is clear and translucent,
it indicates a person who aspires to the Dao and its arts.
When the pupils are positioned closer to the top,
it signifies a person with lowly aspirations.
When the pupils are positioned closer to the bottom,
it indicates a person with noble aspirations.
When the pupils are positioned closer to the inner corner,
it signifies a self-restrained person.
When the pupils are positioned closer to the outer corner,
it indicates an arrogant and foolish person.
Eyes like those of a goat, staring straight ahead,
signify one capable of killing their wife and children.
Arrogant eyes, clear and piercing.
Misfortune and punishment follow one another,
with a gaze like an eagle and a glance like a wolf.
They often harbor jealousy and envy.
The heart of a mole cricket is hard to obtain,
but fingers should be slender and plump like a goose's,
with skin connecting them,
indicating a person of simple and harmonious nature.
Fingers that are square and stubby
signify a slow-witted person.
A person with beautiful features
will be trusted when giving instructions;
an ugly person
will not be obeyed.
Hair with a glossy sheen,
and lips as red as cinnabar,
indicate a person talented in learning and arts.
The heart manifests as the tongue,
and also governs blood.
Blood ends at the hair,
flourishes in the ears,
and is stored in the spirit.
The Classic says:
Fox-like sideburns
indicate unreliability;
ram-like sideburns
signify much suspicion.
Tight lips and exposed teeth
make it hard to befriend them;
broad and well-shaped lips
indicate eloquent speech;
poorly shaped lips and mouth
signify untrustworthy words.
A mouth without charm
likes to expose others' faults;
a mouth pecking like a bird's
should not be lived with,
as they are malicious.
A mouth tense or slack like a bird's,
with clustered speech,
indicates a gossipy person.
Inconsistent in urgency and slackness,
they are seldom trustworthy.
Small, constricted nostrils,
with a low and curved nose tip,
indicate a stingy person.
The lungs manifest as the nostrils,
govern the skin,
and also control breath,
stored in the po.
A good nose
brings reputation.
A thin nose bridge with a sunken ridge
indicates a person prone to illness and misfortune.
A nose without charm
signifies a foolish and dull person.
A dung beetle-like nose
indicates a person with little wisdom.
Small ear canals,
with fine, segmented teeth,
indicate a deceitful and flattering person.
The kidneys manifest as bones,
and also govern marrow.
Marrow ends at the ear canals,
bones end at the teeth,
stored in the zhi.
The Classic says:
Deep and broad ear canals
indicate an open mind and profound understanding.
Ugly and small ear canals
signify lack of wisdom and disbelief in divine principles.
Ears without charm
indicate a vulgar and clumsy person.
Small ear canals with crooked and twisted bones
signify a person without wisdom.
Mouse-like ears
indicate one who survives killings.
It is also said:
People with mouse-like ears
often engage in theft.
Thick and large earlobes,
a round and solid nose tip,
clean and upright nipples,
and a deep, broad, thick chin and jaw
indicate a loyal, trustworthy, cautious, and honest person.
The spleen manifests as flesh,
flesh ends at the orifices,
and also governs the earlobes,
nose tip, nose bridge, chin, and jaw,
stored in the yi.
The Classic says:
A large and tall head
indicates a self-willed person who likes to dominate others.
A low and inferior head
indicates a submissive and petty person.
Therefore, it is said:
A deer-like head, long and slanted,
signifies strong and heroic will;
a rabbit-like head, with a receding chin,
indicates lowly will;
an otter-like head, broad and wide,
signifies an open-minded and understanding heart.
A thin and curved neck
indicates a person who cannot stand independently.
If the skin color is mottled or unclean,
it indicates an adaptable but unstable nature.
Long and slender hands
indicate generosity;
short and thick hands
indicate acquisitiveness;
giving is nearly virtuous,
taking signifies greed and stinginess.
Therefore, it is said:
Hands like chicken feet
indicate narrow-mindedness and limited wisdom.
Hands like pig hooves
indicate confused will.
Hands like monkey palms
indicate diligence and skill.
A broad and thick back
indicates a resolute person;
a thin back
indicates a timid and weak person.
A well-shaped and beautiful abdomen
indicates a talented person.
Therefore, it is said:
An ox-like belly signifies greed,
hoarding wealth and possessions.
A toad-like belly
indicates laziness.
A well-shaped waist
indicates joy and the ability to employ others.
A lizard-like waist
indicates slowness.
Thick and broad arms and thighs
indicate reliability,
a stable and steady person.
A snake-like walk
indicates a venomous person,
with whom one should not collaborate.
The bird-like gait is unsteady,
indicating a nature of poor conduct,
resembling the walk of magpies.
The eagle-like gait is fierce and imposing.
Those with a jackal-wolf walk
are coarse in nature and seek profit.
The ox-like walk
signifies an upright nature.
The horse-like walk
belongs to a person of intense vigor.
Thus, the essence of one's nature resides in demeanor and bearing.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"The King of Yuè, as a person,
has a long neck and a beak-like mouth,
with whom one can share hardships,
but not peace and joy."
Wèi Liáo said:
"Qín Shǐ Huáng,
with a prominent nose and long eyes,
a vulture's chest and a jackal's voice,
shows little kindness or trustworthiness,
and has the heart of a tiger or wolf.
In humble circumstances, he easily submits to others;
when achieving his ambitions, he lightly preys upon people.
One cannot maintain long-term association with him."
When Shū Yú was born,
his mother looked at him and said:
"He has the eyes of a tiger and the heart of a pig,
shoulders like a hawk and a belly like an ox.
Ravines may be filled,
but his greed cannot be satisfied."
Shū Xiàng of Jìn wished to marry a woman from the Wūchén clan,
but his mother opposed it,
saying:
"In the past, the Yǒuréng clan bore a daughter,
dark-skinned yet exceedingly beautiful,
whose radiance could serve as a mirror,
named Xuán Qī.
Yuèzhèng Hòu Kuí married her,
and she bore Bó Fēng,
who truly had a pig's heart,
insatiably greedy,
with boundless resentment and malice,
and was called the 'Great Boar.'
Yǒuqiōng's Hòu Yì destroyed him,
and thus Kuí received no sacrifices.
Moreover, the downfalls of the three dynasties
were all due to such things.
Why would you pursue this?
For possessing extraordinary beauty
is enough to change a person.
If not matched with virtue and righteousness,
it will inevitably bring disaster."
Shū Xiàng, frightened,
then refrained.
King Ān Xī of Wèi asked Zǐ Cóng:
"Mǎ Huí is resolute and upright,
embodying the integrity of a great officer.
I wish to make him chancellor;
is it permissible?"
The reply was:
"With long eyes and a pig-like gaze,
his body may be square, but his heart is round.
Whenever I judge people by this method,
not one in thousands fails.
I observe that Huí is not without a stalwart physique,
yet I deeply suspect his eyes."
Plain Yuán Jūn assessed the Qín general Bái Qǐ,
telling the King of Zhào:
"As for General Wǔ'ān's character,
he has a small head and a sharp chin,
pupils distinctly black and white,
and a gaze that does not shift.
A small head and sharp chin
indicate decisiveness in action;
distinct black and white pupils
show clarity in understanding affairs;
an unshifting gaze
signifies strong determination.
One can engage him in prolonged strategies,
but it is difficult to confront him directly."
Wáng Mǎng had a large mouth and a protruding chin,
bulging eyes with red pupils,
a loud voice, and stood seven feet five inches tall,
with a thrust-out chest and an upward gaze,
looking down upon those around him.
Some said Mǎng had what is called owl eyes and a tiger's mouth,
the voice of a jackal or wolf,
hence he would prey upon people,
and would also be killed by others.
Mǎng later usurped the Hàn throne,
and after his troops were defeated and he returned,
he was indeed killed.
For fate and physiognomy
are like sound and its echo.
The sound arises from the trigger,
the echo fully responds,
an inevitable principle.
Although it is said:
"To judge conduct by words,
one errs with Zǎi Yú;
to gauge nature by appearance,
one errs with Zǐ Yǔ."
Yet the *Zhuàn* states:
"He who grieves without cause,
will surely meet sorrow;
he who rejoices without celebration,
will have joy returned to him."
This mind moves first, and the spirit foreknows,
thus the countenance shows early signs.
Hence, Biǎn Què saw Duke Huán,
and knew he would perish;
Shēn Shū saw Wūchén,
and knew he had stolen a wife.
Some leap on horseback to dine on delicacies,
or soar to feast on meat;
some are slaves in the morning and nobles by evening,
some are punished early but become kings later.
Copper and cliffs cannot sustain life,
jade delicacies end in starvation.
Thus, those who measure the surface and feel the bones,
point to colors and discern patterns,
cannot be dismissed.
Hence, these are listed here.
On Assessing Individuals: Part Seven
I have heard Huáng Shígōng say:
"In the peaceful times of old,
feudal lords had two armies,
regional chiefs had three armies,
and the Son of Heaven had six armies.
When the world falls into chaos, rebellion arises;
when the king's grace is exhausted, alliances form to punish each other.
When virtue is equal and cannot surpass others,
one must win the hearts of heroes."
Thus it is said:
"Gaining men leads to prosperity,
losing scholars leads to collapse."
How can this be demonstrated?
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí went to see the minor official Jì,
making three visits in one day without meeting him,
and his followers tried to stop him.
Duke Huán said:
"Scholars who disdain ranks and emoluments
naturally look down on their rulers;
rulers who disdain hegemony
also look down on their scholars.
Even if the master disdains ranks and emoluments,
how dare I disdain hegemony?"
After five visits, he finally met him.
The Book of Documents says:
"He who can secure a teacher for himself becomes king."
How can this be demonstrated?
When King Xuān of Qí saw Yán Chù, he said:
"Chù, come forward."
Chù also said:
"Your Majesty, come forward."
It is debated:
If Chù comes forward, it is out of admiration for power;
if the king comes forward, it is out of respect for scholars.
Rather than having Chù admire power,
it is better to have the king respect scholars.
King Xuān, with a changed expression, said:
"Is the king noble,
or are scholars noble?"
Chù replied:
"In the past, when Qín attacked Qí,
it issued an order:
'Anyone who dares to gather firewood within five hundred steps of Liǔxià Jì's grave
will be executed without pardon.'
Another order said:
'Anyone who can obtain the head of the King of Qí
will be enfeoffed as a marquis with ten thousand households
and rewarded with a thousand yì of gold.'
From this, it can be said
that the head of a living king
is not even worth as much as the grave of a dead scholar."
King Xuān eventually took him as his teacher.
King Xuān's attendants said:
"Your Majesty rules over a land of a thousand chariots,
and has cast bells weighing a thousand shí.
From east to west, north to south,
none dare not submit.
Yet the so-called lofty scholars
are merely commoners,
walking on foot and living among farmers,
in rustic villages, gatehouses, and alleys.
Are scholars not
extremely lowly?"
Chù said:
"In ancient times, during the era of Great Yǔ,
there were ten thousand feudal states.
Shùn rose from the farmlands to become the Son of Heaven.
By the time of Tāng,
there were three thousand feudal states.
In the present age,
those who face south and call themselves 'the solitary one'
number only twenty-four.
From this, it can be seen
is it not a matter of strategy in gaining or losing?
Gradually, they were destroyed,
and when the time came for their clans to be exterminated,
even wishing to be a gatekeeper or villager
would be impossible.
Does the Yì Zhuàn not say:
'To occupy a high position
without possessing the substance.'
Thus, those who lack substance but delight in fame will be diminished;
those without virtue but expect blessings will be constrained;
those without merit but receive emoluments will be disgraced,
and misfortune will surely grasp them.
Therefore, it is said:
'Boasting of merit leads to no establishment;
empty wishes lead to no attainment.'
These are all about flaunting fame,
flashy but without true virtue.
Thus, Yáo had nine assistants,
Shùn had ten friends,
Yǔ had five aides,
Tāng had three supporters.
From ancient times to the present,
none who could achieve empty fame under heaven
has ever existed.
Therefore, a ruler should not be ashamed to ask frequently,
nor feel ashamed to learn from those below,
and thus accomplish his way.
Lǎozi said:
'Though noble,
one must take humility as the root;
though high,
one must take the low as the foundation.'
Thus, marquises and kings call themselves 'the solitary,' 'the few,' and 'the unworthy.'
These terms—'the solitary' and 'the few'—
refer to those in humble and lowly positions,
yet marquises and kings use them for themselves.
Is this not to humble themselves and honor scholars?
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
King Chéng of Zhōu entrusted the regency to Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
and they are praised as wise through the ages.
This demonstrates the value of scholars."
A proverb says:
"For bathing, one need not go to the river or sea;
the key is to remove the grime.
For a horse, it need not be a Qíjì;
the key is to run well.
For scholars, they need not be sages;
the key is to understand the Way.
For women, they need not be of noble birth;
the key is to be chaste and fair."
How can this be demonstrated?
Chúnyú Kūn said to King Xuān of Qí:
"In ancient times, people loved fine horses,
and you, King, also love fine horses;
in ancient times, people loved fine flavors,
and you, King, also love fine flavors;
in ancient times, people loved beauty,
and you, King, also love beauty;
in ancient times, people loved scholars,
but you, King, alone do not!"
The King said:
"It is not that there are no scholars in the state.
If there were, I too would delight in them."
Kūn said:
"In ancient times, there were Huáliú and Qíjì horses;
today there are none,
yet you select from the masses,
and you love horses.
In ancient times, there were leopard and elephant fetus delicacies;
today there are none,
yet you select from the masses,
and you love flavors.
In ancient times, there were Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī;
today there are none,
yet you select from the masses,
and you love beauty.
If you must wait for scholars like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng
to then love them,
then scholars like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng
would not love you either."
Lǔ Zhònglián said to Lord Mèngcháng:
"You do not truly love scholars."
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"It is because I have not obtained scholars."
He replied:
"In your stables, you have a hundred chariots' worth of horses,
all clad in embroidered clothes and fed beans and grain—
are there any Qíjì or Lù'ěr among them?
In your rear palace, you have ten consorts,
all dressed in fine silk and hemp,
and fed fine grain and meat—
are there any Máo Qiáng or Xī Shī among them?
You seek beauty and horses from the present world;
why must scholars come only from ancient times?
Therefore, it is said:
'You do not truly love scholars.'" Zhāng Chǎng, in his Letter to Zhū Yì, said:
"The hungry find chaff and bran sweet;
the full are sated with fine grain and meat.
Why?
Because their circumstances of having or not having differ.
In the past, though Chén Píng was worthy,
he needed Wèi Qiàn to advance;
though Hán Xìn was extraordinary,
he relied on Xiāo Hé to be trusted.
Thus, scholars each achieve what is timely for them.
If you must wait for ancient heroes,
insisting on recommending only those like Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng,
then such men would not advance through you."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"If one must wait for Yǎoniǎo or Fēitù to ride,
then no one in the world would ever ride a carriage;
if one must wait for Xī Shī or Luòfǔ to take as consorts,
then one would never marry in a lifetime.
Thus, not waiting for ancient heroes but finding sufficiency in the present
means using what one has to the fullest."
The Analects say:
"A jade boat and gem oars
are useless for crossing a river;
a gold bow and jade string
cannot shoot an arrow.
Thus, those who are pure but lack administrative skill
are not tools for restoring order;
those who are refined but lack governance
are not aides for supporting brilliance."
How can this be demonstrated?
Wèi Wúzhī introduced Chén Píng to the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn employed him.
Jiàng, Guàn, and others slandered Chén Píng, saying:
"Píng committed adultery with his sister-in-law and accepted bribes."
The King of Hàn reproached Wèi Wúzhī.
Wúzhī said:
"What I recommended was
his ability;
what Your Majesty has heard about is
his conduct.
Even if one had the integrity of Wěishēng or the filial piety of Xiàojǐ,
but it contributed nothing to the outcome of victory or defeat,
would Your Majesty employ him?
Now that Chǔ and Hàn are locked in conflict,
I recommended a strategist of extraordinary schemes,
considering that his plans
are truly sufficient to benefit the state!
As for adultery with his sister-in-law and accepting bribes,
why should that be cause for doubt?"
The King of Hàn said:
"Well said."
Huáng Shígōng said:
"For men of pure character,
they cannot be won by titles and emoluments;
for men who uphold integrity,
they cannot be coerced by threats and punishments.
To attract men of pure character,
cultivate propriety toward them;
to attract men who uphold integrity,
cultivate the Way for them."
How can this be illustrated?
Guō Wěi advised King Zhāo of Yān, saying:
"A sovereign who would be an emperor treats others as his teachers;
one who would be a king treats them as his friends;
one who would be a hegemon treats them as his ministers;
one who would bring his state to ruin treats them as his servants.
If one bends his will and serves them,
facing north to receive instruction,
then those a hundred times better than oneself will come;
if one is first to hasten and last to rest,
first to inquire and last to fall silent,
then those ten times better than oneself will come;
if others hasten and one hastens too,
then those equal to oneself will come;
if one leans on his desk and grasps his staff,
glancing about and pointing orders,
then menial servants will come;
if one acts recklessly and strikes out violently,
shouting and cursing rudely,
then only convicts and slaves will come."
This is how the ancients served the Way and attracted men of worth.
Huáng Shígōng said:
"Propriety is
what makes scholars commit themselves;
rewards are
what makes scholars devote their lives.
Offer what makes them commit themselves,
show what makes them devote their lives,
and those you seek will come."
How can this be illustrated?
When Crown Prince Jī of Wèi Wénhóu showed courtesy to Tián Zǐfāng,
but Zǐfāng did not return the courtesy,
the Crown Prince was displeased,
and said to Zǐfāng:
"I wonder, is it the poor and humble who are arrogant,
or the rich and noble who are arrogant?"
Zǐfāng said:
"It is the poor and humble who are arrogant.
How dare the rich and noble be arrogant?
If a ruler is arrogant, he will lose his state;
if a high official is arrogant, he will lose his family.
If the poor and humble fail to achieve their aims,
they can just pack their shoes and leave—
where can they go and not find poverty and humility?"
When Sòng Yān was chancellor of Qí,
he was dismissed and returned home,
and said to his various officials:
"Is there anyone who will go with me to serve another lord?"
They all stood in ranks holding their staffs,
silent and unresponsive.
Yān said:
"How sad!
Why are officials so easy to obtain but so hard to employ?"
Chén Ráo said:
"That officials are easy to obtain but hard to employ—
it is you, my lord, who cannot employ them;
if you cannot employ them,
then they feel discontent.
This means you fail in your own duty and blame others."
Yān said:
"What do you mean by that?"
He replied:
"You provide only three shēng of grain to your officials, which is insufficient,
insufficient for the officials,
yet your geese and ducks have surplus grain;
this is your first fault.
The pears and chestnuts from your orchards,
and the women of your inner palace,
are used for mutual entertainment,
yet your officials have never tasted a single one;
this is your second fault.
Silks and satins, fine and beautiful,
adorn your halls,
rotting in the wind,
yet your officials have never had even a trim of them;
this is your third fault.
Wealth is
what you, my lord, hold light;
death is
what officials hold heavy.
If you, my lord, cannot give what you hold light,
yet expect officials to devote what they hold heavy,
it is like hoarding a leaden knife
but expecting to use it as a Gānjiàng sword—
is that not difficult?"
Sòng Yān said:
"This is my fault."
It is said in the Texts:
"Those with the same clarity of sight will see each other;
those with the same acuity of hearing will hear each other.
Those whose virtue matches will feel close without having met;
those whose voices harmonize will respond though dwelling apart."
Hán Zǐ says:
"If inclinations align, they approve each other;
if inclinations differ, they condemn each other."
How can this be illustrated?
King Wēi of Chǔ asked Sòng Yù:
"Sir, have you some misconduct?
Why do the scholars and common people so fail to praise you?"
Sòng Yù said:
"Among birds there is the phoenix, and among fish there is the whale;
the phoenix soars ninety thousand li,
hovering in the vast heavens above;
the sparrow in the hedge—
how can it comprehend the height of heaven and earth?
The whale sets out at dawn from the foothills of Kūnlún,
and rests at night in Mèngjīn;
the minnow in a puddle—
how can it measure the vastness of rivers and seas?
So not only among birds is there the phoenix and among fish the whale—
among scholars too there are such.
The sage, with his extraordinary thoughts and conduct,
stands aloof and dwells alone.
How could the common folk of the world
understand what I do?"
A discussion says:
Good and evil in the world
are hard to know truly;
unless one is the right person,
one cannot discern the boundary.
Why?
If one's literary works are mocked by military men,
it does not necessarily mean they are vulgar;
if they are disparaged by Yáng and Sīmǎ,
then they are truly vulgar.
If a minister is denounced by Jié and Zhòu,
it does not necessarily mean he is foolish;
if he must be denounced by Yáo and Shùn,
then he is truly foolish.
The world's censure and praise
are not to be trusted.
Hence the saying:
"If one does not go out at night,
how can one know there are night travelers?"
Tàigōng said:
"If one's wisdom is the same as the crowd's,
one is not fit to be a teacher of men;
if one's skill is the same as the crowd's,
one is not a master craftsman of the state."
Lǎozǐ said:
"When inferior scholars hear of the Way,
they laugh heartily at it;
if they did not laugh,
it would not be sufficient to be the Way."
Therefore it is said:
"What the common people despise,
the sages value."
How true this is!
It is said in the Texts:
"To know others is not easy,
nor are others easy to know."
How can this be illustrated?
Hàn Míng persuaded Chūnshēnjūn,
and Chūnshēnjūn was pleased with him.
Hàn Míng wished to speak further,
but Chūnshēnjūn said:
"I already understand your meaning, sir."
Hàn Míng said:
"I wonder, how does your worthiness compare with Yáo?"
Chūnshēnjūn said:
"How could I presume to equal Yáo?"
Hàn Míng said:
"Then how do you assess me compared to Shùn?"
Chūnshēnjūn said:
"You, sir, are Shùn himself."
Hàn Míng said:
"Not so.
Allow me to finish my point for you.
Your worthiness is not equal to Yáo's,
and my ability does not reach Shùn's.
Yet to have a worthy Shùn serve a sage Yáo..."
It takes three years to truly know someone.
Now you claim to know me in a single moment,
which would make you wiser than Yáo and me more virtuous than Shùn."
The Records state:
"A fine steed is recognized only by Bó Lè;
if there were no Bó Lè to recognize it,
it would never be acknowledged as a fine horse.
So it is with scholars."
How can this be demonstrated?
When Confucius was trapped between Chén and Cài,
Yán Huí said:
"Our Master's virtue is so great
that the world cannot accept it.
Yet he continues to promote and practice it.
If the world does not employ us,
that is the shame of its rulers.
Why should our Master feel distressed?"
Hence it is said:
When King Wén understood obscurity, the ruler's quality became evident;
when Confucius became a wanderer, the state's condition became clear.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn states:
"After a child is born,
if it falls victim to fire or water,
it is the mother's fault;
when the child comes of age
and is not sent to a teacher,
it is the father's fault
(coming of age
means having the hair cut crosswise;
childhood
refers to being over eight years old);
if studying with a teacher lacks method,
and the mind remains unenlightened,
it is the individual's fault;
when the mind is enlightened,
yet reputation remains unknown,
it is the friends' fault;
when reputation is known,
but officials do not recommend,
it is the officials' fault;
when officials recommend,
but the king does not employ,
it is the king's fault."
Confucius said:
"Failing to cultivate one's conduct
is one's own fault;
having cultivated conduct yet remaining obscure
is the friends' fault."
The Discourses state:
"Those traveling long distances
rely on carriages and horses;
those crossing rivers and seas
depend on boats and oars.
Thus worthy scholars achieve merit and fame
by relying on resources and borrowing means."
How can this be demonstrated?
Gōngshūzǐ could use his ruler's timber
to construct palaces and towers,
but could not build himself a simple hut,
for lack of material;
Ōuyě could use his lord's copper and iron
to make great bells and cauldrons,
but could not make himself pots and dishes,
for lack of material;
a gentleman can utilize his ruler's administration
to harmonize the people and benefit the masses,
but cannot enrich his own family,
for lack of favorable circumstances.
Thus when Shùn farmed at Lìshān,
his kindness did not reach the villages;
when Tàigōng butchered oxen at Cháogē,
his profits did not benefit his wife and children.
But when employed,
their kindness flowed to the eight wildernesses,
their virtue overflowed to the four seas.
So Shùn borrowed from Yáo,
Tàigōng relied on King Wén of Zhōu.
A gentleman can cultivate himself to borrow the Way,
but cannot distort the Way to borrow wealth.
Shènzǐ said:
"The soaring snake rides the mist,
the flying dragon mounts the clouds,
but when clouds disperse and mist clears,
they are no different from earthworms,
having lost what they rode."
Hánzǐ said:
"A thousand jūn floats with a boat,
a small amount sinks without one,
not because the thousand jūn is light and the small amount heavy,
but because one has support and the other does not.
Thus sometimes support cannot be obtained,
and endeavors cannot be accomplished.
Wū Huó finds a thousand jūn light but his own body heavy,
not because his body outweighs a thousand jūn,
but because circumstances are unfavorable;
Lí Lóu finds a hundred paces easy but an eyelash difficult,
not because a hundred paces is near and an eyelash far,
but because the way is obstructed."
The Analects state:
"A ruler of a state
cannot claim there are no deeply strategic ministers in the country or no wise strategists at court,
but rather depends on whether his listening and examination are precise or not, thorough or not."
How can this be demonstrated?
In the past, Emperor Hàn Gāozǔ,
a ruler of keen hearing,
adopted Chén Huī's strategy
and took Nányáng.
He disregarded Lóu Jìng's advice
and was trapped at Píngchéng.
Guǎngwǔ Jūn
was a strategist.
When Hán Xìn adopted his plan,
Yān and Qí fell.
When Chén Yú disregarded his strategy,
they were defeated at Chíshuǐ.
From this we see
that we cannot say successful endeavors have strategic advisors while failures lack deeply planning ministers.
Duke Yú disregarded Gōng Zhīqí's advice
and was destroyed by Jìn;
Qiúyóu ignored Chì Zhāng's words
and perished under Zhìshì;
Jiǎn Shū's weeping
could not prevent the defeat at Xiáomiǎn;
Zhào Kuò's mother
could not avert the disaster at Chángpíng.
These all resulted from the rulers' listening
being imprecise and unthorough.
Every state under heaven
has loyal ministers and strategists.
It is argued:
"When the world is free from calamities,
even those with worthy virtue
have no means to施展 their talents.
Lǎozǐ said:
"When the great Way is abandoned,
humanity and righteousness appear;
when the state is in chaos and confusion,
loyal ministers emerge."
Huáinánzǐ states:
"To know someone's worthiness before achievements
is unique to Yáo's recognition of Shùn;
to know someone's worthiness after success
is how ordinary people recognize Shùn."
Lù Jī said:
"If the flying reins halt in the west,
then Lí Zhū and the blind share the same sight;
if the suspended brilliance shines in the east,
then night-bright pearls and common stones hide their glow.
Thus talent changing with the times leads to shared hardship,
while merit matching the times brings joint accomplishment."
From this we infer,
had Yīn not had the Míngtiáo incident,
then Yī Yǐn would have remained a servant of Yǒushēn;
had Zhōu not had the Mùyě campaign,
then Tàigōng would have remained a fisherman at the Wèi River.
How could they have inscribed their names in imperial records
and had their merits recorded in the heavenly archives?
Therefore it is said:
"Worthiness and unworthiness
depend on talent;
encountering opportunity or not
depends on timing."
How true these words are!
Huáng Shígōng said:
"Gather the heroes,
and the enemy state will be impoverished.
For heroes are
the backbone of the state;
scholars and commoners are
half the state.
Secure the backbone,
win over the half,
and governance will proceed without resentment."
To know people is wisdom,
which even emperors find difficult.
Be cautious!
Chapter Eight: The Essence of Governance
In ancient times, the establishment of emperors and kings
was not to indulge their desires.
It was because among the people under heaven,
the strong oppressed the weak,
the cunning deceived the simple,
so the Son of Heaven was established to unify them.
Considering that the wisdom of one person
cannot illuminate the entire realm,
the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers were established to assist him.
For distant lands with different customs,
unable to receive blessings,
feudal lords were established to instruct them.
The governance of instruction
has existed since ancient times.
How can this be explained?
Guǎnzǐ said:
"To place the state on unshakable ground,
one must possess virtue."
King Wǔ of Zhōu asked Yùzǐ:
"I wish to defend and surely preserve,
attack and surely conquer—
how can this be achieved?"
He replied:
"Attack and defense follow the same principle,
with harmony and strictness
as their preparation.
Thus it is said:
Harmony can preserve while strictness cannot preserve,
strictness is not as firm as harmony;
harmony can attack while strictness cannot attack,
strictness is not as effective as harmony.
Therefore, when feudal lords issue decrees and implement policies,
if governance is fair to the people,
this is called civil governance.
When receiving scholars and employing officials,
if rituals are respectful to people,
this is called civil ritual;
when hearing cases and deciding punishments,
if administration is benevolent to people,
this is called civil punishment.
Thus when these three civilities are established in governance,
and principles are implemented,
yet defense fails to preserve,
or attack fails to conquer—
from ancient times to the present,
this has never been heard of."
《Yuèzǐ》said:
"Virtue is
what heaven, earth, and all things obtain;
righteousness is
what is appropriate for heaven, earth, and all things;
ritual is
the embodiment of heaven, earth, and all things.
When heaven, earth, and all things
all attain their appropriateness and proper ritual,
this is called great benevolence."
Wénzǐ said:
"If people lack shame,
they cannot be governed;
if they don't know ritual and righteousness,
laws cannot be implemented.
Laws can execute people,
but cannot make them filial and fraternal;
they can punish thieves,
but cannot give people shame.
Therefore, when sage kings rule above,
they clarify likes and dislikes to show the way,
guide through criticism and praise,
draw close to the worthy and promote them,
disdain the unworthy and dismiss them,
making punishments unnecessary,
while cultivating ritual and righteousness to employ the worthy."
He also said:
"Righteousness
cannot benefit all under heaven completely,
but benefiting one person makes the world follow;
tyranny
cannot harm the entire realm completely,
but harming one person makes the world rebel.
Therefore, in establishing and abolishing measures,
one cannot but be careful."
To store in inexhaustible granaries,
focus on the five grains.
Cháo Cuò advised Emperor Wén of Hàn:
"Now our land and people
are no less than in ancient times,
without the floods and droughts of Yáo or Tāng's eras,
yet our reserves don't match antiquity—
why?
Because land has unused potential,
people have surplus energy,
grain-producing land isn't fully cultivated,
mountain and marsh resources aren't fully exploited,
and idle eaters haven't all returned to farming.
The urgent task today
lies in valuing grain.
The way to value grain
is to make people use grain for rewards and punishments.
Now recruit people nationwide to deliver grain to the frontiers,
enabling them to receive titles,
and have crimes pardoned.
Thus,
the wealthy gain titles,
farmers gain money,
grain becomes abundant,
and state resources become ample.
Within three years,
frontier grain will surely multiply."
Emperor Jǐng of Hàn decreed:
"Carving and engraving
harm agricultural work;
embroidery and weaving
hurt women's work.
Harm to farming is the root of hunger,
harm to women's work is the source of cold.
When hunger and cold strike together, those who avoid wrongdoing
are few.
We personally plow,
the empress personally tends mulberries,
to serve the ancestral temple,
leading the world by example,
hoping all will focus on farming and sericulture,
maintaining constant reserves,
to prepare for disasters."
《Yántiě Lùn》said:
"When a state has fertile land abundance,
yet people lack sufficient food—
it's because commerce and crafts flourish while fundamental work declines.
When possessing mountain and sea treasures,
yet people lack sufficient wealth—
it's because practical uses are neglected while extravagance multiplies."
To store in inexhaustible treasuries,
grow mulberries and hemp,
raise the six domestic animals.
Emperor Jǐng of Hàn decreed:
"Agriculture
is the foundation of the world.
Gold, pearls, and jade
cannot be eaten when hungry,
nor worn when cold.
Let commanderies and states encourage farming and sericulture,
increase planting,
for adequate clothing and food.
Officials who conscript labor
to mine gold, pearls, and jade
will be convicted as thieves for corruption;
governors (two-thousand-bushel officials)
who permit this share the crime."
《Shēnjìàn》discussed:
"If people don't fear death,
they can't be intimidated by punishment;
if people don't cherish life,
they can't be encouraged toward goodness.
Therefore, rulers must first enrich people's wealth
to settle their aspirations."
To issue decrees at the source of flowing water,
is to follow the people's hearts.
Wèi Liáozi said:
"Decrees
are meant to unify the masses' hearts.
If issued without careful consideration,
they change frequently,
and frequent changes make decrees untrustworthy
even when issued.
The method of issuing decrees:
even with minor flaws,
don't alter them,
then the masses won't follow conflicting orders,
and decrees will be implemented."
《Yǐnwénzǐ》said:
"In civil versus military matters,
some orders must be executed,
some need not be executed.
'Divorce your noble wife,
sell your beloved concubine'—
such orders must be executed.
But saying:
'You dare not resent,
you dare not remember'—
such orders cannot be executed.
Therefore, those above others
must be careful what orders they issue."
Wénzǐ said:
"Governing a state has constants,
with benefiting people as fundamental;
political education has principles,
with implementing orders as ancient wisdom."
To employ scholars in non-contentious positions,
is to let each person use their strengths.
Xúnzǐ said:
"Assessing land quality,
arranging the five grains—
gentlemen are不如 farmers;
handling wealth and goods,
distinguishing value—
gentlemen are不如 merchants;
setting compass and square,
preparing tools—
gentlemen are不如 craftsmen.
But when evaluating virtue to determine rank...
Assign offices according to capability,
speak in accordance with reason,
act in line with necessity,
then these are the strengths of a noble person."
Wénzǐ said:
"If strength can bear the responsibility,
then lifting it is not heavy;
if capable of handling the affairs,
then performing them is not difficult."
To clarify the path leading to certain death,
is to enforce strict punishments.
Discussion says:
Confucius said:
"When those above lose the Way and kill those below,
it is contrary to propriety."
Thus, when the three armies suffer a great defeat,
they cannot be executed;
when prisons are not well managed,
punishments cannot be applied.
Why is that?
Because the teachings from above are not implemented,
the fault does not lie with the people.
To issue orders carelessly but punish meticulously,
is tyranny;
to levy taxes without regard to timing,
is oppression;
to demand results without prior instruction,
is cruelty.
If governance lacks these three,
then applying punishments
is acceptable.
First, persuade them by promoting virtue and morality;
if that still doesn't work,
then honor the worthy to encourage them;
if that still doesn't work,
then remove the incompetent to instill fear;
and if there are still wicked people who do not submit to transformation,
then deal with them through punishments.
Yuánzǐ said:
"Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
are the foundation of law;
decrees and punishments
are the branches of governance.
Without a foundation, nothing stands;
without branches, nothing is accomplished.
Why so?
The methods of ritual education
begin with benevolence and righteousness,
demonstrate propriety and deference,
leading people to improve themselves,
unaware of it in daily practice.
Confucians, seeing this,
thus claim:
Governing a state does not require penal law.
They do not realize that penal law supports from below,
and only then does benevolence and righteousness flourish above.
Laws and decrees
reward good and prohibit excess,
are essential for maintaining order.
Shāng and Hán, seeing this,
thus said:
Governing a state does not rely on benevolence and righteousness as the core,
hence laws and decrees are implemented below.
Therefore, having penal law without benevolence and righteousness makes people resentful,
and resentment leads to anger;
having benevolence and righteousness without penal law makes people negligent,
and negligence gives rise to wickedness.
Base it on benevolence,
complete it with law,
so that both ways are followed without bias,
then governance reaches its peak."
Thus, Zhòngchángzǐ said:
"In the past, Qin used Lord Shāng's laws,
spreading a net as vast as the sky.
Yet Chén Shè shouted loudly in the marshes of Pèi,
and the world responded.
The reason people were not usable
was that resentment and poison had accumulated throughout the world."
Huán Fàn said:
"When Jié and Zhòu applied punishments,
sometimes pickling human muscles,
sometimes cutting out human hearts and guts,
until rebellions became numerous,
and they ultimately faced collapse,
this was because they did not use benevolence and righteousness as their foundation."
Therefore it is said:
"Benevolence
is the forgiveness in law;
righteousness
is the decisiveness in law.
Thus it is known that benevolence and righteousness are the root of punishments."
Hence Sūnzǐ said:
"Command them with civility,
unify them with martial discipline,
this is called certain victory."
This refers to that.
To open the door to certain gains,
is to be trustworthy in rewards.
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"When trust is established, then emptiness is filled,
and rewards can be given.
The entire world can become a treasury.
If a ruler understands this discourse,
his kingship will last long;
if a minister knows this discourse,
he can become an assistant to a king."
Xú Gàn's "Zhōng Lùn" says:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitude,
their nature is the same.
To cut the flesh and harm the body,
is universally detested.
To wear jade and adorn with tassels,
is universally desired.
These two things are constant,
yet some people do not manage themselves properly,
there is a reason for this.
When those who should be rewarded are not rewarded,
and those who should be punished are not punished,
then those who do good lose their fundamental hope,
and doubt their actions;
then those who do evil take the state's laws lightly,
and remain complacent in their ways.
If it is like this,
even if axes are used daily in the market,
people will not abandon evil;
even if titles and emoluments are awarded daily at court,
people will not be inspired to do good."
Shǔ's Zhāng Yì said to Zhūgě Liàng:
"Your rewards do not neglect the distant,
your punishments do not favor the near,
titles are not taken without merit,
punishments cannot be avoided due to power or nobility.
This is why both wise and foolish forget themselves in service."
Do not attempt what cannot be accomplished,
measure human capability.
Wénzǐ said:
"Small debts are easy to repay,
few duties are easy to manage,
light responsibilities are easy to fulfill.
If those above hold to simplicity and few demands,
those below can achieve easy successes,
thus as ruler and minister,
they do not tire of each other over time.
The laws of a declining age,
set high standards and punish those who don't meet them,
impose heavy duties and penalize those who can't bear them,
create dangerous difficulties and execute those who dare not attempt.
When people are distressed by these three demands,
they feign wisdom to deceive superiors,
even with harsh laws and severe punishments,
their wickedness cannot be stopped."
The "Xīnyǔ" says:
"Qín Shǐ Huáng established penal laws,
instituting dismemberment by chariot,
built walls and cities to defend against the Hú and Yuè,
the more he undertook,
the more chaotic below became;
the more laws there were,
the more wickedness spread.
It was not that Qin did not wish for order,
but what it lost was due to
too many measures and too extreme punishments."
Do not seek what cannot be obtained,
do not force people into what they detest.
Hence it is stated:
Governance,
what makes it effective,
lies in conforming to human hearts;
what makes it fail,
lies in opposing human hearts.
People detest worry and toil,
and love ease and pleasure.
Those who enjoy ease and pleasure
detest poverty and low status;
those who are wealthy and noble
detest danger and fall;
those who exist in safety
detest extinction.
Nurture those who produce life.
If you can provide ease and pleasure,
