then people will fear worry and toil;
if you can enrich and ennoble them,
then people will fear poverty and low status;
if you can ensure existence and safety,
then people will fear danger and fall;
if you can enable procreation and rearing,
then people will fear extinction.
Thus, by following these four desires,
the distant will draw near of their own accord;
by enacting these four detestations,
even the near will rebel.
Yànzǐ said:
"Plans measured by righteousness are sure to succeed,
actions rooted in benevolence are sure to achieve.
Acting contrary to righteousness,
moving against benevolence,
I have not heard of such succeeding."
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"When trees are lush, birds and beasts return to them;
when water sources are deep, fish and turtles return to them.
If the ruler is wise, the heroes and elites will come to him.
Therefore, a sage king does not work to make others come to him,
but focuses on what attracts them.
Thus it is said:
If you force someone to smile,
they are not joyful;
if you force someone to cry,
they are not sad;
forcing someone to follow the way
can achieve small things,
but cannot achieve great things.
One cannot remain in an untenable position for long,
nor can one casually take what is suitable for a moment.
Dǒng Zhòngshū discussed strategies for stable borders,
wanting the Hàn to form an alliance with the Xiōngnú,
also taking the Xiōngnú prince as a hostage.
Bān Gù noted that the Xiōngnú were unruly,
and whenever someone surrendered to the Hàn,
they would detain Hàn envoys in return,
so how would they agree to give their prince as a hostage?
During the time of Emperor Xiàowén,
he married a Hàn princess to them,
but the Xiōngnú repeatedly broke the agreements,
ignoring promises for profit,
so why would they not abandon a hostage for significant gain?
To plan affairs and put forward proposals,
one should not only consider temporary stability,
relying on fleeting situations,
but should have a long-term perspective.
Cháo Cuò suggested to Emperor Wéndì of Hàn to accept grain at the borders,
thus allowing people to be granted titles,
and to redeem their offenses,
to which the emperor agreed.
Xún Yuè said:
"The policy of the sage focuses on its principles,
and clearly establishes morality and justice.
Regarding specific strategies,
they would always consult public opinion,
consider timeliness,
and use them only when necessary.
Without significant reason,
they would not deviate from this.
Thus, those who understand the times
can be promptly appointed as leaders.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"When the time has not arrived,
one should not forcibly give life;
If affairs are unfinished,
one should not force completion.
Guǎnzi said:
"A sage can assist the times,
but cannot defy them.
It is said in the Analects:
"The sage prepares and waits for the time.
Those who judge the times correctly,
observe the proper use,
and are able to prepare officials,
can be served as rulers.
The discussion states:
Sūn Qīng stated:
"By stealing the methods of a king,
and doing them with the king's people,
one will also become a king;
by stealing the methods of a hegemon,
and doing them with a hegemon's people,
one will also become a hegemon;
by stealing the methods of a fallen state,
and doing them with the people of a fallen state,
one will also perish.
When one works with gentlemen who accumulate ritual propriety and righteousness,
they will become kings;
When one works with upright, sincere, trustful officials,
they will become hegemons;
When one works with scheming, treacherous people,
they will perish.
These three are the matters a wise ruler carefully chooses,
and this is the ability to discern proper use.
Guǎnzhòng said:
"For those in high position without benevolence,
they should not be entrusted with the state apparatus;
one who does not defer to the worthy
should not be given a higher position;
one who avoids punishing relatives
should not be made in charge of the military;
one who does not enjoy essential affairs
should not be given a city.
He also said:
"If you let the capable feed the worthy,
the superior will show respect;
if you let warriors be rewarded for merit,
the soldiers will risk their lives.
If both practices are implemented in the state,
the whole world will be orderly.
Fùzǐ said:
"The assessments of all provinces and counties have six criteria:
First, teaching and correct conduct,
where officials promote virtue;
Second, purifying fundamentals,
where officials act carefully;
Third, appointing by talent,
where officials make judicious selections;
Fourth, equitable office duties,
where officials manage matters cautiously;
Fifth, agricultural assessments,
where officials attend to affairs diligently;
Sixth, adjudicating litigation,
where officials seek justice carefully.
This is how officials can be thoroughly prepared.
Thus it is said:

Clarify land registration, examine the groupings, set boundaries for lands, define penal titles, establish rulers and chiefs, urgently attend to agriculture and sericulture, discard non-essential crafts, promote learning, evaluate talents, select the vigorous and brave, equip for military defense, enforce strict prohibitions, ensure rewards and punishments are credible, correct pastimes, and inspect harshness and overbearing behavior.
These fifteen principles,
even if sages were to return,
would demand adherence.
When discussing variations in circumstances,
it is crucial to establish governance principles to serve as constants.
Virtue of a Ruler, Chapter Nine
The Three Sovereigns spoke no words,
yet their transformation flowed throughout the four seas,
thus the world had nothing to attribute their merits to.
Fúxī, Nǚwā, and Shénnóng
are referred to as the Three Sovereigns.
The Emperors embodied heaven and emulated earth,
they had words and commands,
and the world was at peace.
Rulers and ministers yielded credit to each other,
their influence spread across the four seas,
and the common people did not know how it came to be.
Therefore, they employed ministers without ritual rewards for achievements,
admirable and without harm.
Huángdì,
complying with the order of heaven and earth,
timely sowed the hundred grains,
diligently applied his mind, strength, ears, and eyes,
frugally used fire, water, and seasonal resources,
and had auspicious signs of earth's virtue,
hence he was titled Huángdì;
Zhuānxū,
nurtured resources by utilizing the land,
carried the seasons to mirror heaven,
relied on spirits to establish righteousness,
governed energies to educate and transform,
purified sincerity in sacrificial rites,
all things moving and still,
spirits great and small,
wherever the sun and moon shone,
none were not honed and refined;
Gāoxīn,
took the wealth of the earth and used it sparingly,
comforted and taught the myriad people, benefiting and instructing them,
followed the sun and moon in welcoming and sending them,
understood spirits and reverently served them,
his demeanor was profound,
his virtue lofty;
Emperor Yáo,
his benevolence was like heaven,
his wisdom like the divine,
approaching him was like the sun,
gazing at him was like clouds,
wealthy yet not arrogant,
noble yet not lax;
Yú Shùn,
no good deed was too small not to be made manifest,
no evil too hidden not to be exposed,
he rewarded and punished according to nature,
entrusted the collective will to establish order.
Thus he could govern through non-action,
operate the Way in ultimate harmony,
the common people used it daily without knowing,
embodying virtue as if it were their own,
such were the virtues of the Five Emperors.
Kings govern people with the Way,
subduing their hearts and winning their allegiance.
Discussion says:
Hán Xìn stated:
"Wherever King Xiàng passed, nothing was left undestroyed,
the people felt no affinity,
only coerced by his might,
forcibly submitting.
Though nominally a hegemon,
in reality, he lost the hearts of the world.
Hence it is said:
his strength is easily weakened."
Zhūgě Liàng said:
"The people of Jīngzhōu,
those who side with Cāo,
do so under the pressure of military force,
not from heartfelt submission.
If you, General, truly command fierce generals to coordinate and unite efforts with Jīngzhōu,
defeating Cāo's army is certain."
From this, it is said,
if people's hearts are not won,
their situation is easily broken.
Therefore, the way of kings
is to subdue hearts and win allegiance.
Establishing norms to prepare for decline,
having discerning governance and military preparations,
yet without the use of conflict and bloodshed,
the world is at peace,
the ruler has no doubts about ministers,
ministers have no doubts about the sovereign,
the state is stable, the sovereign secure,
ministers retire with righteousness,
also admirable and without harm.
In the past, the enlightened kings of the Three Dynasties,
initiated great eras,
with varying systems of refinement and substance,
yet their renowned reputations were consistent.
Hence it is said:
the Xià people esteemed loyalty,
the drawback of loyalty is simplicity,
to remedy simplicity, nothing is better than reverence,
the Yīn people reformed and cultivated it;
the drawback of reverence is superstition,
to remedy superstition, nothing is better than refinement,
the Zhōu people corrected and transformed it;
the drawback of refinement is superficiality,
then it returns again to loyalty.
The Three Dynasties followed one another,
like water aiding fire.
What is called adapting to the times and methods to remedy flaws,
these are the virtues of the Three Kings.
Hegemons control scholars with power,
bind scholars with trust,
employ scholars with rewards.
When trust declines, scholars distance themselves,
when rewards are destroyed, scholars cease to be useful.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Chǔ besieged Sòng,
Sòng reported the emergency to Jìn.
Xiān Zhěn said:
'Repaying kindness, rescuing from distress,
gaining authority, establishing hegemony,
lies in this.'
Hú Yǎn said:
'Chǔ has just gained Cáo and newly allied with Wèi through marriage,
if we attack Cáo and Wèi,
Chǔ is sure to rescue them,
then Qí and Sòng will be spared.'
Thereupon, they held a review at Bèilú,
formed three armies,
deliberated on a commander-in-chief,
and appointed Xì Hú to lead the central army.
The Marquis of Jìn, upon entering, began to educate his people.
In the second year,
wishing to employ them,
Zǐfǎn said:
'The people do not yet know righteousness,
and are not settled in their dwellings.'
Thereupon, they went out to stabilize King Xiāng,
and inward focused on benefiting the people,
so the people cherished life.
When about to use them,
Zǐfǎn said:
'The people do not yet know trust,
and have not demonstrated its use.'
Thereupon, they attacked Yuán to demonstrate trust.
People engaging in trade
did not seek excessive profits,
clearly verifying their words.
The Duke said:
'Is it acceptable now?'
Zǐfǎn said:
'The people do not yet know ritual,
and have not developed respect.'
Thereupon, they held a grand review to demonstrate ritual,
established official ranks to rectify positions,
and only when the people understood without confusion did they then employ them.
They withdrew troops from Gǔ,
lifted the siege of Sòng,
and with one battle achieved hegemony,
all due to the education of Wén."
These are the virtues of the Five Hegemons.
Therefore, it is said:
The foundation of governing a state
lies in punishment and virtue.
These two must proceed together,
and depend on each other to achieve results.
Heaven uses yin and yang to complete the year,
humans use punishment and virtue to accomplish governance,
thus even sages in administration
cannot rely solely on one.
Therefore, those who employed much virtue
and little punishment
were the Five Emperors;
those who balanced punishment and virtue equally
were the Three Kings;
those who relied much on punishment
and employed little virtue
were the Five Hegemons;
those who used punishment purely,
strong yet perished,
was Qín.
Governance says:
In ancient times, those who governed
had three types of governance:
the governance of kings transforms,
the governance of hegemons intimidates,
the governance of strong states coerces.
Thus, if transformation does not bring change, then intimidate,
if intimidation does not bring change, then coerce,
if coercion does not bring change, then punish.
Therefore, reaching the point of punishment
is not what kings value.
Hence, Yú Nán said:
"That Qín emperor,
abandoned benevolence and righteousness to use might and force,
this could achieve annexation,
but not maintain success.
This is the drawback of relying on punishment."
Some say:
"The ways of kings and hegemons,
we have heard instructed.
May I ask about the two emperors Gāo and Guāng,
both rose from the fields,
eradicated calamities and difficulties,
and thus opened royal enterprises.
Emperor Gāozǔ was open-minded and magnanimous,
while Emperor Guāngwǔ was meticulous in regulations.
Each excelled in his own strengths,
soaring like dragons and phoenixes,
thus capable of quelling chaos and protecting the people,
rescuing them from extreme suffering.
Yet comparing their great virtues
and heavenly majesty,
who stands as superior or inferior?"
Cáo Zhí said:
"In the early rise of Hàn,
Gāozǔ rose against the tyrannical Qín,
then destroyed the powerful Chǔ,
possessing all under heaven,
his merit matching Tāng and Wǔ,
his legacy flowing to later generations—
the foremost achievement of emperors,
the grandest deed of rulers.
Yet his reputation was not purely virtuous,
his conduct not entirely upright.
After his death,
at the moment of his demise,
indeed he allowed a vicious woman to unleash cruelty,
a favored consort suffered the 'human swine' punishment.
The King of Zhào was imprisoned,
disaster befell his own flesh and blood,
the various Lǚ usurped power,
the state nearly changed hands.
All these events—
were they not due to Gāozǔ's lack of foresight leading to this?
Yet his fierce generals and strategist ministers
were rare throughout history,
seldom seen across dynasties.
He could employ their talents and use them,
heed their words and discern them,
thus unifying the realm and occupying the imperial throne.
Emperor Shìzǔ embodied the virtuous essence of heaven,
possessed pure and harmonious spirit,
trod the subtle principles of the Mean,
concealed the excellent talent of a near-sage.
In his virtue,
he was intelligent, perceptive, and knowledgeable,
benevolent, wise, clear, and forgiving,
cautious and thorough,
generous in giving and loving toward people.
Encountering an era of calamity,
facing the fate of imperial decline,
like sudden thunder he arose,
majestically and divinely he ascended,
wielding military strategy to repel violence,
raising righteous troops to sweep away remnants.
Before his army left Nánjīng,
Wáng Mǎng had already perished in the Western Capital.
Thus he first secured victory in strategy then mobilized troops,
decided plans then marched the army,
hence no fortress he attacked remained unbreached,
no battle had fleeing soldiers.
Spreading benevolence to harmonize the masses,
extending virtue to attract the distant,
thus Dòu Róng heard his reputation and pledged allegiance,
Mǎ Yuǎn met him once and sighed in admiration.
Fostering harmony among the nine clans,
he earned praise like that of Yáo and Shùn;
noble and pure in simplicity,
he possessed the essence of Fúxī;
humble and accepting of subordinates,
he bore the toil of spitting out food and grasping hair;
attentive to all affairs,
he labored until the sun declined.
Thus measuring merit, his achievements were extraordinary;
comparing glory, his deeds were unmatched;
praising virtue, he was without fault;
in speech and action, without blemish;
assessing circumstances, his power was modest;
evaluating assistants, his ministers were weaker;
yet ultimately he grasped the auspicious signs of heaven's mandate,
established enduring and far-reaching traces,
metal and stone inscribed his splendid deeds,
poetry and books recorded his excellent merits."
Therefore it is said:
Guāngwǔ is the superior.
Xún Yuè said:
"Gāozǔ rose from among commoners,
brandished his sword to seize the realm,
not through abdication like Yáo and Shùn,
not relying on the ranks of Tāng and Wǔ,
like a dragon rising and tiger transforming,
leading amid wind and clouds,
campaigning against chaos and punishing tyranny,
cleansing the imperial domain,
within eight years,
the land was pacified,
thus bearing the heavenly mandate,
ascending to establish imperial rule—
since ancient times,
in recorded texts,
this has never been seen.
Without heroic talent,
broad and wise strategy,
the succession conferred by fate,
the support of spirits and gods,
how could he achieve such merit?
The burning fish and severed snake,
different omens with the same sign—
was this not the response of numinous essence?"
The Shū says:
"Heaven's work, man acts in its place."
The Yì says:
"The revolutions of Tāng and Wǔ
complied with heaven and responded to people."
This refers to such.
Xià governance emphasized loyalty,
its drawback being rustic simplicity,
so Yīn succeeded it with reverence.
Reverence's drawback was superstition,
so Zhōu succeeded it with refinement.
Refinement's drawback was superficiality,
and nothing saves superficiality better than loyalty.
The ways of the Three Dynasties
cycle and begin anew.
Between Zhōu and Qín,
it can be called the drawback of refinement;
Qín did not reform it,
instead imposed harsh punishments.
Hàn succeeded its drawbacks,
yet obtained the legitimate succession.
Kǒng Róng said:
"King Wǔ of Zhōu, from Hòu Jì to himself,
accumulated fifteen generations of succession,
yet had only omens of fish and birds.
As for Gāozǔ,
through his own cultivation of virtue,
had four or five auspicious signs:
the white snake severed,
the divine mother weeping,
entering the pass westwards,
the five planets converging.
Moreover, King Wǔ attacking Zhòu,
beheaded and displayed him.
Gāozǔ entering Qín,
pardoned Zǐyīng and sent him away.
In this generosity,
he was also not equal to Gāozǔ."
Yú Nán said:
"An emperor treats others as teachers,
a king treats them as friends,
a hegemon treats them as ministers.
Hàn Gāozǔ's ministers—
the Three Heroes are such;
Guāngwǔ's assistants—
the Twenty-Eight Generals are such.
How can Dèng Yǔ and Wú Hàn be matched with Zhāng Liáng and Hán Xìn?
Yet Hàn Gāozǔ's meritorious officials
were all executed when they grew powerful;
Guāngwǔ's founding assistants
all received generous ranks and security.
In the relationship between ruler and ministers,
his is truly praiseworthy.
Balancing strengths and weaknesses,
he is slightly inferior."
From this perspective,
Hàn Gāozǔ overcame Qín and Xiàng,
founded the Hàn enterprise,
its culture, rites, and music
passed down to later generations.
Though not reaching the kingly way,
his hegemon virtue was eminent.
Some say:
"Bān Gù claimed:
Zhōu speaks of Chéng and Kāng,
Hàn speaks of Wén and Jǐng—
is this statement appropriate?"
Yú Nán said:
"Chéng and Kāng inherited the legacy of Wén and Wǔ,
with Zhōu and Shào as ministers,
transforming sincere and simple people,
relying on accumulated benevolent virtue—
like wind bending grass,
is an insufficient analogy.
As for Hàn Gāozǔ founding the base,
with no time to spare,
the flaws of fallen Yíng
still remained.
Tàizōng embodied this benevolence and forgiveness,
followed profound silence,
cleansed the cruelty of Qín and Xiàng,
returned to the pure customs of Xuānyuán and Hàodì,
nearly achieving disuse of punishments.
This was truly difficult!
Had he not indulged in Xīnyuán's theories,
nor heeded Dèng Tōng's dream,
awe-inspiringly,
he might have approached the kingly way.
Comparing Jǐngdì to Zhōu Kāng,
there is still shame in virtue."
The Hàn Wén Zàn says:
"Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
for twenty-three years,
his palaces, gardens, and parks,
carriages, horses, clothing, and
He made no unnecessary additions.
Whenever there were inconveniences,
he would relax regulations to benefit the people.
When Nányuè's commander Tuó
proclaimed himself emperor,
Emperor Wén summoned and honored Tuó's brothers,
winning him over with virtue,
and Tuó subsequently pledged allegiance.
He formed marriage alliances with the Xiōngnú,
but they broke the treaty and raided;
he ordered border defenses to hold,
without sending troops deep into enemy territory,
disliking to trouble the common people.
When King Wú feigned illness and did not attend court,
he bestowed him with a stool and cane,
and though his ministers' remonstrations were urgent,
he often tolerated and accepted them.
When Zhāng Wǔ and others accepted bribes,
upon discovery, he rewarded them,
to shame their hearts.
He devoted himself to transforming people through virtue,
thus the realm became prosperous,
and ritual and righteousness flourished.
He adjudicated only a few hundred legal cases,
nearly achieving the cessation of punishments.
Alas!
How benevolent! "
Someone asked Fùzǐ:
"Did Hàn Tàizōng's abolition of corporal punishment
merit being called benevolent?"
He replied:
"That was the benevolence of a common man.
One who rules the world
achieves great accomplishments,
not merely avoiding minor intolerances.
From this perspective,
Bān Gù's assessment of Tàizōng as benevolent
lies not in the abolition of corporal punishment."
The "Eulogy for Jǐngdì" says:
"Confucius said:
'Such men
enabled the Three Dynasties to proceed with upright governance.'
How true!
The failings of Zhōu and Qín,
with their dense laws and harsh statutes,
could not overcome wickedness.
With the rise of Hàn,
burdensome harshness was swept away,
allowing the people to rest.
By the time of Xiàowén,
he added reverence and frugality.
Xiàojǐng continued the enterprise,
and within five or six decades,
customs were transformed,
and the people became honest and sincere.
Zhōu spoke of Chéng and Kāng,
Hàn speaks of Wén and Jǐng—
how splendid!
This is the way of true kings."
Someone asked:
"Hàn Wǔdì had great talent and broad vision—
which ruler of previous eras might he be compared to?"
Yú Nán said:
"Hàn Wǔdì inherited the achievements of six generations,
with a prosperous realm.
Possessing exceptional innate qualities,
he could thus gather heroes,
command the outstanding,
promote rituals and music internally,
expand borders externally,
and his institutions and statutes
were brilliantly commendable.
Compared to Qín Shǐhuáng,
he was superior.
However, in arrogance, extravagance, and cruelty,
they were nearly equal,
both achieving much in merit but lacking in virtue."
The "Eulogy for Wǔdì" says:
"Hàn inherited the failings of numerous kings,
Gāozǔ rectified chaos and restored order,
Wén and Jǐng focused on nurturing the people,
but in examining ancient rituals and culture,
there were still many deficiencies.
Upon ascending the throne, Xiàowǔ
resolutely dismissed the Hundred Schools,
promoted the Six Classics,
consulted widely across the realm,
elevated the talented,
and achieved merits with them.
He established the Grand Academy,
reformed suburban sacrifices,
revised the calendar,
fixed the astronomical system,
harmonized musical tones,
composed poetry and music,
instituted the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
honored various deities,
continued the Zhōu lineage,
and his decrees and writings
were brilliantly commendable.
His successors could follow his grand legacy,
embodying the style of the Three Dynasties.
With Wǔdì's great talent and broad vision,
had he not abandoned Wén and Jǐng's reverence and frugality
to align with the people,
even the praises in the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*
could not surpass him."
From this perspective,
both Hàn Wǔdì and Qín Shǐhuáng
were rulers who achieved merits,
not preservers of established order.
Long ago, Zhōu Chéngwáng succeeded as a child,
and faced the rebellion of Guǎn, Cài, and four other states;
Hàn Zhāodì ascended the throne in youth,
and also confronted the treacherous plots of Yān, Gài, and Shàngguān.
Chéngwáng did not doubt Zhōu Gōng,
Zhāodì entrusted authority to Huò Guāng—
which of the two was superior?
Wèi Wéndì said:
"Zhōu Chéngwáng embodied the virtuous energy of his sage father,
received prenatal teachings from his wise mother,
had Zhōu and Shào as tutors,
and Lǚ Wàng as grand tutor.
When he could speak, envoys articulated words for him;
when he could walk, attendants guided his rituals.
His eyes were filled with majestic beauty,
his ears saturated with virtuous teachings—
what is called immersed in profound currents
and bathed in pure winds.
Yet he still erred,
listening to the slanders of his two uncles,
causing Zhōu Gōng to move east,
until Heaven's wrath
revealed their faults,
and only then did he realize.
Failing to recognize Zhōu Gōng's sage virtue,
but believing the admonitions in the 'Golden Coffer'—
was that not ignorant?
Now, Hàn Zhāodì's father was not like Wǔwáng,
his mother was not like Yì Jiāng,
he was raised only by Princess Gài,
and his minister was the ruthless Guāng.
He lacked nurturing in benevolent filial nature,
and assistance in achieving prosperous governance—
what is called born in deep palaces,
raised by women.
Yet his virtue formed with his nature,
his conduct aligned with ritual,
and at age fourteen,
he was precociously insightful,
exposing the deceit in the Yān letter,
and discerning Huò Guāng's loyalty.
Did he need to open the 'Golden Coffer'
or trust state historians
to realize?
Had Chéng and Zhāo been of the same age at succession,
exchanged eras for transformation,
swapped ministers for governance,
changed music for songs,
then Hàn would not be deemed lesser,
nor Zhōu alone greater."
When Grand General Huò Guāng and Shàngguān Jí held power,
Jí, envious of Guāng's favor,
plotted to kill him,
and forged a letter from the emperor's elder brother, Yān Dàn,
accusing Guāng of imperial protocols in the Shanglin Gardens.
The emperor did not believe it.
Someone asked:
"Hàn Xuāndì governed with clear insight—
was he comparable to Guāngwǔdì?"
Yú Nán said:
"Hàn Xuāndì rose from common alleys,
understood the people's hardships,
thus he attended diligently to governance,
promoted the worthy and capable,
but his method of holding names accountable to reality,
with strict laws and harsh orders,
derived from Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi.
An ancient saying goes:
Aim for kingship and fail,
and the remnants suffice for hegemony;
aim for hegemony and fail,
what then remains?
Guāngwǔdì, with benevolence and righteousness,
was a ruler aiming for kingship;
Xuāndì, with penal codes,
was a ruler aiming for hegemony.
To compare them now,
I fear they are not peers."
A discussion states:
When Yuándì was crown prince,
he once admonished Xuāndì,
believing his enforcement of laws too severe.
The emperor sternly said:
"Our Hàn dynasty blends the ways of hegemony and kingship—
how can we purely rely on virtuous transformation,
to the harm of governance?"
Though this reveals
his vision was not far-reaching,
the balance of leniency and strictness has long origins.
In the past, when Gāozǔ entered Qín,
he simplified the laws into three articles,
which greatly pleased the people of Qín.
This illustrates the virtue of lenient punishments.
Guō Jiā advised Duke Cáo, saying:
"At the end of the Hàn dynasty, governance failed due to excessive leniency.
Yuán Shào continued with leniency,
thus he lacked authority;
you, my lord, corrected this with strictness,
so both superiors and inferiors understand discipline."
This speaks to the appropriateness of severe punishments.
Therefore, the Zuǒzhuàn states:
"When governance is lenient, people become negligent;
when negligent, correct them with strictness;
when strict, people become harsh;
when harsh, apply leniency.
Use leniency to balance strictness,
and strictness to balance leniency,
thus governance achieves harmony."
The Shūjīng says:
"Punishments are light or heavy according to the age."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"For newly established states, use light statutes;
for chaotic states, use heavy statutes;
for stable states, use moderate statutes."
From this perspective,
it depends on what the era requires!
How can severe punishments be considered minor?
Someone asked:
"Hàn Yuándì was talented and refined in arts,
was he not a good ruler who maintained civil governance?"
Yú Nán replied:
"The abilities of a ruler
lie in civil virtue and military achievements.
Civil virtue encompasses ordering heaven and earth,
managing documents and decrees;
military achievements involve suppressing violence and halting warfare,
bringing peace to people and harmony to the masses.
These are the grand designs of rulership.
As for playing the sè and blowing the xiāo,
harmonizing melodies and composing tunes,
these are the duties of musicians,
how can they be the concerns of the Son of Heaven?"
Discussion says:
Yuándì had many talents and skills,
excelling at playing the sè and qín.
Although this is so,
it is not the highest good.
Why?
Xú Gàn's Zhōng Lùn states:
"To elaborate on minor matters while neglecting the great Way,
to examine nearby things while being blind to long-term strategy,
from ancient times to the present,
there has never been such a case without chaos,
nor such a case without ruin.
What is called 'elaborating on minor matters, examining nearby things'
refers to ears sharp for the harmony of strings, bamboo, songs, and ballads,
eyes clear for the patterns of carving and colorful decorations,
mouth skilled in clever, sharp retorts,
mind versed in short sayings and minor tales,
hands practiced in the skills of archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics.
What is called 'long-term strategy, the great Way'
refers to benevolence sufficient to cover all living beings,
kindness sufficient to nurture the common people,
clarity sufficient to illuminate the four directions,
wisdom sufficient to govern all things,
authority sufficient to respond to changes without limit,
righteousness sufficient to enrich wealth and resources,
majesty sufficient to prohibit treachery and wrongdoing,
martial prowess sufficient to pacify calamities and chaos,
attentiveness in listening and discernment in appointing officials,
understanding the origins of rise and fall,
comprehending the distinction between safety and danger.
Only then
is the Way of the ruler complete."
In the past, Lǔ Zhuānggōng had many skills,
and poets criticized him for it;
Lǔ Zhāogōng had fine appearance and demeanor,
yet suffered the calamity of being driven out.
From this perspective,
even if a ruler could see like Lí Lóu, hear like Shī Kuàng, shoot like Yí Yì, and write like Shǐ Zhòu,
it would only mean he was good at the duties of minor officials,
what benefit would it be to governance?
Kuáng Héng's "Letter Advising Yuándì on Changing Governance" stated:
"A king who receives the Mandate
must focus on founding and establishing a legacy
to pass on endlessly.
A successor ruler
must be devoted to inheriting and promoting the virtue of previous kings and glorifying their achievements.
Now Your Majesty's sage virtue covers all under heaven,
cherishing all within the seas,
yet yīn and yáng are not harmonious,
and treacherous evils are not restrained,
likely because critics have not fully extolled the great achievements of the late emperor,
but instead argue that the established systems are unusable.
I privately regret that the state abandons its accomplished enterprise,
and vainly engages in such disputes.
I wish Your Majesty would examine the matters of continuing the legacy,
this is maintaining civil governance."
Someone asked:
"Observing the usurper Wáng Mǎng,
humble, respectful, and courteous,
was he not a famous scholar of his time?
Yet when he became chancellor and assumed supreme power,
he became arrogant, licentious, and tyrannical,
why such extreme contradiction between before and after?"
Yú Nán replied:
"Wáng Mǎng had a cruel nature by heaven's endowment,
a deceitful and hypocritical man.
Before attaining power,
he sought fame and reputation;
after achieving his ambition,
he boasted of his abilities and looked down on others.
Once his pretense was exhausted,
his true nature remained.
Stubborn, rejecting advice, considering himself superior,
he ultimately never reformed or awakened,
causing widespread injustice and cruelty throughout the land,
thus being driven out by Guāngwǔ."
Bān Gù said:
"Wáng Mǎng began as a relative of the imperial family,
humbled himself and acted diligently,
to seek fame and reputation.
During the reigns of Chéngdì and Āidì,
he worked hard for the state,
acted with straightforward integrity,
and his actions were praised,
was this not the so-called 'in the state necessarily heard of,
in the family necessarily heard of,
outwardly adopting benevolence while acting contrary to it'?
Since Mǎng was not benevolent,
and had the talent for deceit and flattery,
coupled with the power inherited from the four generations of his fathers,
encountering the Hàn's middle decline,
with the imperial line thrice broken,
and the Empress Dowager long-lived,
acting as the sovereign matriarch,
thus he could indulge his treachery and evil,
accomplishing the disaster of usurpation.
Inferring from this,
there was also the timing of heaven,
not solely due to human effort.
When he usurped the throne and faced south as ruler,
occupying a position he should not have,
the situation of his overthrow
was more perilous than that of Jié and Zhòu,
yet Mǎng remained complacent,
believing himself the reincarnation of Huángdì and Yáo.
He boasted of his authority and deceit,
committing heinous crimes and oppressing the people,
thus the land was in turmoil,
losing the will to enjoy life,
with resentment and hatred inside and out,
abandonment near and far,
cities undefended,
bodies dismembered,
eventually reducing all cities and towns under heaven to ruins.
In all records of the Shūjīng and traditions,
among rebellious ministers and villainous sons,
and those without virtue,
none were as extreme as Mǎng.
Usurping the imperial color, croaking like a frog,
occupying an illegitimate position in an intercalary period,
he was merely driven out by the sage king."
King Sūn Quán of Wú, discussing Lǚ Méng, said:
"When Zǐmíng was young,
I thought he merely did not avoid difficulty or ease,
being resolute and courageous.
Growing up, he pursued learning and broadened his knowledge,
his strategies became remarkably ingenious,
placing him next to Gōng Jǐn,
in planning to capture Guān Yǔ,
he surpassed Zǐjìng.
Zǐjìng replied to my letter, saying:
'The rise of emperors and kings
always involves those who clear the way.
Yǔ is not worth worrying about.'
This shows Zǐjìng internally could not discern,
yet externally made grand claims.
I also excused him,
not sternly blaming him."
This is the meaning of "driving out."
Xià Shào Kāng and Hàn Guāngwǔ were both restoration rulers,
who was greater?
Yú Nán said:
"These two emperors both revived their ancestors' legacy,
gloriously reopening the path of kingship.
Their names are the same,
but their realities differ.
Why?
In Guāngwǔ's time,
he relied on people longing for chaos,
to punish the brutal usurper Mǎng,
exploiting chaos and overwhelming the doomed,
making his task relatively easier.
As for Shào Kāng,
the Xià lineage had been destroyed for two generations
(Yì and Hán Zhuó).
He was a remote surviving descendant,
still in his mother's womb,
His mother fled into exile,
giving birth to him in another state.
He missed the instruction at the courtyard,
and had no close relatives.
Amidst the calamities of war and chaos,
he found refuge in unsuitable places,
yet managed to navigate through the turmoil of loss and disorder,
ultimately achieving a merit matching Heaven's mandate.
Among the monarchs who restored dynasties,
he stands as the foremost."
The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng of Wèi asked Xún Yǐ:
"After the Xià dynasty declined,
and its rulers were exterminated,
Shào Kāng gathered the remnants of Xià's people,
and restored Yǔ's achievements.
Emperor Gāozǔ rose from the fields,
and eradicated Qín and Xiàng.
Comparing their merits and virtues,
who should come first?"
Xún Yǐ and others replied:
"Creating anew versus inheriting foundations,
differ in difficulty.
Though Shào Kāng's merits and virtues were admirable,
he was still a restorer,
comparable to Emperor Shìzǔ of Hàn.
As for Emperor Gāozǔ,
we consider him superior."
The Emperor said:
"Shào Kāng was born after the dynasty's fall,
reduced to being a subordinate of feudal lords,
yet he could spread his virtue and initiate his strategies,
finally eliminating Guò and Gé,
restoring Yǔ's achievements,
sacrificing to Xià and matching Heaven,
without losing the ancient heritage.
Without supreme virtue and great benevolence,
how could he have accomplished such a feat?
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn capitalized on the collapsing situation,
seizing temporary power.
As a son, he repeatedly endangered his parents;
as a ruler, he imprisoned his virtuous chancellor;
as a father, he failed to protect his son.
After his death,
the state nearly collapsed.
Had he and Shào Kāng exchanged places,
he might not have restored Yǔ's achievements."
Reasoning from this,
Shào Kāng should be esteemed above Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
The decline and chaos of the later Hàn,
stemmed from the two emperors Huán and Líng.
Whose misdeeds were more severe?
Yú Nán said:
"Emperor Huán roused in fury,
executed Liáng Jì,
demonstrating firm decisiveness.
However, eunuchs usurped authority,
factional proscriptions arose,
and the turmoil of the Zhōngpíng era
began with Emperor Huán.
An ancient saying goes:
'When the world cries out in distress,
it provides an opportunity for a new ruler.'
Emperor Líng inherited a weary populace,
making good governance easier;
the people listened attentively,
all hoping for restoration.
Yet he followed the same disastrous path,
worse than his predecessors,
overturning the ancestral temple.
Responsibility lies with the emperor;
his natural death was fortunate enough."
Discussion says:
Emperor Huán asked his attendant Yuán Yán:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
He replied:
"A middling ruler of Hàn."
"Why so?"
"When Chén Fān, the Imperial Secretary, handles affairs, order prevails;
when the eunuchs intervene, chaos ensues.
Thus, we know Your Majesty can do good
or do wrong.
This defines a middling ruler."
Yú Nán said:
"When the Mín River first flows,
its source can fill a wine cup.
As it travels far,
it requires a boat to cross.
During Emperor Yuán's time,
he appointed Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn;
by the time of Huán and Líng,
added Shàn Chāo and Zhāng Ràng.
They corrupted moral principles,
and overturned the state.
This came about gradually.
Hence the saying:
'If a spark isn't extinguished,
what can be done when it blazes?'
It means to be cautious at the start.
Alas!
A hundred generations later,
take this as a mirror!"
An ancient saying states:
"The cold find clothes easy to make,
the hungry find food easy to prepare."
Cháo Cuò said:
"When a state is wealthy and strong while neighboring states are in chaos,
it provides an opportunity for an emperor."
From this perspective,
it's clear that chaotic and incompetent rulers
pave the way for sagely virtue.
Since the fire virtue declined,
the empire fragmented.
Cáo Mèngdé held the emperor to command the lords;
Liú Xuándé relied on Shǔ Hàn's barriers;
Sūn Zhòngmóu possessed Jiāng Huái's strongholds.
They divided the realm into three,
standing like a tripod's legs,
each initiating royal enterprises,
expanding hegemonic plans.
Among these three rulers,
who was superior or inferior?
Yú Nán said:
"Cáo Cāo's military strategy and wisdom
were nearly unmatched,
thus he could establish a foundation,
serving as chancellor centrally,
truly a heroic talent!
However, he was deceitful and inconsistent,
suspicious and jealous,
to the extent of killing Empress Fú,
poisoning Xún Yù,
executing Kǒng Róng,
slaying Cuī Yǎn,
Lóu Shēng died over a single word,
Huán Shào toiled in obeisance.
Abandoning virtue for punishment,
his cruelty was extreme.
To call him a western earl
was unfitting.
Xǔ Shào's description 'a capable minister in orderly times,
a treacherous hero in chaotic times'
is accurate."
"Liú Bèi treated Liú Zhāng with guest rites,
entrusted Zhūgě Liàng without doubt.
A ruler's virtue
is exemplified here.
That Kǒngmíng
was a rare talent of the era,
equal to Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng.
Ruler and minister united in heart,
compared to fish and water.
But with a small state and weak army,
isolated in a corner,
confronting two sides,
resisting the superior state.
Had he and Cáo Cāo exchanged places,
employing his long-term strategies,
unleashing Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi's martial prowess,
exhausting Zhūgě's civil talents,
then the hegemon's enterprise would have succeeded."
"Sūn Quán utilized his brother's legacy,
employed former dynasty's aides,
relied on natural defenses,
barely managed to survive.
Compared to the other two,
he logically falls short."
Chén Shòu said:
"Liú Bèi's strategic ability and resourcefulness
did not match Wèi's Wǔ,
hence his domain was narrower."
Zhāng Fǔ said:
"How can that be?
A ruler who quells chaos
should prioritize recruiting ministers and generals;
personal combat prowess
is not reliable.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng understood rites and adaptability,
nearly a king-making talent.
Xuándé, without strong power, made him submit;
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, both outstanding men,
served under him.
Bright and dark cannot cooperate,
capable and incapable cannot assist each other.
Even if Wǔdì were secure and strong,
he wouldn't be used by him,
especially in crises.
Had Xuándé possessed the central plains,
he could have rivaled the Zhōu dynasty's glory,
not just with two heroes."
The Wèi emperor asked Wú's envoy Zhào Zī:
"What kind of ruler is the King of Wú?"
Zhào Zī replied:
"A ruler of intelligence, wisdom, benevolence, knowledge, valor, and strategy."
The emperor asked for details,
he said:
"Enlisting Lǔ Sù from obscurity
shows his intelligence;
promoting Lǚ Méng from the ranks
shows his wisdom;"
Capturing Yǔ Jìn without harming him,
demonstrates his benevolence;
taking Jīngzhōu without shedding blood,
demonstrates his wisdom;
contending over three provinces while eyeing the empire,
demonstrates his might;
submitting to Your Majesty,
demonstrates his strategy."
Sūn Cè, severely wounded,
called to his younger brother Sūn Quán, saying:
"Raising the masses of Jiāngdōng,
making decisive moves between two battle arrays,
contending for supremacy with the empire,
you are not as good as I;
promoting the worthy and appointing the capable,
each fulfilling their talents,
to preserve Jiāngdōng,
I am not as good as you."
Chén Shòu stated:
"Sūn Quán submitted and endured humiliation,
employed talent and esteemed strategy,
possessing the extraordinariness of Gōu Jiàn.
He was an outstanding man.
Thus he could independently control Jiāngbiǎo,
achieving the enterprise of a tripartite stalemate."
Jìn Xuāndì with his grand strategies and ingenious calculations,
and Zhūgě Liàng, a peerless extraordinary talent of his generation—
who was superior and who inferior?
Yú Nán said:
"Xuāndì rose from being a scholar,
participated in assisting the imperial enterprise,
aided the world in times of crisis and difficulty,
succeeded in clarifying the kingly way;
in both civil and military strategies,
he indeed had commendable aspects.
However, he often relied on covert schemes,
not following benevolence and righteousness,
suspicion, cruelty, deceit, and埋伏,
filled his bosom.
As for displaying false words to Lǐ Shèng,
entrusting the judicial trial to Hé Yàn,
these are actions that shame the heart and betray principle,
which a gentleman would not do.
With such hypocritical sentiments,
applied to all things,
if they had equal strength and balanced power,
meeting on the central plains,
with Zhòngdá's treacherous schemes
facing Kǒngmíng's disciplined command,
I fear he would not be a match."
Wú's Zhāng Yǎn in "Mò Jì" discussed the relative merits of the two chancellors Zhūgě Liàng and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng, saying:
"The Hàn dynasty collapsed and hegemony arose,
the empire fragmented,
both gentlemen encountered this juncture,
entrusting themselves to enlightened lords.
Kǒngmíng arose from the land of Shǔ Hàn,
treading upon a single province's territory,
compared to a great state,
it was about one-ninth its size.
Leading tens of thousands of infantry,
he drove deep into Qí Shān,
fervently aspiring to water his horses at the Hé and Luò rivers;
Zhòngdá held territory ten times larger,
commanding masses from annexed lands,
occupying secure cities,
possessing elite troops,
yet had no intention of capturing the enemy,
focusing solely on self-preservation.
Had that Kǒngmíng not died thus,
then Liáng and Yōng would not have unstrapped their armor,
the central states would not have removed their saddles,
the trend of victory or defeat would already have been decided.
Comparing him to Sīmǎ,
was he not superior?"
Someone asked:
"Jìn Jǐngdì and Wéndì,
which of the brothers was more virtuous?"
Wèi Míngdì passed away,
and his adopted son Qí Wáng Fáng was established,
with a testamentary decree appointing Cáo Shuǎng and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng as regents.
Xuānwáng executed Shuǎng,
and monopolized power.
Xuānwáng died,
and his son Jǐngwáng, named Shī, courtesy name Zǐyuán,
succeeded him as regent,
deposed Qí Wáng Fáng,
and established Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng.
Jǐngwáng died,
and his younger brother Wénwáng, named Zhāo, courtesy字 Zǐshàng,
again succeeded as regent,
killed Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng,
and established Chénliú Wáng.
Later, Chénliú Wáng ceded Wèi to Jìn,
Wǔdì, named Yán, courtesy字 Ānshì,
ascended the throne and pacified Wú,
unifying the empire.
When his son Huìdì succeeded,
the empire fell into great chaos,
and the Five Hú entered the central plains.
Yú Nán said:
"Hé Yàn claimed:
'Only through depth,
can one penetrate the will of the empire—
this is Xiàhóu Tàichū;
only through subtlety,
can one accomplish the affairs of the empire—
this is Sīmǎ Zǐyuán.'
Thus it is known that the talent to assist a king
was evident early on.
By the time of Shuǎng's execution,
his wisdom and strategy were already displayed;
when Qīn and Jiǎn raised troops,
he completely defeated them alone with his army,
this sufficiently shows his heroic plans.
Although his influence was strong enough for a tripartite division,
he remained a subject all his life,
his prestige shook his lord yet his ministerial integrity remained unblemished,
maintaining his marquisate intact and safe,
herein lies his excellence.
Tàizǔ succeeded and prospered,
quelling disasters and chaos,
pacifying Huáihǎi in the south,
subjugating Yōng and Shǔ in the west,
his campaigns not exceeding their time,
his achievements were substantial.
But when Gāoguì usurped the calendar,
despite his innate intelligence and wisdom,
he could not devote loyalty and support,
to emulate the traces of Yī and Zhōu;
instead, he falsely slandered Shì Yàn,
shifted blame to Chéng Jì,
bringing upon himself the stigma of treachery,
ultimately bearing an evil name—
this flaw in his words,
cannot be磨ed away."
Gān Bǎo's "Jìn Zǒng Lùn" stated:
"Previously, Xuāndì with his great talent and broad capacity,
responded to fate and entered service.
Encountering the initial founding of Wèi Tàizǔ's enterprise,
he planned military and state affairs,
his excellent strategies frequently hit the mark,
thus he served in the imperial carriage,
driving through three generations.
His nature was profound and guarded,
possessing depth and reserve,
yet he could be broad and accommodating,
acting with calculation to control things,
and knowing people, he selected and promoted them.
Thus he could capture Mèng Dá in the west,
subdue Gōngsūn Yuān in the east,
internally pacify Cáo Shuǎng,
externally suppress Wáng Líng,
repeatedly withstand the disciplined troops of Zhūgě Liàng,
and in the east support the interdependent situation with the Wú people.
Thereupon, the common people supported the capable,
and the great structure began to form.
Shìzōng inherited the foundation,
Tàizǔ continued the enterprise;
with Xuán and Fēng causing internal chaos,
Qīn and Dàn invading externally,
though their secret plots were tight,
the signs inevitably appeared;
though Huái and Pǔ were disturbed again,
Xǔ and Luò remained unshaken,
all heterodox plans were eliminated,
to glorify the former achievements.
Then they dispatched Zhōng and Dèng with authority,
who drove deep into Yōng and Shǔ.
The three passes were swept away like lightning,
Liú Chán became a subject.
Heavenly signs and human affairs,
thus were believed.
Initially, he received extraordinary rituals,
ultimately, he obtained the full regalia.
As for Shìzǔ,
he then enjoyed the imperial position,
benevolent in generously treating those below,
frugal in节制 expenses,
harmonious yet not lax,
broad yet capable of decision.
Thus people sang of renewal,
and all within the four seas were pleased and encouraged.
Sailing boats through the Three Gorges,
armoring horses in Guìyáng,
campaigns not lasting two seasons,
Jiāng and Xiāng came to submit.
Leveling the fortifications of Wú and Shǔ,
opening up the strategic passes of both regions.
During Tàikāng,
the empire wrote the same script,
used the same gauge for carts.
Though complete peace was not yet achieved,
it was sufficient to illuminate.
Officials performed their duties,
people enjoyed their livelihoods,
it was an era for the ages.
After Wǔhuáng's demise,
before his tomb was dry,
Yáng Jùn was executed,
the empress dowager was deposed,
Court officials and veteran ministers,
dozens of clans were exterminated.
Following the rebellions of the two dukes and the Prince of Chǔ,
the imperial clan lacked support to defend the realm,
and fraternal conflicts like those between Èbó and Shíchén arose year after year.
The high ministers held no esteemed authority for the people to look up to,
yet disasters of downfall, execution, and humiliation occurred daily.
The regional lords had no stabilizing power of even a slight measure,
and the strategic passes lacked the security of a tightly bound thicket.
Lǐ Chén and Shí Bīng
overthrew them in Jīng and Yáng provinces;
Liú Yuān and Wáng Mí
harassed them in Qīng and Jì provinces.
In just over twenty years, the Hé and Luò regions became ruins,
the Róng and Jié tribes claimed imperial authority,
the two emperors lost their dignity,
and had no refuge even in the mountains and forests.
Why was this?
Because the establishment of authority was misguided,
reliance was placed on incompetence,
the four moral pillars were not upheld,
and expedient governance was rampant.
Thus, observing Ruǎn Jí's conduct reveals the reasons for the collapse of rites and teachings;
examining the affairs of Yǔ Chún and Jiǎ Chōng shows the many biases of the high ministers;
pondering Guō Qīn's strategies awakens one to the vulnerabilities regarding the戎狄 tribes;
scrutinizing Fù Xián's memorials and the "Discourse on the God of Money" exposes the blatancy of favoritism and bribery.
With the people's customs and the state's situation as such,
even if governed by a ruler of average talent,
who adhered to established laws,
Xīn Yǒu would surely have foreseen it in the sacrifices,
Jì Zhá would have discerned it in the music,
Fàn Xiè would have pleaded to die for it,
Jiǎ Yì would have wept bitterly over it,
let alone our Emperor Huì, who presided over it with dissolute virtue?
Yet the brilliant legacy had not faded,
so the great mandate once again rested upon Emperor Yuán, the Middle Ancestor.
Of the Eastern Jìn emperors from Emperor Yuán onward,
which ruler was worthy?
Yú Nán said:
"Since the Jìn moved the capital east of the river,
powerful ministers arbitrarily held command,
while the emperors sat facing south with folded hands,
their governance not originating from themselves.
Wáng Dūn, of the firm rock-like imperial clan,
occupied the crucial upper reaches,
proud of his talent and location,
harbored ambitions to inquire about the鼎,
had it not been for Sùzǔ's clear decisiveness
and Wáng Dǎo's loyalty,
the Jìn throne would have shifted to the Wáng family.
If his reign had lasted longer,
relying on the multitude of worthies,
utilizing the remaining people of Chán and Jiàn,
and taking advantage of the declining fortunes of Liú and Shí,
then recovering the central plains
would not have been hard to achieve."
Emperor Yuán encountered the empire's collapse and fragmentation,
founding the regime east of the river.
Later, when Sùzǔ ascended the throne,
the great general Wáng Dūn's power shook both inside and out,
and he plotted rebellion.
The emperor, with Wáng Dǎo, Wēn Qiáo, and others, resolved to campaign against Dūn.
Dūn was defeated and died.
Someone asked:
"The false Chǔ ruler Huán Xuán had extraordinary talent and grand strategy,
yet he ended up destroyed;
why?"
Huán Xuán, courtesy name Jìngdào,
father Wēn.
The Grand Marshal Xuán was versed in various arts,
and regarded himself as a heroic figure.
Emperor Ān of Jìn made him chancellor,
enfeoffed him as Prince of Chǔ,
and then abdicated to him.
Yú Nán said:
"The measure of a ruler
must involve humbling oneself to respond to things,
encompassing and supporting like heaven and earth,
keeping promises as reliable as the warmth and cold of seasons,
only then will the myriad people gladly support and not weary of him.
That Huán Xuán,
possessed but the petty cunning of frivolous craftiness,
lacking the great virtue of magnanimity.
Encountering the late Jìn's decline and chaos,
where authority did not reach below,
thus Xuán could unleash his claws and teeth,
by a stroke of luck,
yet met with the divinely martial fortune,
leading to his extermination;
it was indeed fitting."
Yùzǐ said:
"Issuing governance and enacting decrees
that bring blessing to all under heaven
is called the Way.
Rulers and subjects being close to each other
is called harmony.
The people obtaining what they desire without seeking it
is called trust.
Eliminating the harms of all under heaven
is called benevolence.
Benevolence and trust,
harmony and the Way,
are the tools of emperors and kings."
From this perspective,
the petty wisdom of the heroic and bold,
what benefit is it to being gladly supported?
The Sòng ancestor exterminated Huán Xuán,
reviving the Jìn house once more.
In the Liáng dynasty, Péi Zǐyě considered him superior to Xuānwǔ;
what is this about?
Yú Nán said:
"Wèi's Wǔ,
grandson of Cáo Téng,
enjoyed glory and prominence for generations,
serving the Hàn court with distinction,
for over thirty years.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
he rose with the eastern leaders,
eliminating the chief villain,
yet it was not solely by his own strength.
Jìn's Xuān held successive high ministerial posts,
reaching the pinnacle of the court,
holding the maps of the empire,
situated in a secure position,
upholding the clear decree to punish rebellious elements;
using the analogy of water pouring down from a high roof
is not enough to describe it.
The Sòng ancestor, a commoner raising his sword,
initiated the great enterprise first.
Within months,
he restored the Jìn鼎 securely,
holding but half a province's territory,
driving a single commandery's troops,
he beheaded Qián Zòng in Yōng-Shǔ,
captured Yáo Shào in Xiáo-Hán,
defeated Mùróng Chāo in Qīng province,
and executed Lú Xún beyond the ridges.
Wherever his banners pointed,
there was no advance not victorious.
Observing his openness and magnanimity,
he had the style of the Hàn ancestor;
in his breast for achieving victory,
he was the equal of Guāngwǔ.
Pity his reign was short,
his ambitions immeasurable!
This is why he is considered superior."
Péi Zǐyě said:
"Emperor Wǔ of Sòng,
had more remarkable deeds than Wèi's Wǔ,
and greater virtue than Jìn's Xuān.
Rising from the ranks,
he repelled Sūn Ēn's ant-like swarming masses;
raising his arm in Jīng and Yǐng,
he swept away Huán Xuán's rock-solid clan.
Advancing swiftly on broad fronts, then Sān Qí had no strong fortresses;
turning his blades inward, then the five ridges were cleared of remaining demons.
Ordering Sūn Jìgāo from the vast sea, he rolled up Fānyú like a mat;
promoting Zhū Língshí from among a hundred men, Yōng-Shǔ came to pledge allegiance.
The Qiāng and Hú feared his might,
instead becoming his inner and outer allies.
Leading fierce troops,
he engaged the central plains.
Thence, calling upon the high emperor,
pacing with the former kings,
gloriously possessing the imperial plan,
it is said he righteously seized it."
He also said:
"Huán Jìngdào had extraordinary civil and military talent,
determined to wash away the remaining shame,
cunningly moving amid separation and chaos,
possessing all under heaven without bloodshed.
Then, summoning the six directions,
planning for advancement and conquest,
before a year had passed,
he unlawfully seized the state,
considering himself more renowned than the Hàn ancestor,
his achievements swifter than Wèi and Jìn,
he thought to monopolize his extravagance,
hoping to be revered passively.
Had Wáng Mì and Huán Qiān, with their popular esteem, pacified and led,
and the inner Wáng Suí and Xiè Hùn, with the younger generation, mutually enhancing the glory,
with cousins and brothers
across provinces and connected commanderies,
the people, startled by his speed, would submit to his strength,
with no divergent hopes.
Gāozǔ at that time
was but a commoner from Zhūfāng,
without even a thousand followers,
yet he rallied allied forces,
struck two provinces like lightning,
in less than half a month,
cleansed the capital city,
issued commands to all lords,
drove straight through Jiāng and Hàn,
pushed the dying Chǔ into vulnerable gaps,
lifted the failing Jìn from its collapse,
since the time of Xuānyuán,
the speed of military action
had never been seen before.
Unless one had unparalleled grand strategy,
If the Mandate of Heaven has not ceased,
how could it be like this?
Thereupon, people knew where to turn,
and the kingly path flourished."
Emperor Xiaowu and Emperor Ming of the Liu Song dynasty—
which of the two was more virtuous?
Yú Nán said:
"The cruel nature of these two emperors
was like two bodies sharing one heart.
They executed the virtuous and capable,
cutting off their own branches and leaves.
Internally, they lacked chancellors like Chén Píng or Zhōu Bó;
externally, they were without close relatives like those of Jìn or Zhèng.
Thus, they entrusted the great treasure
to foolish and immature heirs,
allowing the Qí clan to seize the opportunity
to control the empire.
Before a year had passed,
the imperial authority was transferred.
Though the cord and seal were secure,
they merely became assets for the great robbers.
All their considerations led to the same failure—
it is truly lamentable.
The collapse of the imperial altar
was not unfortunate."
Emperor Xiaowu, named Jùn,
was the third son of Emperor Wén,
serving as the governor of Jiāngzhōu.
After his younger brother Shào assassinated the emperor,
he, along with Yán Jùn, raised an army from Jiāngzhōu to campaign against Shào
and pacified him.
Emperor Ming, named Yù,
was the eighteenth son of Emperor Wén.
Upon ascending the throne,
he killed all of Emperor Xiaowu's sons,
indulged in excessive ornamentation,
causing turmoil throughout the land.
After his death,
his son Yù succeeded him,
but he was tyrannical,
and Xiāo Dàochéng had him killed.
During the Jiànyuán and Yǒngmíng eras of the Qí dynasty,
it was hailed as an age of good governance—
was this truly the case?
Yú Nán said:
"Emperor Gāo of Qí, as a founding ruler,
understood the hardships of farming,
maintained a frugal and simple life,
and strived for simplicity and economy.
Emperor Wǔ, however, was preoccupied with his harem,
and his extravagance was excessive.
Yet he was able to appoint Wáng Jiǎn to office,
and regulations were established;
the flourishing of rites and music
was all credited to the Yǒngmíng era.
Having the right person as chancellor
was the beauty of that time."
Discussion says:
When Confucius spoke of Duke Líng of Wèi's tyranny,
Kangzi said:
"If so,
why did he not lose his state?"
Confucius replied:
"Zhòng Shū Yǔ managed foreign guests,
Zhù Tuó oversaw ancestral temples,
and Wángsūn Jiǎ commanded the military.
With such arrangements,
why would he lose it?"
This illustrates the virtue of entrusting duties to the capable.
When Tián Dān served as chancellor of Qí,
he crossed the Zī River
and encountered an elderly man shivering from the cold after wading through it.
Tián Dān took off his fur robe and clothed him.
King Xiāng resented this,
saying:
"Tián Dān's generous acts
are meant to usurp my state, are they not?
If I do not act soon,
I fear it will be too late."
This shows the harm of entrusting power to the virtuous.
Thus, when the Marquis of Qí resented the Chén clan's virtue,
Yànzǐ told the Marquis:
"According to ritual,
household generosity should not extend to the state,
and a minister should not claim public benefits—
this can stop them."
When King Xiāng of Qí resented Tián Dān's generosity,
the pearl stringer advised the king:
"Your Majesty should instead praise Tián Dān's goodness,
declaring:
'I worry about the people's hunger,
and Tián Dān feeds them;
I worry about the people's cold,
and Tián Dān clothes them with his robe.
This aligns with my intentions.'
By commending Tián Dān for his good deeds,
his virtues
become Your Majesty's as well."
Later, the villagers said to each other:
"Tián Dān's care for the people
is taught by the king."
To manage the power of subordinates,
one should follow the examples of Yànzǐ and the pearl stringer.
In the past, when Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was gravely ill,
Empress Lǚ asked about the chancellorship,
and he said:
"Cáo Cān is suitable."
When asked about the next,
he said:
"Wáng Líng is suitable,
though somewhat simple-minded;
Chén Píng can assist him.
Chén Píng has ample wisdom,
but is difficult to rely on alone.
Zhōu Bó is steadfast but lacks refinement,
yet the one who will secure the Liú clan
must be Zhōu Bó.
He can be appointed as Grand Commandant."
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Liú Song was critically ill,
he cautioned the crown prince:
"Tán Dàojì, though capable, lacks long-term vision;
Xú Xiànzhī and Fù Liàng likely have no treacherous intentions;
Xiè Huì, who often accompanied campaigns,
is quite adept at seizing opportunities.
If there is any dissent,
it will surely come from him.
He can be assigned to Kuàijī."
Employing the worthy and capable
should be like Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn and Emperor Gāozǔ of Liú Song.
In the two dynasties of Liú Song and Qí,
five rulers were deposed,
all arrogant, licentious, and tyrannical,
consistent in their behavior.
Some were killed by assassins,
others brought ruin to their ancestral altars.
Was it due to their inherently stubborn and vicious nature,
bringing misfortune upon themselves,
or were they abandoned by Heaven,
leading to the loss of their great enterprise?
Yú Nán said:
"The supremely wise and the utterly foolish
are endowed with unique temperaments;
those of average talent
are shaped by training and habituation.
Since the Liú Song and Qí dynasties,
the tutors of the crown prince
were merely nominal appointments.
Separated by status and ritual,
guidance was inaccessible;
most advanced by rank,
rarely by virtue.
These five rulers,
possessing mediocre natures,
lacked teachers like the Duke of Zhōu or Shào,
were distant from the admonitions of beneficial friends,
and familiar with flatterers and close attendants.
With such inferior qualities,
they were born speaking the language of Chǔ—
the downfall of their state and their own demise
was inevitable by reason and fate."
Discussion says:
Master Jiǎ stated:
"In the past, when King Chéng was young,
still in swaddling clothes,
the Duke of Shào served as Grand Guardian,
the Duke of Zhōu as Grand Mentor,
and the Grand Duke as Grand Preceptor.
The Guardian
protected his physical well-being;
the Mentor
imparted moral righteousness;
the Preceptor
guided his education.
These were the duties of the Three Dukes.
Additionally, three junior positions were established,
namely Junior Mentor, Junior Guardian, and Junior Preceptor,
who accompanied the crown prince in daily life.
Thus, from infancy and early awareness,
the Three Dukes and Three Juniors firmly instructed him in filial piety, benevolence, rites, and righteousness through guidance and practice,
driving away evil individuals,
preventing him from witnessing wicked deeds;
selecting upright scholars, filial and fraternal, widely learned, and possessing moral principles from across the land to protect and assist him,
allowing them to reside with the crown prince.
Hence, the crown prince was born to see proper actions, hear proper words, and follow the proper path.
All around him,
were righteous people.
When one habitually lives with the righteous,
one cannot avoid becoming righteous,
just as growing up in Qí,
one cannot avoid speaking the Qí dialect;
when one habitually lives with the unrighteous,
just as growing up in Chǔ,
one cannot avoid speaking the Chǔ dialect.
Qín had Zhào Gāo mentor Hú Hài, teaching him punishments,
so what he learned was nothing but beheading, nose-cutting, or exterminating three clans.
Thus, the day Hú Hài ascended the throne,
he was shooting people the next.
He labeled loyal remonstrators as slanderers,
and deep strategists as spreaders of heresy,
viewing killing people as mowing down grass.
Was Húhài inherently evil?
The guidance he received was not in accordance with proper principles."
When Crown Prince Yù of Jìn Huìdì committed a crime,
Yán Zuǎn submitted a memorial advising:
"I reflect that Yù was raised deep within the palace,
immersed in wealth and nobility,
spoiled by the late emperor,
and indulged by his parents.
Whenever tutors were selected,
down to the various officials,
they generally chose those from wealthy families living in luxury,
rarely including scholars from humble backgrounds,
such as Wèi Wǎn or Zhōu Wén;
neither the tutors nor attendants
were comparable to Jí Àn or Zhèng Zhuāng,
thus he never learned the way of serving sovereign and father.
According to ancient rites,
the crown prince should observe the rituals of a common scholar and interact with the people,
intending to make him understand humility,
before he assumes nobility.
Recently, the Eastern Palace has also declined,
but it's not only the Eastern Palace that fails due to excessive privilege.
Not only the Eastern Palace,
but also the teachers, friends, and literary officials for the various princes
are selected from powerful families who can obtain such positions—
how can there be refinement,
or mutual improvement?
Now Yù's words are rebellious and contrary,
yet on the day he received punishment,
he did not fail in his duties as a son—
it is still possible to carefully reselect tutors.
Establish wandering scholars and literary officials,
all chosen from those who grew up in hardship and solitude and established themselves through learning and conduct,
and those who have experienced difficulties and established their reputation and conduct,
to let them accompany and interact.
Exclude the children of noble relatives and frivolous guests,
only communicating about filial sons, kind parents, loyal ministers serving their sovereign throughout history,
and reflecting on faults and correcting mistakes,
all hearing of good ways,
so that perhaps he can be preserved."
From this we see,
we know that for a crown prince,
selecting the right attendants,
to teach him through example,
is most urgent.
Liáng Yuándì was intelligent and talented,
capable of quelling disasters and chaos,
yet ultimately led to collapse.
Why?
Yuándì,
the seventh son of Liáng Wǔdì,
named Yì,
was the governor of Jīngzhōu.
He defeated Hóu Jǐng,
established his capital in Jīngzhōu,
but when Wèi's Wànniǔ Yú Jǐn came to attack,
captured and killed him.
Yú Nán said:
"Liáng Yuán's intelligence and skills,
talent in both civil and military arts,
wielding righteousness to crusade against rebellion,
avenging his family's wrongs,
achieving success in his endeavors,
are indeed commendable.
But after the national crisis,
when wounds had not yet healed,
he trusted the sweet words of a strong enemy,
clung to narrow-mindedness in his Chu domain,
alienated his own clan making them enemies,
isolated in a remote and secluded place,
with none to share his worries,
resulting in his death and the end of his reign,
the people suffering greatly,
abandoning Yān and Yǐng—
truly a pity."
Discussion says:
Huáinánzǐ states:
"Benevolence and wisdom
are the beauty of talent.
What is called benevolence
is loving others;
what is called wisdom
is understanding others.
Loving others means no cruel punishments,
understanding others means no chaotic governance.
This is why the Three Dynasties flourished.
Zhì Bó had five exceptional talents,
yet could not avoid dying by others' hands—
because he did not love others;
Qí Wáng Jiàn had three exceptional skills,
but was captured by Qín—
because he did not recognize worthies.
Thus, nothing is greater than loving others for benevolence,
nothing greater than understanding others for wisdom.
Without these two,
even with keen intelligence and quick wit,
one cannot avoid chaos."
Some say:
"With Zhōu Wǔ's heroic talent and military strategy,
leading from the front,
if heaven had granted him more years,
to fully employ his military plans,
he could surely have unified the land,
becoming a brilliant ruler of his era?"
Yú Nán said:
"Zhōu Wǔ was brave, resolute, and decisive,
with extraordinary strategies.
Observing his humility in motivating his men,
and strict enforcement of laws,
even Gōu Jiàn or Ráng Jū
would not be more renowned under heaven.
This suits a fierce general's role,
not the measure of a sovereign."
From this we see,
a ruler who rectifies chaos
should first focus on recruiting ministers and generals as the foundation;
personal prowess in battle
is not to be relied upon.
Thus Liú Xiàng said:
"Understanding people
is the way of kings;
managing affairs
is the duty of ministers.
Skill in arts or battle—
what benefit does it bring?"
Later, Qí Wénxuāndì's
mad and irrational actions,
things even Jié and Zhòu would not do,
yet the state was wealthy and people prosperous,
not leading to chaos and downfall.
Why?
Xuāndì, named Yáng,
second son of Later Qí's Gāo Huān,
received the throne from Later Wèi.
Yú Nán said:
"In the past, Qí Huán's extravagance and loss of propriety
were rejected by human relations,
but he lent his authority to Zhòngfù,
thus becoming hegemon of the feudal lords.
Wénxuāndì was despicable, cruel, and brutal,
unmatched in ancient or modern times,
yet he entrusted state affairs to Zūnyàn,
preserving the ancestral state—
because his appointments found talent,
thus the nation survived."
Discussion says:
Yīn had three benevolent men,
Tàikāng had five brothers,
all worthy individuals,
yet the state became ruins—
why?
Yùzǐ said:
"A gentleman in planning with others
can ensure he follows the right path,
but cannot ensure his advice is accepted;
can ensure his loyalty,
but cannot ensure it is taken in;
can ensure his honesty,
but cannot ensure he is trusted.
Thus, Duke Yú did not adopt Gōng Zhīqí's advice,
and was destroyed by Jìn;
Chóuyóu did not heed Chì Zhāng's words,
and perished under Zhìshì.
Every state under heaven
has loyal ministers and strategists,
but it depends on whether they are used or not.
If not used,
it instead brings blame upon the ruler;
how can worthy gentlemen
save them from defeat and chaos?"
Chén Wǔdì rose from humble origins,
founding an imperial enterprise—
in recent times,
with which ruler can he be compared?
Yú Nán said:
"Wǔdì, with his extraordinary talent and broad strategy,
harboring the ambition to restore,
leaped like a dragon from the seashore,
transformed like a leopard south of the mountains,
swept away heavy miasmas at the crimson palace,
restored the imperial seat in the Purple Tenuity.
Resisting Zhōu's armies in the west,
subduing Qí's invaders in the north,
with grand plans and long-term strategies,
every move without miscalculation—
truly a commendable founder,
a heroic talent in rectifying chaos.
Compared to Sòng Zǔ, he falls short;
measured against Qí Gāo, he is superior."
Suí Wéndì rose from common cloth,
and brilliantly possessed the divine vessel.
Pacifying Yōng and Shǔ in the west,
subduing Jiāngbiǎo in the south—
compared to Jìn Wǔ,
can he be considered his equal?
Yú Nán said:
"Suí Wén, relying on the influence of his maternal relatives,
and the decline of the Zhōu house,
bearing the chart as prime minister,
thus received the precious mandate.
He paid close attention to governance,
diligently bestowed kindness and favor,
thus he was able to pacify both old and new subjects,
bringing peace to distant and nearby regions,
with military and civil administration
all being commendable.
After conquering the Jiānghuái region,
all adopted uniform writing and track standards,
and the common people across the land
eagerly awaited lasting peace.
However, after the fall of Jīnlíng,
the king's heart grew extravagant and decadent;
although his might extended across the four seas,
his attention neglected myriad affairs of state.
Precious jades filled the inner treasury,
and Wú beauties crowded the inner chambers.
The Rénshòu Palace was extravagantly adorned,
rivaling the legendary leaning palace,
exhausting the strength of the populace,
and depleting the wealth of ordinary families.
Moreover, suspicion and jealousy arose in his heart,
leading to incidents of sorcery and witchcraft.
He executed the wife of his beloved son,
and separated the mother of the chief minister
—when the "cat specter" affair erupted,
the wife of the Qín prince and the mother of the minister Yáng Sù
were implicated and punished.
The legal and moral order had become disordered,
and rites and teachings thus perished.
The hen crowed at dawn (a woman meddled in state affairs),
the imperial lineage was decimated,
the innocent were deposed,
and favorites were elevated
—deposing the crown prince Yǒng to commoner status,
and establishing the prince of Jìn, Guǎng, instead.
Meritorious officials and good advisors
were executed without exception.
The failures of his later years
exceeded those of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
and the dynasty's reign did not last long—
was it Heaven that caused its downfall?"
Discussion states:
When Hàn Emperor Gāozǔ wanted to replace the crown prince with the prince of Zhào, Rúyì,
Shūsūn Tōng remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Duke Xiàn of Jìn, because of Lí Jī,
deposed the crown prince,
and established Xī Qí,
causing decades of chaos in Jìn,
and becoming the laughingstock of the world.
Qín, by not early establishing Fú Sū,
allowed Zhào Gāo to deceitfully install Hú Hài,
leading to its own destruction.
This is what Your Majesty has personally witnessed.
Now if Your Majesty insists on deposing the legitimate heir to establish a younger son,
I wish to be executed first,
staining the ground with the blood from my neck."
The emperor said:
"I was only joking."
Tōng said:
"The crown prince is the foundation of the empire;
once this foundation is shaken,
the whole empire will be shaken.
How can one joke about the empire?"
Then he heeded the advice.
Yuán Shào favored his younger son Shàng,
and made the elder son Tán inherit as if he were the son of his elder brother.
Jǔ Shòu remonstrated, saying:
"It is said that when ten thousand chase a rabbit,
and one catches it,
all the greedy stop,
because the division is settled.
Moreover, if age is equal, choose the virtuous;
if virtue is equal, choose the elder—
this is the system of antiquity.
I hope Your Majesty will consider the warnings of past successes and failures,
and reflect on the principle of the rabbit chase and settled division.
If this is not changed,
disaster will begin here."
Yuán Shào did not listen,
and later conflict indeed arose.
Therefore it is said:
"Establishing the嫡子嫡子 (legitimate eldest son)
prevents doubts from lesser favorites.
Doubt leads to unrest,
and having two leads to contention.
When there are two sons in contention for the position,
the family will surely be in chaos;
if there are two sons contending
yet the family is not in chaos,
it is because the parents are still alive.
Relying on the parents prevents chaos,
but losing them will inevitably lead to chaos."
How profound this is.
Some ask:
"Regarding the strategies of kings and hegemons,
I shall follow these words.
May I ask about posthumous naming (shì) after death,
and changing the calendar and
altering the color of garments,
to change what people see and hear—
what do these practices symbolize?"
The response is:
"In ancient times, establishing a posthumous name
was meant to caution later generations,
bestowing a name according to one's conduct,
with no concealment for ruler or parent.
Nowadays, ministers and sons do not consider the reality of the name,
but only strive for honor and elevation—
this practice has long been corrupted."
In the past, Jì Kāngzǐ asked Confucius about the virtues of the Five Emperors,
and Confucius said:
"Heaven has the five agents:
wood, fire, metal, water, and earth.
They divide the seasons to transform and nurture,
thereby completing all things."
In a year of three hundred sixty days,
each of the five agents operates for seventy-two days,
transforming, growing, and nurturing.
Their spirits are the Five Emperor Constellations
—the Five Emperors
are the spirits of the five agents.
Ancient kings,
upon changing dynasties and titles,
modeled themselves on the five agents.
The five agents take turns ruling,
ending and beginning in mutual production,
also symbolizing this principle.
Thus, those who were enlightened kings in life
are matched with the five agents in death.
Therefore, Tàihào is matched with wood
—Gōu Máng was the official of wood;
Yán Dì is matched with fire
—Zhù Róng was the official of fire;
Shǎohào is matched with metal
—Rù Shōu was the official of metal;
Zhuān Xū is matched with water
—Xuán Míng was the official of water;
Huáng Dì is matched with earth
—Hòu Tǔ was the official of earth.
When emperors and kings changed their titles,
for the virtue of the five agents,
each had their preferred element.
They followed the order of the virtue they ruled by
—the wood line follows with fire.
The wood line favors red,
because the virtue of wood signifies universal righteousness,
following its mother (water),
while also including its son (fire).
The Xiàhòu clan ruled by metal virtue and favored black;
the Yīn people ruled by water virtue and favored white
—the water line favors blue,
but they favored white
to avoid the earth line's preference for blue.
The earth line should favor white,
but as earth
is the master of the four agents,
presiding over the four seasons,
and the five agents in operation
start with wood,
thus the earth line favors the color of wood, blue.
The Zhōu people ruled by wood virtue and favored red in color.
This is why the three dynasties differed.
By the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
Gōngsūn Chén and Jiǎ Yì believed Hàn had earth virtue,
based on the transmission of the five agents,
following the unconquered order
—the transmission of succession.
The Five Emperors succeeded each other
always by the method of mutual conquest among metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
Qín was in the water virtue phase,
so they said Hàn, possessing earth, conquered it.
Liú Xiàng and his son believed the emperor emerged from Zhèn (east, wood),
so Páo Xī Shì first received wood virtue,
thereafter passing from mother to son,
ending and beginning again.
From Shénnóng and Huáng Dì,
down through Táng, Yú, and the three dynasties,
Hàn obtained fire virtue.
Thus, when Gāozǔ first rose,
a divine mother cried out at night,
displaying the omen of the Red Emperor,
and he obtained the legitimate succession.
In the past, Gòng Gōng with water virtue intervened between wood and fire,
sharing the same fate as Qín,
not in the proper order,
so both did not last long.
In my view,
the rise of emperors and kings
each bases itself on the lineage of the Five Emperors from which they descend,
to determine the five virtues.
How can this be illustrated?
Hàn
is the descendant of Yáo.
Yáo
ruled with fire virtue.
Thus Han corresponds to Fire.
