During Yuán Shào's time, Gěng Bāo said:
"The virtue of Red has declined and exhausted,
Yuán is the Yellow descendant,
believing that Yuán was a descendant of Shùn,
and Shùn was a ruler of Earth virtue,
therefore he urged advancement."
This shows that the rise of emperors and kings,
each is rooted in their origin,
the descendants of the Five Emperors,
have their reasons for coming.
Now Qin,
being descendants of Zhuānxū,
is of Water virtue.
Thus Qin corresponds to Water virtue.
From this perspective,
even a hundred generations can be known.
Chapter Ten: On Ministers' Conduct
When a subject perceives the subtle signs before they emerge,
discerns the faint indications before they appear,
and clearly foresees the turning points of survival and demise,
the crux of gain and loss,
preventing them before they occur,
enabling the ruler to stand loftily in glory and honor—
such a person
is a sage minister.
With an open mind and full dedication,
he daily presents virtuous ways;
encourages the ruler with ritual and righteousness,
advising him with long-term strategies;
supporting and following his good deeds,
while rectifying and rescuing him from his faults.
Such a person
is a great minister.
Rising early and retiring late,
he tirelessly recommends the worthy,
frequently citing the deeds of ancient times
to inspire the ruler's resolve.
Such a person
is a loyal minister.
Someone asked Yuánzǐ:
"Was not the former Shǎofǔ Yǎng Fù
a loyal minister?"
He replied:
"He may be called an upright scholar,
but I do not know about loyalty.
Why?
For a subject,
upon seeing the ruler's misguided ways,
to point out his errors and publicize his faults—
this may be called an upright scholar,
but not necessarily loyal.
The former Sīkōng Chén Qún, however, was different.
In conversations all day long,
he never spoke of the ruler's faults;
he submitted dozens of memorials, yet outsiders remained unaware.
Gentlemen say that Chén Qún was thus a true elder.
This is loyalty."
Clearly observing success and failure,
preventing and remedying them early,
blocking the gaps,
cutting off the sources,
turning disaster into blessing,
so that the ruler remains free of worry—
such a person
is a wise minister.
Adhering to texts and upholding laws,
serving in office and duties,
accepting no gifts or bribes,
and being frugal in food and drink—
such a person
is a chaste minister.
When the state is in turmoil and confusion,
his actions are not flattering;
he dares to confront the ruler's stern countenance
and speak of his faults to his face.
Such a person
is a straightforward minister.
These are called the Six Uprights.
Huán Fàn's "Shì Yào Lùn" says:
"Some ministers have clumsy words but skillful intentions,
harsh speech but beneficial actions—
should they not be tolerated for their uprightness?
Some ministers are simple and slow of speech,
outwardly coarse but inwardly sharp—
should they not be tolerated for their substance?
Some ministers face hardship for their superiors,
endure slander for the state—
should they not be tolerated for their loyalty?
Some ministers uphold righteousness against popular opinion,
enforce laws against private desires—
should they not be tolerated for their impartiality?
Some ministers do not bend themselves to seek agreement,
nor harm the world to gain fame—
should they not be tolerated for their integrity?
Some ministers, from obscurity, present wise words,
from lowly status, advise on state affairs—
should they not be tolerated for their difficulty?
Some ministers stand alone and uphold principles,
remain independent and face slander—
should they not be tolerated for their firmness?
These seven tolerances
are means to promote goodness."
Holding office and coveting salary,
neglecting public duties,
drifting with the times,
looking left and right—
such a person
is a mere minister.
Saying 'good' to all the ruler says,
'yes' to all the ruler does,
secretly seeking the ruler's preferences to present them,
pleasing the ruler's ears and eyes—
blindly agreeing and flattering,
sharing pleasure with the ruler,
heedless of future harm—
such a person
is a sycophantic minister.
Inwardly treacherous and wicked,
outwardly cautious and careful,
with clever words and ingratiating looks,
yet envious of the worthy—
promoting those he favors by highlighting their virtues,
hiding their faults;
demoting those he dislikes by exposing their errors,
concealing their merits—
causing the ruler's rewards and punishments to be unjust, commands unenforceable.
Such a person
is a treacherous minister.
Intellect sufficient to cover up wrongs,
eloquence enough to promote arguments,
dividing kin within,
sowing discord at court without—
such a person
is a slanderous minister.
Monopolizing power and control,
treating the light as heavy;
forming cliques for private gain,
enriching their families;
forging the ruler's orders,
to elevate themselves—
such a person
is a usurping minister.
Misleading the ruler with cunning and evil,
dragging him into unrighteousness,
forming factions and cliques,
obscuring the ruler's clarity,
blurring right and wrong, black and white;
spreading the ruler's disgrace within the borders and to neighboring states—
such a person
is a minister of a doomed state.
These are called the Six Evils.
Huán Fàn's "Shì Yào Lùn" says:
"Some ministers establish minor loyalty to sell great disloyalty,
display small trust to achieve great deceit—
should they not be guarded against for their fraud?
Some ministers appear stern but are weak within,
outwardly benevolent but act contrary—
should they not be guarded against for their falseness?
Some ministers harm colleagues to monopolize the court,
block lower voices to deceive the ruler—
should they not be guarded against for their envy?
Some ministers advance evil theories to confuse truth,
use semblances to harm the worthy—
should they not be guarded against for their slander?
Some ministers use rewards to repay favors,
use punishments to assert authority—
should they not be guarded against for their treachery?
Some ministers outwardly recommend,
inwardly scheme to remove,
conduct affairs under public guise but with private motives—
should they not be guarded against for their deceit?
Some ministers serve attendants to seek advancement,
rely on powerful ministers to secure ties—
should they not be guarded against for their hypocrisy?
Some ministers harmonize to gain approval,
comply blindly to advance—
should they not be guarded against for their harm?
Some ministers please the ruler's will to gain closeness,
delight in his words to win favor—
should they not be guarded against for their flattery?
These nine cautions
are means to prevent evil."
Zǐgòng said:
"Lord Líng of Chén and his ministers flaunted debauchery in court,
Xiè Yě remonstrated and was killed—
this is like Bǐgān's case;
can he be called benevolent?"
The Master said:
"Bǐgān, to Zhòu,
was kin as his uncle,
in office as Shǎoshī;
his sincere, loyal heart
aimed at preserving the ancestral temple,
so he contended unto certain death,
hoping Zhòu would repent after his death.
His fundamental intent was benevolent.
Xiè Yě held the position of a lower minister,
with no blood ties,
clinging to favor without leaving,
with his single, insignificant self,
trying to correct a state's depravity and folly—
his death was of no benefit;
he may be called devoted!
The 'Shī' says:
'When the people are perverse,
do not make yourself a law.'
Does this refer to Xiè Yě?"
Someone asked:
"Shūsūn Tōng flattered the Second Emperor's wishes—
was that acceptable?"
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Assessing the ruler before advancing
was praised by former sages.
Shūsūn Tōng迎合ed the times,
devised rites according to circumstances,
advancing or retreating with changing times,
and ultimately became the Confucian patriarch of the Hàn dynasty."
The noble persons of antiquity,
were upright yet not rigid,
pliant yet not bending,
the greatest uprightness appears as yielding,
their path akin to the undulating snake,
this saying refers to them indeed. "
Discussion says:
Tàigōng stated:
"Officials who do not intend to remonstrate,
are not my officials. "
Zhū Yún confronted Zhāng Yǔ saying:
"Those who enjoy emoluments and preserve their positions,
incapable of action,
deserve beheading. "
Bān Gù remarked:
"Conforming to the world leads to abandoning the Dào,
defying customs brings peril,
this is why the ancients found it difficult to accept official ranks. "
From this perspective,
survival and death,
what is their righteousness?
The response states:
Fàn Yè asserted:
"Exclusive pursuit of righteousness harms life,
exclusive pursuit of life compromises righteousness.
If righteousness outweighs life,
sacrificing life is permissible;
if life outweighs righteousness,
preserving life is permissible. "
Someone asked:
"Then were Dòu Wǔ and Chén Fān,
who contended with eunuchs in the imperial court,
ultimately executed by them,
in the wrong? "
Fàn Yè said:
"During the Huán and Líng emperors' era,
those like Chén Fān,
all succeeded in establishing moral influence,
resisting corrupt customs through discourse,
navigating treacherous paths,
and contending with decadent men,
yet ultimately faced destruction—
it was not that they failed to purify their aspirations,
or avoid the dust and fog.
They pitied worldly scholars,
who considered detachment from society as noble,
yet showed no mutual compassion in human relations;
deeming withdrawal from the world as unrighteous,
they repeatedly declined but did not depart;
bearing humaneness as their responsibility,
though the Dào was distant, they grew more determined.
When opportunity arose,
coordinating strategies with Dòu Wǔ,
it could be called a rare chance across millennia.
Though their efforts did not culminate,
their integrity and righteousness sufficiently upheld the world's conscience. "
Discussion says:
This exemplifies righteousness outweighing life,
where sacrificing life is permissible.
Another asked:
"Zāng Hóng died in the calamity of Zhāng Chāo,
can this be called righteous? "
Fàn Yè commented:
"During the siege of Yōngqiū,
Zāng Hóng's indignation,
was truly heroic!
Observing him barefoot and wailing,
arming his troops for action,
was indeed pitiable.
Do the choices of heroes
differ from the heart of upholding righteousness?
As for forming alliances and strategies,
harboring deceitful schemes to compete,
they merely follow power and profit.
Moreover, with the isolated city endangered,
and Cáo, Yuán harmoniously aligned,
Hóng merely pointed to external enemies' threats,
to relieve a desperate situation—
an army driven by wrath,
is cautioned against by military strategists,
it may be said he cherished the integrity of weeping for Qín,
but preserving Jīng was unheard of. "
Formerly, Zhāng Chāo, governor of Guǎnglíng, entrusted governance to Zāng Hóng,
later Yuán Shào also befriended him.
When Cáo Cāo besieged Zhāng Chāo in Yōngqiū,
Hóng heard of the siege,
went barefoot weeping,
marshaled troops to rescue Chāo,
and requested reinforcements from Shào,
but Shào refused,
Chāo's city fell,
leading to Chāo's execution and clan extermination.
Hóng thus resented Shào,
severed ties with him,
Shào raised troops to besiege him,
city fell and Hóng was executed.
Discussion says:
Zāng Hóng, in an era of political maneuvering,
practiced commonplace righteousness,
was no achiever of merit.
Another asked:
"Jì Bù was a stalwart man,
yet turned firmness into suppleness,
shaved head, wore clamp, hid in disguise,
was this appropriate? "
Sīmǎ Qiān stated:
"With Xiàng Yǔ's ferocity,
Jì Bù gained renown for bravery in Chǔ,
personally led armies repeatedly,
captured
(pronounced qǐ lián fǎn)
enemy flags multiple times,
could be called a stalwart.
Yet when facing execution,
became a slave without choosing death,
He surely prided on his talent,
thus endured disgrace without shame,
wishing to utilize his unrealized potential,
thus eventually became a famed Hàn general.
The worthy truly value their deaths.
Maidservants and lowly persons,
who kill themselves impulsively,
display no courage,
their options exhausted,
with no alternatives. "
Discussion says:
Grand Historian stated:
"Though Wèi Bào and Péngchéng were originally lowly,
they swept across a thousand lǐ,
declared themselves rulers facing south,
stained with blood, riding victories,
daily heard of achievements.
Harboring rebellious intentions,
upon defeat,
they did not die but were captured,
imprisoned and executed,
why?
Even those of medium talent would be ashamed of such acts,
let alone kings!
They were no different,
their wisdom and strategy surpassing others,
only concerned with preserving life.
Gaining even a slight hold of power,
they transformed like clouds and dragons,
seeking to realize their ambitions,
thus enduring confinement without refusal. "
These were maneuvering strategists,
striving to establish merit.
Also, the "Eulogy of Lord Lìn" states:
"Knowing death necessitates courage,
dying is not difficult,
facing death is difficult.
When Lìn Xiàngrú held the jade, eyed the pillar,
and rebuked the Qín king's attendants,
the worst was execution,
yet some scholars, timid, dared not act.
Xiàngrú, once rousing his spirit,
awed the enemy state with prestige;
retreating and yielding to Lián Pō,
his fame outweighed Tàishān.
In handling wisdom and courage,
he could be called possessing both! "
These were loyal and steadfast ministers,
truly knowing the purpose of death.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Not ashamed of being in bonds,
but ashamed of the world's disorder;
not ashamed of not dying for Prince Jiū,
but ashamed of prestige not extending among the feudal lords. "
This reflects self-confidence in one's talent,
aiming to aid the world as the measure.
These all illustrate scholars' conduct,
clear examples of whether to die or not.
Another asked:
"When Zōng Què was humble,
he was despised by Yǔ Yè.
When he became eminent,
he appointed Yè as chief clerk,
what of this? "
Péi Zǐyě remarked:
"To be poor yet not sorrowful,
humble yet not distressed,
tranquil in natural simplicity,
expanding this great principle,
is the virtue of Zēngshēn and Yuānyuān.
Lowering aspirations, humbling oneself,
bowing brows, bending spine,
enduring subordination beneath common offices,
to gallop above the crowd of heroes when noble,
is the ambition of Hán Xìn and Qíng Bù.
The act of humbling oneself is similar,
but the sentiment while humble differs.
If Zōng Yuángàn felt no shame with coarse meals,
he possessed the measure of Hán and Qíng.
Ultimately forsaking old grievances,
a magnanimous man indeed! "
When Sòng's Zōng Què was humble,
fellow provincial Yǔ Yè, being wealthy,
entertained guests with lavish feasts.
When it was for the sake of Jì Sūn,
even millet rice
could also satisfy hunger.
When he became the governor of Yùzhōu,
he requested Yè to serve as his chief clerk.
The world says Lì Jì sold out friendship,
because he deceived Lǚ Lù.
How is this in terms of principle?
Bān Gù said:
"Those who sell out friendship
are said to see profit and forget righteousness.
As for Jì,
his father was a meritorious minister yet was held hostage;
although he destroyed Lǚ Lù,
it was to stabilize the state.
Preserving righteousness for the ruler and his father can be acceptable."
Someone said:
"Jìn Yǔn abandoned his mother to defend the city—
can this be called loyalty?"
Xú Zhòng said:
"Between Jìn Yǔn and Lord Cáo,
the relationship of ruler and subject was not yet established.
His mother
was his closest kin;
by righteousness, he should have left.
In the past, Wáng Líng's mother was detained by Xiàng Yǔ;
she believed Gāozǔ would surely gain the empire,
so she committed suicide to strengthen Líng's resolve,
showing her heart had no attachments,
so that he could then serve his lord
and fulfill his duty unto death.
The Wèi prince Kāifāng served in Qí,
not returning for ten years;
Guǎn Zhòng considered that he did not cherish his kin,
so how could he love his lord?
Thus, he could not be made chancellor.
Therefore, to seek loyal ministers,
one must look among the doors of filial sons.
Yǔn should have first saved his closest kin.
When Xú Shù's mother was captured by Lord Cáo,
Liú Bèi sent Shù back.
Those who wish to rule the world
should empathize with a child's feelings;
Lord Cáo should also have sent Yǔn away."
When Tàizǔ of Wèi campaigned against Xúzhōu,
he left Chéng Yù to guard Jùnchéng.
Zhāng Miǎo rebelled.
Tàizǔ welcomed Lǚ Bù,
and Bù captured Jìn Yǔn's mother in Fàn county.
Tàizǔ sent Yù to persuade Jìn Yǔn
not to let his mother's situation
prevent him from holding Fàn firmly.
Yǔn wept and said:
"I dare not have divided loyalties."
Emperor Wén of Wèi asked Wáng Lǎng and others:
"In the past, Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
and people could not deceive him;
Zǐjiàn governed Shànfù,
and people could not bear to deceive him;
Xīmén Bào governed Yè,
and people dared not deceive him.
Among these three men's talents,
whose virtue as a ruler was superior?"
The reply was:
"If a ruler relies on virtue,
then ministers are moved by righteousness and cannot bear to deceive;
if a ruler relies on scrutiny,
then ministers fear detection and cannot deceive;
if a ruler relies on punishment,
then ministers fear penalty and dare not deceive.
Relying on virtue to inspire righteousness
is akin to guiding with virtue and aligning with rites,
where people have shame and rectify themselves—
these are of the same direction;
relying on scrutiny to fear wrongdoing
is like guiding with governance and aligning with punishment,
where people avoid penalty but lack shame—
these share the same outcome.
The gap in superiority and inferiority
lies in the balance,
not merely in minute distinctions."
Someone said:
"Jì Wénzǐ and Gōngsūn Hóng—
both men practiced frugality and simplicity,
yet their reputations differ;
why is that?"
Fàn Yè remarked:
"Those who seek profit through benevolence
may use benevolence for gain;
those who embody righteousness
do not expect embodiment to match righteousness.
Jì Wénzǐ's concubines did not wear silk,
and the people of Lǔ praised it;
Gōngsūn Hóng wore cloth garments,
but Jí Àn criticized him as deceitful.
Why are the judgments different when the facts are similar?
Is it the difference between embodiment and profit-seeking?
Thus, earlier records say:
'The benevolent find peace in benevolence,
the wise seek profit through benevolence,
those fearing penalty force themselves to benevolence.'
Comparing their benevolence,
the merit may not differ;
examining their practice of benevolence,
they cannot be the same.
Those at peace with benevolence
are naturally good;
those profiting from benevolence
strive through effort;
those forcing benevolence
act out of necessity.
Comparing these three types of benevolence,
the peaceful one is superior."
A discussion states:
The sage's virtue is complete,
and his capacity lacks nothing.
Below the mean,
talents tend to be one-sided.
Thus it is said:
"Chái is foolish,
Shēn is dull,
Shī is eccentric,
Yóu is rash."
From this, we see
those with complete virtue are rare!
Since complete virtue is rare,
one must rely on restraining emotions to strive for goodness!
Yet the world despises artificial restraint,
and people praise natural authenticity.
If one is truly greedy and foolish and also follows nature,
can that be considered virtuous?
The reply is:
Alas!
How can that be so?
Humans embody the essence of heaven and earth,
bearing yin and embracing yang;
though purity, turbidity, wisdom, and folly differ in nature,
their desires and pursuits
follow similar patterns.
Thus, fine features and smooth skin
are what people delight in;
riding sturdy carriages and driving good horses
are what people love;
enduring hardship with chastity
is what people find difficult;
sacrificing self for public good
is what people suffer.
Without the restraint of ritual teaching,
they would be unrestrained and uncontrollable.
How could they endure bitterness and simplicity,
maintain chastity and public spirit,
and handle wealth with integrity and giving with righteousness?
Therefore, the "Rites" say:
"Desires should not be indulged,
ambitions should not be full."
An ancient saying goes:
"The honest do not dislike wealth;
they acquire it by the right way."
The "Book of Songs" says:
"Like cutting and filing,
like carving and polishing."
All refer to artificial refinement.
If one indulges foolish tendencies
and follows base emotions,
calling it 'natural authenticity' and praising it,
such a person is an offender against the ancient kings.
Thus, I consider artificial restraint
the beginning of ritual and righteousness;
natural authenticity
the source of greed and baseness.
How can those forcing benevolence
be wrongly accused?
Someone said:
"In the affair of Chángpíng,
Bái Qǐ buried 400,000 Zhào soldiers alive—
can he be considered an extraordinary general?"
Hé Yàn said:
"Bái Qǐ accepted the surrender of Zhào soldiers
and deceitfully buried 400,000 of them—
is this merely called cruelty?
It also made it difficult to achieve ambitions again later!
Had the soldiers known surrender meant death,
even empty fists raised in defiance would be fearsome,
let alone 400,000 armored troops?
When the world saw surrendered Qín generals
with heads piled like mountains,
and returned Qín masses
with bones heaped into hills,
then in future battles,
they would fight to the death—
who would willingly submit?
What city would surrender?
Thus, though he ended 400,000 lives,
it only strengthened the world's will to fight.
Seeking instant achievement,
he instead fortified the resolve of other states.
So his military advance undermined his own momentum.
The army triumphs yet returns to mourn its strategy,
Why is this?
Suppose the Zhào forces were to reunite,
and Mǎ Fú were reborn,
then future battles would arise,
certainly not matching past confrontations,
let alone now making all under heaven face such futures!
The reason they ultimately dared not attack Hándān again
was not merely worrying about the patches of the Píngyuán Lord,
or fearing the arrival of rescue from other states,
but simply avoiding mention of it.
Take the Chángpíng incident:
every Qín man fifteen and above
bore arms against Zhào.
With Qín's strength,
yet those fifteen and older
suffered over half casualties—
this shows the achievement of defeating Zhào was small,
while the loss damaging Qín was great.
How can this be called remarkable?"
Discussion says:
Huáng Shígōng stated:
"The soft can control the hard,
the weak can control the strong.
Softness is virtue,
hardness is vice.
The soft
receives human assistance;
the hard
becomes the dwelling of resentment."
Therefore,
though Zhòu had a hundred victories,
he ended without heirs;
though Xiàng Yǔ's troops were strong,
he ultimately lost the empire.
Thus Suí Hé said:
"If Chǔ were to win,
the other states would feel endangered and rescue each other.
Chǔ's strength
would precisely draw the armies of all under heaven."
From this perspective,
if the world were already settled,
relying on a single victory,
deception might be permissible.
But when the realm is in turmoil,
with victory undecided, to break trust and righteousness with all under heaven
is the path to defeat and ruin.
During the Warring States period,
when the states were still strong,
Bái Qǐ buried alive the surrendered Zhào soldiers,
making the states fear him and form vertical alliances.
Such alliances
were not in Qín's interest—
victory in battle turned into defeat.
Hé Yàn's argument is correct.
Some say:
"Yuè Yì not slaughtering the two cities
cost him a grand enterprise—
was this wrong?"
Xiàhóu Xuán said:
"Reading Yuè Shēng's letter to King Huì of Yān,
he nearly understood opportunity and followed the Way,
maintaining ritual from start to finish!
Those who seek the ultimate measure of morality
and focus on the heart of all under heaven—
how could they be confined to the circumstances of their time,
limited to mere conquest?
Conquest
was not what Yuè Shēng valued;
strengthening Yān at the cost of abandoning the Way
was not his pursuit either.
Not stooping to petty gains,
not seeking minor successes,
his intent was to embrace all under heaven.
The campaign against Qí
was how he maneuvered his strategy to move the four seas.
Besieging cities without harming the common people
showed his benevolence reaching far and wide.
Spreading virtuous conduct to lead the states,
he nearly matched the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ.
Yuè Shēng expanded the grand scheme,
sparing the two cities,
gaining trust from the people,
awaiting their decline,
so that the people of Jímò and Jǔ
would turn against their rulers,
opening broad roads
to await the likes of Tián Dān;
fostering a climate of tolerance
to fulfill the aspirations of Qí's scholars.
Drawing them from the Eastern Sea,
connecting them to Huáxià.
His kindness like spring,
people responding like grass,
grateful to the Yān ruler,
looking up to his influence—
the two cities would surely submit,
and royal enterprise would flourish.
Though lingering at two towns,
he accelerated gains for all under heaven.
Unfortunate changes
were beyond his control,
failing at the brink of success
due to shifts of the time.
Had he forced with troops,
coerced with might,
flaunted the cruelty of slaughter,
showing it to all under heaven,
even if the two cities might have been taken quickly,
the path to hegemony
would have vanished far away.
Did Yuè Shēng not know swift capture of the two cities?
He feared that taking them would derail his enterprise.
Did he not consider delay causing change?
He feared haste would bring change alike.
Thus,
Yuè Shēng's not slaughtering the two cities
cannot be underestimated."
Some say:
"With Yuè Yì ministering to weak Yān,
defeating strong Qí,
uniting five states' armies,
avenging the king's shame,
besieging cities without hasty attack,
seeking to win through righteousness when options were exhausted—
this is the army of the benevolent,
all considering his strategy superior to Wǔ Hóu's.
Is this acceptable?"
Zhāng Fǔ said:
"Using five states' armies to attack one Qí
does not count as strength;
the great battle west of Jì River,
with corpses and bloodshed,
does not count as benevolence.
That Kǒngmíng encompassed civil and martial virtue,
waiting calmly for his time.
Liú Xuándé, with his insight into people,
repeatedly visited his cottage,
consulting on saving the world,
his ingenious strategies flowing like a spring.
He then persuaded Sūn Quán in the east,
resisted mighty Wèi in the north,
with victorious troops
aiding the capture of Shǔ.
When Xuándé neared death,
he entrusted the throne to his son,
amid turmoil
establishing a child ruler,
setting up offices and duties,
assigning talents in order,
civilly nurturing within,
martially resisting external threats,
then spreading his kindness to the people.
His military campaigns
saw no lost items on the road,
not a hair harmed.
His achievements nearly succeeded before his death.
Reading his remaining writings,
his strategies were profound and far-reaching.
He yielded benefits to subordinates,
shouldered blame for their shortcomings,
corrected upon seeing goodness,
amended upon receiving advice,
hence his fame shook far and wide.
Mèngzǐ said:
'Hearing of Bó Yí's character,
the greedy become upright.'
I believe witnessing Kǒngmíng's loyalty,
treacherous ministers would turn virtuous.
He nearly rivals Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
how could he merely be paired with Yuè Yì?"
Some say:
"Shāng Yāng rose from humble origins,
served Xiào Gōng,
wielding threefold strategies,
devouring the six states' vertical alliances,
enabling Qín's imperial enterprise—
can he be considered a hegemon's aide?"
Liú Xiàng said:
"Lord Shāng
internally stressed farming and warfare,
externally emphasized rewards for military exploits,
showing no favor to the noble,
no bias against the distant.
Though the Shū says:
'No bias, no faction,'
the Shī says:
'The Zhōu way is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow,'
the Sīmǎ Fǎ's motivation of soldiers,
and Hòu Jì's encouragement of farming
cannot surpass this.
This is how he annexed the states.
Thus Xúnzǐ said:
'Four generations of victory,
not luck,
but inevitability.'
Hegemonic rulers like Qí Huán and Jìn Wén—
Huán did not break the Kē covenant,
Wén did not violate the Yuán agreement,
The Marquis of Jiàng served as Grand Commandant,
holding authority over military power,
yet failed to rectify the situation.
After the Lü clan collapsed,
the ministers joined forces to eliminate the various Lü members,
and the Grand Commandant, in charge of the troops,
happened to achieve success in this endeavor.
What are called "meritorious ministers"
are not necessarily ministers who secure the state."
Later, during the Hàn dynasty, Chén Fān submitted a memorial recommending three individuals: Xú Zhì, Yuán Hóng, and Wéi Zhù.
The Emperor asked Chén Fān,
"Among these three, who should take precedence?"
Chén Fān replied,
"Hóng was born into a noble family,
and gradually learned the Way through training.
Zhù grew up in the Sānfǔ region,
where customs of ritual and righteousness prevail—
what is called 'straight without support,
carved without carving.'
As for Zhì,
he hails from the lowly and humble region of Jiāngnán,
yet he stands out prominently,
and should rightly be given first priority."
Someone asked,
"How might Xiè Ānshí as chancellor be compared to others?"
Yú Nán responded,
"In the past, when Gù Yōng was enfeoffed as a marquis,
his family remained unaware of it,
and previous generations praised his unassuming gravity,
considering him unmatched.
Now, with the Eastern Jìn in decline
and the borders growing increasingly alarmed daily,
moreover, Yǒnggù
(Fú Jiān's courtesy name)
was an eminent ruler of the Six Barbarian tribes,
personally leading a million troops;
Fú Róng, a talented and renowned chancellor,
wielded sharp weapons as the vanguard,
brandishing the claws and fangs of tigers and wolves,
and unleashing the sharp edges of long serpents,
first building guest quarters
to await the Jìn sovereign.
Judging by strength and weakness,
the difference was like that between a swan's feather and Mount Tài—
no analogy could suffice.
Yet Wénjìng (Xiè Ān) firmly rejected Huán Pèi's reinforcements,
and showed no delight at Xiè Xuán's dispatches,
indicating that the outcome of victory or defeat
was already settled in his mind.
Such a man,
how could a mere fief of ten thousand households
stir his heart?
If we speak of his magnanimity,
from recent antiquity onward,
none have been his equal."
When Suí Yángdì was still Crown Prince,
he once asked Hè Ruòbì,
"Yáng Sù, Hán Qínhǔ, and Shǐ Wànsuì are all acclaimed as fine generals;
how do they compare in merit?"
He replied,
"Yáng Sù is a fierce general,
not a strategic one.
Commentary says:
Resolute and daring in spirit,
that is a fierce general;
profound and strategic,
that is a strategic general.;
Hán Qínhǔ is a combat general,
not a commanding one.
Commentary says:
Fist-swift and fiercely brave,
that is a combat general;
disciplined and orderly in leading troops,
that is a commanding general.;
Shǐ Wànsuì is a cavalry general,
not a great general.
Commentary says:
Leading a single contingent,
invincible wherever he goes,
that is a cavalry general;
embracing all heroes,
enabling each talent to serve its purpose,
that is a great general."
The Crown Prince said,
"Well said."
Thus, from the "Six Uprights" to "Inquiring about Generals,"
all illustrate the outcomes of ministers' successes and failures.
An ancient saying goes:
"Yǔ made Xià thrive,
while Jié led Xià to ruin;
Tāng made Yīn prosper,
while Zhòu brought Yīn to its end."
Hélú made Wú victorious in battle,
unrivaled under heaven,
yet Fūchāi was captured by Yuè;
Mùgōng elevated Qín's fame and honor,
yet the Second Emperor was overthrown at Wàngyí.
The reason they ruled as monarchs was the same,
but their achievements differed,
due to whom they appointed.
Thus, King Chéng, while still in swaddling clothes, received homage from feudal lords,
because the Duke of Zhōu was in power;
King Wǔlíng of Zhào, at fifty, starved to death at Shāqiū,
because he appointed Lǐ Duì.
Hence, Wèi had Lord Wújì,
and lost territories were regained;
Zhào employed Lìn Xiàngrú,
and Qín troops dared not advance;
Chǔ had Shēn Bāoxū,
and King Zhāo was restored to his throne;
Qí had Tián Dān,
and King Xiāng recovered the state.
Considering this,
those who rule a state
but cannot mold customs,
evaluate and synthesize individuals,
discern the gains and losses of the crooked and upright,
and grasp the enduring principles of hegemony and kingship—
if any such ruler could achieve merit and fame,
it has never been heard of before.
Therefore, it is known that assigning office according to ability
is the method of ultimate principle.
Dé Biǎo Dì Shíyī (Chapter Eleven: Models of Virtue)
Confucius said:
"By nature, men are nearly alike;
by practice, they get to be wide apart."
This means that the foundation of desires is the same,
but the paths of influence differ.
Deliberate restraint prevents reckless behavior,
while being swayed by external things leads the will astray.
Therefore, the sage guides people to rational nature,
curbing their excesses,
being cautious about what they associate with,
and moderating their biases.
Hence, the "Zhuan" says:
"Examine likes and dislikes,
regulate emotions and nature,
and the kingly way is complete."
The way to cultivate one's nature
must involve assessing one's own excesses
and strengthening one's deficiencies.
For the intelligent and perceptive,
beware of being overly scrutinizing;
the poorly informed and narrow-minded,
beware of being闭塞;
the brave and strong-willed,
beware of excessive violence;
the kind and gentle,
beware of indecisiveness;
the calm and tranquil,
beware of procrastination;
the broad-minded and generous,
beware of forgetfulness.
"Rénwùzhì" says:
"Stern, upright, firm, and resolute,
their talent lies in correction,
their flaw is in being overly critical.
Strong-willed individuals,
stubborn and unyielding,
fail to guard against the abruptness of their strength,
and view compliance as weakness,
thus intensifying their arrogance.
Therefore,
they can help establish laws,
but are hard to involve in subtleties. ;
Gentle, compliant, peaceful, and forgiving,
their virtue lies in tolerance,
their flaw is in lack of decisiveness.
Gentle individuals,
relaxed in mind and lenient in judgment,
fail to guard against their inability to manage affairs,
and view assertiveness as harshness,
thus content in their ease.
Therefore,
they can follow routines,
but are hard to entrust with critical decisions. ;
Bold, fierce, and robust,
their strength lies in courage,
their flaw is in being overly suspicious.
Fierce individuals,
spirited and decisive,
fail to guard against the pitfalls of their bravery,
and view compliance as fear,
thus exhausting their momentum.
Therefore,
they can face difficulties,
but are hard to live with in restraint. ;
Refined, cautious, and fearful,
their goodness lies in respect and prudence,
their flaw is in excessive doubt.
Prudent individuals,
fearful of trouble and full of suspicion,
fail to guard against their timidity in righteousness,
and view courage as recklessness,
thus increasing their doubts.
Therefore,
they can preserve safety,
but are hard to inspire to uphold principles. ;
Strong, model, firm, and resilient,
their use is in support,
their flaw is in stubbornness.
Unyielding individuals,
holding firm to their intentions,
fail to guard against the obstinacy of their feelings,
and view debate as empty talk,
thus reinforcing their rigidity.
Therefore,
they can uphold justice,
but are hard to align with the masses. ;
Argumentative and logical,
their ability lies in unraveling complexities,
their flaw is in being unfocused.
Eloquent individuals,
abundant in reasoning,
fail to guard against the overflow of their words,
and view firmness as constraint,
thus indulging themselves.
Therefore,
they can discuss broadly,
but are hard to establish agreements with. ;
Comprehensive and all-embracing,
their virtue lies in broad tolerance,
their flaw is in being muddled.
Inclusive individuals,
intent on universal care,
do not caution against the confusion in their friendships,
and view integrity as exposure,
thus broadening their muddle.
Therefore,
they can安抚 the masses,
but are hard to reform customs with. ;
Pure, upright, honest, and clean,
their integrity lies in frugality and firmness,
their flaw is in narrow-mindedness.
Scrupulous individuals,
sharp and clear in criticism,
fail to guard against the narrowness of their path,
and view comprehensiveness as impurity,
thus intensifying their拘束.
Therefore,
they can maintain integrity,
but are hard to adapt flexibly. ;
Active and outstanding,
their achievement lies in climbing high,
their flaw is in being scattered.
Active individuals,
aspiring to surpass,
fail to guard against the excess of their ambitions,
and view calmness as stagnation,
thus sharpening their edge.
Therefore,
they can advance aggressively,
but are hard to restrain for the long term. ;
Deep, calm, subtle, and secretive,
their essence lies in profound subtlety,
their flaw is in slowness and timidity.
Calm individuals,
contemplative and cautious,
fail to guard against the delay in their calmness,
and view action as rashness,
thus praising their timidity.
Therefore,
they can ponder deeply,
but are hard to act swiftly with. ;
Simple, frank, and straightforward,
their quality lies in honesty,
their flaw is in lack of subtlety.
Frank individuals,
firm and sincere inside,
fail to guard against the roughness of their nature,
and view subtlety as deceit,
thus exposing their honesty.
Therefore,
they can establish trust,
but are hard to adjust subtly with. ;
Wise and reserved in emotion,
their skill lies in strategy,
their flaw is in indecision.
Reserved individuals,
adapting to please,
fail to guard against the difficulty in rectifying their methods,
and view straightforwardness as folly,
thus valuing their emptiness.
Therefore,
they can assist in good deeds,
but are hard to correct deviations with.
These are the constrained and extreme talents,
not the virtue of the mean."
Wénzǐ said:
"In the way of humans,
the heart should be small,
the will large,
wisdom round,
conduct square,
abilities many,
affairs few."
By "small heart,"
it means to consider dangers before they arise,
guard against calamities and be cautious in细微 matters,
not daring to indulge one's desires;
"large will" means
to encompass all states,
unify diverse customs,
with right and wrong converging,
and oneself as the hub;
"round wisdom" means
endless from start to finish,
flowing in all directions,
like a deep spring that never runs dry;
"square conduct" means
standing upright without bending,
pure white without being stained,
Do not change one's principles in poverty,
nor indulge one's ambitions in prosperity;
"Capable in many" means
being equipped with both civil and martial virtues,
and acting in accordance with propriety in movement and stillness;
"Handling few affairs" means
governing broadly by adhering to simplicity,
and awaiting restlessness while remaining tranquil.
For the way of heaven reaches its extreme and then reverses, becomes full and then diminishes.
Thus, with broad intelligence and great wisdom,
hold to foolishness;
with extensive knowledge and broad debate,
hold to restraint;
with martial prowess and resolute courage,
hold to caution;
with wealth, honor, and vast possessions,
hold to narrowness;
with virtue that benefits all under heaven,
hold to humility.
These five are
how the former kings held on to the world.
The "Zhuàn" says:
"Do not initiate disorder,
do not rely on wealth,
do not depend on favor,
do not oppose consensus,
do not be arrogant in etiquette,
do not be proud of ability,
do not repeat anger,
do not plan against virtue,
do not commit what is unjust.
These nine sayings
are how the ancients established their character."
The "Yù Qián Jīng" says:
"Those who show off their intelligence are shallow,
those who have faults but do not know themselves are flawed,
those who are lost and do not return are adrift,
those who incur resentment through words invite disaster,
those whose orders contradict their hearts are abandoned,
those whose later orders contradict previous ones are ruined,
those who are angry without authority are violated,
those who enjoy humiliating others in public suffer calamity,
those who kill or disgrace their appointees face danger,
those who disrespect those they should revere meet misfortune,
those who are united in appearance but divided in heart are isolated,
those who befriend the flattering and distance the loyal perish,
those who believe slander and abandon the worthy are deluded,
those who appoint officials based on personal connections are frivolous,
those where women's petitions influence public affairs cause chaos,
those whose subordinates seek external favors are doomed,
those who bully inferiors to win are aggressed,
those whose reputation exceeds their reality are depleted,
those who are self-indulgent but harsh to others are abandoned,
those who give little but expect much are unrewarded,
those who reward but forget the humble are not long employed,
those where people do not hold their rightful positions are in peril,
those who choose officials for personal reasons fail,
those who decide with the unrighteous are in danger,
those whose secret plots are leaked fail,
those who levy heavy taxes but give little are withered."
These are the main principles of self-governance.
Xún Qīng said:
"Those who can speak it
and act it out
are treasures of the state;
those who cannot speak it
but can act it out
are vessels of the state;
those who can speak it
but cannot act it out
are tools of the state;
those whose words are good
but actions evil
are monsters of the state."
Thus, Fù Zǐ said:
"The foundation of establishing virtue
lies in nothing higher than rectifying the heart."
When the heart is rectified, then the self is rectified;
when the self is rectified, then those around are rectified;
when those around are rectified, then the court is rectified;
when the court is rectified, then the state is rectified;
when the state is rectified, then all under heaven is rectified.
Thus, if all under heaven is not rectified,
rectify it from the family;
if the family is not rectified,
rectify it from the court;
if the court is not rectified,
rectify it from those around;
if those around are not rectified,
rectify it from the self;
if the self is not rectified,
rectify it from the heart.
The closer the rectification,
the farther the benefit reaches.
Yǔ and Tāng blamed themselves,
and their rise was vigorous.
This is what is meant by "rectifying the heart."
The "Shī Zǐ" says:
"The heart
is the ruler of the body.
The son of heaven receives the mandate for all under heaven from the heart;
if the heart is improper, then all under heaven suffers disaster;
the feudal lords receive the mandate for their state from the heart;
if the heart is improper, then the state perishes;
the common man receives the mandate for his body from the heart;
if the heart is improper, then the body is destroyed."
Chapter Twelve: Order and Chaos
To clearly examine the "Six Types of Rulers,"
is to observe the virtue of a sovereign.
To scrutinize the "Nine Atmospheres,"
is to determine the state's norms.
To probe into the "Four Disorders,"
and verify the "Four Perils,"
then one can know the order or chaos of governance.
What are the "Six Types of Rulers"?
Xún Yuè said:
"Embodies correctness and is benevolent by nature,
clear-minded and united in purpose,
acts for the sake of others,
not for oneself,
this is called the 'Kingly Ruler.'"
Commentary says:
The Kingly Ruler
refers to one with innate benevolence and virtue. ;
Restrains oneself and is forgiving,
fond of inquiry and diligent in action,
acts in accordance with righteousness,
not following personal feelings,
this is called the 'Orderly Ruler.'"
Commentary says:
The Orderly Ruler
refers to one who suppresses emotions and curbs desires;
diligent in duties and preserving the legacy,
not daring to be negligent or lax,
acts with public interest first,
not prioritizing personal gain,
this is called the 'Preserving Ruler.'"
Commentary says:
The Preserving Ruler
refers to one who adheres strictly to laws and regulations;
rebellious and contentious,
public and private interests pursued simultaneously,
with gains and losses,
not purely following the Dao and measures,
this is called the 'Declining Ruler.' ;
Emotions override righteousness,
personal interests outweigh public good,
systems exceed limits,
governance and education lose normality,
this is called the 'Endangered Ruler.' ;
Befriends and employs slanderers and the wicked,
exiles loyal and virtuous officials;
indulges emotions and fulfills desires,
disregarding rites and measures;
comes and goes unrestrainedly,
not bound by etiquette and prohibitions.
Bestows rewards out of personal favor,
exceeding public use;
imposes punishments in anger,
surpassing legal principles.
Persists in errors and covers up faults,
unaware of the need for change,
loyal advice is blocked,
straightforward remonstrators are executed,
this is called the 'Doomed Ruler.' ."
Thus, the Kingly Ruler can achieve prosperity and peace,
the Orderly Ruler can cultivate good governance,
the Preserving Ruler can safeguard the state,
the Declining Ruler, if encountering no calamity, might barely remain intact,
but with calamity, is endangered;
the Endangered Ruler, if encountering no calamity, may luckily avoid disaster,
but with calamity, perishes;
the Doomed Ruler is certain to perish regardless.
What are the "Nine Atmospheres"?
When ruler and ministers are close yet observe propriety,
all officials harmonious yet not uniform,
yielding without contention,
diligent without resentment,
each devoted to their duties.
This is the "Atmosphere of a Ruled-by-Rites State."
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"The superior does not overpower the inferior,
the inferior does not offend the superior,
superiors and inferiors do not overpower or offend each other,
hence prohibitions and orders are implemented,
everyone is selfless,
even through dangers and changes, the state cannot be invaded,
this is a well-governed state."
When rites and customs are not uniform,
positions and duties are not respected,
petty officials engage in slander and jealousy,
commoners voice criticisms.
This is the "Atmosphere of a Declining State."
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"When the ruler is aged,
has many concubines,
few descendants,
and alienates powerful clans,
it is a declining state."
When ruler and ministers contend for prominence,
the court contends for achievements,
great officers contend for fame,
commoners contend for profit.
"This is the 'Atmosphere of a Discordant State.'"
When the superior has many desires,
the inferior has many schemes,
laws are unstable,
governance has multiple authorities.
This is the "Atmosphere of a Chaotic State."
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"When the ruler favors ministers,
and ministers ingratiate themselves with the ruler,
public law is abandoned,
private governance is practiced,
it is a chaotic state."
When extravagance is considered broad-minded,
arrogance is seen as lofty,
excess is taken as sophistication;
following rites is called拘束 (restrictive),
abiding by law is called固执 (stubborn).
This is the "Atmosphere of a Decadent State."
Shū Xiàng said:
"High officials value their emoluments and do not remonstrate to the utmost,
close ministers fear punishment and dare not speak,
the conditions below are not communicated upward,
this is a great calamity."
When superiors and inferiors are estranged,
inside and outside are mutually suspicious;
petty officials contend for favor,
high officials contend for power.
This is the "Atmosphere of an Endangered State."
When the superior does not consult the inferior,
the inferior does not advise the superior;
women's words are heeded,
private governance is practiced.
This is the "Atmosphere of a Doomed State."
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"When the state is poor and small,
but families are rich and large;
the ruler's power is light,
the ministers' influence is heavy,
it is a doomed state.
When internally there is no exclusive favorite,
externally no intimate cronies;
collateral branches flourish,
elders and young are not disordered,
it is a prosperous state.
When farming and sericulture are timely,
granaries are full;
weapons and armor are strong and sharp,
borders are well-maintained,
it is a strong state."
Wénzǐ said:
"A chaotic state appears prosperous,
a well-governed state appears empty;
a doomed state seems insufficient,
a surviving state seems abundant.
Empty does not mean
no people,
but that each keeps to their duty;
prosperous does not mean
many people,
but that all pursue trivial ends;
abundant does not mean
much wealth,
but desires are restrained and affairs few;
insufficient does not mean
no goods,
but people are restless and expenditures high."
What are the "Four Disorders"?
Guǎnzǐ said:
"When internally there are concubines suspicious of the wife,
this is disorder in the family;
when there are sons suspicious of the嫡 (primary heir),
this is disorder in the clan;
when at court there are ministers suspicious of the prime minister,
this is disorder in the state;
when appointed officials are incompetent,
this is disorder among the masses."
Therefore it is said:
"In establishing the Son of Heaven,
do not let the feudal lords be suspicious;
in establishing feudal lords,
do not let the great officers be suspicious;
in establishing the principal wife,
do not let the favored concubines be suspicious;
in establishing the嫡子 (primary son),
do not let the庶孽 (secondary sons) be suspicious.
Suspicion leads to action,
duality leads to contention,
混杂 (mixture) leads to mutual harm.
Thus, if ministers have dual positions,
the state will surely be disordered;
if ministers have dual positions and the state is not disordered,
it is because the ruler still exists,
relying on the ruler it is not disordered,
but losing the ruler, it will surely be disordered.
If sons have dual statuses,
the family will surely be disordered;
if sons have dual statuses and the family is not disordered,
it is because the parent still lives,
relying on the parent it is not disordered,
but losing the parent, it will surely be disordered.
If ministers are suspicious of their ruler,
there is no state not in peril;
if the favored are suspicious of the clan,
There is no state that is not in peril."
What are the "four perils"?
It is further said:
"When high ministers and chancellors fail to gain the support of the masses,
the state is in peril;
when senior officials are not harmonious and united,
the state is in peril;
when the military commander is not sufficiently feared,
the state is in peril;
when the people do not cherish their livelihoods,
the state is in peril.
These are the manifestations of order and chaos.
For all those in positions above others,
if laws and methods are clear and rewards and punishments are certain,
even without words, order will naturally prevail;
if laws and methods are unclear and rewards and punishments are uncertain,
even with daily commands,
chaos will inevitably arise."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"To govern a state, there are three instruments;
to bring chaos to a state, there are six assaults.
If an enlightened ruler can overcome the six assaults and establish the three instruments,
the state will be well-governed;
if an unworthy ruler cannot overcome the six assaults and establish the three instruments,
the state will fall into chaos.
What are the three instruments?
They are:
commands, the battle-axe (punishment), and emoluments (rewards).
What are the six assaults?
They are:
kinship, nobility, wealth, beauty, flattery, and amusements.
What is the use of the three instruments?
It is said:
Without commands, there is no way to direct subordinates;
without the battle-axe, there is no way to awe the masses;
without emoluments, there is no way to encourage people.
How do the six assaults lead to ruin?
It is said:
Even if one disobeys, one can still survive;
even if one violates prohibitions, one can still be exempted;
even if one achieves no merit, one can still become wealthy.
If in a state, there are those who can survive despite disobedience,
then commands are insufficient to direct subordinates;
if there are those who can be exempted despite violating prohibitions,
then the battle-axe is insufficient to awe the masses;
if there are those who can become wealthy without merit,
then emoluments are insufficient to encourage people.
When commands are insufficient to direct subordinates,
the battle-axe is insufficient to awe the masses,
and emoluments are insufficient to encourage people,
then the ruler has nothing with which to secure himself."
Therefore,
when the situation is orderly,
even if left unattended, it will not fall into chaos;
when the situation is chaotic,
even if diligently managed, it will not be well-governed.
Yáo and Shùn folded their hands and did nothing, yet had surplus order,
because the situation was orderly;
Húhài and Wáng Mǎng rushed about frantically, yet it was insufficient,
because the situation was chaotic.
Shāngzǐ said:
"Laws and decrees
are the life of the people,
the foundation of governance.
When one rabbit runs and a hundred people chase it,
it is not because the rabbit can be divided into a hundred parts,
but because its ownership is undetermined.
When the market is full of rabbits for sale,
thieves dare not take them,
because ownership is determined.
Thus, when names and duties are fixed,
it is the way of orderly situations;
when names and duties are undetermined,
it is the way of chaotic situations.
Therefore, an orderly situation
cannot be thrown into chaos;
a chaotic situation
cannot be governed.
To try to govern a chaotic situation
only makes it more chaotic;
to govern an orderly situation
leads to good governance.
Thus, the sage governs order, not chaos.
When the sage establishes laws for the people,
they must be made clear and easy to understand,
so that both foolish and wise can comprehend them.
Therefore, when the sage stands over the world, there are no executed criminals,
not because they could be punished or killed but were not,
but because all people know how to avoid harm and seek good fortune, thus governing themselves.
The enlightened ruler governs by following order,
thus achieving great governance in the world."
Hence it is said:
The skilled
seek it in the situation,
not blame people.
Therefore,
the enlightened ruler examines laws and institutions and promulgates teachings and commands,
and then the world is well-governed.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"When a state is about to perish,
it must have many regulations."
Dù Yù comments:
"It frequently changes its laws."
The discussion says:
Those ministers who can rectify the age and assist in governance
must first understand the ways of prosperity and decline,
be versed in the patterns of success and failure,
discern the tendencies of order and chaos,
and comprehend the appropriateness of employment and dismissal,
then they can face opportunities without confusion,
encounter doubts and yet decide,
becoming assistants to the king—
none have succeeded without these qualities.
Chapter Thirteen: Reversing the Classics
I have heard that the demise of the Three Dynasties
was not due to the loss of laws;
but because those who administered the laws were not the right people.
Thus, we know that laws
are the old traces of the former kings,
and if not applied by the right people,
the Way does not operate in vain.
Therefore, Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music,
names, laws, punishments, and rewards—
these eight
are the methods by which the Five Emperors and Three Kings governed the world."
Thus, benevolence
is used to broadly bestow on all things,
but it can also give rise to partiality and selfishness.
This is the reverse of benevolence.
The discussion says:
In terms of ritual,
family beneficence should not extend to the state,
and great officers should not appropriate public benefits.
Confucius said:
"The Son of Heaven loves all under heaven,
feudal lords love within their domains,
and must not exceed what they should love,
to avoid private favoritism."
Thus, we know that partial and selfish benevolence
is despised by true kings.
Righteousness
is used to establish integrity and conduct,
but it can also lead to ostentation and hypocrisy.
This is the reverse of righteousness.
The discussion says:
Sacrificing oneself for the state,
holding firm to great principles without being swayed—
this is true righteousness.
But like Chancellor Yú Qīng of Zhào,
who abandoned his post and his lord
to relieve the peril of Wèi Qí;
or Xìnlíng Wújì,
who stole tallies and forged orders
to aid Plain Yuán's emergency.
The righteousness of betraying the public for partisan loyalty was achieved,
but the integrity of upholding duty and serving superiors was abandoned.
Thus, Máo Gōng criticized Wújì, saying:
"Toward Zhào, he had merit,
but toward Wèi, it was not correct."
All such cases
are examples of ostentation and hypocrisy.
Ritual
is used to practice reverence and caution,
but it can also give rise to laziness and neglect.
This is the reverse of ritual.
The discussion says:
When Hàn sought to establish rituals,
Emperor Wén said:
"Elaborate rituals and adorned appearances
do not benefit true ritual;
personal transformation is what matters."
Thus, he abandoned them.
Guō Jiā said to Duke Cáo:
"Yuán Shào has elaborate rituals and many formalities,
while you, my lord, act with natural simplicity—
this is the victory of the Way."
For arduous discipline is hard to maintain,
hence giving rise to laziness and neglect. Music
is used to harmonize emotions and will,
but it can also lead to licentiousness and excess.
This is the reverse of music.
The Book of Music states:
"The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is the sound of chaotic times;
the music of Sāngjiān and Púshàng
is the sound of perished states."
Thus Yán Ān said:
"What is magnificent, beautiful, precious, and extraordinary
naturally pleases the ears and eyes.
Thus when nourishment goes astray, it becomes excessive;
when music goes astray, it becomes licentious;
when ritual goes astray, it becomes ornamental;
when instruction goes astray, it becomes hypocritical.
Hypocrisy, ornamentation, licentiousness, and excess
are not the way to guide people." Names
serve to rectify honor and humility,
but also give rise to arrogance and usurpation.
This is the reverse of names.
Discussion says:
In ancient times, when names and positions differed,
rituals also varied accordingly.
Thus the sages established clear rituals to order honor and humility,
and differentiated chariots and robes to manifest virtue.
However, when Hàn Gāozǔ witnessed the majestic dignity of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he sighed and said:
"This is how a true man should be!"
This is how arrogance arises.
The Lǎojīng says:
"As for ritual,
it is the thinning of loyalty and trustworthiness and the beginning of disorder."
How true this is! Laws
serve to unify the multitude and differences,
but also give rise to discord and division.
This is the reverse of law.
Discussion says:
The Dàodé Jīng states:
"The more laws and ordinances are promulgated,
the more thieves and robbers proliferate."
Jiǎ Yì said:
"When laws are issued, wickedness arises;
when orders are given, deceit emerges—
this is division." Punishments
serve to intimidate the disobedient,
but also give rise to oppression and violence.
This is the reverse of punishment.
Rewards
serve to encourage loyalty and ability,
but also give rise to base contention.
This is the reverse of reward. The Wénzǐ says:
"When the sages created writing,
it was to manage all affairs,
so the foolish would not forget,
and the wise could record events.
But when it declines,
it is used for deceit and falsehood,
to exonerate the guilty and execute the innocent."
This is the reverse of writing.
The Wénzǐ says:
"Those who scrutinize the traces of pen and ink
do not know the root of order and chaos;
those accustomed to battlefield affairs
do not know the strategy for victory in the temple."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Confucians use the Shī and Shū to rob tombs.
The great Confucian said:
'The east is growing light!
How goes the affair?'
The lesser Confucian replied:
'The skirt and jacket are not yet removed,
but there is a pearl in the mouth.
The Shī indeed says:
"Green, green the wheat,
growing on the slopes."
In life, he did not give alms;
in death, why hold a pearl?
Grab his temples,
press his cheeks,
and use a metal hammer to pry open his jaw.
Slowly separate his cheeks,
so as not to damage the pearl in his mouth.'"
Thus it is said that the Shī and Lǐ become tools for robbery.
Note: 顪 is pronounced xū huì fǎn,
控 is pronounced kōng. When parks were created,
it was to provide for ancestral temples,
train soldiers,
and prepare for emergencies.
But when it declines,
they gallop and hunt with bows,
depriving people of their time.
This is the reverse of parks.
When King Xuān of Qí saw King Wén's park was large
yet people considered it small,
he asked Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"King Wén of Zhōu's park
was seventy lǐ square.
Gatherers of grass and firewood went there,
hunters of pheasants and hares went there—
he shared it with the people,
so they considered it small.
Was that not fitting?
I have heard that within the suburbs,
there is a park forty lǐ square.
Killing its deer
is treated as murder.
The people consider it large—
is that not fitting?"
When King Líng of Chǔ built the Zhānghuá Terrace,
Wǔ Jǔ admonished:
"When former kings built towers and pavilions,
pavilions were only for military training,
towers only for observing omens.
They did not seize farmland,
did not exhaust resources,
did not burden official duties,
and did not interfere with seasonal work.
Building towers and pavilions
was to teach people benefit, not to cause scarcity."
Elevating the worthy
serves to equalize education,
rectify litigation;
with the worthy in position
and the capable in office;
favor extends below,
and ten thousand cherish virtue.
But when it declines,
cliques form and collude,
each promoting their allies,
abandoning public for private gain,
controlling recommendations inside and out,
with villains in office
and the worthy hidden away.
This is the reverse of honoring the worthy.
Lǚ Shàng said to King Wén:
"If a ruler readily follows common recommendations,
some may take the unworthy as worthy,
or the unwise as wise.
If the ruler considers those recommended by the common as wise and worthy,
and those criticized as unworthy,
then the well-connected advance,
and the less-connected retreat.
Thus crowds of villains collude and obscure the worthy,
and worldly chaos worsens."
King Wén asked:
"How then to elevate the worthy?"
Lǚ Shàng replied:
"Divide duties between generals and ministers,
and let the ruler promote people by office,
examining names and realities,
selecting talent and testing ability—
this is the way to obtain the worthy."
An ancient saying goes:
"Emphasizing cliques obscures the ruler;
contending for fame and profit harms friends;
striving for haste loses virtue."
The Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn says:
"Scholars have five reversals:
Having power and nobility but not using it to love others and uphold righteousness,
instead becoming violent and arrogant."
This is the reverse of nobility.
An ancient saying states:
"Those who enrich others while rich
cannot become poor if they wish;
those who honor others while noble
cannot become humble if they wish;
those who help others succeed while successful
cannot be thwarted if they wish."
Méi Fú said:
"Supporting others is how one establishes oneself; blocking others is how one obstructs oneself."
Having a wealthy family but not using it to relieve poverty and aid the needy,
instead indulging in extravagance without limit.
This is the reverse of wealth.
Having courage and ferocity but not using it to defend superiors and fight battles,
instead using it to bully and engage in private fights.
This is the reverse of courage.
Any general who takes leaving lightly
should not be stationed to guard borders;
only with benevolent virtue can they secure peace. Having intelligence and wisdom but not using it for upright planning and teaching,
instead serving wickedness and practicing deception.
This is the reverse of wisdom.
The Shuō Yuàn says:
"The superior person's stratagems are upright;
the petty person's stratagems are crooked." Having a handsome appearance but not using it to govern the court and lead people,
instead seducing women and indulging desires.
This is the reverse of appearance.
These five
are what is meant by scholars losing their fine qualities.
Lǚ Shàng said: "Clear penalties make people fearful;
when people are fearful, unexpected changes arise."
This is the reverse of clear penalties.
Keen investigation makes people restless;
when people are restless, they migrate;
when people migrate, they do not settle,
and easily instigate change."
This is the reverse of keen investigation.
Tàigōng said:
"Explicit rewards lead to insufficiency,
and insufficiency breeds lasting resentment.
An enlightened king governs people
not by knowing what they favor,
but by knowing what they detest;
not by knowing where they gather,
but by knowing where they depart.
Let each person be content with their livelihood,
and the world will be at peace."
Jìn's Liú Sòng said:
"All supervising officials should focus on major matters and overlook minor ones.
Why so?
For trivial faults and minor flaws,
errors of negligence and forgetfulness—
these are inevitable in human nature.
While they should not be condoned as permissible,
if all are prosecuted according to the law,
then neither court nor countryside will have anyone left standing.
This is what is called bringing disorder through governance." Yànzǐ said:
"When a minister monopolizes his lord,
it is called disloyalty;
when a son monopolizes his father,
it is called unfiliality;
when a wife monopolizes her husband,
it is called jealousy."
This contradicts loyalty and filial piety.
The Annals of Lü Bùwéi states:
"The harmony of yīn and yáng
does not favor one species alone;
the sweet dew and timely rain
show no partiality to any single thing;
the ruler of ten thousand people
should not favor any one individual."
Shēn Zǐ said:
"When one wife monopolizes her husband,
all other wives become disorderly;
when one minister monopolizes the ruler,
all other ministers are obscured.
Thus a jealous wife can easily destroy a household,
and a disorderly minister can easily ruin a state.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler employs his ministers
like spokes converging on a hub,
allowing none to monopolize the ruler." Hán Zǐ said:
"Confucians use culture to disrupt laws,
while knights-errant use force to violate prohibitions."
This opposes both culture and martiality.
"Those who rely solely on martial prowess perish,
those who rely solely on culture fall."
Fūchāi and Yǎnwáng exemplify this.
Wú Zǐ said:
"In ancient times, the ruler of Chéngsāng
cultivated virtue but neglected martial prowess,
thus his state perished;
the ruler of Yǒuhù
relied on numerical strength and favored bravery,
thus he lost his altars of soil and grain.
An enlightened ruler, learning from this,
must internally cultivate cultural virtue,
and externally maintain military training.
Therefore, when facing an enemy who does not advance,
there is no need for excessive courtesy;
mourning over stiff corpses
does not constitute true benevolence."
The Classic of Strategy states:
"One strong in culture with substantial martial ability
can assist the ruler;
one strong in martial prowess with substantial culture
can support the sovereign;
one accomplished in both culture and martiality
can be entrusted with military affairs;
one deficient in both culture and martiality
should not be sent on campaigns."
Zǐlù rescued a drowning person and accepted an ox as reward.
Confucius said:
"The state of Lǔ will surely develop a custom of rescuing people from distress."
Zǐgòng ransomed a person but declined reimbursement from the treasury
According to Lǔ law,
one who ransoms people from other states
receives payment from the treasury. .
Confucius said:
"No one in Lǔ will ransom people anymore."
Zǐlù's acceptance encouraged virtue,
while Zǐgòng's refusal hindered goodness.
From this we see
that integrity has its proper place and cannot be universally practiced.
This opposes integrity.
Kuāng Héng stated:
Confucius said:
"Can one govern a state through ritual deference?
What difficulty is there?"
The imperial court
forms the pillars of the world.
When ministers and high officials mutually cultivate ritual and respectful deference,
then people do not contend;
when they love benevolence and delight in giving,
then subordinates are not violent;
when they uphold righteousness and high principles,
then people emulate their conduct;
when they are tolerant, gentle, kind, and harmonious,
then the masses love one another.
These four qualities
are how enlightened kings accomplish transformation without severity.
Why?
When there are angry words in court,
then there will be strife below;
when there are self-willed officials above,
then there will be unyielding people below;
when there are competitive assistants above,
then there will be harmful intentions below;
when there are profit-seeking ministers above,
then there will be thieving people below.
This is its root.
Shèn Zǐ said:
"Loyalty cannot save a chaotic age,
but rather compounds its errors.
How do we know this is so?
He said:
A father had a good son, yet Shùn exiled Gǔsǒu;
Jié had loyal ministers, yet his transgressions filled the world.
Thus filial sons do not emerge in households with kind fathers
When the six relations are discordant,
filial piety and parental love appear. ,
and loyal ministers do not emerge under sagely rulers
When the state is chaotic and disordered,
loyal ministers appear. .
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler employs his ministers,
their loyalty should not exceed their duties,
and their duties should not exceed their offices."
This opposes loyalty.
Jīng Fáng's discussions
created enmity with Shí Xiǎn.
When Jīng Fáng was appointed governor of Wèi Commandery,
he anxiously submitted a memorial stating:
"My student Yáo Píng told me:
'Jīng Fáng may be called minimally loyal,
but not greatly loyal.
Why?
In former times during Qín,
when Zhào Gāo held power,
there was one Zhèng Xiān
who criticized Gāo and died for it.
Gāo's authority was thereby established,
and Qín's chaos
was hastened by Zhèng Xiān.'
Now that I have been appointed commandery governor,
I beg Your Majesty not to let me suffer Zhèng Xiān's fate
and become Yáo Píng's laughingstock."
From this we see
that what Zhèng Xiān called loyalty
actually hastened Qín's disaster.
What benefit did such loyalty bring?
Guǐgǔ Zǐ said:
"To prevent theft from chests, bags, and cabinets

Opening from the side is called qū. ,
people prepare defenses
by fastening ropes and cords

and securing locks

meaning delicate. .
This is what common wisdom calls intelligence.
Yet when a great thief comes,
he carries off the cabinet, lifts the chest
