and shoulders the bags as he departs.
He only fears that the ropes and locks might not be secure enough.
Thus, what was previously called intelligence
hasn't it merely accumulated goods for thieves?"
This opposes intelligence.
Sūn Zǐ said:
"The stubborn resistance of a small force
leads to its capture by a large force."
What we call sage wisdom -
hasn't it sometimes served to protect great thieves?
How do we know this is so?
In ancient times, the state of Qí
had neighboring towns within sight of each other,
with sounds of chickens and dogs audible between them,
where nets were spread,
and plows and hoes worked the land
across over two thousand square lǐ.
Throughout its four borders,
the establishment of ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
the governance of towns, villages, and communities -
were these not all modeled after sage examples?
Yet Tián Chéngzǐ one morning killed the ruler of Qí and stole his state.
What he stole
was not merely the state itself,
but also the laws of sage wisdom along with it.
Thus Tián Chéngzǐ possessed the name of a thief,
yet enjoyed the security of Yáo and Shùn.
Small states dared not criticize him,
large states dared not punish him.
For twelve generations his family held Qí.
Was this not stealing the state of Qí,
along with its sage wisdom laws,
to protect his thieving person?"
This opposes sage laws.
Formerly, Shūxiàng asked Yànzǐ of Qí:
"What will become of Qí?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"These are last days -
I cannot tell.
Qí will become the Chén family's.
The duke abandons his people, who turn to the Chén family.
Qí's old measures were four:
dǒu, ōu, fǔ, and zhōng.
Four shēng made one dǒu,
each multiplied by four
to reach the fǔ,
and ten fǔ made one zhōng.
The Chén family's three measures
all added one unit each,
making their zhōng larger.
They lent by their household measure,
and the duke collected them.
Timber from the mountains was brought to the market,
yet its price was no higher than in the mountains;
fish, salt, clams, and mussels
were no more expensive than by the sea;
the people exerted their strength,
two-thirds went to the duke while they kept one-third for food and clothing.
The duke's stores rotted and were eaten by worms, while the village elders suffered from cold and hunger;
in the markets of the state,
ordinary shoes were cheap but prosthetic shoes for the amputated were expensive;
the people were afflicted with diseases,
yet some comforted and cared for them.
They loved him like parents,
and flocked to him like flowing water.
Even if he wished not to gain the people,
how could he avoid it?"
Zhí's followers asked Zhí,
"Do robbers also have a Way?"
Zhí said,
"How can there be any place without a Way?
To accurately guess the treasures hidden in a room—
that is sagacity.
To enter first—
that is courage.
To exit last—
that is righteousness.
To know what is feasible and what is not—
that is wisdom.
To divide the spoils equally—
that is benevolence.
One who lacks these five qualities and yet can become a great robber
has never existed under heaven."
At the end of the Eastern Hàn,
when Dǒng Zhuō entered the court,
intending to usurp the throne,
he still recruited famous scholars.
Fàn Yè commented:
"Dǒng Zhuō, with his fierce and reckless nature,
encountering a collapsing and fragmented situation,
thus was able to trample upon the constant moral principles,
and tear apart the imperial domain.
With a character that could carve livers and chop off feet,
the suffering of the masses was insufficient to satisfy his cruelty,
yet he still restrained his will toward the gentry,
hesitated in his plunder,
showing that even he adhered to some way of robbery."
From this perspective,
good people cannot establish themselves without the Way of the sages,
nor can Robber Zhí act without the Way of the sages.
Since there are few good people under heaven,
and many who are not good,
the sages' benefit to the world is little,
while their harm to the world is great.
This is the reversal of benevolence and righteousness.
A discussion says:
Once, Zhòng Yóu was the magistrate of Shào,
and the Jì family started digging a long canal in the fifth month.
At that time,
Zǐlù used his private salary of grain to make porridge,
to feed the canal diggers.
Confucius heard of this,
sent Zǐgòng to overturn the rice,
and smash the containers.
Zǐlù said,
"Does the Master hate my practicing benevolence and righteousness?"
Confucius said,
"According to ritual,
the Son of Heaven loves the whole world,
feudal lords love their domains,
high officials love their offices,
and scholars love their families.
To exceed what one should love
is called encroaching on others' duties."
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
when the King Xiàn of Héjiān came to court,
in his attire and hasty actions,
he always adhered to benevolence and righteousness.
Emperor Wǔ showed a displeased expression and challenged him,
saying,
"King Tāng rose with seventy lǐ,
King Wén with a hundred lǐ;
may you, King, strive accordingly!"
The king understood his meaning,
returned and indulged in drinking.
From this it is said,
that to practice benevolence and righteousness universally,
there must be proper boundaries.
Hence, the "Shīzǐ" says:
"When ruler and father, minister and son,
high and low, elder and younger,
noble and humble, close and distant,
all attain their proper status, it is called order;
when love is properly allocated, it is called benevolence;
when giving is properly allocated, it is called righteousness;
when thought is properly allocated, it is called wisdom;
when action is properly allocated, it is called appropriateness;
when speech is properly allocated, it is called trustworthiness;
only when all attain their proper status can one be considered a complete person."
From this perspective,
the benevolence and righteousness of Zhí's followers
were not within their proper bounds.
Thus it is said,
the ways of benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music, names, laws, punishment, and reward,
the paths of loyalty, filial piety, worthiness, and wisdom,
the principles of civil and martial arts, clarity, and discernment,
are not hidden from people,
but always exist through the ages.
They do not only appear in the times of Yáo and Tāng,
nor do they deliberately flee the courts of Jié and Zhòu.
Used according to the Way, they bring order to the world;
used contrary to the Way, they bring chaos to the world.
Xúnzǐ said:
"Yì's method of archery is not lost,
yet Yì does not appear in every generation;
Yǔ's laws still exist,
yet the Xià dynasty does not rule again.
Therefore, laws cannot stand alone;
with the right person, they survive;
without the right person, they perish."
"Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"A man of Sòng who was skilled at making an anti-chap medicine
for generations made his living by bleaching silk.
A visitor heard of this,
and offered to buy the recipe for a hundred pieces of gold.
The visitor obtained it,
and used it to persuade the King of Wú.
When the Yuè people caused trouble,
the King of Wú put him in command.
In winter,
they fought a naval battle with the Yuè people,
greatly defeating them,
and he was enfeoffed with land.
The ability to prevent chapped hands was the same,
yet one used it to gain a fief,
while the other could not avoid bleaching silk—
this was due to the difference in how it was used."
Thus, we know that systems and methods
are not absent in any age;
it all lies in how they are used.
On Right and Wrong, Chapter Fourteen
Reduction and augmentation follow different paths,
substance and refinement govern differently.
Some uphold authority to manage affairs,
while others honor the Way to pacify customs.
Therefore,
the teachings handed down by past records,
can now all be contradicted by reason.
How to illustrate this?
The affirmative says:
The "Dàyǎ" states:
"Being both intelligent and wise,
to preserve one's person."
The "Yì" says:
"The great virtue of heaven and earth is called life."
The negative says:
The "Analects" says:
"A scholar, seeing danger, is prepared to give up his life."
It also says:
"A gentleman may have to die in order to achieve humanity,
but he never seeks to live at the expense of humanity."
The affirmative says:
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Those who doubt the present should examine the past;
those who do not know the future should look to the bygone."
An ancient saying goes:
"One who shares the same illness as the dead,
cannot live;
one who follows the same path as a fallen state,
cannot survive."
The negative says:
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"If someone dies from eating,
and one wishes to forbid eating throughout the world,
that is absurd;
if someone dies from riding a boat,
and one wishes to forbid all boats in the world,
that is absurd;
if someone loses his state through using arms,
and one wishes to abolish all arms in the world,
that is absurd."
Dù Shù said:
"Treacherous ministers and villainous sons,
from ancient times to the present,
have never been absent.
One in a hundred years,
is considered as frequent as successive footsteps;
one in a thousand miles,
is considered as close as shoulder to shoulder.
Yet to cite this as a warning
is like forbidding eating because of one choke.
Though those who choke are few,
those who starve will be many."
The affirmative says:
Confucius said:
"I detest those who mistake exposing faults for uprightness."
The negative says:
Guǎnzǐ said:
"I detest those who mistake concealing faults for benevolence."
Wèi Cáo Xí's "Essay on Ultimate Impartiality" states:
"What common people call covering faults and extolling virtues
is considered the great righteousness of a gentleman;
protecting and clarifying shared preferences
is deemed the utmost bond of friendship.
Such sayings
are but commonplace talk of the alleys.
They serve to remedy mutual slander born of love and hate,
not the utmost principle of sincere correctness,
nor the impartial judgment of the mean.
Scholars of the world do not consider their rationale,
but cling to these words,
hence good and evil are not distinguished,
and covering up wrongs is seen as magnanimous.
Friends neglect righteousness,
and regard conformity as praiseworthy.
When good and evil are not distinguished,
chaos arises therefrom.
When friends conform blindly,
ruin is sure to follow.
Discussion should value accordance with truth,
not prize excessive fault-finding;
mutual understanding should build friendship on equal footing,
not solidify it through conformity.
Therefore, the enlightened preserve the principle,
not scrutinizing the words;
they discern the heart,
not demanding it from speech."
The affirmative says:
The "Yuèjué Shū" says:
"A woman who flaunts herself is not chaste;
a man who boasts is not trustworthy."
The negative says:
The "Hànshū" says:
"In great conduct, there is no fastidious caution;
in grand rituals, there is no yielding in speech."
The affirmative says:
Huáng Shígōng said:
"Those who seek to expand territory will neglect it;
those who strive to broaden virtue will become strong;
those who possess what is theirs will be secure;
those who covet what belongs to others will be cruel.
A policy of cruelty and destruction,
even if successful, will ultimately fail."
The negative says:
Sīmǎ Cuò said:
"Those who wish to enrich the state
must expand its territory;
those who wish to strengthen the army
must enrich its people;
those who wish to become king
must broaden their virtue.
When these three resources are complete,
then royal achievement follows."
The affirmative says:
The "Zhuàn" says:
"If the heart is without flaw,
why worry about having no home?"
The "Analects" says:
"If there is no transgression in ritual and righteousness,
why worry about others' words?"
The negative says:
The "Analects" says:
"Accumulated slander can melt metal;
gathered calumny can grind bones;
numerous feathers can sink a boat;
a mass of light things can break an axle."
The affirmative says:
Confucius said:
"A gentleman is not a vessel;
a sage's wisdom encompasses all things."
The negative says:
Lièzǐ said:
"Heaven and earth have no perfect achievement,
sages have no complete ability,
and all things have no universal utility.
[None is] entirely complete.
Thus, heaven's duty is to generate and cover,
earth's duty is to bear forms,
and the sage's duty is to teach and transform."
The affirmative says:
Confucius said:
"The gentleman is calm and at ease;
the petty man is always anxious."
The negative says:
Confucius said:
"Jìn's Chóng'ěr developed his ambition for hegemony
while in Cáo and Wèi;
Yuè's Gōujiàn developed his ambition for hegemony
while in Kuàijī.
Therefore, those who dwell in lowly positions without worry
do not think far;
those who live in constant comfort
do not have broad aspirations."
The affirmative says:
Hánzǐ said:
"The ancients,
whose eyes were too short to see themselves,
used mirrors to observe their faces;
whose wisdom was doubtful in knowing themselves,
used the Way to correct themselves."
The negative says:
Lǎozǐ said:
"Hearing inwardly is called acuity;
seeing inwardly is called clarity;
conquering oneself is called strength."
The affirmative says:
Táng Jū said:
"Zhuān Zhū, carrying a dagger, was called brave by all under heaven;
Xī Shī, clad in coarse cloth, was praised as beautiful by the world."
The negative says:
Shènzǐ said:
"Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī
are the most beautiful women in the world,
but if clothed in hideous masks,
all who see them would flee;
if changed into fine black silk,
all who pass would stop.
From this, it is evident
that fine black silk
is an aid to beauty.
If beauty discards it,
then the appeal of beauty is diminished."
The affirmative says:
Xiàng Liáng said:
"Those who rise first subdue others;
those who rise later are subdued by others."
The "Jūn Zhì" says:
"Taking the initiative can seize the enemy's resolve."
The negative says:
Shǐ Yì once said:
"Do not start calamity."
He also said:
"He who starts calamity shall die."
The "Analects" says:
"Do not be the first to cause calamity,
nor the first to seek fortune."
The affirmative says:
Shènzǐ said:
"When the worthy are oppressed by the unworthy,
it is because their authority is light;
when the unworthy submit to the worthy,
It is the position that commands respect.
When Yáo was a commoner,
he could not command his neighbors,
but when he faced south and became king,
his orders were carried out and prohibitions observed.
From this perspective,
virtue alone is insufficient to subdue others,
while power and position are enough to bend even the virtuous."
Counterargument:
Master Jiǎ said:
"From ancient times to the present,
those who oppose the people,
whether sooner or later,
will inevitably be overcome by them.
Thus, Zhòu called himself the Celestial King,
and Jié called himself the Celestial Father,
yet after their downfall,
the people cursed them.
From this perspective,
position does not guarantee respect,
and titles do not confer honor."
Affirmation:
During the reign of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
Yuán Gù and Huáng Shēng debated before the emperor.
Huáng Shēng said:
"Tāng and Wǔ did not receive the Mandate;
they were regicides."
Yuán Gù said:
"Not so.
When Jié and Zhòu fell into chaos and corruption,
the hearts of all under heaven turned to Tāng and Wǔ.
Tāng and Wǔ, aligning with the will of the people,
punished Jié and Zhòu.
The people of Jié and Zhòu,
without being commanded, submitted to Tāng and Wǔ.
Tāng and Wǔ had no choice but to ascend the throne—
if this is not receiving the Mandate, what is it?"
Counterargument:
Huáng Shēng said:
"Though a hat may be worn out,
it must be placed on the head;
though shoes may be new,
they must be worn on the feet.
Why?
Because of the distinction between superior and inferior.
Now, though Jié and Zhòu lost their way,
they were still sovereigns;
though Tāng and Wǔ were sage,
they were subjects.
If a ruler errs,
subjects should remonstrate directly to correct his faults,
thereby honoring the Son of Heaven.
Instead, they capitalized on his errors to execute him,
usurping the throne to face south as rulers—
if this is not regicide, what is it?"
Affirmation:
Tàigōng said:
"Explicit punishments make people fearful,
and fear leads to unexpected changes;
explicit rewards prove insufficient,
and insufficiency breeds resentment.
Thus, an enlightened king governs people
without revealing his preferences
or aversions."
Counterargument:
Master Wén said:
"Punishments without measure lead to slaughter without authority;
rewards without measure result in waste without gratitude."
Hence, Zhūgě Liàng stated:
"Impose authority through law,
and when law is enforced, gratitude is felt;
restrict with ranks,
and when ranks are bestowed, honor is recognized."
Affirmation:
Master Wén said:
"People are influenced by their superiors
not through words,
but through actions.
Thus, if a ruler favors bravery,
the state faces many troubles;
if a ruler favors beauty,
the state falls into chaos."
Counterargument:
The King of Qín said:
"I hear that in Chǔ, iron swords are sharp but entertainers are unskilled.
Sharp swords mean brave warriors,
and unskilled entertainers imply deep strategizing.
With deep strategy commanding brave warriors,
I fear Chǔ has designs on Qín."
Affirmation:
Mòzǐ said:
"Even a worthy ruler
does not cherish ministers without merit;
even a kind father
does not love children who bring no benefit."
Counterargument:
Cáo Zǐjiàn said:
"Overlooking faults and demanding achievements
is the mark of an enlightened ruler;
pitying the foolish and loving the capable
is the kindness of a compassionate father."
The "Three Strategies" says:
"All living beings
wish to realize their aspirations;
therefore, enlightened rulers and worthy ministers
humble themselves to fulfill others."
Affirmation:
The "Zhuàn" says:
"Human hearts differ,
just as faces do."
Cáo Zǐjiàn said:
"Each person has their own preferences.
The fragrance of orchids and huì grass
is loved by many,
yet by the sea, there are those who chase after foul odors;
the melodies of 'Xiánchí' and 'Liùyīng'
are enjoyed by the masses,
yet Mòzǐ criticized them.
How can all be the same?"
Counterargument:
A saying goes:
"Measuring hearts with one's own heart,
there's not even room for a needle."
Confucius said:
"Is it not reciprocity?
What you do not desire,
do not impose on others."
Affirmation:
Guǎnzǐ said:
"When granaries are full,
people know etiquette;
when clothed and fed,
they understand honor and shame."
Counterargument:
An ancient saying states:
"Nobility does not invite arrogance, yet arrogance comes on its own;
wealth does not summon extravagance, yet extravagance arrives unbidden."
Affirmation:
The "Analects" say:
"Loyalty is always rewarded."
Counterargument:
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
"In chaotic times, slander overcomes integrity."
Affirmation:
Hánzǐ said:
"In general, people
agree with those who share their choices,
and oppose those who differ."
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"Like sounds resonate,
like energies attract.
Water flows to dampness,
fire seeks dryness;
clouds follow dragons,
winds follow tigers."
Counterargument:
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"Two women living together,
their wills differ."
A saying goes:
"One roost cannot hold two cocks,
one spring cannot house two flood dragons."
Also:
"In human nature, similarity breeds jealousy."
Hence it is said:
"The beautiful envy each other,
the noble harm each other,
those with shared interests distrust each other."
Affirmation:
Hánzǐ said:
"Discarding laws and techniques to rule by mind,
even Yáo and Shùn could not govern a state;
abandoning compass and square to measure by intent,
even Xī Zhòng could not craft a single wheel.
But let an average ruler adhere to laws and techniques,
and a clumsy craftsman hold to compass and square,
and nothing will be lost."
Counterargument:
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"Arrows pierce far and through hardness
due to the power of the bow;
they hit the target and split the fine
due to the human mind.
Rewarding good and punishing evil
is the role of governance;
but what drives their execution
is sincerity and dedication.
Thus, though the crossbow is strong,
it cannot hit alone;
though decrees are clear,
they cannot implement themselves."
Dù Shù said:
"There are chaotic people in the world,
but no chaotic laws.
If laws alone could suffice,
then Táng and Yú would not have needed the aid of Jì and Qì,
and Yīn and Zhōu would not have valued the support of Yī and Lǚ."
Affirmation:
If plans are not set in advance,
one cannot respond to emergencies;
If military preparations are not made in advance,
one cannot respond to the enemy.
The _Zuǒzhuàn_ says:
"Preparing for unforeseen events
is the good governance of antiquity."
Contradictory view says
The _Zuǒzhuàn_ states:
"Shì Wěi said to the Marquis of Jìn:
'I have heard that:
when there is no bereavement yet one grieves,
sorrow will surely match it;
when there is no warfare yet one builds walls,
enemies will surely occupy them.'"
The _Chūnqiū Wàizhuàn_ says:
"King Jǐng of Zhōu was about to cast large coins.
Dān Mùgōng said:
'This cannot be done.
In ancient times when natural disasters descended,
they would measure resources and currency,
balance light and heavy,
to relieve and save people.
Preparing in advance,
establishing before arrival
is cultivating state preparedness.
Preparing for unforeseen events,
remaining secure while not forgetting danger.
Relieving after arrival
such as putting out fires and curing illnesses,
belongs to measuring resources and currency.
These two do not intermix
each has its appropriate sequence,
they do not intermix.
What can be done first but left unprepared,
is called negligence
negligence means slowness;
what should come later but done first,
is called inviting disaster
meaning when people have no troubles,
making light matters heavy,
alienating people and exhausting wealth,
thus inviting disaster.
Zhōu is indeed a drowning state,
Heaven has not tired of bringing calamities,
and yet you alienate people to assist disaster,
is this not unacceptable!'"
Affirmative view says
The _Zuǒzhuàn_ states:
"The ancients had a saying:
'Releasing an enemy for one day
brings calamity for several generations.'"
Contradictory view says
Jìn and Chǔ met at Yān.
Fán Wénzǐ did not wish to fight,
saying:
"Our former rulers frequently fought for reasons.
Qín, Dí, Qí, and Chǔ were all strong,
if we didn't exert full effort,
our descendants would become weak.
Now three powers have submitted
Qí, Qín, and Dí.
Our enemy
is only Chǔ.
Only sages can be without troubles internally and externally.
Since we are not sages,
external peace must bring internal worries
arrogance and excess
then produce worries and troubles.
Why not release Chǔ to serve as external fear?"
Affirmative view says
The _Sān Lüè_ states:
"Do not let the benevolent manage wealth,
for they bestow much kindness and attract followers."
Contradictory view says
Táo Zhūgōng's middle son killed someone,
and was imprisoned in Chǔ.
Zhūgōng wanted to send his youngest son with a thousand yì of gold to see him.
His eldest son firmly insisted,
so he was sent.
Chǔ killed his brother.
Zhūgōng said:
"I knew he would get his brother killed.
This elder grew up with me,
experiencing livelihood hardships,
thus values wealth.
The younger brother was born into my wealth,
riding fine carriages and horses,
chasing crafty hares,
how could he know where wealth comes from,
so he lightly discards it.
Now the elder indeed got his brother killed,
such is the natural course,
not worth grieving."
Affirmative view says
The _Analects_ state:
"Those with meager salaries cannot be involved in chaos,
those with light rewards cannot be involved in difficulties."
Shènzǐ said:
"Former kings saw that those unwilling to accept salaries shouldn't be ministers,
those without generous salaries
won't share difficulties."
Contradictory view says
Tián Dān was about to attack Dí,
and visited Lǔ Zhòngzǐ.
Zhòngzǐ said:
"General, you cannot take Dí.
Why?
Previously at Jímò,
you sat weaving baskets,
stood leaning on spades,
leading the soldiers.
This defeated Yān.
Now you have eastern Yèyì's revenues,
western Huánshàng's pleasures,
golden belts across,
galloping between Zī and Miǎn,
enjoying life's pleasures,
without death-seeking resolve.
This is why you won't win."
Later it proved true.
Affirmative view says
The _Analects_ state:
"Poor and humble friends should not be forgotten,
wives who shared husks should not be cast out."
Contradictory view says
The _Analects_ state:
"With broad social connections, trust among friends declines;
with high ranks and salaries, loyalty to the ruler declines."
Affirmative view says
The _Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ_ states:
"Chǔ's Chūnshēn Jūn appointed Sūnzǐ as steward.
A guest advised Shēn Jūn:
'Tāng with Bó,
King Wǔ with Hào,
both had no more than a hundred lǐ,
yet possessed the world.
Now Sūnzǐ is a worthy man,
and you lend him power over a hundred lǐ,
I fear for your danger.'
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
'Good.'
Then he dismissed Sūnzǐ.
Sūnzǐ went to Zhào,
where he was made senior minister."
Contradictory view says
Another guest advised Chūnshēn Jūn:
"Previously Yī Yǐn left Xià for Yīn,
Yīn prospered while Xià perished;
Guǎn Zhòng left Lǔ for Qí,
Lǔ weakened while Qí strengthened.
Where the worthy reside,
their ruler inevitably becomes honored,
their state inevitably becomes glorious.
Now Sūnzǐ is a worthy man,
why dismiss him?"
Chūnshēn Jūn again said:
"Good."
He again invited Sūnzǐ.
Affirmative view says
King Xuān of Hán said to Jiū Liú:
"I wish to employ both Gōngzhòng and Gōngshū,
is this possible?"
He replied:
"Impossible.
Jìn used six ministers and the state divided,
Lord Jiǎn used Tián Chéng and Kǎn Zhǐ and was assassinated,
Wèi used both Xīshǒu and Zhāng Yí and lost lands west of the river.
Now you employ both,
the more powerful
will build internal factions;
the less powerful
will borrow external influence.
Ministers may build internal factions
to control the ruler's orders;
or form external alliances
to split your territory,
then your state will be endangered."
Also said:
Gōngsūn Yǎn was Wèi's general,
and didn't get along with minister Tián Xū.
Jì Wénzǐ advised Wèi's king for Yǎn:
"Have you not seen oxen paired with thoroughbreds?
They cannot go a hundred steps.
Now you consider Yǎn fit for command,
so employ him firmly,
yet follow the minister's plans -
this is pairing oxen with thoroughbreds.
Both ox and horse would die without achieving results,
then your state would be harmed.
I hope you will consider this."
Contradictory view says
Fùzǐ said:
"Heaven and earth are supremely divine,
The Way cannot follow the same path yet give birth to all things;
the sage is supremely wise,
yet cannot govern the people with a single standard.
Therefore, using diversity to achieve unity
is the Way of Heaven and Earth;
adapting measures to circumstances
is the governance of the sage.
Once the Way is attained,
even if there are mutually harmful elements,
they do not impair the essence of governance.
The natures of water and fire
extinguish each other,
but those skilled in using them
place cauldrons and pots between them,
kindling and boiling with them,
and thus can fully utilize both,
without mutual harm.
In the world,
things like water and fire are numerous.
Why worry about mutual harm?
Why fear not fully utilizing them?"
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Heaven and Earth are separate,
yet their affairs are the same;
man and woman are separate,
yet their wills communicate;
all things are separate,
yet their affairs are analogous."
Affirmation says:
Chén Dēng advised Cáo Gōng regarding Lǚ Bù, saying:

you must always feed it enough meat,
for if not full, it will bite people."
Negation says:
Cáo Gōng said:
"It is not as you say.
It is like raising a hawk:
when hungry, it serves humans;
when full, it flies away."
Affirmation says:
Liú Bèi came seeking refuge with Cáo Gōng,
who appointed him as Governor of Yùzhōu.
Someone told Cáo Gōng:
"Bèi has ambitious aspirations;
if you do not act against him early,
he will surely become a threat later."
Cáo Gōng consulted Guō Jiā about this.
Jiā said:
"This is true.
However, you raised a righteous army with your sword,
eliminating tyranny for the people,
upholding sincerity and trust,
to summon outstanding talents,
and still feared they might not come.
Now Bèi has a reputation as a hero;
if you harm him when he comes to you in distress,
earning a name for harming the worthy,
then wise men will grow suspicious,
turn their hearts to choose other lords,
and with whom will you stabilize the empire?
To remove one man's threat
at the cost of disappointing the hopes of all under heaven—
this is a critical moment of safety and danger,
which must be carefully considered."
Cáo Gōng said:
"Well said!"
Negation says: [69 Fùzǐ noted:
Guō Jiā said to Tàizǔ:
"Bèi has great ambitions and wins much popular support;
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi are both matchless warriors,
willing to die for him.
In my view,
his schemes are unpredictable.
The ancients had a saying:
'To spare an enemy for a day
brings calamity for generations.'
You should deal with him early."
But Cáo Gōng was then recruiting heroes,
to demonstrate great trust,
and did not follow Jiā's advice.
Affirmation says:
The *Family Sayings of Confucius* states:
Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"May I set aside the ways of antiquity

The Master said:

In the past, the Eastern Barbarians admired the rites of the Central States;
when a woman was widowed,
she took a secret husband privately,
and never remarried.
Not remarrying is one thing,
but it is not the meaning of chastity.
Cāngwú Náo
(pronounced nú niǎo fǎn)
married a beautiful wife
and yielded her to his elder brother.
Yielding is one thing,
but it is not the yielding of propriety.
Now you wish to discard the ancient ways and follow your own ideas—
how can you know your ideas are not mistaking wrong for right?"
The *Analects* say:
"To alter the ancient and disrupt the constant
leads to death or ruin."
The *Book of Documents* states:
"Affairs not modeled on antiquity,
yet able to last long,
I have never heard of."
Negation says:
King Wǔlíng of Zhào wished to adopt Hú attire,
but Prince Chéng was displeased.
The king said:

rites are for facilitating affairs.
The sage observes local customs and adapts appropriately,
establishing rites according to circumstances,
to benefit the people and strengthen the state.
Cutting hair and tattooing,
baring arms and fastening garments left-over-right,
are customs of the Ōuyuè people;
blackening teeth and tattooing foreheads,
wearing tí fish-skin caps and hempen seams,
are practices of the Quǎnróng state.
Thus, ceremonial garments differ,
but their convenience is the same.
Customs vary with locality,
rites change with affairs.
Therefore, the sage devises what can benefit the state,
without uniform practices;
plans what can facilitate rites,
without imitating the past.
Confucians share one teacher but customs differ;
the Central States share rites but teachings diverge—
how much more for the convenience of mountain valleys?
Thus, in choices of adoption or rejection,
even the wise cannot unify;
in garments of near and far,
even sages cannot make identical.
Remote regions have many strange customs;
biased studies harbor many contentious arguments.
Now, Uncle, your words
speak of convention.
My words
aim to shape convention.
You dislike the name of changing attire,
forgetting the reality of effective service—
this is not what I expect of you!"
Prince Chéng then adopted Hú attire.
Affirmation says:
"For transforming customs and changing practices,
nothing is better than music."
Negation says:
Mèngzǐ said:
"The Way of Heaven, when followed, is great;
when forced, becomes small.
Following means
following human nature."
Affirmation says:
Lǐ Xún said:
"To reward and punish based on personal joy or anger,
disregarding seasonal prohibitions—
even with the heart of Yáo or Shùn,
one cannot achieve harmony.
Those skilled in speaking of antiquity
must have efficacy in the present;
those skilled in speaking of Heaven
must have evidence in humanity.
Suppose a skilled farmer wishes to grow crops out of season:
even baring his back to plow deep,
sweating to sow seeds,
they still will not grow—
not due to lack of human effort,
but because the timing of Heaven is not met."
The *Book of Changes* says:
"When it is time to stop, stop;
when it is time to act, act;
in movement and stillness, do not miss the timing—
then the Way will be bright."
The *Book of Documents* states:
"Reverently impart the seasonal duties to the people.
Thus, ancient kings
honored Heaven and Earth,
esteemed yīn and yáng,
revered the ordinances of the four seasons and months,
and complemented them with good governance—
then harmonious energy could be promptly attained,
like drumbeats and their echoes."
Negation says:
Tàigōng told King Wǔ:
"Heaven contributes nothing to military victory;
yet generals rely on it in nine ways:
enforcing laws not by execution but by invasion,
lacking virtue yet using calculations of sun and moon,

Not knowing the terrain yet blaming the timing,
the enemy being timid and weak but not daring to attack while trusting in tortoise shell divination,
soldiers lacking courage yet resorting to ghosts and spirits,

cannot be seen when looked at,

Sīmǎ Qiān said:

Fàn Yè said:

Affirmation says
Yì Fèng said:
"The essence of governance,

If people are sincerely inclined toward righteousness,
even the foolish can be useful;
if they harbor wickedness,
the wise become even more harmful."
Negation says
All rulers love themselves.
Those who don't know how to love themselves,
are not worthy of love.
Thus Huánzǐ said:
"Those who hunt fierce beasts,
do not have beauties raise their hands;
those who fish for giant fish,
do not let children lightly participate.

How can the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
not select the right people?
Therefore it is said:
A dog's ferocity,
manifests in barking at wrongdoing,
without neglecting its duties day and night.
This is the ultimate demonstration of loyalty.
Once there was a wine seller in Sòng,
whose wine turned sour and wouldn't sell,

Because he had a fierce dog.
The dog knew to love its master,
but couldn't consider the problem of sour wine for its master -

Affirmation says
The Analects say:

Negation says

Affirmation says

Negation says

The Emperor again said:

Affirmation says

Negation says

Affirmation says

Negation says

Affirmation says
Confucius said:

It is said:

"The lord of Wèi is worthy,

It is countered:
Hánzǐ said:

Now recluses who do not serve humans
are of the deer kind.
Hence, Tàigōng upon reaching Qí executed Huá Shì,
and Confucius as Minister of Justice put Shǎozhèng Mǎo to death."
Zhào Zhǔfù sent Lǐ Cī to observe if Zhōngshān could be attacked.
He returned and reported:

Zhǔfù said:
"By your words, he is a worthy ruler—

Lǐ Cī said:
"Not so.
If the ruler honors recluses from cliffs and caves,
then warriors grow lax;
if the ruler respects scholars,
then farmers become idle.
If farmers are idle, the state grows poor;
if warriors are lax, the military weakens.
With a weak military abroad and poverty at home,
what awaits but ruin?"
Zhǔfù said:
"Well said."

It is said:

Chén Píng stated:

Sūnzǐ wrote a letter thanking Chūnshēn Jūn, saying:

When a lord is young and prides himself on his talent,
lacking methods to recognize treachery,

resorting to murder to protect themselves.
Thus, they kill the worthy elders and set up the young and weak,
depose the legitimate heir and install the unrighteous.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* warns against this,
stating:
'King Wéi of Chǔ was on a mission to Zhèng;
before leaving the border,
hearing the king was ill,
he returned to inquire,
then used his hat string to strangle the king and killed him,
thereupon establishing himself.
Cuī Zhù of Qí had a beautiful wife;
Duke Zhuang had an affair with her.
Cuī Zhù led his partisans to attack Duke Zhuang.
Duke Zhuang fled,
climbed over an outer wall,
was shot in the thigh,
and was killed,
whereupon his brother was installed.
In recent times, Lì Duì governed Zhào,
starved Zhǔfù at Shāqiū,
and killed him after a hundred days;
Nào Chǐ governed Qí,
pulled out the tendons of King Mǐn,
hung them on the temple beam,
and he died overnight.'
Now leprosy, though a swelling and blistering disease,
compared to ancient times,
does not reach strangling with a hat string or shooting in the thigh;
compared to recent times,
does not reach tendon-pulling or starvation.
Lords who are robbed and killed
suffer mental toil and worry,
physical hardship and pain,
surely worse than leprosy.
From this perspective,
even if the leper pities the king,
it is permissible."
It is said:
The *Yì Jīng* states:
"Preparing things for use,

none are greater than the sage."

Zhuāngzǐ said:

Create dǒu and hú measures to quantify,

create scales and weights to weigh,
and they will steal the scales and weights along with the goods;
create tallies and seals for trust,
and they will steal the tallies and seals along with the goods;
establish benevolence and righteousness to teach,
and they will steal benevolence and righteousness along with the goods.

He who steals a buckle is executed;
he who steals a state becomes a feudal lord.
At the gates of feudal lords,
benevolence and righteousness reside—
is this not stealing benevolence, righteousness, sagehood, and wisdom?

support feudal lords,
steal benevolence and righteousness,
and seize the benefits of dǒu, hú, scales, weights, tallies, and seals—
even rewards of carriages and crowns cannot urge them otherwise,
nor can the threat of axes and halberds restrain them.
This greatly benefits Dào Zhí
and makes it impossible to prohibit—
this is the fault of the sages.
Hence it is said:
'The sharp tools of the state
cannot be shown to others.'
Those sages
are the sharp tools of all under heaven."
This is not the way to enlighten the world. "
Affirmation says

it was an effect of engaging subordinates.
Thus, Chén Píng said to Wáng Líng:
'In openly refuting and court disputation,
I am not your equal;
but in securing the Liú family,
you are not my equal.'
If challenging superiors were superior,
then Wáng Líng should rank above Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng,
and Zhū Yún should surpass Wú and Dèng?"
Affirmation says
The Records of the Grand Historian state:
"Hán Fēi remarked:
'Confucians disrupt laws with writings,
while knights-errant violate prohibitions with force.'
Both are criticized,
yet learned scholars are often praised in the world.
As for those who attain chancellorships and ministers through tactics,
assisting their sovereigns,
there is certainly nothing to say.
But as for Jì Cì, Yuán Xiàn
Jì Cì,
Among the disciples of Confucius,
there was one who never held office,
yet Confucius praised him.
He studied books and cherished independent conduct,
his discussions never carelessly conforming to the contemporary world,
and the contemporary world laughed at him.
Nowadays, the wandering knights,
although their actions do not conform to orthodox righteousness,
their words are always trustworthy,
their actions resolute,
their promises sincere,
they do not cherish their own bodies,
rushing to aid scholars in distress,
and are ashamed to boast of their virtues—
indeed, they have much to commend.
Moreover, crises and emergencies
are something people encounter from time to time.
Yú Shùn was trapped in a well and granary,
Yī Yǐn carried cauldrons and cutting boards,
Fù Yuè hid in Fùxiǎn,
Lǚ Shàng was stranded at Jíjīn,
Yí Wú was shackled,
Bǎilǐ Xī fed oxen,
Zhòngní (Confucius) was besieged in Kuāng,
and suffered hunger in Chén and Cài.
These are all learned men regarded as virtuous and benevolent,
yet they still encountered such calamities.
How much more so for those of average talent navigating the turbulent currents of recent times?
How can one fully recount the harm they encounter!
Yet these commoners,
establishing codes of giving, taking, and keeping promises,
are praised for their righteousness over a thousand lǐ.
Thus, when scholars are in dire straits, they can entrust their lives to them.
Are these not what people call worthy and heroic?
If indeed the knights of the countryside
were compared with Jì Cì and Yuán Xiàn
in weighing authority and strength,
and assessing contributions to their era,
they could not be discussed on the same day.
How can they be considered insignificant!"
Another view says:
The Hànshū states:
"The Son of Heaven establishes states,
the feudal lords establish families,
from ministers and officials down to commoners,
each has their own ranks and distinctions.
Thus, people serve their superiors,
and those below do not harbor ambitions.
Confucius said:
'When the Son of Heaven possesses the Way,
governance does not lie with the high officials.'
The hundred officials and functionaries,
upholding laws and following orders,
cultivate their duties.
Overstepping one's duties leads to execution,
encroaching on others' offices brings punishment.
Hence, superiors and subordinates are in harmony,
and all affairs are well-ordered.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
the rites, music, and military campaigns
emanated from the feudal lords.
After Huán and Wén,
high ministers held hereditary power,
and subordinate officials wielded command.
This decline continued into the Warring States period,
with vertical and horizontal alliances,
and forceful governance contending for supremacy.
Thus, among the princes of various states,
Wèi had Xìnlíng,
Zhào had Píngyuán,
Qí had Mèngcháng,
Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
all leveraging the power of kings and dukes,
competing to be wandering knights.
Even those skilled in crowing like cocks or stealing like dogs
were all received with guest rites.
And the Zhào chancellor Yú Qīng
abandoned his state and ruler
to secure the friendship of Wèi and Qí in their distress;
Xìnlíng Wújì
stole tallies and forged orders,
killed generals and commanded troops,
to rescue Píngyuán in his urgency.
All these gained weight among the feudal lords,
and made their names known throughout the world.
Those who grasped wrists and engaged in wandering debates
considered the four nobles as foremost.
Thus, the discourse of betraying the public for partisan cliques prevailed,
and the principle of upholding duties and serving superiors was abandoned.
By the time Hàn arose,
the legal net was loose and broad,
and this was not rectified.
Figures like Wèijī and Wǔ'ān
vied for followers in the capital;
followers of Guō Jiě and Jù Mèng
galloped through the alleys,
wielding power across regions,
their force overpowering dukes and marquises.
The masses honored their fame and deeds,
gazing with admiration.
Even if they fell into legal punishment,
they identified with those who died to achieve fame,
like Jì, Lù, Qiú, Mù,
and died without regret.
Zēngzǐ said:
'When those above lose the Way,
the people have been dispersed for long.'
If not for an enlightened king above,
showing them likes and dislikes,
and aligning them with rites and laws,
how could people know prohibitions and return to correctness?
The ancient correct laws held:
The Five Hegemons
were offenders against the Three Sovereigns;
and the Six States
were offenders against the Five Hegemons;
moreover, the four nobles
were offenders against the Six States.
How much more so for the likes of Guō Jiě,
with the insignificance of a commoner,
usurping the power over life and death—
their crimes
do not permit even execution!"
Another view says:
The Shīzǐ states:
"For ministers,
recommending the worthy is their achievement;
for rulers,
employing the worthy is their achievement."
The Shǐjì states:
"When Bào Shū recommended Guǎn Zhòng,
the world did not praise Guǎn Zhòng's worthiness,
but praised Bào Shū's ability to recognize talent."
Another view says:
Sū Jiàn once criticized General-in-Chief Wèi Qīng:
"You hold the utmost respect, yet the worthy scholars of the world do not praise you.
I wish to see you emulate ancient and modern famous generals in selecting and recruiting the worthy."
The General-in-Chief apologized:
"Since Wèijī and Wǔ'ān lavishly hosted guests,
the Son of Heaven has often gnashed his teeth.
To personally attach to scholars,
recruiting the worthy and dismissing the unworthy—
that is the ruler's prerogative;
ministers should merely uphold laws and fulfill duties.
Why should they recruit scholars?"
Such was his approach as a general.
Discussion:
Here, one view is affirmed, another denied,
all being contradictions within the classics and histories themselves.
Bān Gù stated:
"In the past, when the kingly Way declined,
feudal lords governed by force,
the rulers of the time
had diverse likes and dislikes.
Thus, the techniques of various schools
swarmed forth simultaneously,
each citing one aspect,
elevating what they esteemed,
using this to spread their theories,
and win over the feudal lords.
Although their words differed,
they were like fire and water extinguishing each other,
yet also able to generate each other.
Benevolence and righteousness,
reverence and harmony,
though matters may be opposite,
can also complement each other."
The Yìjīng says:
"The world reaches the same destination by different paths,
achieves the same goal through a hundred thoughts."
This expresses it.
Chapter 15: Adaptation to Change
In the past, the former kings established laws and institutions according to the times,
addressed affairs based on the tasks at hand.
When laws suited the era, order prevailed;
when actions fit the tasks, achievements followed.
Now times have changed, yet laws remain unchanged;
tasks have shifted, yet actions cling to antiquity.
Thus, laws conflict with the times,
and times diverge from tasks.
Hence, laws are established but chaos intensifies;
tasks are pursued but affairs worsen.
Therefore, when sages govern the state,
they do not imitate antiquity,
nor rigidly adhere to the present,
but achieve merit by aligning with the times,
and avoid harm even in difficulties.
Qín Xiàogōng employed Wèi Yāng.
Yāng wished to reform the laws,
but Xiàogōng feared criticism from the world,
and hesitated.
Wèi Yāng said:
"Hesitant actions gain no fame;
indecisive deeds yield no merit.
Those with superior conduct
are inevitably criticized by the world;
those with unique wisdom
are surely mocked by others.
Fools remain blind to accomplished facts;
the wise foresee what is yet to sprout.
One cannot consult the masses at the start,
but can share joy in success.
Those who discuss supreme virtue
do not conform to customs;
those who achieve great merit
do not consult the multitude.
Thus, if sages can strengthen the state,
they do not follow old ways;
if they can benefit the people,
they do not adhere to outdated rites."
Xiàogōng said:
"Excellent."
Gān Lóng said:
"Not so.
Sages do not change the people to teach;
the wise do not alter laws to govern.
Teaching according to the people
brings success without toil;
governing by existing laws
makes officials familiar and people tranquil."
Wèi Yāng said:
"What Lóng says
is commonplace talk.
Ordinary people cling to customs;
scholars drown in what they've heard.
These two types may serve as officials preserving laws,
but cannot discuss beyond established norms.
The Three Dynasties ruled with different rites;
the Five Hegemons dominated with varying laws.
The wise create laws,
fools are bound by them;
the worthy reform rites,
the unworthy are constrained by them."
Dù Zhì said:
"Without hundredfold benefit,
do not change laws;
without tenfold gain,
do not replace tools.
Imitating antiquity avoids errors;
following rites prevents deviation."
Wèi Yāng responded:
"Governing generations requires no single way;
benefiting the state means not copying antiquity.
Thus Tāng and Wǔ ruled without following old ways,
while Xià and Yīn perished without changing rites.
Those opposing antiquity should not be faulted,
and those adhering to rites deserve little praise."
Xiàogōng said:
"Excellent."
Thus, reforms were implemented.
From this we say:
Therefore, know that such people
each build merit and virtue according to their time.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Though one has tools,
it's better to meet the right season;
though one has wisdom,
it's better to encounter the proper era."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"When the time hasn't come,
don't force life;
when affairs aren't ripe,
don't compel success."
The Analects say:
"Sages cultivate preparedness to await the time."
How do we know this is so?
Huánzǐ said:
"The Three Sovereigns ruled with the Way,
the Five Emperors transformed with virtue,
the Three Kings governed with benevolence and righteousness,
the Five Hegemons used authority and wisdom."
It is said:
Having no decrees or punishments
defines a Sovereign;
having decrees but no punishments
defines an Emperor;
rewarding good and punishing evil,
with feudal lords paying homage,
defines a King;
raising armies,
establishing alliances,
using trust and righteousness to rectify the era,
defines a Hegemon.
Wénzǐ said:
"Emperors
value virtue;
Kings
honor righteousness;
Hegemons
are compelled by expediency.
When the Way narrows, then wisdom is employed;
when virtue weakens, then punishments are used;
when clarity fades, then scrutiny is applied."
Discussion:
In establishing states and achieving merit abroad,
their governance differs thus.
The era before the Five Emperors is too remote,
with no records in classics,
so only the two peaks of Kingly and Hegemonic rule
define the principles of past and present.
Qín and Hàn occupied imperial positions
but practiced hegemonic affairs.
Thus they are considered secondary in virtue.
The rule of the Kingly Way
first eliminates human harms
and provides ample food and clothing.
It is stated:
"On five-mu homesteads,
planted with mulberries,
with women sericulturists,
those aged fifty
can wear silk.
With hundred-mu fields,
for multi-person families,
farming and managing,
they can avoid hunger.
Raising chickens, pigs, dogs, and swine
without missing their seasons,
the elderly can eat meat.
When rulers have no greedy demands,
and subjects no extravagant excesses,
with light taxes and few corvée duties,
those serving as officials
receive salaries only,
not competing for profit with others.
Thus, wealth is balanced without extreme disparity between rich and poor."
Then they are taught ritual propriety.
Thus, enlightened kings examine themselves to correct tradition,
carefully maintain their positions.
Palaces, carriages, and robes
do not exceed ritual standards;
nine concubines are properly ordered within,
three dukes divide duties without.
Establish well-field systems to equalize,
appoint feudal lords to oversee,
so the wealthy don't overspend,
the poor don't lack,
then extend the education of the Imperial Academy,
demonstrate the demeanor of deference,
thus harmonious energy permeates everywhere,
calamities and chaos do not arise—
this is the teaching of sage kings.
And they use punishments and executions to instill awe,
making people understand preferences, aversions, and choices.
Emperor Yú first ordered Yǔ to regulate waters and land,
Hòu Jì to sow various grains,
Qì to promulgate the five teachings,
Gāo Yáo to refine punishments—
thus the world achieved great peace.
Therefore,
when great transformation converges from all directions,
and the world enjoys peace and happiness—
this is the method of Kings.
Kings
regard Heaven as father and Earth as mother,
harmonize yin and yang,
follow the four seasons and order the five elements,
nourish the common people and nurture all beings.
Thus the term 'King'
means 'to go toward.'
It speaks of their generous grace,
skillfully nurturing and moistening the world,
so the world turns toward them—
hence called 'King.'
The greater achievements of Hegemons
honor rulers and humble ministers,
centralize authority,
unify governance,
ensure trustworthy rewards and punishments,
make laws clear,
have officials well-ordered,
and enforce commands strictly.
There will be no need for punishments.
When the ruler treats his subjects
as his own heart and mind,
then the subjects will regard the ruler
as infants regard their loving mother.
In matters of trust,
it should be as constant as the four seasons;
and people's trust in him
will be as certain as the verification of cold and heat.
Thus, viewing the distant as if near,
is not because the Way is near,
but because his illustrious virtue is seen.
Therefore, without moving arms and armor, he commands awe;
without distributing benefits, he gains affection.
This is what is called "the defense of an enlightened king,
which repels the enemy a thousand miles away."
Discussion says:
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng said to Qí Huán Gōng:
"If you, my lord, wish to be a hegemon or king,
and undertake great enterprises,
then you must start from their root.
The common people of the state of Qí
are the root of your lordship.
People are deeply worried about hunger, yet taxes are heavy;
people are greatly afraid of death, yet punishments and governance are harsh;
people are much pained by toil, yet the ruler undertakes projects at inopportune times.
If you lighten their taxes,
relax your punishments,
and undertake projects seasonably,
then the people will be content."
This is called cultivating the root to become hegemon or king.
Zēng Zǐ said:
"What are the 'Three Ultimates'?"
Confucius said:
"The ultimate ritual involves no yielding,
yet all under Heaven is ordered;
the ultimate reward involves no expense,
yet the scholars of the world are pleased;
the ultimate music has no sound,
yet the people of the world are harmonious."
Why is this?
In ancient times, the enlightened king necessarily knew fully the names of all the excellent scholars in the world.
Once he knew their names,
he also knew their substance;
once he knew their substance,
he then employed the ranks of the world to honor them.
This is called "the ultimate ritual involves no yielding, yet all under Heaven is ordered."
Employing the emoluments of the world
to enrich the scholars of the world,
this is called "the ultimate reward involves no expense, yet the scholars of the world are pleased."
Being thus,
the bright reputation of the world then arises,
this is called "the ultimate music has no sound, yet the people of the world are harmonious."
Therefore it is said:
What is called the ultimate benevolence in the world
is the ability to unite the closest bonds in the world;
what is called the ultimate wisdom in the world
is the ability to utilize the harmony of the world;
what is called the ultimate clarity in the world
is the ability to promote the worthiest in the world.
Thus, for the benevolent, nothing is greater than loving others;
for the wise, nothing is greater than knowing the worthy;
for governance, nothing is greater than appointing capable officials.
A virtuous ruler
who cultivates these three things,
then within the four seas,
will only receive offerings and commands.
This is called "repelling the enemy a thousand miles away."
Now, the campaigns of an enlightened king
are necessarily directed against where the Way has been abandoned,
punishing its ruler,
reforming its governance,
comforting its people,
and not seizing their wealth.
Therefore it is said:
The campaigns of an enlightened king
are like the falling of timely rain;
when it arrives, people rejoice.
This is called "withdrawing the army onto the mat and pillow"
— meaning secure and without worry.
Thus Yáng Xióng said:
"The principle of the Six Classics
values preventing disorder;
the victory of military strategists
values preventing war."
This is the method of the Confucian school.
Discussion says:
The teachings of the Confucian school,
emphasize virtuous conduct and righteousness,
representing the Way of the True King.
Mò Zǐ said:
"The people of antiquity did not yet know how to build houses,
so they dwelt by hills and mounds,
living in caves.
Therefore, the sage kings arose,
and built houses.
The method for building houses
was that the height should suffice to avoid dampness,
and the walls suffice to keep out wind and cold.
The height of the interior walls
should suffice to distinguish the propriety between men and women.
Careful attention to this was enough;
it was not for spectacle and pleasure.
Therefore, the people of the world
could have sufficient resources.
The kings of today build houses differently from this.
They heavily tax the common people,
in order to build houses,
with prospects of winding towers and pavilions,
adorned with blue and yellow carvings and engravings.
Building houses like this,
those around them all imitate and emulate them.
Therefore, their wealth is insufficient to cope with famine and disaster,
or to relieve the orphaned and widowed,
so the state becomes poor and difficult to govern.
In building houses, one cannot but be frugal."
Discussion says:
This is about frugality in building houses.
"The people of antiquity did not yet know how to make clothing,
at that time wearing pelts and tying with rushes,
in winter not light yet warm,
in summer not light yet cool.
The sage kings considered this unsuitable to human feelings,
so the sages arose,
instructing women
to make clothing for people.
The method for making clothing
was that in winter, plain silk
sufficed to be light and warm;
in summer, fine and coarse hemp
sufficed to be light and cool;
careful attention to this was enough;
it was not to glorify the ears and eyes,
or for display to fools.
Therefore, the people were frugal and easily governed,
and the ruler's use of resources was economical and easily sustained.
The kings of today,
in making clothing,
are different from this.
They heavily tax the common people,
to make clothes with elaborate patterns and luxurious fabrics,
casting metal for hooks,
using pearls and jade for pendants.
From this perspective,
their making of clothing
is not for the body,
but for visual appeal.
Therefore, the people become dissolute and difficult to govern,
and the ruler becomes extravagant and difficult to remonstrate with.
With an extravagant ruler
ruling over dissolute people,
hoping for the state to be free from disorder
is impossible.
In making clothing, one cannot but be frugal."
Discussion says:
This is about frugality in clothing.
This is the method of Mò Dí.
Discussion says:
The Mohist doctrine
advocates eliminating extravagance and practicing frugality,
representing the Way of strengthening the root.
Shāng Zǐ said:
"Laws and decrees
are the life of the people,
the foundation of governance."
Shèn Zǐ said:
"A ruler of men
who abandons the law and governs personally,
then those receiving rewards, though enriched,
will expect more without end;
those receiving punishments, though appropriate,
will hope for leniency without cease.
If the ruler abandons the law and uses his own mind to decide severity,
resentment will arise from this.
Therefore, using lots to divide horses,
and using a hook to divide land,
is not because the hook and lots possess surpassing wisdom,
but to remove bias and block resentment.
Therefore it is said:
The great ruler relies on the law and does not act personally,
then resentment does not arise,
and superiors and subordinates are harmonious."
One rabbit runs,
a hundred people chase it,
not because the rabbit can be divided into a hundred parts,
but because its ownership is undetermined.
Rabbits fill the market for sale,
yet thieves dare not take them,
because ownership is determined.
Therefore, when ownership is undetermined,
even Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng
would all strive to chase it;
when ownership is determined,
even a poor thief dare not take it.
Therefore, when the sage establishes laws and decrees,
sets up officials,
and appoints clerks,
it is to determine ownership.
《Shī Zǐ》 says:
"When directing the masses,
issuing commands makes them slow,
but dividing land makes them swift.
Why is this?
Because they cannot escape their responsibilities.
Speech also has its domain,
which cannot remain undivided.
If ruler and minister share the same domain,
then ministers can evade their responsibilities.
Thus, when a marking line is stretched, crooked wood is deemed faulty;
when names and duties are examined, ministers who fail in their scrutiny are held accountable."
When names and duties are defined, even great deceivers become honest and trustworthy,
and major thieves become sincere and cautious,
each governing themselves."
Yīn Wénzǐ said:
"When names are fixed, things do not contend;
when distinctions are clear, selfishness does not prevail.
That things do not contend
is not due to lack of intention,
but because names are fixed,
leaving no room for their intentions to act.
That selfishness does not prevail
is not due to lack of desire,
but because distinctions are clear,
leaving no room for their desires to operate.
Thus, intentions and desires are inherent in everyone,
yet they become as if without intention or desire
because the system restrains them effectively."
Shēnzǐ said:
"The ruler is like the body,
the ministers like the hands;
the ruler establishes the foundation,
the ministers handle the details.
A ruler
holds the tally to demand accountability for names.
Names are
the net of heaven and earth,
the tally of the sage.
Spreading the net of heaven and earth
and using the sage's tally,
then nothing can escape."
Discussion says:
Hánzǐ said:
"A ruler
does not need eyes like Shī Kuàng to be perceptive.
Relying not on methods but waiting for one's own eyes to perceive
results in seeing little;
this is not a strategy against being deceived.
Not leveraging circumstances
but waiting for one's own ears to hear
results in hearing little;
this is not a way to avoid being misled.
An enlightened ruler
makes the world inevitably see for him,
makes the world inevitably hear for him.
Residing deep within the palace,
he illuminates all within the four seas,
and the world cannot obscure or deceive him.
Why?
Because the penalty for concealing crimes is severe,
and the reward for reporting treachery is generous."
Sūnqīng said:
"Clarify duties and distinctions,
order tasks and affairs,
assign talents and official abilities,
and all will be well-governed.
Thus,
the virtuous are promoted,
the incorruptible rise,
with comprehensive hearing and clear vision,
and no affairs are neglected.
Hence, the Son of Heaven sees without looking,
hears without listening,
knows without pondering,
achieves without acting,
sitting solidly alone while the world follows him.
This is holding the tally to demand accountability for names."
Shīzǐ said:
"When an enlightened ruler stands,
his appearance is dignified,
his mind is humble,
his gaze is not restless,
his hearing is not indulgent.
He examines duties and responds to words,
establishing himself in court.
Then, even if hidden and distant faults exist,
though there may be errors,
they will certainly be few.
An enlightened ruler does not extend his eyes and ears,
does not employ spies,
does not force himself to hear and see.
When forms arrive, he observes;
when sounds come, he listens;
when events occur, he responds.
If those nearby do not err,
then those far away are orderly;
if the clear is not lost,
then the subtle is respected.
This ensures nothing escapes."
The moving shake,
the still remain calm;
names name themselves,
affairs settle themselves.
Discussion says:
Shīzǐ said:
"The one who controlled the floods
was Yǔ;
the one who sowed the five grains
was Hòu Jì;
the one who judged cases and decided fairly
was Gāo Yáo;
Shùn did nothing,
yet became the parent of the world."
This is names naming themselves.
Tàigōng said to King Wén:
"Heaven has constant punishments,
humans have constant livelihoods.
Sharing life with heaven and humanity,
the world remains tranquil."
This is affairs settling themselves.
Therefore, those with the Way
use names to correct things,
follow affairs to settle them.
Yīn Wénzǐ said:
"Because the worthy are useful,
make it so they cannot but be used;
because the foolish are useless,
make it so they cannot be used.
Used or not used,
each finds their proper use.
Why worry about chaos among things?"
Shīzǐ said:
"The way of holding court
is to give people their roles.
For great goodness,
one must ask who recommended it;
for great faults,
one must ask who appointed them,
and then administer rewards and punishments.
This also serves to observe the worthy and unworthy.
Clear distinctions prevent deception,
correct names prevent falsity.
The worthy are honored,
the unworthy are despised.
Worthiness and unworthiness,
loyalty and disloyalty,
viewed through the Way,
are like black and white."
In ancient times, Yáo governed the world
through names;
his names were correct, so the world was orderly.
Jié governed the world
also through names;
his names were distorted, so the world fell into chaos.
Thus, the sage values the correctness of names."
Discussion says:
A foolish ruler mistakes the unworthy for worthy,
the disloyal for loyal,
the unlawful for lawful,
due to incorrect naming.
Lǐ Sī wrote:
"Hánzǐ said, 'A kind mother may have wayward sons,
but a strict household has no defiant slaves.'
Why?
Because punishment is applied necessarily.
Thus, under Shāngjūn's laws,
those who discard ashes on the road are punished.
Discarding ashes
is a minor offense;
yet being punished
is a severe penalty.
If light offenses are strictly supervised,
how much more so for heavy crimes?
Therefore, people dare not offend.
Now, if one does not focus on preventing offenses
but emulates the kind mother's way that ruins sons,
then one fails to understand the sage's discourse."
Shāngjūn's laws
organized people into groups of ten and five,
mutually supervising and governing.
Those who violated prohibitions were implicated if they failed to report offenses.
He clarified ranks of honor and humility, titles, and grades,
each according to their order;
fields, homes, wives, concubines, and clothing
were allocated by family rank.
The meritorious were glorified,
the meritless, even if wealthy, had no splendor.
He emphasized farming and warfare.
These were Shāngjūn's laws.
These are the methods of Shāng Yāng, Shēn, and Hán.
Huán Fàn said:
"Followers like Shāng Yāng, Shēn, and Hán
valued deceit and cunning,
practiced harshness and exploitation.
They abandoned the teachings of ritual and righteousness,
employed the techniques of punishment and names,
did not follow antiquity,
and began to corrupt customs and damage culture.
They are the criminals against Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Shào.
However, their elevation of the ruler and debasement of ministers...
To enrich the state and strengthen its military,
adhering to laws and mastering strategies,
there are aspects worth adopting.
By the time of the Hàn Dynasty's rise,
there were figures like Nìng Chéng and Zhì Dū,
who emulated the governance of Shāng Yāng and Hán Fēi,
focusing solely on killing, punishment, and brutality as their capability,
catering to the ruler's intentions,
acting in accordance with his wishes,
adapting to the times and pursuing profit,
daring to bring about disaster and ruin.
These, in turn, are the offenders against Shāng Yāng and Hán Fēi.
Yet, in suppressing powerful clans,
comforting the orphaned and weak,
purifying themselves and prohibiting wickedness,
rejecting selfishness to uphold public good,
they still had some governance merits.
As for those deemed capable in later generations,
they violate the laws of the state,
rush to the influence of private factions,
neglect the duties of the common people,
chase after worldly affairs,
resolve complexities and manage tasks,
improvising with shallow arguments temporarily,
ensuring officials bear no burden of blame,
without heeding the grievances of the people below.
They are again the offenders against Shēn Bù Hài, Hán Fēi, Nìng Chéng, and Zhì Dū.
From this perspective,
it is clear that those who govern the world
include proponents of kingly and hegemonic ways,
adherents of Huáng-Lǎo philosophy,
followers of Confucius and Mozi,
and advocates of Shēn Bù Hài and Shāng Yāng.
This is where their differences lie;
although their methods and goals vary,
and their approaches to remedying ills differ,
yet in bringing peace and aid to all living beings,
each has its rationale.
Now, some debaters cite the laws of ancient times,
questioning the discourse on remedying ills,
arguing that:
remedying ills means the Xià people upheld loyalty,
the Yīn people revered respect,
and the Zhōu people valued refinement.
Others invoke the style of emperors and kings,
criticizing the governance of hegemons,
without considering the changes of the times,
but striving to embellish their arguments.
Thus, debates over right and wrong
arise in confusion.
Speaking falsely yet persuasively,
following wrongs and glossing them over,
these are offenders.
Therefore, the noble person prohibits them.
Correct Discourse, Chapter Sixteen
Confucius said:
"The Six Arts converge in principle.
The Rites regulate human conduct,
Music fosters harmony,
the Documents guide affairs,
the Poetry conveys intentions,
the Changes illuminate transformations,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals illuminate righteousness."
Sīmǎ Tán said:
"The Changes delineate heaven and earth, yīn and yáng, the four seasons and five phases,
thus excelling in transformation;
the Rites order human relationships,
thus excelling in practice;
the Documents record affairs of former kings,
thus excelling in governance;
the Poetry records mountains, rivers, valleys, birds, beasts, plants, and the distinction between male and female,
thus excelling in ethos;
Music establishes foundations,
thus excelling in harmony;
the Spring and Autumn Annals distinguishes right from wrong,
thus excelling in governing people."
Therefore it is said:
Enter a state,
and its education becomes evident.
If its people are
gentle, kind, and sincere,
it is the teaching of the Poetry;
broad-minded, understanding, and far-sighted,
it is the teaching of the Documents;
expansive, comprehensive, and good-natured,
it is the teaching of Music;
pure, tranquil, subtle, and refined,
it is the teaching of the Changes;
respectful, frugal, dignified, and reverent,
it is the teaching of the Rites;
skilled in composition and comparing events,
it is the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Thus the fault of the Poetry is foolishness,
the fault of the Documents is misrepresentation,
the fault of Music is extravagance,
the fault of the Changes is harm,
the fault of the Rites is vexation,
the fault of the Spring and Autumn Annals is disorder.
If a person is
gentle, kind, and sincere without being foolish,
then they have deeply mastered the Poetry.
Zǐxià said:
"When sounds form patterns, they are called music.
The music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
reflecting harmonious governance;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
reflecting perverse governance;
the music of a perishing state is sorrowful and thoughtful,
reflecting the people's distress.
Thus for rectifying gains and losses,
moving heaven and earth,
and affecting spirits and gods,
nothing comes closer than the Poetry."
Grand Historian said:
"The Greater Odes speak of kings and lords,
yet their virtue reaches the common people;
the Lesser Odes criticize one's own gains and losses,
yet their influence extends upward.
Though what they speak of differs,
their accord in virtue is one."
During the Jìn period when royal governance declined,
Lǔ Bāo of Nányáng composed the "Theory of the Money God",
and Cài Hóng of Wújùn wrote "Solitary Indignation".
Previous historians considered this the resentful and angry music of a chaotic age,
reflecting perverse governance.
This is what is meant.
Being broad-minded, understanding, and far-sighted without misrepresentation,
then one has deeply mastered the Documents.
The Documents record the way of emperors and kings,
with texts of canons, counsels, instructions, announcements, oaths, and commands,
which the three thousand disciples
all received and understood their meaning.
Being expansive, comprehensive, and good-natured without extravagance,
then one has deeply mastered Music.
The Book of Music says:
"All music
arises from the human heart.
When emotions stir within,
they take form in sound,
and when sounds form patterns, they are called music.
Therefore the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
reflecting harmonious governance;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
reflecting perverse governance;
the music of a perishing state is sorrowful and thoughtful,
reflecting the people's distress.
The way of sound and music
connects with governance.
The gōng note represents the ruler,
the shāng note represents ministers,
the jué note represents the people,
the zhǐ note represents affairs,
the yǔ note represents things.
When these five are not disordered,
then there is no discordant music.
If gōng is disordered, there is dissipation,
and the ruler becomes arrogant;
if shāng is disordered, there is agitation,
and ministers become corrupt;
if jué is disordered, there is sorrow,
and the people become resentful;
if zhǐ is disordered, there is grief,
and affairs become laborious;
if yǔ is disordered, there is peril,
and resources become scarce.
If all five are disordered,
overlapping and encroaching,
it is called dissolution.
If so,
the state's destruction is imminent.
When enlightened kings of antiquity presented music,
it was not merely to entertain and please,
but to stir the blood and pulses,
circulate the essence and spirit,
and harmonize and rectify the heart.
Thus gōng stirs the spleen and harmonizes trust,
shāng stirs the lungs and harmonizes righteousness,
jué stirs the liver and harmonizes benevolence,
zhǐ stirs the heart and harmonizes propriety,
yǔ stirs the kidneys and harmonizes wisdom.
Therefore hearing the gōng note
makes people warm, comfortable, and broad-minded;
hearing the shāng note
makes people upright and fond of righteousness;
hearing the jué note
makes people compassionate and loving toward others;
hearing the zhǐ note
makes people joyful in goodness and fond of giving;
hearing the yǔ note
makes people orderly and fond of propriety.
Rites enter from without,
Music emerges from within.
Thus sage kings make people hear the music of the Odes and Hymns with their ears,
see the rites of dignified demeanor with their eyes,
walk with the bearing of respect and reverence with their feet,
and speak the way of benevolence and righteousness with their mouths.
Therefore gentlemen can speak all day without allowing depravity to enter."
Bān Gù said:
"Music
is what sages delight in,
and it can improve people's hearts,
deeply moving them.
Thus former kings established its teaching.
Humans have the nature of blood, vital energy, heart, and consciousness,
but no constant state of sorrow, joy, anger, or pleasure.
They respond to stimuli and then act,
after which the inclinations of the heart take form.
Thus when delicate and mournful music arises,
the people become anxious;
when harmonious and relaxed music arises,
the people become healthy and happy;
when rough, harsh, and vigorous music arises,
the people become firm and resolute;
when upright, honest, and sincere music arises,
the people become solemn and respectful;
when broad, generous, harmonious, and compliant music arises,
the people become kind and loving;
when decadent, depraved, and dissipated music arises,
the people become licentious and disorderly.
Former kings were ashamed of such disorder,
thus they created the sounds of the Odes and Hymns.
Based on human nature and emotions,
examined by measurements and numbers,
regulated by ritual and righteousness,
in accord with the harmony of vital energy,
guiding the practice of the five constants,
making the yáng not scattered,
the yīn not congested,
the firm energy not angry,
the soft energy not timid,
the four circulating and interacting within,
and manifesting without.
Sufficient to move people toward good hearts,
not allowing evil influences to connect.
This is the method by which former kings established music."
The Annals of Lü Buwei says:
"A destroyed state and executed men
do not lack music,
but their music is not joyful.
A drowning person
does not fail to laugh;
a criminal
does not fail to sing;
a madman
does not fail to dance.
The music of a chaotic age
resembles this."
Fàn Yè said:
"Bell and drum instruments
are not the essence of music,
yet the instruments cannot be discarded;
the three sacrificial animals
are not the core of filial piety,
yet the offerings cannot be abolished.
Preserving the instruments while losing the essence,
The flaw of music lies in its excess.
Regulating the breath to harmonize the sound,
that is the greatness of music.
Overemphasizing nurturing to the detriment of conduct,
that is the burden of filial piety.
Practicing filial piety to achieve nurturing,
that is the essence of filial piety."
Discussion says:
The eastern jiǎo corresponds to benevolence,
the southern zhǐ corresponds to propriety,
the central gōng corresponds to trustworthiness,
the western shāng corresponds to righteousness,
the northern yǔ corresponds to wisdom.
This is the constant principle.
Now Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān believes:
Zhǐ stirs the heart and harmonizes with correct wisdom,
yǔ stirs the kidneys and harmonizes with correct propriety.
Thus, zhǐ governs wisdom,
yǔ governs propriety,
which deviates from the traditional classification.
Therefore, it is not something that later scholars can fully comprehend.
Pure, refined, and subtle without harm,
then one is profound in the "Yì Jīng."
The subtlety of the "Yì Jīng,"
love and hate clash,
distance and closeness interact,
then it cannot tolerate others,
approaching mutual harm.
Respectful, frugal, dignified, and reverent without vexation,
then one is profound in the "Lǐ Jì."
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"I went to the official in charge of grand ceremonies,
observed the additions and subtractions of the Three Dynasties,
and then understood that rituals were established according to human feelings,
and ceremonies were created based on human nature.
The warp and weft of human relations,
myriad rules and regulations,
penetrate everything,
guiding advancement with benevolence and righteousness,
restraining with punishments and penalties,
thus those with abundant virtue hold noble positions,
those with heavy emoluments enjoy honor and glory,
all to unify the realm and regulate the myriad people.
The human body is comfortable with carriages and mounts,
so golden chariots and decorated yokes are made to adorn them;
the eyes favor the five colors,
so embroidered patterns and designs are created to display their beauty;
the ears delight in bells and chimes,
so the eight tones are harmonized to stir the heart;
the mouth savors the five flavors,
so various delicacies and rich tastes are prepared to offer their goodness;
the emotions cherish treasures and excellence,
so jade discs and bi are polished to convey their meaning.
Thus, the grand carriage with grass mats,
leather caps and cloth robes,
red strings and hollow drums,
plain broth and dark wine,
are to prevent extravagance and indulgence,
and remedy their excesses.
Therefore, the order between ruler and minister, court and countryside, noble and humble,
down to the common people, carriages, clothing, palaces, food and drink, marriage, funeral, and sacrifice distinctions,
affairs have their appropriateness,
and things should be regulated and adorned.
When the Zhōu declined,
rituals were abandoned and music corrupted,
the great and small overstepped their bounds,
in Guǎn Zhòng's household,
there were even three returns.
Those who followed the law and upheld righteousness
were insulted by the world;
those who were extravagant and transgressed
were called illustrious and honored.
Even Zǐxià's top disciples,
still said:
'Going out, I see the splendor and magnificence and am pleased;
coming in, I hear the Master's way and am joyful;
the two battle in my heart,
unable to decide.'
How much more so for those below the mediocre,
gradually soaked in lack of education,
and clothed in established customs?
Confucius necessarily rectified names in Wèi,
where he did not fit in,
is it not lamentable!"
Bān Gù said:
"Humans contain the qì of heaven, earth, yīn, and yáng,
have emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
