heaven endows their nature without restraint,
the sages can regulate it,
but cannot eliminate it.
Therefore, they modeled heaven and earth to establish rituals and music,
to communicate with the divine, establish human relations, rectify emotions, and regulate all affairs.
Human nature has the emotions of male and female,
and the distinctions of jealousy,
so the rituals of marriage were established;
there is the order of interaction between elder and younger,
so the rituals of village drinking were established;
there is the emotion of mourning the dead and remembering the distant,
so the rituals of funeral and sacrifice were established;
there is the heart of respect and reverence for superiors,
so the rituals of court audience were established.
Sorrow has the rhythm of crying and leaping,
joy has the expression of singing and dancing,
the upright are sufficient to match their sincerity,
the wicked are sufficient to prevent their errors.
Therefore, if the rituals of marriage are abandoned,
then the way of husband and wife is troubled,
and the crimes of licentiousness and deviance are many;
if the rituals of village drinking are abandoned,
then the order of elder and younger is混乱,
and disputes and fights become frequent;
if the rituals of funeral and sacrifice are abandoned,
then the kindness between flesh and blood becomes thin,
and those who betray their lord and forget life are numerous;
if the rituals of court audience are abandoned,
then the positions of ruler and minister are lost,
and encroachment and aggression gradually arise.
Therefore, Confucius said:
'To secure the above and govern the people,
nothing is better than rituals;
to transform customs and practices,
nothing is better than music.
To govern the world with courtesy and deference,
refers to rituals and music.'"
To compose texts and compare events without confusion,
then one is profound in the "Chūn Qiū."
Hú Suì said:
"Why did Confucius in the past write the 'Chūn Qiū'?"
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"I heard from Master Dǒng:
'Because the way of Zhōu declined,
Confucius became the Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
the feudal lords harmed him,
the high officials obstructed him.
Confucius knew that his words would not be used,
his way would not be practiced,
so he judged the right and wrong of 242 years,
to serve as a model for the world,
criticizing the Son of Heaven,
demoting the feudal lords,
condemning the high officials,
all to achieve the kingly affairs.'
The Master said:
'I would rather express it through empty words,
than demonstrate it through actions that are deep, clear, and evident.'
The 'Chūn Qiū,'
above clarifies the way of the Three Sovereigns,
below distinguishes the principles of human affairs,
resolves doubts,
clarifies right and wrong,
settles hesitations,
praises the good and condemns the evil,
honors the worthy and despises the unworthy,
preserves perished states,
continues broken lineages,
remedies defects and revives the abandoned,
is the great way of kingly governance.
To bring order to a chaotic era,
and return it to the correct path,
nothing is closer than the 'Chūn Qiū.'
Within the 'Chūn Qiū,'
there are thirty-six regicides,
fifty-two fallen states,
feudal lords fleeing unable to protect their altars of soil and grain,
are too numerous to count.
Examining their reasons,
all lost their foundation."
Hú Suì said:
"During Confucius's time,
there was no enlightened ruler above,
and he was not employed below,
so he wrote the 'Chūn Qiū,'
leaving empty texts to judge ritual and righteousness,
as the law of one king.
Now you, Master, have encountered an enlightened Son of Heaven above,
and hold office below,
what do you intend to clarify with your discussions?"
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Fú Xī was of utmost purity and厚道,
and created the eight trigrams of the 'Yì Jīng.'
The prosperity of Yáo and Shùn,
is recorded in the 'Shàng Shū,'
and rituals and music were created.
The grandeur of Tāng and Wǔ,
was sung by the poets.
The 'Chūn Qiū' selects the good and condemns the evil,
promotes the virtue of the Three Dynasties,
praises the Zhōu house,
not merely for criticism and satire.
Since the rise of Hàn,
up to the enlightened Son of Heaven,
receiving the mandate from the pure and majestic,
his grace flows to the four extremes,
the officials and hundred ministers,
strive to extol his sage virtue,
yet cannot fully express his intent.
Moreover, scholars who are worthy and capable but not employed,
is the shame of the state;
the ruler is enlightened and sage,
Yet virtue has not been widely known,
which is the fault of the officials.
Moreover, I oversee this office,
and to neglect the enlightened sages
is a grave offense.
What I call recording
is not what is called creation,
yet you compare it to the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
which is mistaken."
Since Confucius passed away, subtle words ceased,
and with the loss of the seventy disciples, the great principles became distorted.
During the Warring States period, strategies of vertical and horizontal alliances
led to disputes between truth and falsehood,
and the words of the various masters
became chaotic and scattered.
The Confucian school
originated from the office of the Minister of Education,
assisting rulers in harmonizing with yin and yang
and clarifying moral instruction.
They immersed themselves in the Six Classics,
focused on the principles of benevolence and righteousness,
traced their roots to Yáo and Shùn,
modeled themselves on King Wén and King Wǔ,
and revered Confucius as their master—
this represents their highest ideal.
However, the confused lost the subtleties,
while the biased adapted to the times, exaggerating or downplaying,
deviating from the fundamental Way,
merely to dazzle the crowd and seek favor—
this is the flaw of biased Confucians.
Sīmǎ Tán said:
"Confucians
are broad but lack focus,
laborious with little achievement,
hence their methods are hard to fully follow.
Yet their arrangement of the rites between ruler and subject, father and son,
and the distinctions between husband and wife, elder and young,
cannot be changed.
The Confucians
take the Six Arts as their standard,
with classics and commentaries numbering in the tens,
which cannot be fully mastered over generations,
nor their rituals thoroughly studied in a lifetime.
Therefore, it is said:
'Broad but lacking focus,
laborious with little achievement.'
As for establishing the rites of ruler and subject, father and son,
and ordering the distinctions between husband and wife, elder and young,
even the hundred schools cannot alter this."
Fàn Yè said:
"Those who study in schools,
wear Confucian robes,
discuss benevolence and righteousness,
and transmit the methods of the sages.
Thus, people understand the principles of ruler and subject, father and son,
and families know the path to avoid evil and return to righteousness.
From the time between Emperors Huán and Líng,
the court's order daily declined,
and state conflicts frequently arose.
Those of average intelligence and below
all perceived the impending collapse,
yet strong ministers
halted their usurping schemes;
heroic figures
yielded to the righteousness of humble scholars—
because the people recited the words of ancient kings,
and the masses feared the dynamics of rebellion and loyalty.
As for figures like Zhāng Wēn and Huángfǔ Sōng,
whose achievements stabilized half the empire,
whose repute reached beyond the four seas,
if they had looked around and acted,
the great enterprise could have shifted.
Yet they bowed in service under foolish rulers,
awkwardly submitting to commands of ritual,
disbanding troops to accept constraints without regret—
is this not the effect of learning?
Thus, the praise and encouragement of learners by our late teacher
were profound indeed."
The Daoist school
originated from the office of historians,
recording successes and failures through the ages,
grasping essentials and fundamentals,
maintaining purity and emptiness to preserve themselves,
embracing humility and weakness to sustain themselves—
this is the art for rulers facing south.
It aligns with Yáo's yielding virtue
and the modesty in the "Book of Changes,"
which are its strengths.
But when extremists practice it,
they seek to abolish rites and music,
discard benevolence and righteousness,
relying solely on purity and emptiness—
how can this bring order?
This is the flaw of Daoism.
Sīmǎ Tán said:
"Daoism enables people to concentrate their spirit,
act in harmony with the formless,
and provide sufficiently for all things.
Its method
follows the great order of yin and yang,
adopts the strengths of Confucianism and Mohism,
extracts the essentials of the School of Names and Legalism,
moves with the times,
adapts to changes in circumstances,
establishes trust and carries out affairs,
with nothing unsuitable.
Its principles are concise and easy to practice,
with little effort but great results.
Daoist non-action is also called all-action;
its practice is easy,
but its words are hard to understand.
Its technique takes emptiness and non-action as the root,
and adaptation as the function,
having no fixed tendency,
no constant form.
Thus, it can thoroughly understand the nature of all things,
not preceding things,
not following things,
hence it can master all things.
Having methods or no methods,
it acts according to the time;
having measures or no measures,
it aligns with circumstances.
Therefore, it is said:
'The sage is not clever,
but holds to the changes of the times.'
Emptiness
is the constant of the Way;
adaptation
is the net of the ruler.
When all ministers arrive,
they are made to clarify themselves."
The Yin-Yang school
originated from the office of Xī Hé,
reverently complying with the vast heaven,
charting the movements of the sun, moon, and stars,
and respectfully imparting the seasons to people—
these are its strengths.
But when rigid practitioners take it up,
they become entangled in taboos,
stuck in minor techniques,
abandoning human affairs to rely on ghosts and spirits—
this is the flaw of the Yin-Yang school.
Sīmǎ Tán said:
"The techniques of Yin-Yang are overly detailed,
with many taboos,
making people constrained and fearful.
Yet their account of the great order of the four seasons
must not be lost.
For yin-yang, the four seasons, eight positions, twelve measures, and twenty-four solar terms,
each has its directives.
Those who follow them prosper,
those who oppose them perish—
though this is not necessarily so.
Hence it is said:
They make people constrained and full of taboos.
Spring growth, summer flourishing, autumn harvest, winter storage—
this is the great pattern of heaven.
Without following it, there is no basis for the world's order.
Therefore, it is said:
Account of the great order of the four seasons—
must not be lost."
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"Between heaven and humanity,
essences interact and influence each other,
good and evil push against one another.
Events occurring below
manifest as signs above.
The principles of yin and yang
each respond to their stimuli.
When yin changes, the still moves;
when yang is obscured, the bright darkens.
Disasters of flood and drought
follow accordingly.
Therefore, it is said:
Solar eclipses and earthquakes all indicate weak yang and strong yin.
Ministers
are the yin of the ruler;
sons
are the yin of the father;
wives
are the yin of the husband;
barbarians
are the yin of the central states.
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" records thirty-six solar eclipses
and fifty-two earthquakes.
Sometimes barbarians invaded the central states,
sometimes power lay with ministers,
sometimes wives abandoned husbands,
sometimes sons and ministers betrayed rulers and fathers.
Though the events differ,
their category is the same.
Thus, when an enlightened king ascends the throne,
he rectifies the five matters.
The five matters are:
demeanor, speech, vision, hearing, and thought.
Establishing the great mean to uphold heaven's will,
then various auspicious signs will follow below,
and the sun and moon will be regulated above.
If the ruler indulges excessively in the harem,
Indulging in pleasure and hunting excursions,
failing in five personal matters,
the great Middle Way is not established,
then various portents descend and the six extremes arrive.
Whenever disasters and anomalies occur,
they each symbolize faults and errors,
warning people through categorization."
The Tradition states:
"Hunting without proper rest,
feasting without proper offerings,
traveling without moderation,
disrupting people's farming seasons,
and harboring treacherous schemes -
then wood will not bend straight."
It also says:
"Discarding laws and statutes,
abandoning meritorious officials,
killing the crown prince,
making a concubine the principal wife -
then fire will not flame upward."
It further states:
"Fondness for building palaces,
adorning towers and pavilions,
internal debauchery,
offending against relatives,
insulting fathers and elder brothers -
then crops will not mature."
It also says:
"Fondness for launching attacks,
disregarding the common people,
fortifying city walls,
invading border cities -
then metal will not follow transformation."
It further states:
"Ancestral temples,
neglecting prayers and ceremonies,
abandoning sacrificial rites,
going against the heavenly seasons -
then water will not moisten downward."
Guǎn Lù said:
"When noble persons have affairs,
their responses appear in heaven.
In heaven, these are the sun, moon, and stars.
When troops move and people worry,
their responses appear in creatures.
In creatures, these are forests, birds, and beasts."
He also said:
"Though heaven has great images, it cannot speak,
therefore it circulates stellar essences above,
flows spiritual intelligence below,
drives winds and clouds to manifest anomalies,
employs birds and beasts to communicate numinous signs.
Those manifesting anomalies must have signs of sinking and floating,
those communicating numinous signs must have musical responses.
Thus when Duke Xiāng of Sòng lost virtue,
six fish hawks flew backward;
when Bó Jī was about to be burned,
birds cried her lament;
before four states caught fire,
the melting wind had already arisen;
when red clouds flanked the sun,
calamity fell upon Jīngchǔ.
These are heaven's dispatches,
clear tokens of nature."
Later Hàn's Dòu Wǔ memorialized:
"Recently there have been auspicious appearances of blessed grain, magic fungus, and yellow dragons.
Auspicious signs necessarily arise from blessed land,
fortune's arrival truly comes from auspicious people.
With virtue, they are auspicious signs;
without virtue, they become disasters.
Your Majesty's conduct
does not accord with heaven's will,
thus should not be celebrated."
Also Péi Kǎi said:
"According to records since the Spring and Autumn period,
and ancient emperors and kings,
none had the Yellow River run clear.
I believe the River represents
the position of feudal lords.
Clarity belongs to yang,
turbidity belongs to yin.
When the River should be turbid but instead runs clear,
yin desires to become yang,
feudal lords desire to become emperor.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Commentary says:
'When river waters clear,
the world finds peace.'
Now heaven suspends anomalies,
earth spews freaks,
people suffer epidemics -
these three occur simultaneously while the River runs clear,
just as the qilin in Spring and Autumn appeared when it should not.
Confucius recorded it as an anomaly."
During Wèi's Qīnglóng era,
in Zhāngyè commandery's Xuān River,
gushing waters bore treasure stones resembling tripods,
with qilin, phoenixes, dragon-horses,
brilliantly formed patterns.
Contemporary people considered them Wèi's auspicious signs,
Rèn Lìng Yú Chuò brought them to ask Zhāng Jiàn,
Jiàn secretly told Chuò:
"The divine knows what's coming,
doesn't pursue what's past.
Auspicious signs appear first,
then rise and fall follow.
Hàn long perished,
Wèi already obtained it,
why pursue arising auspicious signs?
These stones are present anomalies,
but future auspicious signs."
Later the Sīmǎ clan indeed replaced Wèi.
During Hàn Wǔdì's time,
magicians summoned a divine lord,
of whom only the voice was heard,
not the form seen.
Xún Yuè said:
"The Yì states:
There is the way of heaven,
the way of earth,
and the way of humanity.
Each follows its principle without confusion -
confusion causes ether transformations thus.
As for large stones standing by themselves,
withered willows reviving,
these are formal anomalies;
men transforming into women,
dead returning to life,
these are ether-containing anomalies;
ghosts and spirits vaguely present among humans,
with speech and voices,
these are spiritual anomalies.
Formal and spiritual anomalies
each respond according to kind.
Good produces fortune,
evil produces misfortune -
between essential ethers,
nature's symbolic anomalies.
Therefore, opposing heaven's principle,
spirits lose their measure,
and demonic affairs arise;
opposing earth's principle,
forms lose their measure,
and monstrous humans recklessly appear;
opposing central harmony's principle,
ether-containing beings lose their measure,
and monstrous things recklessly emerge.
This is the main idea.
As for divine lords and such,
they are spiritual anomalies."
The Spring and Autumn Tradition says:
"Acting untimely,
rousing resentment among people,
then non-speaking things will speak."
During Hàn Wǔdì's time,
taxes were numerous,
people impoverished,
hence formless beings spoke.
Regarding the Hóng Fàn's
"improper speech produces temporal monsters" -
this is the category of monsters born from resentment.
Therefore, those comprehending the Way
rectify themselves,
then all things' spirit, form, and ether
each return to their origin."
Later Hàn's Chén Fān memorialized:
"In late Spring and Autumn times,
Zhōu's virtue declined,
for decades
no disasters occurred -
heaven had abandoned it.
Heaven towards Hàn
maintained constant concern,
therefore earnestly showed changes
to enlighten Your Majesty.
Eliminating freaks and evils
truly lies in cultivating virtue.
Thus the Zhōu Documents say:
'When the Son of Heaven sees portents, he cultivates virtue;
when feudal lords see portents, they improve governance;
when high officials see portents, they attend to duties;
when scholars and commoners see portents, they cultivate themselves.'
Spirits cannot harm the Way,
monsters cannot injure virtue."
The Hàn Documents state:
"Move people through actions, not words;
respond to heaven with substance, not ornament.
This is the general principle of heaven and humanity."
The Legalist school
originated from judicial officers,
emphasizing trustworthy rewards and certain punishments
to supplement ritual systems -
this is its strength.
When harsh practitioners emerge,
they abandon moral education,
discard benevolence and love,
exclusively employ penal law,
seeking thereby to achieve order,
even harming closest relatives,
injuring kindness and thickness -
this is Legalism's defect. Sīmǎ Tán said:
"The Legalists are stern and lack benevolence,
yet their rectification of the distinctions between ruler and subject, superior and inferior,
cannot be altered.
The Legalists do not differentiate between kin and stranger,
nor distinguish between noble and humble;
all are judged solely by law,
thus severing the affection due to kin and respect for the honorable.
This can be employed as a temporary strategy,
but cannot be used long-term.
Hence it is said:
'Stern and lacking in benevolence.'
As for honoring the ruler and humbling the subjects,
clarifying duties and roles,
ensuring no overstepping occurs,
even the hundred schools of thought cannot change this."
The School of Names,
likely originated from officials in charge of rites.
In ancient times, as names and positions differed,
so too did the degrees of ritual.
Confucius said:
"Must we not rectify names?"
This is their strength.
But when petty-minded practitioners take it up,
(the character '譥'
is pronounced as gōng jūn fǎn.),
they merely engage in hair-splitting and creating confusion.
This is the flaw of the School of Names.
Sīmǎ Tán said:
"The School of Names makes people meticulous but prone to lose authenticity.
However, their rectification of names and realities
must not be overlooked.
The School of Names,
with its harsh scrutiny and convoluted arguments,
prevents people from grasping the original intent,
focusing solely on names for decisions,
often losing touch with human feelings.
Hence it is said:
'Makes people meticulous but prone to lose authenticity.'
But as for using names to demand reality,
and ensuring consistency without error,
this must not be overlooked."
The character '鈲',
is pronounced pǔ mì fǎn.
The Mohist School,
likely originated from officials of the pure temple,
with thatched roofs and unhewn timbers,
hence they valued frugality;
supporting the three elders and five seniors,
hence they advocated universal love;
selecting scholars through grand archery contests,
hence they exalted the worthy;
reverently worshipping ancestors and strict fathers,
hence they believed in ghosts
(右 here means
to believe in);
following the four seasons in their actions,
hence they rejected fate
(meaning there is no fate of good or bad luck,
only worthiness, unworthiness, goodness, and evil);
demonstrating filial piety to the world,
hence they promoted universal conformity
(meaning all should align with governance).
These are their strengths.
But when biased practitioners take it up,
seeing the benefits of frugality,
they thereby reject rituals,
extending the idea of universal love,
without knowing to distinguish between kin and stranger.
This is the flaw of Mohism.
Sīmǎ Tán said:
"The Mohists are frugal yet hard to follow,
thus their practices cannot be universally adopted.
However, their emphasis on strengthening fundamentals and economizing resources
cannot be discarded.
The Mohists also discourse on Yáo and Shùn,
describing their conduct as:
'The hall only three chǐ high,
the steps to it only three levels;
the thatch left untrimmed,
the timber unplaned.
They ate from earthen bowls,
drank from earthen cups,
consuming coarse grains
and soup of wild herbs.
In summer, wearing hemp clothes;
in winter, deer-skin robes.'
In burying their dead,
they used coffins of tóng wood only three cùn thick,
and the mourning cries did not fully express grief.
They taught funeral rites
must follow this as the model for all people.
If the world were ruled thus,
then there would be no distinction between noble and humble.
But times change and circumstances differ,
and affairs are not the same,
hence it is said:
'Frugal yet hard to follow.'
In essence:
strengthening fundamentals and economizing resources
is the way to ensure every household is well-provided and every person content.
This is the strength of Mohism,
which none of the hundred schools can negate."
Emperor Hàn Wǔ asked Dǒng Zhòngshū in a policy question:
"The frugal do not create ornaments like dark and yellow banners,
yet by the Zhōu dynasty,
they erected twin gate towers,
rode in grand carriages,
with eight rows of dancers in the court, and songs of praise arose.
Is the way of emperors and kings
really different in intent?"
He replied:
"Ornaments like patterned designs and dark yellow colors in institutions
serve to clarify the noble and humble, distinguish the honored and lowly,
and encourage virtuous conduct.
Thus, upon receiving the mandate, the Spring and Autumn period
first established
the correction of the calendar,
and changing the color of garments,
to respond to Heaven.
Therefore, the regulations for palaces and banners
are based on principles.
Confucius said:
'Extravagance leads to arrogance,
frugality to stubbornness.'
Frugality is not the mean system of the sages,
hence it is said:
'Luxury should not usurp the superior's place,
frugality should not oppress the inferior.'
This is the way of true kings."
The School of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances,
likely originated from diplomatic officials.
Confucius said:
"What an ambassador!
What an ambassador!"
Meaning they should act according to circumstances, empowered by their mission but not bound by fixed words.
This is their strength.
But when wicked people practice it,
they engage in deception
(the character '諼'
is pronounced xǔ yuǎn fǎn)
and abandon trustworthiness.
This is the flaw of the Vertical and Horizontal strategists.
Xún Yuè said:
"There are three types of wanderers in the world,
who are thieves of virtue.
The first is the wandering knight,
the second the wandering persuader,
the third the wandering activist.
Those who build up an aura,
wield power and influence,
form private alliances,
to establish strength in the world,
are called wandering knights;
those who adorn their arguments,
devise deceitful schemes,
racing across the land,
to seize opportunities in their time,
are called wandering persuaders;
those who judge by appearances,
迎合时好,
form cliques,
build false reputations,
to gain power and profit,
are called wandering activists.
These three types
are the source of chaos,
injuring the Way and harming virtue,
ruining laws and deluding the age,
and were cautioned against by former kings.
All three types of wanderers emerge
in decadent ages,
especially at the end of the Zhōu and Qín dynasties.
When those above are not enlightened,
those below lack correctness;
when institutions are not established,
and the social fabric slackens and decays;
when praise and blame determine honor and disgrace,
without verifying the truth;
when likes and dislikes dictate benefit and harm,
without considering the reality;
when speakers
weigh gains and losses before uttering words;
when selectors
gauge closeness or distance before writing recommendations.
Then, benefits cannot be sought through righteousness,
and harms cannot be avoided by the Way.
Thus, gentlemen violate rites,
petty people break laws,
embellishing the superficial and neglecting the substantial,
competing for temporal advantages,
thinning the kindness due to kin,
while deepening bonds with colleagues,
forgetting the path of self-cultivation,
yet seeking the praise of the masses,
with bribes filling their courtyards,
and inquiries crowding the roads."
Thus, when vulgar customs prevail, the true path is corrupted.
The foundation of wandering knights lies in martial fortitude and unyielding spirit,
remembering lifelong promises made long ago,
accepting missions in times of danger,
to rescue from contemporary difficulties,
and assist their kind,
those who practice this righteously
are called martial and righteous.
When they deviate severely,
they even become bandits.
The foundation of diplomatic persuasion
stems from distinguishing right from wrong,
being dispatched to the four directions,
without disgracing the sovereign's command.
When crossing borders,
if there is a way to stabilize the state and benefit the nation,
they independently resolve entanglements through dialogue,
their words flowing endlessly,
addressing the people's sufferings.
Those who practice this righteously
are called eloquent and wise.
When they deviate severely,
they descend into deceit.
The foundation of moral conduct
arises from virtue, benevolence, and righteousness,
embracing all with universal love,
befriending others through culture,
harmonious yet not conformist,
cultivating virtue timely,
to establish achievements in the world.
Those who practice this righteously
are called gentlemen.
When they deviate severely,
they end up harming private interests for public affairs,
becoming treacherous conspirators.
How vastly different they are—
is it not lamentable?
Therefore, when the Great Way prevails,
these three wanderings are abolished."
The Eclectic School
likely originated from advisory officials,
combining Confucianism and Mohism,
uniting the School of Names and Legalism,
understanding that state governance includes these elements,
and seeing how royal principles interconnect all,
this is its strength.
But when frivolous practitioners take it up,
it becomes diffuse and lacks a core focus,
this is the Eclectic School's flaw.
The Agricultural School
probably emerged from officials of farming and millet,
sowing various grains,
encouraging plowing and sericulture,
to ensure sufficient food and clothing.
Confucius said:
"What is valued is the people's food."
This is its strength.
But when crude practitioners take it up,
they desire rulers and ministers to farm together,
violating the hierarchy between superior and inferior,
this is the Agricultural School's flaw.
Bān Gù said:
"Sīmǎ Qiān's 'Records of the Grand Historian',
its judgments of right and wrong often diverge from the sages.
Discussing the Great Way,
it prioritizes Huáng-Lǎo thought over
the Six Classics;
narrating wandering knights,
it demotes reclusive scholars
and promotes cunning opportunists;
describing wealth accumulation,
it glorifies profit and power,
while shaming poverty and low status.
This is its shortcoming.
Yet it excels in narrating events and principles,
argumentative without being flowery,
substantial without being vulgar,
its writing straightforward and facts verified,
not exaggerating virtues,
not concealing faults,
thus it is called a true record by the world."
Wén Zǐ said:
"When sages undertake tasks,
they follow different paths but reach the same end.
The songs of Qín, Chǔ, Yān, and Wèi
differ in melody but all bring joy;
the cries of the nine Yí and eight Dí tribes
vary in sound but all express sorrow.
For singing
is the expression of joy;
weeping
is the manifestation of grief.
What is calm within responds outwardly,
thus it depends on what moves them."
Discussion says:
Fàn Yè remarked:
"The hundred schools' discourses on governance
are lofty indeed!
Generally, they aim to stabilize foundations,
and reform contemporary abuses.
But encountered circumstances are ever-changing,
viewpoints are biased and mixed,
hence debates over right and wrong
become chaotically contradictory."
Let us attempt to discuss this:
The world is not an ideal state of simplicity,
people have strayed from natural living,
traces of principles multiply endlessly,
and human complexities continuously emerge.
Even with wisdom encompassing all things,
one cannot fully fathom their adaptations;
the profundity of mountains and rivers
cannot compare to their twists and perils;
thus responding to customs and handling affairs
is hard to bound by fixed rules.
How to explain this?
When a sage rules the age,
great unity reaches its ultimate model,
the ways of giving and withholding
should follow no different norms.
Yet increase and decrease operate differently,
elaboration and simplicity alternate in practice,
using clarity while dwelling in obscurity,
circling back to past times,
raising armies or displaying ritual vessels,
referencing ancient eras.
And when wearing the yellow canopy
or dressed in fine silk,
richness and simplicity may vary,
yet achieving good governance remains the same.
There is also pardoning royal clans
or tattooing national enemies,
leniency and severity already distinct,
but preventing wrongdoing must be identical.
This shows diverging streams sharing one source,
a hundred thoughts converging on one point.
If one applies biased feelings forcibly,
crookedness and straightness will surely be excessive.
Thus wearing hemp sandals in frost
shows the flaw of overvaluing frugality;
dressing in splendid garments
warns against extreme extravagance.
Lax restrictions and generous treatment of inferiors
lead to the tail wagging the dog and bullying the weak;
concentrated authority and harsh laws
cause fragmentation through oppressive severity.
This is why the satires of Cáo and Wèi
illuminate the 'Airs of the States';
the final tracks of Zhōu and Qín
manifest their gradual destruction.
Thus the basis of adoption or rejection
determines rise and fall.
Therefore, complexity and simplicity must suit the times,
leniency and severity complement each other,
inscribing penal codes on tripods
allows detailed examination of affairs,
while the three-article covenant
values concise capability.
Dà Shū caused the decline of harsh governance,
Guó Zǐ shed tears of enduring love.
Xuān Mèng altered the warmth of winter sunlight,
Píng Yáng established uniform laws.
These truly represent the grand application of relaxation and tension,
can we not discern their unifying principle?
The words of these masters
thoroughly investigate the successes and failures
of their contemporary times.
Yet many err in comprehensive teaching,
favoring one-sided arguments.
Those who value purity and quietude
dismiss court debates as rotten discussions;
those constrained by name and reality
consider imperial library talks absurd words.
Some promote former kings' customs
as applicable to their own era,
others cite rules for saving from abuses
that should endure through ages.
Examining them with sincere discourse,
they will prove flawed.
From this perspective,
we know that having methods or lacking them
depends on seizing the moment for achievement,
stopping when the time stops,
acting when the time moves,
acting without missing the timing,
the path will be bright.
Unless one is supremely refined,
who can comprehend such transformation?
Chapter 17: Plans for Hegemony
I have heard that the Zhōu dynasty possessed the world,
and its rule lasted over three hundred years.
During the prosperity of King Chéng and King Kāng,
punishments were set aside for more than forty years without being used;
and when it declined,
it also lasted over three hundred years.
Tàigōng advised King Wén, saying:
"Though bending under one person,
one may extend above ten thousand others—
only a worthy person can achieve this."
Thus, King Wén sought out and met with six individuals,
sought and encountered ten others,
and called upon a thousand to befriend them.
Friends of friends are called companions,
companions of companions form factions,
and factions of factions form groups.
By this means, he befriended the worthy under heaven,
and two-thirds of them turned to him.
Hence it is said:
"He possessed two-thirds of the world,
yet served the Yīn dynasty."
This refers to that.
Thus, the Five Hegemons
(pronounced bà)
rose in succession.
Hegemons often assisted the Son of Heaven,
promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
punishing the violent and restraining the wicked,
rectifying the realm,
to honor the Son of Heaven.
After the Five Hegemons passed away,
no sages or worthies succeeded them,
the Son of Heaven was isolated and weak,
his commands unenforced,
the feudal lords acted arbitrarily,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few.
King Wú asked Wǔ Xū:
"How about attacking Chǔ?"
He replied:
"Chǔ has many in power who are at odds,
none willing to bear responsibility.
If we send three armies to harass them,
one army arrives,
they will all come out,
and when they emerge, we retreat;
when they retreat, we emerge again.
Chǔ will be worn out on the roads,
repeatedly harassed to exhaustion,
misled by multiple strategies.
Once they are weary,
then we follow with three armies,
and will surely achieve a great victory."
Hélǘ followed this advice.
Chǔ thus began to suffer.
King Yuè Gōu Jiàn asked Minister Wén Zhǒng:
"How about attacking Wú?"
He replied:
"There are seven strategies to attack Wú,
roughly as follows:
Honor heaven and serve ghosts,
to expose their depravity;
send them beautiful women,
to dazzle their minds;
send them skilled craftsmen,
to have them build palaces,
thereby exhausting their wealth;
send them flattering ministers,
to make them vulnerable to attack;
strengthen their admonishing ministers,
to drive them to suicide;
with strong armor and sharp weapons,
exploit their weaknesses."
King Yuè then adorned the beautiful woman Xī Shī,
and presented her to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú was delighted.
Zǐ Xū advised against it,
but he was not heeded.
The King of Wú executed Zǐ Xū.
Yuè also made ornate pillars,
inlaid with gold,
and presented them to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú accepted them,
and built the Gūsū Tower,
which took five years to complete,
with commoners dying along the roads.
Yuè also steamed millet seeds and sent them to the King of Wú,
who had people plant them,
but they did not grow,
causing a great famine in Wú.
Duke Huán of Qí wanted to weaken Chǔ,
so he minted coins,
and bought live deer from Chǔ.
Chǔ heard of this,
was pleased,
abandoned farming to raise deer,
while Duke Huán stored five times the grain.
Chǔ had ample coins but lacked grain.
Duke Huán then closed the borders,
and Chǔ's surrendering populace reached four or five out of ten.
At the covenant of Kē,
Duke Huán considered breaking the agreement with Cáo Mèi,
but Guǎn Zhòng upheld it, making it trustworthy,
and the feudal lords hence turned to Qí.
Thus it is said:
"To know that giving is taking—
this is the treasure of governance."
Duke Huán of Zhèng wanted to attack Kuài,
so he first inquired about Kuài's heroes, good ministers, and debaters,
wrote down their names,
selected the best fields in Kuài to promise them,
and recorded official titles and ranks for them,
then buried the list outside the city walls and gates,
sprinkling it with the blood of a chicken and a pig.
The lord of Kuài thought it was an internal rebellion,
and killed them all.
Duke Huán then attacked Kuài.
These are all instances of feudal lords acting arbitrarily,
with the Son of Heaven's commands unenforced.
Tián Cháng usurped Qí,
the six ministers partitioned Jìn,
and together they became the Warring States.
This was the beginning of people's suffering.
The Marquis of Qí and Yànzǐ sat in the open chamber,
and the duke sighed, saying:
"How beautiful this room is!
Who will possess it in the future?"
Yànzǐ said:
"As you say,
might it be the Chén family?
Though the Chén family lacks great virtue,
they give generously to the people.
In measures like dǒu, qū, fǔ, and zhōng,
what they take from the public is little,
what they give to the people is much.
You impose heavy taxes,
while the Chén family gives generously,
so the people turn to them.
The Book of Songs says:
'Though I have no virtue to offer you,
I sing and dance.'
For the Chén family's generosity,
the people sing and dance.
If in future generations there is slight negligence,
and the Chén family does not perish,
then the state may become their state."
Later, they indeed usurped Qí.
Zhì Bó followed the rulers of Hán and Wèi to attack Zhào,
and Hán and Wèi secretly plotted to rebel.
Zhì Guǒ said:
"The two rulers are likely to change,
it would be better to kill them;
if not,
then fully win them over."
Zhì Bó asked:
"How to win them over?"
Zhì Guǒ said:
"Wèi Xuānzǐ's strategist Zhào Jiā,
and Hán Kāngzǐ's strategist Duàn Guī—
both can influence their lords' plans.
Make an agreement with the two lords to defeat Zhào,
then enfeoff these two with counties of ten thousand households each.
If so,
the minds of the two lords will not change."
Zhì Bó did not follow this.
Hán and Wèi indeed rebelled,
and killed Zhì Bó.
Thus, strong states focused on conquest,
weak states on defense,
forming vertical and horizontal alliances,
with chariots galloping and hubs clashing,
armor breeding lice,
and people with nowhere to complain.
By the time of Qín devouring the world,
annexing the Warring States,
unifying the governance of the realm,
destroying the cities of the feudal lords,
with harsh laws and severe governance,
flatterers were numerous.
Méng Tián was sent north to attack the Hú,
and Wèi Tuó led troops to garrison Yuè,
stationing armies in useless lands,
leaving people with no means to live.
When the First Emperor died,
the world rebelled greatly.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng rose up in Chén
(Chén Shè and Wú Guǎng were garrisoning Yúyáng,
encamped at Dàzé.
It happened to rain,
the roads were impassable,
they estimated they would miss the deadline,
and missing the deadline meant execution.
The two then plotted, saying:
"Now we have missed the deadline,
and face execution.
If we launch a great undertaking, we may also die;
since death is equal,
why not die for the state?"
So they first used ghosts and spirits to awe the crowd,
then killed the commanding officer.
He summoned his followers and declared:
"You, gentlemen, encountered rain,
and all have missed the deadline.
Missing the deadline warrants execution.
Even if by chance you are not executed and sent to garrison the frontiers,
the dead will still inevitably be six or seven out of ten.
A brave man does not die in vain—
if he must die, let it be for a great cause.
Are kings, nobles, generals, and ministers
born to such titles?"
The followers all responded:
"We respectfully accept your command."
They then divided forces to conquer territories,
and he proclaimed himself King of Chǔ. ,
Wǔ Chén and Zhāng Ěr rose in Zhào.
Wǔ Chén pacified the land of Zhào,
and was titled Lord Wǔxìn.
Kuǎi Tōng advised the governor of Fànyáng, Lord Xú, saying:
"I am Kuǎi Tōng,
a commoner of Fànyáng.
I privately grieve that you are about to die,
hence I come to mourn you.
Nevertheless,
I also congratulate you for gaining me and thus surviving."
Lord Xú bowed twice and asked:
"Why do you mourn me?"
Kuǎi replied:
"You have served as governor for ten years,
killing people's fathers,
orphaning their children,
cutting off feet,
and branding faces—
all in great numbers.
The reason kind fathers and filial sons dare not thrust blades into your belly
is their fear of Qín's laws.
Now the empire is in great chaos,
Qín's governance is unenforced,
so those kind fathers and filial sons will compete to plunge knives into your abdomen,
to avenge their grievances,
and achieve fame thereby.
This is why I mourn you."
Lord Xú asked:
"Then why congratulate me for gaining you and surviving?"
Kuǎi answered:
"Lord Wǔxìn of Zhào, unaware of my incompetence,
sent someone to inquire about me,
asking whether I live or die.
If I meet Lord Wǔxìn, I will persuade him thus:
'If you must win battles before seizing lands,
and capture cities through attacks to take the realm's strongholds,
I privately believe it is perilous.
Employ my strategy,
and you can gain lands without fighting,
take cities without assaulting,
securing a thousand lǐ by mere proclamations.
Would that not suffice?'
He will then ask:
'What do you mean?'
I would thus advise:
'The governor of Fànyáng ought to organize his troops
for defense and combat.
But he is timid and fears death,
greedy for wealth and honor,
so he wishes to surrender his city to you first.
However, if surrendering first brings him no benefit,
then the border cities will relay the message:
The governor of Fànyáng surrendered first and was killed.
They will surely fortify their walls and defend stubbornly,
turning each into an impregnable fortress,
impossible to attack.
For your strategy,
it is best to welcome the governor of Fànyáng with a grand carriage and red wheels,
sending him to parade through Yān and Zhào's outskirts.
Then the border cities will relay:
The governor of Fànyáng surrendered first and gained wealth and honor.
They will surely follow in succession to surrender,
like pellets rolling down a slope.'
This is what I mean by securing a thousand lǐ with proclamations."
Lord Xú bowed twice again,
prepared carriages and horses, and sent Kuǎi off.
Kuǎi then used this argument to persuade Wǔ Chén.
Wǔ Chén provided a hundred chariots, two hundred cavalry, and a marquis seal,
to welcome Lord Xú.
When Yān and Zhào heard of this,
over thirty cities surrendered,
just as Kuǎi Tōng had strategized. ,
Xiàng Liáng rose in Wú.
Liáng ordered Xiàng Yǔ to kill the acting governor Tōng,
then raised troops to start the uprising in Wú.
Wú
is present-day Sūzhōu. ,
Tián Dān rose in Qí.
Dān, along with young men,
bound a slave intending to kill him,
went to see the governor of Dí,
and took the opportunity to kill the governor and raise an army. ,
Jǐng Jū rose in Yǐng, Zhōu Fú in Wèi,
Hán Guǎng in Yān.
From remote mountains to accessible valleys,
heroes arose together,
and thus the Qín clan was destroyed.
Emperor Gaozu of Hàn, named Bāng,
courtesy name Jì,
surnamed Liú,
was a native of Fēngyì in the Pèi region.
He served as a village chief in Sìshàng.
In the first year of Qín Èrshì's reign,
Chén Shèng and others rose up,
and Shèng proclaimed himself King of Chǔ.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú advised him:
"General, you have risked your life
to rid the world of harm,
yet now, having just arrived in Chén,
you proclaim yourself king—
this reveals selfish intentions to all under heaven.
It would be better to establish descendants of the Six States,
thereby building alliances for yourself,
then advance your army westward.
Then, in the fields, there would be no opposing troops; in the cities, no guarded walls.
Destroy the tyrannical Qín,
occupy Xiányáng,
and command the feudal lords—
then the world could be yours."
Shèng did not listen.
The people of Pèi killed their magistrate
and established Gaozu as the Duke of Pèi.
At that time, Xiàng Liáng was stationed in Xuē,
and the Duke of Pèi went to join him,
together establishing the Righteous Emperor.
Fàn Zēng advised Xiàng Liáng:
"When Qín destroyed the Six States,
Chǔ was the most innocent.
Since King Huái entered Qín and never returned,
the people of Chǔ have pitied him.
Hence the saying:
'Even if Chǔ has but three households,
the one to destroy Qín will surely be from Chǔ.'
Now Chén Shèng initiated the uprising
but did not establish a descendant of Chǔ—
his momentum will not last.
Now you, my lord, have risen east of the river;
the generals emerging in Chǔ
all compete to join you
because your family has served as Chǔ generals for generations,
and they believe you can reestablish Chǔ's descendants."
Liáng then sought out King Huái's grandson, Xīn, and installed him.
They made a pact:
"The first to enter Xiányáng shall be its king."
The Qín general Zhāng Hán
decisively defeated Xiàng Liáng at Dìngtáo.
Liáng died,
and Zhāng Hán, considering Chǔ no longer a concern,
marched north to attack Zhào.
Chǔ sent Xiàng Yǔ and others to rescue Zhào
and dispatched the Duke of Pèi with a separate force to enter the pass westward.
The Duke of Pèi then attacked Wǎn
and accepted its surrender.
When the Duke of Pèi attacked Wǎn,
the Nányáng governor Lǚ Qǐ defended the city and would not surrender.
The Duke of Pèi intended to press westward,
but Zhāng Liáng said:
"With a strong Qín ahead
and Wǎn's troops behind,
this is a perilous path."
So they besieged Wǎn.
Wǎn was in dire straits,
and Qǐ considered suicide,
but his retainer Chén Huī scaled the city wall to see the Duke of Pèi,
saying:
"The officials and people of Wǎn, fearing death, are defending stubbornly.
If you attack all day,
casualties will be heavy;
if you withdraw your troops,
Wǎn will surely pursue you.
You would then break the pact to take Xiányáng ahead
and face the threat of a strong Wǎn behind.
It would be better to accept their surrender,
enfeoff their governor,
then lead their troops westward—
the cities not yet taken
will surely open their gates to welcome you."
The Duke of Pèi said:
"Excellent."
He enfeoffed Lǚ Qǐ as the Marquis of Yīn.
They attacked Wǔguān
and crushed the Qín army.
Zhào Gāo killed Èrshì
and installed Zǐyīng,
sending troops to guard the pass.
Zhāng Liáng said:
"The Qín troops are still strong;
we must not underestimate them.
I suggest we display more banners on the mountains
to create a deceptive force.
Order Lì Yìjī to offer heavy bribes to the Qín generals."
The Qín generals indeed sought to ally and march west together.
The Duke of Pèi was inclined to agree,
but Liáng said:
"This is only their generals wishing to rebel;
I fear their soldiers may not follow,
which would be dangerous.
It would be better to attack them while they are off guard."
They then attacked the Qín army
and defeated them.
Entering Xiányáng,
he made a three-article covenant with the people of Qín.
The people of Qín offered oxen and wine,
but the Duke of Pèi declined to accept.
Thus, the people recognized his virtue.
He sent troops to guard the pass,
intending to rule within it as king.
At this time,
Xiàng Yǔ had defeated the Qín army north of the river
and led 400,000 troops of the feudal lords to Hóngmén,
planning to attack the Duke of Pèi.
The Duke of Pèi, through Xiàng Bó, reconciled with Yǔ.
Yǔ then killed Zǐyīng and moved east, establishing his capital at Péngchéng.
He installed the Duke of Pèi as King of Hàn,
ruling over Bā and Hàn.
The King of Hàn was unwilling to go to his domain
and wanted to attack Chǔ.
Xiāo Hé said:
"Though ruling Hàn is undesirable,
is it not better than death?
Moreover, the Shī Jīng says:
'Celestial Hàn'—
the name is most auspicious.
One who can bend beneath a single person
may then rise above ten thousand—
as did Tāng and Wǔ.
I urge you, Great King, to rule Hànzhōng,
comfort its people,
attract worthy men,
utilize the resources of Bā and Shǔ,
then return to pacify the Three Qín—
and the world can be yours."
Thereupon, adopting Hán Xìn's strategy,
he marched east to campaign,
pacifying the Three Qín upon his return.
The King of Hàn thus went to his domain.
Hán Xìn had fled Chǔ
and followed him into Shǔ,
unknown to anyone.
He spoke with Xiāo Hé several times,
and Hé, impressed by his talent,
recommended him as Grand General.
After Xìn received his appointment,
the King said:
"The Chancellor has often spoken of you, General.
What strategies do you have to advise me?"
Xìn humbly declined,
then asked the King:
"Is not Xiàng Yǔ now the one contending for power over the world to the east?"
The King replied:
"Indeed."
Xìn said:
"In your estimation, Great King, how do you compare to Xiàng Yǔ in courage, fierceness, benevolence, and strength?"
The King of Hàn remained silent for a long while,
then said:
"I am not his equal."
Xìn bowed again and congratulated him:
"Even I believe you are not his equal.
But I once served him,
so allow me to describe Xiàng Yǔ's character.
Xiàng Yǔ roars and shouts,
causing thousands to tremble,
yet he cannot entrust authority to worthy generals—
this is merely the courage of a common man.
Xiàng Yǔ appears respectful and compassionate toward others,
speaking gently;
when someone is ill,
he sheds tears and shares his food and drink.
But when a subordinate achieves merit deserving enfeoffment,
he grinds the seal's edge until it is worn,
unable to bring himself to bestow it—
this is what is called the kindness of a woman.
Though Xiàng Yǔ dominates the Central Plains and subjugates the feudal lords,
he does not reside within the passes but establishes his capital at Péngchéng,
violating the covenant with the Righteous Emperor,
and enfeoffs those he favors among the feudal lords—
this is unjust.
The feudal lords, seeing Xiàng Yǔ banish the Righteous Emperor to Jiāngnán,
all likewise expel their own lords and seize the best lands for themselves.
Wherever Xiàng Yǔ passes through,
nothing escapes destruction;
the world harbors much resentment,
the common people do not support him—
they merely submit out of fear of his might.
Though he is called a hegemon,
he has truly lost the hearts of the people.
Hence it is said:
His strength can easily be weakened.
Now if you, Great King, can indeed oppose his ways,
employing the brave and martial of the world,
who could you not destroy!
Enfeoffing meritorious officials with the cities and towns of the world,
who would not submit!
Leading righteous troops with soldiers who long to return east,
What cannot be dispersed!
Moreover, the three kings of Qín served as Qín generals,
leading Qín's sons and brothers for several years,
causing countless deaths and losses,
and further deceived their masses into surrendering to the various lords.
Upon reaching Xīn'ān,
King Xiàng deceitfully buried over two hundred thousand surrendered Qín soldiers alive,
with only Sīmǎ Xīn, and Dǒng Yì managing to escape.
The fathers and elder brothers of the Qín people resent these three men,
their hatred piercing to the marrow.
Now Chǔ, using its strength and authority, has made these three men kings,
but the Qín people hold no affection for them.
When you, Great King, entered Wǔguān,
you caused not the slightest harm,
abolished Qín's harsh laws,
and made a three-article covenant with the people.
There is no one among the Qín people who does not wish for you, Great King, to rule Qín.
According to the agreement among the various lords,
you, Great King, should be king of Guānzhōng,
and every household in Guānzhōng knows this.
When you, Great King, were deprived of your rightful position and entered Hànzhōng,
there was no one among the Qín people who did not feel regret.
Now if you, Great King, raise your forces and march east,
the three Qín regions can be secured simply by issuing a proclamation.
Thereupon, the King of Hàn was greatly pleased,
and thus heeded and trusted this plan.
Initially,
when the King of Hàn was going to his domain,
Zhāng Liáng escorted him to Bāozhōng,
and advised the King of Hàn, saying:
"Why does the King not burn and destroy the plank roads along the route,
to show the world that you have no intention of returning,
thereby securing King Xiàng's mind."
The King of Hàn then sent Zhāng Liáng back,
and accordingly burned them.
Because of this, Chǔ had no suspicions about the King of Hàn's intentions.
Tián Róng resented King Xiàng for not establishing him,
killed Tián Shì,
and proclaimed himself King of Qí.
Xiàng Yǔ went north to attack and destroy Qí,
and appointed Zhèng Chāng, the magistrate of Wú, as King of Hán to resist Hàn.
Zhāng Liáng sent a letter to Xiàng Yǔ, saying:
"The King of Hàn, having lost his rightful position, went to Shǔ,
desiring only to become king of Guānzhōng,
and will cease once the agreement is fulfilled,
not daring to rebel."
He also sent Xiàng Yǔ a letter about Qí's rebellion, stating:
"Qí wishes to destroy Chǔ."
For this reason, Xiàng Yǔ did not march west,
but instead attacked Qí in the north.
And he had the King of Jiǔjiāng kill the Righteous Emperor in Chēn.
The King of Hàn donned mourning garments and held a funeral for him,
mourning for three days,
and informed the various lords.
Dǒng Gōng advised the King of Hàn, saying:
"Your servant has heard:
Those who follow virtue prosper,
those who lose virtue perish;
If arms are raised without just cause,
endeavors will not succeed.
Therefore it is said:
Make clear that he is a villain,
then the enemy can be subdued.
King Xiàng acts without principle,
having exiled and killed his sovereign,
he is the villain of the world.
Now, benevolence does not rely on bravery,
righteousness does not depend on force,
but let the three armies dress in plain mourning for him,
inform the various lords,
and march east to punish him,
then within the four seas,
none will not look up to your virtue.
This is the action of the Three Sovereigns."
The King of Hàn said:
"Excellent."
The King of Hàn, taking advantage of Xiàng Yǔ's attack on Qí,
led an army of five hundred sixty thousand from the various lords,
struck east to attack Chǔ,
and captured Péngchéng.
Xiàng Yǔ, hearing of this,
left his generals to attack Qí,
and personally led thirty thousand elite troops back to attack Hàn.
The King of Hàn and Xiàng Yǔ fought a great battle beneath Péngchéng.
The King of Hàn was at a disadvantage,
exited through Liáng territory,
reached Yú,
and said to his attendants:
"Who can act as envoy to the King of Huáinán, Qíng Bù,
and command him to raise troops and turn against Chǔ,
detaining King Xiàng in Qí for several months?
Then my capture of the empire
can be perfectly assured."
Suí Hé then went to Huáinán,
to persuade Bù to betray Chǔ.
Suí Hé advised the King of Huáinán, saying:
"The King of Hàn has sent me to respectfully present a letter to Your Majesty's attendant,
and I privately wonder, how are you related to Chǔ?"
The King of Huáinán said:
"I face north and serve him as a minister."
Suí Hé said:
"Your Majesty and King Xiàng are both ranked as feudal lords,
yet you face north and serve him as a minister,
surely because you consider Chǔ strong,
and thus entrust your state to it.
When King Xiàng attacked Qí,
he personally carried building boards and frames,
to set an example for his soldiers.
Your Majesty should have mobilized all the forces of Huáinán,
led them personally,
and served as the vanguard for the Chǔ army.
Yet you only sent four thousand men to aid Chǔ;
is this how one who faces north and serves another as minister
should truly act?
When the King of Hàn battled at Péngchéng,
and King Xiàng had not yet left Qí,
Your Majesty should have swept up Huáinán's troops, crossed the Huái River,
and fought day and night beneath Péngchéng.
You, who command a host of ten thousand men,
did not cross the Huái,
but instead folded your arms and watched to see who would win.
Is this how one who entrusts his state to another
should truly act?
Your Majesty upholds an empty name in allegiance to Chǔ,
yet wishes to deeply entrust yourself;
I privately believe this is not advisable for Your Majesty.
However, if you do not betray Chǔ,
it is because you consider Hàn weak.
Though Chǔ's troops are strong,
the world burdens it with a name of unrighteousness,
because it broke the covenant and killed the Righteous Emperor.
Moreover, the King of Chǔ relies on his victories in battle to strengthen himself,
while the King of Hàn gathers the various lords,
returns to defend Xíngyáng,
brings in the grain of Shǔ and Hàn,
deepens the moats and raises the ramparts,
and stations troops to guard the borders and man the passes.
When the Chǔ troops turn back,
with Liáng territory intervening,
they must penetrate eight or nine hundred lǐ into enemy land;
if they wish to fight, they cannot,
if they attack cities, their strength is insufficient,
and the old and weak must transport provisions from a thousand lǐ away;
when Chǔ troops reach Xíngyáng and Chénggāo,
Hàn holds firm and does not move,
so advancing they cannot attack,
and retreating they cannot escape.
Therefore it is said:
Chǔ is not to be relied upon.
If Chǔ were to win,
then the various lords would feel endangered and fearful and aid each other.
Thus Chǔ's strength
is precisely what summons the arms of the world.
So Chǔ is no match for Hàn;
the situation is easily seen.
Now if Your Majesty does not side with the perfectly secure Hàn,
but instead entrusts yourself to the doomed Chǔ,
I am privately puzzled on Your Majesty's behalf.
I do not claim that Huáinán's troops are enough to destroy Chǔ.
But if Your Majesty raises troops and turns against Chǔ,
King Xiàng will surely be detained in Qí for several months,
and Hàn's capture of the empire
can be perfectly assured.
I request to join Your Majesty, sword in hand, in returning to Hàn;
the King of Hàn will surely apportion lands to enfeoff you,
so why worry about Huáinán?
It will certainly remain Your Majesty's possession.
Thus I, your servant, present this foolish plan,
hoping Your Majesty will consider it carefully."
The King of Huáinán said:
"I beg to follow your command."
He secretly agreed to rebel against Chǔ and join Hàn,
but did not dare reveal it.
A Chǔ envoy was in Huáinán,
urgently pressing Yīng Bù to dispatch troops,
staying at the guesthouse.
Suí Hé entered directly,
sat in the seat above the Chǔ envoy,
and said:
"The King of Jiǔjiāng has already submitted to Hàn;
how can Chǔ order him to dispatch troops?"
Bù was stunned.
The Chǔ envoy rose.
Suí Hé then advised Bù, saying:
"The matter is already set.
Only by killing the Chǔ envoy,
preventing his return,
and swiftly joining Hàn to combine forces."
Bù then acted as the Hàn envoy instructed.
Thereupon, he killed the Chǔ envoy,
and accordingly raised troops to attack Chǔ.
The King of Hàn went to Xíngyáng,
sent Hán Xìn to attack the King of Wèi, Bào,
and captured him.
The King of Hàn asked Lì Shēng:
"Who is the great general of the King of Wèi?"
He replied:
"Bó Zhí."
The King said:
"This one still smells of mother's milk;
cannot match Hán Xìn's cavalry general Féng Jìng."
The King said:
"Cannot match Guàn Yīng's infantry general Xiàng Tuō."
The King said:
"Cannot match Cáo Shēn.
With him here,
I have no worries."
The King then appointed Xìn as Left Chancellor to attack Wèi.
Xìn advanced his troops,
preparing boats to cross at Línjìn,
while Wèi gathered forces to resist him.
Xìn instead set an ambush and crossed his army at Xiàyáng using earthenware jars,
surprised Ānyì,
captured King Bào of Wèi,
then advanced to attack Zhào.
Hàn then faced Chǔ in a standoff at Xíngyáng,
Chǔ besieged the King of Hàn,
who used Chén Píng's plan
to escape through a gap.
The King of Hàn urgently asked Chén Píng:
"What strategy should we employ?"
Chén Píng said:
"Among King Xiàng's loyal ministers like Yàfù and Zhōnglí Mò and their kind,
there are only a few.
If Your Highness can spare tens of thousands in gold,
to carry out counter-espionage,
sow discord among his ministers,
to make him suspicious,
King Xiàng, by nature,
is suspicious and believes slander,
and will surely execute his own internally.
Hàn can then attack,
and defeating Chǔ is certain."
The King of Hàn gave forty thousand catties of gold to Píng,
allowing him free rein,
without questioning expenditures.
Píng used much gold to spread counter-espionage in the Chǔ army,
proclaiming that generals like Zhōnglí Mò had achieved many merits for King Xiàng,
yet never received fiefs:
"They wish to join Hàn,
to destroy the Xiàng clan,
and share the land as kings."
King Xiàng indeed grew suspicious.
He sent an envoy to Hàn.
Hàn prepared a grand feast,
presented it to the Chǔ envoy,
then feigned surprise, saying:
"I thought it was Yàfù's envoy,
but it's King Xiàng's."
They took it away,
and offered poor fare to the Chǔ envoy.
The envoy returned,
and reported fully to King Xiàng.
King Xiàng became highly suspicious of Yàfù.
Yàfù wanted to attack the King of Hàn urgently,
but King Xiàng distrusted him.
Yàfù, hearing of King Xiàng's suspicion,
said:
"The empire's affairs are largely settled!
Your Majesty can handle them yourself.
I beg to retire."
King Xiàng consented.
Yàfù entered the passes to gather troops,
intending to head east again.
Yuánshēng advised the King of Hàn:
"Deploy troops to Wǎn and Yè,
to draw King Xiàng south across the river,
allowing Hán Xìn and others to assemble north of the river."
Yǔ's troops indeed moved south,
as per the strategy.
Yuánshēng advised further:
"Hàn and Chǔ have been stalemated at Xíngyáng and Chénggāo for months,
with Hàn often in distress.
I urge Your Highness to exit Wǔguān,
King Xiàng will surely lead his troops south,
Your Highness can fortify deeply,
allowing rest between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo.
Have Hán Xìn and others gather in Zhào's territory north of the river,
then Your Highness can return to Xíngyáng.
Thus,
Chǔ will have many fronts to defend,
their forces divided,
Hàn can rest,
and fighting them again,
defeating Chǔ is certain."
The King of Hàn followed this plan,
deploying troops between Wǎn and Yè.
King Xiàng, hearing the King of Hàn was at Wǎn,
indeed led his troops south,
as Yuánshēng had strategized.
Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr,
with tens of thousands of troops,
marched east down Jǐngxíng to attack Zhào,
and defeated it.
They reported to Hàn,
requesting to establish Zhāng Ěr as King of Zhào,
to pacify and govern the state.
The King of Hàn agreed.
Initially,
the King of Zhào and Chéng'ān Jūn Chén Yú, hearing Hàn was about to attack,
gathered troops at the Jǐngxíng Pass.
Guǎngwǔ Jūn Lǐ Zuǒchē advised:
"I hear Hán Xìn crossed the Western River,
captured the King of Wèi,
seized Xià Yuè,
and recently bloodied Yānyǔ.
Now aided by Zhāng Ěr,
planning to take Zhào,
this is riding victory to fight far from home,
their momentum is unstoppable.
I've heard:
supplying grain over a thousand miles,
soldiers will still go hungry;
gathering fuel to cook,
the army won't be full overnight.
Now the Jǐngxíng road,
chariots cannot run abreast,
cavalry cannot form columns,
marching hundreds of miles,
their supplies must lag behind.
I beg you to lend me thirty thousand surprise troops,
to emerge from bypaths,
cut off their supply train.
You dig deep moats and build high ramparts,
fortify camps and do not engage,
so they can neither fight forward,
nor retreat back.
My surprise troops will cut off their rear,
leaving nothing to plunder in the wild.
Within ten days,
the heads of their two generals
can be delivered to your tent.
I urge you to consider my plan.
Otherwise,
you will surely be captured by those two."
Chéng'ān Jūn did not heed Guǎngwǔ Jūn.
Guǎngwǔ Jūn's strategy was unused.
Xìn heard of this,
was greatly pleased,
then advanced to attack Zhào,
and defeated it.
After Zhào's defeat,
Hán Xìn ordered his army not to kill Guǎngwǔ Jūn,
offering a thousand in gold
to anyone who captured him alive.
Thus, someone bound Guǎngwǔ Jūn and brought him to the tent.
Xìn untied his bonds,
and treated him as a teacher.
He asked:
"I wish to attack Yān in the north,
and campaign against Qí in the south,
how can I succeed?"
Guǎngwǔ Jūn declined, saying:
"I've heard:
a defeated general
cannot speak of courage;
a minister of a fallen state
cannot plan survival.
Now I am a captive of defeat,
how can I counsel on great matters!"
Xìn said:
"I've heard:
Bǎilǐ Xī lived in Yú and Yú fell,
in Qín and Qín became hegemon.
Not because he was foolish in Yú and wise in Qín,
but due to being heeded or not.
Had Chéng'ān Jūn followed your plan,
even I would have been captured.
I commit my heart to your counsel,
I beg you not to refuse."
Guǎngwǔ Jūn said:
"I've heard:
the wise, in a thousand thoughts,
must have one oversight;
the foolish, in a thousand thoughts,
must have one insight.
Thus it is said:
'Even the words of a madman,
the sage may choose from.'
I fear my plan may not be of use,
but I wish to offer my humble loyalty.
Chéng'ān Jūn had strategies to win every battle,
yet lost them in a day,
his army defeated at Hàoxià,
himself dead at Chíshàng.
Now you, General, crossed the Western River,
captured the King of Wèi,
seized Xià Yuè at Yānyǔ,
took Jǐngxíng in one move,
defeated two hundred thousand of Zhào in less than a morning,
executed Chéng'ān Jūn,
your name known throughout the land,
your might shaking the empire,
farmers leave plows,
weavers leave looms,
dressing finely and eating well,
listening intently for your command.
Such is
your strength, General.
Yet your troops are weary and exhausted,
In reality, it is difficult to employ.
Now, General, you intend to mobilize weary and exhausted troops,
stationing them beneath the strong walls of Yān,
wishing to fight but fearing you cannot,
unable to capture the city by assault,
your true situation exposed and momentum waning,
prolonging the days until provisions are depleted.
And if weak Yān does not submit,
Qí will surely defend its borders to strengthen itself.
With Yān and Qí locked in a stalemate and unyielding,
the authority between Liú and Xiàng remains undivided.
In such a case,
it reveals the General's shortcomings.
I am ignorant,
but I privately believe this is a mistake.
Therefore, those skilled in using troops
do not use their weaknesses to attack others' strengths,
but use their strengths to attack others' weaknesses."
Hán Xìn said:
"Then what course should I take?"
Guǎngwǔ Jūn said:
"Currently, for the General's strategy,
nothing is better than halting the armor and resting the troops,
to pacify Zhào,
comfort its orphans and weak,
within a hundred lǐ,
with oxen and wine arriving daily,
to feast the officers and gentry,
relax the soldiers,
facing north toward the road to Yān,
and then dispatch persuasive envoys bearing a short letter,
displaying your strengths to Yān,
and Yān will surely not dare to disobey.
Once Yān has complied,
send a herald east to inform Qí,
and Qí will surely follow like the wind and submit,
even if there are wise men,
they will not know how to plan for Qí.
If this is done,
then the affairs of the world can be plotted.
In warfare, there are those who first make a show of strength and then follow with substance,
this is what it means."
Hán Xìn said:
"Good."
He followed this strategy,
sent envoys to Yān and Qí,
and they submitted like the wind.
In the twelfth month,
the King of Hàn resisted Chǔ at Chénggāo,
and the army wished to fight again.
The court official Zhèng Zhōng advised:
"Your Majesty, build high ramparts and deep walls,
do not engage in battle,
send Liú Jiǎ to assist Péng Yuè into Chǔ territory,
burn their stockpiles,
and you will surely defeat the Chǔ army."
Xiàng Yǔ then went east to attack Péng Yuè,
leaving Cáo Jiù to guard Chénggāo.
At that time, Hàn was repeatedly besieged at Xíngyáng and Chénggāo,
and planned to abandon Chénggāo and eastward,
stationing troops at Gǒng and Luò to resist Chǔ,
but adopting Lì Shēng's plan,
they again defended Chénggāo.
Lì Shēng advised:
"I have heard:
those who understand what people rely on,
can accomplish royal affairs;
those who do not understand what people rely on,
cannot accomplish royal affairs.
A king regards the people as his heaven,
and the people regard food as their heaven.
Now, the Áo Granary,
has long been the hub of grain transport for the empire,
I have heard there are vast stores of grain beneath it.
The Chǔ people captured Xíngyáng,
but did not firmly hold the Áo Granary,
instead leading eastward,
ordering conscripts to guard Chénggāo in the east,
this is heaven's way of aiding Hàn.
Now Chǔ is easy to take, yet Hàn instead retreats,
forfeiting this advantage,
I believe this is a mistake.
Moreover, two heroes cannot stand together,
Chǔ and Hàn have long been deadlocked without resolution,
the common people are agitated,
the land is in turmoil,
farmers abandon their plows,
weaving women leave their looms,
the hearts of the people are unsettled.
I urge you to quickly advance your troops again,
recapture Xíngyáng,
seize the grain of the Áo Granary,
block the strategic points of Chénggāo,
cut off the Tàiháng Pass road,
hold the Fēihú Pass entrance,
guard the Báimǎ River crossing,
to show the feudal lords the advantage of tangible control,
then the world will know where to turn.
Now Yān and Zhào are already pacified,
only Qí remains unsubdued.
Now Tián Guǎng holds Qí with its thousand lǐ,
Tián Jián commands two hundred thousand troops,
stationed at Lìchéng,
the Tián clan is powerful,
backed by the sea and protected by the river,
Jǐnán is close to Chǔ,
and its people are crafty and deceitful.
Even if you send several hundred thousand troops,
it cannot be taken in months or years.
I request to receive your clear edict to persuade the King of Qí,
to make him a vassal of Hàn in the east."
The King said:
"Good."
He then followed this plan,
again holding the Áo Granary.
And sent Lì Shēng to persuade the King of Qí, saying:
"Does the King know where the world will turn?"
The King said:
"I do not know."
He said:
"If the King knows where the world will turn,
then Qí can be obtained and kept.
If the King does not know where the world will turn,
then Qí cannot be preserved."
The King of Qí said:
"Where will the world turn?"
Lì Shēng said:
"The world will turn to Hàn."
The King said:
"How does the gentleman know this?"
Lì Shēng said:
"The King of Hàn and Xiàng Yǔ joined forces westward to attack Qín,
agreeing that whoever entered Xiányáng first
would be king there.
The King of Hàn entered Xiányáng first,
but King Xiàng broke the promise and did not grant it,
instead making him king in Hànzhōng.
Xiàng Yǔ moved and killed the Righteous Emperor,
the King of Hàn heard of this,
raised troops from Shǔ and Hàn,
attacked the Three Qín,
marched through Wǔguān,
and demanded justice for the Righteous Emperor's fate,
gathering the troops of the world,
and enfeoffing the descendants of feudal lords.
When a city surrenders, he enfeoffs its general as a marquis,
when spoils are obtained, he shares them with his soldiers,
sharing benefits with all under heaven,
so heroes and wise men gladly serve him.
The troops of feudal lords
arrive from all directions;
the grain of Shǔ and Hàn
comes down the river by boatloads.
King Xiàng bears the reputation of breaking promises,
and the burden of killing the Righteous Emperor;
he does not record others' achievements,
nor forget others' faults;
winning battles but not rewarding them,
capturing cities but not enfeoffing them;
unless one is of the Xiàng clan,
none can hold power;
when engraving seals for others,
he wears them down but does not grant them;
capturing cities and gaining spoils,
he hoards them without rewarding;
the world rebels against him,
the talented resent him,
and none will serve him.
Therefore, the talented of the world turn to the King of Hàn,
as can be easily deduced.
The King of Hàn started from Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified the Three Qín;
crossed the waters of the Three Rivers,
and received the troops of Shàngdǎng;
descended the Jǐngxíng Pass road,
punished Chéng'ān's crimes;
northward, he defeated Zhào,
capturing thirty-two cities;
this is like Chīyóu's army,
not by human strength,
but by heaven's blessing.
Now he already holds the grain of the Áo Granary,
blocks the strategic points of Chénggāo,
guards the Báimǎ River crossing,
cuts off the Tàiháng Pass road,
holds the Fēihú Pass entrance,
and those who submit later to the world will perish first.
If the King quickly submits to the King of Hàn,
the state of Qí can be preserved;
if you do not submit to the King of Hàn,
danger and destruction await immediately."
Tián of Qí found this reasonable,
and heeded Lì Shēng's advice,
disbanding the defenses at Lìxià.
The Marquis of Huáiyīn then crossed troops at Píngyuán by night to attack Qí.
The King of Qí boiled Lì Shēng alive,
and led his troops east in flight.
Initially,
when Lì Shēng met the Lord of Pèi,
the Lord of Pèi was sitting arrogantly on his bed.
He had two women wash his feet,
and then received Lì Shēng.
Lì Shēng entered and made a deep bow without kneeling,
saying:
"Do you wish to assist Qin in attacking the feudal lords?
Or do you wish to lead the feudal lords to defeat Qin?"
The Lord of Pèi cursed him:
"Ignorant scholar!
All under heaven have long suffered under Qin,
hence the feudal lords joined forces to attack Qin.
How can you say I'm assisting Qin against the feudal lords?"
Lì Shēng said:
"If you truly wish to gather followers and unite righteous troops,
to punish the unprincipled Qin,
you should not receive your elders with such arrogance."
Thereupon, the Lord of Pèi stopped having his feet washed,
rose and apologized to him.
When Xiàng Yǔ first headed east,
he instructed Cáo Jiù:
"If Hàn challenges to battle,
be careful not to engage,
just don't let Hàn advance eastward."
Jiù then went out to fight,
died,
and the King of Hàn subsequently advanced his troops to take Chénggāo.
Hàn challenged Cáo Jiù to battle,
but the Chǔ army did not emerge.
They sent men to insult them,
and after several days,
Jiù became angry,
leading troops across the Sì River.
When half the soldiers had crossed,
Hàn attacked and defeated them,
capturing all of Chǔ's treasures and goods.
When Xiàng Yǔ heard of Jiù's defeat,
he returned his army to the area of Guǎngwǔ,
built a high platform,
and placed Tàigōng upon it.
The King of Hàn sent Hóu Gōng to persuade Xiàng Yǔ,
requesting Tàigōng's return.
Xiàng Yǔ then made a pact with Hàn:
to divide the world in half,
with the Hóng Gōu as the boundary—west to Hàn, east to Chǔ.
He returned the King of Hàn's parents and Empress Lǚ.
King Xiàng withdrew and headed east,
while the King of Hàn intended to go west.
Zhāng Liáng said:
"Now Hàn holds more than half the world,
and all feudal lords submit,
while Chǔ's troops are weary,
provisions exhausted,
this is heaven's time to destroy Chǔ.
It would be better to take advantage of their eastward movement and seize them."
The King of Hàn then pursued Xiàng Yǔ.
He arranged with the King of Qí, Hán Xìn, and the Chancellor of Wèi, Péng Yuè,
to meet and attack Chǔ together,
but they did not come.
Employing Zhāng Liáng's strategy,
Xìn and others led their troops to besiege Xiàng Yǔ at Gāixià,
and thus destroyed the Xiàng clan.
The King of Hàn asked Zhāng Liáng:
"The feudal lords do not follow;
what should we do?"
Liáng said:
"Chǔ's army is about to be defeated,
yet they have not been allotted lands,
so their absence is natural.
If you, great king, can share the world with them,
they will come immediately.
The establishment of the King of Qí, Xìn,
was not your intention,
and Xìn himself is not secure.
Péng Yuè originally pacified the land of Liáng,
initially, because of Wèi Bào,
Yuè was appointed as Chancellor.
Now Bào is dead,
Yuè also hopes to be king,
but you, great king, have not settled it early.
Now, if you can take the area north of Suīyáng to Gǔchéng,
and make Péng Yuè king there;
and from Chén eastward to the sea,
give it to the King of Qí, Xìn.
Xìn's family is in Chǔ,
his desire is to regain his former territory.
If you can cede these lands,
to satisfy these two men,
making them fight for themselves,
then Chǔ can be easily defeated."
Thereupon, the King of Hàn sent envoys,
and Hán Xìn, Péng Yuè, Liú Jiǎ and others all led troops to besiege Xiàng Yǔ at Gāixià.
He established the capital at Luòyáng.
Adopting Lóu Jìng's advice,
he moved the capital to Cháng'ān.
Lóu Jìng advised the emperor:
"Your Majesty capitalizes at Luò,
do you wish to rival the prosperity of the Zhōu dynasty?"
The emperor said:
"Yes."
Jìng said:
"Your Majesty's way of gaining the world differs from that of the Zhōu house.
The ancestors of Zhōu began with Hòu Jì,
whom Yáo enfeoffed at Tái.
They accumulated virtue and goodness
for over ten generations.
Gōng Liú avoided Jié and dwelled at Bīn,
and Tài Wáng, because of the Róng Dí,
left Bīn,
wielding his horse whip,
settled at Qí,
and the people contended to follow him.
By the time of King Wén,
as the Earl of the West,
he settled the dispute between Yú and Ruì,
and began to receive the Mandate.
Lǚ Wàng and Bó Yí came from the seashore to join him.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
eight hundred feudal lords met at Mèngjīn without prior arrangement,
all saying:
'Zhòu should be attacked.'
Thus they destroyed Yīn.
When King Chéng ascended the throne,
the Duke of Zhōu and others assisted as regents,
and then built the city of Luòyì as Chéngzhōu,
considering it the center of the world.
Feudal lords from all directions presented tribute,
and the distances were equal!
With virtue, it was easy to rule,
without virtue, easy to perish.
All who dwelled here
wished to ensure that Zhōu focused on attracting people through virtue,
not relying on dangerous barriers,
to prevent later generations from becoming arrogant, extravagant, and oppressive.
At the peak of Zhōu's power,
the world was harmonious,
the Four Barbarians admired its influence,
yearning for its righteousness and cherishing its virtue,
attached and served together.
Not a single soldier was stationed in the world,
not a single warrior fought,
yet the people of the great nations of the Four Barbarians all submitted,
offering their tribute.
When Zhōu declined,
it split into two,
the world ceased to pay homage,
and Zhōu could not control it.
Not because its virtue was thin,
but because its strategic position was weak.
Now Your Majesty rose from Fēng and attacked Pèi,
gathered three thousand troops,
with which you swept through Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified the Three Qín,
battled Xiàng Jí at Xíngyáng,
contested the pass at Chénggāo,
fought seventy major battles,
forty minor ones,
causing the people of the world to have their livers and brains spilled on the ground,
fathers and sons exposing their bones in the wilderness,
countless in number,
the sound of weeping not yet ceased,
the wounded soldiers not yet risen,
and yet you wish to rival the prosperity of the Chéngzhōu era,
I humbly believe it is not comparable.
Moreover, the land of Qín is surrounded by mountains and girded by rivers,
fortified by four passes,
so that in sudden emergency,
a million troops can be assembled.
This is what is called the 'Storehouse of Heaven'.
If Your Majesty enters the passes and capitals there,
even if the lands east of the mountains are in chaos,
the old territory of Qín can be held entirely.
When fighting with others,
if you do not grip their throat and strike their back,
