you cannot achieve complete victory.
Now if Your Majesty enters the passes and capitals at Cháng'ān,
controlling the old territory of Qín,
this is also gripping the world's throat and striking its back."
Gāozǔ asked his ministers.
The ministers were all from east of the mountains,
and contended that the Zhōu kings lasted seven hundred years,
while Qín perished in the second generation,
so it was better to capital at Luòyáng.
Luòyáng has Chénggāo to the east,
Yáo and Miǎn to the west,
with the Hé River behind and the Yī and Luò rivers in front,
its defenses are also sufficient to rely on.
Liú Hóu said:
"Although Luòyáng has these defenses,
its area is small,
not more than a few hundred lǐ,
the land is poor,
and it is exposed to enemies on all sides,
this is not a country for military use.
Now, for the land within the passes, with Yáo and Hán to the left,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
fertile fields for a thousand lǐ,
the richness of Bā and Shǔ to the south,
the benefits of the Hú and Yuān to the north,
protected on three sides and guarding only one,
controlling the feudal lords to the east.
When the feudal lords are stable,
The waterways and land transport of the Hé and Wèi rivers
are sufficient to supply the western capital;
if the feudal lords revolt,
one can sail downstream,
ensuring adequate supply transport.
This is what is called a thousand-mile stronghold,
a land of natural abundance,
as Lóu Jìng rightly advised."
Thereupon, Emperor Gāozǔ immediately set off westward,
establishing the capital in Guānzhōng.
When it was reported that the King of Chǔ, Hán Xìn, was rebelling,
he used Chén Píng's stratagem to capture him,
demoting him to Marquis of Huáiyīn.
Emperor Gāozǔ consulted his generals,
who said:
"Quickly send troops to bury that scoundrel!"
The Emperor remained silent.
He asked Chén Píng,
who said:
"Has anyone else heard about the letter accusing Xìn of rebellion?"
The reply was:
"No."
Chén Píng asked:
"Does Xìn know about it?"
The answer:
"He does not.
How does Your Majesty's elite army compare to Chǔ's?"
The Emperor said:
"It cannot surpass it."
Chén Píng said:
"Among Your Majesty's commanders,
is there anyone who can match Hán Xìn?"
The Emperor replied:
"None can equal him."
Chén Píng said:
"Now our troops are not as elite as Chǔ's,
and our generals are inferior;
to raise an army and attack him
would be to rush into battle—
I fear for Your Majesty's safety."
The Emperor asked:
"What should be done then?"
Chén Píng said:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven toured the realms,
meeting the feudal lords.
To the south lies Yúnmèng,
Your Majesty could pretend to tour Yúnmèng,
summoning the lords to Chén.
Chén
is on the western border of Chǔ.
When Xìn hears that the Emperor is on a friendly excursion,
he will surely come to the outskirts to welcome you;
upon his audience, Your Majesty can seize him—
this is merely a task for one strong warrior."
Emperor Gāozǔ agreed,
sending envoys to inform the feudal lords.
The Emperor then proceeded,
and indeed, Xìn met him on the road.
The Emperor had prepared warriors in advance;
upon seeing Xìn,
they immediately captured and bound him.
Tián Xū congratulated the Emperor, saying:
"Excellent.
Your Majesty has captured Hán Xìn,
and now governs Qínzhōng.
Qín,
a land of strategic advantage,
is girded by rivers and fortified by mountains,
isolated across a thousand miles,
with a million halberd-bearing soldiers,
Qín holds a position where two can hold against a hundred.
With such favorable terrain,
to send troops against the feudal lords
is like pouring water from a high roof—effortless.
As for Qí,
to the east, it has the riches of Lángyá and Jímò,
to the south, the solidity of Tài Shān,
to the west, the barrier of the turbid river,
to the north, the benefits of the Bó Hǎi,
its territory spans two thousand miles,
with a million halberd-bearing soldiers,
isolated beyond a thousand miles,
Qí holds a position where ten can hold against a hundred.
These are the eastern and western Qíns;
unless they are your own kin,
none should be made kings of Qí."
The Emperor said:
"Good."
He bestowed five hundred catties of gold.
When Chén Xī, as Chancellor of Dài,
rebelled along with Hán Xìn and Wáng Huáng,
and Xī proclaimed himself King of Dài,
the Emperor personally went to defeat him.
Emperor Gāozǔ pardoned the officials of Zhào and Dài who had been misled by Xī,
but the Chancellor of Zhào recommended executing the prefect and commandant of Chángshān,
saying:
"Of the twenty-five cities north of Chángshān,
when Xī rebelled,
twenty were lost."
The Emperor asked:
"Did the prefect and commandant rebel?"
The reply:
"They did not."
The Emperor said:
"Then it was due to insufficient strength."
He pardoned them,
reinstating them as prefect and commandant.
Upon arriving in Hándān,
the Emperor said joyfully:
"Xī did not secure the Zhāng River to the south
nor hold Hándān to the north—
I knew he was incapable."
He asked Zhōu Chāng:
"Are there any brave men in Zhào who can be made generals?"
The reply:
"There are four such men."
When the four were presented,
the Emperor scolded them dismissively:
"Can you scoundrels be generals?"
Yet he enfeoffed each with a thousand households,
appointing them as generals.
His attendants remonstrated:
"Those who followed you into Shǔ and Hàn to attack Chǔ
have not all been rewarded;
what merit have these men to be enfeoffed?"
The Emperor said:
"You do not understand.
With Chén Xī's rebellion,
all north of Hándān is under Xī's control;
I issued urgent summons for troops from across the land,
but none have arrived.
Now we have only the soldiers within Hándān.
Why should I begrudge four thousand households to enfeoff these four and reassure the hearts of Zhào's people!"
All said:
"Well said."
Then the Emperor asked:
"Who are Chén Xī's generals?"
The reply:
"Wáng Huáng and Mànqiū Chén,
both former merchants."
The Emperor said:
"I understand."
He then offered a thousand pieces of gold each for the capture of Huáng and Chén.
Their subordinates, tempted by the reward,
captured them alive.
Consequently,
Chén Xī's army was defeated.
Initially,
Hán Xìn knew that the Hàn court feared and resented his abilities.
He conspired with Chén Xī to rebel;
when Emperor Gāozǔ personally led troops against Xī,
Xìn pleaded illness and did not accompany him,
intending to rise from within.
A retainer of Xìn offended him,
and Xìn imprisoned the man,
planning to kill him.
The retainer's younger brother reported Xìn's rebellious intentions to Empress Lǚ.
Empress Lǚ wanted to summon him,
but feared his faction would not comply,
so she plotted with Chancellor Xiāo,
deceitfully sending someone claiming to come from the Emperor,
saying that Xī was already dead,
and all the marquises and officials came to congratulate.
The Chancellor deceived Xìn, saying:
"Though ill,
you should force yourself to come and congratulate."
When Xìn entered,
Empress Lǚ had warriors bind him,
and he was executed in the Chánglè Palace.
When Wèi Tuó became king of Nányuè
and rebelled,
Emperor Gāozǔ sent Lù Jiǎ to bestow upon Wèi Tuó the seal and ribbon,
making him King of Nányuè,
ordering him to acknowledge allegiance,
and abide by Hàn's covenants.
When Lù Shēng arrived in Nányuè,
Wèi Tuó received him with hair tied up and sitting sprawled.
Lù Shēng then persuaded him:
"You are a man of the Central Plains,
with relatives, brothers, and ancestral graves in Zhēndìng.
Now you rebel against your nature,
abandoning cap and belt,
seeking to pit your tiny Yuè against the Son of Heaven as an enemy state—
disaster will befall you.
Moreover, when Qín lost its governance,
the feudal lords and heroes all rose up;
only the King of Hàn entered the passes first,
seizing Xiányáng.
King Xiàng broke the covenant,
proclaiming himself Hegemon King of Western Chǔ,
with all the feudal lords under him—
he could be called supremely powerful.
Yet the King of Hàn rose from Bā and Shǔ,
whipping the world into submission,
controlling the feudal lords,
and eventually executed Xiàng Yǔ,
destroying him.
Within five years,
the land was pacified,
This is not by human strength,
but built by Heaven.
The Son of Heaven has heard that you, the King, rule Nányuè,
yet do not assist the world in punishing the violent rebels,
so he intends to move troops to attack you.
However, the Son of Heaven pities the people, who have recently endured hardships,
and wishes to let them rest,
thus sending me to confer upon you the royal seal and ribbons,
carving the tally and exchanging envoys.
You, the King, should welcome me at the outskirts,
face north and declare yourself a subject,
yet instead, with the newly established and still unconsolidated Yuè,
you stubbornly resist here.
If Hàn truly hears of this,
they will dig up the tombs of your ancestors,
exterminate your clan,
and send a lieutenant general with a hundred thousand troops to descend upon Yuè.
Then Yuè will kill you to surrender,
as easily as turning a hand over."
Thereupon, Wèi Tuō sprang up abruptly,
and apologized to Master Lù.
Finally, he paid respects to Wèi Tuō and returned.
Earlier,
Rèn Yáo, the commandant of Nánhǎi, fell ill,
and as he was dying,
summoned Zhào Tuō, the magistrate of Lóngchuān, and said:
"I hear that Chén Shèng has started a rebellion,
and the heroes have turned against Qín, establishing themselves.
Pānyú is backed by mountainous terrain,
blocking Nánhǎi,
stretching thousands of miles east to west,
with quite a few people from the Central Plains assisting.
This makes it the master of a whole province,
suitable for founding a state."
He then immediately put Tuō in charge of Nánhǎi's affairs.
After Yáo died,
Tuō issued a proclamation to the various commaneries, saying:
"Rebel armies are about to arrive,
quickly cut off the new roads,
gather troops to defend yourselves,
and gradually use the law to execute the officials appointed by Qín,
replacing them with your own partisans as acting administrators,
and proclaim yourself King Wǔ of Nányuè."
Emperor Gāozǔ reigned for twelve years,
passed away,
at the age of sixty-two.
Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
with Empress Lǚ overseeing the government.
During Empress Lǚ's time,
Chén Píng was at leisure, deeply pondering.
Master Lù said:
"What are you thinking so deeply about?"
Píng replied:
"Can you guess what I'm thinking?"
Master Lù said:
"Your position is that of the highest minister,
a marquis with a fief of thirty thousand households,
you could be said to be extremely wealthy and without desires.
Yet you have worries,
which are none other than concerns about the various Lǚs and the young emperor."
Píng said:
"Indeed.
What should be done about it?"
Master Lù said:
"When the world is at peace,
attention focuses on the chancellor;
when the world is in danger,
attention focuses on the general.
If the general and chancellor are harmonious,
then the officials will willingly submit;
if the officials are prepared to submit,
even if there are changes in the world,
power will not be divided;
with power undivided,
the fate of the state lies in the hands of you two.
Why not befriend the Grand Commandant,
and form a deep alliance?"
Píng followed his advice,
and eventually eliminated the various Lǚs.
Earlier,
when Empress Lǚ passed away,
the high officials plotted against the various Lǚs.
Lǚ Lù was in command of the Northern Army,
so Grand Commandant Bó could not enter the Northern Army.
At that time, Lì Shāng's son Jì was on good terms with Lǚ Lù.
So they sent someone to coerce Lì Shāng,
and his son, trusted by Lǚ Lù,
thus went out with him on an excursion,
allowing the Grand Commandant to enter the Northern Army and eliminate the Lǚ clan.
During Emperor Jǐng's time,
Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
and he sent an expedition to pacify them.
The Emperor sent Grand Commandant Zhōu Yàfū east to attack Wú and Chǔ.
Yàfū asked his father's guest, Commandant Dèng:
"What strategy should we adopt?"
The guest replied:
"The Wú troops are very sharp,
difficult to confront head-on;
the Chǔ troops are light,
unable to hold out long.
Now, for your plan, General,
it would be best to lead the troops east and fortify at Chāngyì,
using Liáng as bait for Wú.
Wú will surely throw all its sharp troops into attacking it.
You, General, dig deep trenches and build high ramparts,
send light troops to cut off the Huái-Sì River mouth,
sever Wú's supply route.
Let Wú and Liáng wear each other out,
and when their provisions are exhausted,
then use your full strength to strike at their limit,
and defeating Wú will be certain."
Marquis Tiáo said:
"Good."
He then requested of the Emperor:
"The Chǔ troops are swift and light,
hard to confront directly.
I wish to use Liáng as bait for them,
cut off their supply route,
then they can be controlled."
The Emperor approved.
When Yàfū reached Xíngyáng,
Wú was urgently attacking Liáng,
and Liáng, in crisis,
requested rescue.
Yàfū led his troops northeast to Chāngyì,
fortifying deeply and holding.
The King of Liáng sent envoys to request Yàfū's help,
but Yàfū adhered to the advantageous strategy,
did not go,
held firm and did not emerge,
instead sending Marquis Gāogāo and others to station behind the Wú and Chǔ troops,
cutting off their supply line.
The Wú and Chǔ troops ran short of food,
starved,
wanted to retreat,
repeatedly challenged to battle,
but he never emerged.
Once Wú and Chǔ were famished,
they led their troops away.
Yàfū sent out elite troops in pursuit,
and greatly defeated Wú.
He passed away,
and the crown prince Chè ascended the throne.
This was Emperor Wǔ.
He passed away,
and his son Fúlíng ascended.
This was Emperor Zhāo.
Huò Guāng assisted in governance,
but Shàngguān Jié envied Guāng's favor,
forged a letter from the Emperor's elder brother, King Yān Dàn,
accusing Guāng of claiming imperial privileges at the Shanglin Garden,
and privately transferring commandants.
The Emperor did not believe it,
and Shàngguān Jié's forgery was eventually exposed,
leading to his execution.
He passed away,
and Emperor Wǔ's grandson, King Chāngyì Hè, was enthroned.
Hè
was the son of King Bó of Chāngyì.
He reigned for twenty-seven days,
during which he committed one thousand one hundred twenty-seven offenses,
so Huò Guāng deposed Hè as Marquis Hǎihūn.
After his deposition,
Emperor Wǔ's great-grandson Xún was enthroned.
This was Emperor Xuān.
He was the grandson of Crown Prince Wèi.
He passed away,
and the crown prince Shì was enthroned.
This was Emperor Yuán.
He passed away,
and the crown prince Ào was enthroned.
This was Emperor Chéng.
He delegated governance to his maternal uncles, Wáng Fèng and others,
enfeoffing Fèng and his four brothers as marquises on the same day,
called
"the Five Marquises."
The Five Marquises all monopolized power.
He passed away,
and the son of King Gōng of Dìngtáo, Xīn, was enthroned.
This was Emperor Āi.
He reigned for six years and passed away,
without an heir.
He passed away,
and the Emperor's younger brother, King Xiào of Zhōngshān Kàn, was enthroned.
This was Emperor Píng.
The Emperor was young,
and was poisoned by Wáng Mǎng.
He passed away,
and Emperor Xuān's great-great-grandson Yīng was enthroned.
This was the Rúzǐ Emperor,
but Mǎng deposed Yīng and took the throne himself.
The usurper Wáng Mǎng of the fake Xīn dynasty
was the son of Wáng Màn, Emperor Chéng's maternal uncle,
and the nephew of Emperor Yuán's Empress Wáng.
When Emperor Yuán passed away,
and Emperor Chéng ascended the throne,
he appointed his eldest maternal uncle Fèng as Grand Marshal.
Emperor Shìzǔ, the Luminous Martial Emperor, personal name Xiù,
courtesy name Wénshū,
was a native of Càiyáng in Nányáng.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Gāo.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
the empire suffered successive years of locust plagues and disasters,
and bandits rose up like swarms.
In the late years of Wáng Mǎng,
the southern regions experienced famine,
and people flocked into the marshes,
digging for water chestnuts to eat,
while plundering and seizing from one another.
Wáng Kuāng of Xīnshì mediated disputes fairly,
and thus was elected as a leader.
At that time, Liú Xuán was evading officials in Pínglín.
Meanwhile, Shìzǔ was avoiding officials in Xīnyě,
and was selling grain in Wǎn,
where a man named Lǐ Tōng persuaded Shìzǔ using prophetic texts.
Tōng's father, Shǒu,
was fond of apocryphal records.
Tōng had often heard his father say:
"The Liú family will be restored,
and the Lǐ family will assist them."
He privately held this in mind.
When the Xiàjiāng and
Xīnshì troops rose up,
Tōng's younger brother Yì discussed with him, saying:
"Now that the four corners are in turmoil,
the Xīn dynasty is about to fall,
and the Hàn should be restored.
Among the imperial clan in Nányáng,
only Liú Bóshēng and his brother are broadly benevolent and attract followers—
we can conspire with them on great matters."
Tōng laughed and said:
"That is my thought as well."
It happened that Shìzǔ was in Wǎn avoiding official duties,
and upon hearing of this,
Tōng immediately sent Yì to welcome Shìzǔ,
and they formed an alliance.
Not long after,
Shìzǔ went to Wǎn with Bóshēng and Dèng Chén,
and feasted and conversed with men like Cài Gōng Shǎogōng of Rǎng.
Shǎogōng had studied prophetic texts considerably,
and stated that Liú Xiù would be the Son of Heaven.
Someone asked:
"Is that the Imperial Mentor Liú Xiù?"
Shìzǔ laughed and said:
"How do you know it isn't me?"
All present laughed heartily,
but Chén alone was inwardly pleased.
Later, he said to Shìzǔ:
"Wáng Mǎng is cruel and brutal,
executing people even in midsummer—
this is Heaven's time for his demise.
Could it be that the conversation we had in Wǎn
is about to come true!"
Shìzǔ smiled.
When the Hàn troops rose up,
Dèng Chén went to join them.
Shìzǔ then initiated the uprising in Wǎn with Lǐ Yì,
his elder brother Bóshēng rose up in Chōnglíng,
Dèng Chén rose up in Xīnyě,
and they assembled their forces to attack Chángjù.
Wáng Kuāng and others from Xīnshì set up Liú Shènggōng as the Son of Heaven,
and they harmed Bóshēng.
Liú Xuán,
courtesy name Shènggōng,
was a cousin of Shìzǔ.
He was evading officials in Pínglín
when Wáng Kuāng and others established him.
Earlier,
since Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn throne,
Bóshēng had been indignant and harbored plans to restore the state.
He did not attend to family livelihood,
but spent his wealth and depleted his assets,
to befriend the bold and talented across the land.
In the late years of Wáng Mǎng,
bandits arose in groups.
Bóshēng summoned various heroes for consultation,
whereupon he sent his close associate Dèng Chén to rise up in Xīnyě,
Shìzǔ and Lǐ Yì to rise up in Wǎn,
and Bóshēng himself launched from Chōnglíng,
with seven or eight thousand of his clansmen and followers,
deploying his retinue,
and proclaiming himself "Pillar of Heaven Commander."
He sent Liú Jiā to lure the troops of Xīnshì and Pínglín, Wáng Kuāng and Chén Mù, to combine forces and advance,
massacring Chángjù.
The generals discussed establishing a member of the Liú family,
to meet popular expectations,
and the heroes all wished to follow Bóshēng.
But the commanders of Xīnshì and Pínglín enjoyed license,
feared Bóshēng's authority and integrity,
and coveted Shènggōng's weakness,
so they first decided to establish him,
then summoned Bóshēng to inform him of their decision.
Bóshēng said:
"The generals wish to honor and establish a member of the imperial clan—
this is a profound virtue,
but in my humble opinion,
I secretly disagree.
Now the Chìméi have arisen in Qīng and Xú,
with numbers in the hundreds of thousands.
If they hear that an imperial clansman has been set up in Nányáng,
they may fear the Chìméi will also establish someone,
and if so,
this will lead to internal conflict.
Now Wáng Mǎng is not yet destroyed,
and if the imperial clansmen attack each other,
it will sow doubt in the empire and forfeit our advantage,
which is not the way to defeat Mǎng.
Moreover, those who first raise troops and proclaim titles
rarely succeed—
Chén Shèng and Xiàng Yǔ are examples.
Chōnglíng is only three hundred lǐ from Wǎn,
and we have not achieved enough to hastily claim honor for ourselves,
making ourselves the target of the empire,
so that others may capitalize on our weaknesses—
this is not a good strategy.
For now, let us claim kingship to issue orders.
If the one set up by the Chìméi is worthy,
then we can lead our forces to follow him;
if they set up no one,
then after defeating Mǎng
and eliminating the Chìméi,
we can then assume the honored title—
that would still not be too late.
I hope you will consider this carefully."
The generals did not listen,
and so they established Shènggōng.
Because of this,
the heroes were disappointed.
Bóshēng's subordinate commander Liú Jì,
whose courage surpassed the entire army,
heard that Gēngshǐ had been established,
and angrily said:
"The ones who originally raised troops to plan great deeds
were Liú Bóshēng and his brother.
What kind of man is this Gēngshǐ?"
Gēngshǐ and his ministers heard this and were inwardly wary of him.
They then deployed several thousand troops to arrest Jì,
intending to execute him,
and Bóshēng firmly protested.
Lǐ Yì and Zhū Wěi then urged Gēngshǐ to also seize Bóshēng,
and they killed him that very day.
Lǐ Yì and Shìzǔ became estranged,
and later Yì sent Féng Gōngsūn with a secret letter,
seeking to prove his loyalty.
Some advised keeping it confidential,
but Shìzǔ publicized Yì's letter, saying:
"Lǐ Jìwén is full of deceit—
he is not a trustworthy man."
He then circulated the letter to inform the guards and commandants.
Once the letter was exposed,
Zhū Wěi sent someone to kill Yì.
The era was named the first year of Gēngshǐ.
Gēngshǐ appointed Shìzǔ as a lieutenant general
to pacify Kūnyáng.
Wáng Mǎng heard that the Hàn emperor had been established
and was greatly afraid.
He sent the Grand Minister over the Masses Wáng Xún and the Grand Minister of Works Wáng Yì,
leading a million troops,
to attack Shìzǔ at Kūnyáng.
Shìzǔ defeated them.
Earlier,
Bóshēng had captured Wǎn for three days,
but Shìzǔ did not yet know,
so he falsely sent a man with a letter to report to the city,
saying "reinforcements from Wǎn have arrived,"
and deliberately dropped the letter,
which Xún and Yì obtained,
and they were displeased.
The generals, having achieved repeated victories,
grew bolder and more spirited,
each worth a hundred men,
and Shìzǔ then led three thousand daring warriors
to sally forth from the west of the city,
charging the enemy's central strength.
Xún and Yì's formation was thrown into chaos,
and they were crushed by the fierce assault,
resulting in the death of Wáng Xún.
Mǎng's forces were utterly routed,
the fleeing troops trampling over one another,
fleeing and dying over a hundred lǐ,
when suddenly a great storm arose,
rain pouring down in sheets,
the Zhī River swelling and overflowing,
tigers and leopards trembling in fear,
tens of thousands drowning,
and the waters choked with corpses.
The heroes of the Three Adjuncts
together slew Wáng Mǎng
and sent his head to Wǎn.
Gēngshǐ appointed Shìzǔ to act as Grand Marshal,
bearing the imperial credentials to cross the river northward,
to pacify and reassure the provinces and commanaderies.
Dèng Yǔ, grasping his staff, crossed the river northward,
pursuing Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ saw Yǔ and was greatly pleased.
He said to him:
"I have the authority to grant titles and appointments,
and you, sir, have come from afar.
Do you perhaps wish to serve in office?"
Dèng Yǔ replied:
"That is not my wish.
Your Excellency's might and virtue extend across the four seas,
and I only hope to contribute my modest efforts
to leave my name recorded in the annals of history."
Emperor Guāngwǔ smiled
and had Dèng Yǔ stay overnight.
Dèng Yǔ then advised him:
"Although Gēngshǐ has made his capital west of the passes,
the regions east of the mountains remain unsettled now.
The Red Eyebrows, Green Calves, and similar groups
number in the tens of thousands,
while in the Three Adjuncts, pretenders to the throne
frequently gather in hordes.
Gēngshǐ has not yet suffered any setbacks,
yet he does not personally handle affairs or make decisions.
His various generals are all mediocrities who rose suddenly,
their ambitions fixed on wealth and silk,
competing in the use of force
only to gratify themselves from morning to night.
They lack loyal, good, wise, and discerning men who think deeply and plan far ahead, desiring to honor the sovereign and bring peace to the people.
The empire is fragmented and collapsing,
and the situation is clear to see.
Although you, Excellency, have achieved the merit of establishing a supporting domain,
I fear it may still be insufficient for success.
For the present strategy,
nothing is better than recruiting heroes,
striving to win the people's hearts,
establishing the enterprise of Emperor Gāozǔ,
and saving the lives of the myriad people.
If you consider it from your perspective,
the empire is not difficult to pacify."
Emperor Guāngwǔ was greatly pleased.
When he followed him to Guǎng'ē,
he unrolled a map and, pointing to it, said to Dèng Yǔ:
"The commanderies and kingdoms of the empire are like this,
and now I have only obtained one of them.
You previously said that in my consideration,
the empire is not difficult to pacify.
Why is that?"
Dèng Yǔ replied:
"Now the empire is in chaos and disarray,
and the people long for an enlightened ruler,
just as an infant yearns for a loving mother.
In ancient times, those who rose to power
depended on the depth of their virtue,
not on the size of their territory."
Emperor Guāngwǔ smiled with pleasure.
Also, Féng Yì advised Emperor Guāngwǔ, saying:
"The people have longed for the Hàn for a long time.
Now Gēngshǐ's various generals
act arbitrarily, violently, and cruelly,
plundering wherever they go,
causing the common people to lose hope
and have no one to rely on or support.
Now you, sir, have sole command over a region
and can bestow kindness and virtue.
Where there is the chaos of a Jié or Zhòu,
the merit of a Tāng or Wǔ becomes apparent.
When people have long been hungry and thirsty,
they are easily satisfied.
It is appropriate to quickly dispatch officials
to tour the commanderies and counties, redress grievances,
and spread your benevolent influence."
Emperor Guāngwǔ accepted this.
Wáng Láng falsely claimed to be Zǐyú, son of Emperor Chéng,
and set himself up as the Son of Heaven,
making his capital at Hándān.
He sent envoys to subdue the commanderies and kingdoms,
but Emperor Guāngwǔ destroyed him.
Wáng Chāng, also known as Wáng Láng,
was a man of Hándān in the kingdom of Zhào.
He had previously worked as a diviner and physiognomist,
and often believed that north of the Yellow River there was an imperial aura.
At that time, Zhào Miù's son, Lín, was fond of esoteric arts
and practiced chivalry in the regions of Zhào and Wèi,
and Wáng Láng became friends with him.
Earlier,
when Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
someone in Cháng'ān claimed to be Zǐyú, son of Emperor Chéng,
and Wáng Mǎng had him killed.
Wáng Láng therefore claimed to be the true Zǐyú.
In the first year of the Gēngshǐ era,
Pínglín and others led several hundred chariots and cavalry
and entered the city of Hándān at dawn,
establishing Wáng Láng as the Son of Heaven.
Emperor Guāngwǔ attacked Hándān,
and Wáng Láng's junior tutor, Lǐ Lì, turned traitor,
opening the city gate to let the Hàn army in.
Thus, they captured Hándān
and beheaded Wáng Láng.
They collected documents
and found several dozen letters from officials who had communicated with Wáng Láng
and slandered the emperor.
Emperor Guāngwǔ did not examine them
but gathered the generals and burned them,
saying:
"This will let those who were wavering set their minds at ease."
Emperor Guāngwǔ's prestige and fame grew daily,
and Gēngshǐ became suspicious and concerned.
He then sent an envoy to appoint Emperor Guāngwǔ as Prince of Xiāo,
ordering him to disband his troops
and return to Cháng'ān with the generals who had achieved merit.
He appointed Miáo Zēng as Governor of Yōuzhōu
and Wéi Shùn as Administrator of Shànggǔ,
sending them both to their posts in the north.
At that time, Emperor Guāngwǔ was residing in the Hándān palace,
and Gěng Yǎn requested a private audience to advise him, saying:
"Now Gēngshǐ's governance has failed,
with ruler and ministers given to debauchery and disorder.
The various generals act on their own authority outside the capital region,
and the noble relatives run amok within the capital.
The Son of Heaven's commands
do not pass beyond the city gates.
The appointed governors and administrators change positions on their own,
so the common people do not know whom to follow,
and scholars dare not feel secure.
They plunder wealth and goods,
seize women by force,
and those who possess gold and jade
often do not return alive.
The masses beat their breasts in anguish,
longing even for the days of Wáng Mǎng.
Moreover, the Copper Horses, Red Eyebrows, and similar groups, numbering several dozen bands,
add up to a million men,
and Shènggōng cannot handle them.
His defeat is not far off.
You, sir, first raised the cause in Nányáng,
defeating an army of a million men.
Now you have pacified Héběi,
occupying the land of the Heavenly Storehouse.
With righteousness you wage war,
issuing commands to which all respond.
The empire can be pacified by the mere posting of proclamations.
The empire is of utmost importance
and must not be allowed to fall to another family.
Recently, envoys came from the west
wanting you to disband your troops.
You must not comply.
Now many officials and soldiers have died,
and I, Yǎn, wish to return north to Yōuzhōu
to raise more elite troops
to further your great plan."
Emperor Guāngwǔ was greatly pleased.
Gěng Yǎn returned to Shànggǔ
and beheaded Wéi Shùn and others.
Emperor Guāngwǔ declined the summons and did not go,
beheading Miáo Zēng and others.
From this point, he began to break with Gēngshǐ.
At this time,
the government in Cháng'ān was in chaos,
and rebellions broke out on all sides,
all of which he pacified.
Liú Yǒng, Prince of Liáng, acted on his own authority;
Gōngsūn Shù of Suīyáng declared himself king;
Lǐ Xiàn of Bāshǔ proclaimed himself Prince of Huáinán;
Qín Fēng styled himself King of Chǔlí;
Zhāng Bù rose in Lángyá;
Dǒng Xiàn rose in Dōnghǎi;
Yán Cén rose in Hànzhōng;
Tián Róng rose in Yílíng.
They all appointed generals and commanders
and invaded commanderies and counties.
In addition, there were the Red Eyebrows, Copper Horses, and similar groups,
too numerous to count.
Earlier,
when the Copper Horses surrendered to Emperor Guāngwǔ,
they still felt insecure.
Emperor Guāngwǔ, knowing their thoughts,
ordered them each to return to their camps and command their troops,
then rode out with a light cavalry to inspect their formations.
The surrendering troops said to one another:
"The Prince of Xiāo places a red heart in our bellies;
how can we not devote ourselves to death for him!"
From then on, they were completely won over.
Emperor Guāngwǔ sent Gěng Yǎn to attack Zhāng Bù.
When Zhāng Bù heard of this,
he sent his general Fèi Yì to station troops at Lìxià,
and also deployed forces at Zhù'ā,
setting up several dozen additional camps at Tàishān and Zhōngchéng to await Gěng Yǎn.
Gěng Yǎn then crossed the river
and first attacked Zhù'ā.
He began the assault at dawn,
and before noon, he had captured it.
He deliberately left one corner of the siege open
to allow the defenders to flee back to Zhōngchéng.
When Zhōngchéng heard that Zhù'ā had fallen,
they were greatly frightened
and abandoned their walls to flee.
Fèi Yì sent his brother Fèi Gǎn to hold Jùlǐ.
Gěng Yǎn divided his troops to threaten Jùlǐ
and had them cut down many trees,
spreading word that they would fill in the moats and pits.
After several days,
some defectors reported that Fèi Yì had heard Gěng Yǎn intended to attack Jùlǐ
and was planning to come to its rescue.
Yǎn then commanded his army:
"In three days, we shall attack Jùlǐ City with full force."
He secretly released captives,
allowing them to escape back.
The returnees reported Yǎn's plan to Yì.
On the scheduled day, Yì indeed led troops personally to rescue it,
Yǎn joyfully told his generals:
"The reason I prepared siege equipment
was to lure Yì here.
Now that he has come,
it is exactly what I wanted."
He immediately left three thousand men to guard Jùlǐ,
personally leading elite troops up the slopes,
fighting from high ground,
and beheaded Yì in battle.
Afterwards, he displayed the heads to Jùlǐ City.
The city was terrified,
and Fèi Gǎn fled with all his forces to join Zhāng Bù.
Bù was then based in Jù,
with his brother Lán guarding Xī'ān,
and various commandery governors defending Línzī,
forty li apart.
Yǎn advanced his army between the two cities.
Observing that Xī'ān, though small, was strong,
while Línzī, though large, was actually easy to attack,
he ordered his units
to attack Xī'ān in five days.
Upon hearing this, Lán
kept vigilant day and night.
When the time came,
at midnight,
Yǎn ordered his generals to eat heartily,
and by dawn they reached Línzī City.
Catching them off guard,
they captured it in half a day,
occupying the city.
Zhāng Lán, fearing,
led his troops to flee back to Jù.
Yǎn then forbade his soldiers from plundering near Jù,
waiting until Zhāng Bù arrived,
to provoke and anger him.
Bù, upon hearing,
laughed loudly,
and came to Zī to attack Yǎn.
Yǎn first positioned at the Línzī River,
ready to unleash his cavalry.
Fearing to blunt their edge,
which might make Bù hesitant to advance,
he feigned weakness to boost Bù's morale,
then withdrew to a smaller city,
deploying troops inside.
Bù, confident,
directly attacked Yǎn's camp,
engaging in battle with Liú Xīn.
Yǎn ascended a ruined tower of the royal palace to observe,
saw Xīn's forces engaged,
and led his elite troops
to charge horizontally into Bù's formation,
crushing them decisively.
Bù fled and surrendered to Shìzǔ,
while Chén Jùn escaped.
Yǎn sought to rally the remaining troops,
ordering Chén Jùn to pursue and kill the rebels,
pacifying them all.
The Chìméi rebels entered Hánguān,
attacking Gēngshǐ.
Shìzǔ then sent Dèng Yǔ westward with troops,
to exploit the chaos between Gēngshǐ and the Chìméi.
The Chìméi leader Fán Chóng installed Liú Pénzǐ as emperor,
entered Cháng'ān,
killed Gēngshǐ,
and pillaged Guānzhōng.
Then the generals urged the imperial title,
and officials set up an altar at Qiānqiū Pavilion on Wǔchéng Mò south of Hào,
where he ascended the throne.
The generals petitioned:
"Hàn suffered under Wáng Mǎng,
the ancestral temple was abandoned,
heroes were enraged,
and the people in dire straits.
You and Bóshēng first raised righteous troops,
Gēngshǐ used your resources to claim the throne,
but failed to uphold the great lineage,
ruining order and discipline,
bandits multiplied daily,
and lives were endangered.
Your campaign at Kūnyáng
caused Wáng Mǎng's collapse;
later capturing Hándān, Běizhōu, and securing stability,
you held two-thirds of the realm;
spanning provinces and territories,
with a million armored troops,
none dare oppose your might,
and in civil virtue, none can rival.
We hear:
the imperial throne cannot long be vacant,
the world cannot be declined with modesty.
We implore you to consider the state and the people's welfare."
Also, Qiáng Huá from Guānzhōng presented the Red Prophecy:
"Liú Xiù raises troops to capture the unjust,
the four barbarians gather like clouds, dragons battle in the wild,
at the time of four sevens, fire reigns supreme."
Then he assumed the throne.
In October,
he traveled east to Luòyáng,
and the Chìméi surrendered.
Grand Minister over the Masses Dèng Yǔ, Féng Yì, Liú Hóng, etc., campaigned against the Chìméi.
Yì said:
"I previously fought them at Huáyīn,
for dozens of days,
though we captured several brave generals,
their remaining forces are still numerous.
We can gradually win them over with kindness and trust,
it's hard to defeat them quickly by force.
If His Majesty stations generals at Miǎnchí,
blocking their east,
and I attack from the west,
we can take them in one move,
this is a sure plan."
Yǔ and Hóng did not listen,
engaged in major battle,
the Chìméi feigned defeat,
abandoned supplies and fled.
Their carts were loaded with earth,
covered with beans on top.
The soldiers, hungry,
scrambled for them.
The Chìméi turned back to attack Hóng and others,
whose troops fell into chaos and routed,
Yì and Yǔ rescued them.
The Chìméi retreated slightly,
Yì returned to his fort,
setting a date for battle.
Yì had strong men change clothes to match the Chìméi,
ambushing by the roadside.
At dawn,
the Chìméi sent ten thousand to attack Yì's front,
Yì barely sent troops to rescue.
Seeing the weak resistance,
they committed all forces against Yì.
Yì then unleashed his troops in fierce combat.
By afternoon,
the enemy's morale waned,
ambushers suddenly arose,
uniforms mixed up,
the Chìméi could no longer tell friend from foe,
panicked and routed.
The Chìméi leaders bound themselves,
presenting the imperial seal to surrender to Shìzǔ.
After pacifying Wěi Xiāo,
and destroying Gōngsūn Shù,
the realm was greatly settled.
He passed away in the Southern Palace,
at sixty-three.
When Shìzǔ first raised troops,
he was twenty-eight.
His descendant Língdì employed eunuchs like Cáo Jié, etc.,
who forged edicts to execute Grand Tutor Chén Fān, Lí Yīng,
and their partisans were all imprisoned.
In the ninth year of Zhōngpíng,
the Huángjīn rebels arose.
Jùlù's Zhāng Jiǎo called himself "Great Virtuous Teacher",
serving the Huáng-Lǎo Dao,
nurturing disciples,
connecting commanderies and states,
planning a unified uprising on the fifth of March.
Táng Zhōu informed on them,
Jiǎo started early,
all wearing yellow scarves as symbols.
Língdì died,
Crown Prince Biàn succeeded.
Dǒng Zhuō entered the court,
deposed the emperor as Hóngnóng King,
and installed Xiàndì.
Lǐ Jué forced the emperor east;
Cáo Cāo moved the capital to Xǔ,
Cāo died,
and the emperor abdicated to Cáo Pī.
We must not underestimate them.
It would be better to sustain a prolonged standoff.
You, General, hold fast to the natural barriers of mountains and rivers,
command the masses of four provinces,
externally ally with heroes,
and internally cultivate agriculture and warfare.
Then, select your elite troops,
divide them into surprise forces,
and repeatedly launch attacks where the enemy is vulnerable,
to harass the region south of the Yellow River.
If they reinforce the right, strike their left;
if they reinforce the left, strike their right,
making them exhausted from constant rushing,
so that the people cannot live in peace.
Without exerting ourselves, they will already be worn out,
and within three years,
we can subdue them effortlessly.
Now, if we abandon the strategy of careful planning,
and stake success or failure on a single battle,
should it not go as planned,
regret will be too late."
Yuán Shào did not listen,
and thus attacked Cáo Cāo at Guāndù.
Yuán Shào personally led his troops to Líyáng,
and Jǔ Shòu, before departure,
distributed his wealth,
gathered his clan, and said to them:
"When power is strong, no one is beyond its reach;
when power is lost, one cannot even protect oneself.
How lamentable!"
His younger brother, Jǔ Zōng, said:
"Cáo Cāo's forces are no match for ours;
why are you afraid?"
Jǔ Shòu replied:
"With Cáo Cāo's brilliant strategy,
and holding the Emperor as his asset,
even though we have defeated Gōngsūn Zàn,
our troops are truly weary and depleted,
and our leader is arrogant while the generals are wasteful.
The army's defeat lies in this campaign.
Yáng Xióng once said:
'The six states, foolish and confused,
weakened themselves for the Qín to replace the Zhōu.' Is this not referring to the present situation?"
When crossing the river,
he sighed by the boat, saying:
"The superiors are full of ambition,
the subordinates strive for merit.
Vast and endless Yellow River,
am I to cross you?"
Yuán Shào was indeed defeated by Lord Cáo.
Yuán Shào advanced to secure Wǔyáng and faced off against Cáo Cāo.
Jǔ Shòu again advised:
"Though the northern troops are numerous,
their vigor and effectiveness are inferior to the south's;
the south has less grain stores,
but their wealth and supplies are not as ample as the north's.
The south's advantage lies in swift battles,
the north's in prolonged engagements.
We should maintain a lasting standoff,
dragging it out over time."
Yuán Shào did not heed this.
He connected his camps and gradually pressed toward Guāndù.
Xǔ Yōu advised:
"Cáo Cāo has few troops,
and has deployed all his forces to resist us,
leaving the defense of Xǔdū sparse—
it must be vulnerable.
If we dispatch light cavalry in separate forces,
swiftly marching to launch a surprise attack,
and capture Xǔdū,
then Cáo Cāo will be captured.
Even if it does not collapse immediately,
we can make them rush between front and rear,
and surely defeat them."
Yuán Shào again could not employ this plan.
It happened that Xǔ Yōu's family committed offenses,
and Shěn Pèi arrested and imprisoned them.
Xǔ Yōu, discontented,
fled to Lord Cáo.
He then persuaded Cáo Cāo to launch a surprise attack on Chúnyú Qióng.
Qióng was then supervising the army,
stationed at Wū Cháo,
forty lǐ from Yuán Shào's army.
Cáo Cāo personally led a swift assault.
At that time, Zhāng Hé advised Yuán Shào:
"Lord Cáo's troops are elite;
if they go, they will surely defeat Qióng.
If Qióng is defeated,
then your campaign is lost.
We should lead troops to rescue him."
Guō Tú said:
"Hé's plan is wrong;
it would be better to attack their main camp.
They will surely retreat,
thus resolving the situation without a rescue."
Hé said:
"Lord Cáo's camp is fortified;
attacking it will not succeed.
If Qióng and others are captured,
we will all become prisoners."
Yuán Shào only sent light cavalry to rescue Qióng,
while using heavy troops to attack Cáo's camp,
but could not take it.
Lord Cáo defeated Qióng,
burning their stockpiles.
Yuán Shào's army collapsed and fled north,
and Lord Cáo thus defeated Yuán Shào,
his might shaking the world.
Tàizǔ campaigned against Yuán Shào's sons, Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng, at Líyáng,
and Shàng, with Yuán Xī, fled to Liáodōng.
Governor Gōngsūn Kāng beheaded Shàng and Xī,
sent their heads,
and thus Héběi was pacified.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ campaigned against Tán and Shàng at Líyáng,
winning several battles in a row,
the generals wished to press the attack,
but Guō Jiā said:
"Yuán Shào loved these two sons,
but did not firmly establish an heir.
With Guō Tú and Féng Jì as their strategists,
they will certainly contend between them,
leading to mutual alienation.
Pressing them will make them unite;
easing off will breed rivalry.
It would be better to head south to Jīngzhōu and attack Liú Biǎo,
awaiting their internal changes.
Once changes occur and then we strike,
we can settle it in one move."
Tàizǔ said:
"Good."
As Tàizǔ was preparing to attack Liú Biǎo,
Tán indeed contended with his younger brother Shàng over Jìzhōu.
Tán sent Xīn Pí to beg for surrender,
requesting pardon.
Tàizǔ consulted his officials.
Most officials thought Biǎo was strong,
and he should be pacified first,
while Tán was not worth worrying about.
Xún Yōu said:
"The world is in turmoil,
yet Biǎo sits idly between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers—
his lack of ambition to expand is evident.
The Yuán clan holds four provinces,
with armored troops numbering a hundred thousand.
Shào gained followers through leniency,
hoping his two sons would be harmonious
to preserve his achieved legacy,
but the troubles of the world would not cease.
Now that the brothers are at odds,
their situation cannot accommodate both.
If one absorbs the other, their strength will be unified,
and unified strength will be hard to overcome.
Seizing the opportunity while they are in chaos,
then the world can be settled without difficulty—
this moment must not be lost."
Tàizǔ said:
"Good."
He then agreed to peace with Tán,
and defeated Yuán Shàng.
Tàizǔ campaigned against Liú Biǎo,
and it happened that Biǎo died,
and his son, Cóng, surrendered.
Liú Biǎo,
courtesy name Jǐngshēng,
was from Gāopíng in Shānyáng.
In the first year of the Chūpíng era,
an edict appointed Biǎo as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
To the south, it connected to the Five Ridges,
to the north, it held the Hàn River plains,
covering several thousand lǐ in area,
with armored troops over a hundred thousand.
When Cáo Cāo and Yuán Shào faced off at Guāndù,
Shào sent a request for aid,
and Biǎo agreed but did not send troops,
nor did he aid Cáo,
wishing to observe the changes in the world.
Liú Xiānzhǔ advised Biǎo:
"Now heroes contend together,
two powerful rivals are locked in stalemate—
the weight of the world
rests on you, General.
If you intend to act,
you can rise and exploit their weakness.
If not,
you must still choose whom to follow.
How can you hold a hundred thousand armored troops
and sit watching success or failure?
Unable to aid those seeking help,
and unwilling to submit to the worthy—
these two resentments will surely gather upon you, General,
and I fear you will not remain neutral for long.
Cáo Cāo excels in using troops,
and many talented men have joined him;
he will surely defeat Yuán Shào,
then turn his troops toward the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
I fear you, General, will be unable to resist him.
The best strategy now
is to attach Jīngzhōu to Cáo Cāo;
Cáo will surely deeply appreciate you, General.
long enjoy blessings and prosperity,
passing them down to future generations.
This is a perfectly sound strategy."
Liǎobiǎo did not heed this advice.
In the thirteenth year,
Cáo Cāo personally led an expedition against Liǎobiǎo,
but before he arrived,
Liǎobiǎo developed a carbuncle on his back and
died.
Cáo Cāo's army reached Xīnyě,
where Fù Xùn persuaded Cóng to surrender.
Cóng said:
"Now, with all of you, we hold the entire land of Chǔ,
guarding the legacy of our late lord,
and observing the world—
why should that not be possible?"
Fù Xùn replied:
"Resistance and compliance have their fundamental principles,
strength and weakness their fixed tendencies.
For a subject to oppose his sovereign
is an act of defiance;
for a newly established Chǔ to resist the Central Plains
is certain peril;
for Liú Bèi to confront Lord Cáo
is ill-advised.
All three are shortcomings,
and to attempt to withstand the vanguard of the imperial army
is a path to certain ruin.
How does the general assess himself compared to Liú Bèi?"
Cóng said:
"I am not his equal."
Fù Xùn said:
"If indeed Bèi is inadequate to resist Lord Cáo,
then even if we preserve ourselves,
Chǔ cannot survive;
if indeed Liú Bèi is capable of opposing Lord Cáo,
then Bèi would not remain subordinate to the general.
I urge the general not to hesitate."
Cóng then led his forces in surrender.
At that time, Liú Bèi had fled to Jīngzhōu,
but Liǎobiǎo had not employed him.
Hearing of Jīngzhōu's surrender,
he then fled to Xiàkǒu.
The various commanders in Guānzhōng—Mǎ Chāo, Hán Suì, Chéng Yí, and others—rebelled,
and Lord Cáo defeated them.
Lord Cáo and Mǎ Chāo faced each other across the pass as a boundary.
Lord Cáo pressed them urgently,
while secretly sending Xú Huǎng and others to cross at Púbǎn Ford by night,
establishing a camp west of the river.
Lord Cáo crossed north from Tóngguān,
but before he had fully crossed,
Mǎ Chāo rushed his boats to engage fiercely.
Dīng Fěi released oxen and horses as bait for the rebels.
The rebels fell into disorder,
seizing the oxen and horses,
allowing Lord Cáo to complete the crossing,
and set up camp south of the river.
Mǎ Chāo sent a message requesting to cede territory and offer hostages for peace,
which Lord Cáo pretended to agree to.
Hán Suì requested a meeting with Lord Cáo.
At the appointed time,
they met on horseback,
conversing for a while
without touching on military matters,
only reminiscing about old acquaintances from the capital,
clapping hands and laughing joyfully.
After they parted,
Mǎ Chāo asked Hán Suì what was said,
and Suì replied:
"Nothing of importance."
Chāo grew suspicious.
Another day,
Lord Cáo sent another letter to Suì,
with many alterations and deletions,
as if Suì had revised it,
making Chāo even more suspicious of Suì.
Lord Cáo then engaged them in battle,
and decisively defeated them.
Guānzhōng was pacified.
The commanders asked Lord Cáo:
"Initially,
the rebels guarded Tóngguān,
and the route north of the Wèi River was cut off.
Why did you not attack Féngyì from Hédōng,
but instead guarded Tóngguān,
then led the forces and crossed north again—
why?"
Lord Cáo replied:
"The rebels guarded Tóngguān;
if we had entered Hédōng,
they would surely have extended their defense to all the fords,
making it impossible to cross to the west bank.
Therefore, I massed troops toward Tóngguān;
the rebels concentrated all their forces to defend the south,
leaving the defenses west of the river weak,
so our two generals could freely seize the western bank;
then we led the army north to cross,
and the rebels could not contest the western bank with us
because our two generals' armies were there.
Linking carts and erecting palisades to form a corridor southward
both ensured our invincibility
and displayed weakness.
Crossing the river to establish strong fortifications,
and not engaging when the enemy arrived,
was to make them overconfident.
Thus, the rebels did not build their own fortifications
but sought to cede territory.
I complied and agreed,
to follow their wishes,
letting them feel secure and unprepared,
while accumulating our soldiers' strength.
Then, striking suddenly,
it was as they say: 'A sudden clap of thunder gives no time to cover the ears,
a flash of lightning no time to close the eyes.'
The use of military force adapts to change,
and is certainly not confined to one method."
The Son of Heaven decreed Lord Cáo to be King of Wèi.
Sūn Quán declared himself King of Wú,
holding Jiāngdōng;
Liú Bèi seized the position of Governor of Yìzhōu from Liú Zhāng,
occupying Shǔ.
Thus, the empire was divided into three.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he died in Luòyáng.
His son Pī succeeded him.
Pī, styled Zǐhuán,
was Emperor Wǔ's crown prince,
and became known as Emperor Wén. ,
He received the abdication of Hàn.
He passed away,
and his son Ruì succeeded him.
Ruì, styled Yuánzhòng,
was Emperor Wén's crown prince,
and became known as Emperor Míng. .
He passed away,
and his son Prince Qí Fáng was enthroned,
but was deposed after fifteen years.
After his deposition,
the Duke of Gāoguìxiàng Máo was enthroned,
but was killed after seven years.
Following his removal,
the Duke of Chángdàoxiàng Huáng was enthroned.
Huáng abdicated to Jìn.
Jìn enfeoffed him as Prince of Chénliú.
Emperor Xuān of the Jìn dynasty, given name Yì,
courtesy name Zhòngdá,
surname Sīmǎ,
was a native of Wēn in Hénèi.
He served during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
continued through the reigns of Emperors Wén and Míng,
held positions as general and chancellor,
subdued Mèng Dá
(Dá was the Grand Administrator of Xīnchéng
and rebelled),
annihilated Gōngsūn Dù
(Dù claimed the title King of Yān for generations,
occupying Liáodōng),
and captured Wáng Líng
(Líng plotted to enthrone the King of Chǔ as emperor,
and committed suicide after his troops were defeated).
When Emperor Míng of Wèi passed away,
he left an edict appointing the Emperor as Grand Commandant,
to assist the young ruler alongside Grand General Cáo Shuǎng
(the young ruler
was Fáng, the Prince of Qí).
The Emperor executed Cáo Shuǎng
(Shuǎng plotted treason,
so Xuān Emperor feigned illness to avoid him.
Shuǎng's associate Lǐ Shèng was the Assistant Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
The Emperor pretended to be senile,
saying that Bīngzhōu was near the Hú people,
and preparations should be made.
After Shèng left,
he told Shuǎng:
"Lord Sīmǎ is like a corpse with lingering breath,
his spirit and form have already parted;
he is not worth worrying about."
Shuǎng then became arrogant and arbitrary,
resented the Empress Dowager's involvement in governance,
and moved her to the Yǒngníng Palace.
In the first year of the Jiāpíng era,
when the Son of Heaven visited the Gāolíng tomb,
Shuǎng and his brothers led troops to accompany him.
Xuān Emperor then petitioned the Yǒngníng Palace,
and deposed Shuǎng.
Thereafter, he led troops to the Luò River,
welcomed the Son of Heaven,
and accused Shuǎng and his associates of plotting rebellion,
executing them all).
After Xuān Emperor's death,
his son Shī succeeded him as chancellor
(Shī, courtesy name Zǐyuán,
was Emperor Jǐng of the Sùzōng line).
General Zhèndōng Guànqiū Jiǎn and Inspector of Yángzhōu Wén Qīn rebelled,
and he campaigned to pacify them
(When Jiǎn and Qīn first rebelled,
Emperor Jǐng asked Wáng Sù:
"How can the state be secured and the ruler pacified?"
Sù replied:
"In the past, Guān Yǔ led the forces of Jīngzhōu to capture Yú Jìn at the Hàn River banks,
and then harbored ambitions to contend for the empire northward.
Later, Sūn Quán seized the families of his officers and soldiers,
and Yǔ's forces disintegrated overnight.
Now, the parents of the officers and soldiers in Huáinán are all in the province;
if we swiftly advance to resist them,
preventing them from moving forward,
they will surely collapse like Guān Yǔ's forces."
Emperor Jǐng followed this advice,
and thus defeated Jiǎn and others).
After Emperor Jǐng's death,
his younger brother Zhāo succeeded him as chancellor
(Zhāo, courtesy name Zǐshàng,
was Emperor Wén of the Tàizǔ line),
serving as Minister of Works in the regency.
Zhūgě Dàn occupied Shòuchūn,
rebelled,
and he was ordered to campaign and pacify him.
He attacked Shǔ,
capturing Liú Shàn.
At that time, governance was controlled by powerful ministers,
with the emperor merely presiding over sacrifices.
The Wèi emperor could not tolerate this,
and personally led troops to attack the chancellor's residence.
Tàizǔ followed the strategy of his Chief Clerk Jiǎ Chōng,
engaged in battle,
and had his attendant Chéng Jì seize and kill the Wèi emperor
(the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng,
given name Máo,
courtesy name Shìyàn).
He then falsely ordered the Empress Dowager to issue an edict deposing the young emperor,
and shifted the blame to Chéng Jì,
executing his three sets of relatives).
After Tàizǔ's death,
his son Yán received the abdication of Wèi
(Yán, courtesy name Zì'ān,
was the crown prince of Emperor Wén,
and became Emperor Wǔ of the Shìzǔ line).
After receiving the abdication of Wèi,
he employed the strategies of Yáng Hù and Dù Yù,
attacked Wú,
and pacified it.
He reigned for twenty-five years before passing away,
and the crown prince Zhōng succeeded him
(courtesy name Zhèngdù,
was Emperor Huì,
the crown prince of Emperor Wǔ).
Emperor Huì was not wise,
and his consort, the daughter of Jiǎ Chōng, became empress.
The empress wielded power,
killed Yáng Jùn,
and deposed the Empress Dowager
(Empress Jiǎ was licentious and jealous,
treating her mother-in-law disrespectfully.
She falsely accused the Empress Dowager's father Yáng Jùn of rebellion,
had the emperor execute him,
deposed the Empress Dowager to the Jīnyōng City,
and starved her to death),
executed Grand Tutor Liàng, the Prince of Rǔnán, and Grand Guardian Wèi Guàn
(Liàng and Guàn, both renowned for virtue, held power,
and the empress could not act as she wished.
She thus had the emperor's younger brother Wěi, the Prince of Chǔ,
forge an edict to execute Liàng and Guàn,
and subsequently had Wěi executed as well),
killed Wěi, the Prince of Chǔ,
and caused the death of the crown prince Yù
(Empress Jiǎ had no son,
so she pretended to be pregnant
and adopted a son of Jiǎ Mì as her own.
The crown prince Yù
was born to the palace lady Xiè,
intelligent and wise from a young age.
Empress Jiǎ despised him,
slandered the crown prince,
deposed him to the Jīnyōng City,
and then sent a minor eunuch to kill him).
She appointed Lún, the Prince of Zhào, as Chancellor of State.
Lún despised Minister of Works Zhāng Huá
and the upright Attendant Xiè Péi Gù,
and forged an edict to execute them.
Lún then usurped the throne.
Thereupon, Jiǒng, son of Yōu, the Prince of Qí,
along with the emperor's younger brother Yǐng, the Prince of Chéngdū, and others raised a righteous army to execute Lún.
Yǐng then garrisoned Yè,
and Téng, the Duke of Dōngyíng, Inspector of Bìngzhōu, and General Ānběi Wáng Jùn,
also raised troops to attack Yǐng.
Yǐng was defeated,
and fled south with the Son of Heaven to Luòyáng.
Later, Emperor Huì was restored to the throne,
and the emperor's younger brother, the Prince of Chángshā, slandered Jiǒng,
leading to his execution.
From then on, the Róng and Dí peoples rose together,
and the four quarters were in chaos,
eventually splitting into thirty-six states.
Liú Yuānhǎi was a hostage of the Xiōngnú,
staying in Luòyáng.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn spoke with him
and was pleased.
He told Wáng Hún:
"Yuānhǎi's appearance and insight
are like Yóu Yú and Jīndī,
and none can surpass him."
Hún replied:
"Yuānhǎi's appearance is indeed as Your Majesty says,
but his civil and military talents far exceed those two.
If Your Majesty entrusts him with matters in the southeast,
Wú and Kuàijī could be easily pacified."
The emperor praised this.
Kǒng Xún and Yáng Yáo said:
"We observe that Yuānhǎi's talent
is unmatched in the present day.
If Your Majesty underestimates his followers,
it will not suffice to accomplish the task;
if you grant him authority,
after pacifying Wú,
we fear he may not return north.
Those not of our kind
are sure to have different hearts.
Entrusting him with his own tribe,
we privately fear for Your Majesty.
If we raise the natural barriers of the state to aid him,
would that not be inappropriate?"
The emperor fell silent.
Later, when Qín and Liáng fell,
the emperor sought a general,
and Lǐ Xǐ said:
"If Your Majesty can mobilize the five tribes of the Xiōngnú,
grant Yuānhǎi a general's title,
and march westward with drums beating,
the matter can be settled in short order."
Kǒng Xún said:
"Duke Lǐ's words
fail to address the full logic of eradicating troubles.
If Yuān Hǎi can pacify Liángzhōu and behead Shù Jīnéng,
I fear Liángzhōu will then face calamity.
When a flood dragon obtains clouds and rain,
it is no longer a creature confined to ponds."
The Emperor then desisted.
When Emperor Huì lost control,
bandits and rebels swarmed like bees.
Chéngdū King Yǐng garrisoned Yè,
and recommended Yuān Hǎi for the acting position of General of Nìngshuò,
supervising military affairs of the five tribes.
When Wáng Jùn and others campaigned against Yǐng,
Yuān Hǎi persuaded Yǐng, saying:
"Now two garrisons are acting arrogantly,
with forces exceeding one hundred thousand,
I fear they cannot be resisted by the imperial guards and troops near the capital alone.
I request to return and persuade the five tribes on Your Highness's behalf,
to respond to the national crisis."
Yǐng agreed.
Yuān Hǎi reached his homeland,
where Left Virtuous King Liú Xuān and others offered him the title of Great Chányú,
Within twenty days,
his forces already numbered fifty thousand,
then they invaded Píngyáng,
captured it,
and entered Pú.
At that time, the five barbarians threw the Central Plains into chaos.
As for Shí Lè,
he was a Jié barbarian from Shàngdǎng,
who held Zhào.
The Governor of Yōuzhōu, Wáng Jùn, appointed officials of all ranks,
and Lè harbored intentions to annex him,
wishing first to send an envoy to observe the situation.
Those discussing the matter all said:
"It should be like the affair of Yáng Hù and Lù Kàng,
exchanging letters to communicate."
At that time, Zhāng Bīn was ill,
Lè went to consult him,
Bīn said:
"Wáng Jùn relies on the strength of three tribes,
plotting to claim the southern-facing position (of emperor),
though called a vassal of Jìn,
he truly harbors ambitions of usurpation and rebellion.
He must be thinking of uniting with heroes,
to plan the success of his enterprise.
General, your might shakes the land within the seas,
your departure or adherence determines survival or demise,
your location determines lightness or heaviness.
Jùn's desire for you, General,
is like Chǔ's recruitment of Hán Xìn.
If you now cunningly send an envoy without
sincere and earnest appearance,
signs of suspicion will be exposed,
and later, even with ingenious strategies,
there will be no way to implement them.
To establish great deeds,
one must first humble oneself for it,
you should declare yourself a vassal and support him,
yet even then, fear he may not believe;
as for the affair of Yáng and Lù,
your servant does not see it as feasible."
Lè said:
Right Marquis's plan is correct."
Thereupon, he sent his retainer Wáng Zǐchūn to present treasures and a memorial expressing support for Jùn,
Jùn said to Zǐchūn:
"Lord Shí is a heroic and martial figure of the time,
holding the former Zhào,
forming a tripartite confrontation,
why would he declare himself a vassal to me alone,
is this credible?"
Zǐchūn said:
"General Shí's talent is outstanding and exceptional,
his troops and horses are strong and numerous,
truly as in Your Sagely Decree,
yet looking up to you, Illustrious Lord,
esteemed and expected throughout the provinces and commanderies,
with generations of accumulated glory,
stationed to guard the vassal mountains,
your mighty reputation spreads across the eight directions.
Thus, even the Hú and Yuè revere your influence,
the Róng and Yí sing of your virtue,
how could a mere small domain
dare not to fold its lapels before the divine palace?
In the past, did Chén Yīng disdain kingship and not become king,
did Hán Xìn scorn emperorship and not become emperor?
It was only because the imperial throne cannot be contended for by mere courage and strength.
General Shí's comparison to you, Illustrious Lord,
is like the moon compared to the sun,
rivers and streams compared to the vast sea!
Xiàng Jí and Zǐyáng
provide recent examples of overturned carts,
this is General Shí's clear mirror,
why should you, Illustrious Lord, find it strange?
Since ancient times, there have indeed been
sincere barbarians who became famous ministers,
but none have become emperors or kings.
General Shí does not dislike emperorship and yield to you, Illustrious Lord, because of that,
but because taking it would not be permitted by the world.
I hope you, Lord, do not doubt."
Jùn was greatly pleased,
and sent an envoy to report to Lè.
Lè again sent an envoy to present a memorial to Jùn,
expecting to personally go to Yōuzhōu to offer the honorific title.
He also sent a letter to Zǎo Sōng,
begging for the position of Governor of Bìngzhōu and Duke of Guǎngpíng,
to show his sincere commitment.
Lè assembled troops and prepared,
planning to attack Jùn,
but feared Liú Kūn and the Xiānbēi would become his rear concerns,
hesitating and not launching.
Zhāng Bīn said:
"When attacking an enemy state,
one should strike where they do not expect,
the army has been strict for days without moving,
is it because of concerns about three fronts?"
Lè said:
"Yes,
what should be done about it?"
Bīn said:
"Wáng Péngzǔ's hold on Yōuzhōu
relies solely on three tribes,
now all have turned against him,
becoming enemies instead,
this means externally he has no support to resist us;
Yōuzhōu suffers famine and scarcity,
people all eat vegetables,
with masses rebelling and relatives alienating,
his troops are few and weak,
this means internally he has no strong soldiers to defend himself.
If a large army approaches the outskirts,
it will surely collapse and disintegrate.
Now the three fronts are not aware,
if you, General, can swiftly send an army a thousand lǐ to campaign against Yōuzhōu,
with light troops going and returning,
it will not take more than twenty days,
even if the three fronts make a move,
the situation allows for a quick return,
you should act like lightning seizing the opportunity,
do not delay.
Moreover, though Liú Kūn and Wáng Jùn are both nominally vassals of Jìn,
they are actually enemies.
If you send a letter to Kūn,
offering a hostage to seek peace,
Kūn will surely be pleased to gain our support,
and happy at Jùn's destruction,
ultimately he will not rescue Jùn and attack us."
Lè said:
"Good!"
Thereupon, he led light cavalry to attack Yōuzhōu,
Lè reached the north gate of Jì at dawn,
fearing the gate guards might have ambushes,
he first drove several thousand cattle and sheep,
claiming it as a tribute gift,
but actually intending to fill the streets and alleys,
to prevent troops from deploying.
Lè entered,
and Jùn then became afraid.
Lè entered his audience hall,
ordered armored soldiers to seize Jùn and send him to the market of Xiāngguó,
and executed him.
This is the general outline of the thirty-six states.
Emperor Huì reigned for fourteen years,
then passed away.
His younger brother, Yùzhāng King Chì, ascended
courtesy name Fēngdù,
known as Emperor Huái. ,
He established his capital at Cháng'ān,
and was killed by Hú bandits
Later, the Tuòbá clan of Wèi, in the third year of Emperor Huái of Jìn's Yǒngjiā era,
entered from Yúnzhōng into Yànmén,
holding the desert to the north,
and occupying Yīn Mountain to the south,
with a multitude of several hundred thousand.
By the time of Xiàowén,
he changed the surname from Tuòbá to Yuán,
and established the capital at Luòyáng.
When Emperor Sùzōng passed away,
the Grand Commander Ěrzhū Róng plotted to install Emperor Zhuāng.
Róng killed the Empress Dowager Líng and two thousand nobles and officials,
and installed Emperor Zhuāng.
The Emperor killed Ěrzhū Róng.
Left Deputy Ěrzhū Shìlóng led Róng's troops,
attacked the capital from Jìnyáng,
captured Emperor Zhuāng,
and killed him,
then installed Emperor Mǐn,
and later deposed him.
Gāo Huān then installed Guǎngpíng King's son Xiū,
who later was coerced by Húlǜ Sīzhuāng,
and fled into the pass.
Zhōu Tàizǔ Yǔwén Hēitǎ supported the Emperor and established the capital at Cháng'ān,
clearing the rough terrain,
and setting up the court,
known as Western Wèi.
An edict appointed Yǔwén Hēitài as Chancellor.
Tài also harmed the Emperor,
and installed Nányáng King Bǎojù.
Emperor Wu of the Gao ancestor, surnamed Liú,
named Yù,
courtesy name Déyú,
was a native of Péngchéng.
When Huán Xuán usurped the Jìn,
the false Chǔ ruler Huán Xuán,
courtesy name Jìngdé,
was from Lóngkàng, Qiáo Country.
He possessed a remarkable appearance.
As the Governor of Jiāng Province,
he ambushed and killed Yīn Zhòngkān, the Governor of Jīng Province.
The heir of the Prince of Kuàijī, Yuán Xiǎn, monopolized power,
and due to Xuán's overbearing nature,
dispatched troops to subdue him.
Upon hearing of the impending attack,
Xuán immediately led his forces to the capital,
killing Yuán Xiǎn.
An edict appointed Xuán as Chancellor,
enfeoffed him as Prince of Chǔ,
and subsequently abdicated the throne to him. .
The Gao ancestor, along with Liú Yì, Hé Wújì, and others, secretly plotted to restore the dynasty,
raising an army to pacify Xuán.
At that time, Huán Xuán had appointed Huán Hóng to guard Guǎnglíng,
with Liú Dàoguī as Hóng's Central Army Advisor,
and ordered Dàoguī to attack Huán Hóng.
Huán Xiū was stationed at Dāntú,
with the Gao ancestor as Xiū's Central Forces Advisor,
and he personally attacked Xiū.
They coordinated to act simultaneously,
and once Liú Yì and Dàoguī had attacked Guǎnglíng,
beheading Huán Hóng,
they led his troops south across the river;
the Gao ancestor and Hé Wújì attacked the capital,
beheaded Huán Xiū,
and led twelve hundred men from two provinces,
advancing to encamp at Zhúlǐ,
issuing a manifesto to the capital.
It stated:
"Success and failure are interconnected,
and principles do not always remain prosperous;
the cunning run rampant with cruelty,
yet sometimes encounter sagely brilliance.
Since the establishment of our great Jìn,
it has repeatedly faced calamities of extreme adversity.
Since the Lóng'ān era,
the imperial house has suffered many troubles,
with the virtuous perishing by the hands of jackals and wolves,
and loyal ministers shattered in the jaws of tigers.
The traitor Huán Xuán,
daring to indulge in arrogance and disrespect,
halted troops in Jīng and Yǐng,
running amok in the capital,
yet Heaven had not yet ended the calamity.
His vicious power was indeed vast,
and within a year,
he toppled the imperial throne,
causing the sovereign to flee,
wandering to places not his own,
the sacred vessels humiliated,
and the seven temples fallen.
Even compared to the hardships of the Xià dynasty with Zhúo and Yì,
or the Hàn's encounters with Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Zhuó,
measured against this,
it is not enough to serve as an analogy.
Since Xuán's usurpation and rebellion,
it has been years to this day,
with prolonged drought,
leaving the people with no means to live;
scholars and commoners suffer from forced transport,
civil and military officials toil in construction labors.
Families are torn apart,
fathers and sons separated,
is this merely the sorrow of the 'Great East' with its empty looms,
or the resentment of the basket overturned as in 'Plums Fall'?
Looking up at the celestial signs,
and observing human affairs below,
if this can persist,
then what can perish?
All who have a heart,
who would not wring their hands in despair?
Thus, Yù and others, with hearts aching and tears of blood,
have no leisure to rest,
rising at night and toiling by day,
seeking to encourage loyalty and martyrdom,
secretly plotting through treacherous paths,
more perilous than treading on a tiger,
seizing the moment to strive,
righteous without regard for self-preservation.
Generals like Liú Yì of the Supporting Army and Hé Wújì of the Martial Might,
whose loyalty severs metal,
and sincerity pierces the sun,
have thrown back their sleeves and shouldered spears,
determined to give their lives.
Now that the righteous masses have gathered,
civil and military officials vie to lead,
all asserting that without a unified command,
affairs cannot be set in order,
and though reluctant,
I have thus taken charge of the military essentials,
hoping above to rely on the spirits of our ancestors,
and below to exhaust the strength of righteous men,
to cut down the fugitive rebels,
and cleanse Huáxià.
Lords and gentlemen,
some of you have generations of loyalty,
others personally honored with ranks and emoluments,
yet you bow to cunning minions,
with no way to prove your worth.
Gazing upon the way of Zhōu,
is it not lamentable?
Today's events,
are indeed the opportune moment.
Yù, with my inadequacy,
and talent not matching the ancients,
have accepted duty in a time of collapse,
connecting with a critical opportunity,
my sincere devotion not yet expressed,
filled with passionate indignation,
I look to the heavens with eternal longing,
and gaze upon the mountains and rivers with heightened anticipation.
On the day this manifesto is issued,
my spirit races to the traitor's court."
These were the words of Hé Wújì.
Huán Xuán had Huán Qiān station at Dōnglíng and Biàn Fànzhī at Fùzhōu Mountain.
The righteous army ate breakfast,
and with the rest advancing,
reached the east of Fùzhōu Mountain,
ordering weak troops to ascend the heights,
displaying numerous banners,
filling the valleys,
as the Gao ancestor led the charge,
the soldiers fought desperately,
and Qiān's forces quickly scattered and fled.
Xuán, with a single boat and arrows, fled to Jiānglíng,
intending to enter Shǔ,
but upon reaching Méihuí in Sì Province,
encountered the faction of Fèi Tiánzhī, a参军 of Yì Province,
who shot and killed him. ,
They restored the Son of Heaven to the throne,
and thus the Gao ancestor assumed the roles of general and minister,
enfeoffed as Duke of Yùzhāng Commandery.
The Shǔ rebel Qiáo Zòng declared himself king,
and the Gao ancestor sent a general to subdue him.
The Gao ancestor ordered Zhū Língshí to lead twenty thousand troops,
marching from Jiānglíng to attack Shǔ.
The Gao ancestor admonished him:
"Liú Jìngxiān previously went as far as Huángwǔ,
but retreated without success.
Now, as the army sets out,
it should take the Qīngyī route,
for the rebels expect us to act unexpectedly,
and may again come from the inner waters.
If so,
then the garrison at Chénghuó will surely have heavy defenses,
and if we press on Huángwǔ,
we would fall right into their trap.
Now, let the army proceed from the outer waters,
to capture Chéngdū,
while deploying decoy troops toward Huángwǔ,
this is the best strategy to overcome the enemy."
He wrote this in a letter,
inscribed:
"Open at Báidì."
The generals, though on the march,
did not know their course.
Upon reaching Báidì,
they opened the letter,
which stated that all troops should follow the outer waters,
while Zāng Xī would proceed from the central waters to Guǎnghàn.
They had the weak ride on over a thousand tall ships toward Huángwǔ.
Qiáo Zòng indeed sent Qiáo Dàofú with heavy troops to guard Fú City,
while Zhū Língshí encamped at Péngmó,
two hundred lǐ from Chéngdū.
Qiáo Zòng's general Hóu Huī, among others, stationed at Péngmó.
Zhū Língshí said to Liú Zhōng:
"The weather is hot,
and the enemy now holds a strong position,
making it difficult to attack and capture,
only exhausting our forces.
I wish to conserve our energy and rest the troops,
awaiting an opportunity to act;
what do you think?"
Zhōng replied:
"Not so.
Previously, we spread word that the main force would take the inner waters,
so Qiáo Dàofú dared not leave Fú.
Now, with our heavy troops suddenly appearing,
catching them off guard,
Hóu Huī and his men are already terrified.
Huī's defensive troops,
are not firmly entrenched.
If we attack while they are fearful,
the situation makes them easy to overcome.
Once we take Péngmó,
and advance with drums beating,
Chéngdū will be unable to hold."
If we delay our troops and remain locked in stalemate,
our true situation will be revealed.
Once the Fú army returns,
it will be difficult to resist them.
If we advance but cannot fight,
and retreat without supplies,
over twenty thousand men will all become captives of the Shǔ forces."
He followed this advice.
The next day they attacked,
and were victorious in all engagements,
beheading Hóu Huī.
Thereupon they advanced and captured various cities,
where the city defenses crumbled one after another,
and Zòng hanged himself. .
Yáo Hóng usurped the throne in the Western Capital,
and Gāozǔ campaigned to pacify him,
capturing Hóng.
After Gāozǔ had destroyed Qín,
he entered Cháng'ān,
leaving his son Yìzhēn to guard Cháng'ān,
while he returned to Jiāngnán.
At that time, Hèlián was ruling over Tǒngwàn,
and upon hearing this, he was greatly pleased,
saying to Wáng Mǎidé:
"I plan to advance and take Cháng'ān;
you, try to outline a strategy for the campaign."
Mǎidé replied:
"Liú Yù destroyed Qín,
which is what is called using chaos to quell chaos.
He has not implemented benevolent governance to aid the common people.
Guānzhōng is a strategically vital location,
yet he entrusts it to someone of limited talent and shallow wisdom—
this is not a long-term plan.
The reason he hurriedly returned
is that he seeks to hasten his usurpation,
with no time to care for the capital.
Your Majesty, by marching against the rebels in the name of righteousness,
has justice that resonates through both the hidden and visible realms.
The people look to Your Majesty’s banners and drums as if they were your command,
waiting as if each day were a year.
Qīngní and Shàngluò
are key passages for the southern troops;
we should deploy mobile forces there
to cut off their routes of advance and retreat.
Then cross Tóngguān,
block Xiáoxiá,
and sever their water and land routes.
Issue a proclamation to Cháng'ān,
spreading news of your benevolent grace,
and the people of the three adjacent regions will welcome the imperial army with offerings of food and drink.
Yìzhēn will be left sitting alone in an empty city,
with nowhere to flee.
Within ten days, he is sure to be captured under your command.
This is what is called winning without shedding blood,
achieving stability without a fight."
Bóbó approved of this,
and marched south to attack Cháng'ān.
Gāozǔ grew fearful,
summoned Yìzhēn east to guard Luòyáng,
and appointed Zhū Língshí to defend Cháng'ān.
But the people of Cháng'ān expelled Língshí and welcomed Bóbó,
thus losing Guānzhōng. .
The Xiānbēi Mùróng Chāo held Qīngzhōu,
proclaiming himself King of Yān.
Gāozǔ campaigned against him,
and captured Chāo.
Earlier,
Chāo's uncle, Mùróng Dé, had usurped the three Qí regions.
After Dé's death,
Chāo succeeded his position
and began raiding north of the Huái River.
Gāozǔ, intending to focus on central affairs,
took advantage of this invasion
to launch a northern expedition against Chāo.
Grand General Gōngsūn Wǔlóu advised Chāo, saying:
"The Wú troops are swift and sharp;
it is hard to confront them head-on.
Blocking the Tàixiàn Pass to prevent their entry
is the best strategy.
Strengthening defenses and clearing the fields,
destroying the grain stores,
is the middle strategy.
Holding the city and awaiting battle
is the worst strategy."
Chāo said:
"Let them cross the Tàixiàn;
I will crush them with my iron cavalry—
they will be captured.
Why clear the fields
and weaken ourselves?"
When first planning this campaign,
an advisor said:
"If the enemy does not heavily guard the Tàixiàn,
but instead fortifies Guǎnggù,
holding it without emerging,
our army will have no supplies;
how can we sustain ourselves?"
Gāozǔ said:
"Not so.
The Xiānbēi are greedy by nature,
and their planning lacks foresight.
They revel in their victories
and cherish their grain.
They think our army is isolated
and cannot last long,
so they will surely lure us in,
appearing to take the battle lightly.
Once our army enters the Tàixiàn,
what have I to worry about?"
After crossing the Tàixiàn,
with the enemy army yet to emerge,
Gāozǔ joyfully said:
"Heaven is aiding us!"
The officers asked:
"The battle is not yet won;
why are you pleased, my lord?"
Gāozǔ replied:
"Our army has passed the danger;
the soldiers have the will to fight to the death.
Grain remains in the fields,
so the army has no supply worries.
The enemy has fallen into my trap—
victory is assured."
In the sixth month,
Mùróng Chāo sent Wǔlóu to hold Línqú,
leaving the weak and elderly to guard Guǎnggù.
Hearing the army was near,
Chāo also joined there.
Forty lǐ from Línqú lay the Jùmiè River,
and Chāo sent Wǔlóu to secure it,
saying:
"If the Jìn army reaches the water, they will be hard to defeat."
Wǔlóu raced ahead.
The vanguard Mèng Lóngfú rushed to confront him,
and vied to seize the position first.
Wǔlóu retreated.
The main force of four thousand men
divided into two wings
and advanced slowly in parallel formation.
Before reaching Línqú,
enemy cavalry arrived in force.
Lóngfú and others held them off;
as the sun tilted westward,
the battle raged on fiercely.
Gāozǔ said to Tán Sháo and others:
"The enemy's elite troops are all here;
the defenders in Línqú must be few and weak.
You take a covert force around their rear—
if you go, you will surely take the city.
Set up many banners and flags;
this is how Hán Xìn captured Zhào.
Moreover, I earlier mentioned troops coming by sea;
we must make a show of it."
Sháo and others advanced with drums beating.
The enemy saw them and said:
"The naval force has arrived!"
Chāo abandoned the city and fled,
and they captured it.
Upon hearing the city had fallen,
the enemy grew fearful and dared not move.
Gāozǔ personally beat the drums,
and all the soldiers were inspired,
routing the enemy completely.
Chāo fled to Guǎnggù;
they advanced and besieged it.
When the city fell, they captured Chāo,
brought him to the capital,
and executed him in the Jiànkāng market. .
The rebel Lú Xún held Nánhǎi,
and taking advantage of Gāozǔ's northern expedition against Yān,
he attacked Jiànyè in its undefended state.
Gāozǔ returned
and pacified him.
Liú Yì held Jīngzhōu
and turned against Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ sent a general to campaign against him,
and Yì was executed.
Péi Zǐyě commented:
"Among the allies under the righteous banner,
none could preserve both their achievements and reputation—
why is that?
They only saw the swiftness of the initial successes,
without understanding the hardships of establishing a royal enterprise.
They were quick to step forward,
