seeking only their own gain;
while we eradicated the multitude of villains,
how could we have wronged anyone?
Liú Xīlè and Zhūgě Chángmíng were both outstanding men;
how could they have been ignorant of Heaven's mandate?
Or was it the circumstances that led them so?
Had they lived longer,
would their lineages have endured?
How admirable!
When King Wǔ founded the Zhōu,
eight hundred feudal lords gathered together,
saying:
He was summoned back to the capital.
Emperor Sòng Míngdì suspected the Duke lacked the appearance of a subordinate,
and rumors circulated among the people that the Duke would become the Son of Heaven,
deepening his suspicions.
When first summoned,
his subordinates advised against compliance,
but the Duke said:
"The sovereign has executed his own brothers
to secure the throne for his young and weak heir—
a plan for his legacy.
What does this have to do with other clans?
We must act swiftly;
delay would arouse suspicion.
Kinsmen slaughtering one another
is no sign of enduring fortune;
troubles are just beginning,
and I shall join forces with you all."
He was appointed Regular Attendant.
When Emperor Míng died,
his will ordered the Duke and Yuán Càn to jointly handle state affairs.
The Prince of Guìyáng, Liú Xiūfàn, Governor of Jiāngzhōu, raised troops in rebellion,
and the Duke suppressed it.
Initially,
when Xiūfàn rebelled,
the court was terrified.
The Duke, with Chǔ Yǎnhuí,
gathered at the Central Secretariat to deliberate,
but none dared speak.
The Duke said:
"Past rebellions from the upper reaches
all failed due to delays.
Xiūfàn will surely learn from past mistakes,
descending swiftly with light forces
to catch us unprepared.
I request to garrison at Xīntíng
to confront his vanguard."
He then took a brush to write his proposal,
and all others concurred.
He rode out in a simple carriage, dressed in plain clothes, to Xīntíng.
Before the fortifications were complete,
rebel cavalry arrived in force.
He removed his outer garments and lay down calmly,
steadying the troops' morale,
and ultimately defeated them.
He was promoted to Central Army Commander.
Emperor Cāngwú deeply distrusted him.
Once when the Duke was napping naked,
exposed,
Emperor Cāngwú led dozens of riders straight into the Commander's residence,
stood the Duke in the courtyard,
drew a target on his belly,
and drew his bow to full draw to shoot.
His attendant Yáng Yùfū advised:
"The Commander's large belly
is a fine target,
but one arrow would kill him,
leaving none for later shots.
Better use blunted arrows."
One arrow struck the navel,
and Cāngwú threw his bow to the ground. ,
He often told his attendant Yáng Yùfū:
"Watch for the Weaving Maid's crossing,
and report to me."
That night was the Qīxī Festival,
and Yùfū, in fear,
took a dagger and killed him.
Yùfū conspired with Wáng Jìngzé
to assassinate Cāngwú.
They delivered the head to the Commander's residence to inform the Duke.
The Duke donned military attire
and entered the palace that night.
At dawn,
he summoned Yuán Càn and others to deliberate.
As Càn began to speak,
the Duke's hair and beard bristled,
his eyes flashing like lightning.
Jìngzé drew his sword and leaped,
shouting to the crowd:
"All matters under heaven shall be decided by Lord Xiāo!
Whoever dares utter a word
shall stain Jìngzé's blade!"
He then took a white gauze cap and placed it on the Duke's head,
urging him to ascend the throne immediately.
Saying:
"We must strike while the iron is hot."
The Duke sternly replied:
"You truly do not understand."
The Duke then welcomed and installed Emperor Shùndì.
Shěn Yōuzhī, Governor of Jīngzhōu, rebelled,
and the Duke suppressed him.
Initially,
Yōuzhī claimed to act on the Empress Dowager's order
to march on the capital.
Yuán Càn and Liú Bǐng, uneasy about the Duke's growing prestige,
felt threatened,
conspired with Yōuzhī,
and plotted action within the palace.
The Duke ordered Wáng Jìngzé to execute them inside the palace.
He was promoted to Imperial Chancellor,
enfeoffed as Duke of Qí,
and granted the Nine Bestowments.
The proclamation read:
"We, having encountered misfortune,
early faced calamities.
The succeeding ruler lacked virtue,
unrecorded in annals,
defied the Five Elements,
slaughtered the nine clans,
exhausting divine favor,
as seas raged and chaos spread.
The peril of a dangling crown
pales in comparison—
beyond the laments in 'Xiǎo Wǎn'
or 'Shǔ Lí'!
Heaven aided the Imperial Sòng,
revealing a brilliant minister.
In our solitude and ignorance,
we inherited the great enterprise,
your lofty merit and supreme virtue
unparalleled in antiquity.
Even Bǎo Héng assisting Yīn
or Bó Lù upholding Hàn
pale before you.
Now we confer the ceremonies upon you;
reverently accept our mandate.
Previously, Yuán and Liú sowed disaster,
with many followers.
Zǐfáng turned disloyal,
raising troops to join the rebellion,
leaving the palace precincts
nearly overgrown with weeds,
the state
torn by enmity.
At that time,
none held steadfast resolve.
You shook your sleeves to face the crisis,
soaring with fervor.
Mounting war chariots to clear the path,
bearing the golden tally as vanguard.
Once your banners advanced,
the rebels melted like ice.
This laid the foundation of hegemon's work,
the start of royal rescue.
Ān Dū betrayed,
usurping Xú Province,
daring to lead his rabble
across the Huái River.
Suǒ'ér, foolish and perverse,
joined forces in evil,
heaven granting no courage,
turning his back on duty for rebellion,
plunging the northern people
into misery and ruin.
You, charged by the ancestral temples,
with loyalty bright as the sun,
held command at the army gates,
your spirit soaring past the skies;
in the victory of breaking cauldrons,
corpses piled the fields;
at the battle of Shíliáng,
you beheaded their leaders;
securing borders, preserving lives,
Jiāngyáng was pacified.
This again is your merit.
Zhāng Yān, deluded and blind,
disregarded the court,
from the southern regions
plotting against the eastern realm,
sneaking troops secretly,
coveting unprepared lands.
Then the river regions were unsettled,
the imperial way repeatedly blocked.
You, loyal and righteous, aroused,
shone brighter in peril;
with few mastering many,
all directions bowed like grass.
The court had no eastern worries,
Mǐnyuè hoped for deliverance.
This again is your merit.
The Xiōngnú, with wild ambitions,
invaded our borders,
the vile Jié running rampant,
their force shaking Péng and Sì.
You, bearing orders to punish crimes,
set out at dawn's call,
as armies first clashed,
the ominous airs were swept away,
mourning the dead, aiding the wounded,
spreading widely the imperial grace,
so our Huái and Féi
again knew flourishing rule,
this again is your merit.
From then on,
the Xiǎnyǔn grew fiercely aggressive,
like giant boars and long serpents,
When you again looked upon the capital,
the situation remained as before,
the army was already weary,
yet with high-walled corner cities and strong fortifications,
they were destined to fall soon.
You spoke of royal duties,
worked fervently forgetting meals,
personally donned armor,
viewing dangers as level ground,
demarcated borders and boundaries,
opening up Qīng and Yǎn,
this again was your achievement.
Guìyáng relied on its multitude,
lightly questioned the Nine Tripods,
tearing crowns and destroying coronets,
uprooting the base and blocking the source,
fierce fires burned in the royal city,
flying arrows gathered at the lord's house,
all the nobles were anxious and fearful,
the main army had no leader,
you drew your sword and focused your spirit,
then devised unparalleled strategies;
grasping the banner and directing the troops,
you turned cowards into brave men,
within a couple of days,
Xuānyáng was pacified,
this again was your achievement.
Cāngwú ran rampant,
all under heaven was in turmoil,
indulging in cruel punishments for pleasure,
who then was without guilt?
The common people mourned together,
not knowing if they'd see the next morning,
the enterprise of Gāozǔ had already fallen,
who would inherit the path of civilization?
You looked back to the principles of Yīn and Hàn,
followed closely the statutes of Wèi and Jìn,
humbly with your modest self,
entered to serve the ancestral temples,
the seven temples were purified and tranquil,
the nine regions returned to governance,
this again was your achievement.
Yuán and Liú harbored disloyalty,
creating this step toward chaos,
secretly plotting wicked schemes,
crises brewing closely,
occupying Shítóu,
intending to assault the main roads,
you internally devised divine plans,
externally raised frosty blades,
calamities were thereby cleared,
the state's path became harmonious and serene,
this again was your achievement.
Shěn Yōu concealed disaster,
growing more evident over the years,
with the eyes of a bee and voice of a jackal,
relying on force and embracing cruelty,
turning his gaze westward,
distantly akin to foreign lands,
yet as governance was just beginning,
the nine punishments had not been fully applied,
he prolonged his evil without reform,
thus unleashing his vicious rebellion,
you, bearing the battle-axe, marched beyond the pass,
concentrating awe in the river regions,
your upright heart shone as bright as the sun,
your clear strategies vied with autumn clouds in brilliance,
moved by the utmost righteousness,
men multiplied their hearts a hundredfold,
the long-accumulated fugitive from punishment,
was publicly executed in a single morning,
the Xiāng River flowed peacefully,
Zhāngtái followed the proper course,
this again was your achievement.
You have the merit of aiding all under heaven,
augmented with wisdom,
your way protects the living beings,
your will supports the cosmos,
exerting strength and dedicating your heart,
toiling diligently for the royal house,
through dangers and hardships,
you have fully experienced them.
As for the diligence in establishing the ancestral temples,
the grace of initiating creation's materials,
like clouds spreading and mist dispersing,
light reaches the six hidden directions,
assisting me, the one person,
in eternally purifying the four seas.
Distant regions knock at the gates admiring righteousness,
remote territories come to court through repeated translations.
Vast and far-reaching,
it cannot be named. 」 .
In the fourth month,
the Sòng emperor abdicated the throne to Qí.
On Jiǎwǔ day,
he ascended the emperor's throne at the southern suburb,
offering a burnt sacrifice to heaven
saying:
"The emperor, your subject Dàochéng,
dares to use a black bull,
to solemnly announce to the great august sovereign emperor.
Since the beginning of living beings,
rulers have been established to govern them,
in order to elucidate the ultimate and emulate heaven,
initiate the origin and create things,
unfolding this great way,
the mandate is not constant.
In the past, during Yú and Xià, they received the mandate from the previous era;
from Hàn and Wèi,
they yielded the throne in the middle periods.
All are brilliantly recorded in the records,
and preserved in the canonical documents.
The virtue of water was in decline,
successive generations faced many troubles,
indeed relying on Dàochéng's merit of rescue and correction,
to broadly save them from their difficulties,
the great creation was on the verge of collapse,
again he structured the realm,
truly it was heaven and man,
none were not in harmony,
thus looking up to accord with the returning cycle,
clearly belonging to the capable,
hence gathering the great mandate here,
the virtue of Shùn is not to be inherited,
reaching through multiple successions,
yet all the dukes, ministers, and officials,
the various officers and administrators,
extending to the common worthies,
and even all the tribes,
all said:
'The great heaven shows favor and mandate,
it cannot be firmly opposed;
humans and spirits lack a ruler,
they cannot long be without a lord.
Fearing the majesty of heaven,
how dare we not reverently comply with the great calendar,
respectfully choose an auspicious dawn,
devoutly uphold the imperial tally,
ascend the altar to receive the abdication,
announce the category to the high heaven,
to respond to the people's hearts,
and spread this to all states,
may the bright spirits enjoy this offering.' ,
After the ceremony concluded,
he prepared the imperial carriage and proceeded to the Jiànkāng Palace,
presided over the Great Ultimate Front Hall,
issued a great amnesty and changed the era name.
In the fourth year of the Jiànyuán era, he passed away,
and the crown prince Zé was established
as Shìzǔ, the Martial Emperor.
Upon his death,
the eldest grandson Zhāoyè was established
as King Yùlín.
He ascended the throne without virtue,
when the coffin of Emperor Wǔ was lowered to the islet,
the emperor bid farewell inside the Duān Gate,
then the hearse carriage entered the pavilion,
and immediately he had Hu musicians perform,
so Gāozōng had him killed. .
Upon his death,
his younger brother Zhāowén was established
but was deposed as the Hǎilíng King.
After his deposition,
the Marquis of Xīchāng, Luán, was established
as Gāozōng, the Emperor Míng.
He was the son of Dào Shēng, the Prince of Shǐ'ān Zhēn.
Upon ascending the throne, he frequently carried out executions,
and moreover lay ill for years,
preparing the site for his coffin in advance,
thus the sons of Gāo and Wǔ were swept away entirely. .
Upon his death,
the crown prince Bǎojuǎn was established
as the Dōng Hūn Marquis,
who upon accession was brutal and tyrannical,
having golden flowers pasted on the ground,
he made Consort Pān walk on them,
saying:
"This is 'each step produces a lotus flower.' "
Also, he made a market in the garden,
acting himself as the market officer,
with Consort Pān as the market director.
When the righteous army arrived,
he was killed by his attendants.
Upon his death,
the Peaceful Emperor Bǎoróng was established,
the eighth son of Emperor Míng.
He abdicated the throne to Liáng.
Previously,
Crown Prince Wénhuì together with a talented person composed a seven-character poem,
each line ending with the word 'sorrow',
which proved true for the Peaceful Emperor.
In the Dōng Hūn Marquis's palace, they made the 'scattered rebellion' chignon,
with the roots reversed backward.
During the Dōng Hūn Marquis's time,
all under heaven scattered and rebelled.
Also, they established the 'standing hat',
It opens its beak and spreads its two wings,
named:
"The Phoenix Crosses Three Bridges."
Tearing the skirt backward,
tying it together,
named:
"The Reverse-Tied Yellow Oriole."
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's residence was at Three Bridges,
and the phoenix crossed it.
This was an omen of the phoenix's flight.
The Yellow Oriole,
with Huáng Lí representing the sun,
being tied in reverse,
was a response to Dōng Hūn's execution.
Before this,
the common people and court officials filled their chests with silk,
each saying:
"Borrowed rain."
"Borrowed"
is not the proper term.
Storing rain and borrowing it,
clearly means not obtaining the real thing.
Dōng Hūn was killed,
and his son was deposed to commoner status,
reflecting the meaning of stored rain.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Liáng, named Yǎn,
surnamed Xiāo,
served as the legal officer to the Prince of Bālíng,
later becoming one of the Eight Friends of Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglíng.
Initially,
when his deceased father passed away,
he was discontent,
and by the time Yùlín lost virtue,
Emperor Míng of Qí acted as regent,
planning to depose and establish a ruler,
the Emperor intended to assist Emperor Míng of Qí,
to overthrow the heirs of Emperor Wǔ of Qí,
to cleanse his heart of shame.
Emperor Míng of Qí also knew this,
often conspiring with the Emperor.
At that time, Emperor Míng of Qí was about to pursue the Prince of Suí,
fearing he would not comply.
Also, with Wáng Jìngzé in Kuàijī,
he feared a rebellion.
He asked the Emperor,
who said:
"Although the Prince of Suí has a good reputation,
in reality, he is mediocre and inferior,
lacking wise strategists,
his only claws and teeth rely on Sima Yuán Lìshēng and Biàn Báilóng, the governor of Wǔlíng.
These men only seek profit.
If offered prominent positions,
they will rush to serve.
The Prince of Suí only needs a simple letter to be subdued.
Jìngzé's ambition lies in Jiāngdōng,
seeking wealth and honor to the fullest,
it is fitting to select beautiful women to delight his heart."
Emperor Míng of Qí said:
"That is my thought as well."
It indeed went according to his strategy.
When the Wèi general Wáng Sù attacked Sīzhōu,
the Emperor defeated him,
and for his merit, was enfeoffed as the Baron of Jiànkāng Commandery.
Emperor Míng of Qí passed away,
and Dōng Hūn ascended the throne.
The posthumous edict appointed the Emperor as the military governor
and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
During Dōng Hūn's time,
Liú Xuān and five others took turns on duty in the palace,
issuing decrees on alternate days,
known to the world as the "Six Nobles."
There were also eight men like the Imperial Guards,
called:
"The Eight Essentials."
They all arbitrarily spoke the king's words,
wielding state power as they pleased.
The Emperor said to Zhāng Hóngcè:
"With governance coming from multiple sources,
chaos is its stepping stone.
To avoid calamity now,
only this place offers refuge,
diligently practicing benevolence and righteousness,
one can sit and become like the Earl of the West;
but with my younger brothers in the capital,
I fear they may suffer from the times' troubles,
we must plan this with Yìzhōu."
At that time, the Emperor's eldest brother, Yì, had been dismissed from Yìzhōu,
returning to administer Yǐngzhōu affairs,
the Emperor conspired with him,
but he did not agree,
and was soon killed.
With the eldest brother Yì killed,
the Emperor raised an uprising.
He summoned his staff to the main hall,
announcing the raising of troops,
that day the command standard was erected.
Previously, Dōng Hūn had appointed Liú Shānyáng as the governor of Bāxī,
sending him through Jīngzhōu to carry out duties,
with Xiāo Yǐngzhòu to attack Xiāngyáng,
the Emperor knew of this plot,
so he sent Wáng Tiānwǔ to Jiānglíng,
delivering letters to all the provincial officials,
discussing military affairs.
Once Tiānwǔ had departed,
the Emperor said to Hóngcè:
"Today, we sit back and reap the empire.
When Jīngzhōu receives Tiānwǔ,
they will surely be panicked and without a plan,
if they do not align with us,
taking them will be as easy as picking up mustard.
Cut off the Three Gorges,
occupy Bāshǔ,
send troops to secure Xiāngzhōng,
and we will fully control the upper reaches.
With this formidable reputation,
facing the Jiǔ Pài,
severing Pénglí,
issuing proclamations to Jiāngnán,
like wind bending grass,
it is not enough to compare.
It merely delays the matter slightly.
Jiānglíng originally fears the people of Xiāngyáng,
plus with lips gone, teeth feel cold,
they surely will not stand alone,
how can they not align with us?
With the troops of Jīng and Yōng,
sweeping and securing the eastern lands,
even Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ reborn,
could not devise a counter,
let alone an uncalculating foolish ruler,
employing the likes of imperial guards and decree-followers?"
When Shānyáng reached Bālíng,
the Emperor again ordered Tiānwǔ to deliver letters to the Yǐng and Zhòu brothers.
After he left,
the Emperor said to Zhāng Hóngcè:
"The way of using troops:
attacking the heart is superior,
attacking cities is secondary;
psychological warfare is superior,
armed combat is secondary.
Today is such a case."
Recently, I sent Tiānwǔ to the provincial government,
everyone had letters,
but this time only two were for the acting brothers,
all to be conveyed orally by Tiānwǔ.
When questioned,
Tiānwǔ would say nothing.
Tiānwǔ is the trusted aide of the acting officer,
upon hearing this,
they will think the acting brothers are hiding the matter together,
causing everyone to become suspicious.
Shānyáng, confused by the many voices,
will judge them as distrustful,
and if distrustful, the acting officer will have no way to justify his actions,
thus sending two empty letters,
secures one province.
When Shānyáng reached Jiāng'ān,
indeed, his suspicions did not cease.
Yǐng and Zhòu then beheaded Tiānwǔ,
sent him to Shānyáng,
who believed it.
Upon reaching Jīngzhōu,
he rushed into the city,
about to cross the threshold when the hanging gate
sprang shut, breaking his carriage axle,
and he abandoned the cart to flee.
Chén Xiù drew his halberd and pursued him,
killing him outside the gate.
Yǐng and Zhòu immediately sent a courier to deliver his head to the Emperor,
still honoring the Prince of Nányáng with the imperial title,
and reported in discussion:
"The timing is unfavorable,
we must wait until next February."
The Emperor replied:
"Now we have a hundred thousand armored troops sitting idle,
supplies depleting daily.
If we stall for a hundred days,
regrets are sure to arise.
Moreover, Venus appears in the west,
we act upholding righteousness,
with heavenly timing and human strategy,
what is unfavorable?
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he acted against the Year Star,
did he need to wait for the next year?"
The Emperor did not comply,
and thus grandly declared his reign.
On Wùshēn,
the Emperor set out from Xiāngyáng.
The Emperor left his younger brother to guard Xiāngyáng city,
saying to him:
"Place your heart in the hearts of the Xiāngyáng people,
trust them with sincerity,
do not doubt,
under one sky, we are a family,
we shall meet again."
The cities of Yǐng and Lǔ and all the generals surrendered.
Initially,
They established the disciple Qiàn
as Emperor Wén of the Ancestral Lineage.
Upon his demise,
the crown prince Bó Zōng was enthroned
as the Deposed Emperor.
After his deposition,
Xū was established
as Emperor Xuān of the High Ancestral Lineage,
the second son of the illustrious Prince of Shǐxīng. .
Upon his demise,
the crown prince Shū Bǎo was enthroned,
known as the Duke of Chángchéng.
While Shū Bǎo was in the Eastern Palace,
he was studious and skilled in literature.
But upon ascending the throne,
he indulged in wine and women,
with fifty sycophants wearing sable tail ornaments at his side,
and over a thousand women of great beauty in luxurious attire.
He often had eight consorts, including Lady Kǒng, seated beside him,
with Jiǎng Zǒng, Kǒng Fàn, and ten others joining the feasts,
dubbed
"Companions of Intimacy."
First, he had the eight women fold colorful paper,
compose poems in five-character lines,
and the ten guests would immediately respond in verse,
with delays punished by drinking.
Ruler and ministers drank to excess,
from dusk till dawn.
This became their routine.
When Emperor Wén of Suí first received the abdication from Zhōu,
he maintained friendly relations with neighbors.
After Emperor Xuān's demise,
he sent envoys to offer condolences,
observing the rites between rival states,
addressing himself by name and bowing in his letters.
However, the later lord was arrogant and extravagant,
ending his letter with:
"I hope all is well within your realm,
and the universe is peaceful."
Emperor Wén of Suí was displeased,
showing it to his court officials.
Hè Ruò Bì, Yáng Sù, and others considered it an insult to their sovereign,
bowed twice to ask for forgiveness,
and requested a punitive expedition.
Emperor Wén said:
"As a parent to the people,
how can I be hindered by a mere strip of water and not rescue them?"
He ordered the construction of warships.
Someone advised secrecy,
but Emperor Wén said:
"I will openly carry out Heaven's punishment,
what need is there for secrecy?
Let us throw wood chips into the river;
if they can reform,
what more could I ask for!" ,
He appointed Prince Guǎng of Jìn as marshal,
overseeing eighty commanders for the expedition.
Initially,
the Suí army distributed proclamations,
exposing the later lord's evils,
on three hundred thousand sheets of paper,
spreading them throughout Jiāngdōng.
As the armies advanced down the river,
frontier forts reported one after another,
but Shěn Kèqīng, in charge of confidential matters,
suppressed the news.
When the Suí army reached the river,
the later lord said:
"The royal aura is here;
the Qí army came three times,
the Zhōu army twice,
and all were defeated.
Now that the invaders have come,
they will surely defeat themselves."
He continued indulging in wine and composing poems without cease.
The Suí forces advanced, capturing Gūshú,
or cutting off the route at Qū'ē,
so he issued an edict:
"The rabid dogs and sheep run wild,
encroaching upon the suburbs;
even wasps and scorpions have venom,
it is time to sweep them clean."
He appointed Xiāo Móhē as Grand Governor of the Imperial Domain,
deploying troops to guard key points,
with monks, nuns, and Taoist priests
all conscripted for labor.
The Suí army advanced from both north and south,
and the various forces were defeated. .
Hán Qínghǔ entered through the southern side gate,
civil and military officials all fled,
and he captured the later lord.
As the Suí troops entered,
the Vice Director Yuán Xiàn advised sitting upright in the hall,
awaiting them with dignity.
The later lord said:
"Under their blades,
we cannot confront them;
I have my own plan."
He then hid in a well,
and the Suí soldiers pulled him up with a rope,
surprised by his weight,
only to find he was with Consort Zhāng and Lady Kǒng, coming up together.
Emperor Wén of Suí was astonished to hear this.
Bào Hóng replied:
"The Eastern Well constellation corresponds to Qín in astronomy,
which is now where the royal capital lies.
His jumping into the well
must be Heaven's will."
Earlier, in Jiāngdōng, many sang Wáng Xiànzhī's "Song of Peach Leaves,"
saying:
"Peach leaf, oh peach leaf,
cross the river without an oar.
Just cross and fear no hardship,
I will come to welcome you."
When Prince Guǎng of Jìn stationed his army at Liùhé Fort,
the mountain there was named "Peach Leaf,"
and indeed, they crossed using Chén's boats. .
Prince Guǎng of Jìn entered and occupied the capital city,
sending the later lord to the Eastern Palace.
On the third month, Guǐsì day,
the later lord and his officials departed from Jiànyè,
heading to Cháng'ān.
Upon reaching the capital,
they formed ranks with carriages and robes,
leading the later lord and nobles.
An edict was read reprimanding the later lord,
who held his breath, unable to reply.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chángchéng.
When Emperor Wén of Suí toured east,
ascending Mount Máng,
the later lord attended a banquet,
composing a poem:
"The sun and moon glorify heavenly virtue,
mountains and rivers enhance the imperial abode.
In this peace, I've nothing to repay,
but wish to present a petition for the eastern sacrifice."
After he left,
Emperor Wén of Suí watched him go, saying:
"Was his defeat not due to poetry and wine?
Had he used the effort spent on poetry
to ponder state affairs, how much better!" .
By the fourth year of Rénshòu,
he died in Luòyáng.
Earlier,
birds on Jiǎngshān flapped their wings and beat their breasts, crying:
"What to do, Emperor,
what to do, Emperor."
When the later lord was in the Eastern Palace,
a one-legged bird
gathered in his courtyard,
using its beak to draw characters on the ground.
They read:
"One foot ascends the high terrace,
lush grass turns to ash.
To know where my home lies,
a red gate opens by the water."
Interpreters thought "one foot" meant the later lord would act alone without support,
"lush grass" indicated decay and neglect.
Suí inherited the fire element,
so grass meeting fire turns to ash.
When he reached the capital,
he resided at the Dūshuǐ Terrace,
which was the "high terrace by water."
A man from Kuàijī, Shǐ Pǔ, once dreamed of a man in red robes,
with a military cap descending from the sky,
holding a golden plaque.
Pǔ went to look,
and the text read:
"The Chén house, five rulers,
thirty-four years."
When Chén fell,
it was just as in the dream.
A late Liáng nursery rhyme said:
"Alas, the child of the Bā horse,
travels a thousand lǐ in a day.
No longer see the lad on horseback,
only the yellow dust rising.
The yellow dust soils people's clothes,
皂荚 awaits to bury them."
After Wáng Sēngbiǎn's defeat,
officials reported the rhyme,
noting Sēngbiǎn rode a Bā horse to attack Hóu Jǐng.
"The lad on horseback"
signifies the character for 'king';
"dust" refers to Chén;
but "皂荚" was not understood.
Later, Chén was destroyed by Suí,
and interpreters said in Jiāngdōng, goat horns were called皂荚,
and the Suí surname was Yáng,
Yáng
meaning goat.
Thus, it meant final destruction by Suí.
In the late Northern Qí,
many officials in the departments were called department lords.
It speaks of the sovereign and his generals being observed and reflected upon.
Thus, the signs of rise and fall are known,
all having their omens. .
Emperor Gāozǔ of Suí, surnamed Yáng,
named Jiān,
initially served as the Prefect of Suí Province under Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu,
with his daughter as the Crown Prince's consort.
When Emperor Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne,
he was appointed as Grand Marshal.
Upon Emperor Xuān's death,
Jìng Emperor was established,
and he was advanced to the rank of Prince of Suí.
Thereupon, the throne was abdicated to him,
and the era name was changed to Kāihuáng in its first year.
In the ninth year,
Chén was pacified,
the Crown Prince Yǒng was deposed to commoner status,
and Prince Guǎng of Jìn was established as Crown Prince.
Upon Emperor Gāozǔ's death,
the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
this being Emperor Yáng.
Emperor Yáng was without virtue,
and bandits rose up like swarms.
In the thirteenth year, he traveled to Jiāngdū,
Lǐ Mì set up an altar in Gǒng,
and proclaimed himself as the Duke of Wèi.
Mì,
a native of Liáodōng,
was the son of Duke of Púshān, Kuān.
In his youth, he was free-spirited and had great ambitions,
often harboring thoughts of turmoil.
He formed a life-and-death friendship with Yáng Xuángǎn,
but Xuángǎn belittled him based on his status.
Mì angrily said:
"In deciding strategies between two battle arrays,
with fierce shouts and roars,
causing the three armies to crumble,
and seeking achievements in the moment,
I, Mì, am not as good as you;
but if it involves the long journey ahead,
driving and directing the worthy and talented,
enabling each to fulfill their potential,
you are not as good as I, Mì.
How can one belittle the scholars and officials of the world based on rank and grade?"
When Xuángǎn rebelled,
Mì joined him,
serving as his chief strategist.
After Xuángǎn's defeat,
Mì changed his name,
and fled to Zhái Ràng.
Ràng established Mì as the Duke of Wèi,
opened a headquarters,
appointed officials,
totaling over one hundred thousand people. .
Liáng Shīdū occupied Xià Province,
Liú Wǔzhōu killed the Governor of Tàiyuán, Wáng Gōng,
and raised troops in rebellion.
Dòu Jiàndé proclaimed himself King of Xià,
Zhū Càn proclaimed himself King of Chǔ,
and Liú Yuánjìn occupied Wú Capital.
When Emperor Yáng heard of the numerous bandits rising,
he was greatly afraid,
and sent Féng Címíng to conscript troops in the Eastern Capital.
Emperor Yáng heard that bandits were rising like swarms,
summoned his ministers to inquire,
and they all said:
"These are but rats scurrying and dogs stealing,
hardly worth worrying about."
Attendant Censor Wéi Déyù said:
"Now the empire is collapsing,
and order is greatly ruined,
yet the Vice Director of the Secretariat Yú Shìjī,
Censor-in-Chief Péi Yùn, and others,
flatter Your Majesty,
concealing the truth and not speaking.
This is like piled firewood already ablaze;
the ancestral temple will surely not receive sacrifices.
The Zhōu Shū says:
'What is continuous and unbroken
will become rivers and seas.'
Your Majesty must not take these flattering words lightly."
Then an edict was issued for Féng Címíng to go to the Eastern Capital to conscript troops,
intending to campaign against Mì,
but he was captured by patrols,
and taken to Lǐ Mì.
When Mì heard of Címíng's arrival,
he was greatly pleased,
and said to Címíng:
"Heaven is not partial,
but supports only virtue.
The sovereign's poison flows throughout the land,
known to all under heaven.
I, Mì, have gathered the common people,
intent on pacifying the realm.
Warriors like bears and panthers
number over a million.
We hold the grain of Áocāng,
and possess the strategic terrain of Chénggāo,
with well-trained weapons,
and sturdy armor.
We could divert the Eastern Sea to flow west,
or kick Mount Tài to topple east.
With this to resist enemies,
what enemy cannot be crushed?
With this to attack cities,
what city cannot be taken?
The Eastern Capital is in critical danger,
and will surrender any day now.
I hope you will consider slightly
and join in achieving merit and fame."
Címíng said:
"The Duke of Púshān had his name recorded in service to the late emperor,
reaching the highest position at court.
You do not think of the grace that made us,
but instead harbor intentions of rebellion and betrayal,
abandoning the great virtue of the Suí dynasty,
and embracing the stubborn defiance of the rebellious,
accumulating evils until disasters overflow,
with defeat following swiftly,
like a net missing a giant fish,
leading to this day.
In the past, Jù Jūn with all the forces of the empire
was defeated by Emperor Guāngwǔ;
Chǔ Dùn with the armies of Jiāngdōng
was exhausted by Emperor Míng.
You, with a ragtag force
not exceeding several thousand,
arrogant and aggressive like wolves and owls,
tyrannizing villages and forts.
Heaven supports only virtue;
what part do you have in it!"
Mì then imprisoned him in the Minister over the Masses' office,
but Címíng secretly sent someone to the Eastern Capital;
the matter was discovered,
and Zhái Ràng killed him. .
An edict ordered the Duke of Táng, named [Lǐ Yuān], to guard Tàiyuán.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Duke of Táng raised righteous troops,
honoring Emperor Yáng from afar as Retired Emperor,
and established the Acting Prince Yòu as Son of Heaven,
following the precedents of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng.
They issued proclamations throughout the land,
and upon hearing, responses echoed.
This was the strategy of Péi Jì and Yīn Kāishān;
the Acting Prince Yòu was at the Western Capital at the time. .
In the autumn, seventh month,
the Duke of Táng planned to advance west toward Cháng'ān,
wielding white banners,
and pledged to his forces in the wilderness of Tàiyuán,
with thirty thousand armored troops.
He left his son Yuánjí to guard Tàiyuán.
The righteous army encamped at Huò County,
where the Suí General Sòng Lǎoshēng resisted them.
At that time, continuous rain did not cease,
supply routes were cut off,
and rumors spread that the Turks would attack Tàiyuán.
The Duke of Táng feared,
and ordered a retreat.
Following the advice of the Prince of Qín,
he stopped.
The Prince of Qín advised:
"The tyrant runs rampant,
the empire collapses and scatters,
with wolves looking back and bees swarming,
spanning provinces and counties.
Men cannot plow and sow,
women cannot weave and spin.
Thus, we took up arms in Fén and Jìn,
raised banners over the land of Shēn,
to slay the great boar and pacify the myriad people,
and kill the giant fish to cleanse the four seas.
Holding the strategic lands of Xiáo and Hán,
wielding the authority of the Son of Heaven,
we command the feudal lords,
and stabilize the empire.
Therefore, upon hearing, responses echo,
and people join us as if returning home.
Now, encountering a minor enemy,
you wish to turn back the banners.
I fear the righteous army will disband overnight,
and the great cause will be lost.
If the situation cannot be preserved,
and we retreat to guard Tàiyuán,
then we are but bandits in a single city,
and I fear before long,
calamities will arise again."
Thus, they stopped. .
Lǎoshēng arrayed his troops with the city at his back,
and in one battle, he was slain,
and Huò County was pacified.
All other cities surrendered,
only Qūtū Tōng guarding Hédōng
held firm and did not yield. .
In the winter, tenth month,
The righteous army encamped at Chánglè Palace.
Wèi Wénshēng, supporting the Prince of Dài, defended the city walls.
In the eleventh month,
they pacified the capital,
honored the Prince of Dài as the Son of Heaven,
and changed the era name to Yìníng.
They dispatched envoys to tour the commanderies and counties.
The Suí traveling palaces,
the Duke of Táng abolished them all.
The palace women,
he returned to their families.
Initially,
Suí generals often harassed the common people,
who suffered from it.
When the righteous army arrived,
they did not harm the people in the slightest,
and all said:
"Truly, he is our lord."
At that time, Emperor Yáng intended to go to Dānyáng,
but his ministers, generals, and soldiers were all northerners,
unwilling to move south,
and all longed to return north.
Yǔwén Huàjí, capitalizing on the people's unbearable suffering,
killed Emperor Yáng at Jiāngdū,
and the Suí imperial princes, regardless of age,
were all executed.
They established the heir Prince Hào as the Son of Heaven,
with Huàjí as chancellor.
The Emperor once dreamed of a youth in black clothes saying:
"Leaving leads to death,
staying leads to death,
better to take a boat and cross the river."
Péi Yùn and Yú Shìjī, both southerners,
supported the plan.
The generals and soldiers, unwilling to move south,
planned to poison them at a gathering,
but Princess Nányáng, fearing her husband would be killed,
informed Yǔwén Shìjí of the plot.
Shìjí told his brother Huàjí,
who then rebelled,
and seized the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"How have I wronged heaven and earth to come to this?"
Mǎ Wénjǔ replied:
"Your servant has heard:
The myriad people cannot be without a ruler,
hence a lord is established to govern them.
Thus it is known that one person nourishes the myriad people,
not the myriad people nourish one person.
Emperor Wén of the Gāo lineage possessed the lower kingdom,
greatly enhanced the imperial treasure,
abolished harsh governance,
and spread kindness and virtue.
In the south, he destroyed the powerful Chén,
in the north, he subdued the cunning barbarians.
For over twenty years,
the rivers were clear and the seas calm,
and then he passed away and ascended afar.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you distanced yourself from the state,
abandoned the capital,
toured and traveled,
with hardly a year of peace.
Transport canals connected the Hé and Luò rivers,
controlling the Jiāng and Huái regions.
The able-bodied grew weary from labor,
the old and weak exhausted from transporting supplies.
Gāo Jiǒng and Hèruò Bì,
esteemed ministers of the former court,
both accomplished in merit and virtue;
Xuē Dàohéng,
outstanding talent of the age,
a man of strategic ability,
all suffered unjustly,
and were eventually executed,
causing wise and virtuous men to withdraw,
while flattering and deceitful men rose.
Moreover, for years we campaigned against Liáo,
with conscriptions unceasing,
those who left did not return,
state resources were depleted,
white bones covered the plains,
livers and gallbladders stained the marshes.
The countless wronged souls,
having appealed to the Supreme God,
will borrow the hands of men for vengeance.
And at Yànmén,
you were humiliated by the barbarians,
and after the siege was lifted,
it was time to rest and recover,
yet you instead toured Wú and Yuè,
roaming the upper river.
Heavy taxes were levied,
to fund your travels and pleasures.
Soldiers lacked coarse clothing,
while the rear palace tired of silks;
soldiers lacked chaff and bran,
while dogs and horses were fed grain and meat;
armor bred lice,
and warhorses were never unsaddled.
You rejected advice and concealed faults,
with no intention of returning.
Thus, the nine provinces were divided like melons,
and the eight directions torn asunder.
With the wealth of all under heaven and the honor of the four seas,
once abandoned,
and you still claim to be without fault,
I secretly feel shame for Your Majesty."
Then, silently,
they strangled him. .
On the fifth month, day Wǔwǔ,
the Son of Heaven, Yòu, abdicated at a separate palace,
ceding the throne to the Táng,
who established their capital at Cháng'ān.
At the end of the Dàyè era,
a ballad said:
"The peach tree's son, Lǐ,
the great flood is far,
the Yáng mountain garden lies within the flower garden."
Lǐ,
is the surname of Táng;
the great flood,
refers to the Táng king's personal name;
Yáng,
is the surname of Suí;
the flower,
blooms but bears no fruit;
the garden,
is an enclosure,
and the Prince of Dài's name was Yòu,
Yòu sounds like enclosure.
This means that although Yáng Yòu became emperor,
ultimately the mandate had its destination,
and the Táng king would ascend to the throne. .
On day Jǐsì,
Wáng Shichōng, Duàn Dá, and others established Prince Yuè, Tǒng, as emperor in Luòyáng.
In the sixth month,
Yǔwén Huàjí went from Jiāngdū to Péngchéng,
occupied Líyáng,
and declared himself ruler.
Lǐ Mì led a large army,
fortifying Qīngqí.
When Dūnhuáng's Zhāng Shǒuyī heard that Mì was resisting Huàjí,
he advised Prince Yuè to launch a campaign.
Prince Yuè did not adopt his plan,
but followed Mèng Cóng's strategy,
forming an alliance with Mì.
Zhāng Shǒuyī argued:
"Your servant has heard:
Before the swan's wings are fully grown,
its ambition to soar to the sky has already sprouted;
before the tiger or leopard's stripes are complete,
its heart to devour an ox is already formed.
Now, Your Majesty holds the entire Zhōu territory,
with the river at your back and Luò before you,
armored troops numbering a hundred thousand,
grain supplies lasting decades,
these are the resources of a hegemon,
not a situation waiting for wings to grow or stripes to form.
To fortify the city and defend it,
without a mind to save the age,
how is it different from a colony of ants clinging to a single hole?
I dare suggest that Your Majesty should not choose this."
Prince Yuè said:
"What should be done then?"
He replied:
"The rise of the Three Sovereigns,
the actions of the Five Hegemons,
all used military force to achieve great deeds.
Thus, Xià Qǐ had the army at Gānyě,
Qí Huán raised the masses at Shàolíng,
all to campaign against the disloyal,
and punish rebels to awe the wicked.
Now the world is collapsing,
heroes are rising in competition,
and the ones posing a threat to Your Majesty's heartland,
are none other than Xià and Wèi.
If Xià sends troops across the river,
then the eastern capital will no longer be Your Majesty's land;
if Wèi sends troops across the Luò,
seizing the grain at Luòkǒu,
Your Majesty will face a peril more precarious than piled eggs,
with nothing worse to come.
I have heard:
In war, engage with the orthodox,
but win with the unorthodox.
This is how Hán Xìn defeated Chéng'ān,
and how Zǐfáng made Qín surrender.
I request selecting twenty thousand elite troops to guard Luòyáng,
and thirty thousand to guard along the river,
to prepare against Xià's aggression;
Your Majesty should personally lead a large army out of Luòkǒu,
and strike Wèi's forces by surprise,
so that Wèi's ruler and ministers think Your Majesty has descended from heaven,
and in the urgency of the moment,
even the wise will have no time to plan.
Once Lǐ Mì is destroyed,
then Jiàn Dé will be intimidated and lose heart,
Prepare to guard the frontiers,
act according to the opportune moment,
then the achievements of Emperor Wén can be cultivated,
and the foundation of Emperor Shìzǔ will not fall."
The King of Yuè said:
"We have newly received the mandate,
men and spirits are not yet attached,
military conflicts have repeatedly arisen,
fearing that the scholar-officials may disintegrate from us."
Shǒu Yī said:
"Your Majesty, with the endowment of successive sages,
inheriting the enterprise of the two founders,
even as the Xià people longed for the virtue of Yǔ,
they again supported Shào Kāng;
as the Hàn court cherished the Liú lineage,
they revered Guāng Wǔ anew.
Comparing the present with the past,
they would feel ashamed of their virtue,
moreover, Mì has three vulnerable conditions for attack,
why is that?
Initially, Mì and Zhái Ràng together raised a ragtag force,
once the great enterprise was accomplished,
Mì killed Ràng and seized his position.
The soldiers had just lost their leader,
the spirits newly lost their sacrifices.
Men and spirits are not yet attached,
this is the first.
With vast territory and numerous troops,
laws and orders are unclear,
rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
this is the second.
The elite soldiers are all resisting Qín Wáng,
those left in Gǒngluò are all aged and ill,
if we strike while they are vulnerable,
we are sure to achieve our aim,
this is the third.
The chronicles say:
'Seize the initiative from others.'
Also it says:
'Heaven's timing is not as good as earth's advantages,
earth's advantages are not as good as human harmony.'
Your Majesty possesses these three things,
and moreover holds the initiative,
there is nothing you cannot overcome."
The King was about to follow this.
Mèng Cóng said:
"Huàjí leads homesick troops,
their vanguard cannot be withstood;
Lǐ Mì is a hero,
with unparalleled courage and strategy,
without Mì, there is no one to destroy Huàjí;
and if we attack and fail,
we create another Huàjí.
I request to persuade him with interests and harms,
show him the great principle,
make him the commander,
to eliminate the ominous threat,
and deliberate further later,
it is not too late."
The King said:
"Good."
Mèng Cóng went east to persuade Mì, saying:
"You, illustrious sir, with a ragtag force,
close to the royal city,
have few who admire your virtue,
and no strongholds in mountains and marshes,
what military strategy calls 'divided and fragmented,'
is precisely what to fear!
Now in the east, there is Huàjí's army,
in the west, the forces of the eastern capital.
If you resist Huàjí in the east,
then the royal troops will attack your rear;
if you do not move against the eastern capital,
then Huàjí's army will arrive daily,
then the imperial army marches out of Luòkǒu,
Huàjí descends upon Wǔláo,
I truly fear there will be no time to maneuver,
and defeat and ruin will be upon you.
Now the emperor is the son of Shìzōng Chéngdì,
grandson of Shìzǔ Míngdì,
with the endowment of successive generations,
facing the fortune of being gladly supported,
with a million troops and horses,
holding the old capital.
Yǔwén Huàjí shows no sign of submission,
personally acting like an owl and mirror (treacherous).
The master sleeps with his weapon, awaiting dawn,
generals and soldiers conserve strength for the morning.
If you, general, can take the lead and march first,
eradicate the violent and fierce,
then you will have the security of a rock,
and not the danger of piled eggs.
Duke Wén of Jìn forgave the cut sleeve,
Duke Huán of Qí overlooked the shot hook.
Moreover, the sovereign is sage and wise by nature,
broad-minded and tolerant of all,
do not, because of past faults,
hold excessive expectations of the emperor.
A fox fur with lamb sleeves,
you, general, may choose."
Mì initially heard of Zhāng Shǒuyī's plan,
and was greatly afraid;
when Cóng arrived,
he was greatly pleased.
He sent the recorder Lǐ Jiǎn to court,
the King of Yuè was very pleased,
appointed Mì as Grand Commandant and Duke of Wèi.
Lǐ Mì, free from worries about the eastern capital,
used all his elite troops to attack Huàjí,
and defeated him.
After Mì defeated Huàjí himself,
he became even more arrogant,
the King of Yuè ordered Wáng Shìchōng to attack Mì,
Mì did not adopt Zǔ Jūnyàn's plan,
Mì's army was defeated.
He then fled west to the capital,
soon plotted rebellion,
and was killed.
When Wáng Shìchōng attacked Mì,
Mì assembled his officials to discuss it.
Péi Rénjī said:
"Shìchōng now comes with all his elite,
Luòxià must be empty,
we should just firmly hold the vital routes,
not allowing him to go east.
With thirty thousand elite troops, follow the river bend westward,
showing a threat to the eastern capital,
the eastern capital will surely be alarmed,
Shìchōng will surely rescue it.
Wait until he reaches Luò,
then return the army.
In this way,
we have surplus strength,
he is wearied from constant rushing,
as military strategy says: 'When he emerges, we return;
when he returns, we emerge;
fight repeatedly to tire him,
use many methods to mislead him.'"
Mì said:
"You know one aspect,
but not the other.
Now Shìchōng's troops have three irresistible points:
their weapons are elite,
first;
they are determined to advance deep,
second;
their food is exhausted, they seek battle,
third.
We should just defend the city firmly,
conserve strength and await the moment.
He wants to fight but cannot,
seeks to flee but has no path.
Within ten days,
this Shìchōng's head can be delivered under our banner.
What do you all think?"
Shàn Xióngxìn said:
"Using eager troops against homesick soldiers,
hunger and fullness unmatched,
battle will surely overcome."
Zǔ Jūnyàn said:
"No.
An army unjust is weary,
an army righteous is strong;
unjust means hunger,
righteous means fullness.
Shìchōng wields the Sui court's authority,
cannot be considered unjust;
our lord bears the name of rebellion,
cannot be considered righteous.
Péi Guānglù's plan,
is best for the moment;
our lord's strategy,
is best for the long term;
General Shàn's words,
are the worst leading to destruction.
Things cannot both be great,
victory has no constant support.
Thus while celebrants are at the gate,
mourners are at the door.
I truly fear that having overcome Huàjí,
we will surely be endangered by Shìchōng.
I request to lay aside arms and cease troops,
await the time and watch for discord,
Shìchōng has great ambition and strong physique,
a brave heart and much ferocity,
accustomed to self-aggrandizement,
he will surely have treacherous plans.
Within a few years,
calamity will arise.
Then, raising troops with righteousness,
responding to heaven and顺应ing to men;
making Sōng Mountain the wall,
Luò River the moat;
military officers and strong troops campaigning abroad,
civil officials and scholars guarding within.
How does this compare to seizing momentary merit,
and ruining a perfectly secure enterprise?
To take something,
first give it;
to weaken it,
must strengthen him.
To desire to take without giving,
will surely incur Heaven's punishment;
to be about to weaken without strengthening,
will surely suffer Heaven's calamity.
I hope, my lord, you temporarily give to him and strengthen him,
we will take advantage of his decline,
to fully control him afterward,
and there will be no victory not achieved. 」
Mì said:
"How wise. 」
He wished not to fight.
Wáng Bódāng and Shàn Xióngxìn said:
"When the world is peaceful and happy,
and the common people have no troubles,
cultivating literature and wielding ink,
leisurely in the court halls,
martial prowess is inferior to civil arts;
when the four seas are boiling,
and heroes compete to rise,
contending for imperial and kingly titles,
sweeping clear the ominous airs,
civil arts are inferior to martial prowess.
Each has its time,
which cannot be perverted.
The King of Yuè, in the aftermath of his debauchery and tyranny,
has long been despised by Heaven.
Moreover, the Mandate of Heaven is not constant,
and the capable replace others,
so what is there of right and wrong?
We request that quelling chaos be entrusted to military officials,
and governing peace to civil officials.
If we do not fight today,
the great cause is lost. 」
Mì then adopted Shàn Xióngxìn's strategy.
They joined battle,
and Mì's army was defeated.
Shì Chōng took advantage of the victory to advance toward Luòkǒu.
Mì's Left Chief Clerk Bǐng Yuánzhēn surrendered the granary city.
Mì fled to Hǔláo,
but did not dare enter.
He crossed the river northward,
and then fled to Táng.
Initially,
Wáng Bódāng, along with Shàn Xióngxìn and Xú Shìjì, were all generals under Mì,
known in the army as the Three Heroes.
Therefore, Mì trusted them and fought.
In the second year of the Wǔdé era of the Great Táng,
Wáng Shī killed the King of Yuè, Tóng, in Luòyáng,
usurped the imperial title,
and the Suí clan perished.
During the Liáng period, the monk Bǎo Zhì wrote:
"Lead three to approach nine,
the captive barbarian descends the hall fleeing.
Intending to travel southeast,
disaster strikes at Péngchéng's mouth. 」
This March,
a children's rhyme in Jiāngdōng said:
"How coldly the river flows,
how verdant the willows grow,
people now delight in pleasure,
yet again garrison Péngchéng. 」
Leading three to approach nine,
means twelve years;
garrison and capture,
signifies loss;
people of Wú call northerners barbarians,
west of Jiāngdū is Péngchéng Village,
the village has Péngchéng Water,
channeling its water beneath the western pavilion,
and indeed, there he was captured.
Initially,
the emperor was in Jiāngdū,
hearing of heroes rising in competition,
and all said:
"These are but mad rebels,
ultimately achieving nothing. 」
Upon hearing the righteous army had risen,
the emperor was lying down,
started up in shock and said:
"This is the one who will gain it!
Yáng Guǎng, though widely read and knowledgeable,
did not know that Lǐ (avoided name) would become Son of Heaven,
so what use was his sageliness? 」
He sighed, pressing his heart,
and after a long while lay down again,
saying:
"A true king does not die,
Heaven naturally brings it to pass. 」
Commentary says:
Gàn Bǎo stated:
"The rise of emperors and kings,
must await the Mandate of Heaven;
if there is change and succession,
it is not due to human affairs.
Yáo and Shǔn's internal abdication,
embodied civil virtue;
Hàn and Wèi's external abdication,
complied with great names;
Tāng and Wǔ's revolution,
responded to Heaven and man;
Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ's campaigns,
established merit and enterprise.
Each according to their fortune gained the world.
How great is the principle of adapting to the times. 」
Fàn Yè said:
"Since ancient times, the loss of great enterprises,
and the severance of ancestral sacrifices,
the reasons leading to decline, weakness, disaster, and defeat,
gradually have their causes.
The Three Dynasties brought disaster through favored beauties,
the Qín brought calamity through extravagance and cruelty,
the Western Hàn lost the throne due to maternal relatives,
the Eastern Hàn fell because of eunuchs. 」
The arrival of success and failure,
has long been discussed by earlier historians.
From Qín and Hàn down to Zhōu and Suí,
observing their rises and falls,
though there is fate involved,
generally, those who gained the world,
all did so by obtaining worthy and heroic men,
who promoted benefits and eliminated harms for the people;
without exception did so by employing crowds of petty men,
and through excessive luxury and waste.
Confucius said:
'Those who err due to restraint,
are few. ’
Also said:
'Keep away from flatterers,
and remove the wicked and evil. ’
How meaningful! 」
In the past, the King of Qín saw Zhōu's loss of control,
and the dissipation of power among the feudal lords,
so he relied on appointing his own men,
and did not enfeeoff feudal lords,
yet Chén Shèng, Chǔ, and Hàn all rose from commoners,
not from enfeeffed lords with land, and together destroyed Qín.
After Gāozǔ had stabilized the world,
recalling that King Xiàng entered from Hángǔ,
while he himself arrived from Wǔguān,
he only repaired passes and bridges,
strengthened defenses,
internally充实ed the three armies,
and externally posted many long-term garrisons.
When Wáng Wēng seized power,
he did not assault the passes and bridges,
but effortlessly obtained the positions.
Wáng Wēng, seeing he gained power by controlling the state and administration,
then suppressed important ministers,
and centralized power below.
When he lost it,
it also did not arise from the ministers.
Gēngshǐ, seeing Wáng Wēng lost the world by losing the people's hearts,
once he reached the western capital,
relied on people's pleased voices,
and then indulged in comfort and pleasure,
not heeding his admonishing ministers.
With Chìméi besieging from outside,
and close ministers rebelling within the city,
he was thus defeated.
From this we see,
that perils and harms are not singular,
how can one possibly prepare against them all!
Jiǎ Yì said:
"Affairs can invite disaster,
laws can give rise to treachery,
only by appointing the worthy and good,
can there then be no worries! 」
The Eighteenth Strategy: The Seven Powers
Your subject has heard:
The empire is a great vessel,
and the multitudes of people are its precious store.
A great vessel cannot be governed alone,
nor can a precious store be safeguarded by oneself.
Therefore, dividing the land into territories and boundaries
is to facilitate the establishment of feudal lords;
using closeness and distance to check each other
is to hinge upon prosperity and decline.
In the past, the Zhou dynasty, learning from two previous eras,
established five ranks of nobility,
enfeoffed eight hundred states,
fifty-five of which were of the same surname.
With deep roots and a solid foundation,
they were made unshakable.
Thus, in prosperity, the Dukes of Zhōu and Shào assisted in governance;
in decline, the Five Hegemons supported its weakness,
thereby bolstering the royal house,
and steering the course of their age.
This was the intent behind the system devised by the Three Sages
(King Wén, King Wǔ, and the Duke of Zhōu are the Three Sages).
However, the institution of enriching the lower ranks
succumbed to the flaw of the tail wagging the dog.
After the reigns of Kings Yōu and Píng,
it declined daily,
with ranks and emoluments often bestowed by subordinate ministers,
and military campaigns not initiated by the Son of Heaven.
Wú was annexed by Yuè
(King Gōujiàn of Yuè defeated Wú,
intending to relocate the King of Wú to Yǒngdōng,
granting him a hundred families to rule over.
The King of Wú said:
"I am old,
and cannot serve you."
He then took his own life.
Yuè thus annihilated Wú.),
Jìn was divided into three
(Duke Zhāo of Jìn died in his sixth year.
The six ministers sought to weaken the ducal house,
and by law exterminated the entire Yángshé clan,
dividing their cities into ten counties,
with each of the six ministers appointing their sons as grand officers.
Jìn grew weaker,
while the six ministers became powerful.
In the fourth year of Duke Āi,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ, Hán Kāngzǐ, and Wèi Huánzǐ together killed Zhì Bó,
and divided his lands entirely.
By the nineteenth year of Duke Liè,
King Wēi of Zhōu enfeoffed Zhào, Wèi, and Hán as feudal lords.
Jìn was thus extinguished.),
Zhèng was absorbed by Hán
(Duke Huán of Zhèng
was the youngest son of King Lì of Zhōu,
appointed as Minister of Education by King Yōu.
He asked Grand Historian Bó:
"The royal house is fraught with troubles;
where can I escape death?"
Grand Historian Bó replied:
"Only the eastern lands of Luò, south of the Hé and Jì rivers, are habitable."
The Duke asked:
"How so?"
He answered:
"The land is near Guó and Kuài,
whose rulers are greedy and covetous,
and the people do not support them.
Now that you are Minister of Education,
the people all love you;
I beg you to try settling there,
and the people will become your people."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
He eventually established his state there.
By the time of later ruler Yǐ,
he was destroyed by Duke Āi of Hán,
who annexed his state.
Zhèng thus perished.),
Lǔ was extinguished by Chǔ
(In the second year of Duke Qǐng of Lǔ,
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ destroyed Lǔ.
Duke Qǐng of Lǔ fled and was relocated to Biànyì,
becoming a commoner.
Lǔ thus came to an end.).
The realm was without a master,
for over forty years, becoming the "Warring States" period.
Qín, occupying a strategically advantageous position,
unleashed cunning and deceitful armies,
nibbling away at the lands east of the mountains,
which troubled the eastern states.
Sū Qín,
a man of Luòyáng,
allied the states in a vertical coalition to resist Qín;
Zhāng Yí,
a man of Wèi,
shattered the vertical alliance with a horizontal strategy.
This was the origin of the Vertical and Horizontal alliances.
It is discussed:
The "Yì Jīng" states:
"The ancient kings established ten thousand states,
and treated the feudal lords with kinship."
Confucius composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals" as a model for later generations,
criticizing the hereditary ministers for not reforming the system
of hereditary lords.
From this perspective,
the system of feudal lords
has its origins in antiquity.
Xún Yuè said:
"Enfeoffing feudal lords,
each inheriting their positions,
aims to make them regard the people as their children,
love their states as their families,
appoint worthy ministers and grand officers,
assess achievements for promotions or demotions,
granting them land but not dividing the people.
The king unifies the whole,
to oversee the governance.
Thus, if one is tyrannical in his state,
the people will rebel.
When the people rebel below,
punishment is imposed from above.
Hence, they calculate benefits and consider harms,
are encouraged by rewards and fear authority,
each striving to their utmost,
without rebellious intentions.
If the Son of Heaven loses the Way, the marquises and earls correct him;
if the royal house is weak, the great states support it.
Even without virtue,
they do not brutalize the empire,
this is how they assist in accordance with the natural order,
to guide the people."
Cáo Yuánshǒu said:
"The ancient kings knew that governing alone could not last,
so they governed together with others;
they knew that safeguarding alone could not endure,
so they safeguarded together with others.
They employed both the close and the distant,
integrating similarities and differences to advance together.
The weight of importance sufficed to check each other,
closeness and distance sufficed to protect one another.
The path to annexation was blocked,
and rebellious acts did not arise."
Lù Shìhéng said:
"To benefit others is not as good as enriching oneself;
to aid things is not as good as planning for one's own safety;
securing the ruler lies in pleasing the subjects,
and preserving oneself lies in benefiting others.
Thus, the sovereigns facing south,
each took pride in their governance;
the people within the nine domains
knew they had a fixed ruler.
The love from above
thereby emerged;
the trust from below
thereby solidified.
In times of order, it sufficed to strengthen customs;
in times of decline, it sufficed to resist tyranny.
Strong and resolute states could not monopolize the momentum of the era,
and heroic figures had no means to harbor ambitions of hegemony."
This is how the Three Dynasties upheld righteousness,
and the Four Kings established their enduring legacies.
The rise and fall, prosperity and decline,
are inherent in principle;
the preservation or loss of teachings
depends on the people.
The desire for laws hopes they will be pure,
but the bright Way sometimes dims.
Thus, the hereditary system
succumbed to the strong and overbearing;
the institution of enriching the lower ranks
leaked through the unbroken end.
The flaw of gradual weakening
began in the three declining eras;
the disaster of decline
culminated in the "Seven Hegemons."
As the saying goes,
"A large tree is bound to break, a big tail is hard to wag,"
this is the drawback of establishing feudal lords.
When Sū Qín first formed the vertical alliance,
he went to Yān.
King Wǔ of Zhōu, after stabilizing Yīn,
enfeoffed the Duke of Shào in Yān,
which later became a kingdom alongside the six states.
He persuaded Marquis Wén of Yān, saying:
"Yān has Cháoxiān and Liáodōng to the east,
Línhú and Lóufán to the north,
Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán to the west,
and the Hūtuó and Yìshuǐ rivers to the south,
covering over two thousand li in territory,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
six hundred chariots,
six thousand cavalry horses,
and grain reserves lasting for years.
To the south, you have the riches of Jiéshí and Yànmén,
and to the north, the benefits of dates and chestnuts.
Even if the people do not farm,
they have enough from the dates and chestnuts."
This is what is called a heavenly storehouse!
For living in peace and joy without troubles,
without seeing armies destroyed and generals killed,
none surpasses Yān.
Does Your Majesty know why this is so?
The reason Yān does not suffer invasion or don armor
is because Zhào serves as a shield to its south.
When Qín and Zhào exhaust each other,
and Your Majesty uses a intact Yān to control the aftermath,
this is why Yān remains free from invaders.
Moreover, when Qín attacks Yān,
it must cross Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán,
pass through Dài and Shànggǔ,
now known as Yìzhōu,
traversing thousands of miles of land.
Even if it captures Yān's cities,
Qín's plans surely cannot hold them.
Thus, Qín's inability to harm Yān is clear!
Now, when Zhào attacks Yān,
it issues orders and commands,
and within ten days,
hundreds of thousands of troops
are stationed at Dōngyuán.
Crossing the Hūtuó River,
fording the Yìshuǐ,
in less than four or five days,
they reach the capital.
Therefore, it is said:
When Qín attacks Yān,
the battle is fought a thousand miles away;
when Zhào attacks Yān,
the battle is fought within a hundred miles.
To not worry about a threat a hundred miles away,
yet fear one a thousand miles distant,
no strategy is more misguided than this.
Hence,
I urge Your Majesty to ally closely with Zhào,
uniting all under heaven as one,
and then Yān will surely be free from troubles."
Yān Wénhóu agreed to this.
Yuè Yì presented a memorial to the King of Yān, saying:
"The flounder fish,
unless they meet, cannot swim properly,
so the ancients praised them
for joining two into one.
Now, the states east of the mountains cannot unite their weaknesses into one,
showing their wisdom is inferior to that of fish.
Again, it is like soldiers pulling a cart:
three men cannot move it,
but add two more,
and with five, the cart moves.
Now, three weak states east of the mountains cannot resist Qín,
but add two more states,
and they can defeat Qín.
Yet the eastern states do not seek to combine,
so their wisdom is surely less than that of soldiers.
The Hú and Yuè people,
unable to understand each other's speech,
with intentions not communicated,
yet when crossing waves in the same boat,
they assist each other as one.
Now, the cooperation among the eastern states
should be like sharing a boat to cross a river,
but when Qín's troops arrive,
they cannot aid each other as one,
showing their wisdom is even less than that of the Hú and Yuè people.
These three examples
are things humans can achieve.
Yet the rulers east of the mountains remain unenlightened,
which is why I lament for them,
and I hope Your Majesty will deeply consider this.
Now Hán, Liáng, and Zhào have already united.
When Qín sees the solidarity of the Three Jìn,
it will surely attack Chǔ to the south.
When Zhào sees Qín attacking Chǔ,
it will surely attack Yān to the north.
It is natural that different situations can lead to the same calamity:
when Qín long attacked Hán,
Zhōngshān perished;
now if Qín attacks Chǔ,
Yān will surely perish.
I privately plan for Your Majesty:
it is better to send troops south to join the Three Jìn,
agreeing to garrison the western borders of Hán and Liáng.
If the eastern states fail to do this,
they will all surely perish."
Yān indeed sent troops south to join the Three Jìn.
When Zhào was about to attack Yān,
Sū Dài spoke to the King of Zhào on behalf of Yān:
"Just now, as I came from outside,
passing by a stream,
I saw a clam opening its shell to sunbathe,
when a snipe pecked at its flesh.
The clam closed its shell, gripping the snipe's beak.
The snipe said:
'If it doesn't rain today,
and doesn't rain tomorrow,
there will be a dried clam.'
The clam also said to the snipe:
'If you don't come out today,
and don't come out tomorrow,
there will be a dead snipe.'
Neither would let go of the other,
and a fisherman caught them both.
Now Zhào is about to attack Yān,
and if Yān and Zhào long stalemate,
exhausting their masses,
I fear powerful Qín will play the fisherman!
I hope Your Majesty will ponder this carefully."
The King of Zhào then stopped.
King Qí Xuānwāng took advantage of Yān's mourning period,
attacked Yān,
and captured ten cities.
Yān Yìwāng said to Sū Qín:
"Can you, sir, recover the invaded land for Yān?"
Qín said:
"I will retrieve them for Your Majesty."
He then went to Qí,
met the King of Qí,
bowed in congratulations,
then looked up in condolence.
The King of Qí said:
"Why do congratulations and condolences follow so swiftly?"
Sū Qín said:
"I have heard:
the reason a starving person avoids eating crow's beak
is because it temporarily fills the belly but shares the same peril as death.
Now, though Yān is small and weak,
it is the son-in-law of the King of Qín.
Your Majesty covets its ten cities and will long be an enemy of powerful Qín.
If you make weak Yān lead the way,
with strong Qín pushing from behind,
this is like eating crow's beak."
The King of Qí said:
"What then should I do?"
Sū Qín said:
"I have heard:
those skilled in handling affairs in ancient times
could turn disaster into blessing,
and transform failure into success.
If Your Majesty truly listens to me,
return the ten cities to Yān,
and Yān will be greatly pleased.
When the King of Qín learns you returned Yān's cities for his sake,
he will also be pleased.
This is what is called abandoning enmity to forge firm friendship."
The King of Qí said:
"Good."
He then returned the ten cities to Yān.
Sū Qín went to Zhào.
Zhào's ancestors shared lineage with Qín;
King Zhōu Mùwáng had Zào Fǔ drive his chariot,
defeated King Xú Yǎnwáng,
and then bestowed Zhàochéng upon Zào Fǔ,
so the Zhào clan served as ministers of Jìn for generations.
He persuaded Zhào Sùhóu, saying:
"I privately plan for you:
nothing is better than keeping the people peaceful and untroubled,
and not needlessly involving them in affairs.
The foundation of pacifying the people
lies in choosing alliances.
If alliances are chosen well,
the people will be secure;
if chosen poorly,
the people will be unsettled for life.
Let me speak of external threats:
with Qí and Qín as two enemies,
the people cannot be secure.
Relying on Qín to attack Qí,
the people cannot be secure.
Relying on Qí to attack Qín,
the people cannot be secure.
If you truly heed my advice,
Yān will surely present lands of felt, furs, dogs, and horses;
Qí will surely offer seas of fish and salt;
Chǔ will surely contribute orchards of oranges and pomelos;
Hán, Wèi, and Zhōngshān can all provide bathing tributes;
and your noble relatives and elders can all receive marquis titles.
Dividing lands and embracing profits
is what the Five Hegemons sought through destroying armies and capturing generals;
enfeoffing marquises and honoring relatives
is what Tāng and Wǔ fought for through deposing and killing.
Now you can sit high and have both,
which is what I wish for you.
If Qín descends via Zhǐdào,
then Nányáng is endangered;
if it coerces Hán and encircles Zhōu,
then Zhào must take up arms itself;
if it occupies Wèi and seizes Qí and Juǎn,
then Qí will surely submit to Qín.
Once Qín achieves its aims east of the mountains,
it will surely raise troops against Zhào.
When Qín's armor crosses the river and passes Zhāng,
occupying Pānwú,
then battle will surely be fought beneath Hándān.
This is what I fear for you.
In the present time,
among the states east of the mountains,
none is stronger than Zhào.
The state of Zhào spans over two thousand lǐ in territory,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
a thousand chariots,
and ten thousand cavalry horses,
its grain reserves sufficient for several years.
To the west lies Chángshān,
to the south the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
to the east the Qīnghé River,
and to the north Yān.
Yān is inherently a weak state,
not worthy of fear.
Of all the states under heaven, none is as threatening to Qín as Zhào.
Yet Qín dares not raise troops to attack Zhào—
why is that?
It fears that Hán and Wèi will scheme against its rear.
Thus, Hán and Wèi
are the southern屏障 of Zhào.
When Qín attacks Hán and Wèi,
there are no perilous mountains or great rivers as natural barriers,
so it gradually nibbles away at them
until it reaches their capitals.
If Hán and Wèi cannot withstand Qín,
they will surely submit and become its vassals.
Without the restraint from Hán and Wèi,
disaster will inevitably befall Zhào.
This is what I worry about for you, my lord.
I have heard:
Yáo did not have the land of three families,
Shùn not even a foot of ground,
yet they came to possess the empire;
Yǔ did not have a gathering of a hundred men,
yet he became king over the feudal lords;
the soldiers of Tāng and Wǔ did not exceed three thousand,
their chariots no more than three hundred,
their troops no more than thirty thousand,
yet they were established as Sons of Heaven.
Truly, they had the right way.
Therefore,
an enlightened ruler externally assesses the strength and weakness of his enemies,
internally measures the worthiness or unworthiness of his officers and soldiers,
and without waiting for the two armies to confront each other,
the key to victory or defeat, survival or destruction,
is already formed in his mind.
How could he be swayed by the words of the multitude
and decide matters in the dark!
I have privately studied the maps of the empire and found that
the territories of the feudal lords
are five times larger than Qín's;
estimating the troops of the feudal lords,
they are ten times those of Qín.
If the six states join forces
and attack Qín from the west,
Qín will surely be defeated.
Yet now they face west and serve it,
submitting to Qín!
To defeat others versus being defeated by others,
to make others submit versus submitting to others—
how can they be spoken of in the same breath!
Those who advocate alliance with Qín all desire to cut off the lands of the feudal lords
to give to Qín.
When Qín succeeds, they build high towers and pavilions,
beautify their palaces and homes,
listen to the music of shēng and yú,
while their state suffers from Qín's threats without sharing its worries.
Therefore,
these alliance advocates day and night use Qín's power to intimidate the feudal lords,
seeking to carve out territories,
and I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
I have heard:
an enlightened ruler eliminates doubts and dismisses slander,
blocks the path of rumors,
closes the door to factionalism,
so that ministers who honor the ruler and strengthen the army
can present their loyalty before him.
Thus, I privately plan for Your Majesty
that nothing is better than to unite Hán, Wèi, Qí, Chǔ, Yān, and Zhào in a vertical alliance,
to rebel against Qín.
Gather the generals and ministers of the empire,
meet on the banks of the Huánshuǐ River,
exchange hostages,
and swear an oath by slaughtering a white horse.
The covenant would say:
if Qín attacks Chǔ,
Qí and Wèi each will send elite troops to assist,
Hán will cut off its supply route,
Zhào will cross the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
Yān will guard the north of Chángshān;
if Qín attacks Hán and Wèi,
then Chǔ will cut off its rear,
Qí will send elite troops to assist,
Zhào will cross the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
Yān will guard Yúnzhōng;
if Qín attacks Qí,
then Chǔ will cut off its rear,
Hán will guard Chénggāo,
Wèi will block its supply route,
Zhào will cross the Hé at Bóguān,
Yān will send elite troops to assist;
if Qín attacks Yān,
then Zhào will guard Chángshān,
Chǔ will station troops at Wǔguān,
Qí will cross the Bóhǎi Sea
(now Cāngzhōu),
Hán and Wèi will both send elite troops to assist;
if Qín attacks Zhào,
then Hán will station troops at Yíyáng,
Chǔ at Wǔguān,
Wèi at Héwài,
Qí will cross the Qīnghé River
(now Bèizhōu),
Yān will send elite troops to assist.
If any feudal lord fails to abide by the covenant,
the five states will jointly attack it with their armies.
If the six states form a vertical alliance to resist Qín,
then Qín's armor will not dare venture beyond Hángǔ Pass,
to harm the lands east of the mountains!
Thus, the hegemonic enterprise will be achieved. 」
The King of Zhào said:
"Excellent."
After Qín defeated Zhào's army at Chángpíng,
it then planned to attack Hándān.
The people of Zhào were terrified,
and moved eastward.
So they sent Sū Dài with generous gifts to persuade Qín's chancellor Yìnghóu, saying:
"Has Wǔ'ānjūn captured Mǎfúzǐ?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"And does he also intend to besiege Hándān?"
He said:
"Yes."
Sū Dài said:
"If Zhào falls, then the King of Qín will rule the empire!
The cities that Wǔ'ānjūn has captured for Qín in battle
number over seventy,
taking Yānyǐng and Hànzhōng in the south,
and capturing Mǎfú's army in the north.
Even the achievements of Zhōu, Shào, and Lǚ Wàng would not surpass this.
If Zhào falls, the King of Qín will rule the empire.
If Wǔ'ānjūn is made one of the Three Dukes,
could you, sir, serve under him?
Even if you wish not to serve under him,
it would be impossible.
When Qín attacked Hán,
besieged Xíngqiū,
and trapped Shàngdǎng,
the people of Shàngdǎng all turned to Zhào,
having long disliked being under Qín's rule.
Now, Zhào's northern territories are taken by Yān,
its eastern lands by Qí,
and its southern lands by Hán and Wèi.
What you, sir, would gain
is probably not much.
So it's better to seize the opportunity to partition it,
and not let it become a merit for Wǔ'ānjūn."
Thereupon, Yìnghóu spoke to the King of Qín, saying:
"Qín's troops are weary,
I request that we allow the rulers of Hán and Zhào to cede territory for peace."
Once Qín withdrew its troops,
the King of Zhào sent Zhào Shè to make a pact with Qín,
intending to cede six cities to them.
Yú Qīng said to the king:
"Did Qín attack Zhào
and withdraw because it was weary,
or does it still have the strength to advance,
but refrains out of affection for you?"
The king said:
"Qín attacked us
with all its might,
and must have withdrawn due to weariness."
Yú Qīng said:
"Qín used its strength to attack what it could not take,
and withdrew weary;
if you, king, then cede what its strength could not hold and give it to them,
this is helping Qín attack yourself.
Next year, if Qín again demands territory,
will you give it to them?
If not,
you abandon previous efforts and invite future disaster;
if you do,
there will be no land left to give.
As the saying goes:
'The strong excel at attacking,
the weak at defending.'
Now, by complying with Qín,
its troops are not exhausted yet gain much land,
which strengthens Qín and weakens Zhào.
To increase Qín's strength by cutting away your own weakening land—
such schemes will surely not cease.
Moreover, your land is finite, while Qín's demands are endless.
To meet endless demands with finite land
will inevitably lead to the end of Zhào."
The king had not yet decided on a plan
when Lóu Huǎn arrived from Qín,
and the king consulted him.
Huǎn said:
"It is better to give it to them."
Yú Qīng said:
"I advise against giving,
not just to refuse stubbornly.
Qín demands six cities from you, king..."
The king offered six cities to bribe Qí.
Qí,
being a bitter enemy of Qín,
upon receiving the six cities from the king,
would join forces to attack Qín from the west.
Qí's compliance with the king's plan
would not even require the completion of the proposal.
Thus, the king would lose with Qí,
but gain compensation from Qín.
Moreover, the deep-seated enmity with Qí and Zhào could be avenged,
and it would demonstrate to the world the king's capability.
By making this declaration,
before troops even approach the border,
Qín would certainly send substantial bribes to Zhào and instead seek peace with the king.
Once Qín requests peace,
Hán and Wèi, hearing of it,
would surely hold the king in high esteem;
esteeming the king,
they would present valuable treasures to align with the king.
Thus, in one move, the king would gain the allegiance of three states,
and Qín would be increasingly endangered."
The king of Zhào said:
"Excellent."
He immediately sent Yú Qīng east to meet the king of Qí,
to discuss plans against Qín.
Before Yú Qīng could depart,
Qín's envoy had already arrived in Zhào.
Lóu Huǎn, hearing this,
fled.
Qín besieged Zhào,
and the king sent Píngyuán Jūn to Chǔ to form an alliance and request rescue.
Píngyuán Jūn went to Chǔ,
and spoke to the king of Chǔ about the advantages and disadvantages,
talking from sunrise
until noon without resolution.
