Máo Suì then grasped his sword and ascended the steps,
saying to Píngyuán Jūn:
"The pros and cons of the alliance,
can be decided in two words.
Today, discussions began at sunrise,
yet by noon no decision is made,
why?"
The king of Chǔ shouted:
"Why do you not step down!
I am speaking with your lord,
what are you doing here!"
Máo Suì advanced with his sword and said:
"The reason Your Majesty shouts at Suì
is because of Chǔ's multitude.
But within ten steps now,
Your Majesty cannot rely on Chǔ's multitude,
Your Majesty's life hangs in Suì's hands.
With my lord present,
why the shouting?
Moreover, Suì has heard that Tāng became Son of Heaven with only seventy lǐ of land,
and King Wén subjugated the feudal lords with a hundred lǐ of territory.
Now Chǔ has five thousand lǐ of land,
and a million troops bearing halberds,
these are the resources of a hegemon.
With Chǔ's strength,
none in the world can compare, yet it cannot withstand.
Bái Qǐ,
a mere youngster,
leading tens of thousands of troops,
raised an army to fight Chǔ,
in one battle captured Yān and Yǐng,
in a second burned Yílíng,
and in a third disgraced Your Majesty's ancestors.
This is a grievance for a hundred generations,
a shame for Zhào, yet Your Majesty feels no disgrace.
Now, forming the alliance is for Chǔ, not for Zhào."
The king of Chǔ said:
"If it is as you say, sir,
I respectfully offer my state to follow."
Thus, Chǔ sent troops to rescue Zhào.
During the time of King Xiàochéng of Zhào,
Qín besieged Hándān,
and the rescue forces from the feudal lords dared not attack Qín.
The king of Wèi sent Jìn Bǐ to rescue Zhào,
but fearing Qín,
he halted at Yāngyīn and advanced no further.
Wèi sent the guest general Xīnyuán Yǎn to secretly enter Hándān,
to persuade Zhào to acknowledge Qín as emperor.
At this time, Lǔ Lián happened to be traveling in Zhào,
and encountered the siege of Hándān by Qín.
Hearing that Wèi wanted Zhào to honor Qín as emperor,
he went to see Píngyuán Jūn and said:
"Where is the guest from Liáng, Xīnyuán Yǎn?
I ask to reprimand him on your behalf and send him back."
Píngyuán Jūn said:
"Shèng will introduce you."
Lǔ Lián met Xīnyuán Yǎn but remained silent.
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"I see those living in this besieged city
all have requests of Píngyuán Jūn.
Now observing your noble appearance, sir,
you do not seem to have requests of Píngyuán Jūn,
why do you remain long in this besieged city without leaving?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"The world thinks Bào Jiāo died from lack of composure,
but they are all wrong.
Ordinary people do not understand sacrificing for a cause.
That Qín,
is a state that discards rites and righteousness and values military achievements,
using its scholars with authority,
and treating its people like captives.
If it presumptuously becomes emperor,
and extends its governance over the world,
then Lián would rather jump into the Eastern Sea and die,
than be its subject.
The reason I see you, General,
is to wish to aid Zhào."
Yǎn said:
"How will you aid them, sir?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"I will make Liáng and Yān aid them,
while Qí and Chǔ will certainly do so."
Yǎn said:
"As for Yān, I suppose it will follow.
But as for Liáng,
I am from Liáng myself,
how can you, sir, make Liáng aid them?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"It is because Liáng has not seen the harm of Qín declaring itself emperor.
If Liáng sees the harm,
it will surely aid Zhào."
Yǎn said:
"What harm is there in Qín declaring itself emperor?"
Lián said:
"In the past,
King Wēi of Qí once practiced benevolence and righteousness,
leading the feudal lords to pay homage to Zhōu.
Zhōu was poor and weak,
and none of the feudal lords paid homage,
yet Qí alone did so.
Over a year later,
King Liè of Zhōu passed away,
and Qí arrived late.
Zhōu was angry,
and sent a message to Qí saying:
'With heaven collapsed and earth torn,
the Son of Heaven has left his mat.
The eastern vassal Tián Yīng arriving late,
shall be beheaded!'
King Wēi of Qí burst into anger and said:
'Bah!
Your mother was a maid!'
In the end, he became a laughingstock of the world.
Thus, alive, he paid homage to Zhōu,
dead, he cursed it,
truly unable to bear its demands!
That Son of Heaven was indeed so,
and it is no wonder."
Yǎn said:
"Have you not seen servants, sir?
Ten people following one man—
is it because their strength is insufficient or their wisdom inferior?
It is fear!"
Lǔ Lián said:
"Alas!
Is Liáng compared to Qín
like a servant?"
Yǎn said:
"Yes."
Lǔ Lián said:
"I will make the king of Qín boil and mince the king of Liáng."
Yǎn was shocked and said:
"This is too extreme,
your words, sir!
And how can you, sir, make the king of Qín boil and mince the king of Liáng?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"Certainly.
I will explain.
In the past,
Jiǔ Hóu, È Hóu, and King Wén
were the three high ministers of Zhòu.
Jiǔ Hóu had a beautiful daughter,
so he offered her to Zhòu.
Zhòu found her ugly,
and minced Jiǔ Hóu.
È Hóu strongly protested,
arguing vehemently,
so Zhòu made dried meat of È Hóu.
King Wén heard of it,
sighed deeply,
and so was imprisoned in the storehouse of Yǒulǐ,
for a hundred days, intended to be killed.
Why, when all are called kings,
end up as dried meat or mince?
When King Mǐn of Qí was going to Lǔ,
Yíwéi Zǐ drove for him,
holding the whip and following,
said to the people of Lǔ:
'How will you receive my lord?'
The people of Lǔ said:
'We will receive your lord with ten grand sacrifices.'
Yíwéi Zǐ said:
'From where do you take this ritual?
That lord of ours,
The Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven tours the domains,
the feudal lords vacate their residences,
surrender their keys,
tuck in their robes and hold the small tables,
serving meals below the hall.
Once the Son of Heaven has finished eating,
they then withdraw to attend court affairs.'
The people of Lǔ locked their gates,
ultimately not admitting him,
so he could not enter Lǔ.
Intending to go to Xuē,
he sought passage through Zōu.
At that time,
the ruler of Zōu had died,
and King Mǐn wished to enter to offer condolences.
Yíwéizi said to the orphaned heir of Zōu:
'When the Son of Heaven offers condolences,
the host must move the coffin to the opposite side,
set up a ritual table facing north on the southern side,
after which the Son of Heaven faces south to pay respects.'
The ministers of Zōu said:
'If it must be this way,
we would rather fall on our swords and die!'
Thus he dared not enter Zōu.
The officials of Zōu and Lǔ,
while alive could not be properly served and supported,
and when dead could not receive funeral gifts,
yet he still wished to perform the rites of the Son of Heaven in Zōu and Lǔ.
The ministers of Zōu and Lǔ ultimately did not admit him.
Now Qín
is a state of ten thousand chariots.
Liáng is also a state of ten thousand chariots.
Both occupying the status of ten-thousand-chariot states,
sharing the title of king,
upon seeing them win a single battle,
you immediately wish to follow and make him emperor,
then he will proceed to replace the ministers of the feudal lords.
He will remove those he deems unworthy and install those he considers worthy,
remove those he hates and give to those he loves.
Moreover, he will make his daughters and slandering concubines become consorts of the feudal lords,
residing in the palaces of Liáng.
How could the King of Liáng remain at ease?
And how could you, General, retain your former favor?"
Thereupon,
Xīnyuán Yǎn rose,
bowed twice,
and apologized, saying:
"I beg to take my leave,
and dare not speak again of making Qín emperor!"
The Qín general heard of this,
and for this reason withdrew his army fifty lǐ.
Sū Qín went to Hán
Hán's ancestors shared the same surname as Zhōu,
served Jìn,
were enfeoffed at Hán,
and became the Hán clan.
Later, King Liè of Zhōu granted Hán the status of marquis,
enabling it to be listed among the feudal lords. ,
and persuaded King Xuān of Hán, saying:
"Hán has the strongholds of Gǒngluò and Chénggāo to the north,
the passes of Yíyáng and Shāngbǎn to the west,
Wǎn, Ráng, and the Wěi River to the east,
and Xíng Mountain to the south.
Your territory spans over nine hundred lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand.
The powerful bows and strong crossbows of the world
all come from Hán.
Hán soldiers draw and shoot with a leap,
firing a hundred arrows without pause,
piercing the chests of distant targets,
and striking the hearts of nearby ones.
As for Hán's swords and halberds,
such as Lóngquán and Tài'ē,
they can cut through oxen and horses on land,
and slice through swans and geese in water.
With the strength of Hán's troops
and Your Majesty's worthiness,
to face west and serve Qín,
submitting with arms tied,
brings shame upon the state and makes you a laughingstock of the world—
nothing is worse than this!
Therefore,
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
serving Qín will inevitably lead to demands for Yíyáng and Chénggāo.
If you yield them this year,
they will demand more land next year.
If you give it,
you will eventually have no land to offer;
if you do not,
you will abandon previous efforts and suffer future calamities.
Moreover, Your Majesty's land is finite,
while Qín's demands are endless.
To meet endless demands
with finite land
is what is called buying resentment and incurring disaster—
without fighting, your land will already be diminished!
I have heard a common saying:
'Better to be a chicken's beak
than an ox's rear.'
Now if Your Majesty faces west, submits, and serves Qín like a minister,
how is that different from being an ox's rear?
With Your Majesty's worthiness
and the support of Hán's strong army,
to bear the name of an ox's rear—
I secretly feel shame for Your Majesty!"
The King of Hán flushed with anger,
pressed his sword and sighed deeply, saying:
"Though I am unworthy,
I will not serve Qín!"
He followed Sū Qín's advice.
When Hán attacked Sòng,
Qín grew very angry,
saying:
"I love Sòng.
Hán has relations with me,
yet attacks what I dearly love—
why is this?"
Sū Qín spoke to the King of Qín on Hán's behalf, saying:
"Hán's attack on Sòng
is for Your Majesty's sake.
With Hán's strength
augmented by Sòng,
Chǔ and Wèi will surely fear,
and fear will make them face west and serve Qín.
Without losing a single soldier,
without killing one person,
you effortlessly gain Ānyì—
this is what Hán prays for from Qín."
When King Huì of Hán heard that Qín was fond of initiating projects,
he wanted to tire out its people
and prevent them from campaigning east,
so he sent the hydraulics expert Zhèng Guó to infiltrate Qín
and persuade the King of Qín
to excavate the Jīng River for irrigation.
Midway through the project, this was discovered,
and they intended to execute Zhèng Guó.
Zhèng Guó said:
"Initially, I came as a spy,
but the completion of the canal will also benefit Qín.
I have prolonged Hán's life by a few years,
but I am creating benefits for Qín for ten thousand generations."
The king agreed with him.
Sū Qín went to Wèi
Wèi's ancestors
were descendants of Duke Bì Gāo,
sharing the same surname as Zhōu.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he enfeoffed Gāo at Bì,
and this became their surname.
Bì Wàn served Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
who enfeoffed Wàn at Wèi,
making him a senior official.
Later, King Liè of Zhōu granted Wèi the status,
allowing it to become a feudal lord. ,
and persuaded King Xiāng of Wèi, saying:
"Your Majesty's land
has the Hóng Gōu and Chén Rǔnán to the south,
the Huái, Yǐng, Zhǔ, and Zǎo rivers to the east,
the Great Wall as the boundary to the west,
and the Hé River, Juǎn, and Yǎn to the north.
The territory spans a thousand lǐ,
and though the place names may sound small,
the farmhouses and cottages
leave no land for grazing.
The multitude of people,
the abundance of chariots and horses,
moving ceaselessly day and night,
with a rumbling and bustling
like the masses of three armies.
Wèi
is a powerful state in the world;
and you, King,
are a worthy ruler of the world.
Now you actually intend to face west and serve Qín,
calling yourself an eastern vassal,
building an imperial palace,
accepting caps and sashes,
and offering seasonal sacrifices.
I secretly feel shame for Your Majesty.
I have heard that
King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
with three thousand weary soldiers,
captured Fūchāi at Gānsuì;
King Wǔ with three thousand troops
and three hundred armored chariots,
subdued Zhòu at Mùyě.
Was it because of their numerous troops?
It was truly because they could exert their might!
Now I have privately heard that Your Majesty's troops
include two hundred thousand warriors,
two hundred thousand each of servants and assault troops,
one hundred thousand laborers,
six hundred chariots,
and six thousand cavalry.
This far surpasses King Gōujiàn of Yuè and King Wǔ!
Yet now you heed the words of your ministers,
yet you wish to serve Qín as a vassal.
To serve Qín inevitably requires ceding territory as tribute,
so before even employing troops, the state is already diminished.
For a minister to cut his sovereign's land for external alliances,
stealing momentary achievements,
disregarding the consequences,
destroying the public good to enrich private interests,
externally relying on mighty Qín's influence,
internally coercing his sovereign,
seeking territorial concessions—
I urge Your Majesty to examine this carefully!
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
'If unchecked threads persist unbroken,
how can rampant vines be managed?
If not felled at the hair's breadth,
soon axes will be required.'
With prior plans unsettled,
great calamities will follow—
what then can be done?
If Your Majesty truly heeds my counsel,
uniting the six states in alliance,
focusing efforts with combined strength,
then the threat of mighty Qín will surely cease.
Thus, my humble sovereign King of Zhào sent me to offer this simple strategy,
presenting a clear covenant,
awaiting Your Majesty's decree."
The King of Wèi replied:
"I reverently accept your instruction."
Yú Qīng persuaded Chūnshēn Jūn saying:
"Attack Yān
to secure your fiefdom."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"The route to attack Yān
must pass through either Qí or Wèi.
Wèi and Qí recently resented Chǔ;
though Chǔ wishes to attack Yān,
what path can we take?"
He replied:
"Let me secure King of Wèi's permission."
Yú Qīng then went to Wèi
and told the king:
"Chǔ is immensely powerful!
Matchless under heaven!
Now it plans to attack Yān."
The King of Wèi said:
"Earlier you claimed:
'Matchless under heaven',
yet now you say:
'plans to attack Yān'—
why is this?"
He replied:
"To say a horse is strong is true,
but to claim it can lift a thousand jūn is not—
why?
Because a thousand jūn
exceeds any horse's capacity.
Similarly, to call Chǔ powerful is true,
but to cross Zhào and Wèi battling Yān—
is that within Chǔ's capacity?
Undertaking what exceeds its capacity
will exhaust Chǔ.
Exhausting Chǔ strengthens Wèi.
Which benefits Your Majesty more?"
The King of Wèi said:
"Well said."
He consented.
Sū Qín went to Qí
The Grand Duke of Qí, Lǚ Shàng,
served the Zhōu court,
becoming military advisor to King Wén and King Wǔ,
plotting against King Zhòu.
After King Wǔ pacified Shāng,
he enfeoffed Shàngfǔ at Yíngqiū in Qí.
Sū Qín addressed King Xuān of Qí:
"Qí has Tàishān to the south,
Lángyá to the east,
Qīnghé to the west,
and Bóhǎi to the north—
a state fortified on all sides.
Línzī is immensely wealthy and substantial,
where all people play yú, strum sè, pluck qín, strike zhù, stage cockfights, race dogs, play liùbó, and kick cùjū.
On Línzī's roads,
carriage hubs collide,
shoulders rub together,
joined lapels form curtains,
raised sleeves create canopies,
and flung sweat becomes rain.
Households prosper, people abound,
spirits soar high.
With Your Majesty's wisdom
and Qí's might,
none under heaven can withstand you.
Yet now you serve Qín facing west—
I secretly feel shame for Your Majesty!
Moreover, Hán and Wèi fear Qín
because they share borders with it.
When armies engage,
within ten days their fate between survival and destruction is decided.
If Hán and Wèi defeat Qín,
their forces are halved,
borders left unguarded;
if defeated,
their states face imminent peril.
Thus,
Hán and Wèi hesitate to fight Qín
but readily submit as vassals.
Now Qín's attack on Qí would differ:
bypassing Hán and Wèi's territories,
crossing the route through Wèi's Jìnyáng,
traversing the perilous Gāngfǔ pass,
where chariots cannot run abreast,
cavalry cannot ride parallel,
and a hundred defenders at the narrows
thwart a thousand attackers.
Though Qín may wish to advance deep,
it would glance back like a wary wolf,
fearing Hán and Wèi might strike from behind.
Therefore,
it blusters with hollow threats,
posturing arrogantly but daring not advance.
Without deeply considering Qín's inability to harm Qí,
you seek to serve it facing west—
this is your ministers' grave miscalculation.
Now you can avoid the name of serving Qín
while possessing a powerful state's reality—
thus I urge Your Majesty to ponder this slightly."
The King of Qí said:
"Well said."
Sū Qín advised King Mǐn saying:
"I have heard:
those who relish initiating warfare court sorrow;
those who delight in hosting resentful alliances face isolation.
Latecomers
gain advantage;
those avoiding resentment
seize the moment.
Hence the saying:
'When the qíjì steed weakens,
a nag overtakes it;
when Mèng Bēn grows weary,
a woman defeats him.'
Not that the nag or woman possess
greater strength than qíjì or Mèng Bēn—
why then?
The advantage of acting later.
I have heard:
in warfare's art,
without deploying troops,
though facing a million-strong army,
one can triumph in the hall;
though opposed by Mò Yǎ or Wú Qǐ's generals,
they can be captured indoors;
a thousand-zhàng walled city
can be taken over wine vessels;
a hundred-chǐ assault tower
can be toppled at the banquet mat.
Thus, with uninterrupted music of bells, drums, yú, and sè,
territory expands and desires fulfill;
with unceasing laughter of harmonious entertainers,
feudal lords arrive the same day.
Those skilled in royal enterprise
weary the world while resting themselves,
disrupt the world while securing themselves.
When feudal lords lack settled plans,
the state harbors no lingering worries.
How do we know this?
Formerly, the King of Wèi held a thousand lǐ of land,
led three hundred sixty thousand armored troops,
and escorted twelve feudal lords to court the Son of Heaven,
plotting against Qín from the west.
Qín grew fearful,
sleeping restlessly,
eating tastelessly.
Wèi Yāng counseled the King of Qín:
'Why not send me to see the King of Wèi,
where I shall surely make him attack the north.'
The King of Qín agreed.
Wèi Yāng met the King of Wèi
and said:
'Your Majesty's achievements are grand!
Your commands prevail across the land!
Yet your twelve feudal lords
are merely Sòng, Wèi, Zōu, Lǔ, Chén, and Cài.
These are but whips in Your Majesty's hand,
insufficient to rule the world.
Better to conquer Yān northward,
attack Qí eastward,
then Zhào will surely follow;
take Qín westward,
attack Chǔ southward,
then Hán will surely follow.
With intent to attack Qí and Chǔ
and ambition to lead the world,
royal enterprise will manifest.
Your Majesty should first assume royal robes,
then plan against Qí and Chǔ.'
The King of Wèi approved,
thus expanding his palace,
crafting crimson robes,
erecting pillars with nine pendants.
Following the banner of the Seven Stars.
This was the position of the Son of Heaven,
yet the King of Wèi occupied it.
At this, Qí and Chǔ were enraged,
the feudal lords fled to Qí,
the people of Qí attacked Wèi,
killed its crown prince,
and annihilated its army of a hundred thousand.
At this time,
the King of Qín effortlessly received the lands west of the Yellow River.
Thus, when Wèi Yāng first strategized with the King of Qín,
their plans were settled without even leaving their mats,
and the general of Wèi was already captured by Qí;
before their shields and battering rams were deployed,
the territories beyond the Western River had already been taken by Qín.
This is what I mean by defeating the enemy in the hall, capturing the general indoors, seizing cities amid the wine vessels, and repelling the foe at the banquet table."
King Huái of Chǔ sent Zhāo Yáng, the Pillar of State, to lead troops against Wèi,
capturing eight cities,
then shifted his army to attack Qí.
King Mǐn of Qí was troubled by this.
Chén Zhěn said:
"Your Majesty need not worry,
allow me to make him withdraw."
He then went to see Zhāo Yáng in his camp,
bowed twice,
congratulated him on his victory,
rose and asked:
"May I ask, according to Chǔ's laws:
for annihilating an army and killing its general,
what official rank and nobility is granted?"
Zhāo Yáng said:
"The office is Supreme Pillar of State,
the nobility is Supreme Jade Scepter Holder."
Chén Zhěn said:
"What is higher than this?"
He replied:
"Only the Prime Minister."
Zhěn said:
"The Prime Minister is indeed noble!
But one does not appoint two Prime Ministers!
May I venture to offer you an analogy?"
"In Chǔ, there was a man offering sacrifices,
who gave a goblet of wine to his housemates.
The housemates said to each other:
'Several people drinking it would not be enough,
one person drinking it would have surplus.
Let us draw snakes on the ground,
and the one who finishes first shall drink the wine.'
One man finished his snake first,
took the wine and was about to drink it,
but then, holding the goblet in his left hand,
he drew with his right hand on the ground,
saying:
'I can add legs to it.'
Before the legs were done,
another man finished his snake,
snatched the goblet from him,
and said:
'A snake naturally has no legs;
how can you add legs to it?'
Then he drank the wine.
The one who added legs to the snake
ultimately lost his wine.
Now, you have attacked Wèi,
destroyed its army and killed its general,
captured eight cities,
and are shifting troops to attack Qí.
Qí fears you greatly;
this is enough to secure your fame!
There is no room to add more to the highest honor!
To be ever-victorious in battle and not know when to stop,
risking death and loss of nobility,
is like adding legs to the snake."
Zhāo Yáng found this reasonable,
and led his army away.
Sū Qín went to Chǔ.
The ancestors of Chǔ
descended from Emperor Zhuānxū.
During the time of Emperor Kù, Gāoxīn, he held the position of Grand Rectifier,
and was named Zhùróng.
His descendants later served King Wén of Zhōu.
When it came to King Chéng of Zhōu,
he enfeoffed the diligent descendants of Wén and Wǔ,
and granted Xióng Yì land in the barbarian region of Chǔ,
with the rank of viscount or baron,
with the surname Mǐ.
They greatly won the support of the people between the Yangtze and Hàn Rivers.
By the time of Xióng Tōng,
he sent an envoy to Zhōu via Suí,
requesting his title be honored.
Zhōu refused,
Xióng Tōng was angered,
and proclaimed himself King Wǔ.
He persuaded King Wēi, saying:
"Chǔ is the strongest state under heaven;
and you, King, are the worthiest ruler under heaven.
To the west, you have Qiánzhōng and Wū commanderies,
to the east, Xiàzhōu and Hǎiyáng,
to the south, Dòngtíng and Cāngwú,
to the north, Xíngsài and Xúnyáng.
Your territory spans over five thousand lǐ,
with a million armored soldiers,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain supplies for ten years.
These are the resources for a hegemon or king!
With Chǔ's strength
and Your Majesty's worthiness,
no one under heaven can withstand you.
Yet now you face west to serve Qín,
then all feudal lords will face west to pay homage at Zhāngtái!
What Qín fears most
is none other than Chǔ.
If Chǔ is strong, Qín is weak;
if Qín is strong, Chǔ is weak.
Their situations are mutually exclusive.
Therefore, for Your Majesty's strategy,
nothing is better than forming alliances to isolate Qín.
If Your Majesty does not ally,
Qín will surely dispatch two armies:
one exiting Wǔguān,
one descending upon Qiánzhōng.
Then Yānyǐng will be threatened!
I have heard:
govern before chaos arises,
act before events occur.
To worry only after disaster strikes
is too late!
Thus, I urge Your Majesty to consider this early.
If Your Majesty truly heeds me,
I will have the states east of the mountains
offer seasonal tributes,
following Your Majesty's wise decrees;
entrust their altars of land and grain,
serve the ancestral temples,
train soldiers and sharpen weapons,
all for Your Majesty's use.
Thus, with alliances, Chǔ will king,
with horizontal alliances, Qín will emperor.
Now to abandon the hegemon's enterprise
and bear the name of serving others—
I dare say it is not worthy of Your Majesty!
For Qín is a state of tigers and wolves,
with the intent to devour the world.
Qín is the enemy of all under heaven.
Those advocating horizontal alliances all wish to cut feudal lords' lands to serve Qín—
this is what is called nurturing an enemy and serving a foe;
no treachery or disloyalty
surpasses this.
Thus, with alliances, feudal lords will cede land to serve Chǔ;
with horizontal alliances, Chǔ will cede land to serve Qín.
These two strategies are vastly different—
which will Your Majesty choose?
Therefore, my humble king of Zhào has sent me to offer this simple plan,
presenting a clear covenant,
awaiting Your Majesty's command."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent.
I pledge my state to follow."
When King Xiāng of Chǔ had made peace with Qín,
he thought himself free of Qín's threat,
and indulged in wanton extravagance with four companions.
Zhuāng Xīn remonstrated but was not heeded,
so Xīn left for Zhào.
Later, Qín indeed captured Yānyǐng,
and King Xiāng summoned Xīn and apologized to him.
Zhuāng Xīn said:
"I have heard a common saying:
'To look for the hound after seeing the hare
is not too late;
to mend the pen after losing the sheep
is not too delayed.'
I have heard:
Tāng and Wǔ became kings with a hundred lǐ,
while Jié and Zhòu lost all under heaven.
Now, though Chǔ is small,
taking the long to supplement the short,
it still has a thousand lǐ—
how could it be only a hundred lǐ?
Does Your Majesty not see the dragonfly?
With six legs and four wings,
it flies between heaven and earth,
bending down to peck at mosquitoes and gnats for food,
lifting its head to drink the clear dew,
believing itself free from harm,
and having no strife with others.
Unaware that a five-foot child
is preparing sticky paste on a silk thread,
to catch it from four ren above,
and then it becomes food for ants and moles.
The dragonfly is a small example;
the yellow sparrow is likewise!"
Pecking white grains below,
roosting in lush trees above,
flapping wings and stretching pinions,
it considers itself free from troubles,
having no conflicts with humans.
Unaware that noble scions,
with catapults in their left hands,
and pellets in their right,
aim at its head as their target.
By day it rests in lush trees,
by evening it's seasoned with sour and salty flavors.
The yellow sparrow is but a small example,
as is Lord Shèng of Cài!
Traveling south to Gāobēi,
ascending north to Wūshān,
drinking from the Rúxī River's flow,
eating fish from the Xiāng waves,
with a young concubine on his left,
and a favored woman on his right,
galloping with them through Gāocài,
yet neglecting state affairs.
Unaware that Zǐfā was receiving orders from King Xuān,
to bind him with red cords and present him.
Lord Shèng of Cài's case is but a minor one,
and so it is with you, Great King!
With Zhōuhóu on your left,
Xiàhóu on your right,
eating grain from fiefs and salaries,
and carrying gold from the state treasury,
galloping with them through Yúnmèng,
yet neglecting the affairs of the empire and state.
Unaware that the Marquis of Ráng is receiving commands from the King of Qín,
to fill the Ménɡsài Pass within,
and cast you beyond Ménɡsài. "
Upon hearing this, King Xiāng,
trembling with fear,
took the guī scepter and bestowed it upon Zhuāng Xīn,
consulting him on strategies against Qín,
later reclaiming the land north of the Huái River.
A man of Chǔ used a weak bow and fine string to shoot down returning geese.
King Xiāng of Chǔ summoned and questioned him,
and he responded by likening Qín, Yān, Zhào, and Wèi to birds,
to incite the king's anger,
saying:
"The former king was deceived by Qín,
and died abroad,
a grievance unsurpassed!
Now even a commoner can avenge against a mighty state,
as with Wǔ Zǐxū and Báigōng.
Now with Chǔ's territory spanning five thousand lǐ,
and a million armored troops,
it is still enough to leap vigorously in the central plains.
Yet to sit and await subjugation,
I privately advise Your Majesty against it. "
King Xiāng then revived the vertical alliance to attack Qín.
After the six states formed the vertical alliance,
Sū Qín became its leader.
Reporting north to Zhào,
King Sù of Zhào enfeoffed Sū Qín as Lord Wǔ'ān.
They then cast the vertical alliance document toward Qín,
and Qín dared not peek with troops beyond Hángǔ Pass for over fifteen years.
Zhāng Yí promoted the horizontal alliance for Qín.
Qín desired to attack Wèi,
first defeating Hán,
with the Yóuchā army beheading eighty thousand,
terrifying the feudal lords.
Thus, Yí came to persuade the King of Wèi.
Persuading the King of Wèi, he said:
"During the time of Duke Xiào of Qín,
Gōngsūn Yāng requested to attack Wèi,
saying:
'Wèi resides between mountain ridges,
with its western capital at Ānyì,
bordering Qín by the river,
and monopolizing the advantages east of the mountains.
When advantaged, it invades Qín westward;
when troubled, it expands eastward.
Now with your lordship's wisdom and sagacity,
the state thrives by it,
it is fitting to attack Wèi at this time.
If Wèi does not ally with Qín,
it will surely move east.
Moving east, it will rely on the defenses of mountains and rivers,
facing east to control the feudal lords.
This is the path to imperial dominion.' "
From then on,
Wèi indeed left Ānyì,
moving its capital to Dàliáng. :
"Wèi's territory does not reach a thousand lǐ,
its troops not exceeding three hundred thousand.
The land is flat on all sides,
accessible to feudal lords from all directions,
like spokes converging on a hub,
with no great mountains or rivers as barriers.
From Zhèng to Liáng,
it's over two hundred lǐ;
by chariot or on foot,
one arrives before tiring.
Liáng,
borders Chǔ to the south,
Hán to the west,
Zhào to the north,
and Qí to the east.
With garrisons on all sides,
those guarding posts and barriers number no less than a hundred thousand.
Liáng's terrain,
is inherently a battlefield.
Dàliáng,
is present-day Biànzhōu. .
If Liáng allies with Chǔ to the south,
but not with Qí,
Qí will attack from the east;
if allied with Qí to the east,
but not with Zhào,
Zhào will attack from the north;
if not in harmony with Hán,
then Hán will attack from the west;
if not close to Chǔ,
then Chǔ will attack from the south.
This is the path to being torn apart.
Moreover, those feudal lords forming the vertical alliance,
aim to secure the altars of soil and grain,
honor the ruler, strengthen the military, and gain fame.
Now for the vertical alliance,
to unify the world,
swearing brotherhood,
sacrificing a white horse to pledge at the Huánshuǐ River,
to solidify mutual trust.
Yet even blood brothers, born of the same parents,
still quarrel over wealth.
How can one rely on the deceitful and fickle schemes of Sū Qín?
Its impossibility to succeed is already clear.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will send troops to attack Héwài,
seizing Juǎn, Yǎn, and Suānzǎo,
coercing Wèi and taking Jìnyáng,
then Zhào cannot move south;
if Zhào cannot move south, then Liáng cannot move north,
if Liáng cannot move north, the vertical route is cut,
and if the vertical route is cut, for Your Majesty's state to remain unharmed,
is impossible.
If Qín subdues Hán and attacks Liáng,
Hán fears Qín,
Qín and Hán unite as one,
Liáng's downfall,
can be expected momentarily,
this is what I worry about for Your Majesty.
For Your Majesty's strategy,
nothing is better than serving Qín,
serving Qín then Chǔ and Hán will not dare act;
without the threat from Chǔ and Hán,
Your Majesty can rest easy on a high pillow,
and the state will surely be free from worries.
If Your Majesty does not heed Qín,
Qín will dispatch armored troops eastward to attack,
and even if you wish to serve Qín,
it will be impossible.
Moreover, those advocating the vertical alliance often boast with little credibility,
persuading one feudal lord to achieve enfeoffment.
Therefore,
itinerant debaters of the world,
all day and night wringing wrists, glaring, gnashing teeth to extol the vertical alliance's benefits,
to persuade rulers.
Rulers admire their eloquence and are swayed by their arguments,
how can they not be dazzled?
I have heard:
accumulated feathers can sink a boat,
a load of light things can break an axle,
numerous mouths can melt metal.
Thus, I urge Your Majesty to carefully consider and decide. "
The King of Wèi then betrayed the vertical alliance,
and sought peace with Qín.
Fàn Jū advised King Zhāo of Qín:
"For the Marquis of Ráng to cross Hán and Wèi to attack Qín's Gāngshòu,
is unwise.
Sending few troops cannot harm Qí,
sending many harms Qín,
his strategy is flawed.
Moreover, when King Mǐn of Qí attacked Chǔ southward,
crushing armies and killing generals,
expanding territory by a thousand lǐ twice,
yet Qí gained not an inch of land,
was it that Qí did not desire land?
The situation made it unattainable.
When feudal lords saw Qí's exhaustion,
they raised armies to attack it,
shaming its officers and halting its troops.
Thus, Qí's great defeat,
was due to its defeat of Chǔ enriching Hán and Wèi.
This is called lending weapons to bandits and supplying robbers with grain.
Your Majesty should rather befriend distant states and attack nearby ones,
gaining an inch makes it your inch,
gaining a foot makes it your foot.
Now to abandon the near and attack the far,
is it not mistaken?
In the past,
the state of Zhōngshān spanned five hundred lǐ,
and Zhào alone swallowed it,
When achievements are established and fame is secured, benefits follow accordingly,
and none in the world can contend with it.
Now, Hán and Wèi,
situated in the central states, are the pivots of the world.
If Your Majesty wishes to dominate the central states and become the pivot of the world,
to intimidate Chǔ and Zhào.
If Chǔ is strong, then ally with Zhào;
if Zhào is strong, then ally with Chǔ.
When both Chǔ and Zhào are attached,
Qí will also become fearful.
Once Qí submits, it will surely use humble words and generous gifts to serve Qín.
With Qí already attached,
then Hán and Wèi can be dealt with accordingly."
The king said:
"Excellent."
He then appointed Suī as a guest minister,
planning military campaigns to attack Wèi,
capturing Huái and Xíngqiū.
Qí and Chǔ came to attack Wèi,
and the king of Wèi sent envoys to seek help from Qín,
with carriages and caps in constant view, yet Qín's rescue never arrived.
A man of Wèi named Táng Jū,
over ninety years old,
said to the king:
"This old minister requests to go west and persuade the king of Qín,
to have troops dispatched before I return."
The king bowed twice and sent him off.
Táng Jū arrived in Qín,
entered and met the king of Qín,
who said:
"Elder, you have come from afar with such weariness,
this is truly arduous!
Wèi has sent pleas for help many times,
and I am well aware of its urgency."
Táng Jū replied:
"Your Majesty knows of Wèi's urgency yet does not dispatch rescue troops;
I privately believe your strategists are incompetent.
Wèi,
a state of ten thousand chariots,
yet it faces west to serve Qín, calls itself an eastern vassal, builds imperial palaces, accepts caps and sashes, and offers seasonal sacrifices—
all because it believes Qín's strength is sufficient to rely on.
Now the armies of Qí and Chǔ have joined forces at the outskirts of Wèi,
yet Qín's rescue is not sent;
are you waiting until it is no longer urgent?
If driven to desperation,
they will cede territory and form a vertical alliance—
what will Your Majesty have left to rescue?
If you only rescue them when they are desperate,
you will lose an eastern vassal in Wèi and strengthen two powerful states, Qí and Chǔ—
what benefit is there for Your Majesty?"
Thereupon, the king of Qín hastily dispatched troops to Wèi.
Zhāng Yí persuaded King Huái of Chǔ, saying:
"Qín's territory spans half the world,
its military rivals four states,
shielded by mountains and girded by rivers,
fortified by natural barriers on all sides.
Fàn Jū advised King Zhāo of Qín:
"Your Majesty's state,
fortified by natural barriers on all sides,
has Gānquán and Gǔkǒu to the north,
Jīng and Wèi rivers to the south,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
and Guānbǎn to the left;
with a million fierce warriors,
and a thousand war chariots;
when advantageous, they advance to attack,
when不利, they retreat to defend—
this is the land of a true king.
The people fear private conflicts,
but are brave in public battles—
these are the people of a true king.
Your Majesty possesses both these qualities,
and facing the feudal lords,
is like unleashing a hound to catch a lame rabbit.
With over a million tiger-like warriors,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain piled like hills.
Laws and decrees are clear,
soldiers and people are content.
The ruler is wise and strict,
the generals are intelligent and martial.
Even without sending out armor,
they can sweep through the dangers of Chángshān,
surely breaking the backbone of the world—
those who submit later will perish first!
Moreover, those forming vertical alliances
are no different from driving a flock of sheep to attack a fierce tiger.
A tiger against sheep—
it is clear they cannot match!
Now if Your Majesty does not side with the tiger but with the flock of sheep,
I privately believe your strategy is mistaken.
Among all the powerful states in the world,
if not Qín, then Chǔ,
if not Chǔ, then Qín.
If these two states contend,
their situation is such that they cannot coexist.
If Your Majesty does not ally with Qín,
Qín will send troops to occupy Yíyáng,
and the upper lands of Hán will be cut off;
descending to Hédōng and Chénggāo,
Hán will surely submit as a vassal.
Then Liáng will also follow like the wind.
With Qín attacking Chǔ from the west,
and Hán from the north,
how can the state remain without danger?
I have heard:
'If your troops are inferior,
do not provoke a challenge;
if your grain is insufficient,
do not engage in prolonged warfare.'
Qín has Bā and Shǔ to the west,
with great ships laden with grain,
setting out from Wènshān,
floating down the river,
covering over three thousand lǐ to Chǔ.
With boats carrying soldiers,
each load holds five thousand men,
traveling three hundred lǐ a day;
though the distance is great,
it requires no effort from oxen or horses,
and in less than ten days,
they can reach Hánguān;
if Hánguān is alarmed, then from the border eastward,
all cities will be on guard,
and Qiánzhōng and Wūjùn
will no longer belong to Your Majesty.
If Qín raises armor and marches out of Wǔguān,
attacking southward,
then the northern territories will be severed.
When Qín's troops attack Chǔ,
the crisis will unfold within three months.
Yet Chǔ awaits rescue from other states,
which will take over half a year.
The situation will not allow timely aid.
To rely on rescue from weak states,
while ignoring the threat of a strong Qín—
this is what I worry about for Your Majesty.
Your Majesty once battled the people of Wú,
winning three out of five battles,
but your veteran troops were exhausted;
guarding newly acquired cities on the periphery,
the surviving people suffered greatly.
I have heard:
'Those with great achievements are easily endangered,
and exhausted people resent their superiors.'
To uphold precarious achievements,
while defying the will of a strong Qín—
I privately fear for Your Majesty's safety.
In all the world, those who firmly uphold faithful vertical alliances—
Sū Qín was enfeoffed as Lord Wǔ'ān.
Sū Qín served as chancellor of Yān,
then secretly plotted with the king of Yān to attack Qí,
to defeat Qí and divide its land.
He then feigned guilt,
fled and entered Qí,
where the king of Qí accepted him and made him chancellor.
After two years, he was exposed,
and the king of Qí was enraged,
having Sū Qín torn apart by chariots in the market.
With a deceitful man like Sū Qín,
attempting to manage the world,
and unify the feudal lords—
its impossibility is clear.
Now Qín and Chǔ share borders,
naturally forming intimate states.
If Your Majesty can truly heed me,
I will have the crown prince of Qín sent as a hostage to Chǔ,
and the crown prince of Chǔ sent as a hostage to Qín,
and offer a daughter of Qín as a humble servant for Your Majesty,
presenting a city of ten thousand households,
as a fief for bathing and grooming,
so we may long be brotherly states,
never attacking each other for life.
I believe no plan is more advantageous than this."
The king of Chǔ then allied closely with Qín.
Bái Qǐ led troops to attack Chǔ,
and King Xiāng of Chǔ sent Huáng Xiē to persuade King Zhāo of Qín, saying:
"None in the world are stronger than Qín and Chǔ,
yet now I hear Your Majesty wishes to attack Chǔ—
this is like two tigers fighting,
while a worn-out dog suffers the harm;
it is better to befriend Chǔ.
Allow me to explain:
I have heard:
things reverse at their extreme,
as with winter and summer;
stacking to the limit brings danger,
as with piling chess pieces.
Now the territory of your great state,
spans half the world with two frontiers,
such that since the beginning of humankind,
no land of ten thousand chariots has ever existed.
If Your Majesty can uphold fairness and maintain authority,
abandon ambitions of attack,
enrich the virtue of benevolence and righteousness,
then even three kings would not be enough to make four,
and five hegemons not enough to make six;
but if Your Majesty relies on the multitude of people,
and the might of weapons and armor,
To seek to subdue the lords of the world by force,
I fear will bring calamities.
The Book of Songs says:
'All things have a beginning,
but few can sustain it to the end.'
The Book of Changes states:
'When a fox crosses water,
it wets its tail.'
This illustrates that beginnings are easy, but endings are difficult.
How do we know this is so?
Zhì Bó saw the benefit of attacking Zhào but was unaware of the disaster at Yúcì;
King Wú saw the advantage of attacking Qí but did not foresee the defeat at Gānsuì.
These two states were not without great achievements,
but they were blinded by immediate gains and underestimated the ensuing perils.
Now, Your Majesty resents that Chǔ remains undestroyed,
yet forgets that destroying Chǔ would strengthen Hán and Wèi.
For Your Majesty's consideration,
I advise against this course.
Your Majesty holds no generational virtue towards Hán and Wèi,
but rather accumulated grievances over generations.
The fathers, brothers, and sons of Hán and Wèi have died in Qín in succession,
for nearly ten generations.
Those with severed heads and bodies, bones exposed in marshes,
are seen throughout their lands;
those bound by the neck and hands, captured as prisoners,
fill the roads.
Thus, the survival of Hán and Wèi
is a worry for Qín's altars of state.
Now if Your Majesty trusts them,
raises troops to attack Chǔ,
is that not a mistake?
For Your Majesty's consideration,
nothing is better than befriending Chǔ.
If Chǔ and Qín unite to confront Hán,
Hán will surely submit.
Your Majesty, utilizing the natural barriers of Shāndōng
and the advantages of the Hé Qū region,
can make Hán a Marquis within the Pass.
In that case,
with Your Majesty stationing a hundred thousand troops to guard Zhèng, the people of Liáng would be terrified,
Xǔ, Yān, Yílíng, and Yīngchéng would be isolated,
while Shàngcài and Zhàolíng would cease communication.
Thus,
Wèi would also become a Marquis within the Pass.
If Your Majesty befriends Chǔ,
and with two marquises of ten thousand chariots within the Pass,
focusing on Qí's territory,
the right bank of Qí could be taken effortlessly.
Then, threatening Yān and Zhào,
and unsettling Qí and Chǔ,
these four states would submit without needing to be vanquished."
The King of Qín said:
"Well said."
He halted the plan to attack Chǔ.
King Qǐng Xiāng of Chǔ planned an alliance with Qí and Hán,
intending to plot against Zhōu.
King Nǎn of Zhōu sent his minister Wǔ Gōng to persuade Chǔ's chancellor Zhāo Zǐ.
Zhāo Zǐ said:
"There is no plot against Zhōu,
but even so, why can Zhōu not be plotted against?"
Wǔ Gōng replied:
"The land of Western Zhōu,
even if extended and supplemented,
is no more than a hundred lǐ.
Though named the common sovereign of all under heaven,
dividing its land would not enrich a state,
gaining its people would not strengthen an army,
and attacking it would not enhance one's reputation.
Yet, rulers fond of meddling and ministers eager for war,
when issuing orders and deploying troops,
always start and end with Zhōu.
Why is this?
Because the sacrificial vessels are there.
They desire the vessels but forget the chaos of regicide.
Now if Hán gives the vessels to Chǔ,
I fear all under heaven would hold Chǔ accountable for them."
Thereupon,
Chǔ abandoned the plan.
King Wǔ of Qín sent Chū Lǐ Jí with a hundred chariots into Zhōu,
and the Lord of Zhōu welcomed him with great respect.
The King of Chǔ reprimanded Zhōu,
for honoring the Qín guest too highly.
Yóu Shèng spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Zhōu:
"Long ago, Zhì Bó wanted to attack Qiúyóu,
so he gifted a large bell,
transported on a broad cart,
and followed it with troops.
Qiúyóu was ultimately destroyed,
due to lack of preparation.
When Duke Huán of Qí attacked Cài,
he claimed it was 'to punish Chǔ,'
but in truth, he was assaulting Cài.
Now Qín,
a state like a tiger or wolf,
has the ambition to devour the world alone,
and sent Chū Lǐ Jí with a hundred chariots into Zhōu,
causing the Lord of Zhōu to fear.
Taking Cài and Qiúyóu as warnings,
he placed long weapons in front,
and short crossbows behind,
calling it 'guarding Jí,'
but in reality, imprisoning him.
How could the Lord of Zhōu not worry for his state?
He fears that if the state falls one day, it would concern Your Majesty."
The King of Chǔ was then pleased.
When King Xiāng of Chǔ fell ill,
the crown prince was a hostage in Qín,
unable to return.
Huáng Xiè persuaded Qín's chancellor Yìng Hóu:
"Now the King of Chǔ is ill,
and may not recover.
Qín should return the crown prince.
If the crown prince ascends the throne,
he will surely serve Qín diligently;
if not returned,
he is but a commoner in Xiányáng.
If Chǔ installs another crown prince, he will not serve Qín,
losing an ally and severing harmony with a state of ten thousand chariots,
which is unwise.
I hope the chancellor will consider this."
Yìng Hóu spoke to the King of Qín,
but the king refused.
So he fled.
Zhāng Yí went to Hán,
and persuaded King Xuān of Hán:
"Hán's terrain is perilous and harsh,
situated among mountains,
where the five grains grow,
mostly beans and wheat;
the land spans no more than nine hundred lǐ,
with less than two years' supply of food.
Your Majesty's troops,
fully mobilized, number no more than three hundred thousand,
including laborers and porters.
Now Qín has a million armored soldiers,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and warriors like tiger runners,
bareheaded and fierce,
those who charge with spears and halberds,
are too many to count.
The eastern states' soldiers wear heavy armor in battle,
while Qín's men discard armor and charge the enemy bare-chested,
carrying heads in their left hands,
and captives in their right.
Qín's pursuit of the eastern states' troops
is like Mèng Bēn against a coward;
comparing their strengths,
is like Wū Huò against an infant.
The lords do not consider their land's weakness or lack of food,
but listen to the sweet words of persuaders,
who collude and flatter,
misleading their rulers,
with no greater fault than this.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will send troops to occupy Yíyáng,
cutting off Hán's territory;
taking Chénggāo and Xíngyáng to the east,
then the palaces of Hóng Tái and gardens of Sāng Lín
will no longer be yours.
Blocking Chénggāo,
and severing the upper lands,
will divide the state.
Thus, for Your Majesty's strategy,
nothing is better than aligning with Qín.
What Qín desires most
is to weaken Chǔ,
and none can weaken Chǔ better than Hán.
Not that Hán is stronger than Chǔ,
but the situation makes it so.
Now, if you serve Qín to the west,
and attack Chǔ,
the King of Qín will surely be pleased.
Attacking Chǔ without seizing its land,
turning calamity into Qín's favor,
no plan is more advantageous than this."
King Xuān heeded him.
Fàn Jū advised the King of Qín:
"The territories of Qín and Hán intertwine like embroidery,
and Qín having Hán
is like a tree having borers,
or a person having a heart ailment.
If all under heaven remains unchanged, it is tolerable,
but if changes occur,
the greatest threat to Qín
would be Hán.
Why does Your Majesty not subdue Hán?"
The king said:
"I indeed wish to subdue Hán,
but Hán does not comply,
what can be done?"
Fàn Jū replied:
"How can Hán not comply?
If Your Majesty sends troops to attack Xíngyáng,
the route to Chénggāo will be blocked;
cutting off the Tàiháng path to the north,
the troops from Shàngdǎng cannot descend.
Once Your Majesty attacks Xíngyáng,
Hán will be split into three parts,
and it will surely face peril and destruction."
How could I not listen!
If I listen,
then the path to hegemony is worth considering."
The king said:
"Well said."
So he followed the advice.
Zhāng Yí persuaded King Mǐn of Qí, saying:
"Among the powerful states under heaven,
none surpass Qí.
Your ministers, elders, and clansmen are prosperous, numerous, and content,
yet those who strategize for Your Majesty
all offer advice for the moment,
disregarding the benefits for a hundred generations.
Those who persuade Your Majesty
surely say:
'To the west, Qí has the strong Zhào,
to the south, Hán and Liáng;
Qí is a coastal state,
with vast territory and numerous people,
strong armies and brave soldiers.
Even if there were a hundred Qíns,
they could do nothing to Qí!'
Your Majesty praises their words,
but does not consider the reality.
I have heard:
Qí fought Lǔ three times and Lǔ won three victories,
yet the state faced peril and ruin thereafter.
Though they had the reputation of victory,
they suffered the reality of destruction—
why is this?
Because Qí was large and Lǔ was small.
Now, the relationship between Qín and Qí
is like that between Qí and Lǔ.
Now, Chǔ and Qí exchange daughters in marriage,
becoming brotherly states;
Hán has presented Yíyáng,
Wèi has surrendered Héwài,
Zhào has entered Cháogē and Miǎnchí,
ceding Héjiān to serve Qín.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will drive Hán and Liáng to attack Qí's southern lands,
mobilize all of Zhào's troops to cross the Qīnghé River,
advance to Bóguān,
and then Línzī and Jímò will no longer be yours.
Once the state is attacked,
even if you wish to serve Qín,
it will be impossible.
Therefore,
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
The king of Qí agreed.
Yān attacked Qí,
capturing over seventy cities,
leaving only Jǔ and Jímò unconquered.
Tián Dān of Qí used Jímò to defeat Yān,
killing Qí Jié.
The Yān general, fearing execution, held Liáochéng,
not daring to return.
Tián Dān besieged it for over a year,
but could not take it.
Lǔ Lián then wrote a letter,
tied it to an arrow,
and shot it into the city,
addressing the Yān general:
"I have heard:
'The wise do not miss opportunities and abandon gains,
the brave do not fear death and tarnish their names,
the loyal do not put themselves before their lord.'
Now, you act on personal resentment like Hán,
disregarding that the king of Yān is left without a minister—
this is not loyalty;
to die and lose Liáochéng,
with your authority not trusted by Qí—
this is not courage;
achievements ruined and name destroyed,
with no praise from later generations—
this is not wisdom.
Thus, the wise do not hesitate,
the brave do not fear death.
Now, life and death, honor and disgrace, high and low, noble and humble—
this is the moment to decide.
I hope you will consider carefully,
and not follow the common crowd.
Moreover, Chǔ attacks Qí's Nányáng,
Wèi attacks Pínglù,
yet Qí has no intention to face south,
believing the harm of losing Nányáng is small
compared to the great benefit of gaining Jìběi;
hence, they have decided to hold firm.
Now, with Qín sending troops,
Wèi dares not look east,
and if Qín's horizontal alliance succeeds, Chǔ's situation will be perilous.
Previously, they abandoned Nányáng,
severed the right territory,
and preserved Jìběi—
a plan they still pursue.
Now, with Chǔ and Wèi both fighting Qí,
and Yān's rescue not coming,
Qí can use its full force,
free from other threats,
to focus on Liáochéng.
After a year of hardship,
I foresee your inability to succeed.
Qí will surely decide at Liáo—
you have no second chance.
That king of Yān is in great chaos,
with all above and below confused.
Lì Fù with a million troops
suffered five defeats abroad.
A state of ten thousand chariots besieged by Zhào,
lands reduced and the lord distressed,
laughed at by all under heaven.
The state is weakened, disasters abound,
and the people have nowhere to turn.
Now, with the weary people of Liáo,
you resist Qí's full force—
a year without relief,
this is a defense like Mò Dí's;
eating grains and cooking bones for food,
yet soldiers have no thought of desertion—
this is a feat like Sūn Bìn and Wú Qǐ's,
visible to all under heaven!
So, for your sake,
it would be better to withdraw troops and rest soldiers,
return intact to report to the king of Yān,
who will surely be pleased.
The people will greet you like parents,
raising arms to discuss your deeds in the world,
and your achievements will be clear.
Alternatively,
if you resent Yān and abandon the world,
why not travel east to Qí?
I request land be allotted and titles confirmed,
wealth matching Táo and Wèi,
with generations calling you 'the solitary one'—
this is another plan.
These two options,
offer fame and substantial gain—
I hope you will examine them,
think deeply, and choose one carefully.
Moreover, I have heard:
'Those who cling to minor integrity
cannot exercise great authority;
those who detest small shames
cannot achieve glorious fame.'
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng shot Duke Huán,
hitting his hook—
an act of usurpation;
he abandoned Prince Jiǔ,
not dying for him—
an act of cowardice;
bound in fetters—
an act of disgrace.
With these three behaviors,
villages would not associate with him,
lords would not employ him.
Had Guǎn Zhòng remained oppressed and not emerged,
he would not have escaped being a disgraced man with vile conduct.
Yet, Guǎn Zǐ discarded the faults of those three acts,
took control of Qí's government,
unified the world,
assembled the feudal lords nine times,
his name revered under heaven,
his light shining on neighboring states.
Cáo Mò was a general for the lord of Lǔ,
who in three battles lost a thousand lǐ of land.
Had Cáo Zǐ acted without regard for the future,
dying without living on,
he would have been a defeated general captured.
But Cáo Zǐ, relying on his sword,
confronted Duke Huán on the altar,
without changing expression,
without faltering in speech,
and in one morning restored
all lost in three battles,
shaking the world,
his name passed down through ages.
These two men
were not incapable of minor integrity
or dying for small shames.
They believed that to die and vanish from the world,
without establishing merit and fame,
was not wise.
So they cast aside resentment and anger,
and achieved lifelong fame.
Thus, their deeds rival the Three Sovereigns,
their names endure as long as heaven and earth.
Consider this carefully!"
The Yān general, upon reading the letter, said:
"I have respectfully heard your command."
Then he committed suicide.
Once, Yōngmén Zhōu visited Lord Mèngcháng of Qí with his qín,
and Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Sir, when you play the qín,
can you also move people to sorrow?"
He replied:
"What I can evoke sorrow with
is the fall from nobility to lowliness,
from past wealth to present poverty—
unlike being rejected and confined to a poor alley;
cut off from the four neighbors,
It is not as if one's stature were lofty and sublime;
embracing substance and upholding truth,
yet encountering slander and enduring calumny,
grievances accumulate with no means of redress,
it is not as if fostering joy to cultivate affection;
to part without enmity yet be separated in life,
journeying far to another state,
with no hope of meeting again,
it is not as if being orphaned in youth and widowed in prime,
venturing out to take the wild marshes as capital,
returning to use caves and burrows as home,
trapped in the cycle of dawn and dusk,
with nowhere to seek refuge.
For such a person,
merely hearing the cry of fledgling birds or the autumn wind whistling through branches,
wounds the heart.
Whenever I take up the zither and heave a long sigh for them,
none fail to feel sorrow and shed tears.
Now you, my lord, dwell in vast mansions and lofty halls,
with interconnected gates and deep chambers,
lowering silken curtains,
to welcome cool breezes,
entertainers before you,
flatterers at your side,
raising the stirring "Jíchǔ" melodies,
dancing with the beauties of Zhèng,
flowing sounds to delight the ears,
dazzling colors to intoxicate the eyes,
for water revels, you board dragon-prowed boats,
hoist feathered banners and beat drums,
angling in unfathomable depths.
For outings, you ascend the open plains,
gallop through vast parks,
strong crossbows bringing down high-flying birds,
brave warriors grappling with fierce beasts,
setting out wine and music,
沉醉忘归。
In such moments,
you regard heaven and earth as no more than a fingertip,
and even if there were skilled zither players,
they could not move you. "
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Indeed so."
Yōngmén Zhōu said:
"I privately grieve for you, my lord:
He who contended for empire and cornered Qín,
was you;
he who allied five states to attack Chǔ,
was also you.
The world has never been without turmoil,
oscillating between vertical and horizontal alliances,
success in the vertical would make Chǔ king,
success in the horizontal would make Qín emperor.
With the strength of Qín and Chǔ,
to lord over weak Xiē,
is like wielding a sharp axe to cut morning mushrooms.
Those with insight,
all tremble for you.
The way of heaven does not favor constant prosperity,
cold and heat alternate in advance and retreat,
after a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
your ancestral temples will surely lack sacrificial offerings,
high towers will have crumbled,
winding pools leveled,
thorns and brambles overgrowing graves,
foxes and badgers burrowing within,
wandering children and shepherd boys trampling over them, singing atop,
saying:
'With all the honor and nobility of Mèngcháng Jūn,
is this how it ends?' "
Thereupon, Mèngcháng Jūn sighed deeply,
tears streaming down his lashes,
Yōngmén Zhōu took up his zither and played,
and Mèngcháng Jūn, sobbing, approached him saying:
"Sir, your zither playing
makes Wén feel like a man of a fallen state."
Zhāng Yí addressed King of Zhào:
"My humble state's King of Qín,
has sent me to offer my foolish counsel to Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty unites the world to oppose Qín,
Qín's troops dare not exit Hángǔ Pass.
This is due to Your Majesty's might,
prevailing east of the mountains.
My humble state, fearful and submissive,
mends armor and sharpens weapons,
solely because Your Majesty might consider reprimanding us.
Now, with Your Majesty's power,
you've raised Bā and Shǔ,
annexed Hànzhōng,
enveloped the two Zhōu,
moved the nine tripods,
guarded the ford at Báimǎ.
Though Qín is remote,
our hearts have long harbored resentment and anger.
Now, with our worn armor and depleted troops,
stationed at Miǎnchí,
we wish to cross the river,
occupy Pānyú,
and engage in battle beneath Hándān.
We hope to join battle on the jiǎzǐ day,
emulating the campaign against King Zhòu of Shāng.
Thus, I am sent first to inform you.
All that Your Majesty trusts in for the vertical alliance,
relies on Sū Qín.
Sū Qín deluded the feudal lords,
turning right into wrong,
wrong into right,
sought to overturn Qí,
and ended torn apart by chariots in the market.
That the world cannot be unified is clear.
Now Chǔ and Qín are brotherly states,
while Hán and Liáng proclaim themselves eastern vassals,
Qí offers its lands of fish and salt,
this severs Zhào's right arm.
To fight with a severed right arm,
losing allies and standing alone,
hoping to avoid peril,
how can it be done?
Now Qín dispatches three armies:
one blocks the Wǔ Road,
urges Qí to raise troops,
cross the river and camp east of Hándān;
one camps at Chénggāo,
driving Hán and Liáng's forces beyond the river;
one stations at Miǎnchí,
uniting four states to strike Zhào.
Once Zhào submits,
its land will be divided four ways.
Therefore,
I dare not conceal intentions or hide truths,
but inform you first.
I privately advise Your Majesty,
it would be best to meet the King of Qín at Miǎnchí,
face to face to make a verbal pact.
I urge a ceasefire with no attack,
and hope Your Majesty will decide."
King Sù of Zhào agreed.
When Lord Wǔ'ān defeated Zhào's army at Chángpíng,
capturing over four hundred thousand soldiers,
he buried them all alive.
Advancing to besiege Hándān,
yet military supplies fell short,
he sent Mr. Wèi to speak to King Zhāo of Qín:
"Zhào's right leans on the peril of Chángshān,
left girded by the barrier of the river,
benefiting from the steeds and chariots of Dài.
Its people are spirited and brave,
adept at warfare,
often assembling feudal lords as leader of the vertical alliance,
clearly knowing that if Qín does not weaken, the six states will perish.
The reason Qín has not achieved its ambition under heaven,
is due to the threat from Zhào.
Now, by Your Majesty's divine grace,
Zhào's army is broken at Chángpíng,
its trusted ministers and sharp troops nearly all dead.
Hándān lies empty,
all commanderies tremble in fear,
officials and people alike resent their ruler.
If at this time we dispatch supplies and provide ample provisions,
surely Zhào can be destroyed!
Destroying Zhào will awe the feudal lords,
the world can be pacified,
and the kingly enterprise achieved!"
The King of Qín was inclined to agree,
but Marquis Yìng, jealous of his merit,
sought to prevent it,
telling the king:
"Though Qín has crushed Zhào's army,
our own casualties are heavy,
the people are exhausted from distant transport,
the interior is depleted.
If Chǔ and Wèi seize this void to revolt,
we will have nothing to defend ourselves with,
it is best to halt the campaign for now."
The king complied.
Three years later,
he again wanted to send Bái Qǐ to attack Zhào,
but Qǐ refused.
The king then sent Marquis Yìng to reproach him:
"Chǔ's territory spans five thousand lǐ,
with a million halberd-bearing troops,
yet you previously led a mere tens of thousands into Chǔ,
captured Yānyǐng,
burned its suburban temples,
terrifying the people of Chǔ,
who fled east, not daring to look west.
When Hán and Wèi jointly raised vast armies,
your forces were less than half,
yet you crushed them at Yīquè,
bloodshed floating shields,
subjugating Hán and Wèi,
who to this day call themselves eastern vassals.
These are your achievements,
known throughout the world.
Now, of Zhào's soldiers who died at Chángpíng,
already seven or eight out of ten are gone,
hence I wish to have you lead,
determined to annihilate them.
You have always fought few against many,
winning as if by divine power,
Moreover, when striking the weak with strength,
and attacking the few with many?"
Lord Wǔ'ān replied:
"At that time, the King of Chǔ relied on his state's size,
neglected its governance,
while his ministers envied each other's achievements,
flatterers held power,
able ministers were estranged and dismissed,
the common people were disunited,
city walls and moats were not maintained,
there were neither capable generals,
nor defensive preparations.
Thus I could lead troops deep inland,
bypassing many cities,
destroying bridges and burning boats,
to unify our men's hearts;
plundering the countryside,
to supply our army's needs.
At that time,
the Qín soldiers,
treated the army as their home,
their general as parents,
bonding without arrangement,
trusting without consultation.
United in heart and strength,
they would die without retreating.
The Chǔ people fought on their own land,
all concerned for their homes,
each with divided hearts,
none with will to fight,
hence I could achieve success.
In the Yīquē battle,
Hán hesitated looking to Wèi,
unwilling to commit its forces first;
Wèi relied on Hán's sharpness,
wanting to push them as vanguard.
The two armies disputed advantage,
their strength uncoordinated.
Thus I could deploy decoy troops,
to face Hán's formation,
concentrating forces with full sharpness,
striking Wèi unexpectedly,
when Wèi's army was defeated,
Hán's forces crumbled naturally.
For these reasons,
I could achieve success,
all calculated advantages and situational inevitabilities,
what divinity was there?
Now the Qín army defeated Zhào's army at Chángpíng,
but didn't seize the moment,
to destroy them while trembling with fear,
instead fearing released them,
letting them farm to increase stores.
Raising orphans and children to grow their population,
repairing weapons and armor to enhance their strength,
deepening moats and walls to fortify their defenses.
Their ruler humbles himself to serve his ministers,
ministers devote themselves to death-ready warriors.
Down to even the likes of Píngyuán Jūn,
all have wives and concubines mending clothes among troops,
subjects and people united,
high and low concerted,
just like Gōu Jiàn trapped at Kuàijī times.
Attacking present-day Zhào,
they'll surely hold firm;
challenging their army to battle,
they'll surely refuse engagement;
besieging their capital,
will surely prove unconquerable;
assaulting their cities,
will surely prove unbreachable;
plundering their countryside,
will surely yield nothing.
Long campaign without success,
other states will conceive ambitions,
external aid will surely arrive.
I foresee its harms,
see no benefits,
plus am ill and cannot go."
Marquess Yìng withdrew ashamed.
Qín then sent Wáng Hé to lead attacking Zhào.
Chǔ and Wèi indeed rescued them.
Zhāng Yí persuaded King Zhāo of Yān:
"Your Majesty's trusted state,
none equals Zhào.
Formerly, Zhào Xiāngzǐ married his sister to King of Dài,
wanting to annex Dài,
arranged meeting at Gōuzhù Pass.
He ordered craftsmen make a metal ladle,
lengthened its handle,
enabling it to strike people.
Drinking with Dài's king,
secretly told the cook:
'When wine flows merrily,
serve hot soup,
reverse ladle to strike him.'
So when wine flowed merrily,
calling for hot soup,
the cook advanced to pour,
reversed ladle striking Dài's king,
killing him,
entrails smearing ground.
His sister hearing this,
sharpened hairpin and killed herself.
Hence to this day exists Mójī Mountain,
known throughout the realm.
By Hàn高祖's time,
Chén Xī as Zhào's chancellor supervised Zhào-Dài border troops,
raised rebellion,
the Emperor went personally to Hándān,
said gladly:
'Xī not holding Zhāng River south,
nor defending Hándān north,
I know he can do nothing.'
When Xī was defeated,
the Emperor said:
'Dài lies north of Chángshān,
Zhào follows south of mountains,
controlling it is distant.'
Then established two sons as Kings of Dài.
Now the King of Zhào's wolf-like cruelty without kinship,
Your Majesty clearly sees.
And consider Zhào trustworthy?
Zhào raised troops attacking Yān,
twice besieged Yān's capital,
coerced Your Majesty,
Your Majesty ceded ten cities to apologize,
now Zhào's king has entered court at Miǎnchí,
submitting Héjiān affairs to Qín.
If Your Majesty doesn't serve Qín,
Qín sends troops to Yúnzhōng, Jiǔyuán,
driving Zhào to attack Yān,
then Yìshuǐ and Great Wall,
won't be Yours.
If You serve Qín,
the King of Qín will surely rejoice,
Zhào won't dare act recklessly,
thus west having strong Qín's support,
south without Qí, Zhào's threats.
Therefore,
I urge Your Majesty to deeply consider this."
The King of Yān heeded Zhāng Yí,
Zhāng Yí returned reporting to Qín.
The King of Yān sent Prince Dān as hostage to Qín.
Qín wanted to send Zhāng Táng to be Yān's chancellor,
jointly attacking Zhào,
to expand Héjiān territory.
Zhāng Táng told Lǚ Bùwéi:
"I once attacked Zhào for King Zhāo,
Zhào resents me.
Now going to Yān,
must pass through Zhào,
I cannot go."
Bùwéi was displeased,
but couldn't force him.
His retainer Gān Luó, aged twelve,
told Bùwéi:
"Let me persuade him for you."
Then visited Zhāng Táng:
"Your achievements compared to Lord Wǔ'ān's?"
Táng said:
"Lord Wǔ'ān crushed strong Chǔ south,
destroyed Yān, Zhào north,
victorious in battles and captures,
shattered cities and ruined towns,
beyond counting.
My achievements fall short."
Gān Luó said:
"Marquess Yìng's power in Qín,
compared to Wénxìn Hóu's authority?"
Táng said:
"Marquess Yìng less authoritative than Wénxìn Hóu."
Gān Luó said:
"Formerly Marquess Yìng wanting to attack Zhào,
Lord Wǔ'ān opposed it,
ten lǐ from Xiányáng,
was ordered death at Dùyóu.
Now Wénxìn Hóu personally requests you chancellor Yān,
yet you refuse to go,
I don't know where you'll die."
Zhāng Táng feared, said:
"I'll go, following your advice."
Departure date set,
Gān Luó told Wénxìn Hóu:
"Lend me five chariots,
let me precede Zhāng Táng to inform Zhào."
Wénxìn Hóu sent him,
Gān Luó went to Zhào,
persuaded the King:
"Has the King heard Prince Dān of Yān entered Qín?"
Said:
"Heard it."
"Heard Zhāng Táng becoming Yān's chancellor?"
Said:
"Heard it."
Gān Luó said:
"Prince Dān entering Qín,
means Yān doesn't deceive Qín.
Zhāng Táng becoming Yān's chancellor,
Qín does not deceive Yān.
Yān and Qín do not deceive each other,
there is no difference.
Therefore, I wish to attack Zhào and expand the territory of Héjiān.
Your Majesty should bestow upon me five cities,
to expand Héjiān,
and I will request the return of the Yān crown prince,
to join the strong Zhào in attacking the weak Yān."
The King of Zhào said:
"Excellent."
He immediately ceded five cities to Qín.
The Yān crown prince heard of this and returned,
whereupon Zhào attacked Yān,
capturing twenty cities,
with Qín taking ten of them.
Then, Lǐ Sī from Chǔ and Wèi Liáo from Liáng
advised the King of Qín, saying:
"Since Duke Xiào of Qín,
the Zhōu court has declined,
the feudal lords have annexed each other,
and east of the pass there are six states.
Qín, riding on victory, has invaded the feudal lords,
for six generations now.
Now the feudal lords submit to Qín,
as if they were commanderies and counties.
Their rulers and ministers are all fearful,
and if they form a vertical alliance unexpectedly,
this would be how Zhì Bó, Fū Chāi, and King Mǐn perished.
I hope Your Majesty will not begrudge wealth,
but bribe their powerful ministers,
to disrupt their plans.
Qín would only lose 300,000 in gold,
yet the feudal lords could be completely subdued."
The King of Qín followed their plan,
secretly sending strategists with gold and jade to travel among the feudal lords.
Among the feudal lords' renowned scholars,
those who could be won over with wealth
were generously provided for;
those who refused
were stabbed with sharp swords.
Having disrupted the plans of their rulers and ministers,
they then sent skilled generals to follow up,
and thus annexed the feudal lords.
Scholars from all under heaven gathered in Zhào to form a vertical alliance,
intending to attack Qín.
Marquis Yìng said:
"Your Majesty need not worry,
allow me to dismantle it.
Qín holds no grudge against the scholars of the world;
they gather to attack Qín
merely because they desire wealth and honor.
Has Your Majesty seen your dogs?
Hundreds or thousands form a pack,
some lying, some rising,
some walking, some stopping,
without fighting each other.
But throw them a bone,
and they suddenly rise and snarl at each other.
Why?
Because they have the intent to compete.
Now, if we send five thousand in gold with Táng Jū,
along with rare music to reside in Wǔ'ān,
holding grand banquets and drinking together,
spending less than three thousand in gold,
the scholars of the world will fight among themselves."
After Qín had swallowed the world,
it feared the failures of the Zhōu,
believing weakness led to usurpation,
thus it mocked the Three Dynasties,
and eradicated ancient laws.
Kǒng Róng said:
"In ancient times,
the royal domain spanned a thousand lǐ,
and within the realm, feudal lords were not enfeoffed."
Duke Zhài said:
"The system of the former kings
had the甸服 within the state,
the侯服 outside the state,
the宾服 in the侯卫,
the要服 for the Yí and Mán,
and the荒服 for the Róng and Dí.
The甸服 offered daily sacrifices,
the侯服 monthly sacrifices,
the宾服 seasonal offerings,
the要服 annual tributes,
and the荒服 acknowledged kingship.
Daily sacrifices, monthly sacrifices,
seasonal offerings,
annual tributes,
and lifelong kingship
were the teachings of the former kings.
If sacrifices were lacking, they cultivated virtue;
if monthly sacrifices were lacking, they cultivated speech;
if offerings were lacking, they cultivated culture;
if tributes were lacking, they cultivated reputation;
if kingship was lacking, they cultivated virtue.
Once the order was established and still not fulfilled,
then punishments were applied.
Thus, there were punishments for lack of sacrifices,
attacks for lack of monthly sacrifices,
expeditions for lack of offerings,
reprimands for lack of tributes,
and warnings for lack of kingship.
Then came the laws for punishments,
the armies for attacks,
the preparations for expeditions,
the commands for威严 reprimands,
and the proclamations for warnings.
If still not fulfilled,
they further cultivated their virtue,
without troubling people from afar.
This was the ancient system."
Qín abolished the five ranks,
replaced them with commanderies and counties,
proclaimed itself 'Emperor',
and reduced the royal children to commoners.
Internally, there was no support from kin as the root,
externally, not an inch of land for protective vassals.
Wú and Chén raised their wooden clubs
(wooden staffs),
and Liú and Xiàng followed to overthrow them.
Thus it is said:
Zhōu exceeded its destined reign,
Qín fell short of its allotted span,
due to the nature of state power.
Xún Yuè said:
"In ancient times, states were founded small or large
to learn from past弊端,
adapting and making them work.
In the Xià and Yīn eras,
they were no more than a hundred lǐ,
so the feudal lords were weak and the Son of Heaven strong.
Jié and Zhòu could indulge in cruelty,
Zhòu executed the Marquis of Xíng and punished the Marquis of Guǐ,
and even King Wén with his great virtue
was not spared imprisonment in Yǒulǐ.
Zhōu, inheriting these弊端,
thus established large states,
five hundred lǐ square,
to honor the feudal lords and weaken itself.
By the end,
the feudal lords grew powerful,
warring among themselves,
while the Zhōu court declined,
and calamities arose.
Qín, inheriting these弊端,
failed to correct the system to find a balance,
but instead abolished the feudal lords,
replaced them with commanderies and counties,
to unify authority
and monopolize the world,
its intent self-serving,
not for the people.
Thus, Qín could dominate the world's power,
without restraint,
acting extravagantly and licentiously,
brutalizing the world,
yet it fell in just fourteen years.
Therefore, when a ruler loses the Way,
the whole world suffers;
when the people are once disturbed,
they collapse like rotting fish or crumbling earth,
beyond rescue.
Hàn, upon rising,
inherited the弊端 of Zhōu and Qín,
thus mixing and using both systems,
yet the troubles of the six kings and seven states
were truly due to excessive power,
not the fault of feudal lords governing states."
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
the world was newly stabilized,
the imperial clan was few,
learning from the Qín's孤立 failure,
they divided the territory,
establishing two ranks of nobility:
the greater as kings,
the lesser as marquises.
Those enfeoffed as marquises for merit
numbered over a hundred estates.
Honoring the royal sons and brothers,
they greatly opened nine kingdoms,
the largest of which
spanned provinces and commanderies,
with dozens of connected cities,
which could be called overcorrecting the error.
Yet when Gāozǔ founded the enterprise,
he was busy day and night.
Emperor Huì reigned briefly,
Empress Dowager Gāo, a female regent, held power,
yet the world was peaceful,
without worries of rebellion.
Ultimately, quelling the crisis of the various Lǚ
and laying the foundation for Tàizōng
also relied on the feudal lords.
For when the root is weak, the branches grow large;
when the flow is excessive, it leads to overflow.
Minor ones transgress laws through debauchery and excess,
while major ones become isolated and rebellious,
thereby harming themselves and losing their states.
Therefore, Emperor Wen adopted Jiǎ Yì's proposal
to divide Qí and Zhào.
Jiǎ Yì said:
"To ensure the stability and peace of the empire,
nothing is better than establishing many feudal lords while reducing their power.
With less power, they are easier to guide with righteousness;
with smaller states, they harbor no evil intentions.
Let the empire's governance
be like the body directing the arms,
the arms directing the fingers.
Your Majesty should divide the land and establish the system.
Let Qí, Zhào, and Chǔ each be divided into several states,
with their descendants inheriting portions of their ancestors' lands,
until the land is fully allocated.
The Son of Heaven should not seek personal gain from this."
He further submitted a memorial saying:
"If Your Majesty does not establish this system,
given the current situation,
within one or two generations,
the feudal lords will become unrestrained and uncontrollable,
growing powerful and strong,
and Hàn laws will become unenforceable.
What Your Majesty relies on for defense and the Crown Prince's support
are only the two states of Huáiyáng and Dài.
Dài borders the Xiōngnú to the north,
neighboring a powerful enemy;
it is sufficient if it can defend itself.
But Huáiyáng compared to the major feudal lords
is like a small mole on the face,
merely serving as bait for larger states,
insufficient to impose restrictions.
The current system
lies in Your Majesty's hands,
yet your son is made into mere bait—
how can this serve the interests of ten thousand generations?
In my humble opinion,
I suggest allocating the Huáinán territory to strengthen Huáiyáng,
and establishing an heir for the King of Liáng;
cede two or three border cities from northern Huáiyáng and Dōngjùn
to strengthen Liáng.
If this is not feasible,
relocate the King of Dài to establish his capital at Suīyáng.
Let Liáng extend from Xīncài northward,
reaching the Yellow River;
and Huáiyáng encompass Chén southward,
bordering the Yangtze River.
Then any major feudal lords with rebellious intentions
will be too terrified to plot.
Liáng will be sufficient to defend against Qí and Zhào;
Huáiyáng will be adequate to restrain Wú and Chǔ.
Your Majesty can rest easy,
free from worries about the region east of the mountains,
this is an advantage for all eternity.
I have heard:
A sage king consults his ministers
rather than acting solely on his own,
thus enabling his subjects to fully express their loyal advice.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this favorably."
Emperor Wén then followed Yì's plan.
He moved King Wǔ of Huáiyáng to become King of Liáng,
with borders reaching Mount Tài to the north,
and Gāoyáng to the west,
granting over forty large counties;
he moved King Xǐ of Huáiyáng to become King of Huáinán,
to pacify its people.
Later, when the Seven States rebelled,
they could not advance through Liáng territory—
this was due to Jiǎshēng's strategy.
Emperor Jǐng employed Cháo Cuò's plan
to reduce the territories of Wú and Chǔ.
Cháo Cuò advised the emperor:
"When Emperor Gāo first stabilized the empire,
his brothers were few and his sons young,
so he generously enfeoffed those of the same surname.
Thus, the son by a concubine, King Dàohuì of Qí, ruled seventy-two cities;
his half-brother, King Yuán of Chǔ, ruled forty cities;
