his nephew ruled Wú with over fifty cities.
By enfeoffing these three of secondary status,
they divided half the empire.
Now the King of Wú, bearing a grudge since the Crown Prince incident,
though claiming illness and not attending court,
should be executed according to ancient law.
Emperor Wén could not bear to do so,
instead granting him a staff and mat,
showing utmost kindness.
Yet he fails to reform,
growing ever more arrogant and willful.
He mint coins from mountain resources,
boasts salt from the sea,
lures talented men from across the land,
and plots rebellion.
Now, whether we reduce his territory or not, he will rebel;
if we do not reduce it, he will still rebel.
Reducing it leads to quicker rebellion with lesser disaster,
not reducing it delays rebellion but brings greater catastrophe."
Thus, the Hàn court debated reducing Wú's territory,
and Wú indeed rebelled.
Emperor Wǔ implemented Zhǔfù's strategy:
the Decree of Spreading Kindness.
Zhǔfù Yǎn advised the emperor:
"In ancient times, feudal lords held no more than a hundred lǐ,
making control over their strength or weakness easy.
Now some lords possess dozens of cities in a row,
spanning a thousand lǐ of land.
In times of peace, they grow arrogant and extravagant,
prone to debauchery and disorder;
in crisis, they leverage their strength to form alliances,
defying the capital.
If we now reduce them by law,
rebellious tendencies will sprout,
as seen previously with Cháo Cuò.
Currently, among the feudal lords' descendants, only the eldest succeed,
while the rest, though kin,
receive not an inch of land.
This obscures the way of benevolence and filial piety.
I urge Your Majesty to allow the lords to extend kindness,
granting lands to their younger sons as marquises.
They will each rejoice at having their wishes fulfilled.
While appearing beneficent,
this effectively divides their states,
weakening them inevitably."
The emperor followed his advice.
Emperor Jǐng faced the "Rebellion of the Seven States,"
suppressed the feudal lords,
and reduced their officials;
Emperor Wǔ dealt with the plots in Huáinán and Héngshān,
enacting the Law of Left Officials
(serving under a feudal king was termed 'left official'),
and establishing the Law Against Excessive Enfeoffment
(enfeoffing beyond limits was called 'excessive enfeoffment').
Feudal lords were left to collect rents and taxes,
with no part in governance.
By the time of Emperors Āi and Píng,
all were distant descendants,
with remote kinship,
raised behind palace curtains,
unrespected by scholars and commoners.
The imperial clan was stripped of power,
retaining titles without substance.
The empire lay barren,
retracing the path of the fallen Qín.
Thus, Wáng Mǎng, seeing Hàn's internal and external exhaustion and weakness,
with both root and branches frail,
acted without fear or restraint,
nursing treacherous ambitions.
Exploiting the empress dowager's authority,
borrowing the names of Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng,
he monopolized power and favors.
From the court hall,
he ruled the empire without descending the steps.
Once his deceitful schemes succeeded,
he assumed the position facing south,
dispatched officials of the Five Powers,
galloping across the land,
issuing mandates and prophecies.
The Hàn feudal lords kowtowed and bowed,
presenting their seals and ribbons,
fearing to be last—
is this not lamentable?
When Wáng Mǎng fell,
the empire plunged into turmoil.
Wěi Xiāo amassed forces in Tiānshuǐ,
and Bān Biāo sought refuge with him.
Xiāo asked Biāo:
"In the past, Zhōu lost control,
the Warring States contended,
the empire split,
and order was restored only after several generations.
I suspect
that the era of vertical and horizontal alliances
is upon us again!
Or will the rise of a new dynasty
depend on one man?
I wish to hear your opinion."
Biāo replied:
"The rise and fall of Zhōu differed from that of Hàn.
In Zhōu, there were five ranks of nobility,
and feudal lords participated in governance.
The root was weak,
while the branches grew strong.
Hence, in its decline, vertical and horizontal strategies emerged,
a natural outcome of circumstances.
Hàn inherited Qín's system,
establishing commanderies and counties.
The ruler held absolute authority,
while ministers lacked lasting power.
By Emperor Chéng's reign,
he relied on maternal relatives;
Emperors Āi and Píng had short reigns,
and the imperial line was thrice broken.
Thus, the Wáng clan monopolized the court.
They usurped the throne,
with danger arising from above,
leaving the lower levels unharmed.
Therefore, after their accession,
all under heaven looked up and sighed,
Over a span of more than ten years,
turmoil spread both within and beyond the central plains,
with uprisings erupting far and wide.
Pretenders to the throne gathered like clouds,
all claiming allegiance to the Liú clan,
speaking in unison without prior consultation.
The powerful leaders who now command provinces and cities
lack the hereditary foundation of the Seven Warring States,
yet the people sing and yearn for the virtue of the Hàn,
from which one can understand the situation. "
When Emperor Guāngwǔ restored the dynasty,
he succeeded to the imperial lineage,
yet still followed the tracks of the overturned cart,
nurturing the chronic ailment of a bereaved family.
In just a few generations,
corruption became rampant,
with powerful ministers often dominating the court;
then the whole world would follow like the wind;
if one man ran amok,
the city walls would crumble on their own—
is that not perilous?
Consider the difficulties of the Zhōu dynasty in reviving the royal house:
seven ministers defied orders,
three sons usurped positions,
the succeeding king abandoned the Nine Tripods;
malevolent clans seized the capital,
war drums shook the inner chambers,
arrows and blades flew at the crimson gates.
Yet the disaster was confined to the capital region,
the harm did not spread far,
and the realm remained tranquil.
Order awaited chaos,
thus King Xuān rose during the Gònghé period,
and Xiāng and Huì were bolstered by Jìn and Zhèng.
How unlike the two Hàn dynasties, where a brief disturbance at the palace steps
set the four seas boiling;
a treacherous minister enters in the morning,
and by evening the nine regions are in chaos!
Reflecting on Wáng Mǎng's usurpation in the past,
and observing Dǒng Zhuó's seizure of power recently,
millions grieve at heart,
fools and wise alike share the pain.
Is it that the era lacks ministers like those of old,
or scholars have no ambition to restore and unite?
Rather, distant achievements are stifled by changed times,
and grand ambitions are thwarted by humble circumstances.
Lù Jī said:
'Some say that hereditary positions for nobles
need not always be secure;
foolish rulers and tyrants
sometimes leave their traces,
hence the five ranks often lead to chaos.
Today's governors and prefects
are all promoted based on merit,
and though some may err,
their successes are many,
so commanderies and counties are easier to govern.
When virtue is splendid,
promotions and demotions occur daily,
leaders and subordinates are connected,
all fulfilling their duties;
then even debauched and foolish rulers
have no room for error—
why worry about disorder?
Thus earlier eras thrived because of this.
If decline sets in,
all norms become chaotic.
Officials who sell posts
measure talent by wealth,
then greedy and cruel sprouts become lords everywhere—
how can it not lead to chaos?
Hence later kings abandoned it for this reason.
To put it succinctly:
rulers of the five ranks think of order for themselves,
while commanders of counties aim to benefit others.
How to prove this?
Striving for advancement
is the constant aim of officials;
cultivating oneself to pacify the people
is what good scholars aspire to.
The drive for advancement is sharp,
while the reputation for pacifying the people is slow.
Therefore,
those who encroach on the people for self-gain
are not feared by those in power;
those who harm practical affairs to build fame
are what officials pursue day and night.
The ruler lacks plans for the long term,
ministers harbor ambitions for the moment.
The five ranks are not so:
they know the state is their own land,
the people are all their subjects.
If the people are secure, they benefit;
if the state is harmed, their families suffer the illness.
Thus superiors restrain desires to leave a legacy,
descendants think of their ancestral foundations;
those above have no careless hearts,
those below cherish bonds of solidarity.
If both are virtuous and in order,
achievements may vary in magnitude;
if both are foolish and in chaos,
faults differ in depth.
Yet examining the systems of eight dynasties,
one principle almost runs through them;
the statutes of Qín and Hàn
can nearly be summed up in one phrase.'
Emperor Wǔ of the Wèi dynasty, Cáo Cāo, possessed a sage's brilliance
and divine martial strategy.
He soared like a dragon from Qiáo and Pèi,
soared like a phoenix over Yǎn and Yù,
observed the survival and fall of five dynasties,
yet did not adopt their long-term strategies;
witnessed the overturning of preceding carts,
but did not alter their tracks.
He enfeoffed his sons in empty lands,
with no people for them to rule.
Their power equaled that of commoners,
their status no different from ordinary folk.
Internally, they lacked deep-rooted stability,
externally, they had no rock-solid alliances among the clan.
This was not the way to secure the state
as an enterprise for ten thousand generations.
Moreover, today's provincial governors and commandery chiefs,
akin to ancient feudal lords and regional chiefs,
all control territories spanning a thousand lǐ,
bearing military responsibilities.
Some have several men per state,
or brothers holding joint authority,
yet among the imperial clan's descendants,
not a single one is interspersed among them
to provide mutual support.
This does not strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches,
nor prepare for contingencies.
The times did not employ this strategy,
and later it led to decline.
This describes the foundational situations of Zhōu, Qín, Hàn, and Wèi.
Thus, examining the trends of their strength and weakness from start to end,
one can draw clear lessons.
Xún Yuè said:
'Afterward, all ruled through commanderies and counties,
abolishing the feudal lords.
The system of that time
was not necessarily the governance of a hundred kings.'
The discussion states:
The Zhōu dynasty held the realm for over 800 years.
Later generations declined,
and the feudal lords acted recklessly.
Even when its last descendant, King Nǎn, was reduced to a commoner,
he could still rely on interlocking branches for support,
名义上 remaining the shared sovereign of the realm.
At that time,
the Chǔ people inquired about the tripods,
the Jìn lord requested the tunnel burial,
though they wished to covet the Zhōu house,
they were constrained by the various Jī clans.
Was it that there were no ambitious villains?
They relied on the feudal lords to maintain order.
Hence the saying:
'A centipede with a hundred legs
does not stiffen even at death.
It has many supporters.'
This refers to that!
When the Yíng clan took charge,
learning from Zhōu's failures,
they abolished the five ranks,
established commanderies and counties;
the ruler possessed all within the seas,
yet his sons and brothers were mere commoners;
meritorious officials served diligently,
but defenders of the state received no fiefs.
He ruled the world in isolation,
monopolizing its benefits alone.
Upon his death,
the realm split apart.
Chén Shèng, baring his arm, led the cry first,
Liú Jì, grasping his sword, rose up after,
like tigers roaring and dragons glaring,
they extinguished the Qín clan.
Those heroes like Liú and Chén
were commoners,
without the power of Wú or Chǔ, not even land to stand an awl,
yet they drove crowds of untrained followers
and vied with the Son of Heaven for power,
because the people yearned for chaos,
and there were no feudal lords to aid the king to fear.
Therefore, it is said:
'Chaotic governance and cruel punishments
aid heroes and hasten disaster.'
This is what it means.
To cut down deep roots is hard to achieve;
to break dry rot is easy to accomplish.
Now, the five ranks
are the deep roots;
commanderies and counties
are the dry rot.
Thus from Qín onward,
up to Zhōu and Suí,
those who lost the imperial throne were not weakened by invasion,
those who gained the world did not endure long—
such was the nature of the state's situation.
Alas!
When governing through commanderies and counties,
it gives rise to the ambitions of commoners;
when employing the five ranks of nobility to rule the age,
there arise the calamities of horizontal and vertical alliances.
Thus it is known that all systems of governance
have their drawbacks.
It is not that feudal lords and earls lack the means to cause chaos,
nor that commanderies and counties are not tools for achieving order,
but rather that in planning the beginning, one seeks abundant blessings,
and in considering the end, one opts for fewer calamities,
hence the preference for the five ranks of nobility.
The sages, knowing this to be so,
therefore acted with utmost caution and diligence,
growing more prudent with each passing day,
cultivating virtue to stabilize the realm,
and selecting the worthy to employ them.
When virtue is cultivated and the worthy are chosen,
the common people find joy in their livelihoods.
Even with the sagacity of Tāng and Wǔ,
rebellion could not arise.
How much less could a mere commoner,
dare to bare one shoulder and raise a great cry?
This must not go unexamined.
The Nineteenth Discourse on Power among the Three Kingdoms: Shǔ, Wú, Wèi
It is said:
Your servant has heard that in the past, the Hàn dynasty lost its guiding principles,
and its net let the cunning and vicious slip through.
Yuán Běnchū gazed like a tiger upon Héshuò,
Liú Jǐngshēng rose like a magpie in Jīngzhōu,
Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suí heroically held Guānxī,
Lǚ Bù and Chén Gōng usurped command in Dōngxià,
from Liáo River to Hǎi and Dài,
there were over ten princes and lords,
each commanding a million troops and thousands of iron cavalry,
forming alliances and forging ties,
standing as the outstanding figures of their time.
Yet Cáo Cāo, "holding the emperor hostage to command the nobles,"
within six or seven years,
wiped out eight or nine out of ten of them.
Only Wú and Shǔ, insignificant states,
as shown on the map,
possessed merely the land of four provinces,
not comparable to the major cities of the central plains.
Their people were timid in public battles,
but fierce in private fights,
prone to flee and easily defeated in the north,
no match for the warriors of the various Huá states.
In comparing strengths and measuring capabilities,
weighing talents and assessing powers,
they were not as formidable as the two Yuáns, Liú, or Lǚ.
These two heroes, with newly established and unconsolidated states,
relying on a situation of rebellion and incomparable disadvantage,
yet could grasp their swords and look around,
contending with the Cáo clan for supremacy;
leaping on their horses and directing commands,
they reaped benefits all the way to the South Sea.
Why was this?
It was because the advantages of terrain differed,
and circumstances made it so.
Thus the "Yì Jīng" says:
"Kings and marquises set up barriers to guard their states."
An ancient saying goes:
"A thickness of one lǐ,
yet it can sway the power of a thousand lǐ,
is due to the advantage of terrain."
Thus, when Cáo Pī reached the Yangtze River,
saw the turbulent waves surging,
he sighed and said:
"This is what Heaven uses to divide north and south!"
Liú Zī called Nánzhèng the "Heaven's Prison" and the Xiégǔ Path the "Five Hundred Lǐ Stone Cave."
Consulting previous records,
all feared their depth and inaccessibility.
Although it is said:
When the Way of Heaven is followed,
terrain's advantage is not as good as human harmony.
If a person of average talent were to defend it,
they could prolong the period and sustain their fate,
how could the insignificant Dèng Ài and Wáng Jùn have exerted their grand strategies?
From this perspective,
it lies here, not there.
Ah!
"The considerations of the wise
must encompass both advantage and harm,"
thus "without fully understanding the harms of employing military force,
one cannot know the benefits of using it,"
has been a truth since ancient times.
Therefore, selecting the essentials,
this discourse on power is composed.
To encompass the five lakes,
and sweep through all of Shǔ,
one may understand the benefits within the harms,
and clarify the strategy of the Wèi house.
Shǔ
The Celestial Emperor administers governance from Fáng and Xīn constellations,
bringing order to the Shēnfā region.
Shēnfā corresponds to the celestial division of Yìzhōu,
bounded by Dōngjǐng, Nángǔ, and Jù stars,
specifically where Dōngjǐng, Nángǔ, and Jù stars connect with the Yùe constellation.
The Zī star degree lies at the right foot of Shēn,
which is the star held by the Yùjǐng constellation.
The western Jù star is the first star west of the central three stars of Shēn.
According to the "Zhìfāng," it is within the territory of Yōngzhōu,
while based on the "Yǔ Gòng," it belongs to Liángzhōu's domain.
The region spans five thousand lǐ,
encompassing forty commaneries,
truly a major metropolis.
Cháng Qú's "Records of the States" states:
"Shǔ,
its hexagram aligns with Kūn,
hence it abounds in patterned colors;
its celestial branch aligns with Wèi,
thus it emphasizes flavors.
The 'Shī' speaks of King Wén's influence,
reaching the lands of Jiāng and Hàn,
where King Wén's transformation is evident.
Qín and Bīn share the same odes,
Qín and Shǔ share the same division,
hence they possess the Xià sound."
Thus, it has long been called the 'Land of Abundance,'
with fertile plains stretching a thousand lǐ,
and for good reason.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
Gōngsūn Shù occupied Shǔ.
Shù, styled Zǐyáng,
was from Màolíng, Fúfēng,
and served as the Dàojiāng military governor under Wáng Mǎng,
governing Línqióng.
When Gēngshǐ ascended,
local strongmen rose in their counties to support Hàn,
with Nányáng's Zōng Chéng capturing Hànzhōng,
and merchant Wáng Cén also raising troops in Luò County,
proclaiming himself the General Who Pacifies Hàn,
to join Chéng.
Upon hearing this,
Shù sent envoys to welcome Chéng,
but when Chéng and others reached Chéngdū,
they plundered and acted violently,
displeasing Shù,
who summoned local elites and said:
"The world has long suffered under the Xīn dynasty,
yearning for the Liú family.
Now that the Hàn general has arrived,
I rushed to welcome him.
Yet now, innocent people are captured with their women and children,
homes burned—
these are bandits,
not righteous troops.
I intend to protect the commandery and defend it,
awaiting the true ruler.
Those of you willing to join forces may stay,
others may leave."
The elites all kowtowed, pledging their lives.
Shù then had someone pretend to be a Hàn envoy from the east,
appointing him General Who Assists Hàn and Governor of Yìzhōu.
He then selected over a thousand elite troops to attack Zōng Chéng,
defeating him.
He separately sent his brother Huī to Miánzhú to attack Zhāng Zhōng, the Yìzhōu inspector appointed by Gēngshǐ,
and defeated him too,
thus shaking Yìzhōu with his might.
Yìzhōu's officer Lǐ Xióng advised Shù:
"Now the world is in turmoil,
commoners debate recklessly,
yet you control a thousand lǐ,
land tenfold that of Tāng and Wǔ.
If you exert your virtue and power,
seizing heaven's gap,
you can achieve hegemony.
Currently, Shāndōng suffers famine,
people eat each other,
armies ravage,
cities lie in ruins.
Shǔ's fertile plains span a thousand lǐ,
with rich soil,
abundant fruits,
filling without grains.
Its textile industry
clothes the world;
famed timber and bamboo,
plentiful tools,
are inexhaustible.
It also benefits from fish, salt, copper, and iron,
with convenient water transport.
Holding Hànzhōng in the north,
it blocks Bāo Xié's passes;
guarding Bā Commandery in the east,
it secures Hànguān's entrance.
The land spans thousands of lǐ,
with warriors numbering millions.
Seize opportunities to expand,
or farm securely when none arise.
East down the Hàn River,
you can eye Qín lands;
south along the river,
you can shake Jīng and Yáng.
This is using heaven and earth,
the means to success.
Your reputation spreads wide,
yet your title is unsettled,
causing doubt among aspirants.
Assume the throne now,
so distant people have a focus."
Shù said:
"Emperors receive heaven's mandate;
what virtue have I to bear it?"
Xióng replied:
"Heaven's mandate shifts;
the people follow the capable—
the capable should take it.
Why hesitate?"
Thus, he agreed.
In April of the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
founding the 'Chéngjiā' dynasty,
adopting white as its color.
He sent General Hóu Dān to secure Báishuǐ Pass,
guarding Nánzhèng in the north;
General Rèn Mǎn advanced from Lángzhōng to Jiāngzhōu,
occupying Hànguān in the east,
thus controlling all of Yìzhōu.
After Gēngshǐ's defeat,
while Emperor Guāngwǔ focused on Shāndōng,
he had no time to campaign west.
Many Guānzhōng elites joined Shù with their followers.
Later, Pínglíng's Jīng Hán, seeing the east nearly pacified
and troops likely heading west,
advised Shù:
"Military might
is the tool of emperors,
indispensable through ages.
Wěi Áo seized fortune,
ruling Yōngzhōu,
with strong troops and loyal men,
imposing fear on Shāndōng.
Instead of pressing his advantage
to contend for the mandate,
he retreated to act like King Wén of the West,
disarming and resting,
submitting meekly to Hàn,
fancying himself a King Wǔ reborn.
Now the Hàn emperor, free of Guān-Lǒng worries,
concentrates on eastern campaigns,
holding three-quarters of the realm.
If he wins over western elites
to focus on Shāndōng,
sending covert envoys
to lure the wavering,
he'll gain four-fifths.
Marching on Tiānshuǐ,
it would surely collapse.
With Tiānshuǐ secured,
he'd hold eight-ninths.
Your Majesty, with Liángzhōu's land,
serving the court internally,
supplying the army externally,
the people are distressed,
unable to meet demands—
a rebellion like Wáng's may erupt.
My humble plan:
while heaven and people's hopes remain,
and elites can still be won,
swiftly deploy our best troops.
Have Tián Róng hold Jiānglíng,
overlooking the southern rivers' confluence,
secured by Wūshān's firmness,
building strong defenses,
issuing proclamations to Wú and Chǔ—
south of Chángshā
will surely submit like wind-blown grass;
have Yán Cén exit Hànzhōng,
secure Sānfǔ and Tiānshuǐ,
and Lǒngxī will surrender freely.
Thus, the realm will tremble,
promising great gain."
Shù consulted his ministers;
Scholar Wú Zhù said:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
eight hundred lords agreed unprompted,
yet he still waited for heaven's sign,
never launching campaigns
a thousand lǐ away
without support to expand borders."
Hán retorted:
"Now the eastern emperor, with no real power,
leads a motley crowd,
charging into battle,
flattening all in his path.
If we don't seize the moment to compete,
but sit discussing King Wǔ,
we mimic Wěi Áo's futile western ambition."
Fàn Yè commented:
"Raising banners and gathering clans,
He feigned the manifestation of divine traces.
In initiating plans and undertaking affairs,
one can discern his style.
Ultimately isolated in a corner,
positioned between major states,
though the Long slopes were narrow,
lacking the strategic advantage of a hundredfold defense,
with merely two commanderies to resist a formidable advance,
it is known that his methods held enough appeal
to attract outstanding talents from all directions.
When achievements are complete, reputation shines;
when undertakings fail, conflicts arise.
Those who turn defeat into a subject of debate
are perhaps unheard of!
If Wěi had encountered a fate aligned with the mandate,
and his adversaries were not backed by heaven's force,
sitting and discussing like King Wén of the West,
would he have been much ridiculed?
Shù did not heed Hán's advice.
Emperor Guāngwǔ then sent Cén Péng and Wú Hàn to attack Shǔ,
breaching Jīngmén,
and driving straight into Jiāngguān.
Cén Péng was killed by a Shǔ assassin,
and Wú Hàn took command of his army,
entering the boundaries of Qiánwéi,
where all the counties fortified their defenses.
Hàn then advanced to attack Guǎngdū,
capturing it,
and dispatched light cavalry to burn Chéngdū;
the small towns east of Shìqiáo and Yángwǔ all surrendered.
Emperor Guāngwǔ cautioned Hàn, saying:
"Chéngdū has a hundred thousand troops;
do not take it lightly.
Just firmly hold Guǎngdū,
wait for them to attack,
and do not contend with their vanguard.
If they dare not come to attack,
shift camp and pursue them,
waiting until their strength is exhausted
before striking."
Hàn, taking advantage of the situation, led over twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to press toward Chéngdū,
camping over ten lǐ from the city,
setting up defenses north of the river,
and constructing a floating bridge.
He ordered his deputy Liǔ Shàng to station over ten thousand troops south of the river,
about twenty lǐ apart.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ heard of this,
he was greatly alarmed,
and reprimanded Hàn:
"If the enemy sends troops to pin you down,
and uses their main force to attack Shàng,
once Shàng is defeated,
you will be defeated too!
If nothing else happens, fortunately,
quickly lead your troops back to Guǎngdū."
Before the edict arrived,
Shù indeed sent his general Xiè Fēng to attack Hàn,
and dispatched another general to harass Liǔ Shàng,
preventing mutual reinforcement.
Hàn then closed his camp,
not emerging for three days,
erecting many banners,
and keeping smoke and fires continuously lit.
At night, moving silently, he led his troops to join Shàng's forces,
unnoticed by Fēng and others.
The next day,
they divided troops to hold the north bank,
while Hàn personally attacked the south bank,
defeating them
and beheading Xiè Fēng.
Then he withdrew back to Guǎngdū,
reporting the situation to Emperor Guāngwǔ,
who replied:
"Your return to Guǎngdū
is very appropriate;
Shù will surely not dare to bypass Shàng and attack you.
If he attacks Shàng first,
you can lead all your infantry and cavalry from fifty lǐ away in Guǎngdū to assist,
catching them exactly when they are weary and exhausted,
and are certain to defeat them!"
From then on,
Hàn fought Shù in the area around Guǎngdū,
winning eight battles in a row,
and eventually stationed troops in the outer city.
Shù then distributed gold and silk extensively,
recruiting five thousand dare-to-die soldiers,
and assigned them to Yán Cén.
Cén falsely set up flags at Shìqiáo,
beating drums to provoke battle,
while secretly sending surprise troops behind Wú Hàn's army,
launching a surprise attack
that defeated Hàn.
Hàn fell into the water
and escaped by clinging to a horse's tail.
Shù then personally led an attack on Hàn,
engaging three times and winning all.
From dawn until noon,
the soldiers had no food,
and all were exhausted.
Hàn then ordered his strong warriors to charge,
and Shù's troops were badly defeated.
When the army reached Chéngdū,
Shù came out to fight,
was initially defeated and stabbed,
pierced through the chest and died.
Shù's wife and children were executed,
and his palace burned.
Emperor Guāngwǔ heard of this,
angrily rebuking Hàn:
"The city had surrendered for three days,
with officials and people submitting.
To suddenly release troops and set fires
truly violates the principle of executing generals while comforting the people."
He then issued an edict to console them.
Those of loyal integrity and righteous purpose
were all honored and recognized;
Lǐ Yù was promoted for his talent and capability.
Thus, the western lands felt moved and pleased,
and none failed to give their allegiance.
Fàn Yè said:
"In the past, Zhào Tuó ruled over Pānyú,
and Gōngsūn also usurped the title of emperor in Shǔhàn.
Considering they had no other merits or abilities,
yet lasted until later downfall,
was it because their remote border locations
were not prioritized by the kingly influence?
Failing to seize opportunities to achieve deeds,
and adapt to the changes of the times,
they instead sat idly, adorning the fringes,
finding security in their isolation,
as Wú Qǐ once shamed the Marquis of Wèi for.
As for their dismissal of ministers,
and examination of the mandates of rise and fall,
compared to those who bowed their heads in submission,
it is a different matter to discuss."
By the time of Emperor Líng,
governance had declined and deteriorated,
the royal house faced many troubles,
powerful heroes vied for supremacy,
and territories were split apart.
Liǔ Yān was appointed as the Governor of Yìzhōu.
Yān
was a descendant of the Gōng King of Lǔ.
At that time, with rebellions and bandits everywhere,
Yān believed that provincial inspectors lacked authority,
so he proposed establishing regional governors instead,
to pacify the regions,
carefully selecting senior ministers for the posts,
and Yān was made Governor of Yìzhōu.
At that time,
bandits in Liángzhōu gathered thousands of weary conscripts,
first killing the magistrate of Miánzhú,
then attacking Luò County.
The provincial aide Jiǎ Lóng, who had been leading several thousand troops in Qiánwéi,
rallied officials and people to attack the rebels,
defeating them.
He then selected officials to welcome Yān,
who thus assumed the role of Governor of Yìzhōu.
When Yān died,
his son Zhāng succeeded him.
Senior officials like Zhào Wěi, greedy for Zhāng's mild benevolence,
installed him as Inspector.
Initially,
tens of thousands of households from Nányáng and the Sānfǔ regions had migrated into Yìzhōu,
and Yān had enlisted them all as followers,
naming them
the "Eastern Province troops."
Zhāng was gentle and lenient by nature,
lacking authority and strategy,
and the Eastern Province people committed abuses.
Zhào Wěi, exploiting popular discontent,
allied with powerful clans in the province.
The Eastern Province people, fearing execution,
united their efforts
and fought desperately for Zhāng,
beheading Zhào Wěi.
At that time, Zhāng Lǔ also considered Zhāng weak,
and did not submit to him,
establishing his own power in Bāshǔ.
Surrounded by Liú Bèi,
he eventually surrendered.
Bèi relocated Zhāng to Gōng'ān,
returning his treasures.
Later, Zhāng died of illness.
Initially,
Liú Bèi was the Governor of Yùzhōu.
Bèi,
styled Xuándé,
was from Zhuō County in Zhuō Commandery.
He spoke little,
was good at humbling himself to others,
and did not show joy or anger on his face.
Táo Qiān, Governor of Xúzhōu, recommended the First Sovereign as Governor of Yùzhōu.
Later, when Qiān fell ill,
he sent someone to welcome the First Sovereign,
who said:
"Yuán Gōnglù is nearby in Shòuchūn;
this gentleman, with four generations of five lords,
is revered throughout the land.
You should give the province to him."
Chén Dēng said:
"Yuán Shù is arrogant and boastful,
not a ruler capable of bringing order out of chaos.
Now I wish to gather for you, my lord, a force of one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
so that on the grand scale, you may support the sovereign and aid the people,
achieving the feats of the Five Hegemons;
on the lesser scale, you may carve out territory and defend its borders,
recording your merits in the annals of history.
If you, my lord, do not heed this,
then I, Dēng, dare not follow you either."
Kǒng Róng said to the Late Sovereign:
"Is Yuán Shù one who worries about the state and forgets his family?
Why should you mind a dried-up bone in a grave?
In the affairs of today,
the people support the capable.
If Heaven offers it and you do not take it,
regret will be beyond remedy."
Thus, he took control of Xúzhōu.
Chén Dēng sent an envoy to Yuán Shào, saying:
"Heaven has sent down calamity,
disaster has reached our humble province,
and the provincial governor has perished.
The gentry and people are without a leader,
fearing that treacherous heroes might seize the opportunity,
thereby causing you, our alliance leader, concern as the sun sets.
We have therefore jointly supported the Chancellor of Píngyuán, Prefect Liú,
to be our patriarchal leader,
so that the people may forever know they have someone to rely on.
Currently, bandit troubles run rampant,
and we have no leisure to lay down our arms.
We respectfully send a minor official to inform your attendants."
Shào replied:
"Liú Xuándé
is broad-minded, refined, trustworthy, and righteous.
Now that Xúzhōu gladly supports him,
it truly matches my hopes."
He was defeated by Lord Cáo,
and fled to station at Xīnyě.
At that time, Liú Biǎo passed away,
and Zhūgě Liàng advised attacking Cóng,
so that Jīngzhōu could be taken.
The Late Sovereign said:
"When Jīngzhōu faced destruction,
it entrusted me with its orphaned children;
I cannot bear it."
Many people of Jīngzhōu defected to the Late Sovereign,
and the Late Sovereign traveled only over ten lǐ per day.
Someone said:
"We should hasten to secure Jiānglíng."
The Late Sovereign said:
"Those who accomplish great deeds
take the people as their foundation.
Now that the people follow me,
how can I bear to abandon them?"
Xí Zàochǐ said:
"Though Lord Liú faced颠沛流离 and perilous difficulties,
his trustworthiness and righteousness grew even clearer;
though pressed by circumstances and in dire straits,
his words did not stray from the Way;
recalling Liú Biǎo's regard,
he moved the three armies with emotion;
cherishing those who sought righteousness,
he willingly shared defeat with them.
Observing how he won the hearts of the people,
was it merely by sharing wine, comforting the weary, enduring bitterness, and inquiring after the ill?
That he ultimately succeeded in his great enterprise—
is it not fitting?"
Hearing that Zhūgě Liàng was farming personally in Nányáng,
he went three times to visit Liàng in his thatched cottage,
and, dismissing others, said:
"The Hàn house is collapsing,
treacherous ministers have usurped authority,
and the sovereign is covered with dust.
I, despite my limited virtue and strength,
wish to uphold great righteousness
throughout the world,
but my wisdom and methods are shallow and short,
thus I have suffered setbacks,
reaching this day.
Yet my will has not ceased.
What strategy do you advise?"
Liàng replied:
"Since Dǒng Zhuó's time,
heroes have arisen together,
those spanning provinces and commanderies
are too many to count.
Cáo Cāo, compared to Yuán Shào,
had lesser fame and fewer followers,
yet he was able to overcome Shào.
Turning weakness into strength—
it was not only due to Heaven's timing,
but also to human planning.
Now Cáo has a host of a million,
holding the Emperor to command the nobles.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
'To seek the nobles' support,
nothing is better than upholding the king.'
This refers to such a case.
Truly, one cannot contend with him.
Sūn Quán holds Jiāngdōng,
already through three generations,
the state is secure and the people attached,
and the worthy and capable serve him.
He can be allied with for support,
but cannot be taken.
Jīngzhōu, north based on the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
profits extend to the South Sea,
east connecting Wú and Kuàijī,
west linking to Bā and Shǔ—
this is a land for military use,
yet its ruler cannot hold it.
This is likely Heaven's provision for you, General.
Yìzhōu has impregnable passes,
fertile fields,
a land of natural abundance,
which Gāozǔ used to achieve imperial enterprise.
Liú Zhāng is dim and weak,
with Zhāng Lǔ in the north;
though the people are prosperous and the state rich,
he does not know compassion,
so the wise and capable
long for an enlightened lord.
You, General, are a scion of the imperial house,
your trustworthiness and righteousness renowned throughout the land,
you gather heroes,
and thirst for the worthy.
If you hold both Jīng and Yì,
guard their rugged terrain,
make peace with the western Róng tribes,
pacify the southern Yí and Yuè peoples,
form an alliance with Sūn Quán,
and internally cultivate good governance—
when changes occur in the empire,
then order a top general to lead Jīngzhōu's army
toward Wǎn and Luò;
while you personally lead Yìzhōu's hosts
out through Qínchuān.
Would the people not bring food and drink
to welcome you, General?
If it truly be so,
then hegemonic enterprise can be achieved,
and the Hàn house can be revived."
At that time, Lord Cáo took Jīngzhōu,
and the Late Sovereign fled to Wú.
Regarding the Late Sovereign's flight to Wú,
commentators thought Sūn Quán would surely kill him.
Chéng Yù predicted:
"Lord Cáo is unmatched under heaven;
having just taken Jīngzhōu,
his might shakes the lands south of the river.
Though Quán has strategy,
he cannot withstand it alone.
Liú Bèi is a hero,
and Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi are both match for ten thousand;
Quán will surely use them as resources to defend against us.
As the situation is entangled and hard to resolve,
Bèi will succeed with that support—
he cannot be killed."
Quán indeed gave Bèi many troops
to resist the Grand Progenitor.
At that time, Yìzhōu's governor Liú Zhāng heard Lord Cáo was attacking Jīngzhōu,
and sent his Assistant Official Zhāng Sōng to Lord Cáo.
Lord Cáo had already secured Jīngzhōu
and driven away the Late Sovereign.
Lord Cáo did not retain or employ Sōng,
so Sōng advised Zhāng to break with him.
Xí Zàochǐ said:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí once boasted of his achievement,
and nine states rebelled;
Cáo Cāo gradually grew arrogant and self-aggrandizing,
and the empire divided into three.
Both labored for decades,
yet lost it in a moment—
is it not regrettable?
Therefore, the nobleman toils humbly till sunset,
considering how to defer to others;
with high achievement, he maintains it with yielding;
with honored status, he preserves it with humility.
Only then can he possess wealth and honor,
safeguard his accomplishments,
and transmit blessings for a hundred generations.
What room is there for arrogance?
Thus, the nobleman knows that Cáo Cāo could not ultimately unite the empire."
Bèi employed Liàng's strategy,
formed an alliance with Sūn Quán,
and together resisted Lord Cáo at Chìbì,
defeating him.
Lord Cáo returned north,
and Quán then gave Jīngzhōu to Bèi as his base.
Zhōu Yú submitted a memorial advising:
"Liú Bèi, with his fierce hero's bearing,
and with Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi as fierce tiger generals,
will surely not long remain subordinate to another.
I propose a grand plan:
move him to Wú,
build him lavish residences,
and provide him with many beauties and objects of pleasure
to delight his senses."
Divide these three men,
placing each in a separate region.
If someone like Zhōu Yú
could leverage them in battle,
the grand enterprise could be settled.
Now recklessly ceding territory
to empower them,
gathering all three at the border—
I fear they would be like flood dragons encountering rainclouds,
no longer creatures confined to ponds."
Since Sūn Quán recognized Cáo Cāo's presence in the north,
he believed he should broadly recruit heroes,
thus he did not accept this advice.
Páng Tǒng advised Liú Bèi, saying:
"Jīngzhōu is desolate and ravaged,
its population depleted.
To the east is Sūn Quán of Wú,
to the north the Cáo clan.
A tripartite balance strategy
would be difficult to achieve.
Now Yìzhōu enjoys national wealth and military strength,
with a population of a million households,
where troops and horses from its commanderies,
along with all necessary provisions,
are fully self-sufficient without external needs.
You may temporarily borrow it to settle the grand enterprise."
Liú Bèi replied:
"The one who stands against me like fire and water
is Cáo Cāo.
Where Cáo employs haste,
I employ patience;
where Cáo employs cruelty,
I employ benevolence;
where Cáo employs deceit,
I employ loyalty.
Only by consistently opposing Cáo's methods
can affairs succeed.
To lose trust and righteousness over minor matters
is something I cannot accept."
Páng Tǒng said:
"In times requiring flexibility,
matters cannot be settled by one principle alone.
Annexing the weak and conquering the ignorant—
this was the way of the Five Hegemons;
taking by force but guarding through benevolence,
repaying with righteousness—
after affairs are settled,
enfeoffing him with a large state—
how would this betray trust?
If you do not take it today,
it will ultimately benefit others."
Liú Bèi then left Guān Yǔ to guard Jīngzhōu
and intended to take Shǔ himself.
At that time, Sūn Quán sent an envoy to inform Liú Bèi,
proposing a joint campaign against Shǔ,
saying:
"The Rice Bandit Zhāng Lǔ occupies Bāhàn,
serving as Cáo Cāo's eyes and ears,
plotting to take Yìzhōu,
while Liú Zhāng cannot defend it himself.
If Cáo captures Shǔ,
then Jīngzhōu will be endangered.
Now I wish to first attack and capture Zhāng,
then advance against Zhāng Lǔ,
coordinating from start to finish,
unifying Wú and Chǔ—
even if there were ten Cáos,
we would have nothing to fear."
Some advised Liú Bèi to agree to the proposal,
arguing that Wú ultimately could not cross Jīngzhōu to hold Shǔ,
so the land of Shǔ could be taken.
But Registrar Yīn Guān said:
"If we become Wú's vanguard,
and if we fail to conquer Shǔ in the advance,
we might be attacked by Wú on our return—
then the grand enterprise would be lost!"
Liú Bèi followed this advice,
refusing and replying to Quán:
"Yìzhōu has a wealthy people and strong state,
with rugged, defensible terrain.
Though Liú Zhāng is weak,
he can adequately defend himself.
Zhāng Lǔ is duplicitous
and not necessarily loyal to Cáo.
To march troops into Shǔhàn,
transporting supplies over thousands of miles,
expecting every battle to succeed
without loss—
this is something even Wú Qǐ could not plan,
nor Sūn Wǔ execute perfectly.
Now Cáo Cāo holds two-thirds of the realm,
soon to water his horses in the Cāng Sea,
and parade his troops in Wúkuài.
For allies to attack each other without cause,
giving Cáo the advantage—
allowing the enemy to exploit this rift—
is no strategy."
Quán understood Liú Bèi's intent
and desisted.
Meanwhile, Liú Zhāng heard that Cáo Cāo was marching toward Hànzhōng against Zhāng Lǔ,
and felt inner fear.
His Assistant Inspector Zhāng Sōng advised him:
"Cáo Cāo's troops are strong,
matchless under heaven.
If he uses Zhāng Lǔ's resources
to take the land of Shǔ,
who can resist him?
Liú Yùzhōu (Bèi),
is of your own imperial clan,
and Cáo Cāo's bitter enemy.
If you send him to attack Lǔ,
Lǔ will surely be defeated.
With Lǔ defeated, Yìzhōu will be strengthened—
even if Cáo Cāo comes,
he can accomplish nothing."
Zhāng agreed,
sending Fǎ Zhèng to receive the Imperial Uncle (Liú Bèi).
At that time, Huáng Quán admonished:
"General of the Left (Liú Bèi) has a reputation for fierceness.
If treated as a subordinate, he will be dissatisfied;
if treated as a guest, one state cannot accommodate two rulers.
If the guest is secure as Mount Tài,
the host will be in peril like piled eggs.
I urge you to close the borders and await clearer times."
Meanwhile, Liú Bā also admonished:
"Bèi
is a man of heroic caliber.
If he enters, he will surely act—
he cannot be admitted."
After Bèi entered,
Bā added:
"To send Bèi against Zhāng Lǔ
is to release a tiger into the mountains."
Zhāng ignored all such advice.
The Imperial Uncle met Zhāng at Fú.
After Zhāng returned to Chéngdū,
the Imperial Uncle was to campaign north for Zhāng against Hànzhōng.
Páng Tǒng again advised Bèi:
"Secretly select elite troops,
march day and night,
and directly assault Chéngdū.
Since Zhāng lacks martial prowess
and is ordinarily unprepared,
when the great army suddenly arrives,
it can be taken in one move—
this is the superior plan.
Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi,
Zhāng's famous generals,
each command strong troops
guarding the passes.
I have heard they have repeatedly sent letters advising Zhāng
to send you back to Jīngzhōu.
Before you are sent back, contact them;
claim Jīngzhōu is in crisis
and you must return to rescue it,
making preparations
to appear as if departing.
These two admire your reputation
and will be pleased by your departure—
they will surely come lightly mounted to see you off.
Seize them then,
take their troops,
then advance toward Chéngdū—
this is the middle plan.
Return to Báidì,
link up with Jīngzhōu,
and slowly plan later—
this is the inferior plan.
If you hesitate and do not leave,
you will soon face great difficulty—
you cannot remain long."
The Imperial Uncle approved the middle plan.
Earlier,
when Zhāng Sōng and Fǎ Zhèng met Bèi,
Bèi received them with personal attention,
showing utmost courtesy.
He inquired about Shǔ's weapons, treasuries, troop numbers, and strategic points—
Sōng and others told him everything,
even drawing maps
depicting mountains and rivers,
thus revealing all of Yìzhōu's strengths and weaknesses.
The Imperial Uncle went north to Jiāméng
but did not immediately attack Lǔ,
instead building generous favor to win the people's hearts.
The following year,
when Cáo Cāo attacked Sūn Quán,
Quán called for the Imperial Uncle's aid.
Bèi then asked Zhāng for ten thousand troops and supplies,
intending to march east to aid Quán.
Zhāng only granted four thousand troops,
with the rest halved.
Bèi thus incited his troops, saying:
"I campaign for Yìzhōu against a powerful enemy,
my men toil diligently,
with no moment of peace—
yet now he hoards stored wealth
and begrudges rewarding merit.
Can we expect officers to fight to the death
under such conditions?"
He then summoned Zhāng's Báishuǐ Army Commander Yáng Huái.
He was reproached for his lack of propriety,
and executed.
Liú Bèi sent Huáng Zhōng and others to lead the army toward Liú Zhāng.
The Vanguard Lord went directly to the pass,
taking the wives and children of the various generals and soldiers as hostages.
He led his troops to follow Huáng Zhōng and others, advancing to Fú,
and occupied the city.
All the generals sent by Liú Zhāng were defeated.
He then executed Huái and others,
and turned south from Jiāméng to attack Liú Zhāng.
At that time, Zhèng Dù advised Liú Zhāng, saying:
"The Left General has attacked us,
with fewer than ten thousand troops,
his forces not yet loyal,
relying on wild grains for supplies.
The best strategy would be to drive all the people of Bāxī and Zǐtóng
inside the area west of the Fú River,
and burn all their stored and wild grains.
Then build high fortifications and deep moats,
and wait quietly.
When they request battle, do not permit it.
After a long time without supplies,
within a hundred days at most,
they will surely retreat on their own.
If we attack them as they retreat,
we will certainly capture them."
Liú Zhāng did not adopt Zhèng Dù's plan.
The Vanguard Lord then advanced swiftly,
conquering every place he passed,
and thus gained Bā and Shǔ.
When Liú Bèi attacked Shǔ,
the Assistant to the Chancellor, Zhào Jiǎn, said:
"Will Liú Bèi not succeed?
He is clumsy in using troops,
losing every battle he fights,
constantly fleeing with no respite—
how can he plan to conquer others?
Although Shǔ is a small state,
it is secure and fortified on all sides,
a country that can defend itself alone,
difficult to annex quickly."
The recluse scholar Fù Gàn said:
"Liú Bèi is generous, benevolent, and measured,
able to win people's utmost loyalty.
Zhūgě Liàng understands principles and adapts to change,
upright and strategic, serving as his chancellor.
Zhāng Fēi and Guān Yǔ are brave and righteous,
both match for ten thousand men, serving as his generals.
These three men are all outstanding figures.
With Liú Bèi's strategy
and the assistance of these three heroes,
how can he not succeed?"
The Vanguard Lord besieged Chéngdū for several tens of days,
and Liú Zhāng came out and surrendered.
Shǔ was prosperous and abundant,
so the Vanguard Lord held a feast to reward his soldiers,
taking gold and silver from the Shǔ city to distribute among his officers and men,
and returning the grain and silk.
Initially, when attacking Liú Zhāng,
Bèi made a pact with his troops, saying:
"If matters are settled,
all the treasures in the government storehouses,
I will have no part in them!"
After capturing Chéngdū,
the troops all laid down their weapons and rushed to the treasuries,
competing to seize precious items.
Military supplies became insufficient,
and Bèi was very concerned.
Liú Bā said:
"It's easy!
Just cast coins worth a hundred,
stabilize the prices of goods,
and have officials manage the market."
Bèi followed his advice.
Within a few months,
the government storehouses were full.
The Vanguard Lord assumed the role of Governor of Yìzhōu,
with Zhūgě Liàng as his right-hand man,
Fǎ Zhèng as chief strategist,
Guān Yǔ, Zhāng Fēi, and Mǎ Chāo as his military commanders,
and Xǔ Jìng, Mí Zhú, and Jiǎn Yǒng as his guests and friends.
Dǒng Hé, Huáng Quán, Lǐ Yán, and others were originally appointed by Liú Zhāng;
Wú Yī, Fèi Guān, and others were his relatives by marriage;
Péng Yàng was someone Liú Zhāng had rejected;
Liú Bā was someone he had long resented.
Yet all were placed in prominent positions,
and their talents were fully utilized.
Ambitious men all competed to contribute.
The ministers urged the Vanguard Lord to assume the imperial title,
but he initially refused.
Zhūgě Liàng said:
"In the past, Wú Hàn, Gěng Chún, and others urged Emperor Guāngwǔ to ascend the throne.
Emperor Guāngwǔ declined repeatedly.
Gěng Chún then advised, saying:
'The heroes of the world are eagerly looking up,
hoping for something to aspire to.
If you do not follow their advice,
the scholars and officials will each seek another lord,
and no one will follow you, my lord.'
Emperor Guāngwǔ, moved by Gěng Chún's profound words,
then agreed.
Now, the Cáo family has usurped the Hàn,
and the world is without a ruler.
You, Great King, are a descendant of the Liú lineage,
rising to continue the dynasty.
Ascending the imperial throne is indeed appropriate.
The scholars and officials who have long toiled
also hope for some measure of merit and fame,
just as Gěng Chún said."
The Vanguard Lord then assumed the imperial throne.
Qiáo Zhōu and others urged his advancement, saying:
"Before my late father, Qún, passed away,
he said that several times in the southwest, there was yellow vapor,
standing straight up for several zhàng,
appearing over the years,
often accompanied by auspicious clouds and winds responding from the celestial pivot.
This is an extraordinary omen.
Also, in the twenty-second year,
several times there were vapors like banners,
stretching from west to east,
moving across the mid-heaven.
The charts and texts say:
'There must be an Son of Heaven arising from that direction.'
That year,
Venus, Mars, and Saturn often followed Jupiter,
closely pursuing each other.
When the Hàn first rose,
the five stars followed Jupiter's lead,
with Jupiter governing righteousness.
The Hàn's position is in the west,
the direction of righteousness.
Thus, the Hàn method often used Jupiter to await the ruler.
A sage ruler should arise in this province,
to bring about a revival.
At that time, the Emperor of Xǔ was still alive,
so the officials did not dare speak openly.
Recently, Mars has again followed Jupiter,
now in the constellations Wèi and Mǎo.
Wèi and Mǎo form the celestial net.
The Classic says:
'When an emperor resides there,
all evils will vanish.'
We hope the Great King will comply with Heaven and accord with the people,
quickly establish the great enterprise,
to bring peace to the land."
At that time, Lord Cáo captured Hànzhōng.
Initially,
the Grand Ancestor of Wèi defeated Zhāng Lǔ in Hànzhōng,
and Liú Yè proposed a strategy, saying:
"My lord, you have defeated Yuán Shào in the north and campaigned against Liú Biǎo in the south,
uniting eight out of ten commanderies across the nine provinces,
your might shaking the world,
your influence awe-inspiring beyond the seas.
Now, with the capture of Hànzhōng,
the people of Shǔ will tremble at the news,
losing their courage and defenses.
Pushing forward from this,
Shǔ can be pacified by proclamation.
Liú Bèi is an outstanding man,
but he is cautious and slow.
He has not long held Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ are not yet loyal to him.
Their hearts are shaken with fear,
and the situation is naturally unstable.
If we press on this instability,
we will surely overcome.
If we delay slightly,
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng, who excels in governance,
and Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, whose bravery leads the three armies,
will use military might to intimidate
and civil virtue to pacify,
holding strategic points and defenses,
making them unassailable!
If we do not seize this moment,
there will surely be future troubles."
The Grand Ancestor did not follow his advice.
After seven days,
defectors from Shǔ reported turmoil in Shǔ,
and even executions could not stop it.
The Grand Ancestor asked Liú Yè again:
"Can Shǔ be attacked now?"
He replied:
"Now it has slightly stabilized;
we cannot move against it."
Fǎ Zhèng advised the Vanguard Lord, saying:
"Cáo Cāo, in one move, forced Zhāng Lǔ to surrender and secured Hànzhōng,
yet he did not use this momentum to conquer Bā and Shǔ.
Instead, he left Xiàhóu Yuān and Zhāng Hé to garrison the area
and hastily returned north himself.
This is not because his wisdom is lacking
or his strength insufficient,
but because he has internal troubles pressing him."
Now considering the talents and strategies of Yuān and Hé,
they are no match for the generals of our state.
If we raise an army to campaign against them,
we are certain to overcome them.
On the day of victory,
we should expand agriculture and accumulate grain,
watching for signs of conflict and awaiting opportunities.
At best, we can overthrow the enemy forces,
honoring and supporting the royal house;
at a medium level, we can nibble away at Yōng and Liáng,
expanding our borders and territory;
at worst, we can firmly hold strategic points,
as a plan for prolonged resistance.
This is surely heaven granting it to us,
a moment not to be lost."
The Former Lord approved his strategy,
and thus led his generals to advance troops into Hànzhōng,
with Zhèng also accompanying the march.
The Former Lord crossed the Miǎn River south from Yángpíng,
advanced gradually along the mountains,
and set up camp at Dìngjūn Mountain.
Yuān led troops to contest the territory.
Zhèng said:
"Now is the time to attack."
The Former Lord ordered Huáng Zhōng to take the high ground, beating drums and shouting as they attacked,
greatly defeating Yuān's army,
with Yuān and others being beheaded,
thus swiftly capturing Liáng and Hàn.
At that time, Wèi sent Xiàhóu Mào to guard Cháng'ān,
and Shǔ general Wèi Yán requested troops from Zhūgě Liàng to emerge from Bāo Zhōng,
follow the Qín Ridge eastward,
turn north at Zǐwǔ,
to surprise attack Cháng'ān,
but Liàng did not permit it.
The Wèi Lüè states:
"Xiàhóu Mào was the General Pacifying the West,
guarding Cháng'ān.
Zhūgě Liàng was discussing plans with his subordinates in Nánzhèng,
when Wèi Yán said:
'I hear Xiàhóu Mào
is the son-in-law of the young sovereign,
timid and without strategy.
Now if you grant Yán five thousand elite troops,
with five thousand carrying provisions,
directly emerging from Bāo Zhōng,
following the Qín Ridge eastward,
turning north at Zǐwǔ,
in no more than ten days,
we can reach Cháng'ān.
When they hear of Yán's sudden arrival,
he will surely flee by boat.
Cháng'ān will only have the Censor and the Governor of the Capital,
with the granaries at Héngmén and scattered grains,
enough to sustain us.
By the time the eastern forces gather,
it will still take about twenty days,
and you, sir, coming from Xiégǔ,
will also have ample time to arrive.
Thus, in one move, the area west of Xiányáng can be secured!'
Liàng considered it too risky and not as safe as following
a level path to steadily take Lǒngyòu,
ensuring complete success without worry,
hence he did not adopt Yán's plan.
Whenever Yán followed Liàng on campaigns,
he often requested ten thousand troops to take a different route and meet Liàng at Tóngguān,
following the precedent of Hán Xìn.
Liàng restrained him and did not permit it.
Yán often said Liàng was timid,
sighing in regret that his own talents were not fully utilized."
Later, Wú's Sūn Quán attacked Guān Yǔ,
capturing Jīngzhōu.
Liú Bèi had ordered Guān Yǔ to guard Jīngzhōu.
Wú general Lǚ Méng was appointed Governor of Hànchāng, sharing borders with Guān Yǔ,
knowing Yǔ was a fierce hero with ambitions to annex,
and moreover occupied the upper reaches,
making the situation difficult to sustain.
Méng then secretly proposed a strategy, saying:
"Now the Expeditionary General guards Nánjùn,
Pān Zhāng leads mobile troops along the river upstream and down,
responding to where the enemy is.
Méng will advance to hold Xiāngyáng for the state.
In this way,
what worry is there of Cāo?
What reliance is there on Yǔ?"
The general considered it,
and as Yǔ was campaigning against Fán,
he left troops and generals to defend Nánjùn.
Méng submitted a memorial saying:
"Yǔ campaigns against Fán yet leaves many defensive troops,
surely fearing Méng would plot against his rear.
Méng has often been ill,
I beg to take some troops back to Jiànyè,
under the pretext of seeking treatment.
When Yǔ hears of this,
he will surely withdraw the defensive troops,
all heading to Xiāngyáng.
Then our main force can sail up the river,
driving day and night upstream,
attacking their undefended areas,
thus Nánjùn can be taken,
and Yǔ can be captured."
So he claimed to be critically ill,
and Quán openly issued a summons for Méng to return,
secretly planning with him.
Yǔ indeed believed it,
gradually withdrawing troops to Fán.
Quán then sent Méng ahead,
hiding elite troops in merchant vessels,
having them dress in white as merchants rowing,
traveling day and night,
reaching the riverbank outposts set by Yǔ,
capturing them all,
so Yǔ did not hear of it.
Méng entered and occupied the city,
capturing all the families of Yǔ's officers and soldiers,
comforting them all,
ordering the army not to disturb households or make any demands.
As Yǔ was returning on the road,
Quán sent messengers to communicate with Méng,
and Méng always treated his envoys generously.
When Yǔ sent people back,
they all learned their families were safe,
treated better than usual,
so Yǔ's officers and soldiers lost their will to fight,
all abandoning Yǔ to surrender,
and even father and son were captured together.
Initially,
when Sūn Quán campaigned against Yǔ,
he sent envoys to inform Wèi, saying:
"I wish to campaign against Guān Yǔ to prove myself,
and beg you not to reveal it.
If Yǔ becomes prepared,
all ministers say secrecy is appropriate."
Dǒng Zhāo said:
"Military affairs value adaptability,
aiming for appropriateness.
We should reveal the matter.
When Yǔ hears of Quán's advance,
he will immediately return to protect his city,
and the siege will be quickly lifted,
allowing us to gain the advantage.
We can let the two enemies contend with each other,
and we take advantage of their weakness.
If we keep it secret and not reveal,
allowing Quán to succeed,
is not the best plan."
So they shot letters into the besieged area and Yǔ's camp.
The Marquis hesitated and did not leave.
When Lù Xùn arrived,
he captured Jiānglíng.
Yǔ fled to Línjū,
where he was killed by Wú general Pān Zhāng.
The Former Lord was angered at Wú,
attacked them,
but was defeated.
He returned to Shǔ,
and passed away at Yǒng'ān.
Initially,
when Wèi Emperor Wén heard that Bèi was moving east to battle Sūn Quán,
setting up a linked camp over seven hundred lǐ long,
he said to his ministers:
"Bèi does not understand military strategy;
how can a seven-hundred-lǐ camp resist the enemy?
Encamping over plains, marshes, and obstacles,
one will be captured by the enemy,
which is忌讳 in military texts.
News of Sūn Quán's success will arrive soon!"
Seven days later,
Quán defeated Bèi at Yílíng,
and the report arrived.
Later, the Later Lord Shàn ascended the throne.
He issued an edict saying:
"I have heard that those who accumulate good deeds prosper,
and those who accumulate misfortunes perish,
a constant principle through the ages.
In the past, the Hàn destiny declined,
the net let evil slip through,
Dǒng Zhuó created calamity,
shaking the capital region;
Cáo Cāo escalated the disaster,
usurping the imperial authority;
his son Pī, a lowly wretch,
dared to follow the path of chaos,
stealing the sacred vessels,
changing the surname and altering institutions,
perpetuating their wickedness.
At that time,
the world was without a ruler,
and our imperial mandate faltered below.
The Emperor Zhāoliè brilliantly displayed civil and martial virtues,
preserving and restoring the ancestral enterprise,
rightly shouldering the imperial order,
not letting it fall to the ground.
While the myriad states were not yet pacified,
he passed away early,
and I, in my youth,
succeeded to the great task,
not yet trained in the teachings of guardians,
yet bearing the weight of the ancestors,
striving to continue the former legacy.
There has been no success in crossing,
and I am deeply fearful.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng is resolute, loyal, and robust,
forgetting his own safety to worry about the state.
Now, I entrust him with the heavy authority of the commander's banner and axe,
granting him the power to act autonomously,
leading an army of two hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
overseeing the main forces,
reverently executing the celestial punishment,
eliminating troubles and pacifying chaos,
to reclaim the old capital—
all depends on this campaign.
Attack their commander,
and show compassion to their remaining people;
the rest shall follow the edicts and laws."
Prior to this,
the Wu ruler Sūn Quán sought peace.
Wu sent Zhāng Wēn as an envoy to Shǔ,
and Quán said to Wēn:
"You should not travel far,
but I fear that Zhūgě Kǒngmíng does not understand my reasons for communicating with the Cáos.
Thus, I burden you with the duty of an envoy,
accepting the mission but not the specific words."
Wēn replied:
"As a minister, I lack strategic insights inwardly,
and outwardly, I am not adept at independent diplomacy;
I fear I have no merit like Zhāng Lǎo in extending reputation,
nor the effectiveness of Zǐchǎn in presenting affairs.
However, Zhūgě Liàng is perceptive and calculating,
surely he knows the appropriateness of divine considerations for yielding and advancing,
and moreover, he receives the heaven-sheltering grace of the court.
Inferring Liàng's heart,
he will certainly have no doubts or duplicity."
When Wēn arrived in Shǔ,
he went to the court and presented a memorial:
"In the past, Gāozōng used the period of mourning to
prosper the Yin dynasty in its revival;
King Chéng, while young,
elevated the virtue of Zhōu to great peace.
Now, Your Majesty, with your intelligence and talent,
equals the ancients,
entrusting all governance to excellent assistants,
participating in the brilliant radiance of elite officials,
near and far gaze upon your influence,
all rejoicing and relying on it.
The state of Wǔ diligently exerts its strength,
purifying the riverbanks,
wishing to unite the world with the virtuous in peace,
devoting heart and coordinating plans,
as steadfast as the river waters.
I, the humble envoy Wēn, am sent to convey goodwill.
Your Majesty upholds rites and righteousness,
and has not disdained to neglect this.
Since I entered your borders,
and reached the outskirts,
I have repeatedly been welcomed and comforted,
feeling honored yet apprehensive."
Shǔ sent Mǎ Liáng as an envoy to Wú.
Liáng said to Liàng:
"Now, bearing the state's command,
to harmonize the two families,
I hope you will kindly introduce me to General Sūn."
Liàng said:
"You try drafting the text yourself."
Liáng then drafted:
"My humble ruler sends his official Mǎ Liáng to communicate and renew friendship,
to continue the achievements of Kūnwú and Shǐwéi.
He is a virtuous man,
outstanding in Jīngchǔ,
lacking in hasty brilliance,
but possessing the beauty of seeing things through.
I hope you will lower your heart to accept him,
to comfort the envoy's mission."
Quán received him with great respect.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng, fearing that Sūn Quán might have different plans upon hearing of the late emperor's death,
sent Dèng Zhī to repair relations with Quán.
Quán indeed hesitated and did not receive Zhī promptly;
Zhī submitted a request for an audience.
Quán said to Zhī:
"I sincerely wish to make peace and ally with Shǔ,
but I fear the Shǔ ruler is young and weak,
the state small and pressured,
vulnerable to being exploited by Wèi,
unable to preserve itself.
That is why I hesitate."
Zhī replied:
"The two states of Wú and Shǔ,
with four provinces of land,
Your Majesty is a heroic figure of the age,
and Zhūgě Liàng is a standout talent of the time.
Shǔ has the security of formidable barriers,
Wú has the obstacles of the three rivers;
combining these two strengths,
acting as lips and teeth to each other,
advancing, they can conquer the world,
retreating, they can stand as a tripod.
This is the natural course of events.
If Your Majesty now submits to Wèi,
Wèi will surely demand your attendance at court above,
and require your heir to serve within below.
If you refuse,
they will have grounds to attack the rebel,
and Shǔ will surely follow the current,
advancing when the opportunity arises.
In that case,
the lands south of the river,
will no longer be yours."
Quán remained silent for a long time and said:
"You are right."
Thus, he broke off with Wèi,
and allied with Shǔ.
At that time, Minister Huà Xīn, Minister Wáng Lǎng, and others,
wrote to Zhūgě Liàng,
explaining the mandate of heaven,
wanting Shǔ to become a vassal.
Liàng did not reply to the letter,
but wrote "Righteous Argument":
"In the past, Xiàng Yǔ,
rose without virtue,
though he held the central plains,
wielding imperial power,
he ended up in the boiling cauldron,
a warning to later generations.
Wèi fails to learn from this,
and now follows his path.
Escaping with their lives would be fortunate,
but extinction awaits their descendants.
Yet these men indulge in the deceitful rhetoric of Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
presenting the outrageous words of Huān Dōu,
trying to slander the Táng emperor,
and subtly dismiss Yǔ and Jì,
thus merely displaying literary flair,
toiling with brush and ink—
something a noble gentleman would not do.
Moreover, the 'Military Records' say:
'With ten thousand men resolved to die,
they can roam the world unhindered.'
In the past, Xuānyuán led tens of thousands of troops,
subdued the four emperors,
and stabilized the land;
how much more can hundreds of thousands,
upholding righteousness and facing the guilty,
be challenged!"
After Liàng's death,
Wèi ordered Dèng Ài to attack Shǔ,
and the Shǔ army was defeated.
The later ruler followed Qiáo Zhōu's advice and surrendered to Wèi.
Discussion:
A ruler should die for the state if necessary,
or perish for the state if required.
Qiáo Zhōu advised the later ruler to surrender to Wèi—
was this acceptable?
Sūn Shèng said:
"According to the principles of the 'Spring and Autumn Annals',
a ruler dies for the altars of soil and grain,
and ministers die in their posts;
how much more should an emperor avoid humiliation by others?
For Qiáo Zhōu to persuade the ruler of ten thousand chariots
to cling to life and survive ignobly,
abandoning propriety for gain,
seeking trivial glory,
is deluded!
Moreover, considering the circumstances,
the reasoning is incomplete—
why?
Although Liú Shàn was a mediocre ruler,
he was not as cruel as Jié or Zhòu;
though defeated repeatedly in battle,
there was no collapse into chaos.
Even if ruler and ministers could not hold firm,
they could have fought one last battle defending the city,
or retreated to the eastern borders,
to plan for the future.
At that time, Luó Xiàn held Báidì with a strong force,
Huò Yì guarded Yèláng with robust troops;
the land of Shǔ is rugged and narrow,
with steep mountains and rivers isolating it,
sheer cliffs and raging torrents
impassable for infantry.
If they had gathered all boats,
held Jiāngzhōu securely,
recruited troops from the south,
and sought aid from the eastern state,
then generals like Jiāng and Liáo,
would naturally flock like clouds;
the two armies of Wú,
would rush like lightning upon command.
Why think there was no place to turn,
and assume inevitable destruction?
When the Wèi army came,
it was a massive invasion of the state.
If pursued, they had no boats;
if they stayed, the army would grow weary and face many risks.
Moreover, opportunities for advance and retreat arise,
and situations change dynamically;
gradually using those loyal to the old regime to attack the proud and lazy troops—
this is how King Zhāo repelled Hé Lǘ and Tián Dān crushed Qí Jié.
Why act in rash anger,
hastily becoming a captive prisoner, lowering strong walls to the enemy?"
Why must we bear the ultimate regret of cutting stone?
Gě Shēng once said:
'If the endeavor fails, then so be it;
how can one submit to another again?'
How heroic these words are!
They can inspire the timid to find their resolve!
Observing the defeats of ancient Yān, Qí, Jīng, and Yuè,
where states were toppled and rulers perished,
or people were hung like fish or fled like birds,
yet they ultimately achieved merit and established legacies,
restoring the altars of state.
Can it be said it was heaven's aid,
or was it human strategy?
Had they harbored plans for mere survival and heeded Qiáo Zhōu's words,
how could the crumbling foundations have been rebuilt or glorious reputations attained?
Liú Shàn was indeed a dim-witted ruler,
and Qiáo Zhōu a truly inept minister;
compared to Shēn Bāoxū, Tián Dān, Fàn Lǐ, or Wén Zhǒng,
are they not far inferior?"
During the Jìn dynasty,
Lǐ Tè again seized Shǔ.
Initially,
Lǐ Tè acted violently and oppressively in Shǔ,
so Jìn offered a bounty for him and his brothers,
promising great rewards.
Before long,
the proclamation was heard,
and the original document was not concealed.
Lǐ Tè's son Lǐ Xīng saw the notice
and altered all the bounties to read:
"Whoever dares behead the leaders of the six commanaderies—Lǐ, Rén, Yán, Zhào, etc.—and one Dí elder chief,
and present them to the authorities,
will be granted a heavy reward."
The people of the six commanderies were terrified upon seeing this,
and thus all rebelled and joined Lǐ Tè.
The Governor of Yìzhōu, Luó Shàng, sent Wěi Bó to attack Lǐ Xióng at Píchéng,
with victories and defeats alternating.
In the tenth month of winter,
Lǐ Xióng gave Pǔ Tài gold,
then whipped him until he bled,
ordering Tài to feign offense and flee to Luó Shàng,
intending to act as an insider.
Luó Shàng believed him,
and sent troops to follow.
Tài and Xióng attacked from within and without,
crushing Luó Shàng's army.
Xióng pursued the retreating forces,
reaching the city walls by night,
where he shouted "Long live,"
deceiving those in Luó Shàng's city by saying:
"We have already taken Píchéng."
Luó Shàng believed it,
opened the minor city gate,
and Xióng's troops entered.
Luó Shàng then fled,
and thus Xióng captured Chéngdū and declared himself king.
He was later destroyed by Jìn's Huán Wēn.
By the Yìxī era of the Sòng dynasty,
Qiáo Zòng again killed the Governor of Yìzhōu, Máo Qú, in Chéngdū,
proclaiming himself King of Chéngdū.
Initially,
Máo Qú sent Rèn Yuē to join the righteous army,
but when the army reached Zhījiāng,
they encountered Liú Yì's defeat,
and Yuē fled to Huán Zhèn.
Upon hearing of Yuē's flight to Huán Zhèn,
Máo Qú personally led three thousand troops,
advancing via the outer river route.
Qiáo Zòng served as his army consultant,
tasked with leading five hundred Liángzhōu soldiers,
setting out from the inner river.
The Liángzhōu troops were unwilling to head east,
so they pushed Qiáo Zòng to be their leader,
turned back to attack Fúchéng,
and captured it.
When Máo Qú heard of the uprising,
he left Lüèyáng City,
and returned on foot to Chéngdū,
where he was killed by Zòng's partisans.
The Sòng dynasty sent Zhū Língshí to destroy them,
and this is the situation of the Shǔ state.
Discussion says:
Wú and Shǔ are interdependent states like lips and teeth;
if Shǔ falls, Wú perishes—is this credible?
Lù Shìhéng stated:
"Shǔ is but a supportive ally,
not the determinant of Wú's survival or demise.
Why so?
Their borders connect
through layered mountains and accumulated dangers,
with no long-chariot paths on land;
rivers are narrow and flows turbulent,
presenting the perils of startling waves.
Even with a million sharp troops,
those setting forth cannot exceed a thousand men;
with vessels stretching a thousand miles,
those advancing ahead are no more than a hundred ships.
Thus, the Liú clan's campaign against General Lù
can be likened to a long serpent,
such is the nature of the terrain."
Hence Huáng Quán remarked:
"One can advance,
but it is hard to return—
this is the 'entangled ground' in warfare."
An ancient saying goes:
"In narrow paths and perilous roads,
it is like two rats fighting in a hole—
the bolder general will prevail."
Wú
Chǒu corresponds to the stellar division of Xīng Jì,
which is the domain of Wú and Yuè.
Above, it aligns with the constellations of Dǒu and Niú;
below, it occupies the position of Shàoyáng.
Present-day Kuàijī, Jiǔjiāng, Dānyáng, Yùzhāng, Lújiāng, Guǎnglíng, Lù'ān, and Línhuái
all belong to the division of Wú;
while present-day Cāngwú, Yùlín, Hépǔ, Jiāozhǐ, Jiǔzhēn, Rìnán, and Nánhǎi
all belong to the division of Yuè.
The ancients had a saying:
"South of the great river,
amid the five lakes,
the people there have frivolous hearts.
Yángzhōu maintains strength—
bǎo,
meaning to rely on.
In the three dynasties, it was a barely submissive territory,
not governed with proper administration.
When the state is well-ordered, it submits last;
when it is in chaos, it rebels first."
Hence, the "Zhuàn" states:
"Wú is like a giant boar and long snake,
repeatedly preying on the central states,
posing a threat to them—
this did not accumulate in just one day."
During the reign of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Yínghùi, the King of Huáinán, rebelled.
Bù's capital was at Lù'ān,
which is present-day Shòuzhōu.
When the news of the rebellion reached the court,
the emperor summoned his generals
and asked:
"Bù has rebelled;
what should we do about it?"
Téng Gōng, the Marquis of Rǔyīn, said:
"My guest, the former Prime Minister of Chǔ, Xuē Gōng,
has strategies
and can be consulted."
Earlier, when Téng Gōng asked the Prime Minister,
the Prime Minister said:
"He was bound to rebel."
Téng Gōng asked:
"The emperor granted him land to make him a king,
bestowed titles and rewards,
established him facing south,
as a ruler of ten thousand chariots;
why would he rebel?"
The Prime Minister replied:
"Last year, Péng Yuè was killed;
the year before, Hán Xìn was killed.
These three men were comrades in achievement and of one body.
He suspected disaster would befall him,
hence he rebelled."
The emperor then summoned
and questioned Xuē Gōng,
who responded:
"Bù's rebellion
is not surprising.
If Bù adopts the superior strategy,
the lands east of the mountains will no longer belong to Hàn;
if he adopts the middle strategy,
the outcome of victory or defeat is uncertain;
if he adopts the inferior strategy,
Your Majesty can rest easy on your pillow."
The emperor asked:
"What are the superior, middle, and inferior strategies?"
The Prime Minister said:
"Capture Wú to the east
(present-day Sūzhōu),
seize Chǔ to the west
(present-day Jīngzhōu),
annex Qí and take Lǔ
(Qí
is Qīngzhōu;
Lǔ
is Yǎnzhōu),
spread proclamations to Yān and Zhào,
and firmly hold their positions—
then the lands east of the mountains will not belong to Hàn.
Comment:
Forming an alliance east of the mountains
as a long-term strategy
is the superior plan.
What is the middle strategy?
Capture Wú to the east,
seize Chǔ to the west,
annex Hán and take Wèi,
occupy the granaries of Áocāng,
block the pass of Chénggāo—
then the outcome of victory or defeat
is uncertain.
Comment:
Advancing swiftly into Luòyáng
to decide the war in one battle
is the middle plan.
What is the inferior strategy?
Capture Wú to the east,
take Xiàcài to the west,
shift focus to Yuè,
and retreat to Chángshā—
then Your Majesty can rest easy,
and Hàn will be untroubled."
Comment:
Expanding in the region south of the Yangtze,
with no ambition to eye the central plains,
is the inferior plan.
Huán Tán's "Xīn Lùn" states:
"There is a game of wéiqí in the world,
some say it is akin to the art of war.
When playing it,
the superior player spreads his stones widely,
setting them to encircle,
then attacks accordingly,
gaining much advantage—
this is the victory of strategy.
The middling player focuses on blocking and seizing key points,
striving for convenience and profit,
so victory or defeat remains doubtful,
requiring calculation to decide.
The inferior player guards the corners and edges, hastily making small formations,
to survive in limited territory."
Yet, it is also insightful to examine Xuē Gōng's words:
The superior plan mentioned
"taking Wú and Chǔ,
annexing Qí, Lǔ, Yān, and Zhào."
This refers to expanding territory broadly.
The middle plan mentioned
"taking Wú and Chǔ,
annexing Hán and Wèi,
blocking Chénggāo,
and occupying Áocāng."
This is like seizing key points to contend for advantage.
The inferior plan mentioned
"taking Wú and Xiàcài,
holding Chángshā to approach Yuè."
This is like guarding corners and edges, making small formations.
Guà
is pronounced as in wéi guà fǎn.
The emperor asked:
"Which strategy will he adopt?"
The Prime Minister replied:
"The inferior strategy."
The emperor said:
"Why would he abandon the superior and middle strategies for the inferior one?"
The Prime Minister said:
"Bù was originally a convict from Lìshān;
he elevated himself to a state of ten thousand chariots,
all acting for himself without considering the future or planning for eternity.
Thus, he will choose the inferior strategy."
The emperor said:
"Good."
It indeed turned out as predicted.
Xuē Gōng was then enfeoffed with a thousand households.
Later, Liú Bì, the King of Wú, rebelled due to his son's affair.
At the outset of the rebellion,
his general Tián Lùbó said:
"If the troops mass together and march west,
with no other unusual tactics,
it will be hard to achieve success.
I wish to take fifty thousand elite troops,
separately advance along the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
capture Huáinán and Chángshā,
enter Wǔguān,
and rendezvous with Your Majesty—
this would also be an ingenious move."
The crown prince of Wú advised against it:
"Your Majesty is rebelling in name;
such troops are hard to entrust to others—
if entrusted, they might rebel against you."
The King of Wú did not consent.
His junior general, Huán Jiāngjūn, again advised the King of Wú:
"Wú has many infantry,
which are advantageous in rough terrain;
Hàn has many chariots and cavalry,
which excel on flat land.
I hope that as Your Majesty passes through cities and towns,
if they do not surrender,
you should abandon them and press on,
swiftly heading west to seize the armory in Luòyáng,
consume the grain of Áocāng,
hold the strategic barriers of mountains and rivers,
and command the various lords.
Even without entering the passes,
the empire would be firmly secured.
If instead, Your Majesty advances slowly,
lingering to capture cities,
and Hàn's chariots and cavalry arrive,
charging into the regions of Liáng and Chǔ,
then the cause will fail."
The king consulted his elder advisors,
who said:
"This is just the plan of a youth to break the enemy's vanguard;
how could he understand grand strategy?"
The King of Wú did not follow Huán Jiāngjūn's advice
and instead personally commanded all his troops.
Hàn sent Zhōu Yàfū, the Grand Commandant, to attack Wú and Chǔ;
Yàfū employed a strategy from his father's guest
and ultimately defeated Wú.
The guest's strategy is recorded in the Annals of Hegemony.
Liú Ān, the King of Huáinán, harbored resentment over the death of his father, King Lì Cháng,
and plotted rebellion.
He asked Wǔ Bèi:
"If I raise troops and march west,
the various lords are sure to respond;
but what if they do not?"
Bèi replied:
"Gather forces from Héngshān in the south
(Héngzhōu),
to attack Lújiāng
(Lúzhōu).
With the ships of Xúnyáng,
