and guarding the city of Xiàzhì
(located in Jiāngxià,
a county name),
linking the ports of the Jiǔjiāng,
and blocking the entrance of Yùzhāng
(that is Hóngzhōu),
deploy strong crossbows along the river for defense
to prevent the eastern commanderies from advancing.
In the east, gather Jiāngdū
(Yángzhōu) and
Kuàijī
(Yuèzhōu),
open routes to the powerful Yuè in the south,
and stand firm between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
This could still prolong our survival for some time."
The King said:
"Good."
Before he could act,
the plot was leaked,
and he was executed.
Later, during the reigns of Emperor Líng and Xiàn of Hàn,
eunuchs wielded power arbitrarily,
the empire was in turmoil,
and governance fell into the hands of powerful families.
Hé Jìn plotted to eliminate the eunuchs,
but the Empress Dowager did not consent.
Jìn then summoned Dǒng Zhuó to the capital,
to pressure the Empress Dowager.
He secretly instructed Zhuó to submit a memorial stating:
"The eunuchs like Zhāng Ràng have abused their favor and power,
throwing the land into chaos.
In the past, Zhào Yǎng raised troops in Jìnyáng
to expel the evil at the ruler's side.
I shall sound the drums and bells,
march to Luòyáng,
and punish Ràng and others for their crimes."
Before Zhuó arrived,
Hé Jìn failed and was killed.
When Zhuó reached the capital,
he proceeded to depose and enthrone emperors,
plunging the empire into chaos.
It is commented:
"Powerful families"
refer to high officials.
At that time, Sūn Jiān, Governor of Chángshā, killed Zhāng Zī, Governor of Nányáng,
allowing Yuán Shù to seize the commandery.
Jiān allied with Shù,
intending to attack and seize Liú Biǎo's Jīngzhōu.
Jiān was hit by a stray arrow
and died.
Earlier,
when Liú Biǎo held Jīngzhōu,
he heard that bandits were rampant south of the river
and said to Kuǎi Yuè and others:
"I wish to conscript troops,
but fear they will not gather.
What strategy should I adopt?"
The reply was:
"If the masses do not submit,
it is due to lack of benevolence;
if they submit but are not orderly,
it is due to lack of righteousness.
If the ways of benevolence and righteousness are practiced,
the people will flock to you like water flowing downward.
Why worry about their lack of allegiance?
Yuán Shù is brave but lacks strategy;
the clan bandits are greedy and cruel,
causing suffering to the people.
If we offer them benefits,
they are sure to come in numbers.
You can then execute the unprincipled,
pacify and employ the rest.
With people feeling secure,
they will surely come carrying their children on their backs.
With strong troops and loyal followers,
holding Jiānglíng in the south
and guarding Xiāngyáng in the north,
the eight commanderies can be pacified by proclamation.
Even if Shù and others come,
they can do nothing."
Later, it turned out as predicted.
After Sūn Jiān's death,
his son Cè took command of his troops,
attacked Liú Yáo, the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
defeated him,
and thus occupied Jiāngdū.
Cè heard that Yuán Shù intended to claim the throne
and wrote to admonish him:
"In the past, Dǒng Zhuó was tyrannical,
oppressing the royal house,
bringing disaster upon the Empress Dowager,
and violence to Hóngnóng.
The Son of Heaven was displaced,
and the ancestral temples burned.
Thus, heroes rose in indignation,
swiftly rallying together.
Yet in Héběi, there were divergent plots at Hēishān,
Cáo Cāo spread poison in Dōngxú,
Liú Biǎo usurped power in Jīngnán,
and Gōngsūn rebelled in the northern borders.
Zhèng Lǐ hindered with troops,
Xuán Dé contended for alliances.
I had thought you, sir, shared the nation's norms,
but instead, neglecting this,
you calmly harbor ambitions to seize the throne,
which I fear is not what the world expects.
When Chéng Tāng attacked Jié,
he still said:
'The Xià have many crimes.'
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he said:
'The Yīn deserve severe punishment.'
These two kings,
despite their sage virtue,
would have had no pretext to seize power
had the times not been marked by such misrule.
Now, the sovereign has not wronged the empire;
he is merely young
and coerced by powerful ministers,
unlike the times of Tāng and Wǔ.
Your family has served for five generations,
as chancellors to Hàn,
enjoying honors and favor
unmatched by any.
You should demonstrate loyalty
to repay the royal house."
Shù did not accept,
so Cè broke off relations with him.
Cè heard that Cáo Cāo and Yuán Shào were locked in stalemate at Guāndù
and planned to cross the river to attack Xǔ.
Before he could cross,
he was killed by Xǔ Gòng's retainers.
Earlier,
when Cè had this plan,
everyone was fearful,
but Guō Jiā, a strategist for Wèi, assessed:
"Cè
is a hero and a man of prowess,
able to inspire people to die for him.
Yet he is reckless and unprepared;
even with a million troops,
he is like a man walking alone in the central plains.
If assassins lie in ambush,
he faces but a single adversary.
In my view,
he is bound to die at the hands of a commoner."
Indeed, he was killed by Xǔ Gòng's retainers.
After Cè's death,
his brother Quán took command of his forces.
At that time, Wú controlled the region south of the river,
sweeping through Jiāo and Guǎng.
After Lord Cáo defeated Yuán Shào,
his military prestige grew daily,
so he sent a letter demanding Sūn Quán
send a hostage.
Zhāng Zhāo and others convened but could not decide.
Quán then took only Zhōu Yú
to his mother to settle the matter.
Yú said:
"In the past, the state of Chǔ was first enfeoffed by the Jīng Mountains,
with less than a hundred lǐ of land.
But with successive wise and capable rulers,
they expanded their territory,
established their capital at Yǐng,
and thus held Jīng and Yáng,
reaching as far as the South Sea,
passing on their legacy and prolonging their rule
for over nine hundred years.
Now, General, you inherit the foundation of your father and brother,
commanding the forces of six commanderies,
with elite troops and ample supplies,
and officers and soldiers ready to obey.
You mine mountains for copper,
boil the sea for salt,
your domain is prosperous,
and the people have no thoughts of rebellion.
With boats ready and sails raised,
you can set out at dawn and arrive by dusk.
The morale is strong and brave,
unmatched wherever they go.
Why feel compelled to send a hostage?
Once a hostage is sent,
you will have to align with the Cáos;
if the Cáos summon,
you will have to go.
then one would be controlled by others.
How could this be the same as facing south and declaring oneself lord?
It would be better not to send him,
and slowly observe the changes.
If the Cáo family upholds righteousness to rectify the world,
it would not be too late for the general to serve them;
if they plan to commit violence and chaos,
war is like fire,
if not restrained,
it will inevitably burn oneself.
Conceal courage and rest on prestige,
to await the Mandate of Heaven,
what need is there to send a hostage?"
Quán's mother said:
"Gōngyú's advice is correct."
Thus, they did not send a hostage.
Cè passed away,
Quán was young,
initially taking charge of affairs.
The Grand Consort was worried,
and summoned Zhāng Zhāo, Dǒng Xí, and others for an audience.
She asked:
"Can Jiāngdōng be kept secure?"
Xí replied:
"Jiāngdōng's terrain has the solidity of mountains and rivers,
and the late General Who Pacifies Rebels, our wise lord,
his kindness and virtue remain among the people;
the General Who Attacks Barbarians inherits the foundation,
all, great and small, follow orders.
Zhāng Zhāo manages the masses,
Xí and others serve as claws and teeth,
this is a time of advantageous terrain and harmonious people,
there is absolutely nothing to worry about."
All were impressed by his words.
Later, Lord Cáo entered Jīngzhōu,
Liú Cóng surrendered with all his forces.
Initially, when Liú Biǎo died,
Lǔ Sù proposed:
"Now Jīngchǔ borders us,
its rivers flow northward,
externally bordered by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
internally protected by mountainous terrain,
it is a city of metal walls.
With fertile fields stretching thousands of miles,
and its people prosperous and wealthy.
If we can seize and hold it,
this would be the foundation for an emperor.
I request to be sent on a mission,
to condole with Biǎo's two sons,
and also comfort and reward those in charge of the army.
Persuade Liú Bèi to have him care for Biǎo's followers,
and together resist Cáo Cāo."
Before Sù arrived,
Cóng had already surrendered.
Cáo Cāo obtained their naval vessels,
and hundreds of thousands of infantry,
the Wú generals and soldiers heard this and were all afraid.
Sūn Quán summoned his subordinates,
asking for strategies.
Those discussing all said:
"Lord Cáo,
is a wolf and tiger.
In name, he is the Hàn chancellor,
leveraging the emperor to campaign in all directions,
always using the court as his pretext.
To resist him now,
would be even more unfavorable.
Moreover, the general's greatest advantage to resist Cāo,
is the Cháng Jiāng.
Now Cāo has taken Jīngzhōu,
fully possessing its territory,
Liú Biǎo's trained navy,
with assault ships and warships numbering in the thousands,
Cāo deploys them all along the river,
additionally having infantry,
advancing by both water and land,
this means the strategic advantage of the Cháng Jiāng,
is already shared with us!
And the disparity in strength and numbers is beyond comparison.
In my humble opinion, the grand strategy,
is to welcome him rather than resist."
Zhōu Yú said:
"Not so.
Although Cāo claims to be the Hàn chancellor,
in reality, he is a Hàn traitor.
General, with your divine and martial prowess,
coupled with the legacy of your father and elder brother,
holding Jiāngdōng,
a land of thousands of miles,
with ample elite troops,
and heroes willing to serve,
you ought to march across the world,
to rid the Hàn house of its evils.
Moreover, Cāo is coming to his own death,
how can we welcome him?
Allow me to plan for the general:
if the northern lands were already stable,
Cāo had no internal worries,
he could afford a prolonged war,
to contend for borders with us,
then it would be feasible for him to decide victory or defeat with us on boats;
but now the north is not yet stable,
Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suì are still west of the pass,
posing a threat to Cāo's rear;
furthermore, abandoning saddled horses to rely on boats,
to compete with Wú and Yuè,
is not the strength of the central plains;
also, now it is severely cold,
horses lack fodder,
driving the central plains' troops far to navigate rivers and lakes,
unaccustomed to the climate,
they will surely fall ill.
These several points,
are the perils of using troops,
yet Cāo risks them all.
For the general to capture Cāo,
the time is now.
I request thirty thousand elite troops,
to advance and station at Xiàkǒu.
I guarantee to defeat him for the general."
Quán said:
"The old traitor has long wanted to abolish Hàn and set himself up,
only fearing the two Yuáns, Lǚ Bù, Liú Biǎo, and me.
Now those heroes are gone,
only I remain,
the old traitor and I cannot coexist.
You say we should strike,
which greatly aligns with my view,
this is Heaven granting you to me."
At that time, Quán's army was at Cháisāng,
Liú Bèi was at Fán,
Lord Cáo campaigned south against Liú Biǎo,
coinciding with Biǎo's death,
his son Cóng surrendered with all his forces.
The First Sovereign did not know Lord Cáo had suddenly arrived,
only hearing of it upon reaching Wǎn,
so he led his forces south,
but was pursued and defeated by Lord Cáo.
When Liú Bèi reached Xiàkǒu,
Zhūgě Liàng said:
"The situation is critical!
I request to be sent to seek help from General Sūn."
Thus, he went for an audience,
and persuaded:
"General, you raised troops in Jiāngdōng,
while Liú Yùzhōu also gathered forces south of the Hàn River,
competing with Cáo Cāo for the world.
Now Cāo has eliminated major threats,
and is largely pacified.
Having taken Jīngzhōu,
his might shakes the land,
leaving heroes no room to wield their power,
hence Yùzhōu fled here.
General, assess your strength and decide:
if you can oppose the central plains with the forces of Wú and Yuè,
it would be better to break with him early;
if you cannot withstand him,
why not disarm and surrender,
and serve him as a subject?
Now, outwardly, you profess submission,
while inwardly hesitating,
in crisis but indecisive,
disaster will be upon you any day!"
Quán said:
"If it were as you say,
why doesn't Liú Yùzhōu simply serve him?"
Liàng said:
"Tián Héng,
was merely a brave man of Qí,
yet he upheld righteousness and did not disgrace himself,
let alone Liú Yùzhōu, a descendant of the royal house,
with talent surpassing the age,
admired by many,
like water flowing to the sea.
If his endeavor fails,
it would be Heaven's will,
how could he again be subordinate to another?"
Quán flared up:
"I cannot surrender all of Wú's land and a hundred thousand troops to be controlled by others.
My decision is made!
No one but Liú Yùzhōu can stand against Cáo Cāo.
However, after Yùzhōu's recent defeat,
can he withstand this challenge?"
Liàng said:
"Although Yùzhōu's army was defeated at Chángbǎn,
the returning warriors and Guān Yǔ's elite troops number ten thousand,
Liú Qí's forces from Jiāngxià also total no less than ten thousand.
Cáo Cāo's troops,
having come from afar, are exhausted,
having pursued Yùzhōu,
their cavalry traveled three hundred lǐ in a day and night,
this is what is called 'the arrow at the end of its flight cannot pierce the silk of Lǔ.'
Hence, the Art of War warns against it, saying:
'It will surely defeat the commanding general.'
Moreover, northerners are not skilled in naval warfare,
and those in Jīngzhōu who joined Cāo,
did so under military pressure,
not out of genuine loyalty.
Now if the general truly orders a fierce commander to lead tens of thousands of troops,
to coordinate and join forces with Yùzhōu,
We are certain to defeat Cáo Cāo's army!
Once Cáo's forces are crushed,
he will surely retreat northward.
Thus, the power of Jīng and Wú will strengthen, forming a tripartite balance.
The turning point between success and failure
lies in this very day."
Sūn Quán was greatly pleased,
immediately dispatching Zhōu Yú and Lǔ Sù
to accompany Liàng to meet the First Sovereign,
joining forces to resist Lord Cáo.
With thirty thousand naval troops under Zhōu Yú and others,
they united with Liú Bèi to oppose Lord Cáo,
employing Huáng Gài's strategy of fire attack,
thus defeating Lord Cáo at Chìbì.
On the first day of battle,
Lord Cáo's army was defeated,
retreating to station north of the river,
while Yú and others were on the southern bank.
Yú's subordinate general Huáng Gài said:
"Now the enemy is numerous and we are few,
making it difficult to sustain a prolonged fight.
However, observing Cáo's forces,
they have chained their ships together,
with prows and stems connected,
allowing us to burn them and drive them away."
So they prepared several dozen assault ships,
filled them with firewood and straw,
soaked them with oil,
covered them with curtains,
and raised command flags on top.
First, they sent a letter to Lord Cáo,
deceiving him into believing they intended to surrender.
Gài also prepared swift boats in advance,
each tethered behind the fire ships,
then advanced together in formation.
Lord Cáo's officers and soldiers all stretched their necks to watch,
pointing and saying Gài was surrendering.
When they were over two lǐ from the northern army,
they set fire simultaneously.
The flames were fierce, the wind strong,
the ships sped like arrows,
with flying ashes and overwhelming flames,
burning all the northern ships.
The fire spread to the camps on shore,
and in moments,
smoke and flames blazed to the sky,
with men and horses burned or drowned,
resulting in numerous deaths.
Yú led light, elite troops in pursuit,
advancing with thunderous drums.
Lord Cáo left Cáo Rén to guard Jiānglíng,
and headed north himself.
Zhōu Yú then advanced to Nánjùn,
facing Rén,
who subsequently retreated.
After Lord Cáo's defeat,
he headed directly north,
and Sūn Quán thus dominated the region south of the Yangtze.
At that time, Liú Zhāng was the Governor of Yìzhōu,
with external threats from Zhāng Lǔ's incursions.
Yú then went to the capital to see Quán, saying:
"Now Cáo Cāo has recently suffered a setback,
is troubled internally,
and cannot join forces with you, General, for now.
I request to join Fènwēi in advancing to take Shǔ,
annex Zhāng Lǔ after securing Shǔ,
leaving Fènwēi to firmly hold the territory,
and ally well with Mǎ Chāo for support.
Yú and you, General, can then occupy Xiāngyáng to pressure Cáo,
making the north attainable."
Quán agreed.
But Yú died,
and the plan was not realized.
Earlier,
Zhōu Yú had recommended Lǔ Sù, praising his talent for assisting the times,
and Quán immediately invited Sù to drink with him, saying:
"Now the Hàn court is in peril,
with turmoil in all directions.
I have inherited my father and brother's legacy,
aspiring to achieve the merits of Huán and Wén.
Since you have kindly come,
how will you assist me?"
Sù replied:
"In the past, even the great Gāozǔ, with his earnest efforts,
wished to honor and serve Yìdì but could not,
due to Xiàng Yǔ's harm.
Today's Cáo Cāo is like the Xiàng Yǔ of old;
how can you, General, become like Huán or Wén?
In my humble opinion,
the Hàn house cannot be restored,
just as Cáo Cāo cannot be quickly eliminated.
For your strategy, General,
only by establishing a tripartite balance in Jiāngdōng,
and watching for opportunities in the world,
with such a plan,
there should be no issue.
Then, proclaim yourself emperor,
to strive for the empire,
this is the enterprise of Gāozǔ."
Later, when he pacified the riverlands,
and assumed the imperial title,
he stood at the altar and said to his ministers:
"Lǔ Zìjìng once spoke of this;
he can be said to have understood the situation well."
A discussion states:
Lù Shìhéng praised Sūn Quán:
"Holding the whip and bowing respectfully
to enhance Lord Lù's authority;
fully entrusting military defense
to support Zhōu Yú's forces;
maintaining humble palaces and simple fare
to enrich rewards for meritorious officials;
opening his heart and humbling himself
to accept strategists' plans;
holding his breath and treading carefully
to attend to Zǐmíng's illness;
sharing his provisions and reducing his delicacies
to nurture Líng Tǒng's orphans.
Thus, loyal officials competed to exhaust their abilities,
and determined scholars all exerted their efforts,
solidifying the imperial enterprise."
Huáng Shígōng said:
"The governance of a worthy person
subdues people through form;
the governance of a sage
subdues people through heart.
Formal submission can initiate plans,
heartfelt submission can secure the end.
Subdue form with form,
subdue heart with heart."
From this perspective,
Sūn Quán's "holding the whip and bowing respectfully"
is subduing through form;
"opening his heart and humbling himself"
is subduing through heart.
To end well and begin aptly,
is it not fitting?
In the first year of Huángwǔ,
Wèi sent Grand Marshal Cáo Rén with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry toward Rúxū,
where its commander, Zhū Huán, defeated them.
Initially,
Cáo Rén intended to launch a surprise attack on Zhōngzhōu,
first falsely proclaiming he would attack Xiànxī to the east,
leading Huán to dispatch troops to Xiànxī.
Once the troops were sent,
Rén suddenly arrived.
The generals were anxious,
each feeling fearful.
Huán explained to them:
"In any battle between two armies,
victory or defeat depends on the commander,
not on numbers.
Do you think Cáo Rén's skill in employing troops compares to mine?
The Art of War states that 'the attacker needs twice the strength'
refers to battles on open plains,
without city walls for defense,
and assumes equal courage and cowardice among troops.
Now, Rén is neither wise nor brave,
plus his soldiers are very timid,
and they have marched a thousand lǐ,
exhausted and weary.
Huán and you generals hold a high city,
facing the great river to the south,
with mountains and forests to the north,
resting while awaiting the fatigued,
as defenders controlling the attackers—
this is a situation for certain victory in a hundred battles."
Huán thus lowered his flags and silenced drums,
feigning weakness outwardly,
to lure Rén in.
Rán indeed sent his son Tài to attack Rúxū city,
while dispatching other generals to assault Zhōngzhōu.
Zhōngzhōu was
where the families of the troops resided.
As Tài and others retreated,
Huán beheaded their generals.
In the seventh year,
Wèi again sent Grand Marshal Cáo Xiū with a hundred thousand cavalry to Wǎnchéng,
to meet Zhōu Fáng.
Fáng deceived him,
and he returned without success.
Wú's Póyáng Grand Administrator Zhōu Fáng tricked and lured Xiū into a trap.
Xiū welcomed Fáng to Wǎnchéng,
realized he was deceived,
and should have led his army back,
but, confident in his large force,
sought a decisive battle.
Zhū Huán proposed a plan to Field Marshal Lù Xùn:
"Xiū was originally appointed due to kinship,
not as a wise and brave renowned general.
Now, if he fights, he will surely lose,
and if he loses, he will flee,
likely via Jiāshí and Guàchē.
These two routes
are both narrow and perilous.
If we block the roads with ten thousand troops,
his forces will be annihilated,
and Xiū can be captured alive.
I request to lead my troops to cut them off;
if blessed by heavenly might,
If we allow him to rest and prove his loyalty,
we can then ride the momentum of victory and advance swiftly,
capture Shòuchūn,
seize Huáinán,
and set our sights on Xǔ and Luò.
This is a once-in-a-millennium opportunity,
not to be missed."
Sūn Quán first discussed this with Lù Xùn,
but Xùn believed it inadvisable,
so the plan was not implemented.
By the time Sūn Quán passed away,
and Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
he indulged in extreme extravagance and debauchery,
exploited and oppressed the people,
trusted and promoted treacherous individuals,
and persecuted those who offered loyal counsel.
Emperor Shìzǔ of Jìn ordered Dù Yù and others to attack Wú,
and it was destroyed.
A discussion follows:
In the past, Marquis Wǔ of Wèi sailed on the Western River,
turned and said to Wú Qǐ:
"The natural defenses of these mountains and rivers
are the treasures of the state of Wèi."
Wú Qǐ replied:
"Long ago, the Sānmiáo tribe had Dòngtíng Lake to their left and Pénglí Lake to their right,
but they neglected virtue and righteousness,
so Yǔ destroyed them;
the ruler of the Xià dynasty, Jié,
had the Hé and Jì rivers to his left and Tàihuà Mountain to his right,
with Yīquē to his south,
and Yángcháng to his north,
yet he failed to practice benevolent governance,
so Tāng exiled him.
From this, it is evident
that it depends on virtue, not on natural barriers."
Now, Sūn Hào relied on the foundations laid by his father and grandfather,
possessing formidable natural defenses,
with the Wū Gorges to the west,
the vast sea to the east,
the Cháng Jiāng dividing his territory,
and steep mountains encircling his domain,
a land spanning nearly ten thousand lǐ,
with a million troops bearing arms.
Yet in a single day, he abandoned his armor,
and allowed himself to be bound and captured—
does this not affirm that the saying about virtue is an unalterable truth?
The response is:
Why must it be so?
Lù Jī said:
"The Yì Jīng states:
'The revolutions of Tāng and Wǔ
conformed to the will of Heaven.'
The Tài Xuán Jīng says:
'Without extreme chaos,
order does not manifest.'
This speaks of emperors and kings acting in accordance with the timing of Heaven. The ancients had a saying:
Heaven's timing is not as good as Earth's advantages.
The Yì Jīng states:
'Kings and lords establish defenses
to protect their states.'
This refers to a state relying on its natural barriers.
It also says:
'Earth's advantages are not as good as human harmony,
it depends on virtue, not on natural barriers.'
This speaks of defense depending on people.
When Wú rose to power,
it succeeded by balancing all three factors.
As Xúnzǐ called 'integrating the three,'
but when it fell,
it relied solely on its natural barriers."
Lóu Jìng said:
"When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
it split into two parts,
and none in the empire paid homage,
yet Zhōu could not control them.
It was not due to a lack of virtue,
but because its strategic position had weakened."
From this perspective,
the rise and fall of a state also depends on natural barriers,
as the saying goes:
it is not solely about virtue.
By the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
the central plains were in turmoil and chaos,
Emperor Yuán of Jìn crossed the river again,
and ruled south of the Yangtze.
The Sòng, Qí, Liáng, and Chén dynasties
all established their capitals there,
as recorded in the Annals of the Hegemons.
This describes the geographical situation of the state of Wú.

With Your Lordship's divine martiality and brilliant wisdom,

what direction would not be conquered?
Although our army is small now,
it is not like the situation between Chǔ and Hàn at Xíngyáng and Chénggāo.
At that time,
neither Liú Bāng nor Xiàng Yǔ was willing to retreat first,

With only one-tenth of the enemy's forces,
You have drawn a line to defend,

As their situation becomes exposed and their strength exhausted,

This is the moment to employ extraordinary tactics,

Moreover, Yuán Shào's strategist Xǔ Yōu was greedy for wealth,

so he came to join us,
advising Tàizǔ to raid Shào's separate encampments and burn their grain supplies.
Thus, Shào was defeated.
Zhāng Xiù, in Nányáng, allied with Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and Tàizǔ campaigned against them.
A strategist advised:
"Xiù and Liú Biǎo rely on each other for strength,
but Xiù, as a roaming army, depends on Biǎo for provisions,
which Biǎo cannot supply indefinitely.
If we press them hard,
they will unite their forces;
if we ease the pressure,
they will drift apart on their own. "
Tàizǔ did not heed this.
Biǎo indeed sent troops to rescue Xiù,
and Tàizǔ's army was defeated.
In the spring of the third year,
as Tàizǔ returned to Xǔ,
Xiù's troops pursued him,
and Tàizǔ's army could not advance quickly.
He wrote to Xún Yù:
"The enemy is pursuing us,
and though we march only a few lǐ per day,
I predict that by Ānzhòng,
we will surely defeat them. "
Indeed, he set up an ambush with a surprise tactic,
and attacked and defeated them.
Upon returning to Xǔ,
Xún Yù asked:
"Earlier, how did you predict the enemy would certainly be defeated?"
He replied:
"The enemy blocked our retreating army,
forcing us to fight in a death ground;
thus I knew we would win. "
Qū Guāng of Xīpíng killed the commandery administrator and rebelled,
and the generals wanted to attack him.
Zhāng Jì said:
"Only Guāng and his followers are rebelling;
not all the people in the commandery necessarily agree.
If we immediately bring the army against them,
the officials, commoners, and Qiāng and Hú tribes will surely think the state does not distinguish right from wrong,
and instead cause them all to stick together;
this would be like adding wings to a tiger.
Guāng and his followers want to use the Qiāng and Hú as support;
now, if we first have the Qiāng and Hú raid and attack them,
with generous rewards,
and give them all the captives and spoils,
we can externally block their momentum,
and internally break their alliances,
surely settling it without battle. "
Then, a proclamation was issued:
those misled by Guāng and others
would be pardoned;
those who could behead the rebel leader and present his head
would be additionally enfeoffed.
Thereupon, Guāng's followers beheaded him and sent his head.
This is the general strategy by which eight out of ten provinces and one hundred commaderies of the nine provinces were consolidated.
Those who can support the world in its peril,
will then possess the world's security;
those who can eliminate the world's worries,
will then enjoy the world's happiness;
those who can save the world from disaster,
will then obtain the world's blessings.
Dǒng Zhāo and others wished to collectively advance Cáo Gōng,
preparing the nine bestowals and regalia,
and secretly consulted Xún Yù,
but Yù did not consent.
Cāo Cāo was displeased,
and subsequently had him killed.
Fàn Yè commented:
"The world's talk of Xún Jūn's successes and failures
is perhaps excessive.
Often, for those of medium virtue and below,
one does not demand perfection in the Way.
In wisdom and calculation, there are refinements and oversights;
in tracing origins, one need not always reach the end;
this is a principle that cannot be fully interrogated.
With the worth of a Wèi Cì,
one persuasion could destroy two states;
he did not despise benevolence and desire it,
but where there is preservation, there must be loss.
This again shows that achievements cannot be combined.
When the tide of the times is adverse,
without heroic talent, one cannot save its weakness;
with high merit and strong power,
the imperial vessel shifts of itself.
This again is an era that cannot be combined,
so we take his return to righteousness as enough,
also the principle of sacrificing oneself to achieve benevolence. "
The Cáo clan, upholding righteousness, brought order out of chaos,
and for generations carried their achievements;
by the time of Emperor Wén,
heaven and man granted the ability.
Thus, he received the Hàn abdication.
Liú Ruò urged the advancement, saying:
"Your servant has heard:
portents do not appear in vain,
and the hearts of the multitude cannot be opposed.
Thus, Confucius said:
'Was the Duke of Zhōu not a sage?
To yield the empire
is like heaven, earth, sun, and moon lightly abandoning their myriad things.'
Therefore, Shǔn enjoyed the empire,
accepting it without bowing.
Now the virtue of fire is exhausted,
the upward flame's numbers ended.
The emperor transfers to one of bright virtue,
the throne prospers in great Wèi;
the signs and auspices are clear and bright,
the mandate to receive is firm.
Under the bright heavens,
spirits and men respond as one.
Though the phoenix at Yú's court,
and the fish leaping in Zhōu's time,
compared to today's events,
are not adequate analogies.
Yet Your Majesty opposes heaven's mandate to adorn minor conduct,
resists the people's hearts to hold private resolve,
above disobeying the cherished intent of august heaven,
in the middle forgetting the sage's principle of adaptable integrity,
below disappointing the hopes of ministers looking up,
not the way to promote the sagely path on the high road,
or hand down endless glorious achievements.
Your servants have heard:
in serving a ruler, there is the way of presenting the acceptable and rejecting the unacceptable;
in honoring a superior, there is the duty to oppose firmly even against the scale.
Your servants dare to request with our lives. "
The Grand Scribe's Assistant Xǔ Zhī also said:
"The 'Yì Zhuàn' says:

'When a sage with virtue draws the world near,

Your servant hears that emperors and kings
are the essence of the five phases,
the signs of surname change,
the convergence of dynastic rise,
with seven hundred and twenty years as one cycle.
The virtuous exceed eight hundred,
the virtueless fall short of four hundred years.
Thus, the Zhōu house lasted eight hundred sixty-seven years,
the Xià house several hundred forty-some years.
Hàn practices Xià's governance,

Heaven's calendar and numbers
are about to reach their end.
These are all the signs of emperors and kings receiving the mandate and changing surnames.
Gaining the year star
marks the beginning of the Way's rise.
When King Wǔ attacked Yīn,
the year star was in Chúnhuǒ,
the celestial division of Zhōu.
When Gāozǔ entered Qín,
the five planets gathered at Dōngjǐng,
the celestial division of Hàn.
This year, the year star is in Dàliáng,
the celestial division of Wèi.
And heaven's auspicious responses
all gather and arrive.
Humbly thinking, Your Highness embodies the sagely brilliance of Yáo and Shùn,
responds to the seven-hundred-year cycle of abdication,
as all the scholars under heaven have witnessed.
Respectfully, I report this. "
The Court Gentleman Sū Lín and others also said:

The states of kings and dukes

In the first year of the Jian'an era,

In the thirteenth year, again under Daliang,

to the great fortune of the world."
Although the royal house was pacified,

Between Wú and Shǔ, which should be first?"
He replied:

Your Majesty has received the throne in accordance with the times,
ruling over all under heaven.
If you pacify them with civil virtue,

Although Wú and Shǔ are mere small states,

Liú Bèi has great talent,
Zhūgě Liàng excels in governing the state,
Sūn Quán understands strengths and weaknesses,
Lù Xùn perceives military situations,
holding strategic points and guarding passes,

The way of using troops:

In the past, Shùn danced with shield and axe,

Emperor Wén did not accept this,

The state of Sānmiao,
is present-day Yuèzhōu.
The Shǔ chancellor Zhūgě Liàng marched out of Xiégǔ,
and stationed troops south of the Wèi River.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng blocked him.
An edict to Xuānwáng said:
"Just firmly fortify and defend,
to blunt their advance.
They cannot achieve their aims in advancing,
and have no one to fight when retreating,
if they stay long, provisions will be exhausted,
and plundering will yield nothing,
then they are sure to flee!
When they flee, pursue them,
using ease to await their fatigue,
is the way to complete victory."
Liàng sent women's clothing to anger Xuānwáng,
Xuānwáng was about to go out to battle,
but Xīn Pí, holding the imperial scepter, forbade it,
so he stopped.
Xuānwáng, upon seeing Liàng's envoy,
only asked about Liàng's sleep, meals, and the complexity of his duties,
not touching on military matters.
The envoy replied:
"For punishments of twenty strokes or more,
he personally reviews them all,
and he eats no more than a few shēng."
Xuānwáng said:
"Liàng is near his end."
Soon enough, he indeed passed away.
By the first year of the Gānlù era,
Dèng Ài was appointed as General Who Guards the West,
to confront the Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi.
Wéi's army was defeated,
and he retreated to defend Jiàngé.
Zhōng Huì attacked Wéi but could not overcome him,
so he memorialized:
"Now the enemy is defeated and weakened,
we should take advantage of this,
from Yínpíng, take bypaths through Hàndéyángtíng,
head to Fú, emerging 400 lǐ west of Jiàngé,
about over 300 lǐ from Chéngdū,
a surprise force striking at their heart,
the defenders of Jiàngé will surely return to rescue Fú,
then Huì can advance with chariots abreast;
if the Jiàngé army does not return,
then the forces at Fú will be few.
The Military Records say:
'Attack where they are unprepared,
emerge where they do not expect.'
Now, striking at their emptiness,
we are sure to defeat them."
In the winter tenth month,
Ài advanced from Yínpíng over 700 lǐ through uninhabited land,
cutting through mountains to open paths,
with high mountains and deep valleys,
Ài wrapped himself in felt,
and rolled down.
The officers and soldiers all climbed trees and scaled cliffs,
advancing in single file.
They first reached Jiāngyóu,
the Shǔ general Zhūgě Zhān from Fú returned to Miánzhú,
arrayed his forces to await Ài,
Ài sent his son Zhōng and others to give battle,
greatly defeated them,
and beheaded Zhān.
Advancing to Luòxiàn,
Liú Shàn then surrendered.
The Later Emperor, following Qiáo Zhōu's strategy,
presented the seal and document to Ài, saying:
"Bounded by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
encountering deep transgressions,
ascending by means of Shǔ land.
Planning isolated in a corner,
interfering with fate and daring offense,
gradually passing through the years.
Often recalling the Huángchū era,
the warm and confidential edicts proclaimed,
extending the grace of three kindnesses,
showing the way,
the great righteousness clearly revealed.
But with my unworthy virtue and obscurity,
greedily clinging to the remaining legacy,
through successive reigns,
I have not followed the great teaching,
now that the heavenly might has shaken,
in the reckoning where humans and spirits return to capability,
awed by the royal army,
where the divine martiality resides,
how dare I not reform,
and submit to follow orders?"
Ài was greatly pleased,
and replied in a letter:
"When the royal order loses its way,
numerous heroes rise together,
dragons battle and tigers contend,
but ultimately return to the true ruler.
This is the way of heaven's mandate coming and going.
Since ancient times, sage emperors,
down to Hàn and Wèi,
those who received the mandate to become kings,
none did so outside the central land.
The Hé River produced the diagram,
the Luò River produced the writing,
the sages took them as models,
to rise and establish great enterprises.
Those not following this,
have all met with downfall.
Wěi Xiāo relied on Lǒng and perished,
Gōngsūn Shù held Shǔ and was destroyed,
these are indeed warnings from the overturned carts of previous generations.
Our sage emperor is wise and discerning,
the ministers loyal and virtuous,
about to rival the glory of Huángdì and Xuānyuán,
equal the achievements of past ages.
I have been ordered to come on this expedition,
hoping to hear good news,
and indeed, your envoy has troubled to come,
bringing news of virtuous words.
This is not human affairs,
but heaven's will.
In the past, Wēizǐ returned to Zhōu,
and indeed became an honored guest.
The gentleman changes like a leopard,
the righteousness preserved in the Great Change (Yìjīng).
Your words are modest and humble,
presenting the coffin with ritual,
these are all precedents of submission from former sages.
Preserving the state intact is best,
destroying the state comes next.
If not for your wisdom and understanding,
how could one see the righteousness of a king?"
The Later Emperor arrived in Luòyáng,
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Ānlè, with the decree:
"To govern heaven and carry all things,
universal peace is the greatest;
to reside gloriously under heaven,
harmony in times is the splendor.
In the past,
the Hàn house lost its order,
the world was shaken and disturbed.
Our Tàizǔ received the mandate and rose like a dragon,
His grace extended to the eight poles.
Thus, he responded to Heaven and complied with the people,
pacifying and ruling the central region.
At that time,
his late father, taking advantage of the fierce struggles among the heroes,
while the nine domains were unsettled,
seized the opportunity of the remote and obstructed terrain,
secured and held Yōngshǔ,
for nearly five cycles.
I have long pondered over my ancestors,
thinking of pacifying and uniting the four seas,
hence I marshaled the six armies,
displaying our might in Liángyì.
You, my lord, have elevated virtue and magnanimity,
adapting to opportunities like a leopard's swift change,
practicing faithfulness and contemplating obedience,
thereby enjoying the boundless blessings of assisting me—
is this not far-sighted!
Go forth and be reverent!
Respectfully heed my command,
broaden your virtuous heart,
to complete your illustrious achievements."
Initially,
Jìn Wénwáng intended to send Zhōng Huì to attack Shǔ.
Shào Tì said:
"Now Zhōng Huì leads over a hundred thousand troops to attack Shǔ;
I believe Huì is alone and should not bear such a heavy responsibility,
unlike others."
Wénwáng replied:
"Do you think I am unaware of this?
If after destroying Shǔ,
things turn out as you worry,
how could it be resolved?
Generally, a defeated general
cannot speak of courage;
a minister of a fallen state
cannot plan for survival—
because their hearts and courage are already broken.
If Shǔ is destroyed,
the remaining people will be terrified,
unfit to conspire with.
Our central plains' officers and soldiers,
each thinking of returning home,
will not join him.
If he does evil,
it will only lead to his clan's extermination."
Huì indeed rebelled with Jiāng Wéi,
and the Wèi generals, filled with indignation, killed both Huì and Wéi.
By the end of Jìn,
Qiáo Zòng again usurped Shǔ.
Liú Yù of Sòng sent Zhū Língshí to attack Shǔ,
claiming to take Chéngdū via the inner river,
while sending poorly clad, weak elders to the river's mouth.
Qiáo Zòng indeed suspected they were coming up the inner river.
A discussion states:
The inner river
is the Fú Jiāng. ,
He deployed his entire army at Xīnchéng to await them.
Instead, he assigned Zhū Língshí and others elite troops,
going directly via the outer river.
A discussion states:
The outer river
is the Zhī Jiāng.
Which is now the river at Luò Xiàn. ,
They went straight to Chéngdū,
capturing Zòng without a fight.
The event is detailed in the Records of Hegemons. .
This is the situation of destroying Shǔ.
During the Jiāpíng era of Wèi,
Sūn Quán died,
and Generals like Chéngnán Dàjiāngjūn Wáng Chǎng, Chéngdōng Dàjiāngjūn Hú Zūn, and Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Wúqiū Jiǎn,
proposed campaigns against Wú.
The court, finding their strategies divergent,
ordered consultation with Shàngshū Fù Gǔ.
Gǔ responded:
"In the past, Fūchāi defeated Qí and humbled Jìn,
his might prevailed over the central states,
yet he could not avoid the disaster at Gūsū;
Qí Mǐn expanded territory and annexed states,
opening up lands for a thousand miles,
but it wasn't enough to save him from a catastrophic defeat.
Those who have a beginning do not necessarily have a good end—
this is a clear lesson from ancient events.
Since Sūn Quán destroyed Shǔ and annexed Jīngzhōu,
his ambitions swelled and desires were satisfied,
his ferocity reached its peak.
Xiàngguó Xuān and Wénwáng first recognized the principle of seizing disorder and humbling the doomed,
deeply understanding the strategy for grand plans and major actions.
Now that Quán has died,
entrusting his orphan to Zhūgě Kè,
if Kè corrects Quán's harsh tyranny,
abolishes his cruel policies,
so the people are spared brutality,
finding temporary ease in new benevolence,
with internal and external concerns aligned,
sharing the fear as in the same boat,
even if they cannot ultimately preserve themselves intact,
they could still prolong their survival beyond the deep river.
Now, some advisers suggest sailing directly across,
sweeping through Jiāngbiǎo;
others propose advancing with double speed,
attacking their cities and fortresses;
yet others recommend large-scale farming in the border fields,
watching for opportunities to act.
These three are common strategies for dealing with the enemy,
but they succeed only if applied appropriately;
if not executed properly,
they will surely bring future troubles.
Since we began training troops,
it has been three years in and out,
not a surprise attack force.
The enemy has lost their commander,
making retreat and defense advantageous for them.
If they deploy ships at key points,
fortify cities and clear the fields,
the plan for a sweeping advance
would likely be difficult to succeed.
The enemy has been bandits for sixty years,
with a falsely established ruler and ministers,
sharing fortunes and misfortunes.
If Kè removes their弊端,
and Heaven robs them of their vigor,
signs of collapse
cannot be quickly awaited.
Now the enemy has set up defenses,
and is cautious and secretive,
making espionage impossible,
leaving us without intelligence.
An army without intelligence,
with unclear reconnaissance,
yet launching a massive force into great danger—
this is hoping for luck to seek merit,
fighting first and seeking victory later,
not the best strategy for preserving the army.
Only large-scale farming is relatively secure,
with troops deployed beyond the people,
preventing enemy raids,
sitting and consuming stored grain,
without the hassle of transporting soldiers;
attacking when opportunities arise,
avoiding long-distance labor and expenses.
This is the urgent task for the army.
With encampments close together,
both clever and simple tactics can be used,
planning to know the gains and losses,
testing to identify strengths and weaknesses.
Their true situation will have nowhere to hide.
Using the small to oppose the large
leads to exhausting labor and strength;
using the poor to oppose the rich
results in heavy taxes and financial depletion.
Thus, 'tire the enemy when they are at ease,
starve them when they are full'—
this is what it means.
Then, with a mighty host and sharpened weapons to intimidate them,
offering doubled rewards to attract them,
using multiple deceptions to confuse them.
Take unexpected routes,
to strike when they are unprepared.
After three years,
with coordinated efforts,
the enemy will surely disintegrate like ice,
and we can calmly exploit their weakness,
achieving victory through calculation alone.
In the past, the Hàn dynasty long suffered from the Xiōngnú,
with court officials and strategists
deliberating from early morning till late;
armored generals
advocated campaigns;
court scholars
all spoke of peace marriages;
brave and fierce men
desired to fight and devour.
Thus, Fán Kuài wished to lead a hundred thousand to sweep through the Xiōngnú,
but Jì Bù pointed out his shortcomings;
Lǐ Xìn sought two hundred thousand to conquer Chǔ alone,
and indeed brought shame to the Qín army.
Now some generals propose crossing the perilous Jiānglíng,
marching alone into enemy territory—
this is similar to past examples.
With Your Majesty's sage virtue,
assisted by wise and intelligent ministers,
clear laws and well-trained soldiers,
planning from a position of certain victory,
wielding long-term strategies to control them,
the enemy's collapse
is an inevitable outcome.
Thus, the Art of War says:
'Subdue the enemy without fighting,
take their cities without assault.'
If we abandon the certain principle of victory through temple calculations,
and adopt a strategy with less than one percent chance of success,
it is truly what I, a foolish minister, worry about.
Therefore, I consider the plan of large-scale farming to pressure them the best."
At that time, they did not follow Fù Gǔ's advice,
and ordered Wáng Chǎng and others to attack Wú.
The Wú general Zhūgě Kè resisted them.

and Tàizǔ ascended to the throne.
When Wáng Chǎng and others were defeated,

"This is my fault,

Thus, the people of Wei were pleased and harmonious,

By the time of Shìzǔ's reign,
that is, Jìn Wǔdì,
Yáng Hù submitted a memorial to pacify Wú, stating:
"The late emperor followed heaven's will and responded to the times,
pacifying Bāshǔ in the west,
reconciling with Wúkuài in the south,
allowing the realm to rest,
and the people to have peace and contentment.
Yet Wú again betrayed trust,
causing border conflicts to resurface.
Although destiny is bestowed by heaven,
achievements must be realized through human effort.
Without a major campaign to sweep them away,
the multitude of duties will never find peace.
It is also a way to honor the late emperor's merits,

Thus, Yáo had the campaign at Dānshuǐ,
Shùn the expedition against the Yǒumiáo,
both aiming to calm the universe,
and cease arms to harmonize the people.
After Shǔ was pacified,
all under heaven said Wú should fall next.
Thirteen years have passed since then,
which is one cycle.
The time for pacification
is again today.
Critics often say that Wú and Chǔ, when virtuous, submit later,
and when unruly, grow strong first,
but that was in the era of feudal lords.
Now, with unification,
it cannot be compared to ancient times.
Theories that adhere strictly to the Way
often fail to adapt to circumstances,
hence, though many plans are made,
the decision must be singular.
Those who survive by rugged terrain
assume the enemy's equal strength can hold firm;
but if their forces are uneven and strengths differ,
even wise men cannot devise plans,
and the terrain cannot be defended.
The land of Shǔ
was not without perils,
with mountains reaching the clouds,
deep valleys without sunlight,
where horses were tethered and chariots hung
to cross,
and it was said one man with a halberd
could hold off a thousand.
Yet when troops advanced,
there were no barriers to stop them,
generals were beheaded, flags captured,
corpses lay in tens of thousands,
and they swept forward victoriously,
straight to Chéngdū,
while cities in Hànzhōng
perched like birds, not daring to emerge.
Not that they lacked will to fight,
but their strength was truly insufficient to resist.
When Liú Shàn surrendered,
all the garrisons and forts
disbanded in disarray.
Now, the difficulties of Jiānghuái
are no greater than Jiàngé;
the ruggedness of mountains and rivers
no more than Mínhàn.
Sūn Hào's tyranny
exceeds that of Liú Shàn;
the distress of Wúyuè
is worse than Bāshǔ.
And the great Jìn's forces
outnumber those of the past;
its supplies and equipment
are more abundant than before.
If we do not pacify Wú now,
but instead remain entrenched in defense,
with conscripts suffering harsh duties,
and conflicts daily arising,
experiencing rise and fall,
it cannot last long;
we should settle it now,
to unify the four seas.
If we now lead troops from Liáng and Yì,
advancing by land and water;
with forces from Jīng and Chǔ,
approaching Jiānglíng;
pacifying Nán Yùzhōu,
heading straight to Xiàkǒu;
and from Xú, Yáng, Qīng, Yǎn,
all converging on Mòlíng,
using drums and banners to confuse them,
employing multiple strategies to mislead them,
then Wú, confined to a corner,
facing the might of the realm,
will be divided and scattered,
with all defenses under strain.
With surprise troops from Bā and Hàn,
striking where they are vulnerable,
one breach
will cause upheaval throughout.
Wú relies on the river for its state,
with no hinterland,
stretching thousands of miles east to west,
using barriers for defense.
Facing a great enemy,
it finds no respite.
Sūn Hào acts arbitrarily,
suspicious of his subordinates;
officials and generals
no longer have confidence.
Thus, even Sūn Xiù and others
fled out of fear.
Ministers are doubtful at court,
soldiers weary in the fields,
with no secure strategy or steadfast resolve.
In ordinary times,
they consider defection;
when troops approach,
some will surely respond.
They cannot unite to fight to the death,
as is evident.
Their customs are hasty,
unable to endure long;
their bows, crossbows, halberds, and shields
are inferior to ours,
only naval warfare is their advantage.
Once we enter their land,
the Cháng Jiāng will no longer protect them;
if they retreat to defend cities,
they abandon their strength for weakness,
while our troops advance resolutely,
each with a determined spirit.
The Wú people fighting on their soil
have a mindset of relying on walls.
Thus,
the army will not need long,
and victory is certain."
The emperor deeply accepted this.
He then ordered Wáng Jùn and others to destroy Wú.
The realm came to share the same script,
and the same gauge for carts.
At that time, the Wú king Hào had ambitions to conquer the superior state,
and appointed Lù Kàng as governor of Jīngzhōu.
Jìn sent Yáng Hù to confront the Wú forces.
Hù enhanced virtuous governance to win over Wú.
Whenever engaging Wú in battle,
he would set a date beforehand,
avoiding ambushes and surprise attacks,
and if captives were taken in battle,
when the military officials were to execute them,
Hù would say:
"These are ministers loyal unto death."
He would shed tears for them,
personally arrange their burial,
provide for their families,
and when mourners came,
he ensured rich sacrifices before sending them back.
If Wú generals came to him,
he allowed them to go as they wished.
If they wanted to return to Wú,
he would hold farewell ceremonies.
A Wú general had two sons,
both young,
who were playing at the border
and were captured by Hù's troops,
for over a month.
Their father thought they had died,
and held a funeral.
Hù personally cared for and nurtured them,
then sent them back.
Their father, moved by his kindness,
later brought the two sons to surrender.
Thus, Lù Kàng often told his troops:
"He acts solely with righteousness,
while we act with force;
this means submission without battle.
Let each guard their boundaries,
without seeking minor gains."
He praised:
"Even Yuè Yì or Zhūgě Liàng—
how could they surpass Yáng Shūzǐ?"
As Lù Kàng was dying,
he said to the Wú king Hào:
"Xīlíng and Jiànpíng,
are the protective barriers of the state,
located upstream,
facing threats on two fronts.
My father Lù Xùn once stationed at the western frontier,
advised:
"Xīlíng is the western gate of our state.
Should it be endangered,
we must mobilize the entire nation to contend for it."
Humbly, I believe
the feudal lords are young and inexperienced,
not yet managing state affairs.
I request to oversee all matters
to support our border defenses."
When Jìn's Grand General Yáng Hù came to court,
he secretly proposed plans to attack Wú,
commissioning Wáng Jùn to build ships in Shǔ.
These vessels spanned over a hundred paces,
fortified like cities,
with towers at their gates
and monstrous heads carved on prows
to intimidate river deities.
They carried over two thousand men
who could gallop horses aboard.
As wood shavings floated downstream to Wú,
Wūjiàn Prefect Wú Yàn collected them
and presented them to King Wú, warning:
"Jìn surely plans to attack.
We must reinforce Jiànpíng's troops -
if Jiànpíng holds,
they dare not cross the river."
King Hào of Wú disregarded this.
Yàn then forged iron chains
with barbed spikes
to block the river
against our forces.
Learning of this,
Jùn constructed great rafts
with straw dummies,
deploying swimmers beneath
to set bamboo torches and disable the chains,
then launched his assault.
As Jùn predicted,
the obstacles proved harmless.
In the first year of Tàikāng,
General Wáng Hūn attacked Héngjiāng
and triumphed.
General Wáng Jùn captured Jiànpíng and Dānyáng.
Dù Yù separately dispatched six hundred light troops
crossing on bamboo rafts,
landing at Lèxiāng
and stationing at Bā Mountain,
where they unfurled banners
and lit mountain fires
to achieve surprise.
During the capture of Gōng'ān,
commanders argued this century-old foe
couldn't be fully subdued,
especially with spring floods rising
making sustained campaigns difficult,
advising postponement until winter
for major operations.
Yù countered:
"As Yuè Yì once used a single victory to conquer mighty Qí,
our momentum now resembles splitting bamboo -
after the first few nodes,
it cleaves effortlessly!"
His memorial persuaded
the emperor completely.
When Wú sent Zhāng Tì and Shěn Yíng across the river,
Yíng advised Tì:
"Jìn has long built warships in Shǔ.
Now their nationwide mobilization
converges from all directions,
with Yìzhōu's forces
floating downstream.
Our upper river defenses are unprepared -
riverside cities may all fall.
Their navy will surely come here.
We should conserve strength to meet them.
One decisive victory
would clear the river region;
even if upstream falls,
we could reclaim it.
But crossing now to engage
offers no victory guarantee,
and defeat would mean total loss!"
Tì ignored this,
crossed the river,
and pressed forward with full force.
Our imperial troops held firm,
causing enemy retreat and disorder,
whereupon Jìn forces struck
and crushed Wú's army.
King Hào surrendered to Jùn,
as eighty thousand garrison troops
in aligned ships with battle cries
entered Shítóu.
Hào,
bound and with a coffin,
saw Jùn burn the coffin
as ritual demanded.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis Guīmìng.
By Jìn Huì's feeble reign,
northern tribes ravaged the heartland,
the emperor fled dust-covered
to Jiangnan,
and the realm fractured again.
Through five dynasties it passed,
over three hundred years.
When Suí's Emperor Wén received the mandate,
he planned to conquer Chén.
Consulting Gāo Jiǒng for strategy,
Jiǒng replied:
"North of the river, colder climate delays harvests;
southward, warmer soil ripens rice earlier.
Time our maneuvers with their harvest,
mobilizing troops
with feigned attacks.
They'll garrison defenses,
missing farming seasons.
When they mass troops,
we stand down.
Repeating this
makes it routine.
Later when we truly attack,
they'll doubt it,
and in their hesitation,
we cross to engage
with doubled morale.
Moreover, southern soil being thin,
houses use bamboo/thatch,
with underground granaries rare.
Secretly dispatch agents
to wind-spread fires.
When they rebuild,
burn again.
Within years,
their resources will exhaust."
Implementing this plan,
the emperor weakened Chén further.
Later, raising armies,
he appointed Xuē Dàohéng as Secretary
of Huáinán Circuit headquarters,
also overseeing documents.
When imperial troops reached the river,
Gāo Jiǒng summoned Dàohéng
for nighttime counsel,
asking:
"Will this campaign
conquer Jiāngdōng?
Share your view."
Dàohéng answered:
"Assessing major ventures' success
requires fundamental principles.
The Nine Provinces in Yǔ Gòng
were royal domains.
Since Hàn's decline,
warlords rose,
with Sūn Quán's clan
seizing Wú-Chǔ lands.
Jìn's Emperor Wǔ received heaven's mandate,
soon annexing them;
after Yǒngjiā's southern migration,
division returned.
Since then,
warfare never ceased.
Adversity yields to prosperity -
heaven's constant way.
Guō Pú prophesied:
'Jiāngdōng shall harbor separatist kings for three centuries,
then reunite with the heartland.'
Now that period nears completion.
Thus by destiny,
victory is certain - first reason.
Virtuous realms flourish,
virtueless perish -
all dynastic changes
follow this law.
Our sovereign practices frugality
and governs diligently,
while Chén Shūbǎo builds lavish palaces,
drowns in wine and lust,
creating rift between rulers and ruled,
angering gods and men -
thus victory is certain, second reason.
Governing a state
depends on appointments,
yet their ministers
merely fill positions.
Promoting villain Shī Wénqìng
to administer affairs;
Minister Jiāng Zǒng
indulges only in poetry and drink,
unfit for strategy;
Xiāo Móhē and Rén Mánnú,
though senior generals,
possess but brute courage..."
The third certainty of victory lies herein.
We possess the Way and are vast,
while they lack virtue and are small.
Assessing their armored soldiers,
they number no more than a hundred thousand.
From Wūxiá in the west,
to the vast sea in the east,
if dispersed, their situation becomes precarious and their strength weak;
if gathered, they guard one place and lose another.
The fourth certainty of victory lies herein.
The omen of sweeping conquest,
leaves no room for doubt."
Yǐng delightedly said:
"Your discourse on success and failure,
is exceedingly clear in principle.
I am now enlightened.
I had originally expected talent and learning from you,
but never anticipated such strategic insight."
Thereupon, he advanced the troops,
and captured Shūbǎo.
This illustrates the circumstances of conquering Wú.
A discussion states:
In the past, during the Three Kingdoms period,
Shǔ sent Zōng Yù as an envoy to Wú.
Yù said to Quán:
"Although Shǔ is considered a neighboring state,
east and west rely on each other;
Wú cannot be without Shǔ,
nor can Shǔ be without Wú."
Sūn Shèng said:
"What preserves an emperor or king,
is solely the Way and righteousness.
Once the Way and righteousness are established,
even the small can become great,
as with Yīn and Zhōu;
but if one relies on deceit and force,
even the strong will surely fall,
as with Qín and Xiàng.
How much more so for a remote, petty city,
relying on the strength of mountains and rivers,
and seeking to connect over ten thousand miles,
to perpetually depend on each other!
In the past, the nine states devised a plan of vertical alliance,
yet the Qín people ultimately unified the six directions;
Gōngsūn Shù and others plotted mutual support like the cheek and the jawbone,
yet Guāngwǔ ultimately annexed both Lǒng and Shǔ.
With the strength of the nine states and the vastness of Lǒng and Hàn,
none could save each other,
sitting idly by watching the slaughter and overthrow—
why was this?
Because the foundation of the Way and virtue was not universal,
and the hearts of those separated and weak were difficult to unify.
Yet to say:
'Wú cannot be without Shǔ,
Shǔ cannot be without Wú'—
is that not flattery!
From this perspective,
the foundation of governing a state,
lies solely in the Way and righteousness.
If the ruler does not cultivate virtue,
even those within the boat will all become enemy states.
How true this is!"
From the gēngxū year of the tenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era when Chén was destroyed,
to the bǐngchén year of the fourth year of the present Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
altogether one hundred and twenty-six years,
the land under heaven has been unified.
A discussion states:
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says, "A capital city exceeding a hundred zhì
is a harm to the state."
It also says:
"A large capital matching the state,
is the root of chaos."
In ancient times, feudal lords did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
mountains and seas were not enfeoffed,
and closeness to the barbarians was avoided—
indeed, there was good reason for this.
Why?
Master Jiǎ expressed it well:
"I have privately traced past events,
and found that among the feudal lords, generally the strong rebelled first.
Huáiyīn, king of Chǔ, being the strongest,
rebelled first;
Hán Xìn, relying on the Hú, rebelled again;
Guàn Gāo, with Zhào's resources, rebelled again;
Chén Xī, with elite troops, rebelled again;
Péng Yuè, leveraging Liáng, rebelled again;
Qíng Bù, using Huáinán, rebelled again;
while Lú Wǎn, the weakest, rebelled last.
Chángshā had only twenty-five thousand households,
achieved little merit yet remained most intact,
being remote in position yet most loyal.
This was not because their natures differed from others,
but rather due to the circumstances.
Had Fán, Lì, Jiàng, and Guà been enfeoffed with dozens of cities as kings,
they might now be destroyed or lost;
had Xìn, Yuè, and their like
been ranked as marquises and settled,
they might have survived to this day.
Thus, the grand strategy for the land under heaven can be understood.
To make the kings all loyal and submissive,
then nothing is better than making them like the king of Chángshā;
to prevent ministers and sons from being minced into paste,
then nothing is better than making them like Fán, Lì, and others;
to achieve peace and order in the land under heaven,
then nothing is better than establishing many feudal lords and reducing their power."
From this perspective,
those now ruling cities exclusively,
all control territories of a thousand lǐ,
with people within them—
not merely the resources of a hundred lǐ;
officials hold positions by talent,
subordinates are not close kin—
not merely the distance of non-intimacy;
Wú occupies rivers and lakes,
Shǔ blocks with natural barriers—
not merely the advantages of mountains and seas;
spanning provinces and connecting commanderies,
their form constricts and land controls—
not merely the harm of a state matching another.
If encountering a change of ten thousand generations,
with the calamity of the seven sons,
then it cannot be avoided;
those who possess a state must not fail to examine this.
Emperor Míng of Wèi asked Huáng Quán:
"Now that the three states stand like a tripod,
which one is legitimate?"
He replied:
"It should be determined by celestial phenomena.
In previous years, Mars remained in the Heart constellation,
and Emperor Wén passed away,
while the rulers of Wú and Shǔ remained unharmed.
From this perspective,
Wèi holds the legitimate succession."
Chapter Twenty: Heeding Admonitions and Warnings
The Book of Changes says:
"The revolution of Tāng and Wǔ
was in accordance with Heaven and responsive to humanity."
The Book of Documents states:
"He who comforts us is our sovereign;
he who oppresses us is our enemy."
Shīzǐ records:
"When the Duke of Zhōu returned the governance,
Confucius criticized him, saying:
'Was the Duke of Zhōu not sagely!
To yield the empire
was not for the multitude of people.'"
Discussion says:
Yáo of old declared:
"If I give the empire to Shùn,
the empire benefits while Dānzhū suffers;
if I give it to Dānzhū,
the empire suffers while Dānzhū benefits.
I would never benefit one person at the empire's expense,
so I abdicated to Shùn."
Now the Duke of Zhōu did not prioritize the empire,
but sought personal fame through yielding,
thus he was not a sage acting with flexibility,
so Confucius criticized him.
Master Dǒng said:
"Even with hereditary rulers maintaining traditions,
it doesn't preclude sages receiving the mandate."
An ancient saying goes:
"A cornered rat will bite a wildcat,
a commoner may challenge the sovereign."
Thus Huángshígōng stated:
"A ruler cannot be without virtue,
without virtue, ministers will rebel."
Xúnzǐ said:
"He who can eliminate troubles brings fortune,
he who cannot becomes a scourge."
Xúnzǐ stated:
"When the Son of Heaven first ascends the throne,
the high minister advises:
'He who can eliminate troubles brings fortune,
he who cannot becomes a scourge.'
Presenting the first memorial.
The middle minister advises:
'Considering matters before they arise is called preparedness,
preparedness ensures excellent completion;
anticipating troubles before they occur is called precaution,
precaution prevents disasters from arising;
considering matters after they occur is called lagging,
lagging leads to failure;
dealing with troubles after they occur is called passivity,
passivity cannot ward off disasters.'
Presenting the second memorial.
The junior minister advises:
'While celebrations fill the hall,
mourners gather at the gate,
misfortune neighbors fortune,
none know whence they come.
Be cautious!
Be cautious!'
Presenting the third memorial.
This is the ultimate admonition."
How to illustrate this?
When King Wén was at Fēng,
he summoned Tàigōng, asking:
"The King of Shāng unjustly kills the innocent,
you must help me concern for the people,
what should I do now?"
Tàigōng replied:
"Let the king cultivate himself, honor worthies, and benefit people,
to observe the Way of Heaven.
When Heaven shows no calamity,
do not take the lead;
when humanity shows no disaster,
do not initiate plans.
Only when seeing Heaven's calamity,
and humanity's disaster,
may you plan.
Share benefits with the people,
shared benefits bring mutual rescue,
shared feelings bring mutual accomplishment,
shared hatreds bring mutual assistance,
shared preferences bring mutual pursuit.
Win without armor and weapons,
attack without siege engines,
defend without moats and ramparts.
He who benefits others,
the world opens to him;
he who harms others,
the world closes against him.
The world is not one person's world,
gaining the world is like hunting wild beasts -
when caught, all under heaven share the meat.
Like crossing rivers in the same boat -
all share the benefits;
if the boat capsizes,
all share the harm.
Thus all will open to him,
none will close against him.
He who takes nothing from the people,
gains the people;
he who takes nothing from the state,
gains the state;
he who takes nothing from the world,
gains the world."
Discussion says:
When Duke Pei rose,
like a tiger roaring in Fēng Valley,
watering horses at Qín River,
he collected no treasures,
took no women,
made surrendered city commanders marquises,
distributed spoils among his soldiers.
He showed no selfishness,
his self-interest
was interest for all under heaven.
Thus Lǎozǐ said:
"Precisely because he is not self-interested,
he can accomplish his self-interest."
Thus we know taking nothing from others
is the greatest taking.
He who gains the people,
benefits the people;
he who gains the state,
benefits the state;
he who gains the world,
benefits the world.
Thus the Way lies in being unseen,
affairs lie in being unheard,
victory lies in being unknown.
Subtle indeed!
Subtle indeed!
When a bird of prey strikes,
it lowers its body and folds its wings;
when a fierce beast pounces,
it lowers its ears and crouches;
when a sage acts,
he must appear foolish.
Only through culture and virtue,
who can serve as model?
Without observation and examination,
how can one know the ultimate?
Now that Yīn-Shāng
deceives itself with many voices.
I observe its fields -
weeds overcome grain;
I observe its masses -
crookedness overcomes uprightness;
I observe its officials -
violent, cruel, and harmful,
corrupting laws and confusing punishments,
yet the ruler remains unaware,
this is the pattern of a perishing state."
King Wén said:
"Excellent."
Master Jiǎ said:

For a minister to exile his sovereign,
for a subordinate to kill his superior,

Yet they long maintained the empire

continuing through righteousness.
Thus their fame spread throughout the world and passed to later generations."
Tàigōng said:

He who shares benefits with all

Heaven has its seasons,

Where benevolence resides,

Sparing people from death, resolving their difficulties, saving them from calamity, relieving their urgency -
this is virtue.
Where virtue resides,
the world returns.
Sharing worries, joys, preferences, and hatreds with others -

Where righteousness resides,
the world returns.
All people hate death and love life,
appreciate virtue and turn toward benefit.
He who can generate benefits

Where the Way resides,

Discussion:
Liú Xiàng stated:
"There is no ruler who does not desire safety,
yet they are often in peril;
there is no ruler who does not desire preservation,
yet they are often destroyed.
This is due to losing the method of controlling ministers."
When ministers grasp the levers of power and hold the state's administration,
there are none who do not cause harm.
In the past, Jìn had its Six Ministers,
Qí had its Tián and Cuī clans,
Wèi had its Sūn and Níng clans,
Lǔ had its Jì and Mèng clans,
who constantly managed state affairs,
and generationally held the reins of court.
In the end, it came to this:
the Tián clan took Qí,
the Six Ministers partitioned Jìn,
Cuī Zhù assassinated his ruler Guāng,
Sūn Línfǔ and Níng Zhí expelled their ruler Yǎn and assassinated their ruler Piāo,
the Jì clan had eight rows of dancers in their courtyard,
the Three Families used the Yōng hymn to clear the sacrificial vessels,
all monopolized the state's government,
and finally drove out Duke Zhāo.
All these resulted from the yin overcoming and the yang prevailing,
and from those below failing in the way of ministers."
Fàn Jū advised King Zhāo of Qín, saying:
"The reason the Three Dynasties lost their states was
that they often indulged in excess, galloping about hunting,
and did not attend to affairs of government.
Those to whom they delegated power
were jealous of the worthy and envious of the capable,
oppressed those below and deceived those above,
to achieve their private ends,
did not plan for their lord,
and the lord, unaware,
thus lost his state.
Now from the officials of rank and above to all the scribes and the king's attendants,
there is none who is not a man of the Chancellor of State.
I see Your Majesty standing alone at court,
and I secretly fear for you,
fearing that for ten thousand generations to come,
those who will possess the state of Qín
will not be Your Majesty's descendants."
From this perspective,
the *Book of Documents* says that if a minister presumes to dispense majesty and blessings,
he brings harm to your family,
and calamity to your state.
Confucius said:
"When the emoluments leave the ducal house,
and government passes into the hands of the senior ministers,
it is an omen of its demise."
How true are these words!
When Confucius was in Wèi,
he heard that Tián Cháng of Qí was about to foment disorder
(he monopolized Qí's power,
and had the mind of one without a ruler). ,
But he feared the Bào and Yàn clans
(the Bào and Yàn clans
were hereditary ministers and senior officials of Qí). ,
So he shifted his troops to attack Lǔ
(Earlier,
when Tián Cháng was Chancellor of Qí,

to serve in his rear palace,
and guests and retainers came and went without restriction.
Tián Cháng subsequently had over seventy sons,
and through this, he stole the state of Qí). .
Confucius assembled his disciples and said:
"Lǔ
is the land of our parents,
I cannot bear to see it attacked by an enemy.
I wish to humble myself before Tián Cháng to save Lǔ.
Which of you will go?"
Zǐ Gòng requested to be sent,
and the Master agreed.
He then went to Qí
and persuaded Tián Cháng, saying:
"Now, for you to seek achievement by attacking Lǔ is truly difficult,
but if you shift your troops against Wú, it is feasible.
Now Lǔ
is a state difficult to attack;
its city walls are thin and low,
its territory narrow and exposed;
its ruler is foolish and unkind,
its great ministers are hypocritical and useless,
and its officers and people also detest affairs of armor and weapons.
This is not a state you can fight.
Now Wú,
its city walls are high and thick,
its territory broad and deep,
its armor strong and new,
its soldiers selected and well-fed,
with heavy weaponry and elite troops
all contained within it,
and it also has wise senior officials guarding it.
This is easy to conquer."
Tián Cháng angrily changed countenance and said:
"What you consider difficult,
others find easy;
what you consider easy,
others find difficult.
Yet you advise me thus,
why?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Those with internal worries should attack the strong,
those with external worries should attack the weak.
Now your concerns lie within.
I hear you attempted three enfeoffments but none succeeded,
this shows your ministers do not obey.
If you destroy Lǔ to expand Qí,
victory will make your ruler arrogant,
conquering states will honor your ministers.
When Yàn and others lead troops,
if states are broken their prestige increases. ,
Yet your achievements won't be recognized,
so your relationship with the ruler will daily grow distant.
Thus above you'd foster the ruler's arrogance,
below you'd indulge the ministers,
seeking to accomplish great things -
this is difficult.
When superiors are arrogant they become arbitrary,
when ministers are arrogant they contend,
thus above you'd create rift with the ruler,
below you'd struggle with ministers.
In such situation,
your position would be endangered.
Therefore I say:
Better attack Wú.
If you attack Wú and don't win,
people die abroad,
ministers are depleted at home,
thus above you'd have no strong ministerial opponents,
below you'd bear no blame for people's losses,
the solitary ruler controlling Qí -
would be only you."
Tián Cháng said:
"Good.
But troops are already deployed against Lǔ,
cannot be changed,
what to do?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Delay your army.
I'll seek help from Wú,
have them rescue Lǔ and attack Qí,
you meet them with troops."
Tián Cháng agreed.
Zǐgòng then went south to persuade King of Wú:
"A true king doesn't let lineages perish,
a hegemon faces no strong enemies,
a thousand jun weight shifts with added zhu.
Now with ten-thousand-chariot Qí appropriating thousand-chariot Lǔ,
competing with Wú for strength,
this poses grave danger.
Moreover, rescuing Lǔ
brings fame;
attacking Qí
brings great benefit.
To pacify Sì River lords,
punish violent Qí to subdue Jìn,
no benefit greater.
In name preserving perishing Lǔ,
in reality weakening strong Qí,
no wise man would doubt this."
King of Wú said:
"Good.
But I'm truly troubled by Yuè,
Yuè king now trains hard nurturing men,
has intention to repay Wú.
Wait till I first attack Yuè,
then we can proceed."
Zǐgòng said:
"Yuè's strength doesn't exceed Lǔ's,
Wú's power doesn't surpass Qí's,
yet you abandon Qí to attack Yuè,
then Qí will have already pacified Lǔ.
You claim to preserve perishing states,
yet fear strong Qí, attack small Yuè,
this isn't courage.
The courageous don't avoid difficulty,
the benevolent don't abandon the distressed,
the wise don't miss opportunities,
the righteous don't end lineages,
thereby establishing their righteousness.
Now preserving Yuè shows benevolence to all,
rescuing Lǔ and attacking Qí,
imposing might on Jìn,
lords coming to court Wú in succession,
hegemony is achieved.
If you must dislike Yuè,
let me go east to see Yuè king,
have him send troops to follow,
thus actually emptying Yuè,
while nominally joining lords in attack."
King of Wú pleased,
sent Zǐgòng to Yuè.
Yuè king welcomed him beyond suburbs,
personally drove for Zǐgòng,
saying:
"This is barbarian land,
why should great sir honor us with presence?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Recently,
I persuaded Wú king to rescue Lǔ attack Qí,
he desires but fears Yuè,
saying:
'Wait till I attack Yuè then possible.'
Thus,
he'll certainly destroy Yuè.
Having no revenge intention yet making others suspect,
is clumsy;
having revenge intention,
letting others know,
is dangerous;
affairs not started yet known first,
is perilous.
These three are great troubles in undertaking affairs.
Wú king is fierce and violent,
ministers cannot endure;
state wearied by frequent wars,
soldiers discontent;
people resent superiors,
ministers plot internally;
Zǐxū died for remonstrating,
Grand Steward Pǐ handles affairs,
indulging ruler's faults,
to secure his private gain:
this is time for you to repay Wú.
If you can send troops to assist to stir his ambition,
offer treasures to please his heart,
use humble words to show respect,
he'll certainly attack Qí.
This is what sages call bending principles for distant aims.
If he doesn't win,
it's your blessing.
If victorious,
he'll certainly approach Jìn with troops.
I'll return north to see Jìn ruler,
jointly attack him,
weakening Wú is certain.
His sharp troops exhausted against Qí,
heavy armor trapped against Jìn,
you attack while he's weakened,
destroying Wú is certain."
Yuè king agreed,
sent minister Wén Zhǒng with three thousand men to aid Wú.
Wú then attacked Qí at Shàolíng,
indeed approached Jìn with troops,
met at Huángchí.
Yuè king attacked Wú's capital,
thus destroyed Wú.
Confucius said:
"Disordering Qí and preserving Lǔ
was my initial wish.
But strengthening Jìn to weary Wú,
making Wú perish and Yuè hegemonize,
was Cì's persuasion.
Fine words harm trustworthiness,
be careful with words!"
Qín Shǐhuáng toured Kuàijī,
reached Shāqiū,
fell gravely ill.
Shǐhuáng ordered Zhào Gāo write letter for Prince Fúsū,
not yet given to messenger,
Shǐhuáng died.
Then Shǐhuáng had over twenty sons.
Eldest son Fúsū,
sent to supervise troops at Shàngjùn,
Méng Tián as general.
Youngest son Húhài,
beloved,
requested to accompany,
emperor permitted.
Other sons didn't accompany.
Chéngxiàng Lǐ Sī thought emperor died outside,
no true crown prince,
so concealed it.
Ministers didn't know.
Zhào Gāo thus kept the sealed letter for Fúsū,
told Prince Húhài:
"Emperor deceased,
no decree enfeoffing princes but only letter for eldest son.
When eldest son arrives,
ascends as emperor,
you'll have no land at all,
what to do?"
Húhài said:
"So it is.
I hear wise ruler knows ministers,
wise father knows sons.
Father having passed,
not enfeoffing sons,
what can be said!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"Not so.
Now the power over the entire realm,
and the matter of survival or destruction, lie with you, me, and the Chancellor.
I hope you will consider it carefully.
Moreover, to make others one's subjects versus being subjected by others,
to control others versus being controlled by others—
how can these be spoken of in the same breath!"
Hú Hài said:
"To depose the elder brother and establish the younger—
this is unrighteous;
to not obey our father's decree and fear death—
this is unfilial;
with shallow abilities and meager talent,
to forcibly rely on others' achievements—
this is incompetence.
These three acts violate virtue,
and the world will not submit."
Zhào Gāo said:
"I have heard that Tāng and Wǔ killed their sovereigns,
yet the world praised them as righteous—
they were not considered disloyal;
the ruler of Wèi killed his father,
and the state of Wèi bore his virtue,
recorded by Confucius—
he was not deemed unfilial.
It is said:
Treacherous ministers and villainous sons
have existed since ancient times.
Born speaking the language of Chǔ,
one who can cause bitter weeping—
such is Hú Hài.
For great deeds do not fuss over trivial caution,
and great virtue does not shy from yielding.
Local customs each have their appropriateness,
and the hundred officials have different merits.
Therefore, to care for the small and forget the great
will surely bring harm later;
to hesitate and waver
will surely bring regret later.
Decisive and daring action
makes even ghosts and spirits avoid you,
leading to ultimate success.
I hope you will carry it through."
Hú Hài sighed deeply and said:
"Now the great journey has not yet begun,
how can we trouble the Chancellor with such matters!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"The moment, the moment!
There is no time even to plan.
