Carrying provisions and leaping on horses,
we only fear being too late!"
Hú Hài, convinced by Zhào Gāo's words,
then Zhào Gāo said to Chancellor Lǐ Sī:
"The emperor has passed away,
leaving a letter for the eldest son,
to meet with the funeral procession in Xiányáng,
and be established as successor.
The letter has not been sent,
and now the emperor has died,
with no one knowing.
What shall we do about this matter?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"How can you speak such words that would destroy the state!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"Consider your own ability compared to Méng Tián's—
whose achievements are higher?
Who plans more deeply without error?
Who is without resentment in the world?
Who is more familiar and trusted by the eldest son?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"In these five aspects,
I am not as good as Méng Tián,
but why do you press me so deeply!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"I was originally a menial servant in the inner palace,
fortunately entering the Qín palace as a clerk,
managing affairs for over twenty years,
and I have never seen a Qín chancellor or meritorious official dismissed and enfeoffed to the second generation—
they all ended up executed.
The emperor has over twenty sons,
all known to you.
The eldest son is resolute and brave,
trusting and experienced—
upon ascending the throne, he will surely appoint Méng Tián as chancellor,
and you, my lord, will ultimately not return to your hometown holding the marquis seal,
this is clear.
I received the edict to teach Hú Hài laws and methods,
he is benevolent, kind, and sincere,
values people over wealth,
none of Qín's other sons can match him—
he can be made successor.
Consider and decide."
Lǐ Sī said:
"I, Lǐ Sī,
was a commoner from the alleys of Shàngcài.
The emperor graciously promoted me to chancellor,
entrusting me with matters of survival, destruction, safety, and danger.
How can I betray this!
A loyal minister does not avoid death for a chance,
a filial son does not toil and face danger—
please say no more."
Zhào Gāo said:
"I have heard that sages change without constancy,
like dragons transforming with the times,
seeing the tip to know the root,
observing the direction to foresee the end.
This is inherent in things,
how can there be constant rules!
Now the power over the entire realm
hangs on Hú Hài,
and I can achieve my aim.
Moreover, controlling from outside is called confusion,
controlling from below is called treachery.
So when autumn frost falls, grass and flowers wither,
when winds and waters stir, all things arise—
this is the inevitable effect.
Why do you see it so late, my lord?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"I heard that when Jìn changed its crown prince,
three generations were unsettled;
when Duke Huán of Qí and his brothers contended for the throne,
he died a violent death;
when Zhòu harmed his relatives,
and did not heed advice,
his state became a ruin.
These three defied heaven,
their ancestral temples received no sacrifices—
was it not due to their actions!
How can I conspire with you!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"When above and below unite,
it can last long;
when inside and outside are as one,
affairs have no contradictions.
If you follow my plan,
you will long hold your marquisate,
be called 'the solitary one' for generations,
surely have the longevity of Shòu and Qiáo,
the wisdom of Confucius and Mòzǐ.
Now to abandon this and not follow,
disaster will reach your descendants,
enough to chill the heart.
The wise turn misfortune into blessing—
what will you choose?"
Lǐ Sī then looked up to heaven and sighed,
shedding tears and lamenting:
"Since I cannot die,
where else can I entrust my fate!"
So he followed Zhào Gāo in establishing Hú Hài,
altered the sealed decree,
and had Fúsū and Méng Tián killed.
Initially,
Lǐ Sī studied the art of emperorship with Xúnzǐ,
and wished to go west to Qín.
He bid farewell to Xúnzǐ, saying:
"I have heard that when opportunity comes, do not neglect it.
Now states with ten thousand chariots contend for the time,
and traveling persuaders decide affairs.
Now the king of Qín desires to swallow the world,
rule as emperor—
this is the time for commoners to gallop and for persuaders to talk.
So I will go west to persuade the king of Qín."
Arriving in Qín,
he became a retainer of Lǚ Bùwéi,
who valued him
and appointed him as a court gentleman.
He advised the king of Qín to secretly send strategists with gold and jade to lobby the feudal lords.
For the famous scholars of the states,
they were richly provided for;
those who refused
were stabbed with sharp swords.
They sowed discord among the rulers and ministers,
and thus Qín swallowed the world—
all were Lǐ Sī's strategies.
At the end of Qín Èrshì's reign,
Chén Shè rose in Qí,
and his troops reached Chén.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú advised Chén Shè:
"Great King, you have raised Liáng and Chǔ,
focusing on entering the pass,
but have not yet taken Héběi.
We have traveled in Zhào,
know its heroes,
and wish to lead a surprise force to capture Zhào's territory."
So King Chén agreed,
giving them three thousand soldiers.
Crossing the river from Báimǎ
(now within the boundaries of Báimǎ County, Huá Prefecture),
they reached various commanderies and counties,
persuading the local heroes:
"Qín imposes chaotic governance and cruel punishments,
destroying the world.
In the north, there is the corvée for the Great Wall,
in the south, garrisons at the Five Ridges,
inside and out in turmoil,
the people exhausted and destitute,
taxes collected by the head and gathered with baskets,
to supply military expenses,
wealth depleted and strength spent,
further burdened by harsh laws,
causing fathers and sons across the land to live in unbearable misery.
Now King Chén raised his arm to initiate the call for the world,
and none failed to respond.
Each household acted out of anger,
avenging their grievances individually,
counties killing their magistrates and assistants,
commanderies killing their governors and commanders.
Now they have proclaimed the Great Chǔ,
with kings in Chén,
sending Wú Guǎng and Zhōu Wén to lead a million troops westward to attack Qín.
In such a time, those who fail to achieve the feat of enfeoffment as marquises
are not true heroes.
To harness the strength of the world to attack a tyrannical ruler,
avenge the grievances of fathers and brothers, and accomplish the task of partitioning lands—
this is the moment. 」
The heroes all agreed with his words.
So they marched to recruit soldiers,
capturing over ten cities in Zhào.
A discussion states:
Bān Gù said:
"In the past, the 'Shī' and 'Shū' recorded the times of Yú and Xià,
when Shùn and Yǔ received the throne through abdication,
accumulating virtue and benevolence
for several decades
before assuming their positions.
The kings of Yīn and Zhōu
originated from Jì and Xiè,
passing through more than ten generations,
before they were able to depose and execute. "
Qín rose from Duke Xiāng,
gradually nibbling away at the six states,
until reaching the First Emperor,
who unified the world.
Once Qín declared itself emperor,
it feared the failures of the Zhōu,
believing that the feudal lords contended by force,
leading to weakened authority.
Thus, it abolished the five ranks,
dismantled city walls and melted weapons,
suppressed speech and burned books,
internally uprooting the brave and talented,
externally repelling the Hú and Yuè tribes,
employing uniform authority,
thinking it would ensure safety for ten thousand generations.
Yet within a little over ten years,
powerful enemies erupted unexpectedly,
conscripted garrisons became stronger than the Five Hegemons,
commoners were oppressed by the Róng and Dí tribes,
responses were silenced by slanderous talk,
raised arms proved more intimidating than armored soldiers.
The prohibitions of Qín
merely served to aid the heroes,
hastening its own demise.
From this perspective,
the resources for heroes
lie in oppressive governance.
Once Hán Xìn pacified Qí,
he became the King of Qí.
King Xiàng grew fearful,
sending Wǔ Shè from Xūyí to persuade the King of Qí,
urging him to divide the world into three parts.
Xìn did not listen.
After Wǔ Shè left,
Kuǎi Tōng knew that the power of the world lay with Hán Xìn,
and wanted to devise a remarkable strategy to move him,
using physiognomy to persuade Hán Xìn, saying:
"I have often studied the art of reading faces."
Hán Xìn said:
"How do you read faces, sir?"
He replied:
"Nobility or baseness lies in bone structure,
worry or joy in facial expression,
success or failure in decisiveness.
Using these to assess,
there is not one error in ten thousand."
Xìn said:
"How do you read my face, sir?"
He replied:
"I wish to speak in private."
Xìn said:
"Those around me, step away."
Kuǎi Tōng said:
"Reading your face,
you will not exceed the rank of marquis,
and even that is precarious and unstable.
Reading your back,
the nobility is beyond words."
Betrayal would bring great nobility.
Hán Xìn said:
"What does that mean?"
Kuǎi Tōng said:
"When the world first rose in rebellion,
heroes and brave men raised their banners with a single call,
and scholars of the world gathered like clouds and mist,
swarming like fish scales,
surging like smoke and rising like wind.
At that time,
the only concern was the destruction of Qín.
Now Chǔ and Hàn are locked in conflict,
causing the innocent people of the world to have their livers and gallbladders spilled on the ground,
fathers and sons exposing their bones, flesh and blood scattered in the wilderness,
too many to count.
The people of Chǔ rose from Péngchéng,
fighting and pursuing the defeated northward,
reaching Yíngyáng,
rolling up the land with their advantage,
their might shaking the world.
Yet their troops are trapped between Jīng and Suǒ,
forced against the western hills and unable to advance,
for three years now.
The King of Hàn leads several hundred thousand troops,
holding Gǒng and Luò,
relying on the natural barriers of mountains and rivers,
fighting several battles a day,
without gaining an inch of ground,
defeated and unsupported,
defeated at Yíngyáng,
wounded at Chénggāo,
then fleeing between Wǎn and Yè—
this is what is called both wisdom and courage being exhausted.
Their sharp spirit is blunted by treacherous passes,
and their food supplies are depleted from within,
the common people are exhausted to the extreme,
full of resentment and with nowhere to rely.
In my estimation,
the situation requires a sage of the world,
for only then can the world's calamities be quelled.
Now the fate of the two rulers hangs on your decision.
If you side with Hàn, Hàn wins;
if you side with Chǔ, Chǔ wins.
I wish to lay bare my heart,
offer my innermost thoughts,
and present my humble plan,
though I fear you may not use it.
If you truly heed my strategy,
nothing is better than allowing both to benefit and coexist,
dividing the world into three,
standing like the legs of a tripod,
so that none dare move first.
With your wisdom and sagacity,
and the multitude of armed troops you command,
holding strong Qí,
aligning with Yān and Zhào,
emerging from undefended lands to control the rear,
following the people's desires,
heading west to plead for the lives of the common people,
then the world will rise like the wind and respond,
and who would dare not listen!
Carve up the great and weaken the strong,
to establish feudal lords,
and once the lords are established,
the world will submit, listen, and attribute virtue to Qí's initiative,
holding the lands of Jiāo and Sì,
embracing the lords with virtue,
deeply bowing and yielding with courtesy,
then the rulers of the world will take turns coming to court in Qí.
It is said:
If heaven gives and you do not take,
you will instead suffer misfortune;
if the time comes and you do not act,
you will instead incur disaster.
I urge you to consider this carefully."
Hán Xìn said:
"The King of Hàn has treated me generously,
sharing his carriage with me,
clothing me with his clothes,
feeding me with his food.
I have heard:
those who ride in another's carriage share their burdens,
those who wear another's clothes share their worries,
those who eat another's food will die for their cause.
How can I pursue profit and betray righteousness!"
Kuǎi Shēng said:
"You consider yourself loyal to the King of Hàn,
wishing to build an enterprise for ten thousand generations,
but I secretly believe you are mistaken.
Initially, the King of Chángshān and Lord Chéng'ān were commoners,
bound as friends who would cut their throats for each other,
but later they quarreled over the matter of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé,
and the two became resentful.
The King of Chángshān presented Xiàng Yīng's head,
and fled like a rat to join the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn borrowed troops to march east,
killing Lord Chéng'ān south of the Chíshuǐ River,
where his head and feet were separated,
ultimately becoming a laughingstock of the world.
These two men in their relationship,
had the utmost joy in the world.
Yet they ended up capturing each other—
why?
Trouble arises from excessive desires,
and the human heart is hard to fathom.
Now you wish to act with loyalty and trust in dealing with the King of Hàn,
but surely it cannot be as firm as the bond between those two men,
and the matters involved are far greater than Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé's affair.
Therefore, I believe that you are mistaken
to think the King of Hàn will not endanger you.
Great men like Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ,
who preserved the perishing Yuè and made Gōu Jiàn a hegemon,
achieved merit and fame but met their deaths.
As the saying goes:
'When the wild beasts are exhausted, the hunting dogs are boiled;
when the enemy state is destroyed, the strategist ministers perish.'
Speaking in terms of friendship,
yours is not as deep as that between Zhǎng Ěr and Chéng'ān Jūn;
speaking of loyalty and trustworthiness,
it does not surpass that of Great Fū Zhǒng towards Gōu Jiàn.
These two examples
are sufficient for reflection.
I hope you will deeply consider this.
Moreover, I have heard:
those whose courage and strategies intimidate their sovereign face personal danger,
and those whose achievements overshadow the world receive no rewards.
Let me recount Your Majesty's accomplishments and strategies:
crossing the Western River,
capturing the King of Wèi,
seizing Xià Yuè,
leading troops down Jǐngxíng Pass,
executing Chéng'ān Jūn,
subduing Zhào, intimidating Yān, and pacifying Qí,
crushing the Chǔ army of two hundred thousand in the south,
killing Lóng Jū in the east,
and reporting success to the west,
this is what is called achievements unmatched in the world,
and strategies that appear once in a generation.
Now you carry the awe that intimidates your sovereign,
hold merits too great to be rewarded,
if you return to Chǔ,
the people of Chǔ will not trust you;
if you return to Hàn,
the people of Hàn will be terrified;
where do you intend to go with this?
Occupying the position of a subject,
yet possessing the power to intimidate the sovereign,
with a reputation that towers over the world,
I secretly fear for your safety."
Hán Xìn declined, saying:
"Sir, please rest now!
I will think about it."
A few days later,
Kuǎi Tōng again persuaded him, saying:
"Listening
is the sign of affairs;
planning
is the pivot of affairs.
Those who mishear and miscalculate yet remain secure for long
are rare.
Those who rarely err in listening
cannot be confused by words;
those who grasp the entirety in planning
cannot be disturbed by rhetoric.
Those who follow menial duties
lose the authority of a sovereign;
those who cling to meager salaries
—one dàn,
the remainder of a hú—
miss the positions of ministers and chancellors.
Thus, the wise
decide with resolution;
the doubtful
are the omen of affairs.
Pondering trivial calculations
while neglecting the great scheme of the world,
even if wisdom truly knows it,
but dares not act,
brings disaster to all endeavors.
Hence, a hesitating fierce tiger
is less fearsome than stinging bees and scorpions;
a pacing noble steed
is slower than a steady nag;
the hesitant Mèng Bēn
is less decisive than an ordinary man's resolve;
even with the wisdom of Shùn and Yǔ,
murmuring without speaking
is worse than the gestures of the mute and deaf.
Achievements
are hard to attain but easy to ruin;
opportunities
are hard to gain but easy to lose.
Time does not come twice,
I hope you will examine this carefully."
Hán Xìn hesitated, unable to bear betraying Hàn,
and believing his merits were great,
that the King of Hàn would never take Qí from him,
he thus declined Master Kuǎi.
Master Kuǎi said:
"Those pressured by trivial matters
cannot be partnered in great endeavors;
those confined to servitude
truly lack the ambition of a king."
His advice unheeded,
he left,
feigning madness to become a shaman.
Discussion says:
"In the past, Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
Yànzǐ did not die for the sovereign's calamity, saying:
'Those who rule others,
should they oppress them?
They are to govern the state;
those who serve as ministers,
is it for their sustenance?
They are to nurture the state.
Thus, if the sovereign dies for the state, then die for him;
if he flees for the state, then flee with him;
but if he dies for himself,
or flees for himself,
unless they are his intimates,
who would dare take responsibility!'"
Mèngzǐ said to King Xuān of Qí:
"If the sovereign treats his ministers as hands and feet,
then the ministers treat him as their heart and soul;
if the sovereign treats his ministers as grass and weeds,
then the ministers treat him as an enemy."
Although it is said:
"The sovereign,
is heaven.
Heaven cannot be escaped."
Yet ministers gauge their loyalty by the sovereign's favor,
as has been since ancient times.
Hán Xìn, treated generously by the King of Hàn, did not betray his virtue,
is truly pitiable!
King Bì of Wú, due to his son's incident, did not attend court
during Emperor Wén of Hàn's reign,
the Crown Prince of Wú came to court,
and while drinking and gambling with the Crown Prince,
they argued over the game,
and he was disrespectful,
the Crown Prince threw the game board at the Crown Prince of Wú,
killing him.
When the edict to reduce territories arrived,
he then sent Grand Master Yìng Gāo to incite
(tián niǎo fǎn)
the King of Jiāoxī,
without written documents,
orally reporting:
"The unworthy King of Wú,
facing imminent troubles,
dares not act as an outsider,
sends me to convey his heartfelt intentions."
The King said:
"What do you advise?"
Yìng Gāo said:
"Now the emperor has risen among deceitful heroes,
adorned by wicked ministers,
fond of petty virtues,
heeding slanderers,
arbitrarily altering laws and decrees,
encroaching on the lands of the feudal lords,
demanding more and more;
punishing the good and kind,
increasingly severe each day.
There is a saying:
'Licking the chaff reaches the rice.'
Wú and Jiāoxī,
are renowned feudal lords,
once under scrutiny,
I fear they will not rest easy.
The King of Wú has internal ailments,
unable to attend court for over twenty years,
often worried about being suspected,
with no way to clear himself.
Now, even with hunched shoulders and cautious steps,
he still fears not being absolved.
I have privately heard that you, Great King, have been implicated in a matter of rank
(zhí gé fǎn),
and the other feudal lords are having lands reduced,
but their crimes do not warrant this,
this恐怕 goes beyond mere land reduction."
The King said:
"Yes,
that is so.
What do you plan to do?"
Yìng Gāo said:
"Those sharing hatred assist each other,
those sharing interests stay together,
those sharing sentiments accomplish together,
those sharing desires move together,
those sharing benefits die for each other.
Now the King of Wú believes he shares your worries,
hoping to act in time to set things right,
sacrificing himself to rid the world of harm,
would that be acceptable?"
The King was startled and alarmed, saying:
"How dare I do such a thing?
Though the emperor is pressing,
I would rather die,
how can I not uphold him?"
Yìng Gāo said:
"The Imperial Censor-in-Chief Cháo Cuò,
deludes the Son of Heaven,
encroaches on the feudal lords,
blocks loyalty and stifles worthies,
the court is full of resentment,
the feudal lords all have thoughts of rebellion,
human affairs have reached their limit.
Comets appear at night,
locusts swarm repeatedly,
this is a once-in-an-era opportunity,
The customs and laws are without deficiency.
Nányuè submits as vassals,
Qiāngbó bring tribute,
Dōng'ōu surrender,
expanding Chángyáng
fortifying the frontier,
opening Shuòfāng,
the Xiōngnú have broken wings and injured pinions,
losing support and failing to revive.
Though not equaling ancient times of peace,
it is still orderly governance.
If Your Highness wishes to raise an insurrection,
I foresee calamity rather than fortune. 」
The king grew angry,
and Wǔ Bèi apologized for his capital offense.
The king said:
"Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng had not even land enough to set an awl,
yet with a crowd of a thousand men,
they rose in the great marshes,
raised their arms with great shouts and the world echoed in response,
reaching west to Xì
(pronounced xǔ zhí),
with a million troops.
Now though my state is small,
still I can raise over a hundred thousand victorious soldiers,
not merely conscripted masses with scythes and thorn spears
large sickles are called kǎi,
(pronounced wǔ āi).
Or perhaps jī jīn,
(pronounced qí jīn). ,
Why do you, sir, speak of calamity without fortune?"
Wǔ Bèi said:
"Qín was without virtue,
brutalizing the world.
With the chariots of ten thousand,
they built the Ēpáng
(pronounced páng)
Palace,
collecting more than half the taxes,
conscripting the poor from the lanes' left side,
fathers unable to comfort sons,
elder brothers unable to assist younger brothers,
harsh governance and severe punishments,
the world scorched as if burning,
the people all craning their necks to gaze,
inclining their ears to listen,
wailing mournfully to heaven,
beating their breasts and resenting the ruler,
thus with one shout from Chén Shèng,
the world echoed in response.
Now His Majesty rules the world,
unifying all within the seas,
broadly loving the masses,
spreading virtue and bestowing favors.
Though his mouth has not spoken,
his voice is swift as thunder;
though his commands have not issued,
his influence gallops like a god;
what his heart intends,
his authority moves ten thousand miles;
the response from below to above,
is like shadow and echo.
And your great general's ability does not match even Zhāng Hán or Yáng Xióng.
For Your Highness to compare yourself to Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng,
I consider an error."
The king said:
"If it is as you say,
can we not try our luck?"
Wǔ Bèi said:
"I have a foolish plan."
The king said:
"What is it?"
Wǔ Bèi said:
"Now the Shuòfāng commandery has vast fields,
beautiful water and grass,
but the relocated people are insufficient to populate the land.
We could forge a memorial from the chancellor and imperial secretaries requesting,
to relocate the commandery and state's prominent figures, appointed officials, and those with nài crimes or above
minor offenses not warranting head-shaving,
preserving their beards and sideburns,
hence called:
"nài".
Also said:
"by statute".
becoming sīkòu,
or guǐxīn, báicàn.
Nài,
means to endure. ,
pardon their sentences,
those with family wealth over five hundred thousand,
all relocate their families to Shuòfāng commandery,
increasing armored troops,
hastening their assembly date.
Also forge edicts from the Left and Right Chief Commandants of Works and the Shanglin Imperial Prison,
arresting the feudal lords' heirs and favored ministers
the Imperial Clan Superintendent has Left and Right Chief Commandants of Works,
Shanglin has a Water Commandant,
all offices in charge of prisoners. .
Thus the people will resent, the feudal lords fear,
then immediately send Biànwǔ
(a person's name)
to follow and persuade them,
perhaps we might get lucky,
one chance in ten?"
The king said:
"This is acceptable."
He wished to follow Wǔ Bèi's plan.
He sent men pretending to be criminals westward,
to serve the General-in-Chief and Chancellor;
once troops were mobilized
(mobilizing Huáinán's troops),
sending men to assassinate General-in-Chief Wèi Qīng,
and persuade the Chancellor to submit,
as easy as uncovering a blindfold.
He also wanted them to wear constables' clothes,
carry urgent dispatches with feathers,
coming from the east,
shouting:
'Nányuè troops have invaded!'
intending to use this to mobilize troops.
Before it could be launched,
the affair was discovered,
and they were executed.
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
a Zhào man named Xú Yuè submitted a memorial on world affairs saying:
I have heard the world's calamities
lie in collapse from within,
not disintegration from without,
this is constant from ancient to modern.
What is collapse from within?
It is like the late Qín.
Chén Shè lacked the dignity of a thousand chariots, not an inch of territory,
he was no descendant of kings, lords, great men, or renowned clans,
no local reputation for the virtue of a Confucius or Mòzǐ,
nor the wealth of Táozhū or Yī Dùn.
Yet rising from poor alleys,
raising thorn-tipped spears,
baring his shoulders and shouting,
he had the world follow like the wind,
what is the reason?
Because the people suffered while the ruler showed no compassion,
those below resented while those above remained unaware,
customs were chaotic while governance went unreformed,
these three factors
were what Chén Shè used as his capital.
This is called collapse from within.
Hence it is said:
the world's calamities
lie in collapse from within.
What is disintegration from without?
It is said:
the armies of Wú, Chǔ, Qí, and Zhào.
The seven states plotted great rebellion,
each styled ruler of ten thousand chariots,
with armored troops numbering hundreds of thousands,
their authority sufficient to awe their domains,
their wealth enough to motivate their officers and people,
yet they could not seize an inch of land westward,
but were themselves captured in the central plains,
what is the reason?
Not that their power was lighter than a commoner's or troops weaker than Chén Shè's.
At that time,
the former emperor's virtuous influence had not decayed,
and the people content with their land and customs were numerous,
thus the feudal lords had no support beyond their borders.
This is called disintegration from without.
From this perspective,
if the world truly has the momentum for collapse from within,
even commoners in poverty may initiate danger throughout the land,
as with Chén Shè;
how much more if the lords of the Three Jìn survive?
Though the world be vast,
it will lack order.
If truly without the momentum for collapse from within,
even with powerful states and strong troops,
they cannot turn around before being captured,
as with Wú, Chǔ, Qí, and Zhào;
how much less could ministers and commoners
create disorder?
These two forms
are the essential key to safety and danger,
worthy rulers should pay attention and examine deeply.
Recently,
crops have repeatedly failed in Guāndōng,
inferring from patterns and observing governance,
the people may become unsettled in their places.
Unsettled, they are easily moved,
and easy movement
borders on collapse from within.
I hope to address this in the court,
eliminating calamity before it takes form.
Later, Hàn Emperor Líng appointed Huángfǔ Sōng as general,
who defeated the Yellow Turbans,
shaking the world with his might,
yet court governance daily deteriorated,
the land grew empty and exhausted.
Thus Xìndū magistrate Yán Zhōng came to persuade Sōng, saying:
"Hard to obtain yet easy to lose is
timing;
what arrives without turning its heels is
opportunity.
Thus the sage acts in accordance with the time,
the wise seize the moment to advance.
Now you, General, encounter a rare fortune,
tread upon an easily startling chance,
yet you do not embrace this fate,
nor act when opportunity knocks.
How then will you preserve your great reputation?"
Sōng replied:
"What do you mean?"
Zhōng said:
"The Way of Heaven favors none,
the people follow the capable.
You received your command in late spring,
achieved success by winter's end,
moved troops like a deity,
needed no second thought in strategy,
crushing the strong as easily as snapping dry twigs,
melting resistance quicker than hot water on snow.
Within months,
your divine army swept like lightning,
sealing records and carving stones,
reporting achievements southward,
your awe-inspiring name shakes the court,
your fame spreads beyond the seas.
Even the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ
could not surpass yours, General.
Now you've achieved merits beyond reward,
embodying virtues surpassing ordinary men,
yet you serve a mediocre ruler—
how can you seek safety thus?"
Sōng said:
"Serving diligently day and night,
my heart never forgets loyalty—
why should I not be safe?"
Zhōng said:
"Not so.
As the saying goes:
The Strategies mention that
when a birth mother rubs her son's head until it bleeds,
observers think it utmost love.
But if a stepmother does the same,
people deem it cruelty.
The action is identical,
yet perceptions differ.
Now governance decays,
the royal house faces turmoil;
you stand in a stepmother's position,
wielding power that intimidates the ruler.
Though utterly loyal,
I fear minds will change of their own accord.
Secretly, I worry for your peril!
Moreover, I've heard:
when circumstances allow for treachery,
even Bó Yí becomes suspect;
if none doubt,
even Dào Zhī seems trustworthy.
Now you command a million troops,
positioned to do wrong,
holding power that harbors deceit,
placed in a suspect spot.
Even with utmost loyalty and trust,
can you convince others?
This is why Tián Dān, offering his robe,
aroused suspicion.
I urge you to consider this."
Yánshēng gathered such examples to sway his resolve,
citing Hán Xìn as analogy,
yet failed to grasp the meaning of 'heart never forgetting loyalty'.
The crux of persuasion
was missed here.
Hán Xìn, unable to bear a single meal's slight,
abandoned a tripartite domain,
only when a sharp sword was at his throat
did he sigh with bitter regret—
opportunity lost and plans awry.
Now our sovereign is weaker than Liú or Xiàng,
your authority greater than Huáiyīn's,
your command enough to shake wind and clouds,
your shout to summon thunder and lightning.
Arise fiercely,
counter danger and collapse,
honor allies with kindness,
awe the hesitant with might.
Rally Jì region's scholars,
mobilize seven provinces' masses.
Dispatch urgent missives ahead,
let the army's roar follow.
Cross the flowing Zhāng River,
water horses at Mèngjīn.
Punish the eunuchs' crimes,
clear accumulated grievances.
Even children would clench fists to serve,
women lift skirts to obey—
how much more your bear-like troops
riding the swift wind's force!
Once achievements are made,
the world pacified,
then appeal to the High God,
show all under heaven,
unify the six directions,
face south and proclaim rule.
Transfer treasures to the rising,
topple the failing Hàn,
a truly divine opportunity,
a moment to ride the gale!
Rotten wood cannot be carved,
a declining age's court is hard to aid.
To assist an unsalvageable court,
carve decayed wood,
is like pushing a ball uphill or rowing against the current—
can it be easy?
Moreover, eunuchs cluster like rats,
evils crowd the market;
royal decrees go unheeded,
power rests with flatterers;
under a blind ruler,
it's hard to last long;
unrewarded merits
draw slanderers' glares.
If you don't plan early,
regret will be too late."
Sōng, alarmed, said:
"Extraordinary plots
don't fit ordinary times.
Founding a state's great feat
is no task for mediocrity.
The Yellow Turbans are minor rebels,
no match for Qín or Xiàng;
newly formed, easily scattered,
they can't sustain a cause.
Besides, the people haven't forgotten their lord,
Heaven won't bless rebels.
To chase unrealized glory
and hasten daily disaster—
how compare to loyalty to this court,
keeping a subject's duty?
Though slanders may abound,
at worst I'll be exiled—
still leaving a good name,
deathless in death.
Such perverse talk
I dare not hear."
Commentary says:
Bright and dim don't cooperate,
capable and inept don't assist each other.
The wise won't strategize for a brave general,
the brave won't die for a timid commander.
So it has always been.
Thus the Tradition says:
"Loyalty is a fine virtue."
But not for the unworthy—
how much less for the unvirtuous?
The Military Dispositions states:
"Don't use wealth to move the righteous."
Thus the righteous won't die for the unkind,
the wise won't plan for a dim lord.
So Yī Zhǐ left Xià—
no harm to virtue;
Fēi Lián died for Zhòu—
not called wise.
Now the age is dark, the Way lost,
the land burns;
to cling to loyalty in a doomed court,
rest easy in dim favor,
where loyalty can't save the world,
nor death achieve righteousness—
should a wise man
act thus?
Yán Zhōng again argued this point.
Knowing his advice unused,
he fled.
When Dǒng Zhuó monopolized court power,
he summoned Huángfǔ Sōng.
Liáng Yǎn urged him to attack Zhuó.
Also, Táo Qiān and others jointly recommended Zhū Jùn as Grand Historiographer,
preventing his acceptance of Lì Què's summons;
both men refused.
Fàn Yè commented:
"Huángfǔ Sōng and Zhū Jùn, with their superior generals' strategies,
received commands in haste,
encountered a weak sovereign in distress,
fierce bandits running wild—
this was indeed Lord of Yè's moment to roll up his sleeves,
Dí Yì's day to rally troops.
So Liáng Yǎn offered counsel,
Shāndōng formed alliances,
yet they abandoned heaven-high ambitions
for a woman's petty scruples.
Ended up trapped in the tiger's mouth,
laughed at by the wise.
Was Heaven prolonging this chaos?
How could wisdom and courage end so—
alas!"
Discussion says:
Chǔ's Bái Gōng Shèng killed Zǐ Xī,
seized King Huì.
Lord Yè heard that Lord Bái was causing rebellion,
led the people of the state to attack Lord Bái,
and Lord Bái was defeated and fled.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
bandits and rebels arose in groups,
and Mǎng sent General Lián Dān to campaign east of the mountains.
Dān appointed Féng Yǎn as his assistant,
and they traveled together to Dìngtáo.
Mǎng sent a follow-up edict to Dān, saying:
"General, you bear the state's heavy responsibility,
yet you cannot sacrifice your life on the battlefield,
failing to repay the favor and fulfill your duty."
Dān was alarmed and fearful,
summoned Yǎn at night,
and showed him the letter.
Yǎn then persuaded Dān, saying:
"I have heard:
achieving success through compliance
is the great way of the Dào;
accomplishing deeds through defiance
is what authority values.
Therefore,
the goal is to achieve success,
without questioning the means;
when discussing the overall situation,
one should not cling to minor principles.
In the past, Féng Chǒufǔ leaned on the carriage rail and had his lord fetch water,
yet he was praised among the feudal lords;
Zhài Zhòng of Zhèng installed Tuī and exiled Hū,
ultimately enabling Hū to regain the throne,
and was commended in the 'Spring and Autumn Annals.'
For exchanging death for life,
and peril for survival,
is the way of a ruler;
acting contrary to popular opinion
to secure the state and preserve oneself
is the consideration of the wise.
Thus the 'Yì Jīng' says:
'When exhausted, change;
through change, one achieves penetration;
through penetration, one attains lastingness.
Hence, from heaven comes aid,
auspiciousness,
with nothing unfavorable.'
But to insist on doing what one knows is impossible,
destroying armies and decimating troops,
bringing no benefit to one's lord,
upon one's death,
bearing infamy in the world,
is what the wise do not do,
and the brave do not undertake.
Moreover, I have heard:
'When the opportunity arises, do not delay.'
Zhāng Liáng, whose family served Hán for five generations,
attacked the First Emperor of Qín at Bólàng,
his courage surpassing even Mèng Bēn and Xià Yù,
his fame higher than Tài Shān.
Your ancestors, General,
were trusted ministers of Hàn.
With the rise of the new dynasty,
the talented did not submit.
Now the land is in chaos and collapse,
the people cherish the virtue of Hàn,
even more than the poet's longing for Duke Shào.
They loved his gǔtáng tree,
how much more his descendants!
What the people sing and dance for,
heaven will surely grant.
Now, for your strategy, General,
nothing is better than stationing troops in a great commandery,
pacifying and overseeing the officials and soldiers,
honing their integrity;
within a hundred lǐ,
bestow cattle and wine daily,
recruit heroic and outstanding men,
seek loyal and wise counsel,
win the hearts of those to come,
await the shifts of alliance and conflict,
promote the benefit of the state,
remove the harm to the myriad people,
then blessings and emoluments will flow endlessly,
and achievements will be recorded indelibly.
How does this compare to having your army destroyed in the central plains,
your body fertilizing the wild grasses,
your accomplishments ruined and name lost,
shaming even your ancestors?
The sage turns calamity into blessing,
the wise man turns failure into success.
I hope you will plan deeply and not follow the common crowd."
Dān could not accept this,
and as they advanced to Suīyáng,
Yǎn again persuaded him, saying:
"I have heard:
the clear-sighted see what has not yet taken form,
the wise consider what has not yet sprouted.
How much more for what is already evident?
Troubles often arise from negligence,
disasters start from the trivial.
Failure leaves no room for regret,
opportunity must not be lost.
Gōngsūn Yāng said:
'One with superior conduct
is bound to bear blame in the world;
one with unique foresight
is sure to be deemed redundant by the people.'
So, to trust mediocre opinions,
discard rock-solid strategies,
follow the conventions of the age,
and lose one's lofty virtue—
decisiveness
is the master of wisdom;
hesitation
is the servant of affairs.
The moment will not come again,
do not deliberate further."
Dān did not listen,
advanced to Wúyán,
fought the Red Eyebrows,
and died.
At that time, Zhì Yùn of Rǔnán, observing the celestial signs, said to a friend:
"Now Zhèn Suì and Yínghuò
show no Hàn influence in the Yǐ-Zhěn region,
but they depart and return,
so Hàn must receive the mandate again.
If anyone follows heaven's will in strategy,
they are sure to achieve great success."
He used this to persuade Dān,
but Dān did not adopt his advice either.
Yǎn then fled to Hédōng.
Discussion:
In the past, Kuǎi Tōng advised Hán Xìn,
Yán Zhōng advised Huángfǔ Sōng,
Féng Yǎn advised Lián Dān—
these three men
all refused to listen,
willingly heading toward danger and death.
Why?
The response:
Fàn Yè said:
"When life is bitter,
the desire for self-preservation is weak;
when life is comfortable,
the concern for safety runs deep.
Those who climb high without fear
are convicts;
those who avoid sitting under eaves
are children of wealthy families."
From this we see,
in human nature,
comfort breeds a desire for stability,
hardship leads to thoughts of change—
an inevitable trend.
Now, these three either ruled as kings in the south,
or held the highest ranks as generals and ministers,
only scheming for self-preservation,
without considering extraordinary achievements,
unaware that suspicion breeds conflict,
and equal power sparks chaos.
Suspicion had already arisen,
yet they could not withdraw to avoid distrust;
power was already matched,
yet they could not reduce it to attract fortune.
Hesitating and wavering,
they reached peril and death—
their downfall lay in seeking preservation but instead inviting ruin.
As the saying goes:
"Accept death, and you may live;
cling to life, and you will die."
These gentlemen could be said to have clung to life.
Lái Xī advised Wěi Xiāo to send his son to serve at court,
but Xiāo's general Wáng Yuán, thinking the empire's outcome was uncertain,
was unwilling to focus on internal affairs,
and thus persuaded Xiāo:
"In the past, Gēngshǐ made the western capital,
and all quarters responded,
the world looked up with hope,
calling it great peace.
Yet once it collapsed,
you, great king, had almost nowhere to turn.
Now, to the south is Zǐyáng,
to the north is Wénbó,
across the rivers, lakes, seas, and Tài mountains,
there are a dozen kings and lords.
To follow the advice of scholars,
abandon a foundation of ten thousand chariots,
entrust yourself to a perilous state,
seeking absolute safety—
this is to follow the track of an overturned cart,
a plan that must not be adopted.
Now Tiānshuǐ is intact and wealthy,
with the strongest soldiers and horses.
Take Xīhé and Shàngjùn to the north,
gather the Sānfǔ lands to the east,
follow the old traces of Qín,
with mountains and rivers as your defense,
and I, Yuán, ask to use a pellet of mud to seal Hángǔ Pass for you, great king, in the east.
This is the chance of ten thousand generations;
if you do not plan for this,
you should store dried provisions, nurture your troops and horses,
hold the narrow passes and defend yourself,
To prolong the days and endure the duration,
awaiting changes from all directions.
If aspiring to kingship fails,
the remnants would still suffice for hegemony.
In essence,
a fish cannot leave the spring,
and a divine dragon, once losing its power,
is no different from an earthworm."
Xiāo remained indecisive.
Although he had sent his son as a hostage,
he still relied on treacherous terrain,
seeking to control the region independently,
thus betraying the Hàn.
Jiǎ Fù said:
"Those who aimed for the deeds of Yáo and Shùn but fell short were Tāng and Wǔ;
those who aimed for the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ but fell short were Huán and Wén;
those who aimed for the deeds of Huán and Wén but fell short were the Six States;
and those who established the framework of the Six States but failed to maintain it securely were the states that destroyed the Six States."
Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi battled Lǚ Bù at Púyáng,
but was unsuccessful.
Yuán Shào sent someone to persuade Tàizǔ to form an alliance,
suggesting Tàizǔ move his family to Yè,
and Tàizǔ was about to agree.
Chéng Yù came to see him and said:
"I've heard that you plan to move your family to Yè,
to ally with Yuán Shào.
Is this true?"
Tàizǔ replied:
"Yes."
Yù said:
"I suspect you are fearful in the face of events;
otherwise,
why would your consideration be so shallow?
Yuán Shào occupies the lands of Yān and Zhào,
harboring ambitions to unite the realm,
yet his wisdom is insufficient to achieve it.
Do you think you can submit to him?
With your majestic authority like a dragon or tiger,
could you serve as Hán Xìn or Péng Yuè did?
I am foolish and do not grasp grand strategies,
but I believe your aspirations
fall short even of Tián Héng's.
Tián Héng,
merely a brave warrior of Qí,
still felt ashamed to serve under Emperor Gāozǔ.
Now you plan to move your family to Yè,
intending to serve Yuán Shào facing north.
With your intelligence and divine prowess,
how can you not feel ashamed to be beneath Yuán Shào?
I am ashamed on your behalf.
Though Yǎnzhōu is devastated,
three cities remain;
the number of capable fighters
is no less than ten thousand.
If you gather them with Wénruò, Yù, and others and utilize them,
a hegemon's enterprise can be achieved.
I urge you to reconsider."
Tàizǔ then desisted.
Discussion says:
Chén Shòu praised the late ruler for his resolute and generous nature,
his ability to recognize talent and treat scholars well,
possessing the demeanor of Emperor Gāozǔ and the quality of a hero.
In tactical flexibility and strategic acumen,
he did not match Wèi Wǔ.
Yet he remained unyielding and resilient,
never willing to submit,
perhaps because he gauged that the other's capacity would not tolerate him,
not merely competing for advantage but also avoiding harm.
As the saying goes:
"One perch cannot host two mighty birds,
one spring cannot hold two dragons."
From this perspective,
if positions are equal and power balanced,
mutual intolerance is inevitable,
a phenomenon with deep roots.
Cáo Gōng's intention to move his family to Yè,
to ally with Yuán Shào,
was utterly misguided!
Yuán Shào, as alliance leader,
displayed arrogance,
and Zhāng Miǎo, governor of Chénliú, righteously reproached him.
Shào ordered Cáo Cāo to kill Miǎo,
but Cāo refused.
Miǎo felt uneasy.
When Cāo went east to attack Táo Qiān,
he had his general Chén Gōng stationed in Dōngjùn.
Gōng then persuaded Miǎo:
"Now the realm is divided and in chaos,
heroes rise together.
You command a hundred thousand troops,
positioned in a contested land,
holding your sword and gazing around—
that alone makes you a hero.
Yet you are controlled by others;
is that not shameful?
Now the provincial army campaigns east,
leaving the base empty.
Lǚ Bù is a mighty warrior,
unmatched in battle.
If we welcome him,
together we can hold Yǎnzhōu,
observe the realm's situation,
and await opportune changes.
This could be a time for grand strategies."
Miǎo agreed and rebelled against Cáo Gōng.
Discussion says:
Cáo Gōng and Miǎo were very close,
yet Miǎo harbored treacherous intentions
due to circumstances.
Thus, reviewing historical shifts,
they often stem from encroachments and humiliations,
or arise from flaws and conflicts,
like Hán Xìn's heartbreak over losing Chǔ,
Péng Chǒng's accumulated resentment from lack of distinction,
Lú Wǎn's suspicions and fears from past estrangements,
Yīng Bù's anxiety under pressure from exposed secrets—
these are the roots of such events.
From this, it is clear
that rebellious ministers and unfilial sons are not necessarily disloyal;
some act from resentment or peril,
others whose fame intimidates their lord,
thus achieving great deeds—
this has been true since ancient times.
After Zhōng Huì and Dèng Ài conquered Shǔ,
the Shǔ ruler surrendered.
Huì framed Ài,
leading to Ài's arrest and recall in a cage cart.
Huì secretly harbored rebellious plans,
treating Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi and others generously.
Wéi, recognizing his intent,
thought he could exploit the chaos,
gradually planning to reclaim Shǔ.
So he deceitfully advised Huì:
"Since your campaigns in Huáinán,
your strategies have never failed;
the rise of Jìn's path to prosperity
is all your doing.
Now you've pacified Shǔ,
your prestige shakes the world,
the people praise your achievements,
yet the ruler fears your schemes.
Where can you find safety?
Hán Xìn did not betray Hán in turmoil
but was suspected after peace;
Wén Zhǒng did not follow Fàn Lǐ to the lakes,
and ended up dying by the sword.
Was it due to foolish rulers and ministers?
No, it was driven by interests and perils.
Now you've achieved great merits,
and your virtue is renowned;
why not emulate Táo Zhū by sailing away and disappearing,
preserving your achievements and life,
ascending Mount Éméi,
and roaming with Chìsōngzǐ?"
Huì replied:
"Your words are far-sighted,
but I cannot follow them.
For the current path,
there may be more to it."
Wéi said:
"Other matters are within your intellect and power;
no need for an old man's advice."
Thus, their rapport grew very close.
Huì proclaimed himself governor of Yìzhōu and rebelled,
intending to give Wéi fifty thousand troops
as vanguard.
Wèi generals and soldiers, enraged,
killed Huì and Jiāng Wéi.
Zhāng Huá, stationed externally,
was to be recalled as Imperial Secretary.
Féng Dǎn resented this,
and while attending the emperor,
casually discussed stories of Wèi and Jìn,
saying:
"I believe Zhōng Huì's rebellion
was largely due to Tàizǔ."
The emperor flared up,
asking:
"What do you mean?"
Dǎn replied:
"I think a skilled driver
must understand the tension and slack of the six reins;
a skilled ruler
must grasp the appropriate control over officials.
Thus, Hàn Gāozǔ's eight kings
were destroyed due to excessive favor;
Guāngwǔ's generals
achieved good ends through restraint.
It's not that rulers differ in benevolence or tyranny,
or subjects in foolishness or wisdom,
but rather that suppression, promotion, granting, and taking make it so.
Zhōng Huì's talent was limited,
yet Tàizǔ over-praised and enticed him,
applauding his strategies,
elevating his fame and status,
granting him heavy authority...
Thus, Huì believed his strategies left no room for error,
his achievements were beyond reward,
and he exaggerated gains and losses,
thereby plotting treason.
Had Tàizǔ acknowledged his minor talents,
restrained him with grand rituals,
curbed him with authority,
and guided him with rules,
then rebellious thoughts would have had no cause to arise,
and chaos would have found no footing to form."
Shìzǔ replied:
"Indeed."
Dǎn kowtowed and said:
"Since Your Majesty accepts this foolish minister's words,
reflect on the path that leads to solid ice,
and do not allow those like Huì to cause ruin again."
Shìzǔ asked:
"Is there anyone like Huì today?"
Dǎn responded:
"The ministers who devise strategies for Your Majesty,
those who command the military forces—
all lie within Your Majesty's wise consideration."
Shìzǔ fell silent,
and soon after, Huà was dismissed from office.
During the reign of Jìn Huáidì,
Liáodōng Tàishǒu Páng Běn held a personal grudge against Eastern Yi Colonel Lǐ Zhēn,
and Xiānbī leaders Suǒ Lián, Mù Jīn, etc.,
claimed to rise in righteous cause for Zhēn,
but in reality used this as a pretext for rebellion,
thus attacking and defeating various generals.
Mùróng Huì's eldest son, Hàn, advised Huì:
"I have heard:
Nothing wins feudal lords like supporting the king.
Throughout history, capable rulers have all relied on this to achieve great deeds.
Now, Lián and Jīn act arrogantly,
the royal troops are defeated,
and the common people are slaughtered—
can any disaster be worse than this?
These scoundrels use Páng Běn's name outwardly,
but inwardly they seize the chance to plunder.
Liáodōng has fallen for over two weeks,
the central plains are in turmoil,
regional armies suffer repeated defeats—
to support the king and uphold righteousness,
now is the time!
The Chányú should demonstrate the might of the nine punitive expeditions,
rescue those in dire straits,
denounce the crimes of Lián and Jīn,
and unite righteous troops to destroy them.
On one hand, restore Liáodōng,
on the other, annex the two tribes,
display loyalty and righteousness to the court,
and secure benefits for our state.
This marks the beginning of our rise,
and in the end, we will prevail among the feudal lords."
Huì approved of this,
then mobilized forces to attack Lián and Jīn,
executed them,
and reestablished Liáodōng Commandery.
Commentary:
The ancients said that those who start trouble deserve death,
meaning they initiate chaos first.
Deceitful and ambitious individuals,
outwardly raise righteous troops to eliminate rebels,
but inwardly harbor treachery,
using this as a chance to rise—
all under the guise of supporting the king and aiding order, seizing power in due time,
as Huì did.
Later, in Qín, King Fú Shēng killed loyal and good officials,
and the Qín people felt each day
like a hundred years long.
Quán Yì then advised the King of Dōnghǎi, Fú Jiān:
"Now the ruler is blind and cruel,
and the realm is divided in heart.
Those with virtue thrive,
those without meet disaster—
such is the way of Heaven.
Should turmoil arise one day,
who but you, O King, can lead?
The imperial throne is a weighty matter,
it must not fall to others.
I urge you to act like Tāng and Wǔ,
following the people's will."
Jiān agreed,
made him a chief strategist,
then deposed Shēng,
and established Jiān as King of Qín.
Commentary: The "Zhuàn" says:
"The sage transcends norms,
the next best upholds them,
the worst loses them."
Zhònghuǐ said:
"Heaven creates humans with desires,
without a ruler, chaos ensues.
Heaven gives the wise to govern in time.
When Xià's virtue dimmed,
people fell into misery.
But the king shunned sensual pleasures,
and did not hoard wealth.
He eliminated the failing, strengthened the surviving,
and the state prospered.
He fostered the courteous,
overthrew the violent and blind.
Revering Heaven's way,
he secured the Mandate forever."
Xǔ Zhī said:
"The 'Chūnqiū Zhuàn' states:
Why did Zhōugōng not go to Lǔ?
Because even with a successor upholding the rites,
it does not prevent a sage from receiving the Mandate to rule."
Jīng Fáng wrote in the "Yì Zhuàn":
"When a king rules,
the wicked are removed,
the weak are taken from.
Dynasties change names,
Heaven's Mandate is not constant.
Through human plans and spiritual counsel,
the people support the capable."
From this perspective,
Fú Jiān's self-establishment and deposition of Shēng
reflect the sage transcending norms,
acting with the realm as his measure.
In Sòng, Kǒng Xìxiān,
son of Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Kǒng Mò,
had cunning talent,
excelling in astrology,
and claimed:
"The Jiāngzhōu region will produce a Son of Heaven,
and the emperor will be killed by kin."
When Grand General Péngchéng King Yìkāng was confined in Ānchéng Commandery,
Xìxiān thought he was the one,
so he persuaded the Crown Prince's Assistant Fàn Yè:
"My late father once left Guǎngzhōu,
amid court slanders,
but the General deeply intervened to save him,
sparing him from peril.
I long received his final wish,
to repay his virtue with death.
Now the emperor is blind and wayward,
likely abandoned by Heaven.
The General is decisive and wise,
supported by gods and men alike,
yet exiled to the southern border,
causing widespread indignation.
With public sentiment restless,
and astrological signs erratic,
when the time comes, it cannot be resisted—
is this not it?
If we follow the will of Heaven and people,
gather those who admire righteousness,
ally with favored relatives inside,
and unite heroes outside,
secretly plot within and without,
strike like sudden thunder from within,
then eliminate dissenters,
and honor the wise and enlightened,
riding on public expectation,
to command the realm—
who would dare not obey?
I, with my humble frame
and three-inch tongue,
will achieve deeds and credit them to you, sir.
What do you think, my lord?"
Yè was greatly startled.
Xìxiān pressed on:
"In the past, Máo Jú served with utmost loyalty,
yet was not tolerated by Wèi Wǔ;
Zhāng Wēn concluded his counsel,
only to be exiled by Sūn Quán.
Those two men,
trusted ministers of the state,
outstanding talents of their time—
was it due to exposed flaws
or tainted words and deeds
that they met disaster?
No, it was their integrity and uprightness
that conflicted with the wicked;
their noble conduct and fine principles
could not long be endured.
Your standing in this court,
is no deeper than theirs with their rulers,
and your reputation among men
surpasses both ministers.
Slanderers have eyed you with envy
for a long time.
Amid rivals competing,
how can you succeed?
With one word from Yīn Tiě,
Liú Bān was shattered;
Péngchéng's expulsion
made Xú Tóng suspect.
Was it some parental feud,
or generational hatred?
No, they drew swords and thorns
from youth onward,
competing only for fame, power, and precedence.
In the end,
they feared not trapping others deeply enough,
or acting too late.
When execution reached a hundred kin,
Yet it is said to be unsatisfying.
How can distant events recorded in books cause one to feel chilling fear and tremble!
Now, establishing great merit,
serving the wise and sagacious,
planning for difficulties while they are still easy,
replacing danger with safety,
comparing it to Mount Tài Shān while discarding a pile of eggs—
why hesitate to pursue it?
Moreover, elevating a sage and enlightened ruler
is the highest virtue;
personally enjoying the rank of minister or chancellor
is a grand achievement;
receiving a mandate while living in seclusion
is a great reputation;
matching the deeds of Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng
is an honorable title.
As for the highest virtue, grand achievement, great reputation, and honorable title,
these are what the Three Sovereigns and Five Hegemons fought for, even at the cost of armies destroyed and generals slain.
To encompass them all at once—
is that not fitting?
There is something even closer to this,
but I dare not speak of it foolishly."
Fàn Yè said:
"What do you mean?"
Xú Xīxiān said:
"You, sir, come from generations of pure and illustrious lineage,
yet you have not been able to marry into the imperial family.
The state treats you as if you were an animal,
and you, sir, have never felt ashamed of this?"
Fàn Yè lacked integrity in his private conduct,
so Xú Xīxiān used this to provoke him.
Fàn Yè fell silent,
and from then on, their relationship grew close,
and secret plots were formed.
Xú Xīxiān solely took the role of mastermind,
and when the affair was exposed, all were executed. [37 Péi Zǐyě said:
"Those with talent surpassing the crowd
are bound to aspire to soar to the heavens;
possessing a capacity beyond the ordinary,
they remain obscured beneath the common lot.
To guide them with the Way,
lead them with wisdom,
act without straying from righteousness,
and proceed without violating rites—
this is nearly impossible!
As for Fàn Yè and others, clinging to ambition and coveting power,
flaunting their talents to follow rebellion,
while Heaven offered no opening,
they sought to interfere with the times.
When their crimes were exposed and punishments carried out,
father and son wept together,
and generations of noble tradition
were destroyed in a single day.
This is what is meant by intelligence and ability becoming tools for self-destruction.
Treacherous and perilous at heart—
is this not referring to them?"
The Great General of Zhōu, Guō Róng, was sent on a mission to Suí's Gāozǔ,
Gāozǔ Yáng Jiān, who was then in Dìngzhōu.
Gāozǔ said to Guō Róng:
"I have always cherished mountains and rivers,
and do not care for official trappings.
By chance, I relied on the opportunities of the times,
and thus undeservedly gained fame and position.
I wish to return to my estate as a marquis,
to safeguard my remaining years—
what do you think?"
Guō Róng replied:
"Now the ruler is without virtue,
and people are filled with fear and apprehension.
The Mandate of Heaven is not constant,
and those with ability arise in turn.
Your virtue, illustrious sir, surpasses even that of the Western Earl,
and your prestige reaches the pinnacle of the state's glory.
You should instead seize the entire realm
to bring comfort to the common people—
how can you echo the words of children and women about jumping into pits and traps!"
Gāozǔ was greatly startled and said:
"Do not speak recklessly,
or it will mean the extermination of your clan."
When Gāozǔ became chancellor,
he said to Guō Róng with a laugh:
"Your earlier words indeed came true."
He later went on to replace the Zhōu dynasty.
A discussion states:
In the past, when King Wǔ reached Yīn,
about to engage in battle,
Zhòu's troops were exceedingly numerous.
King Wǔ feared, saying:
"The world considers Zhòu great,
and Zhōu small;
considers Zhòu numerous,
and Zhōu few;
considers Zhōu weak,
and Zhòu strong;
considers Zhōu in peril,
and Zhòu secure;
considers Zhōu a mere feudal state,
and Zhòu the Son of Heaven.
With these five shortcomings,
to strike against his five strengths—
can we possibly achieve success and accomplish our task?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Do not be afraid or fearful, O King.
What is called greatness
means winning over all the people of the world;
what is called numerous
means gaining the multitude of the world;
what is called strength
means utilizing the strength of the entire world;
what is called security
means fulfilling the desires of the world;
what is called the Son of Heaven
means the world loves each other like father and son—
this is what is meant by the Son of Heaven.
Today, we act to rid the world of cruelty and villainy.
Though Zhōu is small,
has it ever wronged even one person with cruelty or villainy?"
King Wǔ was greatly pleased,
and said:
"What is meant by cruelty and villainy?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Collecting the world's pearls, jade, beautiful women, gold, silver, and silks,
hoarding them without cease—
this is called cruelty;
employing violent and oppressive officials,
killing innocent people,
not according to laws and standards—
this is called villainy."
From this perspective,
if one engages in cruel and villainous conduct,
even if great,
they will perish.
Thus, it is understood that the power of a true king
does not lie in numbers, few or many.
This has been so from the beginning.
When Suí Gāozǔ passed away,
he was buried in the Tài Líng tomb.
Initially, when he fell ill,
an imperial edict summoned Prince Hàn, Liàng,
who was then stationed in Bìngzhōu.
Liàng, upon hearing of Gāozǔ's death,
and rumors that Yáng Sù had usurped the throne,
grew greatly fearful,
believing it to be a deception.
He raised troops to defend himself,
secretly plotting rebellion,
and attacked Púzhōu from the south,
capturing it.
When Liàng first rebelled,
Wáng Qǔ advised Liàng, saying:
"The families of Your Highness's officers and officials
are all west of the pass.
If you employ these men,
you should immediately march deep inland,
directly seizing the capital—
what is called 'swift thunder that leaves no time to cover the ears.'
If you only wish to carve out the old territory of Qí,
then you should appoint men from the east."
Liàng did not follow his advice,
and thus was defeated.
Sīmǎ Cānjūn Péi Wén'ān advised Liàng, saying:
"In war, swiftness even if crude is valued;
one never hears of cleverness that is slow.
Now, the late emperor's coffin is still at Rénshòu,
and by the time they muster troops to advance eastward,
it will take ten days to a month.
If with ten thousand swift and brave cavalry,
armor rolled, marching by night,
heading straight for Cháng'ān,
it will take less than ten days.
Then, the discontented elements,
promoted to high positions,
entrusted with your confidence,
can together guard the capital,
and the prefectures and counties east of the mountains will not belong to them.
After that, Your Highness can march west with drumbeats,
and once the momentum is joined,
the world can be settled with a wave of the hand."
Liàng did not follow this,
and instead personally led a large army,
stationing it between Bìng and Jiè.
The emperor, hearing of this, grew greatly fearful,
and summoned Hè Ruòbì to discuss it.
Bì said:
"Prince Hàn
is the late emperor's son,
and Your Majesty's younger brother.
He holds the heavy responsibility of a regional commander,
overseeing the duties of a feudal lord,
his fame and influence resound,
and he is admired throughout the land—
his rebellion is already complete.
However, his strategies for advancement are three:
to march swiftly into the pass,
directly seizing the capital,
resisting the imperial army in the west,
and capturing the lands east of the mountains in the east—
this is the best strategy."
If so,
then the potential of the empire cannot be measured.
Stationing a large army at Pǔzhōu,
sending five thousand cavalry to block Tóngguān Pass,
restoring the former territory of Qí,
occupying it and establishing a capital there,
is a middling strategy.
If so,
to contend by force
Commentary says:
The former territory of Qí,
refers to the lands during the Northern Qí period,
not the present-day Qí of Qīngzhōu. .
If he personally resides in Tàiyuán,
merely dispatching his generals to come,
is a lower strategy.
If so,
he will be captured. ”
The Emperor said:
“You, sir, try to plan for me,
what strategy will emerge? ”
Bì said:
“Xiāo Móhē,
is a general of a fallen state,
and cannot be partnered with to plan great affairs.
Péi Wén'ān,
though talented in his youth,
is not employed.
The rest are all petty men,
caring for and attached to their wives and children,
merely seeking their own safety,
unable to venture far.
They will surely send an army to attack Pǔzhōu,
while he personally resides in Tàiyuán,
using it as his lair.
I believe they will certainly adopt the lower strategy. ”
It indeed turned out as Bì had planned.
So he appointed Yáng Sù as general,
and defeated them.
Commentary says:
Initially,
the Prince of Hàn secretly plotted rebellion,
claiming to campaign against Sù.
Marshal Huángfǔ Dàn admonished:
“The Great Suí has possessed the empire for over twenty years,
the masses are peaceful,
making it hard to shake,
first;
the people are weary of chaos,
everyone longs for peace and happiness,
even if Shùn or Yǔ were reborn,
their hopes would not be followed,
second;
the Crown Prince is intelligent and divinely martial,
his name corresponds to prophecies,
Sù has not even had the chance to serve his chariot,
how dare he harbor rebellious intentions,
third;
currently, the various princes guard the provinces and commanderies,
controlling each other internally and externally,
making the situation impossible to rally,
fourth.
With these four solid reasons,
overseeing the empire,
to be able to initiate turmoil,
has never been heard of before. ”
The Prince of Hàn did not listen,
hence his defeat.
From this perspective,
when the empire has no desire for chaos,
even signs of collapse,
though possessing the numbers of Wú and Chǔ,
still cannot succeed,
let alone insignificant ones?
Therefore, the former kings amplified their virtuous reputation,
diligently sympathized with the people's hidden sufferings,
precisely for this reason.
Emperor Yáng of Suí personally led the six armies to attack Gāolì.
Minister of Rites and Duke of Chǔ, Yáng Xuángǎn, rebelled based in Líyáng.
Lǐ Mì advised Xuángǎn:
“The Son of Heaven is on a distant campaign in Liáodōng,
a land distant from Yōuzhōu,
separated by a thousand lǐ,
with the vast sea to the south as a barrier,
and the threat of northern barbarians,
the single route in between,
is extremely perilous.
Now you command troops,
strike unexpectedly,
drive straight into Kuǎi,
and seize his throat.
With Gāolì ahead,
and no retreat route behind,
within ten days,
their supplies will surely be exhausted,
raise your banner and summon,
his troops will surrender on their own,
achieving victory without battle,
is the superior strategy
Another version states:
with the imperial carriage in Liáo,
unaware of this move.
Dispatch over ten thousand troops swiftly,
defend Línyú Pass,
cut off their retreat,
within a month,
their granaries will surely be depleted.
Pressed by the great enemy to the east,
and our forces to the west,
with no reliance ahead,
and no foothold behind,
a million troops,
can be made to perish like fish.
This is subduing the enemy without battle,
the superior strategy. .
Guānzhōng, surrounded by natural barriers,
is the land of abundance,
with Wèi Wénshēng there,
but not a major concern.
If you lead the masses into Cháng'ān now,
even if the Son of Heaven returns,
he will have lost his strategic hold,
and you can confront him from a vantage point,
thus surely overcoming him,
a fully secure strategy,
is the middling strategy
Another version states:
Since the emperor ruled, all under heaven have resented him.
You, illustrious sir,
son of a high general,
have kindness covering the common people.
Drive straight into the pass,
is the middling strategy. .
If following proximity and convenience,
heading first to the Eastern Capital,
stationing troops under its strong walls,
victory or defeat remains uncertain,
this is the lower strategy
Another version states:
Fán Zǐgài does not grasp the greater scheme,
with cunning plans and decisive actions,
holding the entire Zhōu region,
relying on strong armor and soldiers,
he won't come if summoned,
and won't fall if attacked.
Stationing troops under a fortified city,
with no allied forces outside.
Attacking Luòyáng,
is the lower strategy. . ”
Xuángǎn, coveting the treasures of Luòyáng,
said:
“Your lower strategy,
is my superior strategy. ”
So he besieged it.
Xuángǎn suffered defeat,
fled overnight,
and the imperial forces pursued and beheaded him.
Commentary says:
When Xuángǎn rebelled,
Venus entered the Southern Dipper.
A proverb says:
“When Venus enters the Southern Dipper,
the Son of Heaven walks off his hall. ”
Thus, the empire held conflicting loyalties.
Therefore, The Three Strategies says:
“Exaggerated words go too far. ”
Péi Zǐyě said:
“Those with heterodox ways and strange practices,
deluding and deceiving with fantasies,
can enough to move the masses,
but not enough to achieve success. ”
Now observing through the proverb,
that heterodox ways can move the masses,
is indeed true!
Hence, the king prohibits them.
Lǐ Mì then fled,
and joined Zhái Ràng.
Commentary says:
Tàigōng stated:
“Those who benefit the world take the world,
those who pacify the world possess the world,
those who love the world endure in the world,
those who are benevolent to the world transform the world. ”
The Annals of Lü Buwei says:
“A cook blends flavors but dares not eat,
thus can be a cook.
If the cook blends flavors and eats them,
then cannot be a cook.
The same applies to a hegemon or king.
Punishing the violent without selfishness,
to enfeoff the worthy of the world,
thus can become a hegemon or king;
if a hegemon or king punishes the violent for personal gain,
then cannot become a hegemon or king.
From this perspective,
to give is to take,
These are the treasures of governance.
Now Yáng Gǎn covets the treasures and goods of Luòyáng,
how could he accomplish the deeds of a hegemon or king?"
When Suí Yángdì first grew suspicious of Táng Gāozǔ,
the latter became aware of it,
and constantly harbored fear and apprehension.
The Duke of Táng was the garrison commander of Tàiyuán,
and when Emperor Yáng returned to the capital from Liáodōng,
the Duke of Táng went to the imperial temporary residence to pay respects,
but due to an unhealed illness,
he could not attend the audience in time.
The Duke of Táng's niece, a woman of the Wáng family,
was selected to join the rear palace,
and Emperor Yáng asked her:
"Why has your uncle arrived so late?"
The niece replied truthfully,
and the Emperor said:
"Could he be dying?"
Gāozǔ learned of this,
and was constantly filled with fear and apprehension.
As the garrison commander of Tàiyuán,
due to unsuccessful military campaigns,
he feared being reprimanded by Emperor Yáng,
and was deeply troubled by this.
At that time, Tàizōng was accompanying him in the army,
and knowing that the Suí dynasty was nearing its end,
he secretly planned a righteous uprising,
to bring peace to the world.
He then advised:
"Why is my father so deeply worried?
The current ruler is without virtue,
the people are filled with sorrow and resentment,
outside the city gates,
all have become rebels.
If we merely cling to minor principles,
we will surely face death sooner or later.
If we raise an army of righteousness,
it would truly align with the people's desires.
Moreover, Jìnyáng is a strategic place for military operations,
with ample food and soldiers,
and you, father, reside here.
This is heaven's grant,
precisely an opportunity to turn disaster into fortune,
and achieve great deeds.
If heaven gives but we do not take,
what good is worry?"
Gāozǔ was greatly startled,
and firmly rejected him.
Tàizōng hurried out,
and the next day advised again:
"This is a foolproof strategy,
to save us from the fate of clan extermination.
Now the imperial laws are lax and disordered,
bandits are everywhere under heaven,
and you, father, are ordered to suppress them,
but can they be entirely eliminated?
Since the bandits cannot be fully eradicated,
you will inevitably be held guilty.
Moreover, it is widely said that the Lǐ family is destined to receive the celestial mandate,
Lǐ Jīncái held high position and prestige,
yet his clan was exterminated in a single day.
Even if you, father, can pacify the bandits,
your achievements would be too great to reward,
and seeking survival through this,
is it possible?"
Gāozǔ's resolve slightly softened,
and he said:
"I have thought it over all night,
and your words make great sense.
Today, the destruction of our family and my death will be because of you,
and turning our family into a state will also be because of you."
Thus, the plan was decided,
and he ordered Tàizōng with the Jìnyáng magistrate Liú Wénjìng,
and his followers Zhǎngsūn Shùndé, Liú Hóngjī, and others to recruit soldiers.
Within ten days,
the crowd reached nearly ten thousand.
They executed the deputy commanders Wáng Wēi and Gāo Jūnyǎ,
because they deceitfully invited Gāozǔ to pray for rain at Jìncí,
intending harm.
Adopting Péi Jì's strategy,
following the precedents of Yī Yǐn exiling Tàijiǎ and Huò Guāng deposing Chāngyì,
they honored Emperor Yáng as Tàishàng Huáng,
established the代王 Yòu to stabilize the Suí court,
issued proclamations to various comman,
to manifest their righteous cause.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
with thirty thousand elite troops,
they marched west to plan the capture of Guānzhōng.
Gāozǔ held a white banner,
and pledged to the masses in the wilderness of Tàiyuán,
leading the army on the road,
thus ending the Suí lineage,
and establishing our central land.
The Jìnyáng magistrate Liú Wénjìng once secretly observed Tàizōng,
and said to Péi Jì:
"He is no ordinary man.
His magnanimity resembles that of Hàn Gāozǔ,
his divine might matches that of the Wèi Emperor.
Though young in age,
he is endowed by heaven."
Later, Wénjìng, being a relative of Lǐ Mì,
was imprisoned.
Tàizōng, secretly harboring grand ambitions,
visited him in prison.
Wénjìng was overjoyed,
also sensing Tàizōng's extraordinary intent,
and sighed:
"Under great chaos in the world,
without the talent of a Tāng, Wǔ, Gāo, or Guāng,
it cannot be stabilized."
Tàizōng, understanding his meaning,
replied:
"How do you know there is none?
Only fear that ordinary people cannot recognize it."
Wénjìng rose and clapped:
"I have long known you, young master, are a hidden dragon.
Now that the times are like this,
it is precisely the season to soar.
You inherently possess the quality to receive the mandate,
and still hold the way to quell chaos,
this gives the people hope for relief,
and I, Wénjìng, know where to attach myself."
Tàizōng joyfully said:
"What plan do you propose?"
Wénjìng replied:
"Now Lǐ Mì has long besieged Luòyì,
and the emperor is wandering in Huáinán.
Major bandits span provinces and comman,
minor thieves block mountains and marshes,
numbering in the tens of millions.
But only a true ruler can drive and capture them.
If you can truly respond to heaven and accord with the people,
raise a banner and give a great shout,
then the four seas can be stabilized without difficulty.
Now the people of Bīngzhōu fleeing bandits,
all enter this city.
I, as magistrate for several years,
know its heroes,
once called upon,
tens of thousands can be gathered instantly.
The troops under your honored father also number tens of thousands,
once a word is spoken,
who would dare not follow?
Take advantage of the void to enter the passes,
command the world,
in less than half a year,
imperial enterprise can be achieved."
Tàizōng laughed and said:
"Your words are excellent,
and match my thoughts."
Thereupon, he arranged his followers,
secretly planning the uprising.
Gāozǔ then ordered Wénjìng to forge an edict from Emperor Yáng,
conscripting men aged twenty to thirty from several comman including Tàiyuán, Yànmén, Mǎyì,
to gather at Zhuōjūn by year's end.
This caused great unrest among the people,
and those desiring chaos increased.
He also ordered Wénjìng and Péi Jì to counterfeit tallies and edicts,
to withdraw goods from the palace warehouse,
to supply the garrison's needs.
Thus, they recruited soldiers and gathered the masses to rise,
changing flags to manifest their righteous cause.
Also, Wénjìng was ordered to ally with the Turks.
The Turkish Shǐbì Khagan said:
"The Duke of Táng raises a righteous army,
what does he intend to do?"
Wénjìng replied:
"Emperor Wén deposed the rightful heir,
passed the throne to the later ruler,
thus causing this calamity and chaos.
The Duke of Táng,
a close relative of the state,
cannot bear to stand by and watch success or failure,
wishes to depose the improperly enthroned,
and hopes to join the Khagan's troops in entering the capital.
The people and land will go to the Duke of Táng,
the wealth, silks, gold, and treasures to the Turks."
Shǐbì was greatly pleased,
and immediately sent troops with Wénjìng,
thus enhancing their military prestige.
From this, we can see:
it is known that
the world
is not the world of one person,
but the world of all under heaven.
Therefore, a true king must understand the three unities,
and know that the mandate of heaven is bestowed broadly,
not exclusively on one family.
In the past, when Confucius discussed the "Book of Songs",
upon reaching "The officers of Yīn are handsome and alert,
they assist in the capital's rituals,"
he sighed deeply and said:
"Wealth and honor are not constant,
if it were not so,
how would kings and dukes be cautioned and careful,
and how would the common people be encouraged and urged!"
The "Book of Changes" says:
"In safety, do not forget danger,
in existence, do not forget perish."
Thus, personal safety and the state can be preserved. "
Therefore, knowing fear and reflecting on caution,
is indeed the blessing of a nation.
Timely Strategies: Chapter Twenty-One
There are matters that appear similar yet differ in circumstances,
not because the matters are deceitful,
but due to changes in the times.
How can this be demonstrated?
In the late Qín dynasty,
Chén Shè rose from Qí,
and his troops reached Chén.
The local elites of Chén advised Chén Shè, saying:
"General, clad in armor and wielding sharp weapons,
leading soldiers to punish the tyrannical Qín,
restoring the state of Chǔ,
your merits and virtues warrant you becoming king."
Chén Shè consulted Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr,
and the two replied:
"General, with wide-eyed courage,
embarking on a plan risking death without regard for survival,
you aim to rid the world of remnants of evil.
Now, upon just reaching Chén, declaring yourself king
would reveal selfish intentions to the world.
We urge you not to become king,
but instead quickly lead your troops westward,
send envoys to reestablish the descendants of the six states,
thereby building alliances for yourself.
In this way,
there would be no conflicts in the fields,
you could destroy the tyrannical Qín, occupy Xiányáng,
and command the feudal lords,
thus achieving imperial enterprise.
If you solely proclaim yourself king in Chén now,
I fear the world will fall apart!"
During the Chǔ-Hàn conflict,
Lì Yìjī, strategizing for Hàn to undermine Chǔ's power,
said:
"In the past, Tāng attacked Jié,
enfeoffing his descendants in Qǐ;
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
enfeoffing his descendants in Sòng.
Now Qín has lost virtue and abandoned righteousness,
invading the states of the feudal lords,
extinguishing the descendants of the six states,
leaving them without land to stand on.
If Your Majesty can truly reestablish the descendants of the six states,
their rulers, ministers, and common people will surely revere Your Majesty's virtue,
all turning toward your influence and admiring your righteousness,
willing to become your subjects.
With virtue and righteousness put into practice,
Your Majesty facing south could claim hegemony,
and Chǔ would surely straighten its garments and come to court."
The King of Hàn said:
"Good."
Zhāng Liáng said:
"If you truly follow this advisor's plan,
Your Majesty's cause will be lost."
The King of Hàn asked:
"Why?"
Liáng then raised eight difficulties,
summarizing as follows:
"In the past,
when Tāng attacked Jié,
he enfeoffed his descendants in Qǐ
because he could control Jié's fate.
Can Your Majesty now control Xiàng Jí's fate?
This is the first impossibility.
When King Wǔ entered Yīn,
he honored Shāng Róng's neighborhood,
released Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
and built a tomb for Bǐgān.
Can Your Majesty now build tombs for sages
and praise the neighborhoods of the worthy?
This is the second impossibility.
He distributed grain from Jùqiáo,
scattered wealth from Lùtái,
to relieve the poor.
Can Your Majesty now disperse the treasury to aid the impoverished?
This is the third impossibility.
After the Yīn affairs concluded,
he converted war chariots to civilian use,
stored away weapons,
showing the world he would no longer use force.
Can Your Majesty now abandon arms and cultivate culture,
never again employing troops?
This is the fourth impossibility.
He released horses on the south of Huàshān,
showing he had no further use for them.
