Can Your Majesty release horses and not use them again?
This is the fifth impossibility.
He rested oxen in the fields of Táolín,
showing the world no more transport of supplies.
Can Your Majesty do this?
This is the sixth impossibility.
Moreover, the wandering scholars of the world,
who left their families, abandoned graves, departed from old friends to follow Your Majesty,
day and night hope for a tiny piece of land.
If the six states are restored now,
establishing descendants of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Zhào, Qí, and Chǔ,
with no others left to establish,
the wandering scholars will return to serve their own lords, rejoin their families, and revert to old ties;
with whom will Your Majesty conquer the world?
This is the seventh impossibility.
Furthermore, only if Chǔ is not strong,
would the six states be submissive;
it's only when Chǔ is not strong
that the six states, weakened, would follow.
How could Your Majesty then make them your subjects?
This is the eighth impossibility.
If you truly follow this advisor's plan,
then the great enterprise is lost."
At that moment, the king was eating;
he spat out his food,
scolded Lì Yìjī, saying:
"Pedantic scholar!
You nearly ruined my affairs!"
He urgently ordered the seals destroyed.
This illustrates differing circumstances.
Xún Yuè said:
"The methods for formulating strategies and securing victory
have three essentials:
first is form,
second is momentum,
third is sentiment.
Form refers to
the overall assessment of gains and losses.
Momentum refers to
the immediate situation and the opportunities for advance or retreat.
Sentiment refers to
the actual state of morale and determination.
Thus, even with the same strategy and similar matters,
the three methods differ.
Initially,
Zhāng Ěr advised Chén Shè to restore the six states' descendants,
to build alliances for himself.
Lì Yìjī also used this to persuade the King of Hàn;
though the advice was the same,
the outcomes differed.
Why?
When Chén Shè rose,
the whole world desired the fall of Qín;
but during the Chǔ-Hàn division, it was uncertain
if the world necessarily wanted Xiàng's fall.
Moreover, Xiàng Yǔ had the strength to lead the six states,
unlike Qín's situation,
which could not.
Therefore, establishing the six states for Chén Shè
meant increasing his own allies
and exacerbating Qín's weaknesses.
Besides, Chén Shè did not exclusively control the land under heaven;
it was about taking what wasn't his
to bestow virtue upon others,
offering empty favors to gain real benefits.
Establishing the six states for the King of Hàn,
however, meant cutting his own possessions
to aid the enemy,
setting up empty titles and incurring real harm.
This is a case of similar matters but different forms."
During the Warring States period,
the King of Qín said to Chén Zhěn:
"Hán and Wèi are attacking each other,
unresolved for a year.
Some say it's better to intervene,
others say not to;
I cannot decide,
please decide for me."
Zhěn said:
"Once, Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was about to stab a tiger,
when a stable boy stopped him,
saying:
'Two tigers are feeding on an ox;
the ox is tasty, so they will fight,
and fighting will lead to combat,
where the larger gets injured and the smaller dies.
Then, stabbing the injured one,
with one move, you gain the fame of two tigers.'
Now Hán and Wèi are fighting,
unresolved for a year;
surely the larger state will be injured, the smaller destroyed.
Attacking the injured one then,
with one move, you gain the substance of both.
This is like Biàn Zhuāng stabbing the tiger."
King Huì said:
"Good."
It turned out as he said.
Initially,
when the feudal lords rebelled against Qín,
Qín general Zhāng Hán besieged the King of Zhào in Jùlù.
King Huái of Chǔ sent Xiàng Yǔ, Sòng Yì, and others north to rescue Zhào.
They reached Ānyáng
(now Ānyáng County in Xiàngzhōu),
and halted without advancing.
Yǔ said to Yì:
"Now the Qín army surrounds Jùlù;
quickly lead troops across the river,
with Chǔ attacking from outside,
and Zhào responding from within,
we will surely defeat the Qín army."
Sòng Yì said:
"Not so.
A gadfly that bites an ox
cannot break a louse.
(The gadfly metaphorically refers to Qín.)
The louse metaphor refers to Zhāng Hán.
It advises our current commander leading troops,
who intends to destroy Qín,
not to exhaust all strength in immediate battle with Zhāng Hán.
Now Qín attacks Zhào;
if they win, their troops will be exhausted,
and we can capitalize on their weakness;
if they lose,
then we lead our troops westward with drums beating,
and will surely conquer Qín.
Therefore, it's better to let Qín and Zhào fight each other.
In striking with swift and sharp forces,
I am not your equal;
in sitting to devise strategies,
you are not my equal."
Yǔ said:
"You, General, joined forces to attack Qín,
yet have long delayed action.
This year brings famine and impoverished people,
soldiers eat half beans
soldiers eat vegetables,
mixed half with beans.
The army has no visible grain supplies.
Yet you drink at grand feasts,
not leading troops across the river,
to utilize Zhào's food resources,
and join forces to strike Qín,
instead saying:
'Capitalize on their weakness'.
With Qín's strength,
attacking the newly established Zhào,
they are bound to conquer Zhào.
If Zhào falls and Qín grows stronger,
what weakness is there to capitalize on?
Moreover, our state's army was recently defeated,
the King cannot rest easy,
and has entrusted the entire territory to you, General.
The safety of our state
hinges on this one move.
Now you show no compassion for the soldiers but serve private interests,
you are no minister devoted to the altars of soil and grain."
That night, he entered Sòng Yì's tent and beheaded him.
He led all troops across the river,
sank the boats and smashed the cooking pots,
showing the soldiers there was no turning back,
no thought of retreat,
and decisively defeated the Qín army.
This is a case of different circumstances.
Xún Yuè said:
"Sòng Yì waiting for Qín and Zhào to weaken each other
is similar in event but different in circumstance from Biàn Zhuāng's tiger-stabbing affair.
Why?
Applied in the Warring States period,
when neighboring states attacked each other,
without immediate urgency,
it could work.
The establishment of the Warring States
had a long history;
the victory or defeat in one battle
did not necessarily lead to destruction.
The situation did not urgently require the destruction of the enemy state.
Advancing meant seizing advantage,
retreating meant self-preservation,
hence accumulating strength and awaiting the right moment,
to capitalize on weakness was appropriate.
But now Chǔ and Zhào are newly risen,
their strength and Qín's power cannot coexist;
the pivot of safety and danger,
changes with every breath,
advancing secures achievement,
retreating brings disaster,
this is a case of similar events but different circumstances."
Hán Xìn attacked Zhào,
stationed at Jǐngxíng,
selected two thousand light cavalry,
each holding a red banner,
and had them ascend the mountains via hidden paths to observe the Zhào army,
instructing them:
"When Zhào sees us retreat,
they will empty their fortifications to pursue us.
Then swiftly enter the Zhào camp,
pull down the Zhào banners,
and set up the Hàn red banners."
Hán Xìn then sent ten thousand men ahead,
deploying them in a back-to-the-river formation.
At dawn,
Hán Xìn raised the general's flags and drums,
and marched out of the Jǐngxíng Pass.
Zhào opened their fortifications and attacked,
a great battle ensued for a long time.
Then Hán Xìn abandoned his flags and drums,
and retreated to the riverbank army.
The riverbank army opened ranks to let them in,
and resumed fierce fighting.
Zhào, having emptied their fortifications, vied for the Hàn flags and drums,
pursuing Hán Xìn.
By the time Hán Xìn and others had entered the riverbank army,
all soldiers fought desperately,
and could not be defeated.
The two thousand surprise cavalry Hán Xìn had sent out,
waiting for Zhào to empty their camp in pursuit of gain,
galloped into the Zhào camp,
pulled down all the Zhào banners,
and set up two thousand Hàn red banners.
When the Zhào army could not capture Hán Xìn and others,
and wanted to return to their camp,
they saw all were Hàn red banners,
and were greatly alarmed,
thinking that Hán Xìn had already captured the Zhào king's generals.
Thus thrown into confusion,
they fled in disarray,
and even though Zhào's generals executed some,
they could not stop the rout.
Thereupon, the Hàn troops pressed the attack,
decisively defeating them,
and captured the Zhào army.
The various generals presented heads and captives,
all congratulating Hán Xìn.
They then asked him:
"According to military strategy:
'Right and rear should be against mountains and hills,
front and left facing water and marshes.'
Yet now you deployed with your back to the river,
and still won in the end.
What strategy is this?"
Hán Xìn said:
"Does not military strategy say:
'Place them in a fatal position to seek life,
put them in a hopeless situation to seek survival'?
Moreover, I have not had the time to win the trust and train the officers and men;
this is what is called driving market folk to battle.
In such a situation, unless placed in a fatal position,
to make each fight for their own survival,
if given a chance to live,
they would all flee,
how then could they be used?"
Also, Gāozǔ rallied the troops of five feudal lords,
and entered Péngchéng.
Xiàng Yǔ heard of this,
led his troops away from Qí,
and engaged the Hàn in a great battle at the Suī River,
decisively defeating the Hàn army,
killing many soldiers,
so that the Suī River was blocked with bodies.
This is a case of different conditions.
Xún Yuè said:
"In the campaign against Zhào,
Hán Xìn stationed his army at the Zhī River,
yet Zhào could not defeat him.
Why?
In the Péngchéng disaster,
the Hàn king fought at the Suī River,
soldiers plunged into the Suī River, and the Chǔ troops won a great victory,
Why?
The Zhào troops left their state for a nearby attack,
advancing when they saw advantage,
retreating when they knew difficulty,
deeply concerned about their homeland,
not committed to a fight to the death;
Hán Xìn's isolated army stood by the river,
determined to fight to the death,
with no thought of survival,
this is why Hán Xìn won.
The Hàn king, having entered the enemy's territory,
was drinking at grand feasts,
his troops were at ease and complacent,
their will to fight was not united.
Chǔ, with its great might,
had lost its capital,
Xiàng Yǔ returned from outside,
the soldiers were filled with indignation and fervor,
rushing to save the defeat and avert destruction,
staking their lives on one decisive battle.
This is why Hàn was defeated.
Moreover, Hán Xìn selected elite troops for defense,
while Zhào attacked with soldiers worried about home;
Xiàng Yǔ selected elite troops to attack Hàn,
while the Hàn king responded with lax and weary soldiers.
This is a case of similar events but different conditions."
Therefore it is said:
Authority cannot be preset,
changes cannot be preplanned.
Move with the times,
adapt to the changes of circumstances,
that is the essence of strategy.
When the Hàn king was in Hànzhōng,
Hán Xìn advised him:
"Now the soldiers are all from Shāndōng,
standing on tiptoe, gazing homeward.
Harness their sharp morale,
and heading east, you can contend for the empire."
Later, Hàn Guāngwǔ traveled north to Kuǎi,
heard that the Hándān troops had arrived,
and Shìzǔ wanted to return south.
He summoned his officials to discuss plans.
Gěng Yǎn said:
"Now the enemy comes from the south,
we cannot go south."
The Grand Administrator of Yùyáng, Péng Chǒng,
was a fellow townsman of the Lord;
the Grand Administrator of Shàngjùn,
was none other than Yǎn's father.
Deploying these two commanderies,
with ten thousand mounted archers under control,
Hándān would not be a concern."
Emperor Shìzǔ's officials did not follow,
so they galloped south,
and the officials dispersed.
Discussion says:
Returning armies are one category,
yet some fail and some succeed,
why is that?
The response states:
Sūnzǐ said:
"Do not intercept a returning army."
When King Xiàng sent three kings to Qín,
they intercepted King Hàn's return route,
hence their vanguard was unstoppable.
Again, Sūnzǐ stated:
"When feudal lords fight in their own territory,
it is called scattered ground."
Emperor Guāngwǔ's troops came from the south,
heading south into scattered ground,
thus they lacked fighting spirit and dispersed.
So returning armies are one,
yet one succeeds and one fails.
Later, in the Hàn dynasty, Lǐ Jué and others pursued and trapped the Son of Heaven at Cáoyáng.
Jǔ Shòu advised Yuán Shào:
"General, your family has served as high ministers for generations,
upholding loyalty and righteousness through the ages.
Now the court is displaced,
and the imperial temples are destroyed.
Observing the various provinces and commanderies,
though outwardly they raise righteous armies,
inwardly they scheme against each other,
with none showing concern for the state or compassion for the people!
Moreover, your province is now roughly stabilized,
with strong soldiers and loyal followers.
If you welcome the imperial carriage to the west,
and establish the palace in Yèdū,
holding the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords,
gathering troops and horses to punish the disloyal,
who could withstand you?
If you do not decide early,
someone will surely beat you to it.
Authority does not tolerate missed opportunities,
achievement does not disdain speed,
I hope you will consider this."
Shào did not listen.
Cáo Cāo indeed welcomed the Hàn emperor,
and Shào consequently failed.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, Xiāo Yǎn, raised a righteous army,
Dù Sīchōng urged the emperor to welcome Prince Nánkāng,
establish the capital in Xiāngyáng,
and assume the rightful title,
but the emperor refused.
Zhāng Hóngcè said:
"If we now place Nánkāng in others' hands,
they will hold the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords,
and you, my lord, going forward,
will be at others' mercy.
Is this a plan for enduring hardship?"
The emperor replied:
"If our great enterprise ahead fails,
then indeed orchids and weeds will burn together;
but if we achieve success and establish our cause,
who would dare not follow?
How could we mediocrarily accept others' arrangements in Jiāngnán,
establishing Xīnyě Commandery to gather new adherents?"
He did not comply.
Thus he advanced his troops,
captured Jiànyè and possessed Jiāngzuǒ.
Discussion says:
"Holding the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords,
the act is the same,
yet some succeed by it,
and some fail by it,
why is that?"
The response states:
"The world
is not one person's world.
Those who perpetrate violence and cruelty,
even successors cannot preserve themselves;
where the people's hopes converge,
a commoner can achieve great deeds.
When the Mandate of Heaven reaches its end,
only those whom the people gladly support
have their origins here.
When the Fire Virtue declined,
and heroic tigers contended,
though the Hàn destiny waned,
the people's hopes remained unchanged,
so Cáo Cāo honored the Son of Heaven to follow popular desire,
wielding great legitimacy to command the realm,
causing the world's scholars to devote loyalty to his hegemonic plan.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
'To seek feudal lords, nothing is better than rescuing the king.'
This refers to such cases.
In the Qí period, it was not so,
when the whole world desired chaos,
and the seas raged,
at a time when the people supported the capable,
and the three spirits mandated change,
to cling to an old ruler
would be contrary, would it not?
Hence the Zuǒ Zhuàn criticizes Cháng Hóng for trying to support what Heaven would destroy,
and praises Cài Mò's theory of 'thunder mounting over heaven'.
Therefore, the act is the same,
yet some succeed by it,
and some fail by it."
This is the difference between "sentiment" and "circumstance" or "momentum".
One must adapt to the times,
and not cling to one way.
Zhūgě Liàng said:
"Fàn Lǐ considered leaving glory as nobility,
Yú Qīng regarded abandoning ministerial rank as achievement;
Tàibó was deemed benevolent for thrice yielding,
while Yān Kuài brought disaster by relinquishing the state;
Yáo and Shùn were sage for abdicating,
but Kǎo and Āi were foolish for handing power to Dǒng;
King Wǔ was righteous for taking over Yīn,
while Wáng Mǎng was a usurper for seizing Hàn;
Duke Huán became hegemon thanks to Guǎn Zhòng,
while the Qín king lost the state because of Zhào Gāo.
These all share similar motives but differ in outcome.
The wise use them to bring order and prosperity,
the foolish to incur disgrace and chaos."
Book 22: Assessing Sentiments
Confucius said:
"To speak without observing the countenance
is called being blind." He also said:
"If not trusted,
one will be accused of slandering."
Xun Qing stated:
"Speaking appropriately
is wisdom;
remaining silent appropriately
is understanding."
The "Shīzǐ" records:
"When listening to words,
if the ears and eyes show no respect,
and the attention is not deep,
then good words will not be received."
Thus, it is known that those about to speak
must first gauge human feelings,
as it has been so since ancient times.
Hán Zǐ noted:
"The difficulty of persuasion
lies in knowing the mind of the person being persuaded so that our words can match it.
If persuaded with substantial profit,
they will see it as lowly and encounter baseness,
and will surely discard and distance it.
If the person truly seeks substantial profit,
they may covertly use the advice
while overtly abandoning the advisor,
which must not be unknown.
If persuaded with high reputation,
they will see it as aimless and detached from reality,
and will certainly not accept it.
If the person truly seeks high reputation,
they may superficially accept the advisor
but实质上疏远 them.
This must not be unknown.
Affairs succeed through secrecy,
and fail through leakage.
It may not be that the person themselves leaked it,
but if the persuasion touches upon their hidden matters,
in such cases, the advisor is endangered.
If the favor is not yet deep,
and one speaks of ultimate knowledge,
if the advice is followed and succeeds, the credit is forgotten;
if it fails and leads to defeat, one is suspected,
in such cases, the advisor is endangered.
If a noble has faults,
and the advisor explicitly points them out to push the blame,
the advisor is endangered.
If a noble has a successful plan and wishes to claim the credit,
and the advisor is aware of it,
then the advisor is endangered.
Forcing them to do what they will not,
or stopping them from what they cannot cease,
endangers the advisor."
He also said:
"Discussing great men with them,
they may think you are creating distance;
discussing petty men,
they may think you are trading power.
Talking about their loved ones,
they may think you are seeking favor;
discussing their hated ones,
they may think you are testing them.
Presenting ideas顺从ively,
they may say you are timid and incomplete;
planning broadly and freely,
they may say you are rustic and arrogant.
This must not be unknown.
If they are confident in their plan,
do not use their faults to corner them;
if they are proud of their judgment,
do not oppose them to anger them."
Generally, persuasion requires long duration,
with deep favor established,
so that deep plans are not doubted,
and debates do not incur blame.
Then, clarify the advantages and disadvantages
to achieve success.
Point directly to right and wrong
to refine their character.
Maintaining this approach,
is how persuasion succeeds.
Xún Yuè said:
"Why is it difficult for ministers to speak?
What is the reason?
Words leave the body, and blame and regret follow."
Hence it is said:
Pointing out errors and exposing faults,
brings the blame of offense;
advising and instructing,
invites criticism of presuming superiority.
If words are appropriate,
they resent being outshone;
if inappropriate,
they despise the folly.
Agreeing before they do,
they hate being robbed of insight;
agreeing after,
they see it as compliance.
Opposing subordinates to follow superiors,
is seen as flattery;
opposing superiors to follow subordinates,
is seen as conformity.
Speaking with the crowd,
is considered following the majority;
speaking alone against the crowd,
is seen as seeking glory.
If words are shallow and exposed,
they are dismissed as simplistic;
if profound and far-reaching,
they are misunderstood and rejected.
Unique insights and wisdom,
make others envy being overshadowed,
so even if correct, they are not praised;
sharing common wisdom,
is seen as附和,
so even if successful, it is not credited.
Being humble and non-confrontational,
is seen as easily exhausted;
not speaking fully,
is thought to hide intentions;
advising with full sincerity,
is considered overstepping.
If words bear no result,
one faces抱怨 and blame;
if they lead to success,
it is deemed理所当然.
Benefiting the superior but not the subordinates,
or convenient for the left but not the right,
or fitting the past but opposing the future,
this is why the feelings of those below often go unheard.
Confucius, in frustration,
exclaimed, 'I wish to speak no more,'
precisely because of the difficulty of speech.
How to illustrate this difficulty?
Once in Sòng, a rich man's
wall collapsed due to rain.
His son said:
'If not repaired,
there will be thieves.'
His neighbor said the same.
That night, indeed, much was stolen,
and the family praised their son's wisdom but suspected the neighbor's father.
When Duke Wǔ of Zhèng wanted to attack Hú,
he married his daughter to its ruler,
then asked his ministers:
'I wish to use arms;
whom should we attack?'
Guān Qí Sī said:
'Hú can be attacked.'
The duke had him executed,
saying:
'Hú
is our brother state;
why do you speak of attacking it?'
Why do you say to attack it?'
The ruler of Hú heard this,
thought Zhèng was friendly and left defenses down,
so the people of Zhèng attacked Hú
and captured it.
In these two cases,
the advice was correct,
yet one was severely executed,
the other lightly suspected.
It's not that wisdom is hard,
but applying it is difficult.
A man from Wèi welcomed a bride;
as she boarded the carriage,
she asked:
'The side horses,
whose are they?'
The driver replied:
'Borrowed.'
The bride told the servant:
'Gently drive the side horses,
don't whip the main ones.'
When the carriage reached the gate,
she urged:
'Mother-in-law, don't put out the torch,
or there might be a fire.'
Entering the house,
she saw a mortar,
and said:
'Move it under the window,
it hinders passersby.'
The host laughed at her.
These three remarks
were all pertinent,
yet she was ridiculed
because the timing was improper.
Such is the difficulty of speech.
Knowing this difficulty,
speakers must always gauge
to understand human feelings.
How to illustrate this?
When the queen of Qí died,
the king wished to appoint a new one but had not decided,
He ordered his ministers to deliberate.
Xuē Gōng Tián Yīng, wishing to align with the king's intentions,
presented ten earrings but made one exceptionally beautiful.
The next day,
he inquired where the beautiful earring had gone,
and thus advised that its wearer be made queen.
The King of Qí was greatly pleased,
and thereafter valued Xuē Gōng highly.
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through objects.
When Shēn Bùhài first sought to align with the King of Hán,
he was unsure of the king's desires,
fearing his words might not hit the mark.
The king asked Shēnzǐ:
"With whom should I ally?"
He replied:
"This is crucial to our safety or peril,
a major affair of state.
I beg to ponder it deeply and think hard."
Then he privately said to Zhào Zhuō and Hán Cháo:
"You,
are both skilled debaters of the state;
as ministers,
why must your words always be heeded?
Simply exhaust your loyalty."
The two each presented their views on the matter to the king.
Shēnzǐ secretly observed what pleased the king,
and then spoke accordingly,
greatly delighting the king.
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through words.
When Wú attacked Yuè,
Yuè took refuge on Kuàijī Mountain,
Gōu Jiǎn sighed deeply and said:
"Is this my end?"
Minister Wén Zhǒng replied:
"Tāng was imprisoned in Xiàtái,
King Wén confined in Yǒulǐ,
Chóng'ěr fled to Dí,
and Qí's Xiǎo Bái fled to Jǔ,
yet they eventually became hegemon-kings.
From this perspective,
how can we say this will not turn to fortune?"
After Gōu Jiǎn was spared,
he focused on avenging Wú.
Minister Wén Zhǒng said:
"I observe the King of Wú's governance has grown arrogant;
let me test it."
So they borrowed grain to probe the situation.
Wǔ Xū advised against giving it,
but the king gave it anyway.
Wǔ Xū said:
"Since the king ignores advice,
in three years,
Wú will be in ruins!"
Grand Steward Pǐ heard this,
and slandered him:
"Wǔ Yún appears loyal but is truly cruel."
Wú then killed Wǔ Xū.
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through events.
A guest introduced Chúnyú Kūn to King Huì of Liáng,
who dismissed his attendants,
but after two meetings,
Kūn remained silent.
The king found it strange
and reproached the guest.
The guest spoke to Chúnyú Kūn,
who said:
"The first time I saw the king,
his mind was on hunting;
the second time,
his mind was on music.
Hence, I remained silent."
The guest reported this fully to the king,
who exclaimed in astonishment:
"Master Chúnyú
is truly a sage!
Earlier, someone presented a fine horse,
and before I could try it,
he arrived;
later, someone presented a singer,
and before I could listen,
he came again.
Though I dismissed others,
my private thoughts were elsewhere."
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through observing inclinations.
When Zhì Bó led the rulers of Hán and Wèi to attack Zhào,
Hán and Wèi used a plan by Zhào minister Zhàng Mèngtán
to secretly plot against Zhì Bó.
Zhàng Mèngtán went to see Zhì Bó
and met Zhì Guǒ outside the camp gate.
Zhì Guǒ entered to see Zhì Bó,
saying:
"The two rulers are likely to turn against you.
I encountered Zhàng Mèngtán
and observed his proud demeanor and lofty actions;
seeing the changed expressions of the two rulers,
they will surely betray you."
Zhì Bó did not listen.
Zhì Guǒ left
and changed his surname to Fǔ.
Zhàng Mèngtán went to see Zhào Xiāngzǐ, saying:
"I met Zhì Guǒ outside the camp gate,
and his gaze showed suspicion of me.
He entered to see Zhì Bó and then changed his clan.
If we do not attack tonight,
we will be too late."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Agreed!"
So they killed the officials guarding the dikes with Hán and Wèi,
breached the waters to flood Zhì Bó's army.
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through observation.
Yīn Hào served in Jìn,
enjoying great fame,
and people of the time watched his actions and retirements
to predict the rise and fall of Jiāngzuǒ.
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through worthiness.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"When a state is about to fall,
those with the Way leave first."
The *Qián Jīng* states:
"Joy
shows in a radiant expression;
anger,
in a fierce and contemptuous look;
desire,
in a flushed and pleased face;
fear,
in a timid and subdued manner;
worry,
in a fearful and quiet demeanor."
This illustrates how feelings can be hooked through expressions.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
"Those about to betray
speak with shame;
those with doubts in their hearts,
their words are scattered.
The words of the auspicious are few,
the words of the restless are many.
Those who slander the good
speak evasively;
those who have lost their integrity
speak hesitantly."
The *Zhōulǐ* describes five ways of listening:
first, listening to words—
if insincere, they become verbose;
second, listening to expressions—
if insincere, they show shame;
third, listening to breath—
if insincere, it becomes panting;
fourth, listening to ears—
if insincere, confusion arises;
fifth, listening to eyes—
if insincere, they appear dull.
From this, it is seen
that human feelings must manifest in things.
In the past, the Jìn ruler favored beauty,
and Lí Jī used her looks to manipulate him.
The King of Wú desired to expand territory,
so Grand Steward Pǐ advocated campaigns to manipulate him.
Duke Huán loved fine flavors,
so Yì Yá steamed his child to manipulate him.
Such dark, unfathomable schemes
are truly fearsome.
Thus, a ruler's likes and dislikes
must not be revealed outwardly.
If they are shown,
then ministers and concubines will exploit them to exercise control.
Therefore, it is said:
If the ruler reveals his intentions,
he becomes bait for his subordinates.
This is what it means.
Those who understand this
can effectively present their counsel to the ruler.
Second Thirteen: On Feigned Sincerity
Confucius said:
"The noble person is steadfast but not rigidly faithful."
He also said:
"When trust approaches righteousness,
words can be fulfilled."
From this perspective,
only righteousness matters,
not necessarily keeping faith.
Discussion says:
Subtle indeed!
Subtle indeed!
All matters under heaven
cannot flourish without something being abandoned.
If loyal to this,
one must be insincere to that -
this is the natural principle.
Thus we observe
that what we call loyalty
may be what others call deception.
So between loyalty and deception,
how shall we determine our choice?
Yet I have heard:
Between ruler and minister exists great righteousness,
between superior and inferior are fixed roles -
this is the unchanging Way through all generations.
Therefore, to practice loyalty,
observe the established righteousness between ruler and minister;
to practice trust,
consider the clear distinction between superior and inferior.
If one's role and righteousness remain unviolated,
even clever stratagems may be acceptable.
How to illustrate this?
Duke Shè of Chǔ asked Confucius:
"In my village there is an upright person
whose father stole a sheep and the son testified against him."
Confucius replied:
"The upright persons in my village differ from this:
fathers conceal for sons,
sons conceal for fathers -
uprightness lies therein."
When the King of Chǔ besieged Sòng,
Sòng sought help from Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xiè Yáng to Sòng,
ordering them not to surrender to Chǔ,
saying:
"The Jìn army has fully mobilized
and will arrive soon."
The people of Zhèng captured and delivered him to Chǔ,
where the King of Chǔ offered rich bribes
to make him reverse his message.
He pretended to agree.
When mounted on the siege tower,
summoning the people of Sòng to deliver the message,
he instead conveyed his ruler's command.
The King of Chǔ prepared to execute him,
sending word:
"You promised me but broke your word -
why?
The faithlessness is not mine
but yours!
Quickly face your punishment!"
He replied:
"I have heard:
When a ruler can issue commands, that is righteousness;
when a minister can receive commands, that is trust.
Trust carrying righteousness into action brings benefit.
Plans that don't lose benefit
while protecting the altars of soil and grain
serve the people's sovereign.
Righteousness cannot have double trust,
trust cannot have double commands.
Your bribing me
shows ignorance of true command.
Having received my mission and departed,
I'd rather die than fail -
what use are bribes?
My pretending to agree
was to fulfill my mission.
Dying while completing my mission
is my good fortune!
My humble ruler has a trustworthy minister,
and I, your servant, achieve completion
(completion
means accomplishment),
what more could I seek in death!"
The King of Chǔ released him to return home.
Hán Fēizǐ said:
"In Chǔ there was an upright person
whose father stole a sheep and he reported it to authorities."
The Prime Minister said:
"He must be executed!"
Considering him upright to the ruler but crooked to his father,
he arrested the son and punished him.
From this we see
that the ruler's upright minister
is the father's unfilial son."
A man of Lǔ following his ruler to battle
fled three times in three engagements.
Zhòngní asked his reason,
and he replied:
"I have an aged father -
if I die, no one will support him."
Zhòngní considered this filial
and recommended him for office.
From this we see
that the father's filial son
is the ruler's deserter.
Thus, though the Prime Minister executed people,
Chǔ's crimes didn't cease;
when people heard of Zhòngní's rewards,
the people of Lǔ easily surrendered.
The interests of superior and inferior
differ so greatly
that when rulers simultaneously encourage common people's conduct
while seeking the state's prosperity,
they will certainly not succeed.
Yán Shuài wanted to see Gōng Zhòng,
but Gōng Zhòng refused.
Yán Shuài told Gōng Zhòng's receptionist:
"Gōng Zhòng must think me hypocritical,
hence he won't see me.
Gōng Zhòng loves women -
I call him lover of scholars;
Gōng Zhòng is stingy with wealth -
I call him generous;
Gōng Zhòng lacks virtue -
I call him righteous.
From now on,
I shall simply speak truthfully."
The receptionist reported this to Gōng Zhòng,
who immediately rose and received him.
Discussion says:
The saying "hating exposure while claiming uprightness"
matches the Yìjīng:
"The noble person checks evil and promotes good."
If Yán Shuài were truly loyal and upright,
Gōng Zhòng's faults would be exposed.
Thus Yán Shuài's deception
became Gōng Zhòng's blessing.
When Qí attacked Yān,
it captured ten cities.
The King of Yān sent Sū Qín to persuade Qí,
and Qí returned the ten cities to Yān.
When Sū Qín returned to Yān,
some slandered him saying:
"Sū Qín is a double-dealing traitor,
an inconsistent minister
who will rebel."
The King of Yān distanced himself from him,
dismissing and not employing him.
Fearing punishment, Sū Qín
sought audience with the king saying:
a humble man from Eastern Zhōu,
had not an inch of achievement,
yet you personally honored me in the temple
and received me in court.
Now that I've repelled Qí's troops for you
and gained ten cities' worth of merit,
I should be drawn closer.
Yet now you give me no office -
someone must have damaged my credibility with you.
Moreover, my lack of credibility
is your blessing.
The King of Yān once told Sū Dài:
"I greatly dislike deceitful speech."
Sū Dài replied:
"In Zhōu they despise matchmakers
for praising both sides.
To the man's family they say:
'The woman is beautiful,'
to the woman's family:
'The man is wealthy.'
Yet Zhōu's custom
doesn't allow arranging one's own marriage.
If a maiden has no matchmaker,
she ages unmarried;
if she promotes herself without matchmakers,
she wears out unsold.
To marry without slander,
to be accepted unworn -
only matchmakers can achieve this.
Moreover, affairs won't stand without flexibility,
nor succeed without adaptation.
Those who make people sit receiving accomplished matters -
only the deceitful can do this."
Deceit
(pronounced similar to tuó).
"If I were as faithful as Wěi Shēng,
as incorruptible as Bó Yí,
as filial as Zēng Shēn -
these three being the highest conduct under heaven -
and served you with these,
would that work?"
The King of Yān said:
"It would."
Sū Qín said:
"Having such a minister,
I will not serve a king either.
As filial as Zēng Shēn was,
he would not leave his parents to stay overnight away from home;
how could Your Majesty make him walk a thousand miles to serve the endangered king of weak Yān?
As incorruptible as Bó Yí was,
he refused to succeed his father as lord of Gūzhú,
would not become a subject of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
did not accept the marquis title,
and starved to death at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain.
With such incorruptibility,
how could Your Majesty make him walk a thousand miles
to advance and achieve success in Qí?
As trustworthy as Wěi Shēng was,
he waited for a woman under a bridge pillar,
and when she did not come,
even as the water rose he would not leave,
holding the pillar until he died.
With such trustworthiness,
how would he be willing to promote the prestige of Yān and Qín,
and repel the strong army of Qí?
Hán Zǐ said:
"Xǔ Yóu, Jì Yá, Biàn Suí, Wù Guāng, Bó Yí, Shū Qí—
these several men
all showed no joy at seeing profit,
and no fear when facing difficulty.
To show no joy at seeing profit—
even with generous rewards, nothing can encourage them;
to show no fear when facing difficulty—
even with severe punishments, nothing can intimidate them.
These are called ungovernable people,
whom even the sage kings of antiquity,
all could not subdue as subjects.
In the present age,
how would one use them?"
Moreover, trustworthy conduct
is for self-cultivation,
not for serving others;
it is a method of self-preservation,
not a way of aggressive advancement.
Moreover, when the Three Dynasties rose in succession,
and the Five Hegemons flourished one after another,
none preserved themselves by inaction.
Do you, my lord, consider self-preservation acceptable?
Then Qí would not have expanded beyond Yíngqiū,
and you, sir, would not be peering beyond the border cities.
In the past, when Zhèng Zǐchǎn reported the victory of invading Chén to Jìn,
the people of Jìn asked him:
"Why did you invade a small state?"
He replied:
"By the mandate of the former kings,
wherever guilt lies,
each should receive their punishment.
Moreover, in the past, the Son of Heaven's land was one qí,
and the feudal states each had one tóng.
By this measure it decreased,
but now great states often have several qí.
If there were no invasion of small states,
how could they have become so large?"
The people of Jìn could not refute him.
Furthermore, I have an elderly mother in Eastern Zhōu;
leaving her to serve you, sir,
I abandon the method of self-preservation
and practice the way of aggressive advancement.
My pursuits
fundamentally do not align with yours, sir.
You, sir,
are a ruler of self-preservation;
I,
am a minister of aggressive advancement.
What I call 'offending the ruler through loyalty and trustworthiness' is this."
The King of Yān said:
"But if a servant is trustworthy,
how can there be any offense?"
He replied:
"You, sir, do not understand.
My neighbor had a man who served as an official far away,
and his wife had a lover.
When her husband was about to return,
the lover was worried,
but the wife said:
'Do not worry.
I have prepared poisoned wine to serve him.'
Two days later,
the husband arrived,
and the wife had a concubine present a cup of wine to him.
The concubine knew it was poisoned wine;
presenting it would kill the master,
but revealing it would get the mistress expelled.
So she pretended to stumble and spilled the wine,
and the master, enraged, flogged her.
The concubine's spilling of the wine
saved the master's life above,
and preserved the mistress below.
Her loyalty was utmost,
yet she could not avoid the flogging—
this is offending through loyalty and trustworthiness.
My service
unfortunately resembles the concubine's spilling of the wine.
Moreover, in serving you, sir,
I have upheld righteousness and benefited the state,
yet now I am accused of an offense.
I fear that in the future, those under heaven who serve you, sir,
will not dare to be certain of their standing.
Furthermore, when I persuaded Qí,
I never deceived them.
Those who persuade Qí after me,
if their words are not like mine,
even with the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn,
they will not dare to adopt them."
The King of Yān said:
"Well said!"
And treated him generously again.
From this, we see
that cunning can be trustworthiness,
and deceit can be loyalty.
Deceptive and cunning actions
are the foundation of loyalty and trustworthiness.
Twenty-Four: Doubts About Loyalty
Praise and blame, right and wrong, cannot be fixed absolutely.
Take the strategies of Hàn Gāo and the schemes of Chén Píng:
if criticized, they become estranged;
if praised, they grow closer.
With the clarity of Wén Dì and the loyalty of Wèi Shǎng,
applying the law makes them guilty,
while applying virtue makes them meritorious.
Those who understand the world's listeners
know they often have biases.
Having biases,
their hearing must be distorted.
Bias means fault.
How do we know this is so?
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"A man who lost his axe
suspected his neighbor's son.
In his gait, expression, speech, actions, and demeanor—
everything seemed that of a thief who had stolen the axe.
Later, digging in a valley, he found his axe.
Valley means pit.
Another day, seeing his neighbor's son again,
his actions and demeanor showed no resemblance to a thief.
The neighbor's son had not changed;
he himself had changed.
The change had no other cause—
it was due to bias.
In the state of Zhū's case,
they made armor skirts with silk.
Using silk to attach armor,
Gōngxī Jì told the ruler of Zhū:
'It would be better to use woven cords.'
The ruler of Zhū said:
'Excellent!'
He issued an order
that officials must use woven cords for armor.
Gōngxī Jì then had his whole household make cords.
Someone slandered him, saying:
'The reason Gōngxī Jì wants to use cords
is that his household makes many cords for armor skirts.'
Slander means to harm.
The ruler of Zhū was displeased
and thus stopped the order,
discontinuing the use of cords.
The ruler of Zhū had a bias.
If using cords for armor was indeed convenient,
even if Gōngxī Jì made many cords,
what harm was there?
If using cords was inconvenient,
even if Gōngxī Jì made no cords,
what benefit would that be?
Whether to make cords or not
should not discredit Gōngxī Jì's proposal.
Discredit means to disgrace.
In all listening, one must examine carefully.
Lóu Huǎn said:
'Gōngfǔ Wénbó served in Lǔ,
fell ill and died,
and two women killed themselves in his chambers.'
His mother heard this
and did not weep.
Her steward said:
'How can you not weep when your son has died?'
His mother said:
'Confucius,
a worthy man,
was driven from Lǔ, and this man did not follow him.
Now that he is dead, women kill themselves for him.
If so,
he must have been cold to the worthy and warm to women.'
Thus, from the mother's perspective,
she is a worthy mother;
from the wife's perspective,
she cannot avoid being a jealous wife.
So the words are the same,
but the speakers differ, and people's minds change.
Yuè Yáng, as a general of Wèi, attacked Zhōngshān.
His son was in Zhōngshān,
and the ruler of Zhōngshān boiled his son and sent the broth to him.
Yuè Yáng drank it all.
Wén Hóu said:
'Yuè Yáng, for my sake,
ate his son's flesh.'
Dǔshī Zàn said:
'He would eat his own son;
who wouldn't he eat?'
When Yuè Yáng returned from Zhōngshān,
Wén Hóu rewarded his achievements but doubted his heart.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
'A birth mother picking fleas for her son
until his ears bleed
is seen as the ultimate love for her child.
If it were a stepmother,
onlookers would consider it cruelty.'
The reality is the same,
but the observers differ.
Viewing an ox from a city wall, it looks like a sheep;
viewing a sheep, it looks like a pig—
it's due to the height.
Looking at one's face in a pan of water, it appears round;
in a cup, it appears
suí,
meaning deficient.
The face's shape doesn't change;
the reason it appears round or deficient
is the difference in what one uses to look.
Now, even if I wish to correct myself and interact with others,
how can I know how the world views me?
Thus, we know that right and wrong in the world are not fixed.
The world each affirms what it affirms and denies what it denies.
Now, if I wish to choose the right and abide by it,
and choose the wrong and avoid it,
without knowing what the world considers right and wrong,
who can tell which is right and which is wrong?
Discussion says:
Forgetting family and sacrificing for the state
is seen as not caring for one's kin;
how can such a one love the ruler?
Examples are Wèi's Prince Kāifāng, Wú Qǐ, and Yuè Yáng.
But if one favors their kin,
it is said:
'Upon receiving orders, they forget their family;
in military command, they forget their kin;
grasping the drumstick, they forget themselves.'
Ráng Jū executing Zhuāng Jiǎ is an example.
Thus, the "Zhuàn" says:
'If you want to impute a crime,
can you lack a pretext?'
Those who examine right and wrong
can grasp the truth of matters.
Thus, there are those loyal yet suspected—
this must be carefully examined.
The Use of the Useless: Twenty-Fifth
The ancients said:
'What catches the bird
is one mesh of the net.
But spreading a net with only one mesh
will never catch a bird.
The reason birds can fly far
is the strength of their six primary feathers.
Yet without the aid of the numerous small feathers,
they cannot fly far.'
Inferring from this,
the usefulness of the useless is great.
Thus, Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
'Your words are useless.'
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'Only by knowing the useless can one begin to discuss the useful.
Heaven and earth are not unvast and great,
yet what humans use
is only enough for their feet.
But if we cut away the ground around our feet down to the yellow springs,
would the space still be useful?'
Huìzǐ said:
'It would be useless.'
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'Then the usefulness of the useless
is also clear.'
In the past, Chén Píng had abundant wisdom but was suspected,
while Zhōu Bó, simple and loyal, was trusted.
When benevolence and righteousness are insufficient to secure mutual trust,
the wise are suspected for their abundance,
and the simple are trusted for their lack.
Hàn summoned recluses Fán Yīng and Yáng Hòu,
and the court treated them as divine.
Upon their arrival,
they showed no extraordinary abilities.
Lǐ Gù and Zhū Mù thought these recluses merely stole empty fame
and were of no practical use.
Yet later aspirants looked up to them and achieved greatness,
and rulers honored them to win the masses.
Confucius said:
'Promote the reclusive,
and the hearts of all under heaven will turn to you.'
Yān Zhāo honored Guō Wěi
to attract Jù Xīn and Yuè Yì;
Qí Huán respected the art of nines-times-nines
to recruit the class of outstanding talents.
Considering the useless,
it is also a means to be useful.
But the confused neglect untrodden ground,
dismiss the achievements of the useless,
even to the point of ridiculing distant arts
and despising the nation's brilliance.
Is that not a mistake?
Gratitude Begets Resentment: Twenty-Sixth
The tradition cites a saying:
"Do not resent those whom you should not resent.
Yet I, the ruler, have resentment."
This shows that those who harbor resentment
do not resent the distant,
but inevitably resent the intimate.
How can this be demonstrated?
Gāo Zǐ said:
"The 'Xiǎo Biàn'
is the poem of a petty man."
Mèng Zǐ asked:
"Why do you say so?"
Gāo Zǐ replied:
"It expresses resentment."
Mèng Zǐ said:
"How rigid!
Old Master Gāo's interpretation of poetry.
If a man from Yuè were here,
drawing his bow to shoot at me,
I would speak of it with laughter and banter.
For no other reason
than that he is a stranger.
But if my brother drew his bow to shoot at me,
I would speak of it with tears and sobs.
For no other reason
than that he is kin.
Thus, the resentment in 'Xiǎo Biàn'
is due to closeness to kin.
Being close to kin
is benevolence."
The "Xiǎo Biàn"
criticizes King Yōu of Zhōu,
composed by the crown prince's tutor.
When Jìn sent Hán Jiǎnzǐ to observe the Qín army, he reported:
"Their army is smaller than ours,
but their warriors outnumber us twice over."
The duke asked:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"We relied on their resources when leaving,
used their favor upon returning,
and ate their grain in famine.
Three kindnesses went unrequited—
hence their arrival."
Seeing Qín's anger in coming,
we know that the deepest kindness must breed the deepest resentment.
Dù Yè advised Wáng Yīn:
"I have heard that where human affection runs deep,
care is meticulous;
where love is utmost,
expectations are exacting.
To be close yet not treated differently,
intimate yet not distinguished—
'close' means near,
'distinguished' means set apart from strangers.
Who then would bear no resentment?
This is why 'Táng Dì' and 'Jiǎo Gōng' were written."
From this we see
that resentment, indeed,
stems from closeness;
and kindness
is the source of resentment.
This cannot be overlooked.
Chapter 27: Feigned Compliance
Zhào Zǐ said:
When clouds and thunder gather in tumultuous times,
and the roosting birds have not yet settled.
At such a moment,
one serves the ruler to whom one has pledged allegiance and governs the people,
each performing their duties for their own lord.
Thus, Emperor Gāozǔ rewarded Jì Bù despite his crime,
and Duke Wén of Jìn praised the fault of the courtier,
bearing no resentment for past harassment,
which can be said to comprehend the greater principle.
Long ago, when Duke Wén of Jìn first fled into exile,
Duke Xiàn sent the courtier Pī to attack him at Púchéng,
and Pī cut off his sleeve.
Upon his return to the state,
Lǚ and Xì feared persecution,
and plotted to burn the duke's palace and kill him.
The courtier Pī requested an audience,
and the duke sent a message reproaching him:
"At the battle of Púchéng,
the ruler's command was to arrive in one night,
yet you came immediately.
Later, when I was hunting by the Wèi River with the lord of Dí,
you came on behalf of Duke Huì,
seeking to kill me,
ordered to arrive in three nights,
yet you came by the second night.
Though you had the ruler's command,
why were you so swift?"
Pī replied:
"I thought that upon your return,
you would have understood this.
If not yet,
you will again face calamity.
A ruler's command admits no second thoughts,
such is the ancient rule.
To eliminate the ruler's enemies,
I exerted all my strength.
Whether it was a man of Pú or a man of Dí,
what were they to me?
Now that you are on the throne,
will there be no more Pú or Dí?
Duke Huán of Qí set aside the arrow-hook incident and made Guǎn Zhòng his minister,
if you act differently,
why trouble to command me?
Those who leave will face great punishment,
not just a mutilated servant!"
If a ruler holds grudges against commoners,
many will live in fear.
The duke met him,
and Pī informed him of the impending trouble,
thus averting the disaster from Lǚ and Xì.
Hán Zǐ said:
"That Qí and Jìn lost their heirs,
was it not fitting?
Duke Huán could utilize Guǎn Zhòng's achievements,
yet forget the resentment of the arrow-hook;
Duke Wén could heed the words of the courtier,
and overlook the crime of the cut sleeve.
Dukes Huán and Wén were able to tolerate these two men.
Later rulers,
in wisdom, cannot match these two dukes;
later ministers,
in virtue, are not equal to these two men.
With disloyal ministers
serving unenlightened rulers,
if the ruler is unaware,
then there occur the usurpations of Zǐ Hǎn and Tián Cháng;
if aware,
they then use Guǎn Zhòng and the courtier as excuses.
The ruler inevitably refrains from punishment,
and considers himself to possess the virtue of Huán and Wén,
thus employing his enemies while failing to see the flaws in their abundant leisure,
deeming himself wise and free from delusion,
then even without heirs,
is it not also fitting?"
Chén Zhěn and Zhāng Yí both served King Huì of Qín,
and the king valued them both.
The two vied for favor,
and Yí slandered Zhěn to the king, saying:
"Zhěn heavily bribes and lightly serves between Qín and Chǔ,
intending to engage in state relations.
Now Chǔ is not friendly with Qín but is friendly with Zhěn,
so Zhěn favors Chǔ and neglects Qín.
Zhěn wishes to leave Qín for Chǔ,
why does Your Majesty not let him go?"
The king then summoned Zhěn and questioned him.
Zhěn said:
"I do wish to go to Chǔ.
If I leave, I will indeed go to Chǔ,
thus making clear whether I am for Chǔ or not.
In the past, there was a man in Chǔ with two wives,
has Your Majesty heard of this?"
The king said:
"I have not."
Zhěn said:
"There was a man in Chǔ with two wives;
someone flirted with the elder,
and the elder scolded him;
he flirted with the younger,
and the younger reciprocated.
Not long after,
the man with two wives died,
and a friend asked the flirtatious man:
'Shall you marry the younger one?
Or the elder one?'
The flirtatious man said:
'I will marry the elder.'
The friend said:
'The elder scolded you,
the younger flirted with you.
Why do you choose the elder?'
The flirtatious man said:
'When she was another's wife,
I wanted her to flirt with me;
as my own wife,
I want her to scold others.'
Now the King of Chǔ is a wise ruler,
and Zhāo Yáng is a virtuous minister.
If I, as a minister, were to constantly leak state secrets to Chǔ,
the King of Chǔ would not keep me,
and Zhāo Yáng would not work with me.
Why would I go to Chǔ?
If I leave, I will indeed go to Chǔ,
sufficiently proving whether I am for Chǔ or not."
Zhěn left,
and Yí entered and asked the king:
"Does Zhěn really wish to go to Chǔ or not?"
The king said:
"He does."
Yí said:
"If Zhěn is not for Chǔ,
why would the King of Chǔ want him?"
The king repeated Yí's words to Zhěn,
and Zhěn said:
"It is so."
The king said:
"Then Yí's words are indeed credible."
Zhěn said:
"Not only Yí knows this,
but everyone on the street knows it.
Wǔ Zǐxū was loyal to his lord,
and all under heaven vied to have him as minister;
Zēng Shēn and Xiào Jǐ loved their parents,
and all under heaven wished to have them as sons.
Thus, maidservants sold within the neighborhood
are good maidservants;
divorced women remarried in the village
are surely good women.
Now if I, Zhěn, am not loyal to my lord,
why would Chǔ want me as a minister?
Being loyal yet cast aside,
if I do not go to Chǔ,
where else should I go?"
The king found his words reasonable,
and thus treated him generously.
King Huì eventually made Zhāng Yí his minister,
and Zhěn then fled to Chǔ.
Zhāng Yí initially slandered Chén Zhěn to King Huì, saying:
"Zhěn is still friendly with Chǔ,
and strives hard to seek territory for them."
Zuǒ Shuǎng said to Chén Zhěn:
"Yí is on good terms with the King of Wèi,
who trusts him deeply.
Even if you plead a hundred times,
he will not listen.
You might as well use Yí's words as evidence,
and thus return to Chǔ."
Zhěn said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he had someone report Zhāng Yí's words to the King of Chǔ,
who was pleased,
and wanted to restore him,
so Zhěn fled to Chǔ.
When Hán Xìn was first King of Qí,
Kuǎi Tōng advised Xìn,
urging him to divide the empire into three,
but Xìn did not listen.
Later, realizing that Hàn feared and resented his abilities,
he conspired with Xì to rebel.
The plot was exposed,
and Empress Dowager Lǚ captured him by stratagem.
As he was about to be executed,
he said:
"I regret not following Kuǎi Tōng's plan,
and being deceived by a woman and a child.
Is it not heaven's will!"
Emperor Gāozǔ personally led the army,
to attack Chén Xì at Jùlù,
and Xìn pleaded illness and did not follow,
intending to rise up from within.
A retainer of Xìn offended him,
and Xìn imprisoned him, intending to kill him.
The retainer's younger brother submitted a report exposing Xìn's plot to rebel to Empress Lǚ,
who wanted to summon him,
but feared his faction would not comply,
so she conspired with Chancellor Xiāo Hé,
deceivingly sent someone claiming to come from the emperor,
saying Xì had been captured and killed,
and all the marquises and ministers came to congratulate.
The chancellor deceived Xìn, saying:
"Although ill,
force yourself to come and congratulate!"
Han Xin entered,
Empress Lǚ had warriors bind Han Xin,
and executed him.
When Emperor Gāozǔ returned,
he then ordered Qí to arrest Tōng.
When Tōng arrived,
the Emperor said:
"Did you teach Huáiyīn Hóu to rebel?"
He replied:
"Yes.
I certainly taught him.
That fool didn't use my strategy,
so he ended up destroying himself here.
Had that fool used my plan,
how could Your Majesty have destroyed him?"
The Emperor angrily said:
"Boil him!"
Tōng said:
"Alas!
Boiling me is unjust."
The Emperor said:
"You taught Hán Xìn to rebel,
what injustice?"
He responded:
"When Qín's laws slackened and order collapsed,
the east of the mountains was in great turmoil,
men of different surnames rose together,
heroes gathered like crows.
Qín lost its deer,
and all under heaven chased it,
so those with great talent and swift feet got it first.
Zhí's dog barks at Yáo,
not because Yáo is unvirtuous,
but because a dog barks at anyone not its master.
At that time,
I only knew Hán Xìn,
not Your Majesty.
Moreover, many under heaven sharpened their weapons,
wanting what Your Majesty sought,
but lacked the strength to succeed—
could you boil them all?"
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Release him!"
And pardoned Tōng's crime.
Diāo Bó often spoke ill of Tián Dān,
saying:
"Ānpíng Jūn
is a petty man."
Ānpíng Jūn heard this,
so prepared wine and summoned Diāo Bó,
saying:
"How have I offended you, sir,
that you often praise me at court?"
Diāo Bó said:
"Zhí's dog barks at Yáo,
not because it honors Zhí and scorns Yáo,
but because a dog barks at strangers.
Suppose now Gōngsūn Zǐ is virtuous,
and Xú Zǐ is unworthy,
yet if Gōngsūn Zǐ and Xú Zǐ fight,
Xú Zǐ's dog would seize Gōngsūn Zǐ's calf and bite it.
If it could leave the unworthy for the virtuous,
would it merely seize the calf and bite?"
Ānpíng Jūn said:
"I respectfully heed your words."
And recommended him to the king.
Later, when Tián Dān avoided slander from nine sons,
it was due to Diāo Bó's efforts.
Earlier,
when King Bì of Wú plotted rebellion with seven states,
and it began,
the King of Jìběi wanted to kill himself.
Gōngsūn Jué
(pronounced jù bì)
said to the King of Jìběi:
"I ask to try to clearly persuade King Liáng for Your Majesty,
and convey your intent to the Son of Heaven.
If persuasion fails,
it's not too late to die."
Gōngsūn Jué then saw King Liáng,
saying:
"Jìběi's territory,
borders strong Qí to the east,
is tied to Wú and Yuè to the south,
and pressed by Yān and Zhào to the north—
a state torn four ways.
Its power is insufficient for self-defense,
its strength inadequate to resist invaders,
and it lacks extraordinary advisors for crisis.
Though it fell
(fell,
meaning lost)
to Wú,
it wasn't its true plan.
In the past, Zhài Zhòng of Zhèng agreed to Sòng's demand to install Prince Tū,
to save his lord's life—
not righteous,
but the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded it
for exchanging life for death,
and survival for ruin.
Had Jìběi shown its true stance,
displaying refusal clearly,
then Wú would first pass through Qí,
conquer Jìběi,
and rally Yān and Zhào together.
Thus,
the east's alliance would form without gaps.
Now the kings of Wú and Chǔ drill feudal lords' troops,
drive untrained masses,
west to challenge the Son of Heaven,
while Jìběi alone holds firm, not yielding,
making Wú lose allies and support,
staggering alone,
crumbling like tiles and earth,
defeated without rescue—
surely due to Jìběi's effort.
For tiny Jìběi
to contend with feudal lords
is like a weak lamb
fending off tiger-wolf foes.
Upholding duty unyieldingly
shows true devotion.
With such merit and righteousness,
if still doubted by the emperor,
hunching shoulders, bowing head,
clasping feet, smoothing robes,
making it regret not advancing
(regretting not joining Wú west),
is not the state's interest.
I fear vassals upholding duty would doubt.
I privately reckon
that only you, Great King, can cross the Western Hills,
pass Chánglè,
reach Wèiyāng,
roll up sleeves and speak forthrightly.
You alone, Great King,
can achieve the feat of preserving the fallen above,
and gain fame for calming the people below,
with virtue deep as marrow,
and grace extending endlessly.
I urge you, Great King, to consider this carefully."
King Xiào was greatly pleased,
sent someone swiftly to report,
and the King of Jìběi avoided punishment,
moved to Zīchuān.
Chén Lín managed Yuán Shào's documents;
when Yuán fell,
Lín joined Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ said to him:
"You once wrote manifestos for Běnchū,
criticizing only me—
hatred should stop at the person,
why extend to my ancestors?"
Lín apologized:
"When Chǔ and Hàn were undecided,
Kuǎi Tōng offered strategies to Hán Xìn.
At the battle of Gānshí,
Guǎn Zhòng fought hard for Zǐ Jiū.
They only wished to serve their lords,
aiding fortune momentarily.
So Zhí's follower could assassinate Yóu,
and Jié's dog could bark at Yáo.
Now if you, enlightened lord, can promote worthies after anger,
and discard fools despite affection,
all directions will reform,
and heroes will sincerely submit.
It's for you, enlightened lord, to decide."
Tàizǔ said:
"Good!"
And treated him generously.
From this we see
why the Marquis of Jìn killed Lǐ Kè,
Emperor Gāozǔ executed Dīng Gōng,
Shí Lè put Zǎo Sōng to death,
Liú Bèi slighted Xǔ Jìng—
all with good reason.
Thus Fàn Yè said:
"One who keeps faith with an old lord
can serve a new one;
one ashamed to be honored with his crowd
can receive great honor."
If the speaker is sincere,
but the listener doesn't grasp it,
is it that flattery for advancement
is easily accepted with emotion,
while upright opposition
is hard to appreciate with reason?
If one can renounce profit to follow the Way,
and abide by principles to uphold righteousness,
that is the measure of a noble person.
Difficulty and Necessity, Chapter 28.
Every ruler desires loyalty from his ministers,
yet loyalty does not always earn trust.
Thus Wǔ Yuán was cast into the river and Cháng Hóng died in Shǔ;
their blood transformed into jade after three years.
Every parent desires filial piety from their children,
yet filial piety does not always earn affection.
Thus Xiào Jǐ suffered anxiety and Zēng Shēn knew grief.
This illustrates the uncertainty of expectations.
How can this be explained?
As the saying goes:
"When Yì draws his bow, the Yuè people remain unperturbed;
when a child draws his bow, even his loving mother retreats indoors and closes the door."
Thus, when certainty exists, the Yuè people do not doubt Yì;
when uncertainty exists, a loving mother flees from her own child.
Wèi Wén Hóu asked Hú Juànzǐ:
"Can one rely completely on the virtue of father and son, brothers, or ruler and minister?"
He replied:
"One cannot rely completely.
Why?
No father was more virtuous than Yáo,
yet his son Dān Zhū was exiled;
no son was more virtuous than Shùn,
yet his father Gǔ Sǒu was imprisoned;
no elder brother was more virtuous than Shùn,
yet his brother Xiàng was arrogant;
no younger brother was more virtuous than Zhōu Gōng,
yet his brothers Guǎn and Cài were executed;
no minister was more virtuous than Tāng and Wǔ,
yet they attacked their rulers Jié and Zhòu.
Those who place hopes on others will see them unmet;
those who depend on others will not last long.
If you wish to govern well,
you must start with yourself.
How can one rely on others!"
During the Hàn dynasty,
Liáng Xiào Wáng concealed Yáng Shèng and Gōngsūn Guǐ.
Hán Ān Guó tearfully persuaded Liáng Xiào Wáng, saying:
"Your Majesty, consider your relationship with the Emperor
(the Emperor
refers to Jǐng Dì,
elder brother to Liáng Xiào Wáng) -
how does it compare to that between Tài Shàng Huáng and Gāo Huáng Dì,
or between the Emperor and Lín Jiāng Wáng?"
Lín Jiāng Wáng
was Crown Prince to Jǐng Dì.
Xiào Wáng replied:
"It does not compare."
Ān Guó said:
"Now Tài Shàng Huáng and Lín Jiāng Wáng
were related as father and son,
yet Gāo Dì declared:
'It is I who seized the empire with a three-foot sword!'
Thus Tài Shàng Huáng ultimately could not govern affairs
and resided in Lìyáng.
As for Lín Jiāng Wáng,
he was the legitimate eldest son and Crown Prince,
but was demoted to Prince of Línjiāng due to offensive remarks.
When Jǐng Dì entrusted the imperial consorts to the Crown Prince's mother,
Consort Lì spoke disrespectfully,
leading to the Crown Prince's demotion
and Consort Lì's death from sorrow.
Because of palace wall affairs,
he eventually committed suicide in the Commandant's office.
Why?
Because governing the empire ultimately cannot allow private interests to harm public good.
As the saying goes:
'Though he be one's own father,
who knows he won't become a scourge?
Though he be one's own brother,
who knows he won't become a wolf?'
Now you, Great King, ranked among the feudal lords,
delight in evil ministers,
follow reckless advice to offend the sovereign,
and obstruct clear laws.
The Son of Heaven, for the Empress Dowager's sake,
cannot bear to bring you to justice.
The Empress Dowager weeps day and night,
hoping you will reform yourself,
yet you remain unawakened.
If the Empress Dowager should suddenly pass away,
whom will you rely upon then?"
Before he finished speaking,
Xiào Wáng produced Yáng Shèng and others.
Liáng Xiào Wáng, brother of Jǐng Dì, followed the schemes of Yáng Shèng and Gōngsūn Guǐ,
seeking to become Crown Prince of Hàn.
Fearing the ministers would not consent,
he secretly sent assassins to kill Yuán Àng, the influential policy-making minister.
When the Emperor learned of Guǐ and Shèng's plot,
he sent ten groups of envoys
to conduct a nationwide search,
seeking to capture Guǐ and Shèng,
but they were not found.
Neishi Hán Ān Guó, hearing that Guǐ and Shèng were hidden in Xiào Wáng's residence,
went to see the King
and persuaded him.
The King produced Guǐ and Shèng,
whereupon Guǐ and Shèng committed suicide.
From this we can see -
where lies any certainty?
As the saying goes:
"Those who unite for power and profit
will become estranged when these are exhausted."
Another says:
"Those who serve others with their beauty
will lose favor when their beauty fades."
This shows that wealth and beauty cannot be relied upon.
Mòzǐ said:
"Even a loving father
will not cherish a worthless son."
Huáng Shí Gōng said:
"A ruler cannot be without virtue,
for without virtue ministers will rebel."
This shows that ministers and sons cannot be relied upon.
The Book of Songs says:
"Seek your own blessing."
How profound!
How profound!
Twenty-ninth: On Fate and Fortune
The Way of Heaven, human nature, and destiny
are rarely spoken of even by sages.
Though their essence exists,
it is difficult to obtain detailed understanding.
Yet by examining past and present,
interweaving their patterns,
and riding upon the three tendencies,
one can roughly grasp their outline.
How can this be explained?
Xún Yuè said:
"All three luminaries
Discussion states:
The three luminaries
are the sun, moon, and stars.
When essential energies transform abnormally,
these are all essences of yīn and yáng.
Their foundation lies in the earth,
yet they manifest above in heaven.
When governance fails here,
changes appear there -
is this not indeed so?"
King Wén asked Tài Gōng:
"When a ruler acts and undertakes affairs,
are there responses of calamity,
or blessings from spirits and gods?"
Tài Gōng said:
"There are.
If a ruler favors heavy taxes,
grand palaces,
then people will often suffer from epidemics,
frost and dew will kill the five grains;
if a ruler enjoys hunting,
not avoiding seasonal prohibitions,
then the year will have great winds,
and grains will not ripen;
if a ruler likes to destroy famous mountains,
block great rivers,
or redirect famous waters,
then the year will have great floods that harm people,
and the five grains will not grow;
if a ruler favors military affairs,
with weapons and armor never resting,
then the sun and moon will be eclipsed,
and Venus will stray from its course."
King Wén said:
"How true!"
Now citing the "Hóng Fàn" about portents of fault,
there were Yáo and Tāng's flood and drought disasters;
for dispelling disasters and unusual phenomena,
there was King Xuān of Zhōu's "Cloudy Han" - would you not listen to me!
The "Yì Jīng" states:
"Accumulating good deeds brings surplus blessings."
Yet there were Yán and Rǎn's misfortune of early death.
The retribution for good and evil,
manifests in countless ways,
cannot be uniform,
thus observers become confused.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"The "Shū Jīng" states:
'The Way of Heaven shows no partiality,
it constantly supports the good person.'
Among the seventy disciples,
Confucius particularly recommended Yán Huí as loving learning,
yet Huí was often in want,
not even satisfied with coarse food and died young.
How does Heaven reward good people?
What is it like?
Robber Zhí daily killed innocents,
ate human livers,
was cruel and unrestrained,
gathered followers numbering thousands,
rampaged across the world,
yet ultimately died of old age -
by following what virtue was this?
I am greatly confused."
Let me attempt to explain:
Confucius said:
"Life and death are matters of destiny."
Also said:
"Cannot obtain their proper death."
Also said:
"Fortunate to escape" -
that life and death are destined,
is the normal principle;
not obtaining proper death,
means one should not die but dies;
fortunate to escape,
means one could die but does not.
These are all principles of the three tendencies of nature and destiny.
Formerly the crown prince of Guó died,
Biǎn Què treated him and he lived,
Biǎn Què said:
"I cannot give life to the dead,
I can only treat those who can live."
Yet without meeting Biǎn Què,
he would not have lived.
As for illness in the vital regions,
even Yī Hé could not cure it.
Therefore it is said:
Life and death are destined,
that is the normal principle;
not obtaining proper death,
means one should not die but dies;
fortunate to escape,
means one could die but does not.
This is Xún Yuè's discussion of the three tendencies of nature and destiny.
Yáng Zǐ's "Fǎ Yán" states:
Someone asked:
"Can lifespan be increased?"
Said:
"By virtue."
Someone asked:
"Huí and Niú practiced virtue!
Why were their lives not extended?"
Said:
"Virtue was precisely why.
As Huí was impaired,
Niú was harmed,
how could they obtain long life?"
Said:
"The impaired and harmed sometimes live long."
Said:
"Those are erroneous cases,
the noble person is not erroneous."
Extending this to education and transformation,
it is also like this.
Some people become accomplished without education,
some need education to become accomplished,
some never accomplish despite education,
therefore the highest wisdom and lowest stupidity cannot be changed,
while average people can move up or down
Discussion states:
The "Zhuàn" says:
"The capable nurture it with blessing,
the incapable ruin it with misfortune."
This refers to those who can move up or down.
Extending this to the Way of Heaven,
it is also like this.
The responses of calamity and auspice,
leave no doubt.
Therefore Yáo and Tāng's floods and droughts,
were numbers of Heaven.
Discussion states:
When yīn is still and yáng moves,
heaven revolves and earth circulates,
the Great Unity calculates cycles,
forming the hardship of one hundred and six,
when the Grand Year's number peaks,
it becomes the disaster of one origin.
These are inevitable signs,
that cannot be changed.
Therefore the "Zhuàn" says:
"Beauty and ugliness complete their cycles and must return."
Also says:
"Heavenly disasters spread,
each generation of states has them."
Meaning they are certain.
Therefore called numbers of Heaven.
In Hàn times, Gōngsūn Hóng thought otherwise,
believing when Yáo encountered floods,
he made Yǔ control them,
and we haven't heard of Yǔ having floods.
As for Tāng's drought,
it was the remaining violence of Jié.
Jié and Zhòu practiced evil,
receiving Heaven's punishment.
Yǔ and Tāng accumulated virtue,
thus ruling the world.
Viewing from this,
Heaven shows no private favoritism.
Complying brings harmony,
opposing creates harm.
This is the principle of astronomy, geography, and human affairs.
Examining Gōngsūn Hóng's words,
he believed virtue influences floods and droughts,
not numbers of Heaven.
This is one school's opinion,
not correct theory.
The "Hóng Fàn" about portents of fault,
concerns human affairs.
Discussion states:
The "Zhuàn" says:
"Fortune and misfortune have no gates,
they are summoned by people themselves."
Referring to the five affairs corresponding to good and bad omens,
therefore called human affairs.
Duke Xī of Lǔ's excessive rain,
was a response that could be remedied.
The Zhōu court's severe drought,
was a situation difficult to change.
Discussion states:
Confucius said:
"Sacrifice as if present."
Meaning sacrificial methods lie in sincerity.
It is said:
"Respond to Heaven with substance,
not with ornate words."
Heaven is not moved by falseness.
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"Goodness unaccumulated
cannot achieve fame."
An ancient saying states:
"Earth's nature overcomes water,
yet a handful of soil cannot block a river;
metal's nature overcomes wood,
yet an inch-long blade cannot destroy a forest."
The Tradition says:
"Small favors not sincere,
the spirits will not bless."
This means scant goodness cannot move things.
Now rain sacrifices are identical yet responses differ—
some say because benevolence is too meager
while seeking blessings too numerous;
others merely perform empty rituals
without genuine sincerity.
Hence the differences.
Yán Huí and Rǎn Gēng's misfortunes
stemmed from their inherent nature.
Discussion says:
Duke Jǐng of Qín asked Shì Yǎng:
"Which Jìn minister's clan will fall first?"
Reply:
"Perhaps the Luán clan?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"Due to their extravagance?"
Reply:
"Indeed, Luán Yǎn's excesses are extreme,
yet he may escape.
The danger lies with Yíng!"
Duke Jǐng asked:
"Why?"
Reply:
"Wǔzǐ's virtue remains among people,
like the Zhōu people missing Duke Shào!
They cherished his pear tree—
how much more his son?
When Luán Yǎn dies,
Yíng's goodness cannot reach others;
Wǔzǐ's benefactions fade,
while Yǎn's resentments manifest—
will it happen then?"
A year later,
Jìn destroyed the Luán clan.
Thus we see
though Yǎn was extravagant,
through his father Wǔzǐ's virtue,
he personally received blessings;
though Yíng was wise,
through his father Yǎn's excesses,
he met with disaster.
Therefore fortune and misfortune
depend not on our own worthiness or cruelty.
Fàn Yè said:
"Chén Píng employed many schemes,
yet knew his line would end;
Bǐng Jí accumulated hidden virtue,
so Xiàhóu Shèng predicted his ennoblement would extend to descendants.
Ultimately Chén Zhǎng lost his marquisate,
while Bǐng Chāng continued the state.
Though cases differ,
none can be disputed—
the general principle returns to virtue.
When Yuán Ān confronted the Dòu clan with sincere emotion,
guiding the imperial house with righteous elegance,
he exemplified ministerial excellence.
When adjudicating the Chǔ case,
he never convicted anyone of corruption.
His benevolent heart sufficiently blessed his descendants—
his lineage's prosperity
is fitting indeed!"
Thus we see
the decline of Chén Píng's line and prosperity of Bǐng Jí's and Yuán Ān's
lay in their ancestors' virtue,
not their own gains or losses.
Yú Shìnán said:
"Buddhism's giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom
how differ they from
benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faithfulness?
Therefore cultivation becomes cause,
its fruit becomes reward.
People cultivating these six practices
often do so incompletely—
one deficiency,
and the fruit diminishes accordingly."
Thus Zōngmíng was ugly but wise;
Zhào Yī talented but low-ranked;
Luó Póu wealthy but unrighteous;
Yuán Xiàn poor but principled—
their differences
are this extreme.
Rise and fall, gain and loss
all necessarily follow this.
Thus we say:
Incomplete personal conduct means incomplete blessings—
hence good fortune and disaster are uneven.
Thus some people with wicked conduct enjoy wealth and longevity,
while some accumulating goodness die young.
Now common folk
seeing Bǐgàn's heart excised
think loyalty futile;
hearing King Yǎn's kingdom lost
think benevolence worthless.
Is this not mistaken?
The Yì Jīng says:
"There is Heaven's way,
Earth's way,
and Humanity's way"
—speaking of their differences;
"Combining the three forces in pairs"
—speaking of their unity.
Thus Heaven and Earth's ways
have both unity and difference.
Focusing on differences
to blame unity
causes confusion;
clinging to unity
while seeking differences
leads to error.
Speed and slowness, depth and shallowness
interweave with variations—
hence irregularity prevails over uniformity.
The principles of Heaven, Earth, humanity, and things all follow this.
Therefore the gentleman exhausts heart and strength
to engage with destiny.
Discussion says:
Xúnzǐ stated:
"Heaven's cycles are constant,
not existing for Yáo's sake,
nor perishing for Jié's sake.
Responding with order brings fortune;
responding with chaos brings disaster.
Strengthening fundamentals while practicing frugality—
Heaven cannot impoverish you;
adequate provisions and timely labor—
Heaven cannot sicken you;
following the Way unswervingly—
Heaven cannot harm you;
betraying the Way recklessly—
Heaven cannot bless you.
Thus understanding Heaven-human distinction
makes one a supreme person.
Like falling stars or sounding trees—
these Heaven-Earth changes
may be wondered at,
yes;
feared,
no.
Only human portents
are truly fearsome.
Why?
Tyrannical governance loses people,
fields lie barren, crops wither,
grain prices soar, people starve,
roads fill with corpses—
this is called human portent.
Unclear decrees,
ill-timed actions,
neglected fundamentals—
this is called human portent.
Ritual-righteousness uncultivated,
inner-outer undefined,
men-women debauched,
father-son distrustful,
superior-subordinate alienated,
banditry daily increasing—
this is called human portent.
These three disordered
leave no peaceful state."
His reasoning is profound,
his warnings dire.
The Tradition says:
"Monsters among the myriad things
books do not discuss.
Useless debates,
unurgent inspections
are abandoned ungoverned."
Mò Dí said:
"Ancient sage kings
promoted filial sons to encourage service to parents;
honored worthies to promote goodness;
issued decrees for instruction,
clarified rewards-punishments for deterrence.
Thus chaos became order,
danger became safety.
If unconvinced,
consider: Jié's chaos
was ordered by Tāng;
Zhòu's chaos
was ordered by King Wǔ.
The world unchanged, people unaltered—
yet rulers changing policies transforms teaching.
Thus safety-danger, order-chaos
depend on rulers' governance.
How can this be called fate?"
Previously King Huì of Liáng asked Wèi Liáo:
"I hear Huángdì had penal-virtue tactics
ensuring hundred-battle hundred-victory—
is this true?"
Wèi Liáo replied:
"Not so.
What Huángdì called 'punishment and virtue'
means using punishment to attack,
and using virtue to defend,
not what the world calls punishment and virtue.
What the world calls punishment and virtue
concerns celestial officials, auspicious times, yīn-yáng, and directional orientations.
Huángdì's approach
was solely about human affairs.
How can this be explained?
Suppose there is a city here,
attacking it from east and west,
it cannot be taken;
attacking it from north and south,
it cannot be taken.
These four directions,
are they not all following timely advantages?
Yet it cannot be taken,
why is that?
Because the walls are high, the moats deep,
weapons and preparations complete,
and it is defended with strategy.
From this perspective,
celestial officials and auspicious times are not as good as human affairs.
The celestial officials' battle formations say:
'An army with its back to water
is a doomed army;
an army facing a slope
is a defeated army.'
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he had his back to the Zhāng River,
facing a mountain slope,
leading twelve thousand men against Zhòu's one hundred and eighty thousand,
cut off Zhòu's head,
and hung it on a white banner.
Did Zhòu not have the celestial officials' formations?
Yet he was not victorious,
why?
Because he failed in human affairs.
Huángdì said:
'One who first examines his own wisdom
is called the Son of Heaven.'
From this, it is clear
that it is all about human affairs."
Note:
The theories of Xúnzǐ, Mòdí, and Wèi Liáo
state that good and bad fortune, calamity and blessing lie with humans.
The Duke of Zhōu admonished King Chéng, saying:
"In the past, King Zhōngzōng of Yīn
governed the people with reverence and caution,
not daring to be idle or indulgent,
and enjoyed the throne for seventy years.
As for Gāozōng,
he brought peace to the Yīn state,
so that from great to small,
there was no resentment at any time,
and he enjoyed the throne for fifty-nine years.
As for Zǔjiǎ,
he understood the clothing and food of the common people,
was able to protect and benefit the masses,
and did not oppress the widowed or orphaned,
enjoying the throne for thirty-three years.
From that time onward,
the kings established were born into leisure,
only pursuing indulgence and pleasure,
and none could achieve longevity.
Some reigned ten years,
some seven or eight years,
some three or four years.
Alas!
