May the succeeding kings take this as a mirror."
The "Records of the Grand Historian: Chén Family" says:
"Chén
was a descendant of Shùn.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed him at Chén.
The Grand Historian says:
Shùn's virtue
was supreme.
He abdicated to the Xià,
and his descendants continued the sacrifices,
through three dynasties.
When Chǔ destroyed Chén,
the Tián clan gained power in Qí,
eventually establishing a state,
lasting for a hundred generations without end."
Also, the "Biography of Nányuè" states:
"Although Yuè was a barbarian region,
did its ancestors not have great merit and virtue towards the people?
How could it last so long?
Through several generations,
they served as rulers,
with Gōujiàn once becoming a hegemon.
This was due to Yǔ's legacy."
It also says:
"Duke Huán of Zhèng, Yǒu,
was the youngest son of King Lì of Zhōu.
King Yōu made him a Minister of Education,
and he asked the Grand Historian Bó:
'The royal house faces many troubles,
where can I escape death?
I wish to go south to the river,
what do you think?'
He replied:
'In the past, Zhùróng served as fire official for Gāoxīn,
his merit was great.
Yet in Zhōu,
none of his line has risen.
Chǔ
is his descendant.
When Zhōu declines,
Chǔ will surely rise,
and its rise will not benefit Zhèng.'
The Duke asked:
'When Zhōu declines,
which states will rise?'
He replied:
'Qí, Qín, Jìn, and Chǔ!
Now Qí,
of the Jiāng surname,
are descendants of Bóyí.
Bóyí assisted Yáo in rituals.
Qín,
of the Yíng clan,
are descendants of Bóyì.
Bóyì assisted Shùn,
pacifying all creatures.
As for the ancestors of Chǔ,
all had merit under heaven.
And King Wǔ enfeoffed Shūyú at Táng,
a land rugged and perilous,
thus possessing virtue.
If Zhōu declines,
these will surely rise together.'"
Note:
The discussions of the Duke of Zhōu, Sīmǎ Qiān, and Grand Historian Bó
state that rise and fall, longevity and brevity
must depend on virtue.
This briefly states the root without detailing the specifics.
Let me attempt to discuss it:
Fate is
what heaven bestows;
virtue is
the root of fate.
Although the heavenly spirits secretly determine human affairs,
settling them in unseen signs,
yet rise and fall, longevity and brevity
are measured by virtue.
If virtue was cultivated in the past,
then fate is determined in the present.
Thus, the fate determined now
is clearly all due to past virtue.
Since fate lies in virtue,
then good and bad fortune, calamity and blessing do not come from heaven;
since fate is determined now,
then even sages and spirits cannot change it.
Therefore, the noble person exhausts their heart and strength,
to seek fate.
This is the ultimate understanding of fate.
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"Exhaust principle and fully develop nature,
to reach fate."
This is what it means.
Discussion:
Good and bad fortune depend on humans,
rise and fall lie in virtue.
Examining previous records,
it is certain that it depends on virtue.
Some argue that Yáo and Shùn had no heirs,
attributing it to fate,
but this is mistaken.
Why?
Those who assist as meritorious ministers
must have rising descendants;
if the throne were passed to sons,
then the virtue of the ministers would be discarded.
How can this be explained?
In the past, Duke Huán of Zhèng asked Grand Historian Bó:
"When Zhōu declines,
which state will rise?"
He replied:
"In the past, Zhùróng served as fire official for Gāoxīn,
his merit was great.
Yet in Zhōu,
none of his line has risen.
Chǔ
is his descendant.
When Zhōu declines,
Chǔ will surely rise.
Qí,
of the Jiāng surname,
are descendants of Bóyí,
who assisted Yáo in rituals.
Qín,
of the Yíng clan,
are descendants of Bóyì,
who assisted Shùn in pacifying all creatures.
If Zhōu declines,
these will surely rise together."
Therefore, Bān Gù's "Diǎn Yǐn" states:
"Táo Táng (Yáo) passed over his own descendants and abdicated to Yǒuyú (Shùn),
Yǒuyú also commanded Xiàhòu,
Jì and Xiè carried on their work with brilliance,
extending to Chéng Tāng and Wǔ,
with ministers and assistants already complete,
Heaven then credited the merit to the sovereign,
preparing to bestow it upon Liú of Hàn. "
From this perspective,
how can it be said there is no successor!
It is also said:
"The Chǔ army slaughtered the Hàn troops,
the Suī River clogged with their bodies;
the Qín people buried the Zhào soldiers alive,
the boiling sound like thunder.
Even with the talents of Yóu and Xià,
or the near-perfection of Yī and Yán,
how could they resist it!"
This reveals its fallacy.
In response, it is said:
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
Mars was in the Heart constellation.
The duke feared,
and asked Zǐwéi,
Zǐwéi said:
"The Heart,
corresponds to Sòng's celestial division,
the calamity should fall upon the ruler.
However,
it can be transferred to the people."
Based on this statement,
when the ruler faces disaster,
the people should bear it.
If at the time of the ruler's crisis,
then the people suffer extreme hardship.
Even with Yī, Yán, Yóu, or Xià,
what could they do to resist?
Therefore, Zhuāngzǐ said:
"In the times of Yáo and Shùn,
there were no impoverished people under heaven,
not because of gained wisdom;
in the times of Jié and Zhòu,
there were no successful people under heaven,
not because of lost wisdom.
It was the circumstances that made it so."
This is what is meant.
It is also said:
"Those Róng and Dí,
human-faced but beast-hearted,
find comfort in poison,
regard slaughter as morality,
and consider incestuous relationships as righteousness.
Since the virtue of metal declined,
heaven and earth were in turmoil,
they overran Chán and Luò,
and toppled the five capitals.
Alas!
The idea that good is blessed and evil is punished,
is but an empty saying." □
This argument,
attributing the Róng and Dí's invasion
simply to fate,
is what is called not weighing virtue.
Why so?
Formerly, Duke Mù of Qín asked the Róng man Yóuyú:
"The Central States govern with the Odes, Documents, Rites, Music, laws, and regulations,
yet still experience periodic chaos.
Now the Róng and Yí lack these,
how do they achieve order?"
Yóuyú laughed and said:
"This is precisely why the Central States are chaotic.
Since the supreme sage Huángdì created the rites, music, laws, and regulations,
he personally practiced them first,
achieving only minor order.
In later ages,
rulers grew increasingly arrogant and decadent daily,
relying on the authority of laws and regulations
to demand and supervise their subordinates;
when the people were exhausted and weary,
they resented their rulers in the name of benevolence and righteousness.
Upper and lower classes mutually contended and resented, leading to usurpation and slaughter,
even to the extinction of clans,
all due to this.
The Róng and Dí are not like this;
their superiors embody pure virtue
in dealing with their subordinates;
the subordinates harbor loyalty and trust
in serving their superiors.
The governance of the whole state
is like managing one's own body.
Without knowing how it is governed,
this is truly the governance of a sage.
Such is the virtue of the Róng and Dí."
Now, at the rise of Jìn,
the imperial clansmen provided no support like a surrounding wall,
and the conflicts like those between Èbó and Shíchén arose every year;
the high ministers lacked the dignity of being looked up to,
and the disasters of overthrow, execution, and humiliation occurred daily.
Xuān and Jǐng encountered times of many troubles,
focusing on attacking heroes,
and executing numerous stalwarts to facilitate affairs.
Their overthrow and massacres
were not limited to mere executions.
Customs became depraved and aberrant,
with both integrity and shame lost.
Marrying prematurely,
acting on whims,
none felt ashamed of the faults of debauchery and idleness.
Unrestrained by the evils of jealousy and envy,
some opposed their in-laws,
some reversed the roles of strength and gentleness,
some killed their concubines,
some defiled the hierarchy between superior and subordinate.
Their lewdness, turmoil, and vicious rebellion
were not limited to incestuous relations.
From this perspective,
the virtue of the Jìn house,
how could it surpass that of the Xiōngnú!
Now, seeing the Róng and Dí throwing Huá into chaos,
and attributing it to fate rather than virtue,
how excessive such words are!
The Great Private, Thirtieth
Guǎnzǐ said:
"To know that giving is taking
is the treasure of governance."
The Zhōushū says:
"If you wish to take something,
you must first give it."
How can this be proven?
Huáng Shígōng said:
"When you gain, do not possess;
establish but do not take;
the action is yours,
the possession belongs to the officers.
How then can one know where the profit lies?"
People often strive for achievement,
few are those who yield.
Only the Son of Heaven does not compete with subordinates for merit and fame.
Therefore it is said:
"The possession belongs to the officers,
how then can one know where the profit lies?"
They become feudal lords,
while he becomes the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven does not claim credit from all things,
thus he can attain his height;
he does not compete for fame among the masses,
thus he can achieve his greatness. ,
Let the city defend itself,
let the officers take for themselves
all the wealth of the enemy city,
allowing them to take it.
This is what is called using the greedy and using the foolish. .
This is the way of a true king.
Shīzǐ said:
"Yáo cared for the helpless,
Yǔ loved the guilty,
this is how the ancient kings brought safety to the endangered and won over the distant."
The sage, in his great private, is selfless.
Tāng said:
"If I have sinned,
let it not affect the myriad regions;
if the myriad regions have sinned,
let me bear it."
Tāng was not private about his person but was private about the myriad regions.
King Wén said:
"If there is a benevolent person,
why must they be closely related!"
King Wén was not private about his kin but was private about the myriad states.
The ancient kings were not without private interests,
but what they considered private differed from others,
this is understanding the great private.
From this, it is said,
only by not being private
can one achieve their private aims;
by not seeking benefit, yet benefiting others,
one attains the greatest benefit.
The Failure of Merit, Thirty-First
Wénzǐ said:
"Those who achieve merit yet stray from benevolence and righteousness
will be viewed with suspicion;
those who commit crimes but do not lose the people's hearts
will surely be trusted."
Thus, benevolence and righteousness
are the most honored virtues in the world.
How can this be explained?
Long ago, King Gōng of Chǔ fell ill
and summoned his ministers, saying:
"I, the unvirtuous one,
have poorly governed the state,
failed to maintain the legacy of previous rulers,
and brought defeat upon Chǔ's armies -
these are my crimes.
If by the grace of the ancestral temples
I can preserve my head until death,
I request the posthumous names 'Líng' or 'Lì' -
do you ministers consent?"
When he passed away,
Zǐnáng said:
"Not so!
Those who serve a ruler
should follow his virtues,
not his faults.
He magnificently ruled over the great state of Chǔ,
pacified the southern regions,
and his influence reached the central states -
his achievements were grand indeed.
Having such honor
yet recognizing his own faults -
can this not be called 'Gōng' (Reverent)?"
The ministers followed this suggestion.
This is an example of turning faults into merits.
When Wáng Chǎng and Chén Tài, generals of Wèi, suffered defeat,
the Grand General took the blame upon himself.
The people of Wèi were moved by his acceptance of responsibility,
all became pleased,
and sought to repay him.
Xí Zàochǐ commented:
"The Grand General Sīmǎ took responsibility for the two defeats as his own fault,
thus eliminating blame while prospering his enterprise -
this may be called wisdom."
When subordinates forget their defeat and think of repayment,
even if one wishes not to prosper,
how could it be avoided?
If instead one conceals defeat and shifts blame,
attributing fault to everything,
then superiors and subordinates become estranged,
the wise and foolish abandon their duties -
this would be like Chǔ suffering repeated defeats and Jìn achieving repeated victories,
a grave error indeed.
If a ruler can grasp this principle
and apply it to governing the state,
though actions may fail, reputation will flourish;
though troops may be thwarted, victory will be won;
even a hundred defeats would be acceptable,
let alone two defeats!
This is achieving success through failure.
Thus we know that when the wise undertake endeavors,
they turn calamity into blessing,
transform defeat into victory -
this has been so since ancient times.
Discussion:
When Bái Qǐ of Qín buried alive over four hundred thousand surrendered Zhào soldiers,
he caused the various states to resent Qín and form alliances against it.
The massacre of Zhào's surrendered troops
was not a victory,
but rather an opportunity for Qín's defeat.
When Lord Shāng deceived Wèi
and captured Prince Áng,
he caused Qín's credibility to be lost throughout the world -
this was an omen of self-defeat,
not a hegemonic achievement.
Yuè Yì, upholding righteousness,
captured Qí's cities,
yet was defeated at Jímò -
this was not true defeat,
but rather the momentum to conquer the world.
Liú Bèi, pitying those who had submitted to him,
traveled only ten-some lǐ per day,
and was defeated at Chángbǎn -
though he had no time even to flee,
this marked the beginning of his royal enterprise.
Thus we know that only hegemons can utilize defeat.
When the Qí people used purple to ruin plain silk,
its value increased tenfold.
Though this saying is small,
it can illustrate greater truths.
Thirty-second: Clouded Judgment and Wisdom
The spirit is
the wellspring of wisdom;
when the spirit is clear, wisdom is bright.
Wisdom is
the manifestation of the mind;
when wisdom is impartial, the mind is balanced.
This is quoted from "Wénzǐ".
Now, among scholars, there are those with clear spirits and bright wisdom who are yet ignorant of success and failure—
not because they are foolish,
but because sounds and sights, power and profit, anger and affection have clouded their wisdom.
How can this be explained?
In the past, when Confucius acted as the prime minister of Lǔ,
Duke Jǐng of Qí heard of it and became fearful,
saying:
"With Confucius in government,
Lǔ will surely become a hegemon.
Since we are near neighbors,
we will be the first to be annexed."
Lí Jǔ said:
"To remove Zhòngní is as easy as blowing away a feather.
Why not offer him a generous salary to delay him,
and present Duke Āi with female musicians?
If Duke Āi personally enjoys the music,
he will neglect governance,
and Zhòngní will surely remonstrate.
If his advice is not heeded,
he will lightly sever ties with Lǔ."
Thereupon, they selected eighty beautiful women from Qí,
all dressed in embroidered garments to dance the Kānglè.
They were presented to the ruler of Lǔ,
who accepted Qí's female musicians,
neglected his duties,
and for three days did not attend to governance.
Confucius said:
"With those women's allure,
one must depart."
He then went to Wèi.
This is an example of being clouded by sounds and sights.
When the Róng king sent Yóu Yú to observe Qín,
Duke Mù of Qín, considering Yóu Yú wise and sagely,
asked Nèishǐ Liào:
"I have heard that a sage in a neighboring state
is a worry for a rival country.
Now Yóu Yú
is a threat to me—
what should be done?"
Nèishǐ Liào replied:
"The Róng king resides in a remote place,
and has never heard the music of the central states.
Try presenting him with female musicians
to divert his will;
request Yóu Yú's service,
to create a rift between them;
detain him without sending him back,
so he misses his deadline.
The Róng king will find it strange,
and will surely suspect Yóu Yú.
Moreover, if the Róng king enjoys the music,
he will neglect governance."
Duke Mù said:
"Excellent!"
He presented the Róng king with two rows of eight female musicians each,
and the Róng king accepted them with delight,
remaining in his place all year without moving.
Yóu Yú remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Duke Mù sent someone to secretly invite Yóu Yú,
and Yóu Yú then surrendered to Qín.
When the King of Liáng feasted the feudal lords at his garden terrace,
the ruler of Lǔ said:
"In ancient times, the emperor's daughter ordered Yí Dí to make wine, which was excellent,
and presented it to Yǔ.
Yǔ drank it and found it sweet,
yet he distanced himself from Yí Dí
and abstained from fine wine,
saying:
'Later generations will surely have those who lose their states because of wine.'
When Duke Huán of Qí felt unsatisfied at midnight,
Yì Yá would fry, simmer, roast, and grill,
blending the five flavors to present to him.
The duke ate until he was full,
and said:
'Later generations will surely have those who lose their states because of taste.'
When Duke Wén of Jìn obtained Nánzhīwēi,
he did not hold court for three days,
then pushed Nánzhīwēi away and distanced himself from her,
saying:
'Later generations will surely have those who lose their states because of beauty.'
When the King of Chǔ ascended the Qiángtái and gazed upon the Bēngshān,
with the river on the left and the lake on the right,
he found such joy that he forgot death,
yet he refrained from ascending again, saying:
'Later generations will surely have those who lose their states because of high terraces and ponds.'
Now, your lordship's wine cup
is like Yí Dí's wine;
your lordship's flavors
are like Yì Yá's cooking;
with Báitái on the left and Lǘxū on the right,
it is the beauty of Nánzhīwēi;
with Jiālín in front and Lántái behind,
it is the pleasure of Qiángtái.
If a ruler has even one of these,
it is enough to lose his state.
Now your lordship possesses all four—
should you not be warned?"
The King of Liáng repeatedly praised him.
From this, it can be said
that what clouds wisdom
is not limited to one path.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Lord Píngyuán
was an elegant nobleman in a corrupt age,
yet he failed to see the greater picture.
As the saying goes:
'Profit confounds wisdom.'
Lord Píngyuán, greedy for Féng Tíng's deceitful advice,
caused Zhào to lose over four hundred thousand troops at Chángpíng,
and nearly led to the fall of Hándān."
This is an example of being clouded by profit.
"Rénwùzhì" states:
"Benevolence arises from compassion,
yet there are those with compassion but no benevolence.
The benevolent show sympathy,
yet there are those with benevolence but no sympathy.
The stern possess firmness,
yet there are those who are stern but not firm.
For instance, one may shed tears at the sight of pity,
yet be stingy when it comes to sharing—
this is having compassion without benevolence.
One may feel distress at witnessing danger,
yet fear harm when about to rescue—
this is having benevolence without sympathy.
One may appear stern in empty righteousness,
yet waver inwardly when facing profit and desire—
this is being stern without firmness.
Thus, compassion without benevolence
is due to stinginess overpowering it;
benevolence without sympathy
is due to fear overpowering it;
sternness without firmness
is due to desire overpowering it."
The "Hòu Hàn Shū • Bān Gù Zhuàn"评论道:
"In the past, Bān Gù lamented about Sīmǎ Qiān, saying:
'Qiān was erudite and widely informed,
yet he could not use his wisdom to avoid extreme punishment.'
However, Bān Gù himself also fell into grave execution
Bān Gù attached himself to the Dòu clan's power,
and when the Dòu clan fell,
Bān Gù was implicated,
dying in the Luòyáng prison. ,
It can be said that he attained wisdom but could not maintain it.
Is this not what the ancients meant by discussing the eye being unable to see its own lashes?
This is an example of being clouded by power."
It is discussed:
Bān Gù's lament for Qiān
was a fair judgment.
His own fall into execution
was due to partiality.
When the mind harbors partiality,
wisdom cannot be maintained.
"Shīzǐ" says:
"The states of Wú and Yuè
used servants and concubines for burials.
The central states heard of this and condemned it.
Yet when angered,
they would sacrifice their own relatives over a single word.
When wisdom is impartial, one pities the servants of Wú and Yuè;
when partial, one forgets one's own relatives.
It is not that wisdom is diminished,
but that anger obscures it.
This is an example of being clouded by anger.
The same applies to fondness."
As the saying goes:
One does not know the faults of one's own child.
It is not that wisdom is diminished,
but that love obscures it.
This is an example of being clouded by love.
Therefore,
in discussing nobility and baseness, or distinguishing right and wrong,
one must speak from a public-minded heart,
and listen from a public-minded heart,
before understanding can be reached.
Hence, Fàn Yè said:
"When profit does not concern oneself,
in planning affairs,
then wisdom and consideration are not selfish;
in judging righteousness,
then stern sincerity can prevail.
With the wisdom to observe things,
and the introspection to reflect on oneself,
one can be forgiving and self-aware."
It is discussed:
Confucius said:
"I have never met a truly firm person."
Someone replied:
"What about Shēn Chéng?"
The Master said: [199"Chéng is full of desires;
how can he be firm?"
From this perspective,
if the heart harbors selfishness,
it loses its original nature.
Shīzǐ states:
"When the swan is soaring above,
and the crossbow is drawn to await it,
whether to shoot or not,
if you ask Èr-Wǔ,
he would say:
'I do not know.'
It is not that Èr-Wǔ finds it hard to decide,
but his desire for the swan confuses his mind.
This shows that when attention is fixated on gain,
the fundamental heart becomes disordered."
Chapter Thirty-Three: Humble Governance
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Offering gold and jade to a drowning person in Qí
is not as useful as an ordinary rope."
Hánzǐ says:
"If one refrains from eating for a hundred days
waiting for fine grain and meat,
the starving person would not agree."
Hence it is said:
"To relieve hunger, one does not await a tripod feast;
to rescue the drowning, one does not wait for measured conduct."
This speaks of governance valuing humility to accomplish tasks.
Why is this said?
Hán Fēi states:
"What are called the subtle and profound words of the wise
are difficult even for the highest intellect to grasp.
Now if we make laws for the masses based on what challenges the highest intellect,
then people will have no means to understand them.
Thus, those not sated with bran and husks
do not await fine grain and meat to be full;
those lacking complete coarse garments
do not require embroidered silks to feel well-dressed.
From this perspective,
the affairs of governing the world—
if the urgent cannot be obtained,
then the non-urgent should not be pursued.
Now the governance we administer
concerns ordinary human affairs.
If what is clearly understood by common couples is not used,
but we admire what challenges the highest intellect's discussion,
then it becomes too remote from people.
Thus we know subtle and profound words
are not the people's business."
He also says:
"Those the world calls staunch knights
detach themselves from the crowd and act alone,
seeking to differ from others.
They engage in quietistic studies
and discuss nebulous theories.
Your servant believes
quietism
is a useless teaching;
nebulous theories
are lawless words.
Now human life necessarily involves serving rulers and supporting parents;
serving rulers and supporting parents
cannot be done by quietistic individuals—
it must be through loyal and trustworthy speech,
and loyal speech cannot be nebulous.
Therefore, nebulous theories and quietistic learning
are the delusive arts of the world."
He further states:
"Thorough investigation before understanding
cannot be considered complete wisdom.
For people cannot all investigate thoroughly,
and only the worthy can subsequently practice it,
so it cannot be made a standard."
Hence the Yīnwénzǐ says:
"Any principle that does not benefit governance
the noble person does not speak;
any ability that does not benefit affairs
the noble person does not perform."
Therefore, what the noble person speaks of
does not exceed names, laws, authority, and methods;
what the noble person performs
does not exceed farming, agriculture, and military formations,
but serves practical needs entirely.
It also says:
What petty persons speak of
reaches extremes in Confucian-Mohist debates on right and wrong;
what petty persons perform
reaches extremes in stubborn, hypocritical, biased, and confrontational conduct.
They seek fame only,
thus the enlightened ruler punishes them.
People of the present age
in conduct desire uniquely virtuous standing,
in affairs desire uniquely capable performance,
in debate desire surpassing the crowd,
in courage desire exceeding all others.
Uniquely virtuous conduct
is insufficient to accomplish transformation;
uniquely capable affairs
are insufficient to serve practical needs;
crowd-surpassing debate
cannot be explained door-to-door;
all-exceeding courage
cannot be deployed in proper formations.
These four qualities
are the sources of chaos.
Hence it is said:
Those who do good
make it impossible for others to follow;
those who display skill
make it impossible for others to participate.
Such exclusive goodness and exclusive skill
have not fully understood the principles of skill and goodness.
Therefore, what we value in the sage's governance
is not his exclusive rule,
but his ability to govern together with the multitude.
What we value in craftsman Chuí's skill
is not his exclusive skill,
but his ability to be skilled together with the multitude.
The Wénzǐ states:
"Foreknowledge and far-sightedness
represent the height of human talent,
yet well-governed ages do not value these in people.
Broad learning and strong memory,
eloquent speech and ready rhetoric,
represent the overflow of human intellect,
yet enlightened rulers do not seek these from subordinates.
Defying the world and despising material things,
remaining untainted by vulgar customs,
represent the noble conduct of scholars,
yet well-governed ages do not take these as human transformation.
Therefore, what is too high to reach
is not made the human standard;
conduct that cannot be matched
is not made the state custom.
Thus the state's order can be maintained with the simple,
and the army can unite with the timid.
Not awaiting ancient heroes yet people being self-sufficient
comes from utilizing what they already possess collectively."
Discussion:
According to Wénzǐ's words,
he believes sages should not use three things—foreknowledge, broad learning, and defying worldly values—
to transform the common people,
making everyone practice these ways
and adopt them as customs.
Instead, they should follow local conditions,
transforming through farming and military formations,
adapting flexibly to circumstances,
and bending to align with customs,
not valuing exclusive ability or courage.
Thus the sage employs the Way
to navigate difficulties.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Those who embody the Way rest without exhaustion,
those who rely on technique labor without achievement.
Lí Zhū with his keen eyesight
could discern a needle tip a hundred paces away,
yet could not see fish in deep water.
Shī Kuàng with his acute hearing
could harmonize the eight winds' tones,
yet could not hear beyond ten lǐ.
Thus relying on one person's ability
is insufficient to manage a three-mǔ homestead;
following the numbers of the Way's principle,
according to heaven and earth's spontaneity,
then the six directions become manageable."
This is employing the Way to navigate difficulties.
Establishing laws to manage differences.
The Wénzǐ says:
"Farmers, scholars, merchants, artisans—
different in villages and districts.
Farmers among farmers discuss storage,
scholars among scholars discuss conduct,
artisans among artisans discuss skill,
merchants among merchants discuss numbers.
Therefore,
scholars have no neglected conduct,
artisans no crude work,
farmers no wasted effort,
merchants no lost goods.
Each secures their livelihood."
This is establishing laws to manage differences.
Making the worthy and simple not reject each other,
the capable and crude not abandon each other—
this is the method of perfect order.
Thus when Shūsūn Tōng wanted to establish rites,
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn said:
"Won't it be difficult?"
He replied:
"Rites
are patterned restraints based on contemporary conditions and human feelings."
When Zhāng Shì spoke of expedient matters,
Emperor Wén said:
"Lower it!
No excessively lofty discussions,
make it practicable now."
From this perspective,
governance
should not prize the strange while ignoring contemporary practical needs—
this would be like starving people waiting days for fine grain,
or offering gold and jade to rescue a drowning child.
Discussion:
Formerly, Chǔ's Gōngshū and Sòng's Mò Dí
could make wooden kites fly alone,
yet it served no practical use.
Hàn's Zhāng Héng
could make three wheels turn autonomously;
Wèi's Mǎ Jūn
could make wooden figures play flutes;
if done without practical benefit,
it wastes effort and expends strength,
causing much harm.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Zhū Pēngmàn learned dragon-slaying from Zhīlí Yì,
exhausted a thousand gold,
mastered the skill yet had no use for his artistry."
The Wénzǐ says:
"Governing a state lies in benevolence, righteousness, rites, music, names, laws, punishments, and rewards—
Beyond this point,
even if one encompasses heaven and earth,
intertwines with all things,
outside the way of governance,
it is not what the masses can partake of or rely on,
thus the sage sets it aside and does not speak of it."
From this perspective,
what matters in affairs is timeliness,
not the pursuit of distant achievements,
and this has been so from the beginning.
On the Perishability of Goodness, Chapter Thirty-Four
The "Yì" says:
"A family that accumulates good deeds
will surely have abundant blessings."
It also says:
"Without accumulating good deeds,
one cannot achieve fame."
How can we prove this?
Mèngzǐ said:
"Goodness overcoming unkindness
is like water overcoming fire.
But now those who practice goodness
are like using a cup of water to save a cartload of burning firewood.
If the fire is not extinguished, they claim water cannot overcome fire—
this only aligns them with the most unkind.
Moreover,
even the finest grains,
if they do not ripen,
are inferior to weeds.
So, goodness too must be brought to maturity."
Maturity
means completion. ."
The "Shīzǐ" says:
"Food is what makes one fat,
but if someone eats one meal and asks others,
'How am I?'
everyone would laugh at them.
Governing the world
is a great task.
This is like those who ask 'How am I?' after just one meal."
Commentary:
This shows that a little goodness is not enough to build a reputation.
The same applies to evil.
How can we illustrate this?
The "Shū" says:
"The crimes of Shāng filled to the brim,
so Heaven ordained its punishment.
If I do not comply with Heaven,
my crime would be equal."
From this,
if crimes are not full,
even if there is wickedness,
it is not yet destroyed.
Now, when people see evil not immediately punished,
they think it is not to be feared,
hence those who perish follow one another in succession through the ages.
Therefore, it is said:
"Without accumulating evil,
one cannot bring about self-destruction."
This is the warning of the sages.
From this perspective,
we know that goodness
lies in accumulation alone.
Now, when people see Xú Yǎn's state perish,
they say benevolence and righteousness cannot be relied upon;
when they see Chéngsāng lose its rule,
they claim cultural virtue is not dependable
(for the ruler of Chéngsāng,
cultivated virtue but neglected martial prowess,
leading to his state's destruction). .
This is akin to the arguments of using a cup of water to fight fire or asking about fatness after one meal—
such confusion is profound indeed.
On Perverse Customs, Chapter Thirty-Five
There are matters that, when followed, lead to loss of righteousness;
those loved can cause harm;
what is disliked by oneself may turn out beautiful;
and what benefits the individual may damage the state.
How can this be explained?
Liú Liáng said:
"In the past, King Ling of Chǔ was arrogant and decadent,
brutal and without restraint.
Qiǎn Yǐn Shēn Hài indulged the king's desires,
burying him at Gānxī
with two maidens sacrificed to him.
This is following yet losing righteousness."
Commentary:
When the ruler is correct and ministers follow,
it is called compliance;
but if the ruler loses righteousness and ministers follow,
that is not true compliance.
At the battle of Yānlíng,
when Jìn and Chǔ faced off,
Gǔ Yáng offered wine,
leading to Zǐ Fǎn's death—
this is love causing harm.
When Emperor Wén of Hàn favored Lady Shèn,
in the palace,
she often shared a mat with the empress.
During a visit to the Upper Forest Garden,
the official arranged mats,
and Lady Shèn's mat was placed equal to the empress's.
Yuán Àng moved Lady Shèn's seat.
The emperor grew furious,
but Yuán Àng stepped forward and explained:
"I have heard
that when尊卑 are ordered,
上下 achieve harmony.
Now that Your Majesty has established an empress,
Lady Shèn is but a concubine.
How can the mistress and concubine sit together?
Moreover, if Your Majesty favors her,
bestow generous gifts instead.
What you do for Lady Shèn
may indeed bring disaster upon her.
Has Your Majesty not heard of the 'human pig'?"
The emperor then was pleased.
Thus,
the harm from love
has its origins here.
Zāng Wǔzhòng said:
"Mèngsūn's dislike of me
is like medicine;
Jìsūn's love for me,
a sweet sickness.
The poison of sickness grows thick,
yet medicine can still revive me."
This is disliking turning into beauty.
Xúnzǐ said:
"Those who criticize me rightly
are my teachers;
those who affirm me rightly
are my friends;
those who flatter me
are my enemies."
Shāng Jūn said:
"Superficial words
are flowery;
profound words
are substantial;
bitter words
are medicine;
sweet words
are disease."
Hánzǐ said:
"Doing favors for old friends in private
is called loyalty;
distributing public wealth
is called benevolence;
轻视俸禄 and valuing personal well-being
is called integrity;
twisting the law for relatives
is called righteousness;
abandoning office to indulge friends
is called chivalry;
withdrawing from society
is called lofty integrity;
defying orders through dispute
is called firmness;
winning followers with kindness
is called gaining support.
But loyalty
hides official corruption;
benevolence
depletes public funds;
integrity
makes people hard to command;
righteousness
ruins legal systems;
chivalry
leaves posts vacant;
lofty integrity
discourages public service;
firmness
undermines orders;
gaining support
isolates the ruler.
These eight traits
are the private praise of commoners,
yet great failures for a ruler."
If a ruler ignores the state's interests
and heeds commoners' private praise,
it is impossible
for the family and state to avoid danger and chaos.
Thus,
the preferences of customs
often contradict practical affairs,
and only the discerning can perceive this.
Hánzǐ said:
"The interests of ruler and minister differ,
so no minister is wholly loyal—
thus, the minister's gain means the ruler's loss."
This illustrates the divergence of interests.
Chapter 36: Ceasing Debate
Discussion says:
Human conduct is always manifested through traces;
by examining these traces through fundamental conduct,
then good and evil cannot remain hidden.
How can debaters escape their deceit?
The "Zhōng Lùn" states:
"The coldness of water,
the heat of fire,
the hardness of metal and stone -
these things have never spoken,
yet no one fails to know their nature,
because trustworthiness is embodied in their substance."
Therefore it is said:
If the trustworthiness of my conduct
were like those things,
who would doubt me?
Now if people don't trust my conduct,
yet I complain that others don't trust me -
this is extreme delusion.
Thus we know conduct has fundamentals and affairs leave traces.
If we carefully observe their substance,
then nothing can conceal the truth.
What are the fundamentals of conduct?
Confucius said:
"Establishing oneself requires righteousness,
with filial piety as the foundation;
mourning rituals require propriety,
with grief as the foundation;
battle formations require order,
with courage as the foundation."
Tàigōng said:
"If people don't exhaust their efforts,
they are not my people;
if officials aren't fair, clean, and loving toward people,
they are not my officials;
if the prime minister cannot enrich the state and strengthen the military,
harmonize yīn and yáng,
secure the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
train the various ministers,
establish their names and realities,
and clarify rewards and punishments,
he is not my prime minister."
These are the fundamentals of conduct.
What are the traces of affairs?
Formerly, King Wēi of Qí summoned the magistrate of Jímò and told him:
"Since you took residence in Jímò,
slander reaches me daily.
However, when I sent people to inspect Jímò,
the fields were cultivated,
the people were prosperous,
official business saw no delays,
and the eastern region was peaceful.
This shows you don't serve my attendants to seek praise."
He enfeoffed him with ten thousand households.
Then he summoned the magistrate of Ē and told him:
"Since you guarded Ē,
praise reaches my ears daily.
However, when I sent people to inspect Ē,
the fields were not cultivated,
the people were poor and suffering.
When Zhào attacked Zhēn,
you couldn't rescue it;
when Wèi took Xuēlíng,
you were unaware.
This shows you constantly bribe my attendants to seek praise."
That day he boiled the magistrate of Ē and those attendants who regularly praised him,
and Qí state became greatly ordered.
During Hàn Yuándì's reign,
Shí Xiǎn monopolized power.
Jīng Fáng had a banquet audience
and asked the emperor:
"Why did rulers Yōu and Lì fall into peril?
Who were those they appointed?"
The emperor said:
"The rulers were unenlightened and appointed cunning flatterers."
Jīng Fáng said:
"Did they know they were cunning flatterers yet employed them?
Or did they consider them worthy?"
The emperor said:
"They considered them worthy."
Jīng Fáng said:
"Then how do we now know they were unworthy?"
The emperor said:
"We know from the era's chaos and the ruler's peril."
Jīng Fáng said:
"Duke Huán of Qí and Èrshì of Qín also heard about these rulers and ridiculed them.
Yet they appointed Shù Diāo and Zhào Gāo,
whereupon governance daily deteriorated,
and bandits filled the hills.
Why didn't they use Yōu and Lì as omens and awaken?"
The emperor said:
"Only those possessing the Dào
can use the past to know the future."
Jīng Fáng said:
"Does Your Majesty consider the present era ordered
or chaotic?"
The emperor said:
"Extremely chaotic."
Jīng Fáng said:
"Who are those employed now?"
The emperor said:
"Still, fortunately they're better than those,
and I don't think the problem lies with these people."
Jīng Fáng said:
"Those two former rulers
were also like this.
I fear later generations viewing our present
will be like our present viewing the past."
These are the traces of affairs.
From this we can say:
Establishing oneself and engaging in governance
all have fundamentals;
order and chaos, capability and incapability,
all leave traces.
If we grasp the fundamental conduct
and measure it against the traces of affairs,
it's like the coldness of water or the heat of fire -
then good and evil cannot escape detection.
Chapter 37: Measuring Faults
Confucius said:
"People's faults
each accord with their category.
Observing their faults,
one then knows their virtue."
"Category"
means type or group.
Petty people cannot perform gentlemanly conduct -
this isn't the petty person's fault,
so we should forgive and not blame them.
Why say this?
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān stated:
"Formerly, Guǎn Zhòng served as Qí's minister,
nine times assembled the feudal lords,
and unified the world.
Yet Confucius belittled him, saying:
'Guǎn Zhòng's capacity was small!'
Was this not because the Zhōu Dào had declined,
Duke Huán was worthy,
yet he didn't urge him to become a true king,
but only made him a hegemon?"
Discussion says:
Kuí, Lóng, Jì, and Qì
were aids to true kings;
Hú Yǎn and Jiù Fàn
were aids to hegemons.
Confucius stated:
"Without Guǎn Zhòng,
we'd be wearing hair loose and lapels left!"
This praises Guǎn Zhòng for having talent fit to aid a king.
Having talent fit to aid a king yet conducting hegemonic governance -
if not small capacity, then what?
From this we see,
Confucius classified Guǎn Zhòng with Kuí, Lóng, Jì, and Qì's group when judging his fault.
Yú Qīng persuaded King of Wèi
Yú Qīng persuaded Chūnshēn Jūn to attack Yān to secure his own fief,
but Chǔ's attack on Yān
required passing through Wèi.
Fearing Wèi wouldn't permit passage,
Yú Qīng persuaded Wèi's ruler for Chūnshēn Jūn to borrow the route. :
"Chǔ is indeed powerful,
matchless under heaven,
and now plans to attack Yān."
The King of Wèi said:
"Earlier you said 'matchless under heaven',
now you say 'plans to attack Yān' -
why?"
He replied:
"Now if we say a horse is strong, that's acceptable,
but if we say it can lift a thousand jūn, that's not so -
why?
Because a thousand jūn
is not within a horse's capacity.
Now saying Chǔ is powerful is acceptable,
but crossing Zhào and Wèi to wage war on Yān -
is that within Chǔ's capacity?"
From this we see,
Guǎn Zhòng nine times assembled the feudal lords,
unified the world,
yet Confucius belittled him;
the Chǔ people couldn't attack Yān,
yet Yú Qīng considered them powerful and matchless under heaven.
This isn't deceptive argument -
each spoke according to their category.
This cannot go unexamined.
Chapter 38: Circumstantial Momentum
In the world, there are noble individuals,
there are petty persons,
and there are rituals and courtesies.
These matters
do not necessarily stem from their inherent nature,
nor are they necessarily their consistent conduct;
they are all influenced by circumstances and trends.
How can this be explained?
Wénzǐ said:
"When people have surplus, they yield;
when they are in want, they contend.
Yielding gives rise to ritual and righteousness,
while contention leads to violence and chaos.
When goods are abundant, desires diminish;
when needs are met, strife ceases."
Discussion says:
Guǎnzǐ stated:
"When food and clothing are sufficient,
people understand honor and shame."
This illustrates yielding when there is surplus.
Hànshū records:
"When Hán Xìn was a commoner,
he was poor and lacked virtuous conduct,
and could not be recommended for official position.
Later, in Hànzhōng,
Xiāo Hé said to Emperor Gāozǔ:
'Hán Xìn is
a state scholar without equal.'" This illustrates contention when in want.
Therefore, Fùzǐ said:
"If Bóyí and Shūqí were given duties but provided meager salaries,
with parents starving before them,
and wives and children famished behind them,
few could maintain their integrity unshaken."
Huáinánzǐ states:
"A swimmer cannot save a drowning person
because their limbs are preoccupied with their own struggle;
a burning person cannot rescue others from fire
because their body is in pain.
In forests, firewood is not sold;
on lakes, fish are not vended
because there is abundance."
Thus, in times of order, even petty persons uphold righteousness,
and cannot be tempted by profit;
in times of chaos, even noble individuals turn to wickedness,
and punishments cannot restrain them.
Shènzǐ said:
"When Jié and Zhòu possessed the empire,
all within the four seas was in chaos.
Guān Lóngpáng and Prince Bǐgān did not participate in it,
yet it was called universal chaos
because the chaotic were numerous.
When Yáo and Shùn possessed the empire,
all within the four seas was well-governed,
and Dānzhū and Shāngjūn did not partake in it,
yet it was called universal order
because the orderly were numerous."
Hence, Zhuāngzǐ said:
"In the eras of Yáo and Shùn, there were no impoverished people under heaven,
not because wisdom was attained;
in the eras of Jié and Zhòu, there were no successful people under heaven,
not because wisdom was lost.
It was the appropriateness of the times and circumstances."
Xīnyǔ states:
"Lands near rivers are damp,
trees near mountains grow tall
because like influences like.
When the four great rivers flow east,
no hundred streams run west,
for the small follow the great and the few follow the many."
Thus it is known that the noble individuals of the world
may not truly be noble.
Discussion says:
Kuāng Héng stated:
"By adhering to rituals and showing respectful deference,
people do not contend;
by loving benevolence and delighting in charity,
the populace is not violent;
by exalting righteousness and high principles,
people are inspired to virtuous conduct;
by being tolerant, gentle, kind, and harmonious,
the masses love one another.
These four qualities
are how enlightened kings accomplish transformation without severity."
From this perspective,
the noble individuals of the world
are transformed by those above. .
The petty persons of the world,
may not truly be petty.
Discussion says:
Shàngshū records:
"In Yīn, none, great or small,
were not given to plunder and villainy.
Ministers and officials emulated one another,
obtaining nothing without transgressing norms."
This describes the late period of Yīn,
when ministers, officials, and noble individuals all acted unlawfully,
none finding the mean,
all following the transformation from above.
Hence, it is understood that the petty persons of the world
may not truly be petty. .
The rituals and courtesies of the world,
may not be true courtesy.
Discussion says:
Zuǒzhuàn records:
"Fàn Xuānzǐ loved yielding,
and his subordinates all yielded;
Luán Yǎn was domineering,
yet none dared oppose him.
Jìn state was thereby pacified,
and several generations relied on this,
a manifestation of goodness."
When Zhōu rose to power,
its odes said:
'Emulate King Wén,
and all states will trust you.'"
This is a manifestation of goodness.
When it declined,
its odes said:
'The great officers are unjust,
yet I alone toil with virtue.'"
Indicating a lack of yielding.
From this,
Luán Yǎn's yielding
was due to circumstances and trends.
Thus, it is known that the rituals and courtesies of the world
may not be true courtesy. .
Circumstances and trends
must not be left unexamined.
Discussion says:
Zhènglùn states:
"Even among those consistently wealthy,
or inherently pure in character,
not one in a hundred
can adapt to the changes of the world."
Therefore, it is understood that noble individuals and petty persons have no fixed essence,
as most are shaped by circumstances and trends.
Thirty-Nine: Disdain for Ritual
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Do not be disrespectful in ritual."
The Qūlǐ states:
"Be reverent in all things."
Yet the ancients used disrespect as a form of ritual,
what was the reason for this?
They wished to highlight others' virtue.
How can this be explained?
Long ago, Hóu Yíng served as gatekeeper of the Yí Gate in Dàliáng,
Lord Wèi heard of him,
and prepared a grand banquet.
When the guests were seated,
the lord took his carriage and retinue,
left the honored left seat empty,
and personally went to welcome Hóu Yíng at the Yí Gate.
Hóu Yíng led the lord through the market,
and upon arriving home,
was treated as an honored guest.
Hóu Yíng told the lord:
"Today, I have done enough for you.
I am but a lowly gatekeeper,
yet you personally troubled your carriage and retinue.
In the midst of a crowded public place,
it was improper to go out of your way,
yet you deliberately did so.
I wished to establish your reputation,
so I made you stand long with your carriage in the market,
to observe your reaction -
you grew even more respectful.
The market people all thought me petty,
while considering you a noble gentleman
capable of humbling yourself before scholars."
Earlier,
when the lord went to welcome Hóu Yíng,
Hóu said:
"I have a friend in the market butcher shop,
I wish you would trouble your carriage to visit him."
Hóu descended to see his friend Zhū Hài,
conversed with him,
while secretly observing the lord -
the lord's expression grew even more serene.
The market people all watched,
the retinue secretly cursed Hóu Yíng,
but Hóu saw the lord's expression never changed,
so he bid farewell and mounted the carriage.
When Zhāng Shìzhī stood at court,
with all the high ministers assembled,
the elder Wáng Shēng said:
'My socks have come loose.'
He then turned and asked Court Commandant Zhāng to tie them for him.
Someone asked Wáng Shēng:
"Why publicly humiliate Court Commandant Zhāng?"
Wáng replied:
"I am old and lowly,
and know I can be of no help to Court Commandant Zhāng.
Court Commandant Zhāng
is currently a famous minister in the land.
So I briefly humiliated him,
making him kneel to tie my socks,
wanting thereby to elevate his status."
When the officials heard this,
they admired Wáng Shēng and respected Court Commandant Zhāng more.
Jí Àn often treated the Grand General as an equal,
someone criticized him saying:
"Since the Son of Heaven often wants his ministers to defer to the Grand General,
you should not fail to bow."
Jí replied:
"If the Grand General has guests who merely bow with clasped hands,
wouldn't that actually make him more esteemed?"
When the Grand General heard this,
he thought even more highly of Jí Àn.
From this we can see
that using disrespect as ritual
can elevate others.
Discussion:
Lǎozǐ said:
"When the country falls into chaos, loyal ministers appear;
when the six relations are discordant, filial piety and compassion arise."
This means that loyal ministers and filial sons
reveal their integrity
precisely through discord and chaos.
Had Hóu Yíng not been disrespectful,
people wouldn't have known the lord could humble himself before scholars.
Had Wáng Shēng not been arrogant,
the high ministers wouldn't have known the Court Commandant could humble himself.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who are not good
are the material for the good."
How true this is!
Chapter Forty: Defining Concepts
Principles understood in the heart
cannot be expressed without words;
objects defined in the external world
cannot be distinguished without names.
If words fail to convey intentions,
there is no means for mutual understanding;
if names fail to distinguish objects,
then perception and judgment remain unclear.
Tracing their origin,
investigating their basis,
neither do objects possess inherent names, nor do principles have fixed designations.
To distinguish their essence,
different names are created;
to express one's intentions,
designations are established.
Hence they are designated as:
Dào, Dé, Rén, Yì, Lǐ, Zhì, Xìn.
Dào (the Way)
is what humans tread upon.
Knowing what to do while at rest,
knowing where to go while moving,
knowing what to rely on in affairs,
knowing where to stop in actions—
this is called Dào.
It is also said:
Dào
refers to what humans tread upon,
enabling all things not to lose their proper course.
Dé (Virtue)
is what humans attain.
Enabling everyone to obtain what they desire—
this is called Dé.
Rén (Benevolence)
is love.
Bringing benefit and eliminating harm,
loving universally without selfishness—
this is called Rén.
It is also said:
Rén
is what makes humans intimate,
having a heart of compassion and sympathy,
thus achieving growth and completion.
Yì (Righteousness)
is appropriateness.
Clarifying right and wrong,
establishing what can and cannot be done—
this is called Yì.
It is also said:
Yì
is what is appropriate for humans.
Rewarding good and punishing evil,
thereby achieving merit and establishing affairs.
Lǐ (Ritual)
is practice.
Advancing and retiring with measure,
honorable and humble having distinction—
this is called Lǐ.
It is also said:
Lǐ
is what humans practice,
rising early and retiring late,
to complete the order of the sovereign.
It is also said:
Establishing good and preventing evil—
this is called Lǐ.
Zhì (Wisdom)
is what humans know.
Determining the circumstances of gain and loss, right and wrong—
this is called Zhì.
Xìn (Trustworthiness)
is what humans uphold.
Issuing commands and decrees,
to unify people's hearts—
this is called Xìn.
Seeing the root and knowing the branches,
grasping one to respond to ten thousand—
this is called technique.
It is also said:
Wielding the power of life and death,
unblocking obstructed paths,
weighing the numbers of light and heavy,
discussing the ways of gain and loss,
making near and far, true and false, necessarily visible to the ruler—
this is called technique.
The "Shuō Yuàn" says:
"Following orders to benefit the ruler
is called obedience.
It is also said:
The ruler is correct and the minister follows—
this is called obedience.
Following orders to harm the ruler
is called flattery.
It is also said:
Should speak but not speak—
this is called concealment;
should remonstrate but not remonstrate—
this is called flattery.
It is also said:
The ruler is perverse and the minister follows—
this is called rebellion.
Opposing orders to benefit the ruler
is called loyalty.
It is also said:
Distributing wealth to others
is called generosity;
teaching others what is good
is called loyalty.
Xún Qīng said:
Covering the ruler with virtue and transforming him—
this is great loyalty;
harmonizing the ruler with virtue and supplementing him—
this is secondary loyalty;
admonishing against wrong with what is right and angering him—
this is inferior loyalty.
Opposing orders to harm the ruler
is called chaos.
It is also said:
Rewarding the meritless
is called chaos.
When the ruler has faults
that will endanger the state,
if one can fully speak to the ruler,
being employed then staying,
not employed then leaving—
this is called remonstrance;
being employed then acceptable,
not employed then dying—
this is called forceful remonstrance.
Leading the multitude to remonstrate with the ruler,
resolving the state's great calamities,
removing the state's great harms—
this is called assistance.
Resisting the ruler's commands,
opposing the ruler's actions,
securing the state in danger,
removing the ruler's disgrace—
this is called correction."
Thus remonstrance, forceful remonstrance, assistance, and correction
can be called ministers of the altars of soil and grain,
valued by enlightened rulers.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Advancing without regard
is called sycophancy.
Guiding words according to intention
is called flattery.
Speaking without choosing right or wrong
is called adulation.
Enjoying speaking of others' evils
is called slander.
Praising deceit and falsehood,
to ruin and vilify others,
is called concealment.
Not distinguishing good and bad,
accommodating both sides with smooth cheeks,
secretly extracting what one desires—
this is called treachery."
An ancient saying states:
"Using the possible to aid the impossible
is called harmony;
likes and dislikes not differing
is called sameness.
Replacing the worthy with the worthy
is called replacement;
replacing the worthy with the unworthy
is called usurpation.
Lax orders with urgent punishments
is called tyranny;
taking good for oneself
is called theft;
punishing without knowing faults
is called cruelty;
respect not conforming to ritual
is called rudeness;
prohibiting but not stopping
is called disobedience.
It is also said:
Respect not conforming to proper conduct
is called disobedience.
It is also said:
Ordering but not implementing
is called obstruction.
Prohibiting wrong and establishing right
is called law;
knowing good but not practicing it
is called recklessness;
knowing evil but not reforming
is called confusion."
Tài Gōng said:
"Collecting the world's pearls, jades, beautiful women, gold, silver, and colored silks
is called rapacity.
Employing cruel and oppressive officials,
killing innocent people,
not according to laws and measures,
is called villainy.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
The villain who severs friendships and alienates the new.
Xun Qing said:
Those who do not care about the ruler's honor or disgrace,
do not concern themselves with the state's good or ill,
but instead flatter and conform merely to secure their position,
maintaining their stipends and cultivating connections,
are traitors to the state.
When worthy men do not come,
it is called obstruction.
When loyal ministers do not come,
it is called blockage.
Pretending to accept someone while actually opposing them,
is called hypocrisy.
Not treating one's ministers with sincerity,
yet expecting them to serve oneself sincerely,
is called foolishness.
What is divided from the Way,
is called nature
— division means the beginning of becoming human.
What is formed into one,
is called destiny
— receiving the nature of yin and yang, hardness and softness,
hence it is said:
formed into one.
All humans encompass the nature of the five constants,
yet differ in hardness and softness, slowness and urgency, tones and voices,
which are tied to the qi of water and soil,
and this is called custom.
Liking and disliking, choosing and rejecting, action and stillness are not constant,
but follow the ruler's desires,
and this is called convention.
Someone asked:
"Are music and sound the same?"
The reply was:
"Formerly, Marquis Wèn of Wèi asked Zǐxià:
'When I dress formally and listen to ancient music,
I fear I might fall asleep;
but when I hear the sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
I do not know weariness.
May I ask why ancient music is like that,
and new music like this?'
Zǐxià said:
'What you are asking about now
is music.
What you enjoy
is sound.
Music and sound are close but not the same.'
Marquis Wèn said:
'May I ask how they differ?'
Zǐxià said:
'Ancient music
follows heaven and earth with the four seasons in order,
the people have virtue and the five grains flourish,
diseases and plagues do not arise, and there are no omens,
this is called great harmony.
Then the sages established the relationships of father and son, ruler and minister,
making them the guiding principles.
Once the principles are correct,
the world is greatly settled;
when the world is greatly settled,
then the six pitch standards are rectified and the five tones harmonized,
with strings, songs, poems, and hymns,
this is called virtuous sound,
and virtuous sound is what is called music.
The Book of Songs says:
"Vast is his virtuous sound,
his virtue can shine.
Able to shine and to categorize,
able to lead and to rule,
he kings this great state.
Able to follow and to compare,
comparing to King Wén.
His virtue knows no regret,
having received divine blessings,
they extend to his descendants."
This refers to it.
What you enjoy now,
is drowning sound!
The sound of Zhèng is excessive,
and confuses the will;
the sound of Sòng indulges women,
and drowns the will;
the sound of Wèi is hurried,
and troubles the will;
the sound of Qí is arrogant and eccentric,
and makes the will proud.
All four indulge in sensuality and harm virtue.
Therefore, they are not used in sacrifices.
This is the difference in music.'"
Dǒng Shēng said:
"In ancient times, before music was created,
they used the music of former kings that suited the time,
to deeply educate and transform people,
and only after achievements were made was music created.
It celebrated their virtue.
Thus, the lewd customs of the state airs are present in the pipes and strings."
The Book of Music says:
"Those who know sound but not tone
are birds and beasts;
those who know tone but not music
are the common people;
only the gentleman can know music.
Therefore,
examine sound to know tone,
examine tone to know music,
examine music to know correctness,
and the way of order is complete."
This again is the difference between sound and tone.
Someone asked:
"Tone and music,
we have heard explained.
May I ask if ceremony and ritual are the same?"
The reply was:
"Formerly, Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Tàishū about the ritual of bowing and yielding, and circumspect movement,
Tàishū said:
'That is ceremony,
not ritual.
I have heard from the late minister Zǐchǎn:
"Ritual
is the constant of heaven
— constant means
the regularity of the Way.
It is the principle of earth
— principle means
what is appropriate for benefit.
It is the conduct of the people
— conduct means
what humans practice."
The constants of heaven and earth,
the people indeed follow them.
They follow the brightness of heaven
— the sun, moon, stars, and constellations
are the brightness of heaven.
They accord with the nature of earth
— high and low, hard and soft
are the nature of earth.
They produce the six qi
— meaning yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
They use the five phases
— metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
The qi forms the five flavors
— sour, salty, pungent, sweet, and bitter,
manifests as the five colors
— blue, yellow, red, white, and black,
appearing in distinctions of right and wrong.
They are expressed as the five tones
— gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
Excess leads to confusion and disorder,
and the people lose their nature
— flavors, sounds, and colors,
in excess, harm nature.
Therefore,
ritual is created to uphold it
— establishing ritual to uphold their nature.
Humans have likes and dislikes, joy and anger, sorrow and pleasure,
born from the six qi
— these six
all receive the qi of yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
Therefore,
examine the principles and appropriate categories,
to regulate the six emotions
— creating ritual to regulate the six emotions of liking, disliking, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
so they do not exceed moderation.
Sorrow has weeping,
pleasure has song and dance,
joy has giving,
anger has fighting.
When sorrow and pleasure are not lost,
they can harmonize with the nature of heaven and earth,
thus enduring long
— through harmony.
Therefore, one who can bend and straighten to follow ritual
is called a complete person.'" Someone asked:
"Then what is called ceremony?"
The reply was:
"Nurturing the state's youth,
teaching them the six ceremonies:
the demeanor for sacrifices,
solemn and majestic;
the demeanor for guests,
respectful, careful, dignified, and solemn;
the demeanor at court,
orderly and measured;
the demeanor in mourning,
sorrowful and distressed
pronounced lèi,
顛,
pronounced tián).
The appearance of worry and contemplation. ；
The demeanor of military ranks,
resolute and stern.
Stern,
pronounced as è.
The manner of commands and orders. ；
The bearing of chariots and horses,
swift and orderly.
These are the variations in ritual and propriety.
The flaw in defining names
lies in splitting hairs and dissecting words.
Splitting,
pronounced as pìmì fǎn. 。
If such flaws are absent,
then the subtlety of defining names is achieved. 」
It is discussed:
Bān Gù's nine schools,
the ninth being the Eclectic School,
combining Confucianism and Mohism,
uniting the School of Names and Legalism.
Fùzǐ's nine categories,
the ninth being miscellaneous talents,
used for extensive remonstration and discussion.
From this perspective,
the benefits of eclectic theories
have existed for a long time.
Hence, this piece is written,
to establish principles and narrate events,
for the future gentlemen and military affairs.
Master Zhào said:
"The Book of Songs says, 'Truly civil and truly martial,'
the Book of Documents praises, 'Both martial and civil.'"
Confucius said:
"A gentleman engaged in civil affairs
must have military preparedness."
The Commentary states:
"Heaven produced the five materials,
and the people use them all;
none can be dispensed with—
who can eliminate the military?"
Huángdì battled Chīyóu,
Zhuānxū contended with Gònggōng,
Yáo attacked Huāndōu,
Shùn campaigned against the Yǒumiáo,
Qǐ fought the Yǒuhù,
Tāng conquered the Xià,
King Wén attacked Chóng,
King Wǔ overthrew Zhòu,
Hàn Gāozǔ had the battles of Jīngsuǒ,
Guāngwǔ raised the army at Kūnyáng,
Wèi mobilized forces at Guāndù,
Jìn launched the campaign to pacify Wú.
Thus, the Annals of Lü Buwei states:
"The sage kings have armies of benevolence and righteousness,
but they do not abandon arms."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"To abolish the unrighteous and bestow upon the virtuous."
From this, it is clear that establishing authority and hegemony—
how could it be achieved without this!
Since ancient times, military texts have numbered nearly a thousand;
if one does not understand integration and adaptation,
what use is having many?
Therefore, it is said:
Less brings attainment,
more leads to confusion.
Hence, the essence is summarized in creating "Military Authority."
Now, weapons are
instruments of calamity.
Warfare is
a perilous affair.
The battlefield of armed conflict,
is the place where corpses lie;
it is only as a last resort that the sovereign employs it.
Whenever in the heavens there are white clouds like a bolt of cloth spanning from Chǒu to Wèi,
there will be much warfare in the land,
and if they are red, it is especially severe.
Sometimes there are clouds like a bolt of cloth covering the sky,
or clouds resembling Hú people arrayed in battle formation,
all indicating widespread warfare in the land.
Sometimes on a Rénzǐ day, when looking out in all four directions there are no clouds,
yet alone one sees red clouds like banners unfurled,
then armed uprisings will occur across the land.
If they spread throughout the four directions,
then the whole land will be embroiled in war.
Or if when looking out in all four directions there are no clouds,
but alone one sees black clouds reaching across the sky,
this too means armed uprisings will occur in the land,
but if within three days there is rain,
the disaster will be averted.
Sometimes there are strikingly vivid red clouds;
in the region where they are seen,
great warfare will arise.
Whenever there are white clouds like the robes of immortals,
countless and interconnected,
as if troops are chasing one another,
ceasing and then rising again,
there will be warfare spanning a thousand lǐ.
Or if there are clouds like men holding knives and shields,
this is the qi of violent troops.
Sometimes there are white clouds six zhàng wide,
stretching east to west across the sky;
this too indicates the rise of warfare.
If they are blue,
it signifies a great mourning.
Therefore it is said:
To rescue from chaos and punish the violent,
is called righteous troops;
troops that are righteous will rule.
When an enemy attacks us,
and we have no choice but to use them,
it is called responding troops;
responding troops will be victorious.
To contend over petty grievances,
unable to overcome furious anger,
is called忿 troops;
忿 troops will be defeated.
To covet others' land, treasures, and goods,
is called greedy troops;
greedy troops will be crushed.
To rely on the state's greatness,
boast of its numerous people,
and desire to display power before the enemy,
is called arrogant troops;
arrogant troops will be destroyed.
Now, to suppress violence and rescue from chaos,
is called righteous troops,
and can be subdued by propriety;
to rely on numbers to attack,
is called strong troops,
and can be subdued by humility;
to raise an army out of anger,
is called rigid troops,
and can be subdued by rhetoric;
to abandon propriety and covet profit,
is called violent troops,
and can be subdued by deception;
when the state is in peril and the people exhausted,
yet to initiate actions and mobilize the masses,
is called rebellious troops,
and can be subdued by strategy.
Thus we know that when the sage employs troops,
it is not because he delights in it,
but rather to punish the violent and quell chaos.
To use righteousness to punish the unrighteous,
is like releasing the waters of a river to douse a firefly's glow,
or standing at the edge of an unfathomable abyss and intending to push it over—
victory is certain.
Why then must one be serene and detached?
To avoid further harm to people and things.
Hence it is said:
"When distant people are not submissive,
then cultivate civil virtue to attract them."
If they do not come through virtue,
only then order the general to lead the army out.
Now, the general is
the support of the state,
the arbiter of human fate.
Therefore it is said:
If a general does not understand warfare,
he is handing his ruler over to the enemy;
if a ruler does not choose his general well,
he is handing his state over to the enemy.
Once the general understands warfare,
and the ruler has chosen his general,
the Son of Heaven sits in the main hall and summons him, saying:
"The safety or peril of the state
rests entirely with the general.
Now, such-and-such a state is insubordinate;
I wish to trouble the general to respond to it."
Then he orders the Grand Historian to perform divination and select an auspicious day,
and confers upon him the axe and yuè.
The ruler enters the ancestral temple,
stands facing west,
while the general stands facing north.
The ruler personally grasps the yuè,
holds its head,
and presents its handle, saying:
"From this upward to the heavens,
the general controls it."
Then he again takes the handle,
and presents the blade, saying:
"From this downward to the abyss,
the general controls it."
Once the general has received his mandate,
he bows and replies:
"Your servant has heard:
A state cannot be governed from outside,
an army cannot be commanded from within the court.
A divided heart cannot serve its ruler,
a doubtful will cannot respond to the enemy.
Since your servant has received the mandate,
and exclusively holds the authority of the axe and yuè,
I dare not return them."
Then he takes his leave and departs,
breaking through the Gate of Ill Omen as he goes out.
Hence the "Sīmǎ Fǎ" says:
"Advance and retreat only according to the situation,
without referring to the sovereign."
Sūnzǐ says:
"When the general is with the army,
the sovereign's commands may not always be accepted."
An ancient saying goes:
"Inside the threshold,
the sovereign controls it;
outside the threshold,
the general controls it."
The "Hànshū" says:
"Only the general's orders are heard,
not the Son of Heaven's edicts."
Thus we know that assembling the army and gathering the masses,
lies outside the threshold;
entrusted with the responsibility of pushing the chariot's axle,
one bears the weight of the command staff.
With no heaven above,
no earth below,
no enemy in front,
no sovereign behind,
only then can great achievements be accomplished.
Therefore it is said:
"When the general is capable and the sovereign does not interfere, there is victory,"
this is what it means.
When a king leads an army,
he must select and train outstanding talents,
understand the capabilities of his officers,
and assign positions according to their abilities.
Each should utilize their strengths
to serve as his limbs and wings,
thereby establishing majestic authority,
after which all affairs will be accomplished.
One trusted strategist
is responsible for advising on plans and responding to emergencies,
assessing celestial signs to avert disasters,
overseeing strategic planning,
and ensuring the state's security and preservation.
Five tacticians
manage the state's safety and perils,
anticipating unforeseen events,
evaluating talents and skills,
clarifying rewards and punishments,
appointing officials,
resolving doubts,
and determining what is feasible.
Three astronomers
specialize in observing stars and calendars,
monitoring wind and weather,
managing timing,
verifying omens,
examining disasters and anomalies,
and discerning the will of Heaven.
Three geographers
oversee army movements and halts,
analyzing terrain advantages and disadvantages,
distances and difficulties,
droughts and mountain barriers,
ensuring no errors in geographical understanding.
Nine military strategists
discuss variations and similarities in tactics,
analyze successes and failures of operations,
drill with weapons,
and oversee all battlefield formations,
rectifying any irregularities.
Four quartermasters
manage ample provisions,
secret stockpiling,
securing supply routes,
procuring grains,
ensuring the army never faces food shortages.
Four vanguard officers
select skilled warriors,
train troops and horses,
lead swift as wind and lightning strikes,
never losing direction,
serving as elite forces.
Three signal officers
manage drums, flags, tallies, and orders,
moving swiftly back and forth,
appearing and disappearing like spirits.
Four work officers
erect banners and poles,
handle heavy and difficult tasks,
dig trenches,
build fortifications,
and maintain defenses all around.
Three versatile aides
rectify oversights and correct errors, organize meetings, and handle techniques,
circulating widely and gathering intelligence,
receiving guests,
engaging in discussions,
resolving disputes and untying knots.
Three deception specialists
devise unusual and deceptive schemes,
beyond ordinary comprehension,
executing endless variations.
Seven intelligence gatherers
travel to listen and gather information,
observe events in all directions,
exposing truth and falsehood in the army,
daily presenting findings.
Five morale officers
boost military prestige,
inspire the troops,
brave difficulties in fierce attacks,
making the army courageous.
Four propagandists
spread reputation,
shake distant and near,
influence all borders,
weakening enemy morale.
Eight scouts
observe signs and omens,
monitor openings and closings,
and spy on enemy plans.
Two occultists
practice deception,
invoking ghosts and spirits,
to confuse the enemy.
Two accountants
manage army logistics,
overseeing supplies and resources.
Two physicians
prepare medicines,
to heal the wounded and sick.
In the army:
Those with great courage, willing to die, or delighting in wounds
are grouped into a unit
named the Blade-Bravers.
Those with vigorous spirit, robust bravery, or fierce strength
are grouped into a unit
named the Formation-Breakers.
Those trained in unconventional and conventional tactics, long swords, and carved bows,
marching in step and aligned ranks,
are grouped into a unit
named the Sharp Cavalry.
Those who can break barriers and straighten hooks,
fierce and strong,
shattering gongs and drums,
destroying banners and flags,
are grouped into a unit
named the Mighty Warriors.
Those who can leap high and far,
light-footed and swift runners,
are grouped into a unit
named the Vanguard Troops.
Those who are former ministers of fallen kings,
seeking to restore their merits,
are grouped into a unit
named the Death-Duelers.
Those with death sentences,
or brothers seeking revenge for their commanders,
are grouped into a unit
named the Death-Resenters.
Those who are poor and angry,
wanting to vent their frustrations,
are grouped into a unit
named the Certain-Death Troops.
Those who are former son-in-laws sent as hostages,
seeking to clear their names and gain fame,
are grouped into a unit
named the Hardship-Endurers.
Those with eloquent speech and cunning words,
skilled in slander and praise,
are grouped into a unit
named the Spies and Rumor-Spreaders to Weaken the Enemy.
Those who are former convicts pardoned,
wanting to escape their shame,
are grouped into a unit
named the Opportunistic Troops.
Those with exceptional skills,
able to carry heavy loads for hundreds of miles,
are grouped into a unit
named the Awaiting-Orders Troops.
If the troops are strong but the general weak,
it is called slackness;
if the officers are strong but the troops weak,
it is called collapse;
if the army lacks a vanguard,
it is called defeat.
This is an inevitable principle.
Hence it is said:
"Which side has stronger military forces?
Which side has better-trained soldiers?"
"Those who know this will win,
those who do not will not win."
This cannot be neglected.
Tàigōng said:
"When deploying troops for campaign,
setting up camps and arranging formations,
take six as the standard."
The six,
refers to six hundred paces,
or alternatively sixty paces,
depending on what suits the terrain and the troops,
placing markers for the twelve celestial branches.
The general should position himself above the Jiǔtiān
Qīnglóng is also considered Jiǔtiān,
if considering where to station or rest,
reside under the Yùzhàng,
generally the three celestial branches preceding the month branch are Yùzhàng,
for instance, the Sì position in the first month is such.
After a full ten-day period,
again relocate and open the main gate,
always turning one's back to Jiàn and facing Pò
not facing Tàisuì or Tàiyīn,
do not drink from stagnant water,
do not camp on deadly terrain,
do not occupy Dìzhù,
do not reside in Dìyù,
avoid Tiānzào,
do not position at Lóngshǒu.
Stagnant water means
water that does not flow;
deadly terrain refers to
areas among mounds and tombs;
Dìzhù means
high ground within low areas;
Dìyù refers to
low ground within high areas;
Tiānzào is
the mouth of a valley;
Lóngshǒu means
the summit of a mountain.
Hence it is said:
Whenever establishing a camp or arranging a formation,
the general resides at Qīnglóng,
the army drums at Féngxīng,
soldiers at Míngtáng,
ambushes hidden at Tàiyīn,
the army gate at Tiānmén,
junior officers at Dìhù,
executions at Tiānyù,
judgments at Tiāntíng,
army provisions at Tiānláo,
military equipment at Tiāncáng.
This is called modeling heaven in establishing camps,
so that nothing can harm them.
For example, in the Jiǎzǐ cycle,
Zǐ is Qīnglóng,
Chǒu is Féngxīng,
Yín is Míngtáng,
Mǎo is Tàiyīn,

Sì is Dìhù,
Wǔ is Tiānyù,
Wèi is Tiāntíng,
Shēn is Tiānláo,
Yǒu is Tiāncáng.

Hài is Féngxīng,
Zǐ is Míngtáng,
Chǒu is Tàiyīn,

Mǎo is Dìhù,
Chén is Tiānyù,
Sì is Tiāntíng,
Wǔ is Tiānláo,
Wèi is Tiāncáng.

There are three situations where troops should not be deployed:
if there is discord in the state,
do not deploy the army;
if there is discord within the army,
do not deploy the formation;
if there is discord within the formation,
do not engage in battle.
Hence Sūnzǐ said:
The first is the Way.
The Way
means making the people share the same will as their superiors.
Thus they can face death together,
and share life together,
without fearing danger.
Danger
means doubt.
This means if the ruler has consistently shown benevolence to his subjects,
then the soldiers can advance to meet the enemy,
thus sharing difficulties of survival or demise,
without fearing the risk of defeat.
Like during the siege of Jìnyáng,
where stoves sank and frogs bred,
yet the people did not betray or doubt.
Huángshí Gōng said:
"Before the army's well is reached,
the general does not speak of thirst;
before the army's tents are set up,
the general does not speak of fatigue.
In winter, he does not wear fur;
in summer, he does not use a fan.
This is called a courteous general.
Sharing safety
and danger with them,
his troops can be united but not divided,
can be used but not exhausted."
Treat them with courtesy,
encourage them with words
—inspiring soldiers with words about facing danger and sacrificing life,
then the soldiers will die for him.
Thus, by enduring hardship and inquiring after the sick,
the King of Yuè dominated among the feudal lords;
by sucking pus and caring for his soldiers,
Wú Qǐ surpassed the enemy states.
Mourning at Yángmén,
he defeated the armies of the Three Jìn;
pouring a single cup of wine into the river,
he moved the entire army's soldiers.
The brave fight for him,
the wise worry for him.
Viewing death as returning home,
without a second thought in their plans,
it is because he has consistently nurtured them with kindness,
and his strategies are harmonious and unified.
Therefore it is said:
"Accumulate kindness unceasingly,
and with one, you gain ten thousand."
As the saying goes:
"If you ceaselessly accumulate kindness,
you can command the whole world."
This is the essence of the Way and its virtue.
Sūnzǐ said:
"If soldiers are not yet devoted and close to you when you punish them,
they will not submit,
and if they do not submit, they are difficult to employ.
If soldiers are already devoted and close to you, yet punishments are not enforced,
then they cannot be used.
Therefore it is said:
Regard soldiers as infants,
then you can lead them into deep ravines;
regard soldiers as beloved sons,
then you can dwell with them in fatal terrain.
But if you are generous yet cannot employ them,
loving yet cannot command them,
and they become disorderly without knowing discipline,
