they are like spoiled children,
and cannot be used."
The Classic says:
"In war, rewards serve as the exterior,
punishments as the interior."
It also says:
"Command them with civility
—civility being kindness—
and align them with martiality
—martiality being law—
this is called certain victory."
Thus, Wǔhóu's military prohibitions numbered seven.
Sūnzǐ said:
"Suspension without law,
orders without governance."
The Simǎ Fǎ says:
"Make oaths when facing the enemy,
grant rewards when observing achievements—
these are for times of urgent encirclement,
when normal regulations cannot be applied."
When managing military affairs against an enemy state,
maneuvering across the wilds,
the essential principles and key points
must be predetermined:
First is negligence,
second is slowness,
third is theft,
fourth is deception,
fifth is betrayal,
sixth is disorder,
seventh is error—
these are the prohibitions in governing the army.
If one fails to arrive at the appointed meeting,
does not advance upon hearing the drum,
lingers freely taking advantage of leniency,
avoids duties and halts efforts,
starts close but later stays distant,
does not respond when called by name,
lacks complete armor,
or has unready weapons—
this is called 'negligent army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
Receiving orders but not transmitting them,
transmitting them inaccurately,
thereby confusing officers and soldiers;
not hearing the gongs and drums,
not seeing the flags and banners—
this is called 'sluggish army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
Not distributing food provisions,
not deploying troops by unit,
unequal distribution of rewards,
favoritism towards close associates,
taking others' belongings,
not repaying debts,
seizing others' heads
to claim merit and fame—
this is called 'thieving army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
Changing names,
wearing unclean clothes,
incomplete gongs and drums,
unsharpened blades,
unsteady weapons,
arrows without fletching,
bows without strings;
officers and soldiers
disobeying laws and orders—
this is called 'deceptive army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
Not advancing upon hearing the drum,
not stopping upon hearing the gong,
not crouching when the flag is lowered,
not rising when the flag is raised,
not following commands,
hiding behind while avoiding the front,
disrupting formations when advancing,
weakening the force of weapons,
retreating without fighting;
wavering left or right,
carrying the wounded and dead,
using this as pretext to return—
this is called 'betraying army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
When the army marches,
soldards scrambling ahead,
in chaotic confusion,
cavalry and troops intermingling,
blocking the roads,
hindering those behind,
shouting and clamoring,
making commands inaudible,
breaking formation and order,
injuring with weapons,
senior officers failing to manage,
chaos among ranks—
this is called 'disorderly army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
When encamped,
inquiring about hometowns,
sticking closely together,
eating together for mutual protection,
not responding to summons,
entering others' positions,
disrupting the order,
unable to be restrained;
entering and leaving camp beyond limits,
not using the gates,
not reporting;
knowing of treacherous acts
but not reporting,
sharing equal guilt;
sharing meals together,
accepting private favors,
spreading alarming rumors,
confusing officers and soldiers—
this is called 'erring army.'
Those with such offenses
shall be executed.
After executions are carried out,
all matters will be in order.
Thus, when a fellow villager stole a bamboo hat,
Lǚ Méng first wept then executed him.
When a horse trampled wheat,
Cáo Gōng cut his hair as self-punishment.
Therefore, Tàigōng said:
"Punishments reach the highest,
rewards extend to the lowest."
Sūnzǐ said:
"Whose laws and orders are implemented?
Whose rewards and punishments are clear?
Through this, I know victory."
This is what it means.
Confucius said:
"To fail to train people for warfare
is to abandon them."
Hence it is known that if soldiers are not well-trained,
their daily drills are not perfected,
their front attacks while their rear disintegrates,
and they fail to follow the sounds of bells and drums,
then a hundred of them cannot match one enemy
- this is what abandoning them means.
Therefore, when commanding the three armies
and training them for warfare,
there must be bells, drums, and binding orders
to unify the soldiers.
Train them in weapon handling, daily drills,
and the changing signals of banners and flags.
Thus, train one person in warfare,
and when trained, combine him with ten others.
Train ten in warfare,
and when trained, combine them with a hundred.
Gradually build up to the multitude of three armies.
The method of major warfare
involves organizing battle formations
each with its own principle.
The left formation is the Green Dragon,
the right formation is the White Tiger,
the front formation is the Vermilion Bird,
the rear formation is the Black Tortoise,
the central formation is Xuānyuán.
Where the great general positions himself,
spears are on the right and halberds on the left,
shields in front and crossbows behind,
with drums and flags in the center,
all rising and moving together.
Hear the drum - advance;
hear the gong - halt.
Follow his directional commands,
and the five formations are properly arranged.
The method of the five formations
takes drums and flags as essential.
One drumbeat raising the blue flag
forms the curved formation;
two drumbeats raising the red flag
forms the sharp formation;
three drumbeats raising the yellow flag
forms the circular formation;
four drumbeats raising the white flag
forms the square formation;
five drumbeats raising the black flag
forms the straight formation.
The curved formation
corresponds to wood;
the sharp formation
corresponds to fire;
the circular formation
corresponds to earth;
the square formation
corresponds to metal;
the straight formation
corresponds to water.
These five elemental formations
cyclically generate each other,
determining victory or defeat.
The method for organizing the five formations
requires mutual protection in fives,
five men form one leader's unit,
five leaders form one division,
five divisions form one command,
five commands form one regiment,
five regiments form one brigade,
five brigades form one legion,
five legions form one army -
then preparations are complete.
The efficiency of troops
lies in understanding organization.
The short carry banners and flags,
the brave carry gongs and drums,
the weak handle supplies and logistics,
the wise serve as strategists.
Neighbors support each other,
maintaining mutual protection in fives.
First drum - stand ready;
second drum - take meal;
third drum - prepare equipment;
fourth drum - form ranks.
Listen carefully to orders,
then raise flags and deploy troops,
following where the command banners direct.
Therefore it is said:
"Governing many is like governing few -
it is a matter of organization.
Units and divisions create organization,
squads and teams create numbers."
"Fighting with many is like fighting with few -
it is a matter of signals.
Banners and flags are the visible signals,
gongs and drums are the audible signals."
When voices cannot be heard,
drums and bells are used;
when vision is obstructed,
banners and flags are used.
Gongs, drums, banners and flags
unify the senses of the troops.
Night battles多用torches and drums,
day battles多用banners and flags
to adapt to human perception.
Thus we know that drums and gongs
command the ears;
banners and flags
command the eyes;
prohibitions and punishments
The ears commanded by sound
must hear clearly;
the eyes commanded by sight
must see distinctly;
the heart commanded by punishment
must feel sternness.
If these three are not established,
even victory will turn to defeat.
Therefore it is said:
"Where the general points,
all follow and move;
where the general directs,
all advance to death."
In chaotic turmoil,
fight disordered yet remain ordered;
in confused chaos,
form circles yet remain unbroken -
this is the method of employing multitudes.
When soldiers are well-trained
and equipment is sharp,
the general then grasps the command staff to address the troops
Yǒuyú shì gave warnings at court,
Xiàhòu shì made oaths in camp,
Yīn made oaths outside the camp gates.
Zhōu made oaths when blades were about to cross -
though the oath locations differed,
I follow Zhōu,
making this oath:
"Alas!
Under the vast heaven,
all is the king's land;
within the sea's boundaries,
all are the king's subjects.
Now a certain state insults the five elements
and abandons the three fundamentals,
compelling our multitudes
to reverently execute heaven's punishment.
Those who obey orders
will be rewarded without delay;
those who hesitate or retreat
will be executed on the spot.
Life, death, wealth, and honor
rest on this single action.
O you numerous officers,
each strive with all your hearts!"
Thereupon morale soars to the clouds,
and even charging into boiling water or walking through fire
becomes possible.
This is the method of training for warfare.
Sūnzǐ said:
"The second is celestial timing.
Celestial timing refers to
yin and yang, cold and heat,
governed by seasonal rhythms."
The "Sīmǎ Fǎ" states:
"Do not raise armies in winter or summer,
so as to extend care to our people."
Tàigōng said:
"Three specialists in astronomy,
take charge of observing winds and atmospheres,
understanding the inclinations of heaven's intent."
Hence the "Classic" says:
"Those who know the three births,
face blades without fear,
follow solitude to strike emptiness,
one woman equals five men."
Thus, in marching the army, one must turn away from the Great Yin and face the Great Yang,
observe the radiance of the five planets,
watch the eclipses of the two luminaries,
with Tàibái (Venus) as the primary reference,
and Chénxīng (Mercury) as the indicator.
When they conjoin,
it signals a time for inevitable battle;
when they oppose,
it reveals a situation for avoiding combat.
Avoid days of solar depletion,
turn away from lunar punishments.
Strike with royal force against exhaustion,
with vitality against demise,
thus knowing the way of employing heaven,
executing punishments in accord with heaven,
is not a matter of a single day.
If a fine rain bathes the army,
facing opportunity will surely bring victory;
if contrary winds clash,
the path back will be fruitless.
Clouds resembling a flock of sheep,
foretell a route of flight;
an aura like startled deer,
signals a situation of certain defeat.
Black clouds emerging from the fortress,
red vapors approaching the army,
winds rising from six directions of extremity,
fogs arising from three punishments,
all these presage seeing the army depart but not return.
If it looks like smoke but is not smoke,
this is auspicious cloud;
if it looks like a star but is not a star,
this is a returning anomaly;
if it looks like fog but is not fog,
this is the army's lament;
if it sounds like thunder but is not thunder,
this is heaven's drum.
When auspicious cloud parts,
there is virtue;
with a returning anomaly,
there are surrendering men;
with the army's lament,
many generals will be slain;
with heaven's drum,
many armies will be defeated.
Thus, the practice of divining winds and clouds,
and observing the signs of years and months,
has a long history.
Therefore, when appointing a new general in ancient times,
at the initial erection of the command flag upon departure,
they would invariably observe the signs of wind and cloud.
In all plans for military affairs,
campaigns in all directions,
mobilizing troops and moving masses,
avoid great winds, thunderstorms, and rain,
and gloom that obscures the sun.
The hours of Chén, Wǔ, Yǒu, and Hài,
are days of self-punishment.
The command flag,
is the essence of the general.
Whenever erecting the command flag,
it must be on a controlling day.
A controlling day
means the upper overcomes the lower.
Upon first establishing the command gate,
offer a sacrifice and say:
"The two polarities have their norms,
the four seas have their king,
precious mandate lies with heaven,
worldly virtue shines ever brighter.
Petty and vicious rebels,
dare to plot against constant order,
the Son of Heaven commands me,
wielding the battle-axe to lead the campaign.
Thus I marshal my forces,
to punish those disloyal.
Heaven's way aids the compliant,
spirits and gods harm the...
May the vicious wretches be timely annihilated,
and the borders swiftly cleansed.
With blades unstained by blood,
triumphantly return to the capital.
Divine aura increases in radiance,
eternally witnessing this accomplishment.
Truly relying on uprightness,
and all the spirits' power,
urgently as the statutes command."
Generally, when vapor first appears like steam from a cauldron,
vigorously rising upward,
vapor accumulates into fog,
fog is yin,
yin energy congeals into rainbows,
halos, and similar phenomena.
If vapor does not accumulate or congeal,
but scatters aimlessly,
it cannot cause disaster.
It must mix with lethal energy,
rising swiftly and densely,
to be significant.
In discussing divination,
often observe at dawn, late afternoon, and sunrise/sunset times;
if there is wind or rain within the period,
the disaster will not materialize.
If the wind does not blow fiercely from the sides,
flags and banners appear haloed,
lifting smoothly with the wind,
or facing the enemy all day,
then the army's advance will achieve merit,
a sign of victory.
If the energy above the enemy army resembles trees on a mountain slope,
do not engage in battle;
if above our army, great victory.
If resembling flames,
also great victory.
If white energy above the enemy flutters like a tower,
edged with red vapor,
their troops are strong, do not attack;
if above our army, certain great victory.
If the enemy's energy is yellow-white, thick, moist, and heavy,
do not fight.
If clouds spread like three bolts of silk,
the march of the main army before and after will be favorable.
From a distance, if clouds above the army resemble fighting cocks,
with red and white following each other,
they have celestial aid in their energy,
do not attack.
When two armies face each other,
if energy above like a snake,
raising its head toward the enemy,
will surely triumph in battle.
If five-colored energy above the military camp,
connects to the sky,
this is an army responding to heaven,
do not attack.
If red-yellow energy reaches the sky,
also do not assault.
If clouds resemble the sun and moon,
with red vapor encircling them,
like a solar halo,
and glowing,
the location where seen will achieve great victory,
do not attack.
If energy above the enemy is shaped like a mouth,
their army cannot be attacked.
These are all victorious energies.
If adverse winds respond,
energy flares sideways,
the flagpole breaks,
gloom obscures the sun,
banners whip violently,
these are signs of defeat.
If cloud energy comes from the enemy's direction,
lasting all day without cease,
the army should not advance,
advancing would be不利.
If wind and energy come together,
this is a sign of defeat,
requiring urgent attack.
If the enemy's energy color resembles horse liver,
or like dead ashes,
or similar to a toppled canopy,
all are signs of defeat.
If black energy like a collapsing mountain,
falls upon the army,
the army will surely be defeated.
If energy above the army appears dimly,
illuminating people through the night,
then military affairs will be scattered and chaotic.
If the army's energy halves,
one break means one defeat,
a second break means another defeat.
If white emerges in the east,
the disaster is deep.
If five-colored energy above the army is disorderly,
shifting unpredictably east, west, north, south,
the army is about to be defeated.
If red energy above the army blazes, descending from the sky,
the general will die, the troops will be in chaos.
If black energy above the army takes the form of oxen or horses,
descending from the mist into the army gradually,
It is called the celestial dog descending to feed on blood,
signifying a defeated army.
If there are clouds covering the path, obscuring daylight into darkness,
one should abandon cooking before the food is even done,
and leave urgently,
as these are all signs of defeat.
If subordinates disrespect their general,
supernatural occurrences arise simultaneously,
and rumors spread confusion among the masses,
one must cultivate virtue and clarify orders,
sharpen weapons and armor,
diligently pledge sincerity to the troops,
to avoid heaven's wrath.
Then, select an auspicious day again,
sacrifice to the banner,
prepare offerings of the grand sacrifice,
resound with the sounds of drums and bells,
sincerely pray and request,
to prepare for heaven's inquiry,
observe its auspicious responses,
and thereby predict good or ill fortune.
If the men and horses are joyful and leaping,
banners and flags all point forward to high hills,
the sound of metal bells is clear and rising,
the war drums' rhythm is smooth and resonant,
this indicates receiving divine assistance,
which can be used to calm the hearts of the multitude,
making it feasible to employ.
Although it is said that appointing the virtuous and employing the capable
brings success without divination;
with clear commands and thorough laws,
plans succeed without consulting the oracle;
enfeoffing merit and rewarding toil,
blessings follow without prayer;
sharing hardships and joys alike,
even facing adversity leads to accomplishment.
Yet, adapting to circumstances and applying strategies,
there are five types of assistance:
first, assistance in planning,
second, assistance in momentum,
third, assistance for the timid,
fourth, assistance in doubt,
fifth, assistance from terrain.
These five aspects
are methods to aid victory.
Hence the saying:
"Know the earth and know the heaven,
then victory can be complete."
This must be carefully examined.
Master Sūn said:
"The third is terrain advantage.
Terrain advantage refers to
distance (far and near), difficulty (dangerous and easy), scope (wide and narrow), and condition (fatal and viable).
Therefore, those who do not know the forms of mountains and forests, perilous obstacles, and marshy swamps
cannot march an army;
without using local guides,
they cannot gain terrain advantage.
Thus, in employing troops:
there are scattering ground, light ground, contentious ground, intersecting ground, thoroughfare ground, heavy ground, treacherous ground, encircled ground, and fatal ground—
the names of the nine grounds.
When feudal lords fight in their own territory,
it is scattering ground.
Fighting on land within their borders,
the soldiers' minds are not focused,
and they have a tendency to disperse on their own.
Therefore, the Classic says:
'In scattering ground,
I will unify their will.'
Entering enemy territory but not deeply is
light ground.
Having entered enemy land not deeply,
the soldiers' minds are not yet steadfast,
and they are prone to flee lightly.
Hence, the Classic says:
'In light ground,
I will keep them continuous.'
Ground that if I obtain is advantageous,
and if the enemy obtains is also advantageous,
is contentious ground.
It allows the few to defeat the many, the weak to overcome the strong,
meaning mountain passes and narrow openings that offer the advantage of natural defenses,
contested by both sides.
Therefore, the Classic says:
'In contentious ground,
I will hasten to its rear.'
Where I can go,
and the enemy can come,
is intersecting ground.
Roads cross and interlace there,
with multiple paths on level ground,
allowing free movement and communication,
impossible to block entirely.
Thus, the Classic says:
'In intersecting ground,
I will strengthen my alliances.'
The territory of a feudal lord bordered by three states,
where I face the enemy
and there are other states nearby,
and whoever arrives first gains the support of the masses under heaven,
is thoroughfare ground.
Arriving there first,
one can win over the masses of the feudal lords as allies.
Therefore, the Classic says:
'In thoroughfare ground,
I will consolidate my defenses.'
Entering deep into enemy territory that is difficult to return from,
with many cities and towns behind,
is heavy ground.
Having left one's own city walls far behind,
penetrating deep into enemy land,
requires single-minded focus,
hence it is called heavy ground.
Thus, the Classic says:
'In heavy ground,
I will ensure a continuous supply of provisions.'
Traveling through mountains and forests, perilous obstacles, and marshy swamps—
any terrain that is difficult to traverse—
is treacherous ground.
Treacherous means
waterlogged, boggy land.
Therefore, the Classic says:
'In treacherous ground,
I will press on along the routes.'
Where the entrance is narrow,
and the return route is circuitous,
so that a small enemy force can attack our large one,
is encircled ground.
The intended entry point is dangerously narrow,
and the way back is long;
prolonged stay leads to exhaustion of supplies,
hence the enemy can attack our large force with a small one—
this is encircled ground.
Thus, the Classic says:
'In encircled ground,
I will block the gaps.'
Where a swift battle brings survival,
and delay means destruction,
is fatal ground.
With high mountains in front,
and great waters behind,
advancement is impossible,
retreat is obstructed,
and supplies are cut off,
so it is fatal ground.
Those in fatal ground
should act while the soldiers are still well-fed,
strengthening their resolve for a desperate fight,
so they can face death together.
Therefore, the Classic says:
'In fatal ground,
I will show them there is no way out.'
Thus,
in scattering ground, do not engage
because the soldiers are concerned about home,
they cannot be fought.
In light ground, do not stop
as you have entered enemy territory shallowly,
the troops' will is not yet firm,
they should not encounter the enemy;
instead, solidify their resolve.
In contentious ground, do not attack
from multiple directions;
one must first secure the terrain advantage.
If the enemy has taken the ground first,
do not attack it.
In intersecting ground, do not become isolated
but maintain connectivity.
In intersecting ground,
both sides can advance or retreat;
do not let your forces be cut off.
In thoroughfare ground, form alliances
to gain support from feudal lords.
One should establish ties with the feudal lords.
In heavy ground, plunder
to store up provisions.
Having penetrated deeply,
with the soldiers steadfast,
one can seize goods and supplies.
In treacherous ground, keep moving
and do not halt.
In encircled ground, devise stratagems
to counter the enemy's plans.
Then, one must employ clever and deceptive tactics
to escape danger.
In fatal ground, fight
with a desperate struggle.
Before the battle, motivate them by saying:
'Do not worry about foolishness or stupidity;
if the use of troops is not clear,
and we end up in a trapped and desperate situation,
it adds to the worries of the officers,
and it is all the general's fault.
Today's matter
hinges on this one action.
If we do not exert our strength,
our bodies will fatten the wild grasses,
eaten by insects and beasts,
with no one to seek out our wives and children;
if we overcome, we gain personal glory,
with rewards and emoluments awaiting—
can we not strive hard?'"
Additionally, there are six types of terrain:
accessible,
entangling,
stalemated,
constricted,
precipitous,
and distant—
the names of the six terrains.
Where I can go,
and the enemy can come,
is called accessible.
This means both sides are on flat or hilly ground,
with easy movement back and forth.
When occupying accessible terrain,
first take the high and sunny positions,
secure supply routes,
and then fighting will be advantageous.
It is better to impose on the enemy
than be imposed upon.
Having first occupied high ground,
deploy troops to guard the return routes,
preventing the enemy from cutting off your supply lines.
Where one can go
but finds it hard to return,
is called entangling.
Entangling means
being hooked or entangled.
In entangling terrain, it is said:
if the enemy is unprepared,
sally forth and defeat them;
if the enemy is prepared,
sallying forth will not lead to victory,
and it will be difficult to return,
Unfavorable.
When the enemy is unprepared and we launch an attack,
victory is possible;
if they are prepared,
and we cannot achieve victory,
then it is difficult to retreat safely. .
If our attack is unfavorable,
and the enemy's attack is also unfavorable,
it is called a stalemate
stalemate,
meaning prolonged.
Neither side benefits from a prolonged standoff. .
Regarding the stalemate terrain, it is said:
Even if the enemy tempts us,
we should not advance,
but instead lure them away;
wait until the enemy is halfway out and then strike them,
favorable.
Those who tempt us,
feign retreat to lure us,
do not pursue them,
wait for them to advance and then strike,
thus they can be defeated. .
Regarding the narrow terrain, it is said:
If we occupy it first,
we must fully deploy our forces to await the enemy
fully deploy,
meaning to fill.
Deploy troops to fill the narrow passage,
preventing the enemy from advancing or retreating. ;
If the enemy occupies it first,
do not follow if they are fully deployed,
but if they are not fully deployed, then follow them
Narrow terrain refers to
a valley between two mountains.
If the enemy is enraged,
their momentum will not spare us.
Occupying it,
we must array troops at the narrow entrance,
and defend it with unexpected tactics.
If the enemy has already occupied this place and arrayed at the entrance,
do not follow.
If they are only halfway deployed in the narrow passage,
then engage the enemy,
as this is advantageous. .
Regarding the hazardous terrain, it is said:
If we occupy it first,
we must take the high ground facing the sun to await the enemy
Occupying high ground facing the sun,
to wait for the enemy.
If the enemy approaches from the shaded low ground,
strike them,
and victory is assured. ;
If the enemy occupies it first,
then lure them away and leave,
do not follow them
In hazardous terrain,
one must not be forced into by the enemy. .
As for distant terrain,
with equal conditions,
it is difficult to provoke battle,
and unfavorable
Provoke,
means to approach the enemy.
Distant terrain,
means far from one's own state.
With equal conditions,
neither side has a unique advantage,
initiating battle first,
is unfavorable. .
All these six points,
are principles of terrain.
They are the utmost responsibility of a general,
and must not be overlooked.
Hence it is said:
Dense and overgrown grass
is for concealing retreat;
deep valleys and hazardous obstacles
are for stopping chariots and cavalry;
narrow passes and forested mountains
are for the few to attack the many
the few can attack the enemy by night;
marshes and obscure places
are for hiding one's form.
A ditch fifteen feet wide,
water that submerges chariots
submerge,
means to soak.
Pronounced as "zī lián fǎn". ,
mountain forests and rocky paths,
rivers and hills
rivers,
refer to flowing streams. ,
where grasses and trees are present,
these are lands for infantry,
where chariots and cavalry are worth less than half.
Rolling hills interconnected
interconnected,
means linked and extended;
connect,
means continuous,
pronounced as "zhī yù fǎn". ,
open plains and vast fields,
these are lands for chariots and cavalry,
where infantry are worth less than one-tenth.
Plains that are distant
distant,
means separated. ,
high ground overlooking below,
these are lands for bows and crossbows,
where short weapons are worth less than one-tenth.
When two formations are close,
on flat ground with short grass,
allowing advance and retreat,
these are lands for long halberds,
where swords and shields are worth less than one-third.
Reeds, bamboo, and tall grass
tall grass,
means weeds. ,
where vegetation is dense,
and forest leaves thickly intertwined,
these are lands for spears and lances,
where long halberds are worth less than half.
Winding paths with ambushes,
and dangerous narrow passes,
these are lands for swords and shields,
where bows and crossbows are worth less than one-third.
Therefore, it is said:
"Terrain is
an aid to the military."
It is also said:
"In the art of using troops,
terrain advantage is a treasure."
Zhào Shē rushed to the mountain,
leading to the defeat of the Qín army;
Hán Xìn deployed with his back to the river,
enabling the Hàn troops to achieve victory.
This is the strategy of utilizing terrain advantage.
The Classic states:
"Using water to assist an attack makes one strong,
using fire to assist an attack makes one brilliant."
From this we know that water and fire are
aids to warfare.
Thus, there are five types of fire attack:
The first is called firing personnel
—ignite the grass near the enemy,
and burn them by leveraging the wind. ,
The second is called firing provisions
—burn their accumulated stores,
the third is called firing baggage
—burn their heavy equipment and supplies,
the fourth is called firing arsenals
—one should send spies into the enemy camp,
to burn their weapon stores. ,
The fifth is called firing with projectiles
—projectiles
mean to drop.
It is to drop fire into the enemy camp.
The method of fire-headed arrows,
is to fill iron with fire,
attach it to arrowheads,
and shoot them into the enemy camp with powerful crossbows,
to burn and cut off their supply routes. .
Executing fire attacks must have a basis
—the basis is having covert agents,
and fire-making materials must always be prepared.
Launching fire has its appropriate season,
and igniting fire has its specific days.
The season refers to
when the weather is dry;
the days refer to
when the moon lodges in the constellations Jī, Bì, Shēn, and Zhěn,
for all these four constellations are
days when wind rises.
Xiāo Shìchéng said:
"On the Bǐng-Dīng days in spring, Wù-Jǐ days in summer, Rén-Guǐ days in autumn, and Jiǎ-Yǐ days in winter,
there will be fierce winds and heavy rain on these days.
Residing and examining the Tàiyǐ,
within it are the ten essences of flying birds,
indicating the periods of wind and rain,
the cyclical movement of the five elements,
each awaiting its time,
when fire can be used."
Hence it is said:
"Using fire to assist an attack makes one brilliant."
Why is this said?
In the past, Yáng Shān met with rebels in Guìyáng,
Shān made large bellows from leather,
placed lime inside them,
set them on carts,
created fire tunnels,
tied them to horses' tails,
and then from the upwind direction,
pumped the bellows to blow the lime,
blinding the crowd of rebels,
then set fire to the horses' tails,
sending them charging into the rebel formation,
causing the rebels to flee and collapse—
this is the momentum of using fire.
When Yīn Hǎo campaigned north,
his chief secretary Jiāng Yóu took several hundred chickens,
connected them with long ropes,
and tied fire to their feet.
Releasing them all at once,
the flock of chickens flew scattered into the Qiāng camp,
setting the entire camp ablaze,
whereupon he attacked,
and Yáo Xiāng retreated and fled—
this is the momentum of using fire.
Lǐ Líng was in the marshes amid grass,
when the enemy set fire from upwind;
Líng set fire from downwind,
using this fire to counteract the fire's momentum.
I have heard that if the enemy burns the gate,
fearing the fire might go out and the gate open,
one should pile more firewood to feed the fire,
ensuring the fire does not die out—
this is also a method to counteract fire.
Tàigōng said:
"Strong crossbows and long weapons
are for crossing waters to fight."
Sūnzǐ said:
"Water can be used to cut off."
This means flooding a city.
He also said:
"When crossing water,
one must stay far from the water
to lure the enemy into crossing.
If the enemy crosses the water to approach,
confront them within the water,
striking when they are half across—
this is advantageous.
If intending to fight,
do not cling to the water to receive the enemy,"
referring to troops positioned on the water."
Hence it is said:
"Using water to assist an attack makes one strong."
Why is this said?
In the past, Hán Xìn secured Línzī and drove out King Tián Guǎng of Qí,
and Chǔ sent Lóng Qiě to rescue Qí.
King Guǎng of Qí and Lóng Qiě combined their armies,
engaging Xìn in battle.
Someone advised Lóng Qiě, saying:
"The Hàn troops fight desperately from afar,
their vanguard is unstoppable,
while Qí and Chǔ fight on their own territory,
where soldiers are prone to defeat and dispersion.
It would be better to fortify deeply,
and have the King of Qí send his trusted ministers
to recruit the lost cities.
When the cities hear their king is present
and Chǔ has come to rescue,
they will surely turn against Hàn.
With the Hàn troops residing as guests two thousand miles away,
and all Qí cities rebelling,
their situation will leave them with no means to obtain food—
they could surrender without a fight."
Lóng Qiě said:
"I have always known Hán Xìn's character,
he is easy to deal with.
Moreover, to subdue him without fighting—
what achievement would I have?"
Thus, he engaged in battle
and was defeated.
I have heard:
"Those known in ancient times as skilled in warfare prevail,
while those who seek easy victories are defeated.
The victories of the skilled
bring no fame,
no brave feats.
Thus, their triumphs are not martial;
not being martial means
their victories are secured
over those already defeated."
Lóng Qiě did not heed his advisor's plan,
seeking instead glorious achievements—
how foolish! .
At the Wéi River
(pronounced wéi)
battle formation,
Hán Xìn had men make over ten thousand sacks overnight,
filled them with sand to block the river upstream,
led his troops halfway across,
attacked Lóng Qiě,
feigned defeat,
and retreated.
Lóng Qiě indeed rejoiced, saying:
"I knew Xìn was timid!"
He pursued Xìn across the river,
whereupon Xìn had the sandbags breached,
and a great flood came down.
Most of Lóng Qiě's army could not cross back,
and Xìn immediately pressed a fierce attack,
killing Lóng Qiě.
Lóng Qiě's naval forces scattered and fled east.
This is the counter to the 'half-crossing' tactic.
I have heard the art of war states:
When crossing water,
one must stay far from it.
Strike the enemy when they are half across—
it is advantageous.
Hán Xìn half-crossed,
his army feigned entering perilous ground,
luring Lóng Qiě to attack,
then breached the dammed water.
This is what is called:
"Mix with advantages and tasks can be accomplished divinely,
mix with harms and calamities can be resolved."
Both reversed the military principles to apply the art of war.
Subtle indeed!
Subtle indeed!
Lú Wǎn assisted Péng Yuè in attack,
capturing over ten cities in Liáng territory.
Xiàng Yǔ heard of this,
and told his Grand Marshal Cáo Jiù:
"Guard Chénggāo carefully;
even if Hán challenges,
do not engage them in battle."
Hán indeed provoked the Chǔ army,
but the Chǔ army did not emerge,
so they sent men to insult them.
Sūnzǐ said:
"If he is principled,
he can be insulted."
The Grand Marshal grew angry,
crossed the Fàn River
(pronounced fán),
and when his troops were half across,
Hán struck,
routing them utterly.
This illustrates the principle of not clinging to the water when intending to fight.
Thus, we understand the variations in using water and fire,
It has long been possible to secure victory,
a practice with ancient origins.
The Qín people poisoned the upper reaches of the Jīng River,
causing many Jìn troops to perish;
the King of Jīng burned the stockpiles of Chǔ,
leading to Xiàng Yǔ's capture;
Cáo Gōng diverted the Sì River at Xiàpī,
resulting in Lǚ Bù's execution;
Huáng Gài employed fire attack at Chìbì,
forcing Wèi's founder (Cáo Cāo) to flee in defeat.
This is the utmost responsibility of a commander,
and indeed among the most critical matters in warfare,
which must not be overlooked.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"Those who travel through the state spreading intelligence
are counter-spies."
Lǚ Wàng said:
"Spies,
who fabricate flying rumors,
are gathered into one unit."
This shows the way of using spies
did not begin in a single day.
Whenever there are white vapors moving in groups,
lingering and forming arrays approaching,
it means people from other states are coming with plotting intentions;
one should not engage them,
but observe where they go,
follow and attack them,
then victory can be achieved.
If there is black vapor hovering over our army,
moving like cart wheels,
it means the enemy has penetrated deeply,
plotting to corrupt our state's ministers.
If there is black vapor drifting,
containing five colors within,
hovering over our army,
the enemy must be planning to ally with various lords to attack our state;
when the lords turn their plots against the army,
the army will defeat itself.
If there is black vapor like a banner,
emerging from the camp,
black above and yellow below,
the enemy wishes to come seeking battle.
They lack sincerity,
their words and trustworthiness contradict each other;
within nine days this will surely be discovered,
prepare against it,
for good fortune.
If the sun and moon are overcast and dark,
without light yet not raining,
or if for ten days and nights the sun and moon cannot be seen,
this is called 'obscuration',
indicating ministers plotting against the ruler.
Therefore it is said:
Prolonged overcast without rain,
means ministers plot against the ruler.
Thus there are five types of spies:
there are local spies,
inside spies,
counter-spies,
living spies,
and dead spies.
When all five types of spies are activated,
none can know their methods.
Local spies
are those employed from among the local villagers.
This means people from the enemy's villages and towns,
who know the enemy's external and internal weaknesses and strengths,
can be used to wait upon and listen observe,
convey messages and deliver statements.
Therefore it is said:
In employing them,
rewards and emoluments come first.
Inside spies
are those employed from among the officials.
They utilize those who have lost their positions,
such as descendants of executed criminals or punished families.
Taking advantage of their grievances,
approach and employ them.
Counter-spies
are those who turn the enemy's spies to our use.
Duke Cáo said:
"When enemy spies come to observe us,
we know of them.
Then with generous bribes and promises,
we turn them into our spies,
hence called counter-spies."
Xiāo Shìchéng said:
"When the enemy sends people to observe us,
we pretend not to know and show them false information,
advancing and retreating at scheduled times,
making them return and report to each other,
hence called counter-spies."
Living spies
are those who return to report.
Select those among us with talent, wisdom, and strategy,
able to establish connections with the enemy's relatives and nobles,
observe their movements,
learn their plans and actions,
after knowing the actual situation,
return to report,
hence called living spies.
Dead spies
are those who carry out deceptive operations externally,
making our spies aware of them,
then waiting for the enemy's spies.
Creating false deceptive operations externally,
pretending to leak them.
Making our spies aware of them.
When our spies go among the enemy,
if captured by the enemy,
they will certainly report the false information to the enemy;
the enemy then prepares accordingly,
but our actual operations differ,
thus the spies will die.
Also,
another explanation:
enemy spies come into the camp,
learn our false information and take it back,
yet none of it matches our actual plans.
Neither spy can know the hidden truth,
hence called dead spies.
Xiāo Shìchéng said:
"Captured enemies or our own soldiers with serious crimes imprisoned,
deliberately pardoned,
instructed not to泄露,
yet pretending not to be secretive,
allowing the prisoners to overhear secretly.
Then treat them leniently,
making them escape;
escaping they must return to the enemy,
reporting what they heard;
the enemy will surely believe them,
and they will go without suspicion.
Thus dead spies achieve their purpose."
In former times, Bān Chāo, Protector-General of the Western Regions in Hàn,
initially as Chief Clerk Leading Troops,
mobilized all states' infantry and cavalry totaling twenty-five thousand to attack Shāchē,
Shāchē sought help from Qiūcí.
The King of Qiūcí sent his Left General to mobilize troops from Wēnsù, Gūmò, and Wèitóu,
totaling fifty thousand men to assist.
Bān Chāo summoned his officers and the kings of Yútián and Shūlè to discuss, saying:
"With few troops we cannot oppose them,
the plan is for all to disband and leave.
Yútián goes east from here,
the Chief Clerk also goes west from here.
At midnight, upon hearing drumbeats, depart immediately."
All thought this reasonable.
Then he secretly loosened control of a captured informant,
the informant returned,
reporting Bān Chāo's words to Qiūcí.
Qiūcí heard this,
rejoiced,
sent the Left General with ten thousand cavalry to intercept Bān Chāo at the western border,
and the King of Wēnsù with eight thousand cavalry to intercept the King of Yútián at the eastern border.
After everyone had settled,
Bān Chāo secretly ordered his various marshals,
to prepare troops and encourage officers.
At cockcrow,
they raced to the Shāchē army camp,
surprised and overran it,
the Hú all fled in panic,
five thousand heads were taken,
and Shāchē surrendered.
Also,
Gěng Yǎn campaigned against Zhāng Bù,
Bù heard of this,
then sent his general Fèi Yì to station troops at Lìxià,
and divided forces to garrison Zhù'ā,
separately setting up several dozen camps at Tàishān Zhōngchéng to await Yǎn.
Previously, Liú Bèi went east and engaged Sūn Quán in battle,
Wèi Wéndì heard that Bèi had built connecting camps over seven hundred lǐ,
and told his ministers:
"Bèi does not understand military authority;
how can a seven-hundred-lǐ camp resist the enemy?
Encircling plains, marshes, and dangerous terrain to station an army
leads to capture by the enemy;
this is a military taboo."
Seven days later,
news arrived that Quán had defeated Bèi.
Now Zhāng Bù arrays several dozen camps,
unable to support each other in emergencies.
Once one army collapses,
the morale of all becomes hard to maintain.
This is why Qíng Bù fled from the King of Jīng.
Bù's plan is unwise,
his defeat is appropriate.
Yǎn crossed the river,
first attacked Zhù'ā,
and captured it,
deliberately leaving one corner of the siege open,
allowing its troops to flee to Zhōngchéng.
The people of Zhōngchéng, hearing Zhù'ā had fallen,
were greatly terrified,
and abandoned their walls to flee.
Master Sūn said:
"The three armies' morale can be seized,
the general's resolve can be shaken."
Gěng Yǎn opening the siege at Zhù'ā,
letting its troops flee to Zhōngchéng,
to terrify them,
was also a stratagem of seizing morale and shaking resolve.
How brilliant!
Fèi Yì sent his brother Gǎn to guard Jùlǐ separately,
Yǎn advanced his troops,
First, he threatened Jùlǐ,
cut down many trees,
and spread word of filling in the moats.
After a few days, there were defectors
who reported that the city had heard Gǎn intended to attack Jùlǐ,
and they planned to send reinforcements.
Gǎn then strictly ordered his troops to hasten the preparation of siege equipment,
declaring they would fully assault Jùlǐ in three days.
Secretly, he released captives,
allowing them to escape back,
and the returnees informed the enemy commander of Gǎn's planned date.
On that day, the enemy commander indeed personally led troops to rescue it,
and Gǎn joyfully told his generals:
"The reason I prepared the siege tools
was to lure the enemy commander here.
Now that he has come,
it is exactly what I sought."
Immediately, he assigned three thousand men to guard Jùlǐ,
while he led elite troops to position on the hillside,
engaging the enemy from high ground in a combined battle,
crushing them decisively,
and beheading the enemy commander in the fray.
Someone once asked Sūnzǐ:
"If the enemy is numerous and well-organized,
and about to advance,
how should we respond?"
He replied:
"First seize what they cherish,
and they will become compliant."
He also said:
"A skilled warrior
dictates to the enemy and is not dictated by them."
Gǎn's spreading word of attacking Jùlǐ
was also seizing what they cherished,
a strategy to make them come of their own accord.
This exemplifies the use of exploiting opportunities through intelligence.
During the Jìn dynasty,
Yìzhōu's governor Luó Shàng sent Wěi Bó to attack Lǐ Xióng at Píchéng,
with alternating victories and defeats.
Lǐ Xióng then recruited Pǔ Tài from Wǔdū,
had him whipped until he bled,
and sent him to deceive Luó Shàng,
pretending to be an insider
using fire as a signal.
Shàng believed him,
dispatched all his elite troops,
and sent Wěi Bó and others to follow Tài.
Lǐ Xióng had previously ordered Lǐ Xiāng to set an ambush along the route,
and Tài propped a long ladder against the city wall and lit a fire.
When Bó's troops saw the fire rise,
they all scrambled up the ladder.
Tài then used a rope to haul up over a hundred of Shàng's soldiers,
and beheaded them all.
Xióng then unleashed his forces,
attacking from inside and out,
and routed Shàng's army completely.
This exemplifies the use of an inside agent.
Duke Wǔ of Zhèng wanted to attack Hú,
so he first married his daughter to the ruler of Hú.
Then he asked his ministers:
"I wish to launch a military campaign;
whom should we attack?"
The senior official Guān Qīsī said:
"Hú can be attacked."
Duke Wǔ feigned anger and executed him, declaring:
"Hú
is a brotherly state to us.
Why would you suggest attacking it?"
The ruler of Hú heard of this,
believed Zhèng was friendly and left his defenses unprepared.
Zhèng launched a surprise attack on Hú,
and conquered it.
The Hàn envoy Lìshēng persuaded King Tián Héng of Qí,
leading Héng to stand down his troops
and feast with Lìshēng.
The Hàn general Hán Xìn took advantage of their unpreparedness,
attacked Qí,
and defeated them.
Tián Héng had Lìshēng boiled alive,
and Lìshēng unwittingly became Hán Xìn's sacrificed spy.
When Táng's Lǐ Jìng attacked the Xiōngnú,
he sent Táng Jiǎn first to discuss peace,
then used his troops to strike while they were off guard,
defeating them.
This is Lǐ Jìng using Táng Jiǎn as a sacrificed spy.
This exemplifies the use of a sacrificed spy.
Chén Píng used gold to carry out counter-espionage in the Chǔ army,
sowing discord against Fàn Zēng,
and the King of Chǔ grew suspicious of him.
This is the use of counter-espionage.
The details are recorded in the Annals of the Hegemon.
Thus it is known:
In the army, none are closer than spies,
rewards none greater than for spies,
affairs none more secret than those of spies.
Only the sagacious and wise can employ spies,
and only through meticulous subtlety can one grasp the truth of espionage.
This is crucial to the army,
and only a worthy general pays it due attention.
The "Wàn Jī Lùn" states:
"Even with a million-strong army,
the act of vanquishing the enemy in the moment
lies with the general."
Wǔ Zǐ says:
"When people discuss generals,
they often judge them by courage alone.
But courage for a general
is merely one part in ten thousand."
Thus, the "Liù Tāo" states:
"If the general is not benevolent,
the three armies will not be close;
if the general is not courageous,
the three armies will not be moved to action."
Sūn Zǐ says:
"A general must possess
courage, wisdom, benevolence, trustworthiness, and resolve."
With courage,
he cannot be transgressed;
with wisdom,
he cannot be thrown into chaos;
with benevolence,
he loves others;
with trustworthiness,
he does not deceive others;
with resolve,
he has no second thoughts.
These are what are called the 'Five Talents'."
The multitude of the three armies,
the million-strong host,
the arrangement of priorities,
rests on one person,
which is called the 'opportunity of morale'.
Precipitous paths and narrow roads,
famous mountains and great passes,
guarded by ten men,
can hold back a thousand,
this is called the 'opportunity of terrain'.
Skilled in using spies,
dividing the enemy's forces,
causing ruler and ministers to resent each other,
this is called the 'opportunity of affairs'.
Sturdy chariots and sharp boats,
well-trained soldiers and horses,
this is called the 'opportunity of strength'.
These are what are called the 'Four Opportunities'."
A general should be made joyful, not worried,
plans should be profound, not doubtful.
If the general worries, internal doubts arise
if the general shows a worried expression,
then inside and outside become mutually suspicious.
Hence it is said there is no trust.
If plans are doubted, the enemy state becomes emboldened
much doubt leads to confused strategies,
confusion allows the enemy state to exert its might.
Launching campaigns with this
can only lead to chaos."
Therefore, a general
must be able to be pure,
able to be tranquil
purity means incorruptible with wealth,
tranquility means not causing disturbances.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Heavy is the root of light,
tranquil is the master of restless."
Able to be impartial,
able to be orderly,
able to accept advice,
able to hear cases,
able to recruit talent
accepting the worthy from among the multitude of heroes,
such as Yuè recruiting Fàn Lí or Qí recruiting Nìng Qì.
Able to gather good counsel,
able to know the customs of states,
able to map mountains and rivers,
able to assess difficulties
dangers, hardships, and obstacles,
all must be clearly understood.
Able to control military authority.
Those in peril, secure them;
those fearful, reassure them;
those who rebel, win them back
if some generals leave due to disagreements,
comfort and persuade them to return,
like Xiāo Hé pursuing Hán Xìn.
Those wronged, vindicate them;
those with complaints, investigate them;
those humble, honor them
soldiers suffering from low status,
elevate them.
As in the past when Wú Qǐ shared food and clothing with his soldiers.
The strong, restrain them;
the defiant, crush them
among the lowly, there are base ones,
who oppose the noble,
disrupting the rites of hierarchy,
crush and kill them.
The greedy, enrich them
hang rewards to satisfy their hearts,
thus utilizing the greedy.
The desirous, employ them
when facing the enemy about to battle,
some desire to achieve merit and fame,
some desire profit from the enemy,
permit and employ them all,
this is what is called using the brave and using the greedy.
The fearful, conceal them
soldiers who have fears,
shelter them in the rear,
do not let them be the vanguard,
for army defeat stems from vanguard timidity.
The strategic, keep them close;
the slanderous, verify them
if there are slanderous disputes,
verify before trusting.
The demoted, restore them
those whose offices were ruined and dismissed,
repair and reinstate them.
The rebellious, depose them;
the arrogant, humble them;
the submissive, spare them
those who confess their crimes first,
spare them.
The surrendering, release them
release means
to let go.
Those capturing cities, reward them
to honor meritorious officials,
those seizing lands, grant them
to bestow upon the honored achievers,
those conquering states, appoint them to guard
upon gaining a state,
must enfeoff the worthy to guard it.
As in the past when Wú attacked Yuè,
captured but did not guard it,
thus ultimately failed.
Seize strategic points and secure them,
seize difficult positions and garrison them,
seize wealth and distribute it.
When the enemy moves, observe them;
when the enemy is strong, yield to them
if the enemy formation is strong, yield,
do not engage in battle.
As when the Qí army attacked Lǔ,
they drummed,
but Cáo Guì did not move.
After three drum rolls,
he defeated Qí,
by yielding first.
When the enemy arrogantly presses, bide time
if the enemy's imposing momentum advances upon us,
should hold firm and wait,
do not engage in battle.
As when Chǔ pressured Hàn,
seeking a decisive battle,
Hàn's founder, knowing his weakness,
did not consent,
this is the case.
When the enemy is brutal, pacify your own
if the enemy acts with brutality,
then pacify and encourage your troops,
so as to enrage our masses.
As when Yān attacked Qí, Tián Dān,
not surrendering,
the Yān army dug up Qí graves,
Tián Dān pacified and encouraged his people.
When the enemy acts recklessly, respond with righteousness
if the enemy engages in violent disorder,
then respond with righteousness to counter them,
they are reckless, we are righteous,
thus overcome them.
When the enemy is harmonious, divide them;
with righteous action,挫之
acting rightly to挫 the rebellious,
exploit the situation to defeat them,
spread rumors to exaggerate
disseminating exaggerated slanders,
to deceive and mislead the enemy,
to anger one's own troops. ,
with a four-sided net to ensnare them.
This is the way of being a general.
Thus if a general rejects advice,
then heroes will disperse;
if strategies are not followed,
then strategists will rebel;
if good and evil are treated alike,
then meritorious officials will become weary
if rewards and punishments are not clear,
and good and evil are not distinguished,
then all ministers with achievements will slacken and tire. .
If a general is self-centered,
then subordinates will blame him
being self-centered and self-reliant,
not consulting with subordinates,
all will attribute faults to the general and hold him accountable. ;
if a general boasts of his own merits,
then subordinates achieve little
zāng (good),
means good.
If the general claims credit for achievements,
forgetting his subordinates and being self-serving,
thus it is said they achieve little. ;
if a general listens to slander,
then subordinates will have divided loyalties;
if a general is greedy for wealth,
then corruption cannot be prevented
if those above are greedy,
then those below will steal. ;
if a general is inwardly preoccupied,
then soldiers will become licentious
inwardly preoccupied,
means thinking of wives and concubines. .
If a general has one of these,
then the masses will not submit;
if he has two,
then the army will have no discipline
shì,
means law. ;
if he has three,
then the army will rebel;
if he has four,
then disaster will reach the state.
The "Military Records" say:
a general's plans should be secret,
the troops should be unified
the general and troops as one body,
attacks on the enemy should be swift.
If the general's plans are secret,
then treacherous intentions are blocked;
if the troops are unified,
then all hearts are bound together
bound as one;
if attacks on the enemy are swift,
then deceit cannot be set up.
If an army has these three,
then its strategies cannot be thwarted.
If the general's plans are leaked,
then the army loses its advantage;
if outsiders spy on internal affairs,
then disaster cannot be controlled
kuī,
means to see.
If plans are leaked,
then outsiders see the reality of one's situation,
and the disaster cannot be controlled. ;
if wealth enters the camp,
then all sorts of corruption will gather
whenever in the military,
allowing outsiders to bring goods and wealth into the camp,
then corrupt schemes will secretly gather at its heart. .
If a general has these three,
the army will surely be defeated.
If a general lacks foresight,
then strategists will leave
if the general lacks foresight,
he cannot follow advice,
so they leave. ;
if a general lacks courage,
then officers and soldiers will fear
if the general is timid,
then subordinates have nothing to rely on,
so they fear. ;
if a general vents his anger,
then the soldiers will be afraid.
Foresight,
strategy,
are what a general values;
courage,
anger,
are what a general uses with intent.
Thus it is said:
one who is determined to die,
can be killed;
one who clings to life,
can be worried;
one who is quick-tempered,
can be insulted;
one who is honest and clean,
can be shamed;
one who loves people,
can be troubled.
These five,
are faults of a general,
disasters in employing troops.
Therefore, the key to all warfare,
is first to assess the enemy general and observe his talents.
By applying methods and using authority accordingly,
then without toil, success will arise.
If the general is foolish and trusts others,
he can be deceived with schemes;
if he is greedy and neglects reputation,
he can be bribed with goods;
if he is prone to change,
he can be wearied and trapped;
if the superiors are wealthy and arrogant,
and the subordinates poor and rebellious,
they can be divided and estranged;
if the general is negligent and soldiers slack,
they can be secretly attacked.
One who is wise but slow-minded,
can be pressured;
one who is brave and reckless with death,
can be provoked;
one who is impatient and hasty,
can be lured;
one who is greedy and fond of profit,
can be ambushed or bribed.
One who is benevolent and cannot bear to harm others,
can be wearied;
one who is trustworthy and easily believes others,
can be deceived;
one who is honest and clean but does not love others,
can be insulted;
one who is resolute and self-reliant,
can be served to manipulate;
one who is cowardly and likes to be used by others,
can be made to be deceived.
These are all essentials in employing troops,
the strategies for being a general.
When two states engage in warfare,
with armies meeting and weapons crossing,
deciding matters in the fog of war,
one must first investigate the enemy's situation.
Thus Sunzi said:
"The victorious army first secures victory and then fights."
He also said:
"By pondering, we understand the plans for gain and loss;
by observing, we comprehend the principles of movement and stillness."
Adapting to circumstances to achieve victory visible to all,
this is the essence of employing troops.
If one wishes to first know the enemy commander,
one should order low-ranking but courageous soldiers
to lead light and sharp troops to confront them.
Observe the enemy's approach:
their movements and halts,
if their administration is orderly.
When pursuing retreating forces,
they pretend not to catch up;
when seeing advantages,
they feign ignorance.
Such a commander
must be intelligent—
do not engage them lightly in battle.
Generally, if the enemy's upper energy is yellow-white and glossy,
the commander possesses authority and virtue.
If energy rises from the army,
gradually spreading like clouds,
transforming into mountain shapes,
the commander has deep stratagems.
If the enemy has energy black outside and red inside appearing ahead,
the commander is elite and fierce—
all such should not be attacked.
Generally, when energy connects upward to the sky,
the army has worthy and capable commanders.
When energy resembles dragons or tigers amid slaughter,
or takes the form of fire and smoke,
or appears like flames,
or resembles mountains and forests,
or looks like dust,
with large heads but low positions,
or when energy is purplish-black,
like towers over gates,
or like boiling white powder,
these are all signs of fierce commanders' energy.
If their troops are noisy with disordered flags,
soldiers stopping and moving arbitrarily,
formations sometimes vertical, sometimes horizontal,
pursuing retreating forces fearfully as if unable to catch up,
seeing advantages fearfully as if unable to obtain them—
such a commander
must lack strategy;
even with numerous troops, they can be captured.
Generally, if the enemy's upper energy is blue and scattered,
the commander is cowardly and weak.
Large in front but small behind
indicates the commander's nature is unclear.
Therefore it is said:
When the enemy is near yet quiet,
they rely on their terrain's advantage;
when distant yet provocative,
they want us to advance;
when trees move,
troops are coming;
when grass has many obstacles,
it's a ruse.
Dense grass with many obstructions
means they will surely flee,
fearing our pursuit,
creating many barriers
to make us suspect ambushes within.
Birds rising
signals ambush.
Generally, when army energy appears turbid, round, and long
with red energy within,
or energy like red pestles in black clouds,
there are ambushes below.
If two armies face each other
with red energy before, behind, left, or right of the army,
there are ambushes—
guard according to where the energy appears.
Some clouds appear twisted and continuous—
this indicates cavalry ambushes.
Clouds like spread mats—
this indicates infantry ambushes.
Clouds resembling mountains outside—
these are ambushes,
requiring careful examination.
Birds startled—
means surprise attack;
dust low and widespread—
infantry approaching;
scattered and streaking far—
firewood gatherers coming;
little dust moving back and forth—
camp-building troops.
Little—
means few.
Humble words yet increasing preparations—
means advance;
the enemy enhances readiness;
strong words yet advancing aggressively—
means retreat.
Unexpected peace offers—
mean deception;
half advancing, half retreating—
means enticement;
leaning on spears standing—
means hunger;
drawing water and drinking first—
means thirst;
seeing advantage not advancing—
means fatigue;
birds gathering—
means emptiness;
night cries—
means fear;
army disturbances—
mean commander lacks authority;
flags moving—
means disorder;
officers angry—
means exhaustion;
feeding grain to horses, eating meat,
army without hanging cooking pots
(pronounced tuò),
not even a basket of food—
not reaching their shelters—
means desperate foe;
murmuring and whispering,
slowly persuading people—
means losing their troops;
this shows the commander losing their troops' support;
frequent rewards—
mean distress;
frequent punishments—
mean hardship;
frequent looking back—
means losing their group;
coming to apologize—
means wanting rest.
Troops angry yet approaching,
long without engaging,
nor withdrawing—
must carefully observe them.
Enemy newly arrived,
formations not settled—
can be attacked.
Formations settled but
men and horses not fed—
can be attacked.
Marching long distances,
rear troops not rested—
can be attacked.
Moving slopes crossing dangers,
half concealed half exposed—
can be attacked.
Fording rivers halfway—
can be attacked.
Dangerous paths narrow roads—
can be attacked.
Banners disordered moving—
can be attacked.
Formations frequently shifting—
can be attacked.
Men and horses often looking back—
can be attacked.
Whenever seeing these,
attack without doubt.
However, warfare
is the way of deception.
Able yet appearing unable,
using yet appearing not to use.
Thus the Xiōngnú feigned weakness,
and Hàn Gāozǔ suffered the siege of Píngchéng;
Shílè concealed his sharpness,
and Wáng Jùn faced the fall of Yōuzhōu.
These are the proofs—
can we not be cautious!
Master Sūn said:
"Courage and timidity
are matters of momentum;
strength and weakness
are matters of formation."
He also said:
"That which enables weak water
to float rocks
is momentum."
How can this be demonstrated?
In the past, Lord Cáo campaigned against Zhāng Lǔ
and pacified Hànzhōng.
Liú Yè advised him:
"Your Lordship, with five thousand infantry,
punished and executed Dǒng Zhuó,
defeated Yuán Shào in the north,
and campaigned against Liú Biǎo in the south.
Of the nine provinces and hundred commanderies,
you have united eight-tenths,
your might shakes the world,
your influence extends beyond the seas.
Now that you have raised Hànzhōng,
the people of Shǔ tremble at the news,
their courage broken and defenses lost.
Pushing forward from this,
Shǔ can be pacified by proclamation alone.
Liú Bèi
is a man of distinction,
possessing wisdom but slow to act.
He has held Shǔ for only a short time,
and its people are not yet reliant on him.
Now that Hànzhōng has fallen,
the people of Shǔ are shocked and fearful,
their situation naturally unstable.
With Your Lordship's divine intelligence,
pressuring them in their instability
means
nothing cannot be overcome.
If we delay even slightly,
Zhūgě Liàng, who is clear in strategy, serves as chancellor,
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, whose courage tops the three armies, serve as generals.
Once the people of Shǔ are settled,
holding strategic points and guarding passes,
they will be unassailable.
If we do not take them now,
they will surely be a future worry."
Lord Cáo did not heed this.
After seven days,
a defector from Shǔ reported:
"In Shǔ, there are dozens of panics daily,
and even though Bèi executes people, he cannot stop them."
Lord Cáo summoned Yè and asked:
"Can we still attack now?"
Yè replied:
"They have now stabilized somewhat,
so it is not possible to attack."
Also,
when Tàizǔ campaigned against Lǚ Bù
and reached Xiàpī,
Bù was defeated
and firmly guarded the city,
making it unassailable.
Tàizǔ wanted to retreat,
but Xún Yōu said:
"Lǚ Bù
is brave but lacks strategy.
Now his entire army is defeated,
and their morale has declined.
The army takes its general as the core;
if the core weakens, the army has no will to fight.
Chén Gōng has wisdom but is slow to act.
Now, while Bù's spirit has not yet recovered,
and Gōng's plans are not yet settled,
if we press the attack urgently,
Bù can be captured."
So they diverted the Yí and Sì Rivers to flood the city,
the city collapsed,
and Bù was captured alive.
From this, we observe that
at that time,
even with Zhūgě's wisdom,
Chén Gōng's strategies,
Lǚ Bù's courage,
and Guān and Zhāng's strength,
there was nothing to be done.
This is what is meant by "Courage and timidity
are matters of momentum.
Strength and weakness
are matters of formation."
Thus, in warfare, there are three types of momentum.
In warfare, there are three types of momentum:
first, the momentum of morale,
second, the momentum of terrain,
third, the momentum of opportunity.
If the general is brave and scorns the enemy,
the soldiers delight in battle,
the masses of the three armies
have aspirations reaching the blue clouds,
morale like a whirlwind,
and voices like thunder,
this is called the momentum of morale.
If there are narrow passes and mountain paths,
high mounds and deep ravines,
coiled like dragons and snakes,
winding like sheep intestines or dog gates,
where one man guarding the danger
prevents a thousand from passing,
this is called the momentum of terrain.
If we take advantage of the enemy's weariness, labor, hunger, and thirst,
their disturbance by wind and waves,
their officers acting arbitrarily,
their vanguard not yet encamped,
and their rear crossing in confusion,
this is called the momentum of opportunity.
Those skilled in warfare
always seek to create momentum.
When momentum is present,
Lì Shí Jì persuaded with ease,
and over seventy cities of Qí surrendered;
Xiè Shí crossed the Féi River
and crushed Qín's million-strong army.
When momentum is lost,
Xiàng Yǔ, with strength to pull up mountains,
could only weep vainly for his concubine Yú;
Tián Héng, with strength to rely on the sea,
ended up cutting his own throat.
Therefore, it is said:
"The power of a victorious army
makes each man a hundredfold;
the soldiers of a defeated army
never recover
—forever broken.
This means that when morale is wounded,
even with a million-strong army,
it is of no use."
Thus, "that which enables weak water
to float rocks"
is the essence of momentum strategy.
Master Sūn said:
"Attacking the heart is superior,
attacking cities is inferior."
How is this illustrated?
During the Warring States period, someone advised the King of Qí:
"The way to conquer a state:
attacking the heart is superior,
attacking cities is inferior;
victory through the heart is superior,
victory through arms is inferior.
Therefore,
when a sage conquers a state and attacks an enemy,
he must first subdue their hearts.
What does attacking the heart mean?
Cutting off what they rely on
is called attacking the heart.
Now what Qín relies on for its heart
is Yān and Zhào,
so we should seize the power of Yān and Zhào.
When persuading the rulers of Yān and Zhào,
do not use empty words or rhetoric,
but must offer substantial benefits
to turn their hearts,
this is what is called attacking the heart."
When Duke Pei entered Wǔguān from the west,
he wanted to attack Qín's Yáo
(pronounced yáo)
garrison with twenty thousand men.
Zhāng Liáng said:
"Qín's troops are still strong,
we cannot underestimate them.
I have heard:
their general is a butcher's son, a merchant easily moved by profit.
I hope Duke Pei will temporarily remain in camp,
send men ahead,
prepare food for fifty thousand men,
and display more banners on the mountains
as a deceptive force."
He ordered Lì Yìjī to take precious treasures to bribe Qín's general
who was greedy and disregarded reputation,
and could be bought with bribes.
The Qín generals indeed wanted to form an alliance,
and together march west to attack Xiányáng,
Duke Pei intended to agree.
Liáng said:
"This is only their generals wanting to rebel,
the soldiers probably won't follow.
If they don't follow,
it will certainly be dangerous,
better to attack them while they are unprepared."
Duke Pei then led troops to attack the Qín army,
and heavily defeated them.
When Zhūgě Liàng captured Mèng Huò,
he released and captured him seven times,
and during Liàng's lifetime, the southern tribes
dared not rebel.
Also,
when Chǔ songs came from all sides, Xiàng Yǔ fled;
when Liú Kūn played his reed instrument, the Hú people dispersed.
The strategy of attacking the heart
is not limited to one approach.
This is what attackers of the heart do.
Master Sūn said:
"Those skilled in using troops
prevent the enemy from joining forces."
How is this illustrated?
Formerly, the Mò Áo of Chǔ was about to form an alliance with Èr and Zhěn
(Èr and Zhěn
were two state names),
when the Yún people stationed troops at Pú Sāo,
planning to join Suí, Jiǎo, Zhōu, and Liǎo in attacking Chǔ's army,
the Mò Áo was worried about this.
Lián said:
"The Yún army is encamped in its outskirts,
they certainly won't be vigilant,
and daily they anticipate the arrival of the four cities
(anticipate
means expect).
The four cities:
Suí, Jiǎo, Zhōu, and Liǎo.
You should station at Jiāo Yǐng
to defend against the four cities.
I will lead elite troops to attack Yún by night,
Yún is overconfident and relies on its city,
and lacks fighting spirit.
If we defeat the Yún army,
the four cities will certainly withdraw."
The Mò Áo followed this advice,
and indeed defeated the Yún army at Pú Sāo.
During the Hàn Emperor Xuān's reign,
Xiānlíng and Hǎnjiān Qiāng ended their feud
and allied to raid.
The emperor ordered Zhào Chōngguó to first attack Hǎnjiān,
but Chōngguó held to the advantageous strategy,
did not comply,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"The Xiānlíng Qiāng barbarians
want to rebel,
so they ended their feud with Hǎnjiān,
but in their hearts they cannot forget it,
fearing that when Hàn troops arrive, Hǎnjiān will betray them.
In my foolish opinion,
their plan is always to rush to Hǎnjiān's aid in emergencies,
to strengthen their alliance.
If we attack Hǎn Qiāng first,
Xiānlíng will certainly assist them.
Now the enemy's horses are fat and supplies abundant,
attacking them
might not inflict damage,
but would just allow Xiānlíng to bestow favor on Hǎn Qiāng,
strengthen their alliance,
and unite their faction.
If the barbarians strengthen their alliance and unite,
subduing them would require several times the effort,
I fear the state's troubles would accumulate,
lasting over ten years,
not just one or two years.
If we first attack Xiānlíng,
then Hǎnjiān and others
can be subdued without military effort."
The emperor followed this advice,
and it turned out as planned.
When Tàizǔ of Wèi first attacked Guānzhōng,
each time a rebel faction arrived,
Tàizǔ would be pleased.
After the rebels were defeated,
the generals asked the reason.
Tàizǔ said:
"The roads in Guānzhōng are long,
if each (faction) held their strategic points,
subduing them would take one or two years,
and could not be settled.
Now they have all gathered here,
although numerous,
none can submit to another,
the army has no unified command,
they can be destroyed in one move,
making the attack relatively easy,
that's why I am pleased."
As the saying goes:
"Tethered chickens cannot roost together,
they can be separated and resolved."
Lord Cáo understood this.
This is attacking alliances.
Master Sun said:
"One can make them move by threatening what they hold secure."
He also said:
"Attack where they must rush to defend."
How can this be illustrated?
In the past, the King of Chǔ besieged Sòng,
and the Duke of Sòng sent a messenger to Jìn to report the emergency.
Hú Yǎn of Jìn said:
"Chǔ has just acquired Cáo,
and newly formed a marriage alliance with Wèi.
If we attack Cáo and Wèi,
Chǔ will surely rescue them,
then Qí and Sòng will be spared."
The previous year,
Chǔ had stationed troops at Gǔ to pressure Qí.
Indeed, the plan proceeded as expected.
When Wèi attacked Zhào,
Zhào urgently requested aid from Qí.
King Wēi of Qí appointed Tián Jì as general,
with Sūn Bìn as strategist,
who devised plans while residing in a supply carriage.
Tián Jì wanted to lead troops to Zhào,
but Master Sūn said:
"To untangle a knotted mess,
one does not use fists;
to stop a fight,
one does not join the fray.
Strike at their vital point, assault their weakness;
when their situation is constrained and momentum blocked,
they will resolve it themselves.
Now Liáng and Zhào are attacking each other,
their elite troops exhausted abroad,
the old and weak weary at home.
You should lead troops swiftly to Dàliáng,
seize its thoroughfares,
strike where it is vulnerable;
they will surely abandon Zhào to save themselves,
thus we lift the siege of Zhào in one move,
and reap the spoils from Wèi's exhaustion."
Tián Jì followed this,
and Wèi indeed withdrew from Hándān.
Also,
when Cáo Cāo was governor of Dōngjùn Commandery
(Dōngjùn,
present-day Wèizhōu),
governing from Dōngwǔyáng,
with troops stationed at Dùnqiū,
the Hēishān bandits
(Hēishān,
in present-day Wèizhōu area)
Yú Dú and others attacked Dōngwǔyáng.
The Grand Ancestor (Cáo Cāo) considered leading troops west into the mountains,
to attack Dú's main camp.
His generals all thought they should return to save their own,
but Cáo Cāo said:
"In the past, Sūn Bìn saved Zhào by attacking Wèi,
and Gěng Yǎn aimed for Xī'ān to assault Línzī.
If the bandits hear we head west and return,
then Wǔyáng is saved.
If they don't return,
we can destroy their lair,
while they cannot take Wǔyáng—
this is certain."
They proceeded,
Dú heard of it,
indeed abandoned Wǔyáng to return,
Cáo Cāo ambushed them,
and crushed them utterly.
Earlier,
when Guān Yǔ besieged Fán and Xiāngyáng,
Cáo Cāo, with the Hàn emperor in Xǔ,
close to the enemy,
wanted to move the capital.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng and Jiǎng Jì advised Cáo Cāo:
"Liú Bèi and Sūn Quán,
are outwardly close but inwardly distant.
If Guān Yǔ succeeds,
Quán will surely be displeased.
Send someone to urge him to follow behind Yǔ,
promising to grant him lands south of the river to enfeoff Quán,
then the siege of Fán will lift itself."
Cáo Cāo agreed,
and Yǔ was subsequently captured.
This illustrates that by attacking what they cherish,
one can make them move.
Thus, those skilled in warfare
gain no fame for wisdom,
no merit for courage.
They do not contend before naked blades,
nor prepare after the loss has occurred.
This is what is meant.
As the saying goes:
"If troops are cast into scattered lands,
even kin cannot protect each other;
if crossing the river in the same boat,
why worry about Hú and Yuè having different hearts?"
Master Sun said:
"Those skilled in using troops
are like the shuàirán."
How can this be illustrated?
During the Hàn Emperor Xuān's time,
the Xiānlíng tribes rebelled,
and the emperor ordered Zhào Chōngguó to suppress them.
He led troops to where the Xiānlíng were,
the enemy had long been camped there,
relaxed and off guard,
but upon seeing the large army,
abandoned their heavy carts,
and tried to cross the Huáng River,
where the path was narrow and confined.
Chōngguó advanced slowly to drive them.
Someone said:
"Pursue advantage with speed."
Chōngguó said:
"These are desperate foes,
not to be pursued.
If we ease up,
they flee without looking back;
if we press hard,
they turn and fight to the death."
All his officers said:
"Well said."
The enemy indeed rushed into the water,
where hundreds drowned,
and thus they were defeated.
After Yuán Shàng was defeated,
he fled to Liáodōng,
with several thousand followers.
Earlier,
Gōngsūn Kāng, governor of Liáodōng, relied on remoteness and defied authority.
After Cáo Cāo defeated the Wūwán,
someone advised him:
"March there now,
and the Yuán brothers can be captured."
Cáo said:
"I shall have Kāng behead and send Shàng and Xī himself,
without troubling our troops."
Cáo led his army back.
Kāng indeed beheaded and sent Shàng and Xī,
delivering their heads.
Some generals asked:
"You withdrew, yet Kāng killed Shàng and Xī—
why?"
Cáo said:
"He always feared Shàng and Xī;
if pressed,
they'd unite against us;
if given respite,
they'd plot against each other—
such is the situation."
When Cáo Cāo attacked Zhāng Xiù,
Xún Yōu said:
"Xiù and Liú Biǎo rely on each other for strength,
but Xiù, as a roaming force, depends on Biǎo for supplies;
Biǎo cannot sustain him long,
so they are bound to split.
Better to delay and wait,
luring them to us.
If we press them,
they will surely aid each other."
Cáo Cāo did not listen,
advanced to Rǎng,
and fought Xiù.
Biǎo indeed came to rescue,
and the battle turned unfavorable.
Thus Master Sun said:
"Those skilled in using troops
are like the shuàirán;
the shuàirán
is a snake from Chángshān.
Strike its head, and the tail responds;
strike its tail, and the head responds;
strike its middle, and both head and tail come."
Someone asked:
"Can troops really be made like the shuàirán?"
Master Sun said:
"They can.
Though the people of Wú and Yuè despise each other,
when crossing the river in the same boat,
they rescue each other like left and right hands.
Therefore,
tethering horses and burying chariot wheels
are not reliable;
unifying courage as one
is the way of command."
This is what is meant.
Master Sun said:
"Those skilled in warfare
first make themselves invincible,
then await the enemy's vulnerability."
How can this be illustrated?
Bandit leader Wáng Guó of Liángzhōu besieged Chéncāng.
Huángfǔ Sōng and Dǒng Zhuó were appointed,
each leading twenty thousand troops to resist him.
Zhuó wanted to advance quickly to Chéncāng,
but Sōng disagreed.
Zhuó said:
"The wise do not wait for opportunities,
the brave do not hesitate.
Swift battle preserves the city,
no rescue means its destruction.
The choice between preservation and destruction
lies here."
Sōng replied:
"Not so.
Winning every battle
is inferior to subduing the enemy without fighting.
Therefore, first make yourself invincible,
then await the enemy's vulnerability.
Invincibility lies with us,
vulnerability lies with the enemy.
Fàn Lǐ said:
'When the time is not right,
do not force growth;
when matters are unresolved,
do not force completion.'
This applies here.
Their defense is insufficient,
our attack has surplus strength.
Those with surplus
move as if from the highest heaven;
those with insufficiency
sink as if into the deepest earth.
Now though Chéncāng is small,
its city defenses are solid and prepared,
not like sinking into the deepest earth;
though Wáng Guó is strong,
attacking where we cannot be rescued
does not give him the advantage of the highest heaven.
Without the advantage of the highest heaven,
the attacker suffers harm;
without sinking into the deepest earth,
the defender cannot be overcome.
Wáng Guó is now in a position to suffer harm,
while Chéncāng maintains an impregnable city.
We need not trouble our troops or mobilize the masses,
yet achieve complete victory -
why should we rescue them?"
Thus he did not listen.
Wáng Guó besieged Chéncāng
for over eighty days from winter through spring,
but the city remained firm and strongly defended,
ultimately unconquered.
The bandit forces grew weary and exhausted,
and indeed withdrew on their own.
Sōng advanced to attack them,
but Zhuó said:
"Do not.
The Art of War states:
'Do not press a desperate enemy,
do not pursue a returning army.'
Now if we pursue Guó,
