we are pressing a returning army and pursuing a desperate enemy.
A cornered beast will still fight,
bees and scorpions possess poison -
how much more so a large force?"
Sōng said:
"Not so.
Earlier I did not attack
to avoid their sharpness.
When the enemy is well-rested, prepare against them;
when strong, avoid them;
do not attack keen troops -
this is the essence of warfare.
Now I attack
because I await their decline.
I am attacking weary troops,
not a returning army;
Guó's forces are fleeing,
with no will to fight.
Using order to strike chaos,
they are not desperate enemies."
So he alone advanced to attack them,
having Zhuó provide rear support.
In consecutive battles,
he achieved great victory.
Guó fled and died.
Zhuó was greatly ashamed and resentful.
Master Sun said:
"Provoke them when they are angry."
This means wait for their decline.
He also said:
"Feign weakness to make them arrogant."
This means when the enemy angrily advances,
outwardly show submission and weakness
to heighten their arrogance,
then when they withdraw,
follow and strike them.
He also said:
"Lure them to tire them out."
This means observe their changes through advances and retreats,
then attack where they are unprepared,
strike where they don't expect.
These are the victories of military strategists,
not to be transmitted lightly.
When the Huángjīn rebels of Qīngzhōu, numbering over a million, reached Dōngpíng,
Liú Dài wanted to attack them.
Bào Yǒng advised:
"Now the rebels number a million,
the people are all terrified,
our soldiers lack fighting spirit -
we cannot oppose them.
Observe the rebel masses:
they move in disorderly groups,
their army lacks supplies,
relying solely on plunder for sustenance.
If we now conserve our troops' strength,
first establishing solid defense,
they will be unable to fight when they wish,
unable to succeed when they attack,
and their situation will inevitably collapse.
Then select elite troops,
occupy strategic points,
and strike them -
they can be defeated."
Dài did not listen,
and was indeed defeated by the rebels.
When the Dài army of Jìn attacked Yè city of Yān,
Mùróng Dé resisted them,
and the Dài forces were defeated.
Dé wanted to attack them further,
but his assistant Hán Tán advised:
"Formerly Hàn Gāozǔ said:
'I would rather fight with wisdom
than with brute strength.'
Therefore the ancients first secured victory in the temple hall,
then engaged in battle.
Now there are four reasons not to attack Dài,
and three reasons Yān should not move:
Dài's army has penetrated deeply far from home,
favoring open battle - first reason not to attack;
they have reached near the capital,
stationed in deadly terrain - second reason not to attack;
though their vanguard was defeated,
their rear remains firm - third reason not to attack;
they outnumber us - fourth reason not to attack.
Our troops fight on their own land -
first reason not to move;
moving without victory
makes morale hard to maintain - second reason not to move;
defenses are not repaired,
leaving us unprepared if the enemy comes - third reason not to move.
These are all essentials of warfare.
Deepen moats and raise ramparts,
awaiting the tired with rest.
They supply food over a thousand miles,
find nothing to plunder in the wilds -
prolonged, their three armies consume resources;
attacking, their numerous troops grow weary.
When the army tires, opportunities arise -
plan carefully against them,
and victory can be achieved."
Dé said:
"Assistant Hán's words
are strategies worthy of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng."
Master Sun said:
"Use distance to await proximity,
use rest to await fatigue,
use fullness to await hunger -
this is mastering strength."
This means first secure victory then engage in battle.
Master Sūn said:
"When surrounding an enemy, you must leave an outlet."
How can this be illustrated?
When the Yellow Turban rebel Hán Zhōng occupied Wǎn,
Zhū Jùn and Zhāng Chāo besieged him.
They built fortifications and raised earthen mounds overlooking the city,
then beat drums to attack its southwest.
The rebels all rushed to defend there,
so they struck at the northeast,
scaling the walls to enter.
Hán Zhōng retreated to defend the inner city
and begged to surrender.
The various generals wished to accept.
Zhū Jùn said:
"In warfare, situations may appear identical yet differ in essence.
In the era of Qín and Xiàng Yǔ,
the people had no fixed ruler,
so rewards were given to encourage defections.
Now the realm is unified,
with only the Yellow Turbans creating rebellion.
Accepting surrender does not encourage goodness -
suppressing them suffices to punish evil.
If we accept them now,
it will further foster rebellious intentions.
When advantage favors them, they advance and fight;
when disadvantaged, they beg to surrender.
To spare the enemy is to nurture rebellion -
this is no good strategy."
They intensified their attacks,
but could not conquer it.
Zhū Jùn ascended an earthen mound,
looked back and said to Zhāng Chāo:
"Now I understand.
The rebels are completely surrounded,
with our camps pressing urgently,
their surrender refused,
and no means to escape -
this is why they fight desperately.
Ten thousand men united as one
are already irresistible,
let alone a hundred thousand!
The danger is extreme!
Better to lift the siege,
consolidate our troops and enter the city.
When Hán Zhōng sees the siege lifted,
he will inevitably come out.
Once out, their resolve will scatter -
this is the way to easily defeat them."
After lifting the siege,
Hán Zhōng indeed came out to fight,
and was subsequently defeated along with his forces.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi besieged Húguān Pass,
he decreed:
"When the city falls, all shall be buried alive."
Months passed without success.
Cáo Rén advised Tàizǔ:
"When besieging a city, you must show them a gate -
this opens their path to survival.
Now you have promised certain death,
so everyone will defend desperately.
Moreover, the city is strong with ample supplies.
Attacking will cost many soldiers,
while defending allows prolonged resistance.
To station troops beneath strong walls,
attacking doomed enemies -
this is no good strategy."
Tàizǔ followed his advice,
and the city surrendered.
Generally, the qi of surrendering forces
appears like groups of tens and fives,
all with clasped hands and bowed heads.
It is also said:
When facing each other, if there is qi yellow above and white below,
it is called auspicious qi.
The army it approaches
will seek peace and withdrawal.
Whenever white qi resembling banners appears in a city,
it cannot be taken.
If yellow clouds approach the city,
there will be great celebration.
If blue qi like an ox head charges toward people,
the city cannot be slaughtered.
If qi emerges from the city toward the east,
yellow in color,
this is the Heaven's Axe -
do not attack,
for attackers will perish.
If city wall qi resembles fire smoke,
the defenders wish to sally forth.
If this qi is boundless,
do not attack.
If qi appears pestle-shaped,
pointing outward from the city,
the garrison wishes to break out -
the defenders will prevail,
do not attack.
If clouds above the city split like twin comets,
attack will not succeed.
If misty qi encircles the city without entering,
outside troops cannot enter.
Generally, when besieging, any qi moving from city to our forces
is hostile qi.
When besieging cities and towns,
if ten days pass without thunder rain,
the city has divine support -
quickly withdraw,
do not attack.
These are all victory qi.
When besieging cities and towns,
if red qi appears atop walls
surrounded by yellow qi,
a great general inside will die,
and the city will surrender.
If red qi like flying birds appears over walls,
attack urgently -
it can be taken.
If qi flows in and out,
people wish to flee.
If ash-like qi
emerges and covers their army,
many soldiers will fall ill,
and the city will be slaughtered.
If no cloud qi appears over walls,
soldiers are dispersing.
If red qi resembling multiple heads appears over city camps,
there will be much death and bloodshed below.
If white qi encircles and enters during attack,
urgent assault will succeed.
If a curved rainbow enters from outside,
the city will be slaughtered within three days.
These are all defeat qi.
This is the way of surrounding armies.
Master Sūn said:
"Those skilled at moving the enemy
create a deceptive appearance,
and the enemy is sure to follow it."
How can this be illustrated?
When Wèi and Zhào attacked Hán,
Qí's general Tián Jì went to rescue it,
marching directly toward Dàliáng.
Wèi's general Páng Juān left Hán and returned,
but the Qí army had already advanced westward past them.
Sūn Bìn said to Tián Jì:
"The troops of the Three Jìn
are traditionally fierce and brave and despise Qí,
considering Qí to be cowardly.
One skilled at employing the army
leads them by exploiting this tendency.
The Art of War states:
'One who races for advantage over a hundred lǐ
will exhaust his commanding general.'
Have the Qí army enter Wèi territory and build a hundred thousand cooking stoves,
the next day fifty thousand stoves,
and the next day twenty thousand stoves."
Juān joyfully said:
"I always knew the Qí troops were cowardly.
After entering our territory for three days,
more than half their soldiers have already deserted."
He then abandoned his infantry,
and with his light, elite forces marched double time in pursuit.
Bìn calculated they would reach Mǎlíng at dusk,
where the road was narrow and full of hazards,
suitable for an ambush.
He then stripped a large tree of its bark and wrote on it:
"Páng Juān will die beneath this tree."
He ordered ten thousand skilled crossbowmen to lie in ambush on both sides of the road,
commanding them:
"Shoot when you see a fire raised."
Juān arrived at the stripped tree at night,
saw the writing,
then struck a fire to illuminate it,
and read the words.
The Qí army's ten thousand crossbows fired simultaneously,
throwing the Wèi army into chaos,
and Juān then cut his own throat,
saying:
"So I've helped make that scoundrel famous after all."
When Yú Xǔ was governor of Wǔdū commandery,
the Qiāng tribesmen led their forces to intercept him at Chéncāng Xiáogǔ.
Xǔ ordered his officers and soldiers each to make two cooking stoves,
doubling their number daily,
and the Qiāng dared not press him.
Someone asked:
"Master Sūn reduced his stoves, yet you increase yours.
The Art of War states:
'March only thirty lǐ per day
to guard against the unexpected.'
Now you're marching nearly two hundred lǐ daily,
why is that?"
Xǔ replied:
"The enemy is numerous;
if we proceed slowly we'll be easily overtaken,
but by moving swiftly they cannot fathom our intentions.
Moreover, when the enemy sees our numerous stoves,
they'll think large reinforcements have arrived.
Master Sūn showed weakness,
I display strength—
the circumstances differ."
In former times, Wáng Jùn was in Shǔ,
building ships to attack Wú,
and floated wood shavings down the river to intimidate them.
Later, when Táng general Lǐ Jìng wanted to attack Jīngzhōu,
and assault Xiāo Xiǎn,
he threw wood shavings into the river,
making Xiāo Xiǎn see them.
Jìng then followed with his troops downstream behind the shavings,
and Xiāo Xiǎn, unprepared,
was captured,
and Jīngzhōu was pacified.
The methods of war require adaptation;
one cannot cling to a single approach.
These gentlemen understood this.
Thus it is said:
Assessing the enemy lies in the mind,
discerning opportunity lies in observation,
and creating victory through adapting to circumstances before the masses
is the pinnacle of excellence.
This is the principle of adaptation.
Master Sūn said:
"Place them in a fatal position, and they will survive;
cast them into a desperate ground, and they will live."
He also said:
"When considering advantages, ensure tasks can be accomplished;
when considering harms, ensure calamities can be resolved."
How can this be illustrated?
When the Hàn general Hán Xìn attacked Zhào,
Zhào amassed troops at Jǐngxíng Pass.
Hán Xìn then led his troops to a point thirty lǐ from Jǐngxíng Pass,
where he encamped.
At midnight, he issued orders,
selecting two thousand light cavalry,
each carrying a red banner,
to take a hidden path and conceal themselves in the mountains
(pronounced bì)
to observe the Zhào army.
He instructed them:
"When Zhào sees us retreat,
they will certainly empty their fortifications to pursue us.
Then swiftly enter the Zhào camp,
pull down the Zhào banners,
and raise the red banners of Hàn."
He ordered his lieutenant to distribute a meal,
saying:
"Today, we will defeat Zhào and feast together."
None of the officers believed him,
but they pretended to agree:
"Yes."
Hán Xìn told his officers:
"Zhào has already occupied favorable terrain for their camp,
and since they have not yet seen my commander's flags and drums,
they are unwilling to attack our vanguard,
fearing we might turn back upon reaching difficult terrain."
Hán Xìn then sent ten thousand troops forward,
forming a battle array with their backs to the river.
When the Zhào army saw this,
they laughed heartily.
Tàigōng said:
"If one's wisdom is the same as the crowd's, one is no teacher of men;
if one's skills are the same as the crowd's, one is no champion of the state.
No action is more divine than the unexpected;
no victory is greater than the unrecognized."
Had the Zhào army recognized Hán Xìn's strategy,
how could they have been defeated?
Thus, they laughed but were defeated.
At dawn,
Hán Xìn raised his commander's flags and drums,
and marched out of Jǐngxíng Pass with drums beating.
The Zhào army opened their gates and attacked,
engaging in a fierce battle for a long time.
Thereupon, Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr abandoned their flags and drums,
and fled toward the river.
The troops by the river opened their formation to let them in,
then resumed fierce fighting.
The Zhào army emptied their camp to seize Hàn's drums and flags,
pursuing Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr.
By the time Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr reached the river troops,
all the soldiers were fighting desperately,
and could not be defeated.
The two thousand surprise cavalry Hán Xìn had sent out,
waiting for the Zhào camp to be emptied in pursuit of gain,
charged into the Zhào camp,
pulled down all the Zhào banners,
and raised two thousand red Hàn banners.
When the Zhào army failed to capture Hán Xìn and others,
and wished to return to their camp,
they saw it full of red Hàn banners
and were greatly alarmed.
Tàigōng said:
"Between two battle arrays,
a deceptive formation emerges.
Allowing troops to move in disorder
is a means to create change."
This describes the situation.
Thinking that Hàn had captured all of Zhào's commanders,
they fell into chaos,
fled in disarray,
and even though Zhào's generals tried to stop them by execution,
they could not be restrained.
Master Sūn said:
"Await the disordered with order,
await the clamorous with calm:
this is mastery of the mind."
Once the troops' morale is broken,
even with excellent generals,
no strategy can be devised.
Thereupon,
the Hàn troops attacked from both sides,
routing them utterly,
executing Chéng'ān Jūn by the Chí River,
and capturing King Xiē of Zhào.
When the officers presented the heads and prisoners and rested,
they all congratulated him and asked Hán Xìn:
"According to military strategy:
'Right and rear should be against mountains and hills,
front and left facing water and marshes.'
Yet you ordered us to form a battle array with our backs to the river,
saying:
'Defeat Zhào and feast together.'
We were unconvinced,
but ultimately we won.
What strategy was this?"
Hán Xìn replied:
"This is in the military texts,
but you gentlemen failed to notice it.
Does not the Art of War say:
'Place them in a fatal position, and they will survive;
cast them into a desperate ground, and they will live'?
To be in a fatal position means that when forces are evenly matched,
one can win by using the fatal position.
But if the extremely weak face the extremely strong,
casting weak troops into a fatal position
is to invite their doom.
Thus, Sūn Bìn said:
'If troops are terrified,
they cannot be saved.'
Also, the Classic says:
'When the masses are plunged into harm,
then they can determine victory or defeat.'
Thus, to grasp the opportunity of the fatal position,
one must use the masses.
Moreover, I had not previously trained and cared for these officers and men;
it was what is called 'driving market folk to battle.'
Under such circumstances, unless I placed them in a fatal position,
making each fight for himself,
had I given them safe ground,
they would have all fled.
How then could I have used them?"
The officers said:
"Excellent!
This is beyond our reach."
Master Sūn said:
"When troops are in deep peril, they fear nothing;
when there is no alternative, they fight."
Therefore,
such troops need no training to be vigilant,
seek nothing yet gain everything,
require no bonds to be close,
and need no orders to be trustworthy.
To cast them into a position with no escape
is the courage of the commanders.
This describes it.
When Tàizǔ of Wèi campaigned against Zhāng Xiù,
he once withdrew his army,
and Zhāng Xiù pursued him.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"Do not pursue."
Zhāng Xiù did not listen
and was indeed defeated upon returning.
Jiǎ Xǔ told Zhāng Xiù:
"Quickly pursue them again,
and you will surely win the battle."
Zhāng Xiù gathered his scattered troops,
pursued Tàizǔ,
and indeed won the battle.
Upon returning,
he asked Jiǎ Xǔ:
"With elite troops, I pursued a retreating army, yet you said I would lose;
with defeated troops, I attacked a victorious army, yet you said I would win.
Both turned out as you said.
Why were these contrary predictions both validated?"
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"This is easily understood.
Military situations vary widely,
and circumstances differ.
Though you are skilled in warfare,
you are no match for Lord Cáo.
When the Wèi army first withdrew,
Lord Cáo surely took personal command of the rear guard.
Though your pursuing troops were elite,
your command was no match for his,
and his soldiers were also sharp,
so I knew you would lose.
Lord Cáo attacked you without error,
yet withdrew before exhausting his strength,
so there must have been trouble at home.
Having defeated you,
he would certainly advance lightly and swiftly,
leaving his generals to guard the rear.
Though these generals are brave,
they are no match for you in command.
Thus, even with defeated troops, you could win."
Zhāng Xiù then acknowledged his ability.
This illustrates the transformation of advantage and harm.
Thus it is said:
"Place them in a fatal position, and they will survive;
when considering harms, ensure calamities can be resolved."
This describes it.
Tàigōng said:
"If one cannot divide and maneuver,
one cannot speak of the extraordinary."
Sūnzǐ said:
"In war, the orthodox is used to engage,
but the extraordinary is used to secure victory."
How can this be illustrated?
When Wèi king Bào rebelled against Hàn,
Hàn king appointed Hán Xìn as Left Chancellor to attack Wèi.
King of Wèi massed troops at Púbān,
blocking Línjìn.
Hán Xìn then created additional decoy forces,
lining up boats as if to cross at Línjìn,
while secretly moving troops from Xiàyáng using wooden jars to cross the river,
and launched a surprise attack on Ānyì.
Sūnzǐ said:
"When you are distant, show the enemy you are near;
when you are near, show them you are far."
This is what it means.
King of Wèi Bào was shocked,
led his troops to confront Hán Xìn,
whereupon Hán Xìn captured Bào,
and pacified Wèi, establishing HéDōng commandery.
Thus we know that the extraordinary and orthodox
are crucial in warfare.
The "Classic" says:
"Victory in battle is nothing more than the use of extraordinary and orthodox.
The variations of extraordinary and orthodox
are inexhaustible,
like a circle without beginning,
who can exhaust them?"
This is what it means.
Sūnzǐ said:
"Those skilled in war
create situations of peril,
with momentum that is swift."
"Lure them with profit,
then await them with troops."
He also said:
"Those skilled in moving the enemy
create appearances,
and the enemy will certainly follow."
How can this be proven?
When Yān pacified Qí,
they besieged Jímò city.
The people of Jímò appointed Tián Dān as general to resist Yān.
Tián Dān wanted to anger his soldiers,
so he declared:
"I only fear that the Yān general will cut off the noses of captured Qí soldiers,
and dig up graves outside the city walls.
Harming our ancestors
would be heartbreaking."
The Yān general acted as predicted,
and the people of Jímò all wept,
eager to go out and fight,
their anger increased tenfold.
Tián Dān then collected gold from the people,
obtaining a thousand yì,
and ordered wealthy families of Jímò to present it to the Yān general,
with a letter saying:
"Jímò is about to surrender,
we beg you not to enslave our families."
The Yān general was greatly pleased,
and became lax.
Tián Dān then gathered a thousand cattle,
tied reeds to their tails,
set the ends on fire,
dug dozens of holes in the city walls,
and released the cattle at night.
Five thousand warriors followed behind them,
the cattle ran toward Yān when their tails became hot,
the Yān army was greatly alarmed,
and the following five thousand troops attacked silently with gag bits in their mouths,
the Yān army was badly defeated,
their general Qí Jié was killed,
and over seventy cities of Qí were recovered.
When Lǚ Méng was stationed west at Lùkǒu,
and Guān Yǔ was attacking Fán,
he left troops to defend Gōng'ān and Nánjùn.
Lǚ Méng submitted a memorial saying:
"Guān Yǔ is attacking Fán but leaves many defensive troops,
certainly fearing I might attack his rear.
I am often ill,
I request to take some troops back to Jiànyè,
using illness as a pretext.
When Guān Yǔ hears of this,
he will certainly withdraw his defensive troops,
and send them all to Xiāngyáng.
Then our main force can sail up the river,
advancing day and night,
attacking where he is undefended,
then Nánjùn can be taken,
and Guān Yǔ can be captured."
So he claimed to be seriously ill,
Sūn Quán then openly issued a summons for Lǚ Méng,
and Guān Yǔ indeed believed it.
He gradually withdrew troops to Fán,
when Sūn Quán learned of this,
he proceeded with the plan.
First sending Lǚ Méng ahead,
concealing elite troops in merchant ships,
having them dressed in white and rowing,
wearing merchants' clothing,
advancing day and night,
they reached the riverbank outposts set up by Guān Yǔ,
captured and bound them all,
thus Guān Yǔ received no news.
Tàigōng said:
"Feigning to be envoys
is a means to cut off supplies;
using deceptive orders and wearing enemy uniforms
is preparation for defeating the enemy."
From this we can see,
in matters of clothing and orders,
one cannot be insufficiently careful.
They then reached Nánjùn,
where Shì Rén and Mí Fāng both surrendered.
Lǚ Méng entered and occupied the city,
found the families of Guān Yǔ's officers and soldiers,
treated them all kindly,
ordered the army not to disturb the households,
and items dropped on the road were not picked up.
In the past, Duke of Qín saw the advantage of attacking Zhèng,
but did not consider the defeat at Xiáohán;
King of Wú boasted of his success in attacking Qí,
but forgot the disaster at Gūsū.
Therefore it is said:
"Those who cannot fully understand the harms of using troops
cannot fully understand the benefits of using troops."
This is what it means.
The "Classic" says:
"Employ the feudal lords by giving them tasks."
As the saying goes:
"Use their strength to strengthen yourself,
then the enemy can be broken."
When Guān Yǔ attacked Fán,
though not deceived by others' schemes,
he also acted by employing and strengthening himself.
When Guān Yǔ returned,
while on the road,
he repeatedly sent messengers to communicate with Lǚ Méng,
Lǚ Méng treated his envoys generously,
had them move about the city,
conveying greetings to every household,
sometimes with handwritten letters to show sincerity.
When Guān Yǔ's envoys returned,
they privately inquired around,
and all learned their families were safe,
treated even better than before,
so Guān Yǔ's soldiers lost their will to fight.
When Sūn Quán arrived and captured Guān Yǔ,
he thus secured Jīngzhōu.
This exemplifies the change from concealment to action.
Therefore it is said:
"At first be like a maiden,
and the enemy will open his door;
later be like a fleeing hare,
and the enemy cannot resist."
This is what it means.
Master Sūn said:
"To raise an army of a million men
costs a thousand pieces of gold daily."
Master Yù said:
"When the army consumes emptiness,
the state has no reserves."
Therefore it is said:
"Transporting provisions over a hundred lǐ,
there will be no food for one year;
over two hundred lǐ,
no food for two years;
over three hundred lǐ,
no food for three years.
This is called emptying the state.
When the state is empty, the people become poor;
when the people are poor, superiors and inferiors cannot be close.
The superiors have no means to establish their kindness,
the inferiors have no means to sustain their lives,
then thoughts of desertion and rebellion arise.
This is winning the battle but defeating oneself."
Thus even if the enemy is defeated abroad,
and achievements are made at home,
yet for those who win battles,
they are treated with funeral rites.
The general dons plain white mourning garments,
and confesses his crime before the ruler.
The ruler says:
"Where the army was deployed,
was a state without virtue.
Capturing the enemy and achieving victory,
the general bears no blame or calamity."
Then he honors him with office,
to strip him of his power.
Therefore it is said:
"When the high-flying birds die,
the good bows are stored away;
when the enemy state is destroyed,
the strategist ministers perish."
Perishing does not mean losing their lives,
but means sinking them into the abyss.
Sinking them into the abyss
means stripping them of their authority and abolishing their power.
Enfeoffing them at court,
granting them the highest ministerial positions,
to display their achievements;
giving them the finest states in the central region,
to enrich their hearts.
The multitude of benevolent people
can be united but not separated;
authority and power can bring joy,
but are difficult to suddenly transfer.
For this reason,
withdrawing the army and disbanding the troops
is the step between survival and demise
as seen with Wèi Tuó and Zhāng Hán. .
Therefore weaken them with position,
strip them with fiefdoms.
Thus the arguments of a hegemon's assistants
are驳也
驳,
not purely virtuous. .
If the ruler deeply understands this principle,
he can control his ministers and generals
as when Hàn Gāozǔ seized the Qí army;
if the ministers deeply understand this principle,
they can preserve their achievements and protect their lives
as when Zhāng Liáng studied grain avoidance,
abandoning worldly affairs. .
This is the method of withdrawing troops.
It is said:
The mechanism of orthodox and unorthodox tactics,
the essence of the five types of espionage,
the changes of heaven and earth,
the ways of water and fire,
are like sounds not exceeding the five tones,
yet the variations of the five tones
cannot all be heard;
colors not exceeding the five hues,
yet the variations of the five hues
cannot all be seen.
It lies in adapting to opportunities and employing flexibility,
one cannot adhere rigidly to one method.

Colophon
This book is mentioned in Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán,
which states:
"Zhào Ruí
was from Yántíng County, Zǐzhōu.
He was widely learned in military strategy,
excelling in statecraft.
Both husband and wife had moral integrity,
and did not respond to official summons.
He authored ten volumes of Cháng Duǎn Jīng,
discussing the ways of kings and hegemon,
which circulates in the world."
It also appears in Táng Shū · Yì Wén Zhì:
"Miscellaneous school: Zhào Ruí's Cháng Duǎn Yào Shù in ten volumes.
Ruí, courtesy name Tàibīn,
was from Zǐzhōu.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he declined summons to office."
Cháo's Jùn Zhāi Dú Shū Zhì also records:
"Cháng Duǎn Jīng in ten volumes,
authored by Táng's Zhào Ruí,
discussing the strategic flexibility of kings and hegemon,
and methods of orthodox, changing, long and short tactics.
Sixty-three chapters in total,
with chapters nine and ten containing military strategy and covert plans."
I previously sought to purchase it but failed,
until this summer when Mr. Bào Yǐwén entrusted me with the Bàijīng Lóu manuscript for correction,
finally allowing me to read it with pleasure.
Its main ideas largely match what Masters Sūn and Cháo described,
but its citations are numerous and rich,
making verification difficult.
Considering my limited knowledge,
I long hesitated to begin.
After the year-end,
I gathered all books from my studio,
and collated them in sequence,
completing in twenty days.
Errors were corrected,
omissions filled,
doubts verified,
and ambiguous passages retained.
Though not perfectly aligned,
it should be readable now.
Traditionally called ten volumes,
sixty-three chapters; the current edition's author's preface says the same.
But examination shows only nine volumes,
with sixty-four chapters.
Initially suspicious,
upon reading Wén Xiàn Tōng Kǎo quoting Cháo,
it first cites Suǒ Yán,
then states the tenth volume on covert strategists was originally missing.
Now sixty-four chapters survive,
revealing this book long lacked a complete version.
The existing author's preface
is no longer fully original.
Recent editions of the reading record
contain significant omissions and errors.
But Wáng Ruǎntíng once saw a Sòng edition,
said to be obtained by Xú Jiàn'ān in Rènchéng,
its colophon also stating "ten volumes,
totaling sixty-three chapters,
written by Zhào Ruí of Táng, from Ānchāng Rock, Chángpíng Mountain, Qī County, Zǐzhōu, a commoner subject,"
matching the current edition,
showing the error dates back to Sòng.
Suǒ Yán says Ruí was from Yántíng,
but mentions Qī County.
Sìchuān Zǒng Zhì states:
"Ruí,
from Yántíng,
lived in seclusion at Ānchāng Rock, Chángpíng Mountain, Qī County.
Extensively studied similarities and differences in classics and various schools,
authored Cháng Duǎn Jīng,
and annotated Guān Lǎng's Yì Zhuàn.
Emperor Míng repeatedly summoned him without success,
Lǐ Bái once visited his cottage to request advice."
Note: Tàibái Jí contains "Huáinán Lying Ill, Writing My Thoughts, Sent to Zhào Ruí, Recluse of Shǔ,"
and Guǎng Yú Jì states:
"Ruí devoted to learning, never held office,
was a commoner friend of Bái,
authored Cháng Duǎn Jīng."
Zǐzhōu Zhì praises him as an outstanding person.
Ruǎntíng also quotes Yáng Tiānhuì's Zhāngmíng Yì Shì:
"Tuójiāng's Zhào Ruí,
chivalrous and spirited,
excelled in纵横学,
authored Cháng Duǎn Jīng."
These are noteworthy for readers of this book,
hence detailed here.
As for Zǒng Zhì calling its text akin to Shēn Jiàn and Lùn Héng,
I observe this book's title draws from Zhàn Guó Cè,
its anecdotal style imitates Lǚ Lǎn,
and its eclectic quotes
greatly resemble Hóng Liè.
